Forensic expert says his analysis of autopsy photos suggests Epstein was killed
- Published
This article contains distressing details and references to suicide
A forensic expert has said he believes that convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein's death in prison was the result of a homicide, not suicide.
Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor Michael Freeman said that after reviewing the New York City medical examiner's file he believes Epstein was strangled, most likely from behind.
The medical examiner who carried out the autopsy concluded in 2019 that Epstein's injuries were consistent with suicide and there was no evidence of the defensive wounds expected if his death had been a homicide.
Epstein was found dead in prison on 10 August 2019 in New York as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.
Dr Barbara Sampson, chief medical examiner at the time of Epstein's autopsy, who ruled that Epstein's death was a suicide, has previously said: "I stand firmly behind our determination of the cause and manner of death for Mr. Epstein." The BBC has approached Sampson for further comment.
Freeman has served as a cause-of-death expert to attorneys-general in the US for death in police custody cases, including George Floyd in Minnesota.
He published his research and the New York City medical examiner's files after presenting his findings in London on Monday evening.
Freeman, who did not see the body, based his conclusions on the files and photographs from the examiner's report provided to him by Epstein's brother, Mark Epstein, who has always maintained that his brother was murdered.
Freeman said his analysis is independent and that he was not paid by Mark Epstein. His research has not been peer reviewed.
He told the BBC that he believed there are signs indicating an assault on Epstein, including a deep haemorrhage to his left shoulder and injuries that appear to be consistent to being struck in the face.
Freeman said he believed the evidence was most consistent with strangulation using a ligature and then that same ligature was probably used to suspend the body from the bunk bed.
He said there appeared to be fingernail marks above the ligature mark on Epstein's neck, which "would be consistent with strangulation, particularly from behind. And the attempt by the victim to try to remove the ligature from the neck".
He said "the injuries and the way the body was found don't match up. There's only one remaining explanation then, and that is that the death was as a result of a homicide."
The medical examiner who performed the autopsy at the time told the Department of Justice (DoJ) Office of the Inspector General , externalthat Epstein's injuries were more consistent with, and indicative of, a suicide by hanging rather than homicide by strangulation, adding there was no evidence of defensive wounds consistent with what is seen in victims of strangulation.
Freeman said he would have expected in an investigation of a death by hanging in custody for there to be a photograph before the body was taken down.
According to a DoJ investigation into Epstein's time in prison, the guard who found Epstein immediately called for a second colleague to help, lowered Epstein's body to the floor and began attempts to resuscitate him.
Epstein's death came a month after he was briefly placed on suicide watch, the DoJ report said.
When asked who might have killed Epstein if his interpretation of the evidence was correct, Freeman said he had "no idea".
"That is not something I have an opinion about. That isn't any part of any investigation that I've done," he said.
Challenged on whether his views veered into conspiracy theory, Freeman said: "I have the luxury of being able to say, don't take my word for it, let everybody look at it."
"If you think I'm still a conspiracy theorist because I'm looking at something that looks like a strangulation and say, I think it is a strangulation and I don't think it could be a hanging, show me where I got it wrong."
"I'm wide open to that. I'm an academic. I'm quite happy to hear people's theories on things that are informed," he said.
Epstein was convicted in 2008 of soliciting prostitution from a minor, for which he was registered as a sex offender. He escaped a heavy jail sentence as a result of a plea deal.
Eleven years later, Epstein was charged with running a network of underage girls for sex. He was awaiting trial in 2019 when he was found dead at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City.

Timing of Climate Science Reports Ignites a Hot Fight at U.N. Talks
Several countries that rely heavily on fossil fuels want to delay the next round of scientific assessments that governments use to inform their climate policies.
A squabble over the publication timetable for several climate reports has turned into one of the burning issues of this year’s United Nations climate conference, as some warn that fossil fuel interests might be interfering with the world’s pre-eminent climate science organization.
The U.N.-backed Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change produces landmark reports that generally come out every five to seven years. The next round of reports would take on topics like physical changes to the earth and greenhouse gas emissions.
Timing is critical because in 2028 nations are supposed to assess their progress and then ramp up their efforts to do more, based on the best science. That process, known as a stocktake and occurring every five years, is the engine of the Paris Agreement.
Saudi Arabia, India and Russia are among those pushing to delay the reports so that at least two of them come out after 2028.
The fact that those nations rank among the largest fossil fuel exporters or importers has led to accusations that coal, oil and gas interests might be interfering with science.
“Saudi Arabia is trying to destroy the I.P.C.C. in order to prevent the next global stocktake from using the accurate scientific data on fossil fuels,” said former Vice President Al Gore, who is in Turkey for the talks.

‘Should be held accountable, penalised’: SC warns states, UTs and districts of fines over Yamuna pollution
It also ordered tougher monitoring of treatment plants, drains and water quality, and called for shared accountability across the river basin.
The Supreme Court has directed that states, Union territories and even individual districts be fined if the quality of Yamuna water deteriorates on any parameter while flowing through and exiting their respective jurisdictions, seeking to fix accountability for pollution in the river.
A bench of justices Manoj Misra and Manmohan said that any state, UT or district where deterioration in water quality is detected should be held accountable and penalised, with the compensation or fine deposited in the Supreme Court registry.
The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has been asked to suggest a formula for calculating the penalty. States and UTs would, however, be free to recover the amount from polluters and officials found remiss in discharging their duties after conducting an inquiry.
The decision could have particularly significant implications for Delhi, where the Yamuna flows through a 22-km stretch between Wazirabad and Okhla -- just 2% of the river’s length -- but contributes the most to its overall pollution load.
In a detailed order released on Monday, the court laid down a framework for monitoring water quality at the entry and exit points of every state, UT and district along the river, with financial penalties for any deterioration. It also prescribed measures to ensure that sewage treatment plants (STPs) and common effluent treatment plants (CETPs) function efficiently, industrial waste is checked at source and untreated wastewater is prevented from entering the river.
Also Read | Pollution in Yamuna increased despite huge expenditure on cleaning: Supreme Court
The bench observed that the Yamuna’s condition reflected the failure of civic administration across towns, cities and villages along its banks.
“Everything that is wrong with civic administration in the towns, cities and villages situated along the banks of the river is reflected in the poor health of the river and in the 520 drains” discharging wastewater into it, the court said. This, it added, explained why pollution had continued to increase despite huge sums being spent on cleaning the river.
The court said industrial pollution and untreated sewage must be curtailed, if not stopped altogether, at source. Where that was not possible, sewage must first be tapped and then treated. It acknowledged, however, the difficulty of laying sewer networks in unauthorised colonies that had developed without proper grid layouts and have little space for such infrastructure.
It also said illegal and unauthorised colonies, JJ clusters along drains and settlements on the riverbed would have to be removed after rehabilitating eligible occupants. Otherwise, sewage from these areas would continue to pollute the river. The bench flagged the problem of illegal and unaccounted-for dairies, particularly in Delhi, noting that proposed biogas plants would not address waste generated by dairies outside the authorised network.
On ecological protection, the court said Zone ‘O’, designated as a green zone under Delhi’s Master Plan 2047, should be protected and, if feasible, extended upstream and downstream from the Yamuna’s source to its confluence with the Ganga. No permanent structures, other than green parks and essential public infrastructure, should be permitted. Recreational and tourism activities should be restricted to semi-permanent facilities such as cycling and walking tracks. Existing structures should be removed in accordance with law, after providing alternative accommodation to those entitled to rehabilitation.
Also Read | Delhi Police arrests BSP worker who posted videos of dead fish in the Yamuna
Shared responsibility
The court called for treating the Yamuna as one continuous ecosystem rather than a collection of state-wise stretches. Invoking the principle of “common, but differentiated responsibilities”, it said all states sharing the river had a common obligation to protect it, while each state’s specific responsibilities should be calibrated according to the pollution it contributed and its capacity to address the problem. A state’s responsibility, it said, could not be confined to what happened within its own stretch.
The Yamuna flows through Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh, making its conservation a shared responsibility.
CPCB has been directed to submit details of chemical composition and water quality parameters — including biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD), faecal coliform and total suspended solids (TSS) — at points where the river and major drains entering it cross state, UT and district boundaries. The court noted that CPCB already monitored the river at entry and exit points quarterly and suggested that samples collected simultaneously be analysed by institutions such as the IITs for independent verification.
The bench also ordered stricter monitoring of treatment infrastructure. Every STP, CETP and government-commissioned biogas plant must install tamper-proof smart energy meters within a month. STPs and CETPs must additionally install inlet and outlet meters with continuous sensors to record wastewater volumes and parameters such as pH, BOD, COD, TSS and ammoniacal nitrogen. Faecal coliform levels must be tested weekly in accredited laboratories.
All readings must be uploaded live, plant-wise, on CPCB and state pollution control board websites, allowing authorities and the public to track the hours of operation, electricity consumed, volume of wastewater treated and quality of discharge.
A break in the data feed exceeding 24 hours, it said, would be presumed to indicate that the plant was not operating, unless its operator could establish otherwise. Biogas plants must additionally record the quantity of waste received and gas produced.
CPCB has been asked to arrange unannounced inspections and sampling of every STP with a capacity of 5 million litres per day (MLD) or more, as well as CETPs, at least once every quarter through IITs, NITs or accredited third-party laboratories. Results must be published within 30 days, and environmental compensation recovered from operators for every day of non-compliance.
Other measures include real-time water quality monitoring stations along the river and major drains in all basin states, with data shared with CPCB through an integrated system. Urban local bodies must register all septage tankers, install GPS tracking systems and develop portals to track septage generated by households, collected and ultimately disposed of.
Also Read | Will Yamuna get its Sabarmati makeover? Delhi plans 52-km riverfront in two phases
The court also mandated unrestricted access for CPCB and its designated agencies to treatment plants, installations and records for surprise inspections and technical assessments. Police commissioners, district magistrates and superintendents of police must assist inspection teams when required. Chief secretaries of the basin states and UTs, and secretaries of the concerned central ministries, must nominate senior officers, not below the rank of special secretary, as nodal officers within two weeks.
The officer in charge of every treatment plant and major drain must be identified on a public portal and submit a monthly compliance affidavit before the court.
The directions follow the court’s examination of a comprehensive Yamuna Action Plan prepared by a committee headed by the Union home secretary. The plan envisages 125 new STPs with a combined capacity of 4,401.30 MLD, upgrades to 20 existing STPs, 12 new CETPs in Haryana, 10 municipal solid waste processing plants and 23 biogas plants. It also proposes intercepting and treating 520 drains that currently discharge around 9,666.81 MLD of wastewater into the Yamuna and its tributaries.
While describing the plan as a significant step forward, the bench cautioned that constructing more treatment plants alone would not revive the river. It flagged inconsistencies, including discrepancies over encroachments on water bodies and wetlands in Delhi’s Zone ‘O’, and noted that none of the Capital’s 37 existing STPs met all prescribed standards.
The matter will now be heard on January 13, 2027.

Defending champion Jharkhand will look to continue its winning run when it takes on Rajasthan in the second round of the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy on Monday. Jharkhand began its title defence with a commanding six-wicket win over Mizoram, chasing down a target of 77 in just 8.3 overs. Rajasthan, meanwhile, also made a winning start, beating Uttar Pradesh by six wickets.
Two-time former champion Karnataka will aim to build on its 19-run victory over Bengal when it faces Uttar Pradesh, which will be eager to bounce back from its opening-day defeat to Rajasthan. Tamil Nadu, the tournament’s most successful team with three titles, will also look to make it two wins in a row when it takes on Jammu and Kashmir. The former champion edged past Railways by six runs in its opening fixture, while J&K suffered a 103-run defeat against Delhi.
Mumbai and Gujarat will be involved in one of the day’s most anticipated contests after making impressive starts to their campaigns. Mumbai chased down Hyderabad’s 172 in just 13.1 overs, with Suryakumar Yadav smashing an unbeaten 60 off 21 balls. Gujarat, meanwhile, posted 250 for nine against Odisha, the tournament’s highest total on the opening day, before securing a 21-run win. Both sides will look to maintain their momentum in what promises to be an intriguing Group D encounter.
Delhi and Punjab will also face off in a clash between two opening-day winners. Delhi produced one of the most dominant performances of the first round, defeating Jammu and Kashmir by 103 runs after posting 243 for six. Mayank Yadav starred with the ball, claiming five wickets for 14 runs. Punjab, meanwhile, pulled off a four-wicket win over last season’s finalist Haryana, chasing down a target of 191 with five balls to spare.
Haryana will look to get its campaign back on track when it takes on Saurashtra, while Baroda, a two-time former champion, will aim to recover from its narrow three-wicket defeat to Chandigarh against Mizoram. Maharashtra, which lost to Puducherry by 15 runs despite scoring 189 for five in reply to 205, will face Kerala as it seeks its first victory.
Among the other teams looking to build on winning starts, Vidarbha will take on Odisha after registering a seven-wicket win over Goa. Hyderabad, meanwhile, will be keen to bounce back against Chhattisgarh after its defeat to Mumbai. With several former champions already facing contrasting fortunes, the second round offers an early opportunity for the contenders to strengthen their positions in the group standings.

Warren Buffett's final weeks as Berkshire Hathaway chairman were fittingly free of fireworks.
The low-key investor's conglomerate only made minor tweaks to its stock portfolio during the three months to September 30, a regulatory filing showed on Monday.
Berkshire cut several smaller positions, including Capital One by 62%, VeriSign by 34%, Nucor by 15%, and Kroger by 10%. It once again trimmed its Bank of America stake by about 6% to around 456 million shares, worth close to $25 billion as of September 30.
On the other hand, it boosted its Delta Air Lines stake by 12% to around 65 million shares, worth about $5.4 billion at September's close.
It also bolstered its bet on homebuilder Lennar, increasing its volume of Class B shares by 86% and Class A shares by 99%. Those purchases propelled the total value of the position from $1.2 billion to $2.1 billion.
The only new position was Bending Spoons, but the Italian tech conglomerate previously disclosed Berkshire invested in its IPO this summer, then took part in a private placement that raised its stake to about 4%.
It's unclear whether Buffett, CEO Greg Abel, or investment manager Ted Weschler were behind the portfolio changes. Buffett said this summer that he initiated Berkshire's stake in Alphabet last year, a holding worth $36 billion at the end of September.
The disclosure came hours after Buffett announced he was donating $5.5 billion of his Berkshire stock to four of his family's foundations, in line with his plan to gift his entire Berkshire fortune by 2034.
Buffett, 96, championed kindness in a surprisingly short Thanksgiving message, telling his shareholders they'd "heard plenty" from him in the letter announcing his retirement as chairman in September.
Berkshire investors were prepared for a pretty humdrum third-quarter portfolio update. The company's recent third-quarter earnings revealed that it bought $2.4 billion of stocks and sold $2.8 billion worth during the three-month period — tiny sums relative to its $335 billion stock portfolio.
However, Berkshire did spend a record $9.6 billion on stock buybacks last quarter. Those purchases look well-timed so far, as Berkshire's share price has jumped 19% since the start of October, closing at record highs of around $593 a share.
Buffett — who ran Berkshire for six decades before stepping down as CEO and chairman in the past year — struggled to find bargains during his final years in charge as both public and private company valuations soared. That made quiet quarters the norm, with Berkshire making few stock purchases or acquisitions.

An analysis of more than 180 epidemiological studies examining the health impacts of air pollution across India has found that over 91% of them reported at least one adverse health association with air pollution exposure.
These studies, published between 1975 and 2025, also noted that health impacts extend beyond respiratory diseases to cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, pregnancy complications, impaired child growth, tumours, blood disorders, mental and neurocognitive disorders, among others.
The analysis, released on Friday, was done by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), an independent research organisation focused on revealing the trends, causes, and health impacts, as well as the solutions, to air pollution.
Notably, out of 180 studies, only 40 examined air pollution's impact on rural populations, of which 38 reported at least one adverse health association, indicating that air pollution's health impacts are not confined to urban areas.
Further, most studies were conducted on Delhi (26) to examine the link between health and air pollution. The national capital was followed by Punjab with 13 studies, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh with 11 each, West Bengal with 10, Tamil Nadu with nine, Karnataka with eight and Telangana with seven, the report said.
In a statement, CREA analyst Manoj Kumar said, "The findings highlight the need to move beyond a city-centric approach and explicitly include rural areas through a regional, airshed-based approach in the next phase of National Clean Air Programme (NCAP 2.0)."
Studies examined a range of air pollutants, with 45 investigating both particulate matter and gaseous pollutants. PM2.5 was examined in 32 studies, PM10 alone in four, and both PM10 and PM2.5 in 16.
Among studies examining gaseous pollutants, statistically significant adverse health associations were reported for increased mortality, acute respiratory hospital and emergency visits, asthma-related hospital admissions, and impaired lung function.
Beyond their direct health effects, gaseous pollutants such as SOx and NOx also contribute to secondary PM2.5 formation by undergoing atmospheric chemical reactions to form sulphate and nitrate particles, respectively.
Kumar said, "Air pollution mitigation must adopt a multipollutant approach, addressing gaseous precursors that contribute to secondary PM2.5 and ground-level ozone formation. This requires emission reductions at major sources, including industries, power plants, residential cooking, and other combustion activities."

Chennai breathes far cleaner air than Delhi. A study that followed 12,064 adults in the two cities put the typical yearly level of fine particles around Chennai homes between 2010 and 2016 at 40.2 micrograms per cubic metre, just above the national standard of 40, against 101.5 in Delhi. In both cities, the dirtier a person’s air, the likelier they were to develop type 2 diabetes.
The World Health Organization’s theme for World Diabetes Day, on November 14 this year, is early action. The sixth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6), carried out in 2023-24, found 17.8% of women and 20.9% of men aged 15 and above had high blood sugar or were on medicine for it, up from 13.5% and 15.6% per cent in NFHS-5, conducted in 2019-21. In Chennai district, nearly 3 in 10 women fall in the group.
That said, there are limitations to this data: NFHS teams prick a finger at whatever hour they visit, so people may or may not have eaten, and a reading above 140 milligrams per decilitre counts as high. One such reading cannot diagnose diabetes. However, what is most routinely blamed for the rising burden of diabetes in the country -- and it is rising -- are weight and diet. And while these are significant factors, dirty air is rarely blamed. Perhaps it’s time it is.
The outdoor evidence
Siddhartha Mandal of the Centre for Chronic Disease Control in New Delhi and his colleagues used satellite and weather data to estimate daily levels of fine particles, called PM2.5, near each participant’s home.
Over a median of almost five years, 743 people developed type 2 diabetes. Each extra 10 micrograms in a person’s yearly average accounted for a 22% higher risk, after the researchers allowed for age, socio-economic status, tobacco and alcohol use, diet and exercise. Studies in richer, cleaner countries have put the rise at 7 to 11%.
A 2024 global review of 46 studies also linked PM2.5 and the coarser PM10 to type 2 diabetes. Its authors point mainly to inflammation and oxidative stress (damage from reactive oxygen), which blunt the body’s response to insulin, the hormone that moves sugar into cells. The Global Burden of Disease project puts about a fifth of the healthy years lost worldwide to type 2 diabetes in 2019 down to PM2.5, about 14% from outdoor air and 6% from household smoke.
Smoke in the kitchen
Between 2018 and 2021, researchers from the Madras Diabetes Research Foundation tested adults in 30 villages of Cheyyur taluk in Chengalpattu district as part of a project called TREND.
All but 208 of the 13,877 adults lived in homes cooking on traditional fuels such as firewood or kerosene. Diabetes was more common among them, 14.2% against 12%, and more common still, 16.5%, in homes without a separate kitchen. Among women, traditional fuel use was linked with 80% higher odds of diabetes of diabetes, after the researchers allowed for age, weight, family history, education and income.
One round of testing, however, cannot prove what causes diabetes, and the group using clean fuel was small. Even so, a 2022 review of nine studies with 45,620 people found that those who cooked with solid fuels had 46% higher odds of diabetes. However, in homes that burned only biomass like wood or dung, the link was too weak to be certain.
Short of gas, short of data
The NFHS used to report cooking fuel and blood sugar from the same homes. Clean fuel, mostly LPG, reached 58.6% of homes in 2019-21, up from 43.8% in 2015-16, as the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana distributed connections. Even at that pace, about 3 homes in 10, mostly in villages, would still have cooked on fuels such as wood, dung and kerosene by 2023-24. The NFHS-6 fact sheets, released on May 29, leave this figure out. The Health Ministry has said this, and other missing statistics are being monitored through dedicated national surveys and administrative databases; however these other surveys do not take blood samples, leaving possible connections unable to be made.
Much of India’s LPG comes from abroad. About 90% of those imports pass through the Strait of Hormuz, which the West Asia war choked in early March, leading to shortfalls across the country. Poor homes, though, used little gas even before the war. The average Ujjwala household bought 4.71 cylinders in 2025-26, and about one in seven in Bihar bought none, the Petroleum Ministry told the Lok Sabha. The ministry has since cut subsidised refills from nine a year to four, about half of what a family cooking only on gas needs, as per figures cited by think tank, the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW).
Every return to the wood stove brings back smoke tied to diabetes, and even a month of dirtier air nudged up blood sugar in the Delhi and Chennai study, a worry for anyone already living with the disease. As long as India’s kitchens depend on imported gas, the next war or blockade can push them back to wood, and more people towards diabetes.
The Kerala puzzle
If dirty air alone drove the numbers, the least polluted States would sit at the bottom of the survey’s tables. A satellite study of 2024 pollution by independent research organisation, the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), put Kerala among the seven States and Union Territories with the cleanest air. Yet Kerala has the highest share of women with high blood sugar of any State or Union Territory, 28.9%, according to NFHS-6. Meghalaya, where CREA found every district above the national pollution standard outside the monsoon, has the lowest of any State, 7.1%. Kerala also has the oldest population of any State, and diabetes grows more common with age. This complicates the picture.
What could help, would be more data, and long-term studies that could tease apart the effects of air, with those of age, weight, diet and access to doctors, of the same people.
The NFHS, though, could provide answers sooner than any new study. The Health Ministry has said that a more detailed NFHS-6 national report will be released, though it is not clear if this will include cooking fuel numbers. If the report and household data include cooking fuel, researchers could compare blood sugar in homes using wood and gas, taking age and weight into account, and use data from before the shortage as a baseline. The Petroleum Ministry already tracks Ujjwala refills by State, and could publish this information monthly for every district.
It remains to be seen, however, if the data will materialise. Until then, India remains the country with the highest burden of diabetes, and one of the highest levels of air pollution.
(Dr Margubur Rahaman is a public health researcher at MAMTA Health Institute for Mother and Child, New Delhi. margubur48@gmail.com; Ankit Mishra is an ICSSR Doctoral Fellow at the Govind Ballabh Pant Social Science Institute, Prayagraj. ankitmishrakoraon@gmail.com)

Littler hits triple-bull, but Price checkout doesn't add up
- Published
Gerwyn Price and Luke Littler both made it through to the Grand Slam of Darts knockout stage on a night featuring a bizarre maths error and a sensational triple-bull checkout.
Littler suffered a 5-4 defeat by Dutchman Niels Zonneveld but claimed the three legs he required to progress from the group stage.
The 19-year-old, egged on by the crowd at the Aldersley venue in Wolverhampton, improbably landed three darts on the bullseye to produce a remarkable 150 checkout and level the match at 4-4, only to lose the deciding leg.
Price, meanwhile, claimed a 5-2 victory over Sebastian Bialecki - although he was the beneficiary of an unusual mathematical mistake.
The Welshman was 2-1 up against Poland's Bialecki and required 135 to win the fourth leg.
Price's first dart hit treble 19, leaving him with 78, but he asked referee Charlie Corstorphine what he had left to score and was incorrectly told 88.
In good faith, Price promptly threw treble 16 and then double 20 to win the leg, having scored 145 - which should have bust him.
"A rare scoring error was made by the referee in the fourth leg of the match between Gerwyn Price and Sebastian Bialecki," organisers the PDC told BBC Sport in a statement.
"Under Darts Regulation Authority (DRA) rule 6.4, as the error was not corrected before the next leg began, the leg score stands as announced."
Price said he was unaware of the miscalculation until it was flagged up to him before he walked into a post-match news conference.
"I hit the first treble and I asked 'what have I got left?' and he said 88, so I threw treble 16 and double top, then he said 'game shot'," said fourth seed Price.
"I'm glad I didn't know, because it probably would have played on my mind."
What do DRA rules say about Price error?
The DRA's rulebook is clear if there has been an error in scoring which, although rare in professional darts, can sometimes occur.
The following clauses are what the rulebook, external says about the mistake involving Price:
- 6.4.6 Errors in arithmetic shall stand as detailed on the scoreboard unless corrected prior to the next throw of the player whose score is in error. Any error in the score can be corrected by the referee at any time until game shot is called in that leg.
- 6.4.7 If the incorrect score resulted in a leg win the result will stand unless corrected prior to the start of the next leg.
- 6.4.8 If the incorrect score resulted in the winning of a match the result will be considered as final when both players and the referee have left the playing area believing the match to be successfully completed.

US basketball player arrested with 34kg of cannabis at Nigerian airport
- Published
A professional American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria with 33.95kg (75lbs) of cannabis in his luggage at the main airport in Lagos.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) identified the player as Greene Da'monte Khiree, 28, from the US state of Georgia, who it said had arrived from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.
According to the agency, the suspect said he had been playing professional basketball in Thailand and was visiting to Nigeria to "build networks" for his career. He has not publicly commented on the allegations.
The agency said an examination of the suspect's phone had pointed "to his knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity".
In statement on Sunday, the agency he was arrested on Wednesday after airport officials noticed him abandoning his two checked-in bags and attempting to leave with his carry-on bag.
The two bags, which bore his name, contained 32 packs of the drug known as "Loud", a potent strain of cannabis, the agency said.
A tracking device was also recovered from the bags, the agency added.
The International Basketball Federation (FIBA) lists a player by the name Damonte Greene, with the most recent appearance at the Phuket Elite Cup in Thailand, on 26 September.
Nigeria, once regarded primarily as a transit hub for drug trafficking, has increasingly become a producer, consumer, and distributor of illegal drugs, according to the UN.
Recent NDLEA operations have uncovered several industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratories, raising concerns about links between Nigerian drug producers and Mexican cartels seeking to manufacture and export the drug.
In September, the agency said it had dismantled a meth lab and arrested a Mexican suspected drug kingpin who was allegedly attempting to flee Nigeria through Lagos.
Methamphetamine, commonly known as meth, is a highly addictive synthetic drug that can cause severe psychosis, heart attacks or stroke.
In August, a social media influencer suspected of links to an international drug trafficking network was arrested after the authorities seized cocaine worth nearly $28m (£21m), which was destined for the UK.

Chris Van Hollen says he can beat Chuck Schumer. Here's his case
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., on his challenge for Senate majority leader
Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Monday that he is gaining momentum in his bid to unseat longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, taking a traditionally private Senate leadership contest into public view.
"Well, I'm the underdog, but we are really moving in the right direction here," Van Hollen told NPR's Steve Inskeep on Morning Edition.
Over the weekend, he appeared on CNN, ABC and Fox News to make his case for new Democratic leadership after his party's sweeping midterm victories. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, says he has enough votes to remain leader.
Van Hollen is hardly a Washington outsider. The progressive Democrat has spent nearly 25 years on Capitol Hill, served as a deputy to then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and led Democratic campaign efforts in both chambers. He has been a vocal opponent of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and dismantling of the U.S. Agency for International Development, and he has called for investigations into the administration's foreign aid cuts.
Schumer has continued to support U.S. military assistance to Israel despite his criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Van Hollen, by contrast, has pushed to restrict weapons sales and military aid to the Israeli government over its war in Gaza, while pressing for more humanitarian aid to Palestinians.
"I certainly oppose the idea of an American taxpayer blank check to the government of Israel, regardless of its actions," Van Hollen said.
Van Hollen also wants Democratic leaders to stay out of contested primaries. He pointed to the victories of incoming Sens. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.
"We have two senators-elect who would not be there if the current majority leader had his way," he said.
He described the midterm victories as a populist rejection of President Trump, rather than an election orchestrated by Washington Democrats.
Van Hollen also cited legislation to strengthen labor unions, which never received a vote on the Senate floor. On the war in Iran, he called for an end to further funding.
"We should not be voting for one penny in mid-December to continue this war," he said.
Van Hollen will need close to 30 votes, a simple majority of the Senate Democratic caucus, to win. The election will be decided by secret ballot behind closed doors, making it difficult to know how many votes either candidate secured.

India and nine other nations have signed a joint declaration to safeguard supply chains and infrastructure that are central to the development and deployment of advanced AI systems. The agreement, called the San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity, was signed on November 15 at the Pax Silica retreat, which was convened by US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg. Besides India, the declaration was also signed by representatives of the governments of the US, Australia, Israel, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Qatar, Singapore, the UAE and the UK. “The declaration affirms that economic security is fundamental to national security, sets out the participants’ common understanding of the sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure that underpin super intelligence (or AI) supply chains, and declares that safeguarding them is a shared endeavor,” read a statement by the US state department. For context, the US government refers to AI as super intelligence (SI) after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename it. The declaration has termed the protection of two strategic assets – “critical” AI infrastructure and “sensitive technologies” – as a “shared endeavour” essential to the prosperity and independence of participating countries. The document defines sensitive technologies as goods, software, knowledge, components, inputs and means of production used in AI supply chains. The declaration noted that these technologies could provide a military advantage, create undue economic leverage and pose risks if transferred without authorisation or misused. It also defines “critical infrastructure” as the physical and digital systems that support AI supply chains, including ports, terminals, transport, communications and logistics networks, information technology and digital platforms. The declaration adds that disruption, hostile control or unauthorised exposure of data flowing through these systems could cause significant harm. In addition, the signatories also agreed that AI resilience would be “best” achieved through diversified and trusted supply chains and by building trusted capabilities among participants. The declaration also underscored the importance of coordinated efforts to address AI supply chain disruptions and non-market policies that distort the AI market. It also called for protecting private investment and ensuring a level playing field for innovation and growth. To aid this, the declaration also proposed the setting up of working groups across five separate spaces: Pro-innovation policy frameworks AI adoption in key sectors Supply chain cooperation across the AI stack Safe harbours and supply chain security hubs AI security and resilience “We, the undersigned participants,... reaffirming (reaffirm) the importance of cooperation on the enforcement of our respective policies to protect sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure from undue access, influence, or control, as stated in the Pax Silica declaration…,” added the document. The San Francisco Declaration is part of the broader US-led Pax Silica initiative. The framework aims to build secure and resilient supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors and AI infrastructure. For India, the multilateral platform offers an avenue to coordinate with other economies on AI supply chains and critical infrastructure. This comes as India seeks to expand its domestic manufacturing in semiconductors and advanced computing, while reducing reliance on foreign sources for components and equipment.

Cloud storage certainly has a lot going for it. For a start, if you drop your laptop into the sink, it's likely that a lot of your important work will be backed up somewhere in the cloud, as long as you’re using services such as Google Drive, OneDrive, and iCloud.
Then there's file sharing: Not too many years ago, swapping large amounts of data with other people meant dragging and dropping and running around with USB drives (and perhaps even mailing them). Now, via a couple of clicks and a link, you can share just about anything with just about anyone, anywhere in the world.
However, this comes with security risks attached. You don't want those links making their way to anyone they weren't intended for, otherwise they've got access to your files and folders. They could potentially see what's in them, and maybe even make changes or delete files, depending on the permissions you've set.
It's worth emphasizing that sharing files through these cloud storage services isn't inherently insecure—these shared links are actually very well protected, by default. However, the longer they stick around, the bigger the risk gets. Your links could get mistakenly forwarded in an email, or one of your contacts could have their email account hacked.
With that in mind it's prudent to run a regular audit on the cloud sharing links you've got active. It shouldn't take long: The apps involved usually make this pretty straightforward. Once you've closed a link down, no one else can get to it.
Microsoft OneDrive
If you head to the Microsoft OneDrive portal on the web, you'll see a Shared link in the navigation pane on the left: Click this, then select By you up at the top of the file list to see everything you've shared with other people. Use the Modified header if you want to sort the files and folders by the oldest or most recent.
Click the three dots next to any file or folder, then Manage access to control who can get to it. If you've shared the file with specific people, you can remove some or all of them; if the file or folder is shared more widely with just a link, clicking the trash can gets rid of it. You can also open up Office files to manage access there.
It's worth knowing that when you opt to share a file in OneDrive on the web (via the three dots and Share), if you click the cog icon on the Share panel you can set an expiration date for the sharing—which saves you the trouble of having to tidy it up afterwards.
Apple iCloud
If iCloud Drive is your cloud storage service of choice, once you've got the main interface up on the web, you can click Shared on the navigation pane on the left to go straight to the files and folders you're sharing with other people. There's no easy way to sort them, but you can use the search box up in the top right corner.
Click the three dots next to a file and folder, then Managed Shared File, to make changes. The next screen lets you block access for specific contacts, and to change permissions (from editing to just viewing, for example). If you want to cancel the sharing altogether, click Stop sharing.
Unlike OneDrive, iCloud doesn't give you any way of putting expiration periods on shared links, so you have to clear them up manually.
Dropbox
Dropbox is one of the more aggressive services when it comes to tidying up shared links, and if you use the Dropbox apps you might see reminders to review the files and folders you've shared with others. From Dropbox on the web, click Shared in the left-hand navigation pane to see files and folders you're currently sharing.
You can get quite a detailed breakdown here, including by Files or by Folders. Click the three dots next to any entry, then Share, to see the current sharing options: You can remove access for contacts one by one, or click the cog icon (top left) to find the Unshare button that ends all sharing completely.
Dropbox does have link expiry features built in: If you open up the share settings whenever you're sharing a file or folder, you'll see Link expiry is one of the options. It's an easy way to tidy up after yourself, provided the people you're sharing the file or folder with get around to viewing it in time.
Google Drive
Google Drive, surprisingly, isn't quite as on top of shared links as other cloud storage services. If you open up the web portal, there's no easy to access list of everything you've shared: The closest thing to it is clicking the People filter, and then choosing contacts to see files and folders you've shared with them specifically. If you pick Anyone with the link from the drop-down list, you'll see everything shared with a simple link.
To change the sharing settings for a file or folder, click on the three dots, then Share. Click the cog icon on the panel that pops up, then you can remove contacts as needed and turn the visible link off.
As with iCloud, there's no link expiry feature you can rely on here, so shared files and folders can't be set to become unshared after a certain time has elapsed. It has to be done manually, so it's a shame Google doesn't make it as easy as it could be.

Organizing a film festival is a challenge at the best of times, figuring out the logistics with the threat of war on the doorstep requires an extra layer of resilience.
It is a quality Fatma Al Remaihi, CEO of the Doha Film Institute (DFI) and her team have had to muster in spades as they prepared for the second edition of the rebooted Doha Film Festival, setting in place logistics for a trio of different scenarios.
“We knew that no matter what, we will have a festival… we were exploring differing scenarios, that it could be just for locals, that it could be for everyone, or that it could just be an online competition. We’ve planned for every eventuality,” Al Remaihi tells Deadline on the eve of the festival which is due to open on Thursday.
She is speaking nine months after Israel and the U.S. launched a major military campaign against Iran’s Islamic Republic government at the end of February, which retaliated with missile and drone strike on all its Gulf neighbours.
The DFI was forced to move its popular annual Qumra project and talent incubator online in March, with the team applying lessons learned during the Covid-19 pandemic. While guests, including Gael García Bernal and Diego Luna and Alice Diop, could not make it to Qatar, Al Remaihi says the event still fulfilled its mission.
“The filmmakers and the projects didn’t miss this edition. It was fantastic to be able to be there for them. Even though a lot of our staff here were suffering with scary times, they’re still pulled through and made it happen for the filmmakers.”
The situation has calmed down since April and Qatar has been heavily involved in negotiations to deescalate the conflict, with its diplomats regularly traveling to the Iranian capital Tehran as part of international efforts to broker a peace deal.
Al Remaihi is confident that the festival, running from November 19 to 27, will unfold at full capacity, alongside other events set to take place in Doha in the period including the Fashion Trust Arabia Awards on November 28 and the Formula 1 Grand Prix from November 27 to 28.
“We’re so happy that we are a few days away from the festival, and excited now to open and experience it with everybody, and it’s not smaller, we have more films and more guests,” she says.
The festival expands on the DFI’s long-running family-focused festival of Ajyal which ran for more than a decade during the same period, with Media City Qatar and the territory’s Film Committee coming on board as new partners as part of their mission to build the country’s media and entertainment sector. 
“I don’t like to call it a second edition as I don’t see it as a new festival. It’s a continuation of what we do,” notes Al Remaihi, while acknowledging that the repositioning gave the festival fresh impetus last year.
The first edition of the reboot last year set the tone for a festival focused on cinema and rather than big name stars.
“The guests that we invite are from the program. That’s what is important for us. They have a role in the program and something to give in the festival. It’s never been about big names and stars for us,” says Al Remaihi.
She points nonetheless to the presence of Japanese director Naomi Kawase as jury president for the main International Competition; James Gray, for a gala screening of Paper Tiger, and Oscar-winning documentarian Gianfranco Rosi ,who is also on the jury alongside rising actor Adam Bessa, Tunisian producer Dora Bouchoucha and Palestinian director Kamal Aljafari.
	Indian filmmaker and actor Nandita Das (Manto, Zwigato) and regional star, the Syrian actor Taim Hassan (Al Hayba, Mawlana), will also be in attendance to receive the festival’s Creative Excellence Award.
“We have big names. Maybe for the public eyes, it’s different. But for people who work in the industry and who value filmmaking and the craft itself, they know these names and they’re very excited to have them in Doha. In that sense, I’m very happy with the caliber of the guests who are coming to the festival,” she explains.
Watch on Deadline
	DFI-backed Yemen-set drama The Station by Sara Ishaq – set against the backdrop of woman-only petrol stations in the war-torn country – opens this edition.
“We confirmed The Station for the opening months ago. It’s very rare to have an opening film confirmed from that early, but we saw in this film everything that embodies the festival and the spirit of the festival,” says Al Remaihi.
“It’s a simple story that sheds light on a very complicated background, and we thought it was very brave to make a film like this. We don’t see a lot coming out of Yemen. Yes, it had its premiere in Cannes, but we wanted to give it center stage in the festival.”
The Station is among 15 films playing in the International Competition at the heart of the festival, competing for close to $200,000 in combined prize money.
It features a raft of titles which have garnered acclaim on the festival circuit over the past year including Cameroonian director Auguste Bernard Kouemo’s House of the Wind, which won Venice’s Lion of the Future for a Debut Film when it premiered there in its Orizzonti sidebar in September.
Further contenders include Moroccan director Tala Hadid’s Bardi, which played at the New York Film Festival, and Thai filmmaker Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s 9 Temples to Heaven, which premiered in Cannes Directors’ Fortnight and is Thailand’s submission to the 99th Academy Awards.
Other Oscar hopefuls in the lineup include the Philippines’ entry Filipiñana by Rafael Manuel and Chilean director Manuela Martelli’s The Meltdown.
There are four films by Palestinian filmmakers including Rabab Khamis’ documentary Sama, about a ten-year-old girl who collects plastic and cardboard in Deir al-Balah in Gaza to sell as fuel and help sustain her family, which world premieres
It is joined by Hosam Abu Dan’s Gaza-shot drama Thirteen in Gaza, about a 13-year-old living with her father in a Gaza displacement camp, which won the NETPAC Award in Toronto; Muayad Alayan’s Venice–selected Conversation with the Sea, about a Palestinian man caught in the crosshairs of Israeli bureaucracy, and Mohanad Yaqubi’s Revolutionaries Never Die, revolving around 113 reels of films preserved by Lebanese filmmaker Jocelyne Saab.
The final contenders are Asmahan Bkerat’s Concrete Land, Hugo Salvaterra’s My Semba, Zou Jing Cannes Critics’ Week Fipresci-winner A Girl Unknown, Alessandra Sanguinetti’s The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer and Alexander Murphy’s Tin Castle.
Eleven of the films have received the support of the DFI’s grantee programs, with Al Remaihi explaining it is at the heart of an interconnected process developed over the institute’s 16-year existence. 
“It just shows that we don’t do anything on a singular basis. Everything we do is connected. We have an ecosystem that we built a long time ago, and we’ve seen the benefits of having something like this,” she says.
“A lot of the films in our competition are grantees because it speaks to the type of funding that we do, choices that we make, the people that we work with, and we love to celebrate all of this during the festival with all of that community. It’s a great moment for us also to have all of that come together.”
Outside of the competition, there will be gala screening for Paper Tiger, Rami Kodeih’s DFI-backed Beirut-set heist thriller Furies, Maiken Baird’s Toronto-selected Edward Said: Between Worlds and Bruno Dumont’s Red Rocks.
	
There will also be Special Screenings for Abderrahmane Sissako’s Artou, Daniele Rugo’s Life Support, following international doctors working alongside local medical staff in Gaza in 2023; Ginevra Elkann drama The Roses of Marrakech and Ali El Arabi’s 52 Blue.
Another key strand is the Made In Qatar sidebar. This has traditionally showcased short films but makes history this year as it premieres four locally produced features, spanning Jodari Meno by Jamal Al Khanji, A Very Ordinary Life by Mohamed Deniz, First to Fly by Rodrigo Vazquez Salessi and When the News Breaks You by Hamad Al Hajri.
	“It’s a testament to all of the work that we’ve been doing over the years and how the industry has developed in Qatar. We’ve been doing this for a long time, but now its not just the Doha Film Institute. We the Film Committee, Media City Qatar, and Katara Studios, all the film production houses,” she says. “You feel that there is a huge movement and a huge shift in the industry here.”
A new addition to the program is the Cinema Alkhaleej sidebar showcasing cinema from across the Gulf region, with highlights including the world premiere of horror feature Soulala by Saudi director and actor Hisham Fqih as well as the Qatar premiere of Ahd Kamel’s My Driver and I, which originally premiered at Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea International Film Festival in 2024. 
“We wanted to bring the Khaleeji (Gulf) industry together and have them more involved in the festival, not just as guests but also as participating guests. A lot of these films were not available here, so they are still fresh for our audiences. I loved watching all these films as we programmed the section and I’m excited to share them with the audience here.”

Upasana Kamineni Konidela, wife of Telugu actor Ram Charan, has spoken about the unequal expectations society places on mothers and fathers when it comes to parenting. She questioned why fathers receive appreciation for performing everyday childcare responsibilities, while mothers are expected to take on the same duties without receiving similar recognition. Emphasising the need for a change in this mindset, Upasana said that the shift must begin within families and eventually reflect in professional spaces as well.
Upasana Kamineni Konidela speaks about unequal parenting expectations, questions why fathers are praised for parenting; says, “The father is not doing anybody a favour”
Speaking at the CII Partnership Summit 2026 in Visakhapatnam, where she interacted with Andhra Pradesh Minister Nara Lokesh, Upasana highlighted how routine parenting activities are often viewed differently depending on whether a mother or father performs them. She pointed out that when a father feeds a child or changes a diaper, people tend to praise him, whereas mothers rarely receive the same appreciation for carrying out these responsibilities.
“When a father feeds a child or changes the diaper, the mother and everyone are clapping, saying, 'Oh, that's so nice, you're such a good father.' But when the mother does it, why aren't they clapping for me? Unless this mindset changes at home, it'll never change in the boardroom. This is what we really need to work on. It should be part of the curriculum, people's mindset, people's changes. The father is not doing anybody a favour. He's parenting. And I think that's the most important thing,” she said.
Upasana also acknowledged that she has sometimes been part of this mindset herself. Admitting that she finds it adorable when Ram Charan feeds their children, she said she has now come to understand that such gestures should be considered a normal part of parenting rather than something extraordinary.
“If we have that in our mindset, if we have that in our education, if children are brought up that way, and if mothers also don't make a big deal when their sons do good work, then I think the whole system will progress. As a wife, I sometimes do it too. I find it extremely cute when he feeds our children. But now I understand that it's normal. It's a normal thing for parents to do,” she said.
She further stressed that children should grow up understanding that childcare and household responsibilities are shared duties. According to her, bringing this change into children's upbringing and education can help challenge traditional gender expectations.
Ram Charan and Upasana got married in 2012 and welcomed their first child, daughter Klin Kaara Konidela, in June 2023. The couple expanded their family in January 2026 with the arrival of twins, a boy and a girl, named Shivram and Anveera Devi.

In the weeks since Jane Doe alleged she was gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity party in 2024, the plague of campus sexual assault has once again become the topic of a heated national debate.
Preventing campus sexual assault could start in kindergarten
The Cornell case shows that something’s missing in how young people learn about sex. Fixing it could change a lot.
Those discussions inevitably land on familiar solutions. Experts, pundits, and parents argue for stricter criminal laws and a more transparent and punitive Title IX campus adjudicatory process. But these solutions have been tried in the past and not proven effective: Campus climate surveys show persistently high rates of assault, and Cornell’s own data show that reported incidents rose from 23 percent to 35 percent between 2023 and 2025.
It’s increasingly clear that to make meaningful progress requires a focus on prevention — not just punishment. Anyone horrified by the Cornell fraternity text thread published by the New York Times would agree that enforcement is only part of the story, and a fuller solution would begin with raising young people who don’t think it is remotely okay to treat each other’s bodies and emotions this way. There is a group of scholars and advocates across the country who are working on one surprisingly effective policy that might get us closer to that goal: comprehensive sex education.
Yes, you read that right: sex ed. But not sex ed as it’s currently taught in most American public schools — a haphazard set of state programs, often deeply political, which often stress abstinence over how to be in healthy sexual relationships with other people. This other version, known as comprehensive sex ed and currently required in just seven states, takes a holistic approach with focus on how to refuse unwanted sexual advances, establish clear boundaries, and have intimate relationships based on open communication and mutual desire, not force, coercion, or extreme intoxication.
An important step in the prevention of sexual assault is making comprehensive sex ed more common in American schools, and, in the states that do, making that education start earlier and comply with the National Sex Education Standards. Evidence suggests that this kind of instruction can reduce sexual violence.
Giving young people information about contraception and how to avoid STIs is an essential part of sex ed, but it isn’t enough. Far too many of our children head off to college without the interpersonal skills required to have healthy relationships involving physical intimacy, which are critical to their psychological development into caring and fulfilled adults.
The consequences can be devastating, and I see them firsthand. I am a law professor who runs a clinical program at the University of San Francisco that trains second- and third-year law students by having them litigate real cases under close supervision. Since 2018, we have been representing Title IX clients — the accusers and those they accuse — at colleges and universities all over the United States. In every case, every time, the end result is the same: pain, heartbreak, and ruined lives. The legal “resolution” is almost beside the point.
The allegations in the Cornell case are at the extreme end of the spectrum. In nearly all of the cases we handle, there is no malicious intent or casual cruelty. Instead, there are two young people who are inexperienced, hesitant to convey their real feelings, and bad at reading nonverbal cues. They drink excessively and use drugs to overcome their awkwardness and insecurity, which only makes the poor communication worse. My colleague and I joke bleakly that we are in the wrong business. What we really need to be doing is going to secondary schools and preaching the value of comprehensive sex ed to tweens and teens to stop these assaults from happening in the first place.
Recently, I interviewed Jennifer Hirsch, who is a professor at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and the co-author with Princeton sociologist Shamus Khan of the book Sexual Citizens, which synthesizes the findings of a five-year study of campus sexual assault that surveyed 2,000 students attending Columbia and Barnard.
“Thinking ambitiously about prevention requires that we get some more tools in the toolbox.”
— Jennifer Hirsch, Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health
Sex education needs to start in kindergarten, she said, by teaching children to respect the bodies of their classmates by keeping their hands to themselves and refraining from playground activities like chasing down a classmate trying to kiss them. In higher grades, she explained, the instruction should change to become more age-appropriate, gradually adding topics relating to sexual health for tweens and teens “to teach the things you need to know, to grow into being a person who can have sex without hurting other people or yourself.” Currently, only Washington and Oregon start this early. (A few other states begin in first grade.)
While it is true that many colleges and universities have mandatory trainings for students that involve learning about consent, bystander intervention, and how intoxication is a risk factor for sexual assault, it is too little, too late. By then, Hirsch said, “there is a non-trivial possibility that they’ve already experienced sexual violence or perpetrated sexual violence.” She compared it to “starting with calculus when they’ve never done arithmetic.”
The need for such education is even more urgent today when kids snap and text instead of talk face-to-face as they are fed a diet of toxic social media messages and violent pornography that tells them what women want is to be dominated, degraded, and objectified.
Gen Z in particular is in desperate need of a sexual education that is designed to dispel the fear, shame, and ignorance most young people feel around this topic and replace it with candid instruction on how to set boundaries, read cues, and treat intimate partners — whether it is a long-term relationship or a casual hook-up — with a basic modicum of respect and care.
Study after study has shown that there is widespread bipartisan support for having sex ed incorporated into secondary school instruction that teaches students the skills they need to have safe and healthy sexual relationships. Comprehensive sex education holds promise in combatting sexual assault, although the data is limited. A 2016 survey of more than 1,600 college students led by John Santelli, who is also a professor at Columbia’s Mailman School (and Hirsch’s spouse) found that when high schoolers received comprehensive sex education, it lowered their risk of sexual assault in college. Instruction stressing abstinence or how to avoid unwanted pregnancies and STIs did not.
This makes intuitive sense. If a young person learns early on how to extricate themselves from a sexual encounter that has turned uncomfortable or scary, they will be more likely to leave before an assault happens. If he or she is taught that other people’s bodies are not theirs for the taking, they will be less likely to violate them and instead ask for clarity whenever there is ambiguity about consent.
Still most schools shy away from such instruction. “It is better to tell kids that rape is bad than to say nothing,” but to stop there and hope for the best is not effective, Hirsch told me. “Thinking ambitiously about prevention requires that we get some more tools in the toolbox.”
But comprehensive sex ed, despite its popularity, has for decades been blocked by a minority of loud opposition, often motivated by religious beliefs, in states that consider adopting it. Since 2017, New York state lawmakers have advocated for a law mandating comprehensive sex ed for students in grades K-12. Every year, Hirsch told me, it dies in committee. At the federal level, the Trump administration has eliminated most of the federal grant money for sex ed that isn’t abstinence-only even though the research has shown that telling kids to “just say no” to sex has no impact on their behavior.
Suspension, expulsion, even criminal prosecution are not the solutions. They are the inadequate answers on offer by the adults in the room, who are trained only to react once the problem has become too big and ugly to ignore in any particular case before bracing for the next one. Reducing the accused to monsters and the accuser to a pitiable victim reinfects the wound, it does nothing to heal it. Wringing one’s hands and asking why, a generation later nothing has changed, virtually guarantees that nothing ever will.
If we really want to combat the plague of sexual assault on campus, we need to vaccinate our children in the same way we would against a lethal virus. Comprehensive sex ed is the best place to start.

Tamil Nadu Minister for Health K.G. Arunraj inaugurated the Centre for Advanced Genomics at Christian Medical College (CMC) in Ranipet on Monday (November 16, 2026).
Health officials said that the new facility is aimed to provide high-end genetic testing within CMC. Such genetic testing will support precision healthcare, translational research, and medical education.
The Minister inspected the new facility in the presence of Minister for Cooperatives V. Gandhiraj, Collector N. Priya Ravichandran and Biju George, Director, CMC. The facility is equipped with advanced Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) platforms for high-throughput genomic testing, as well as high-performance bioinformatics pipelines.
The facility also has the capacity to process hundreds of samples at a time. In healthcare, it will enable rapid, accurate diagnosis of many conditions that include complex cancers, rare inherited disorders, and infectious diseases as well as susceptibility to lifestyle diseases. “Such an advanced research facility helps for early detection of diseases. Such research helps in treatment of rare and communicable diseases,” Mr. Arunraj said.
Health officials said that by decoding genetic profiles of individual patients, the multidisciplinary team at the new facility will empower clinicians to deliver personalised, targeted therapies. As a hub within a premier teaching hospital, the facility will also serve to train current and coming generations of physicians, geneticists, and biomedical scientists.
Through close collaboration between clinicians and researchers within a hospital setting, the Centre for Advanced Genomics will facilitate scientific discoveries that will impact healthcare. Anderson Diagnostic Service Private Limited has provided the technological infrastructure and operational service.
