- Jason will play a central role in GTA 6 alongside the series' first female protagonist, Lucia.
- The character will have a Bonnie and Clyde-like dynamic with Lucia in GTA 6.
- Rockstar has yet to confirm the official voice actor for Jason, but rumors have linked him to Dylan Rourke.
Jason Duval is one of the two playable protagonists in GTA 6, with his story being closely tied to Lucia Caminos. While Rockstar Games initially kept Jason a bit mysterious, the second trailer and the recent GTA 6 Extended Look on Netflix have given us a clearer picture of who he is and how he fits into the main story. So, if you’re looking to learn more about Jason in GTA 6, check out this comprehensive guide.
Who Is Jason in GTA 6?
Jason Duval is one of the dual protagonists in GTA 6 and plays a prominent role in the narrative alongside Lucia. The character grew up around grifters and crooks, but eventually joined the army in an attempt to set things straight. However, this endeavor capsized at some point, and Jason found himself in the Leonida Keys region working for local drug runners.
Around this time, he meets Lucia, and the pair strike a formidable bond as they go around pulling off audacious scores together. Despite a penchant for being on the wrong side of the law, Jason prefers the easy life, but “things just keep getting harder.”
We caught a first glimpse of the character in the 2023 GTA 6 trailer 1. However, his presence in the initial reveal can be described as brief at best. Fortunately, Jason was effectively the focal point of the GTA 6 trailer 2, as we got a proper look at his character model, his colorful associates, and an Extended Look at his relationship with Lucia.
Now that the GTA 6 Extended Look is out, we have gotten the most substantial look at who Jason is so far. He is placed in shootouts, driving, robberies, exploration, and interactions with Lucia. Plus, we got to see more of his romantic dynamic with her.
In LOVE Magazine’s recent GTA 6 issue, Senior Vice President of Narrative Rupert Humphries revealed that Jason turns to a life of crime “because of his material circumstances”.
He also mentioned that Jason is “wired differently from other people,” sparking community discussions about what that could mean. Some players speculate that Jason may be neurodivergent, while others think he might be a bit introverted, given how Lucia often seems to call the shots.
Bonnie and Clyde Dynamic with Lucia
Both trailers and the elaborate GTA 6 Extended Look clearly show the duo as partners in crime. In the first, we saw them pull off a daring vehicle escape alongside separate shots of Jason and Lucia in GTA 6.
The second trailer also features multiple shots of the pair having lighthearted conversations and getting intimate. This quote typifies their dynamic from Jason: “If anything happens, I’m right behind you.” The duo is hell-bent on earning the ‘good life’ together and will do whatever it takes.
One important aspect that the Extended Look reveals is that Jason and Lucia’s romantic relationship is optional in GTA 6. It’s an important distinction because Jason’s role isn’t simply serving as Lucia’s love interest. He is a protagonist in his own right, and he can work independently by taking jobs and exploring the open world.
Jason’s Friends & Associates
The second trailer and its official page have provided a ton of new information about the various side characters in GTA 6. Some of them have proclaimed ties to Jason, starting with his friend, Cal Hampton. The homebody has a taste for alcohol and the internet, a typically dangerous combination, but we’ll have to see how that plays out.
As for his appearance in the trailer, the character can be seen calling for a round of shots and hauling cargo onto a plane. Given this, it’s safe to assume that Cal will likely assist Jason in his criminal endeavors.
Another character worth highlighting is Brian Heder. We see the wise veteran during the first few seconds of the trailer, as he nags Jason about some collection jobs. While that sums up his appearance in the trailer, he even lets our protagonist stay rent-free at one of his properties.
As dingy as those dwellings might be, we suspect Heder could be the primary mission-giver during the initial section of the game. It also seems likely that Jason will be moving some drugs for the character, as we saw him lending Cal a hand in those above ‘hauling cargo’ shots.
The final character of note is Raul Bautista, a seasoned bank robber connected to the larger heist side of GTA 6’s story. The LOVE Magazine GTA 6 issue confirms that Raul will mentor Jason and Lucia, passing on the criminal knowledge and experience they lack when they first arrive in Vice City.
The latest footage shows Bautista and Jason using some of the best weapons in GTA 6 to escape the cops. Additionally, Raul tells them to keep in touch after the police chase in GTA 6 Extended Look, suggesting Jason and Lucia will become part of his crew.
It’ll be interesting to see how Jason and Raul’s dynamic evolves as the story progresses and the two pull off more heists together.
Could Jason Betray Lucia in GTA 6?
It’s well established that Rockstar loves weaving a major betrayal into their narrative. There are countless examples of this, and things have reached a point where players can see it coming from miles away. This spawned a popular theory that Jason could turn his back on Lucia at some point in the story.
The genesis of this theory is the very first shot of the 2023 trailer, which shows Lucia in an orange jumpsuit inside a prison.
However, we can safely put this speculation to rest since the second trailer and the Extended Look reveal that Jason and Lucia are a great duo and will take on numerous tasks in the GTA 6 map of Leonida. Regardless, only time will tell what Rockstar has in store for Jason’s fate at the end of the story.
GTA 6 Jason Voice Actor Speculation
Despite uttering a single word during the entire first GTA 6 trailer, Jason was linked to multiple voice actors. We hear a lot more of his VA in the second trailer, but there’s still no official confirmation on who his actor really is. As far as speculative guesses go, these four actors stand out for voicing Jason in GTA 6:
Gregory Connors
American actor Gregory Connors emerged as the most likely candidate behind Jason’s voice. The 37-year-old has appeared on TV Shows such as The Blacklist, The Good Fight, and FBI: Most Wanted, alongside some on-stage roles.
Rumors surrounding his involvement began after fans online discovered a ‘Lead’ voice-over role for Rockstar Games on his resume. Furthermore, his CV has no media credits in 2023, which aligns with Rockstar’s potential voice-over timeline. Of course, this is just speculation at the moment, and the actor himself has yet to comment on these rumors.
Troy Baker
Troy Baker is a well-established voice actor credited with iconic roles such as Joel from The Last of Us and Sam Drake from Uncharted 4. Fans linked the actor to Jason purely out of speculation, but he was quick to shoot down those claims in an interview.
Bryan Zampella
Actor Bryan Zampella was linked to Jason shortly after the emergence of the 2022 leaks. He went on to lean into these rumors by posting images of himself cosplaying as the character, gray tank top and all.
He is also connected to Rockstar employees on social media, which stoked the fire even more. Without an official confirmation, it’s hard to deduce if the New York City native is actually involved in the game or if he’s taking fans for a ride.
Dylan Rourke
One of the more recent names associated with Jason is Dylan Rourke, after his name appeared on an IMDb listing connected to the Grand Theft Auto 6 Extended Look. Since the IMDb credits can be edited by users, the listing doesn’t establish any real proof that Rourke is the one who actually voices Jason.
The Extended Look also sparked new discussions about the character’s voice direction, as some players don’t like Jason’s deep voice. The voice is described as difficult to understand and overly monotone. However, it might have something to do with his army background and his introverted personality.
That is pretty much everything we know about who Jason is in GTA 6 so far. We’ll be sure to update this article as we learn more about the character. Until then, let us know in the comments if you have your own voice actor theories for Jason.

Constellation Energy – America’s largest operator of nuclear power plants – does not share Wall Street’s concerns that the Democrats will slow down data center development. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Joe Dominguez was, for lack of a better word, unbothered as he addressed the blue wave.
Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers
They may have a point.
They may have a point.
“I do think we’ve seen a bit of an overreaction in the market to the election results based upon fear that Democrats won’t let data centers get built,” Dominguez said.
Many of the Democrats who seized control of the House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections ran on anti-data-center campaigns, which triggered a historic $2.5 trillion sell-off in AI-adjacent stocks that reached well beyond tech to the energy, construction, and materials sectors.
Up until a few years ago, many of Constellation’s nuclear power plants were in severe financial distress and in danger of shutting down early. But the data center development boom and its enormous demand for electricity have dramatically reversed the nuclear industry’s fate.
Now, Constellation and other companies like it are signing major deals with Big Tech companies to provide power to data centers. Microsoft, for instance, signed a deal with Constellation to fund the revival of a nuclear plant at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania. (Three Mile Island is the site of what the Nuclear Regulatory Commission refers to as the “most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power plant operating history.”)
Constellation also signed major contracts in the third quarter to provide power to Amazon and Google data centers, Dominguez said.
Nuclear energy has had bipartisan support for years. The US Department of Energy classifies nuclear as a “clean” energy source because the act of operating a nuclear reactor does not directly produce carbon emissions. This makes nuclear an appealing investment to Big Tech companies that have to balance aggressive data center development with the ambitious climate goals they set long before the AI race took off. Still, nuclear energy has its issues. One of the biggest is nuclear waste, which the US government has not figured out how to dispose of at scale.
Big Nuclear and Big Tech also tout these deals as good for the economy and job creation.
“The market scare that people got last week was not lost on Democrats,” Dominguez said on the call. “They do not want to be the reason that the economy takes a nosedive by halting data center development.”
Of course, Constellation’s future is essentially staked on the data center buildout, and Dominguez’s job is to convince investors they have nothing to worry about.
In this instance, however, Dominguez really does seem genuinely unconcerned by the new Democratic majority in the federal government. It could be that he understands that, yes, while the Democrats won the midterms on promises of data center regulation and the blue wave included many new Democratic governors, data centers aren’t necessarily a strictly partisan issue. Some Democrats have opposed harsh measures like moratoriums — though on the flip slide, Constellation may also have to deal with challenges from the other side of the aisle.
In Virginia, some of the state lawmakers who have been the most vocal about data centers are actually Republican. Virginia Sen. Richard Stuart, a conservative Republican, has aggressively pursued data center regulation. Last month, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, denied Stuart’s request for a special session to address a concerning new report from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality on the state’s groundwater supply, which has become strained amid rampant data center growth.
For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
The fight against data centers so far has been highly fragmented and hyperlocal, but that could change soon. The Trump administration loves data centers, and the federal government is working on wresting some control over data center development away from the states. But even then, Democrats and Republicans at the federal level tend to view data centers as an inevitable part of the future that needs some guardrails rather than out-of-control corporate growth infringing on the average American’s quality of life.
Just look at the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which was co-sponsored by two Democrats. The Senate is expected to vote on a passage of a sweeping bill which is being marketed as a way to speed up the permitting process for new power plants and transmission lines and connect new data centers to the grid faster. New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, one of the Democrats backing the bill, has touted its inclusion of provisions designed to protect utility customers from rising rates due to data centers, ensuring Big Tech pays its fair share of costs. Researchers at Columbia University SIPA’s Center on Global Energy Policy called the bill’s protections “mixed,” noting they do not account for wholesale capacity and energy prices, a “principal way” data center electricity demand can lead to higher household bills.
Senate Democrats are sharply divided on the bill, which critics say will fast-track data center projects at the expense of public input and environmental oversight and lead to a massive overbuild of energy projects that Americans will end up paying for.
On Constellation’s earnings call, Dominguez pointed out that Virginia and Illinois, states with Democratic governors already in place before the election, have seen “a great deal of data center development.”
“The bottom line is that Democrats care deeply about economic growth and they care very deeply about the many labor jobs that go with data center construction,” Dominguez said. “With labor such a key constituent for Democrats, it’s hard to imagine that we are going to halt work …There might be some differences and certainly there are going to be some local areas, I think, that are not going to want data centers.”
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns. He also has a good point. Grassroots efforts to stop local data center development have been successful and have contributed to broader opposition to data center development across the country. But data center developers can also abandon projects and go elsewhere. Until a few years ago, data centers were largely concentrated in Northern Virginia, but with the AI boom, developers have fanned out across the country in search of available power and land. A total of 38 states have welcomed them with open arms and generous tax breaks, per the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns.
Thanks to the convoluted way the US electric grid and energy markets work, Constellation’s power plants don’t even need to be located in the same state as their data center customers — the plant supplying the power just needs to be connected to the same region from which the grid is drawing power. The purchase agreement, in that sense, is symbolic: Because the data center needs more electricity than it can draw from the local grid without causing disruptions for everyone else, the data center pays for independent power providers like Constellation to supply the grid with extra electricity.
That’s why data centers and the enormous amount of electricity Big Tech says it needs to power them have been such a boon for the nuclear industry. For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
Nuclear lobbyists will tell you that’s because the NRC’s safety regulations are overly restrictive and lead to untenable upfront capital costs that make projects impossible to finance. (This has been an industry talking point since 1979, after the NRC seriously overhauled its safety standards following the partial meltdown at Three Mile Island. That site is now owned by Constellation, which has signed a 20-year deal with Microsoft.)
Both the Biden and Trump administrations have worked to support the development of nuclear power in the US by passing developer tax credits. The Trump administration has gone even further, pushing for a sweeping reform of the NRC that would make it much easier for new reactors to obtain operating licenses.
And the Department of Energy this month approved a $5 billion loan to Constellation, which the company will use to upgrade its existing nuclear fleet. Another nuclear energy company, Vistra, received a $4.2 billion loan.
It’s not totally unlike the Biden administration’s passage of the Civil Nuclear Credit Program in 2022, which planned to loan $6 billion to struggling nuclear companies in the US.
That’s not lost on Dominguez.
“Interestingly, in many respects the election had the Republicans saying a lot of the same things that the Democrats were saying,” Dominguez told investors on the call. “And I believe that the policy solutions are going to be somewhat similar.”

The Pan American Health Organization has revoked the United States’ measles-elimination status after 26 years, because the country did not halt continuous transmission of the highly contagious virus for more than a year, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday (November 13, 2026).
The international health body did not immediately respond to a request from Reuters for comment on the report, which cited people familiar with the matter.
The reported decision by the Americas branch of the World Health Organization comes as the U.S. battles the highest number of measles cases it has seen in more than three decades.
Some 7,500 people in the U.S. have been infected with measles and 13 have died since 2025. That period coincides with falling immunization rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines.
As part of its evaluation, PAHO reviewed epidemiological and laboratory evidence to determine whether the same strain of measles had been circulating in the United States uninterrupted for 12 months or longer, a sign of local transmission rather than imported cases.
As of Thursday (November 12, 2026), 5,182 confirmed cases of measles had been reported in 2026 to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from 45 States, New York City and the District of Columbia, surpassing last year’s total of 2,289, making it one of the country’s worst measles resurgences in decades.
The U.S. achieved its measles-elimination status in 2000. A country can halt transmission when 95% of its population is vaccinated, creating so-called herd immunity that also protects those unable to receive the vaccine.
Two doses of the measles vaccine — by far the best way to prevent infection and transmission — provide 97% protection against the virus, which can cause blindness, deafness, brain damage or death.

Guatemala ramps up security operations following declaration of state of siege
Guatemala's interior and defense ministers have inspected security operations in two departments bordering Honduras
GUATEMALA CITY -- GUATEMALA CITY (AP) — Guatemala’s interior and defense ministers on Monday inspected security operations in two departments bordering Honduras, days after President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency to curb drug-related violence in the Central American country.
The decree, announced on Saturday, suspends for 30 days several constitutional rights, including freedom of movement and assembly, and allows security forces to disperse groups by force, make arrests and enter homes without warrants.
Interior Minister Marco Antonio Villeda said Monday that the emergency measure also targets groups allegedly linked to drug trafficking that are involved in illegal jade and gold mining in the region.
“We are carrying out a series of coordinated and planned actions with the Defense Ministry and the public prosecutor’s office. We have a plan that we will execute over 30 days,” Villeda said.
Defense Minister Henry Sáenz said authorities are “establishing territorial control through checkpoints on routes and patrols along roads bordering Honduras."
This area in the eastern part of Guatemala has been the scene of a wave of violence over the past three months.
On Sept. 27, an armed attack left eight people dead in the municipality of Huité, in the department of Zacapa.
Initially, the army claimed the attack involved clashes between organized crime groups; however, days later, it announced that 107 military personnel had been placed at the disposal of the authorities to determine their potential involvement in the massacre, which claimed the lives of three women, including a young girl.
The prosecutor’s office is investigating whether the army’s actions were linked to the detention of suspected drug traffickers.
Separately, on Nov. 7, Congressman Julio César Portillo Paz and three members of the National Civil Police — who were part of his security detail — were gunned down by armed men in broad daylight in the municipality of Río Hondo, also in Zacapa.
Early on Friday morning, five people were killed in the same department. According to preliminary investigations, armed men arrived in several vehicles at a small village and abducted a man, whose whereabouts remain unknown. They then killed his mother, two brothers and two friends at the scene.
Also on Friday, the U.S. State Department designated three local drug-trafficking groups as terrorist organizations for financing violence and crime in the region. Among those designated are two family clans — Los Lorenzanas and Los Mendoza — which, according to authorities, maintain deep ties to Mexican drug cartels and operate within the area.

When medical student Emmanuel Oyebadejo went to watch his friend's American football game, he had no idea he would end up being scouted himself for a sport he had never even played.
He wasn't even interested in it. In fact, while still at school in Manchester he'd delivered a speech titled 'I have a dream' in which he outlined plans to do "very well in basketball, return from the NBA and be the prime minister of the United Kingdom".
But now, four years later, he is being tipped to become the first Briton to be a first-round pick in the NFL Draft.
It is a rapid rise for the 22-year-old, who had to learn the game from scratch and win over his parents who "begged" him not to play and instead focus on his medical studies.
His biggest challenge at the start, though, was finding a pair of boots big enough for his size 16 feet.
It was 6ft 6in Oyebadejo's physique that had caught the eye of the coaching staff at Exeter Demons when he was a spectator for his friend's university game that was taking place at the club's home ground, The Crumb.
"I was talking to one of the other coaches, Jack Mullins, and we sort of turned around [and thought] 'that guy's freaking huge! We should go talk to him'," Lydon Ward-Best, one of the Demons' coaches, tells BBC Sport.
Oyebadejo had been a talented basketball player, playing for Manchester Magic - one of England's top junior clubs - from the age of 11 to 18. But by the time he was at the University of Exeter he was no longer playing competitively.
Lydon Ward-Best persuaded him to give a new sport a go.
"He started coming to training and just had the most ridiculous intro to American football I think I've ever seen," the coach adds.
A straight-A pupil, who had also learned the piano, guitar and drums while studying medicine, Oyebadejo had always been a quick learner.
"I always say that American football is kind of like violent chess," says Mullins, the Demons' current head coach.
"[Emmanuel] got the violent bit pretty quickly. He was fine at that - 'I am much bigger than you, watch me go'.
"The chess bit took a little longer because there's all these things that you have to think about."
But as Ward-Best puts it, "he's not just a big sort of jock athlete, he's a smart guy. He is so dedicated and disciplined with everything."
Oyebadejo played for the Demons at the end of the 2022-23 season, before the team went unbeaten in his first full season, 2023-24. When back home he also played for the Manchester Titans and helped them win the Britbowl in September 2023.
By December 2023, he decided he wanted to take things further. Could he make it in the United States? Would college teams be interested if he sent them videos of his highlights?
Coach Ward-Best told Oyebadejo it would be "tough", adding: "You know the percentages are not on your side here, but you are 6ft 6in and 280 pounds (20 stone), so you've got a better chance than most.
"I wanted to be realistic with him," he adds. "But I said I'd do whatever I could to help get him out there."
Emmanuel's father Oladini says he thought it was a "joke" and that he did not support him playing this "dangerous" game, explaining: "He had never played this game before. He'd only done it for a few months, so why would anybody from America want him?"
But they did.
There was interest from several colleges and Oyebadejo ended up at Jacksonville State, where he would study biology and play under legendary college coach Rich Rodriguez, having managed to win his parents round thanks to the influence of an uncle who lived in Dallas and understood the sport.
His first season was hit by injury but, despite coming up against players who have played American football since they were young children, his second was a big success.
As a defensive end, Oyebadejo's job is to get past the offensive linemen trying to block him and tackle the ball carrier or claim a sack - when a defensive player tackles the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage.
He recorded 4.5 sacks, forced two fumbles and had 41 total tackles during the 2025 season.
Now the big college teams were paying attention.
College football is America's most passionate sporting pastime. While the NFL plays on Sundays, the college game dominates Saturdays during the autumn months.
And Oyebadejo transferred to the University of Florida to play for one of college football's biggest teams in the most prestigious conference, the Southeastern (SEC).
The Florida Gators are three-time national champions, have about 50 former players currently in the NFL and get home crowds of 90,000 at 'The Swamp'.
Oyebadejo was undaunted as he burst on to the scene. He had 2.5 sacks in a win at rivals Auburn in September and followed that up by impressing in big wins over Mississippi and Texas, the latter in front of 103,989 people.
After barely being on the radar of NFL scouts at the start of the season, Oyebadejo's form has propelled him into contention to be an early-round draft pick in 2027.
NFL teams do not have youth systems or academies. Almost all players have come through the US college system and they are recruited via the NFL Draft when they graduate.
One of the biggest events in the American sporting calendar, the NFL Draft takes place over three days in April, with the 32 teams taking turns to select players across seven rounds.
First-round picks in April will be guaranteed a rookie contract of at least $19.1m (£14.4m) and they are often fast-tracked into starting roles. The contract values decrease in a sliding scale so, for example, a third-round pick (top 96) will be guaranteed $7.3m (£5.5m).
Among the latest prospects, ESPN's veteran draft analyst Mel Kiper has ranked Oyebadejo as the fifth-best edge rusher (defensive end). That is regarded as the sport's second-most important position behind quarterback - and therefore the second-best paid in the NFL.
The reason is that Oyebadejo has everything needed to be a starting defensive end in the NFL. Firstly, his height and weight are ideally suited for the grappling battle required in what is known as 'the trenches'.
He has very long arms (7ft wingspan), perfect for winning a wrestling match against the kind of enormous opponent he faces, and unusually for a man as big as him, he's extremely quick. That's the money-making trait.
Although he now weighs about 300lbs (more than 21 stone), it is believed he has a remarkable body-fat percentage of about 12%. All his measurables are seen as ideal for a defensive end, if not better.
There are simply very few people with Oyebadejo's physical talent, and given the fast-tracked nature of his rise in American football, he does not look as raw as you might expect.
"He's British and has only played the sport for three [full] seasons," says his mentor and former coach Ward-Best. "You'd therefore think he must be very green, but he doesn't look that way.
"The physical qualities are clearly there but he's worked a lot on mastering aspects of the position as well."
Menelik Watson, also from Manchester, holds the record for being the highest-drafted British player. He was the 42nd pick in 2013 and spent six years in the NFL, earning a total of $16.4m (£13.7m).
London-born Osi Umenyiora, the 56th pick in 2003, enjoyed an illustrious 12-year career - winning two Super Bowls with the New York Giants.
"I have spoken to Osi, he's a really cool guy," says Oyebadejo, who is also of Nigerian heritage.
"To be a first-round pick out of the UK, it would be amazing. It would do so much for the American football community back home."
Oyebadejo impressed again in an upset win at Kentucky on Saturday and has 4.5 sacks with two regular-season games left. Florida could then play in a 'bowl' game, an end-of-season exhibition.
After that, Oyebadejo is expected to participate in a physical-testing event called the 'scouting combine', where he will be assessed by representatives of all 32 teams in March.
The draft then begins in Washington DC on 27 April, and if Oyebadejo hears his name called, he will complete an unlikely journey and make his now fully supportive parents very proud.
"It's mad," says Ward-Best. "I've been doing this for 20 years and I've never seen anything like this. We almost have to pinch ourselves."
Oyebadejo has stayed in touch with his former coaches in Exeter. The Demons hold watch parties for Florida games and there is a real sense of pride over where his journey began.
"It was just complete chance that he wanted to wander up to The Crumb and watch a game, just being there for his mate," says coach Mullins.
"If those things didn't happen, we wouldn't be having this conversation. He would be four years into his medical degree."

I usually can’t pinpoint the moment I stop using a software feature, with most tools drifting out of fashion without an expiration date. That’s not the case with YouTube Music’s “Beyond the Beat,” an AI-generated DJ that explains songs to you.
YouTube Music is my music-streaming service of choice. And since I’m a software reporter, I always enable the beta features available through YouTube Labs, which include Beyond the Beat. YouTube’s AI DJ randomly interjects for about 30 seconds between songs, teeing up the vibe shift and providing context about the next track.
More listeners are encountering synthetic commentary built into their music streaming apps. While YouTube launched this experimental AI DJ in 2025, Spotify first introduced a similar tool back in 2023. It doubled down on its AI DJ efforts in November, expanding the different personalities available to users and adding more controls over the commentary.
These AI DJs aren’t just annoying. Their attempts to provide helpful context and mimic human candor ultimately fall flat. Lucky for me, both features are optional and avoidable.
After months of leaving it enabled, a bad experience with Beyond the Beat this week pushed me to swear off AI DJs altogether. I was listening to a pop divas playlist as part of my morning workout and got slapped with 30 seconds of exposition after a Slayyyter track:
“Hey Boy delivers that high-energy surge perfectly, but we're shifting our focus to a sharper, more visceral reality. In Rock Music, Charli XXC [sic] weaves in a biting, dark sense of humor regarding the physical toll of her relentless 2024 and 2025 touring. She turns the genuine nerve damage she sustained on the road into a strange sort of battle scar, reclaiming the exhaustion of a weary party girl as a badge of honor. It's an unflinching look at the cost behind the spectacle, where the grind of the industry becomes the actual subject matter. Here is Rock Music by Charli XXC [sic].”
What a lengthy paragraph of platitudes with little substance. That’s not even mentioning how the AI DJ butchered the pronunciation of a little-known, indie act called Charli XCX. This flub reflected my overall experience with YouTube Music’s AI DJ. It took me out of the groove and didn’t feel additive.
In another example, it went in-depth on the meaning of Olivia Rodrigo’s Expectations remix featuring Chappell Roan, calling it a "structural interpretation” that unpacks the “nuances of queer dating.” Then YouTube Music played the original track, sans Roan; so much for the queer yearning.
Curious how Spotify’s AI DJ experience would compare, I upgraded my account to the premium tier for access to that beta software. One of the biggest recent changes to Spotify’s AI DJ was adding new voices to the lineup, so I went into my settings and played the introduction clips for each of the eight English-language voices.
Maybe I was already a bit miffed from my YouTube Music experience because these voices immediately started to frustrate me. Multiple voices leaned into filler words such as “you know” and “like,” as the AI described the next songs it would play. Knowing an AI voice is being trained to use filler words to sound more human gave me the uncanny-valley ick.
Spotify’s AI DJ was fairly different from YouTube Music’s version. On Spotify, the AI DJ is also an algorithmically guided experience that picks songs for you based on past listening habits and song requests. Overall, Spotify’s synthetic commentary felt tighter and more tolerable than YouTube’s blabbering DJ. That said, neither software experience was enjoyable enough for me to return.
Although Spotify claims it has “80 percent of listeners coming back to DJ week after week,” according to the company’s launch blog, I won’t be one of them. My rejection of AI DJs isn’t based on how they audibly sound. The voices, from both companies, are decent and sound convincingly human. The content of their commentary is what truly turns me off. Whether it’s empty platitudes or mimicking human mistakes, I’ve heard enough.

Researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology-Kanpur have identified a molecular pathway through which immune cells in the pancreas can rapidly suppress insulin release, opening up a potential new avenue for developing therapies to protect insulin production in people with obesity and Type-2 diabetes.
The findings, published in ‘Journal of Clinical Investigation’, show that immune cells called macrophages can switch off insulin secretion by neighbouring beta cells within minutes, rather than gradually damaging them through inflammation over months or years, according to a note issued by IIT-Kanpur on Thursday.
Simran Singh and Ashish Kumar led the study as co-first authors under the supervision of Sai Prasad Pydi, assistant professor, department of biological sciences and bioengineering, IIT-Kanpur.
“We discovered that immune cells that are present next to beta cells can switch off insulin release within minutes,” Pydi said.
The researchers found that the process involves sphingolipids, a class of fats released by macrophages, rather than the inflammatory proteins traditionally associated with obesity-related pancreatic damage.
The team traced the trigger to GPR18, a receptor on macrophages. Once activated, it prompts the immune cells to release sphingolipids, which are taken up by neighbouring beta cells through a surface transporter, and interfere with their insulin-producing machinery.
Using a precision genetic technique, the researchers found that activating this pathway reduced insulin secretion in mouse models, while switching it off improved insulin release. Blocking GPR18 or other steps in the pathway also restored insulin secretion.
The team, working with the Indiana Biosciences Research Institute in the US, confirmed that the same pathway was present and active in human pancreatic tissue.
Activating it in donated human tissue also suppressed insulin secretion, according to the communique.
While the study does not offer an immediate treatment for diabetes, the findings establish a potential target for developing drugs to preserve insulin production in people with obesity and Type-2 diabetes, it said.

Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
- Published
Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment.
"People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC.
After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter.
"Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion.
Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next."
Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.
But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force.
Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements.
Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority.
Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat.
"The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage."
Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says.
Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost.
Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC.
He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy."
The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability.
It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored.
Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes.
Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days.
"We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active.
Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents.
The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives.
As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds.
Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded.
Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC.
Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations.
However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael.
Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. "The TPLF may continue a low-level insurgency and guerrilla campaign, but that is not war. I do not think there will be a wider-scale conflict between the federal forces and the TPLF."
He says the TPLF no longer possesses the size, strength or military capability required to effectively confront federal forces, which he says have significantly expanded and modernised in recent years. "The TPLF has also lost much of its public support and cannot easily rebuild its ranks through recruitment," he says.
Yared, on the other hand, points to the TPLF's history of overcoming setbacks as evidence that the movement could recover to sustain a prolonged struggle. "The TPLF has overcome many major challenges in the past. It is wrong to conclude that it has no public support. It is a political movement with a history stretching back more than 50 years," he says.
What Yared sees as a strength, Hudson sees as a weakness, saying the TPLF is still "trapped in the past", and continues to behave as a dominant party within Tigray, even though the situation has changed. "It is a movement that has not evolved, modernised or expanded."
While Hudson argues that the TPLF is not equipped to sustain a major military campaign, the TPLF spokesman says the group obtains weapons and logistical supplies from the Ethiopian military. "We seize weapons from our enemy, and the weaponry that has entered Tigray will, sooner or later, become ours."
In early October, eyewitnesses told the BBC they had seen Eritrean troops in Tigray amid reports they were backing the TPLF. However, they appear to have returned home and Hudson thinks the country would be wary of becoming further embroiled in the conflict.
"First, Eritrea does not have unlimited resources. Second, the TPLF is no more an effective military force, and Eritrean leaders may have concluded that supporting it at this stage would not yield significant military gains," he says. "Third, Eritrea would have to consider the risk of provoking a confrontation with Ethiopia if it openly backs the TPLF."
Sources in the Ethiopia army tell the BBC that senior members of the TPLF's political leadership were briefly based in Eritrea, however, they say the authorities ordered them to leave in early November, shortly after President Isaias Afwerki returned from Russia. According to the sources, the move was driven by concerns that Ethiopia could use their presence as a reason to invade.
Hudson also argues that Eritrea's renewed diplomatic engagement with the US, whose relations with the TPLF have long been strained, could further discourage Asmara from providing meaningful support to the movement.
In September, seven Ethiopian rebel groups led by the TPLF announced the formation of a new coalition called the Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.
Yared believes the alliance could give the TPLF the strength to keep on fighting. "Its members can combine their strengths. The TDF [the TPLF's military wing] has leadership experience and organisational capacity, while Fano [an ethnic Amhara militia] is believed to have between 70,000 and 80,000 fighters.
"If conditions emerge that allow the forces to co-ordinate effectively, the TPLF's current difficulties may not last long," he says.
Hudson, however, rejects that argument, insisting that the alliance is unlikely to alter the balance of power. "I don't think the TPLF can be saved by this alliance. The ethnic militias have not demonstrated the capacity, either individually or collectively, to pose a serious threat to federal forces. We should not underestimate the strength of the federal army," he says.
Abraha from Mekelle University argues that the conflict in Tigray will only truly be over if the federal government addresses the region's feeling that it has been marginalised, both economically and politically by the current government.
However, many Tigrayan elites and political observers remain wary of the federal government's intentions. They question whether the authorities in Addis Ababa are genuinely seeking to address Tigray's problems, or whether they are taking advantage of the region's weakness to boost their influence.
In the meantime, many ordinary people in Tigray say their priority is peace.
"Peace seems slow in coming. Most people are tired of politics. Whatever happens, we only want peace and a chance to rebuild our lives," says Firut from her beauty salon in Mekelle.

A video purportedly showing Union Home Minister Amit Shah saying in the Lok Sabha that the government is more concerned about elections than the situation in Manipur is going viral on social media (here, here, and here). Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Union Home Minister Amit Shah saying in the Lok Sabha that the government is more concerned about elections than the situation in Manipur.
Fact: The video is from a Lok Sabha discussion on the Delhi Services Bill in August 2023. Amit Shah’s remarks about the government being more concerned about elections than Manipur were made sarcastically while criticising the opposition and accusing it of prioritising its political interests over democracy and the welfare of the nation. He was not expressing his own views or stating the BJP’s position. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a video uploaded to Sansad TV’s YouTube channel on 03 August 2023. In this video, Amit Shah is seen wearing the same outfit and speaking against the same background as in the viral video. According to the description, Union Home Minister Amit Shah was responding to a discussion on the National Capital Territory of Delhi (Amendment) Bill, 2023, in the Lok Sabha. During the discussion, he also criticised the opposition.
At the 12:26-minute mark in the original video, Amit Shah can be heard making the same remarks as those in the viral clip. However, a careful viewing of the full video shows he wasn’t expressing his own views or explaining the BJP’s position. Instead, he was sarcastically quoting what he alleged to be the opposition’s priorities.
Amit Shah made these remarks to taunt the opposition. At the 12:28-minute mark, he says, “We’re not concerned about Manipur, we’re concerned about elections. We’re not concerned about democracy, we’re concerned about elections. Our party has no principles; we’re in politics solely to win elections.“
Before making these remarks, Shah was seen criticising the opposition over its response to the Manipur situation. In this context, he was accusing the opposition alliance of prioritising its political interests and the survival of its coalition over democracy and the welfare of the nation. Thus, the viral video omits the context in which he made these remarks, making it appear as though he was expressing his own views or stating the BJP’s position.
We also found multiple media reports (here, here) published in 2023, stating that the Delhi Services Bill was passed in the Lok Sabha on 03 August 2023. During the discussion, Home Minister Amit Shah launched a verbal attack on the opposition parties. The reports also stated that the bill was passed by a voice vote after opposition MPs staged a walkout.
To sum up, a video of Amit Shah criticising the opposition over Manipur is shared out of context as his own remarks on the BJP’s priorities.

United Halts Flights as It Addresses ‘Widespread System Outage’
The disruption, after a nationwide ground stop last week, added to concerns about air travel ahead of a busy Thanksgiving travel period.
United Airlines reported a “widespread system outage” on Monday, grounding planes and stranding passengers even as the nation’s aviation system was recovering from the ground stoppage that paralyzed air traffic late last week.
The airline said in statement that it was “troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights.” There was “no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” it said, referring to its regional network.
In a separate statement on social media, United said that “our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible.”
United did not immediately provide additional details about the outage, which was reported as federal officials were trying to get to the bottom of the nationwide ground stop that halted all air travel nationwide for hours on Friday.
It also comes ahead of the busy Thanksgiving travel period.
Airlines sometimes experience short-lived technical disruptions and can recover quickly if the problem is swiftly addressed. But a lengthy outage can become destabilizing as pilots and flight attendants reach legal working limits and delays and cancellations ripple throughout a carrier’s network.
This is a developing story.
Niraj Chokshi and Ryley Ober contributed reporting.

CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team) has now flagged new security flaws in eMudhra's digital signature utility unit, emBridge, weeks after the cybersecurity firm faced a major cybersecurity incident. On November 13, the national nodal agency for cyber security incident response, issued a vulnerability note on emBridge, highlighting that the software could potentially allow unauthorised entities on the same local area network (LAN) to access files and directory names on an impacted device. The agency classified this threat as a ‘low-severity’ cybersecurity flaw. The issue came into picture after cybersecurity expert Karan Saini reported the vulnerability to CERT-In. What Is the emBridge Flaw? Web browsers cannot talk directly to the USB tokens that hold a user's digital signature certificate (DSC). emBridge bridges that gap. It is a client-side application that allows web portals to communicate with DSC and hardware tokens installed on a user's computer. According to CERT-In, a set of file-browsing functions inside this interface did not check whether the request came from an authorised source. These functions run with the highest system privileges on Windows. An attacker on the same local network could use a malicious webpage to send requests to emBridge and map out the file and folder names on the targeted machine. The affected versions are 5.9.1.x to 5.9.3.x on Windows, 3.2.4.x to 3.2.6.x on macOS, and 3.2.0.x to 3.3.0.x on Ubuntu and Red Hat Linux. CERT-In asked users to upgrade to version 5.9.4.x or later on Windows, 3.2.7.x or later on macOS, and 3.3.1.x or later on Linux. Several government portals rely on emBridge for DSC-based signing, including the Ministry of Corporate Affairs’ MCA V3 portal, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) and the National Single Window System. The Income Tax Department also recommends it for managing DSCs. However, the agency said that the flaw does not give access to the contents of files, does not allow files to be changed or deleted, does not allow code to run, and does not expose cryptographic keys or token PINs. eMudhra published its own advisory on the CVE and said it fixed the issue on November 11, two days before CERT-In's note, by removing the file-browsing functions from emBridge altogether. "With these endpoints removed, the file enumeration capability is no longer available through emBridge," the company said. eMudhra rated the flaw's impact and risk as low. According to its advisory, an attacker could at most see the names of drives, files and folders on a user's computer. File contents, cryptographic keys, token PINs, and signing operations were not exposed. An attack would also need several conditions at once: an affected emBridge version, a malicious webpage hosted on the same local network, the user opening it, and a browser without Local Network Access restrictions. The company added that its firewall and local-only request handling block direct access from other machines. Expert Saini, who had first uncovered the vulnerabilities, posted on X that while the bug was trivial, eMudhra’s own advisory has further downplayed it. eMudhra in its statement to Inc42 said that every digital signature certificate needs the user to enter the token PIN before it can be used, and pointed out that CERT-In’s note confirmed keys and token PINs had not been exposed. “Identifying and fixing vulnerabilities is a routine part of responsible software development,” a company spokesperson said, adding that large global vendors like Microsoft, Oracle, Google, and Adobe addressed thousands of vulnerabilities every month. The October Incident On October 17, a security researcher reported that the private keys behind eight of eMudhra's intermediate certificate authority certificates had been generated so weakly that they could be worked out from public data in under a second. eMudhra revoked the certificates on October 18, and browser makers moved to block them and distrust the root they chained to. The company traced the weak keys to a script error during an April 2025 key-generation ceremony. The fallout was swift. eMudhra said it would exit the global SSL/TLS certificate business, its shares fell sharply over two days, the Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY) set up a special team to probe the incident, and on October 30 the company appointed KPMG as an independent reviewer of the incident and its security controls.

The World
The U.S. economy hitched its wagon to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Now that he has stepped down, the company faces deep uncertainty.
A week ago, we learned the news that Jensen Huang, the rock star C.E.O. of the chip-making company Nvidia, had acknowledged an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy. It turns out that may have been just the beginning. Shortly after revelations of a second affair, this time with a subordinate, Huang resigned.
Nvidia’s stock has tumbled in the days since, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in value, and analysts have begun trying to process just how the downfall of one of the most important figures in the A.I. industry is going to play out. One Silicon Valley venture capitalist recently called him “irreplaceable.”
But why are Huang and Nvidia so irreplaceable — and is anything that cannot be replaced automatically vulnerable? Today I’m writing about power, vulnerability and choke points.
Why there’s only one Nvidia
Last week, as it became clear that Jensen Huang’s future at Nvidia might be in jeopardy, a meme began making the rounds on the internet. It showed a complicated, multitiered structure, delicately balanced on a tiny block. The structure was labeled “entire global economy”; the block was labeled “Jensen Huang’s wife.”
The meme is already outdated: Huang has resigned from his role as Nvidia’s C.E.O. (and it never made sense to put any of this on his wife). But the image still captured the idea that so much of the business world somehow came to depend on one man and his — now, it seems, questionable — judgment.

For book lovers, a library represents something much bigger than a room filled with shelves. It serves as a repository of knowledge, history and ideas, offering readers a space to explore, learn and discover. The Supreme Court's latest remarks on the shifting of nearly 8.5 lakh books from the Central Secretariat Library have renewed attention to the importance of preserving such collections. On Monday, the apex court adjourned the matter concerning the relocation of the 135-year-old Central Secretariat Library (CSL) until Friday. It also directed that the books housed in the library should not be shifted in the meantime, LiveLaw reported. Expressing concern over the manner in which the 8.5 lakh books were being handled, Justice Sanjay Kumar accused the Centre of adopting what appeared to be an ad hoc approach towards preserving the library's heritage. The apex court observed: "You are just in a hurry to get done with this. What are you planning to do with these books? There seems to be an ad hoc approach. You are not bothered about… this is some heritage. Basically, a heritage for us dating back to 1702. If you don't want them, give them to some other country that will value them...Show some respect to these books; two lakh books thrown to the wind." The hearing comes after the apex court took suo motu cognisance of the lack of space allotted to the CSL, which currently houses 8.5 lakh books, under the Central Vista plan. Earlier in October, the court sought an affidavit detailing the space allotted to the library and its layout. The apex court's intervention was sought on 3 October, after reports suggested that the library, currently located in Shastri Bhawan, could face relocation in view of the proposed demolition of the building as part of the redevelopment plan. Questions have emerged over whether an appropriate space can be provided for the 135-year-old library and how its vast collection will be safeguarded during the relocation. The Indian Express reported in October that the CSL, which is currently spread across four floors, was facing uncertainty as the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) had allotted only two rooms for it in the Kartavya Bhawan-2 complex under the redevelopment plan. The MoHUA had directed all ministries to vacate Shastri Bhawan by the end of September to pave the way for its demolition and redevelopment, the report added. When the matter came up for hearing, a two-judge bench comprising Justice Sanjay Kumar and Justice Sanjeev Sachdeva was informed that the Centre had filed an affidavit. Although the affidavit had not been placed on record, amicus curiae Senior Advocate Haripriya Padmanabhan told the court that efforts were being made to expedite the shifting of the books by November. She urged the court to put a stop to the move and sought greater clarity from the Centre on the space available at the proposed new location. "I would like them to give a breakup of how much is presently being used for bookshelves and compare it with how much is used in the new place," she told the court. Padmanabhan also raised concerns about some of the books kept at RK Puram. She said she had visited the site and found them in "atrocious condition". According to her, the books had remained in this state for the past 15 years and were part of the library's original collection. Her submissions prompted strong oral observations from the court. The apex court then questioned the Additional Solicitor General about the urgency of shifting the books and directed the Centre: "You will not shift the books then." The court passed an order stating: "ASG says the books will not be shifted until next hearing. Listed on 20th November. In the meanwhile, the affidavit came to be filed today shall be placed on record." A tiny, $900 wearable device being developed by an Indian billionaire entrepreneur and showcased by some of the country’s top sportspersons has sparked criticism from doctors who say its claims of tracking blood flow to the brain are exaggerated.
The Temple device is less than 1 inch (2.54 cm) wide and weighs under 2 grams (0.07 oz). It sticks to the side of the head between the forehead and the ear, or the temple area.
Promotional materials for the device, developed by Deepinder Goyal, say that its BrainFlow feature shows how well the brain is being supplied with blood in real time and its Entropy feature can detect how hard the body works to shed heat.
It can also measure thermal, immune, digestive, cognitive and emotional readings that help to transform how a person regulates their health, they say.
Priced at 85,000 rupees ($907), the device comes in six colours. India’s cricket captain Shubman Gill and Olympic medal-winning badminton player P.V. Sindhu have worn it.
Some well-known doctors in the country, however, are sceptical of the claims, saying the device’s capabilities are not backed by peer-reviewed research. In prime-time shows and on social media, they are calling for the device to come under the purview of medical regulators.
Prominent Indian hepatologist Cyriac Philips, known as “TheLiverDoc”, has been criticising the device on his X account with 328,000 followers, calling Temple “the biggest health scam”.
“People must be aware of wellness hacks such as wearables also, even though they are not marketed as health devices,” he told Reuters.
On one prime-time TV discussion, paediatrician and nephrologist Sanjeev Bagai called Temple a “gimmick”, saying it had “no formal approval or clearance”.
Goyal has hit back at the criticism from doctors, saying Temple is a “fitness tracker, and wellness device”, not a medical one.
Indian doctor Jason Philip wrote on X that assessing blood flow to the brain was not easy, and optical signals placed over the temple skin would only give data on the “superficial temporal artery” that supplies blood to the face and skin.
In a statement to Reuters, Temple said BrainFlow and Entropy were new metrics “with emerging science”, and that more research would follow, adding that some metrics would eventually need regulatory approval.
India’s health ministry did not respond to Reuters queries, and the government has so far not reacted to the public debate.
The debate on Temple comes as wearable makers overseas also face questions on when a fitness feature becomes a medical one.
Some Apple Watch features, such as hypertension notifications, have received US Food and Drug Administration clearance as software-based medical features. Last year, the US FDA warned Whoop, saying its wrist-worn fitness tracker’s blood-pressure feature looked like a medical one — a view the company disputes.
Goyal is best known for co-founding Eternal, which houses India’s biggest listed food-delivery company Zomato and has a market value of about $35 billion. The 43-year-old stepped down as chief executive of Eternal this year to focus on Temple.
Temple, which has professors from the University of Ottawa and Harvard on its advisory board, raised $54 million in February at a valuation of about $190 million.
Goyal said Temple has received orders from more than 62 countries since November 1.
On its website, Temple says it is also working on detecting conditions including snoring and jaw clenching.
