Quick Answer
You can run AI models locally on Android and iPhone using Google AI Edge Gallery or PocketPal AI, and on Mac and Windows using LM Studio or Ollama. Simply install the app, download a compatible AI model, and start using it offline. Your data stays on your device, with no cloud access required after setup.
While many think AI is a bubble that is going to burst one day, it might be true, or it might not be at all. Only time will tell. But we should all accept that AI is fundamentally changing how we interact with our devices and do work.
For me, my life revolves around AI: I hand off some of my work to it and do things that once weren’t possible.
AI models are rapidly evolving. If you don’t know what an AI model is, it powers the apps and interfaces you interact with. For instance, the ChatGPT app uses GPT models, and the Claude app is powered by Claude models, which run behind the scenes.
While AI is fundamentally changing how we interact with devices and making work easier, handing your sensitive data to it has remained a major privacy concern.But thanks to rapid AI model development, many capable, powerful AI models enough to run locally on your device, without your data leaving your device
Companies like Google and Meta offer free AI models that can run locally on most consumer devices, including your mobile phone. Apps like Google’s AI Edge Gallery and PocketPal AI also make it easy to discover and run AI models locally without technical expertise.
If you have a capable computer with decent RAM, you can also run AI models locally to use them for writing your email, summarising PDFs, data analysis, coding, using their vision capabilities, and much more.
However, setting up an AI model locally involves downloading the app, choosing the model yourself, and understanding its capabilities first.
To help you out, I have created this detailed, comprehensive guide to set up and run local AI models on your device on Android, iPhone, Mac, or even on Windows.
I wrote this guide with beginners in mind, so every step is comprehensive and easy to follow. If you have questions, comment below. I am happy to help you. Most of these models can run locally on many consumer applications, but before that, don’t forget to check our prerequisites because that’s where your journey starts.
Table of Contents
Pre-Requirements To Run AI Models Locally on Device
Your device’s RAM determines whether it can run AI models.
Technically, a model loads into your RAM to run. As a general rule of thumb, a model needs about as much free RAM as its download size.
So, more RAM leaves room to run large AI models. A minimum of 6 GB of RAM is required to run decent, capable AI models locally on your device
Similarly, you need enough storage to download and store models locally. A model can generally range from 2 GB to 20 GB or even more, depending on its size and capabilities.
Finally, you need an internet connection and enough data to download the model so you can run it offline.
As I said before, these models can range from 2 GB to 20 GB. So it requires an internet connection to download the model and store it locally on your device.
Of course, Other minimum specifications, such as a capable Processor, Operating system, and platform, also matter but not as much as RAM does.
How to check how much RAM your device has
On Android:
Go to About Device to see how much RAM your smartphone has. To do that: Open Settings on your device, tap on the search bar at the top, and search for “About Device”. On some phones, scroll down and tap “About Device”. Look at the RAM specifications.
On some phones, you will see extra visible RAM after the plus sign, for example, 16GB + 12GB. However, only the first number is the real memory.
iPhone:
Apple generally doesn’t disclose the RAM used in iPhones. However, iPhone 15 Pro and newer devices generally have at least 8GB, while older iPhones have less than 6GB, which can run 1 billion to 2 billion models. You can check how much RAM your iPhone has from here.
Mac:
To check how much RAM on your MacBook: From the home screen, click on the Apple icon in the top left corner screen and tap on About This Mac. From here, you can check chip and memory options. Apple MacBooks running on Apple Silicon are especially good for running local AI models since the graphics chip shares all the memory.
Windows:
On Windows, you can go to Settings > System > About. From there, check the installed RAM, graphics card, and system type (x86 or ARM-based), which determines which applications you can download to run AI models locally.
Once your device meets the minimum RAM requirement, follow these steps to set it up to run AI models locally. Use the table of contents above to go to the device you want to set up. This guide covers Android, iPhone, Mac, and Windows.
How to Run AI Models Locally on Any Device
Android:
Method 1: Run Gemma 4 on Android with Google AI Edge Gallery
You can run Google’s family of Open-weight AI models locally for free on your Android device using Google’s own AI Edge Gallery app (Free).
Gemma 4 is Google’s latest open-weight model. It comes in five model sizes. Gemma 4 E2B and Gemma 4 E4B are suitable for running on Android devices. 2B requires at least 8GB of RAM, and 4B requires at least 12GB of RAM.
Gemma 4 also supports vision capabilities, so it is not just text; you can also use it to understand images.
How to install and run the latest Google Gemma 4 models locally on your Android phone
Step 1: Download Google AI Edge Gallery from the Play Store. Here is the direct download link.
Step 2: Open the app and tap on AI Chat.
Step 3: Under the recommended models, tap Download below. To download the model you want. Gemma 4 E2B is 2.6 GB and best for starters, while Gemma 4 E4B is 3.7 GB and smarter, but your phone needs at least 8 GB of RAM to run it locally.
Step 3: Once the model is downloaded, tap Try it.
Step 4: Type your prompt in the Type prompt box and tap the send button.
Step 5: Like the other AI apps, the model replies to your prompt. You can also see how fast the model runs, measured in tokens per second, and how much RAM it uses. On my Android phone, the Gemma 4 E2B model ran at about 30 tokens per second, and my model comes with 16 GB of RAM.
Method 2: Run any open model on Android with PocketPal AI
PocketPal is a popular free and open-source app for running AI models locally on Android.
Unlike Google’s AI Edge Gallery, it supports a wide variety of third-party models, including Google’s Gemma, Meta’s Llama, Microsoft’s Phi, Qwen, and more. It also supports GGUF models, including compressed versions.
How do I use the PocketPal app to run AI models locally on my device?
Step 1: Download and install the PocketPal app from the Google Play Store. Here is the direct download link.
Step 2: Open the app and, during onboarding, tap Download Model.
Step 3: Pick any available model to download and tap Download,
or tap the plus option to find more. To get a new model, tap the plus icon, select Hugging Face, then tap Choose and add from Hugging Face.
Step 4: From here, you can search for any model. In this case, I searched for the Qwen3 1.7B parameter model and tapped the download icon to download it locally.
Step 5: Once done, open the Models tab and select the model to load it. Now go to the chat interface and enter the prompt, and the model uses the model that you have loaded, in this case, the Qwen3 1.7 billion parameter model, to answer your queries. You can also see how much time it takes to run this model on your device.
iPhone
Method 1: Run Gemma 4 on iPhone with Google AI Edge Gallery
Google’s AI Edge Gallery is also available on iPhone and supports the latest Gemma 4 family of open-weight models, similar to Android. You can download and use E2B (around 2.6 GB) and the E4B model (around 3.7 GB).
Apple doesn’t disclose the RAM used on iPhones. However, the latest iPhone models, including the iPhone 15 Pro and later, support up to 8 GB of RAM, which can run these models faster and more reliably. However, older iPhones may struggle with slow responses, battery drain, and overheating, so keep that in mind.
Step 1: Download the Google AI Edge Gallery app on your iPhone. Here is the link.
Step 2: Open the app and tap on AI chat
Step 3: Now download the compatible AI model. In this case, I’m downloading Gemma 4 E2B, which is about 2.59 GB. Click on the download icon under the model.
Step 4: Wait for the model to download, then tap Try It, enter the prompt, and wait for a reply. If you want to use the vision capabilities, tap on the plus icon and upload an image
Method 2: Run open models on iPhone with PocketPal AI
Similar to Google’s AI Edge Gallery app, the PocketPal app is also available on iPhone. It also gives access to some of the popular Hugging Face model library and other third-party models, including models from Meta, Cohere, and more. It also supports Google Gemma 4 models.
Step 1: Install the PocketPal AI app on your iPhone. Here is the link.
Step 2: Open the app, tap Download Model, select a model, and tap Download. In this case, I am downloading the Qwen3 1.7B model.
Step 3: Once downloaded, tap the Load option at the top, enter the prompt, and wait for the reply
Mac
Method 1: Run AI models on a Mac with LM Studio
You can use LM Studio on Mac to run AI models locally.
It supports a wide range of models, including models from Google Gemma, Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, and more. Like the mobile app, you can install LM Studio on your Mac, download a model, and start chatting. It also supports GGUF and Apple-optimized MLX models.
Depending on the model, you can have text conversations, image analysis, and more. You can also use it as a local API for other apps.
However, LM Studio is only available on Apple Silicon Macs (M1 or later). Intel Macs are not supported.
How to install and run AI models locally using LM Studio on Mac
Step 1: First, go to lmstudio.ai/download and download the LM Studio app for Mac. Select the compatible version and drag and drop LM Studio into Applications to install it.
Step 2: Open LM Studio on the Mac, click on the model search in the sidebar, and search for the model; for example, in this case, I searched for the Gemma 4 E4B model
Step 3: You can also pick a different model, select it, and click Download. A likely fit badge here means that it is suitable to run locally on your Mac using your Mac’s available memory. Once the model is downloaded, tap on Use in the new chat instead.
Step 4: On the home screen, click Load Model in the dialog and select the model. You can also raise the context length here if you are planning for long conversations.
Step 5: Now enter the prompt and press Enter. The model returns with an option. You can also click the model server in the sidebar and turn on the status to use the model for other apps via an OpenAI-compatible API at http://localhost:1234.
Method 2: Run AI models on a Mac with Ollama
You can also run AI models on your Mac using Ollama. It is a free, lightweight tool by Meta that lets you run local AI models in the terminal with one command. It also works with many local apps that support local AI.
Step 1: To run Ollama locally on your device, go to ollama.com/download and click on the Download manually option. You can also directly paste the command into the terminal if you are a developer.
Step 2: Next, open the Ollama.dmg, drag it into Applications, and open it
Step 3: On the onboarding screen, while setting up an account, Ollama asks you to sign up for an account; however, you can tap on No thanks, I will use Ollama locally’
Step 4: Next, to run ollama run llama3, copy the ollama run llama3 command, open Terminal, and paste it. Wait for the model to download completely. Ollama can run Qwen3 4B parameters and other models. In this case, I am going to run the Ollama run Qwen3 4B model. So, wait for the model to download completely.
Step 5: Finally, you can start using the Ollama model right there. You can enter the prompt directly, and it will reply in the same terminal.
Windows
Method 1: Run AI models on Windows with LM Studio
You can use the same LM Studio on Windows as well to run AI models locally on your device
Step 1: Download and install LM Studio for Windows. Here is the download page link.
Step 2: Open the LM Studio app and, in the left sidebar, tap Model Search and search for the model you want to run locally. In this case, Iam using Qwen3 1.7 billion parameters; on the model details page, click the download option.
Step 3: Wait for it to download, and once it has downloaded, tap on Use in new chat
Step 4: Now, on the home screen, in the model box, select the downloaded model. You can tap on the model to select and enable it, then enter the prompt and press enter.
Method 2: Run AI models on Windows with Ollama
Ollama is also available on Mac. It supports NVIDIA and AMD graphics cards, as well as the latest ARM-based Snapdragon PCs. You can download models and use them directly from the terminal. Here is how.
Step 1: First, download Ollama on Windows. Go to ollama.com/download/windows and click Manual download. If you are a developer, you can install it directly in PowerShell using the PowerShell command.
Step 2: Now install the Ollama app on Windows. While setting up, click Continue, and then tap on No thanks, I will use Ollama locally, so you can skip creating an account.
Step 3: Next, copy the command shown in the app, open Terminal, and run this command: ollama run qwen3:1.7b, and press Enter. It downloads the model. Wait for the download to complete.
Step 4: Now enter your question and press Enter.
This is how you can set up and run AI models locally on Android, iPhone, Windows, and Mac. Choosing the right model is important to get high-quality output. Bigger models don’t always mean better outputs, as their capabilities can vary. Our guide to the best AI models to run locally should help you choose the right model for your needs. If you have any issues setting them up, feel free to comment below, and I’ll be happy to help.

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.
Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.
“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.
From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.
Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.
Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.
The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.
Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.
Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.
Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.
“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.
It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.
That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.
On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.
Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.
It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.
In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.
Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”
A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.
Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.
It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.
In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.
In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.
In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.
The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.
Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.
As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.
Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.
The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.
The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”
Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.
The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”
Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.
Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

BJP national president Nitin Nabin arrived in Mathura on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) to attend the last day of the party's two-day brainstorming session, where senior leaders are deliberating on a strategy to secure a third consecutive term in power in Uttar Pradesh in the 2027 Assembly elections.

BJP's Uttar Pradesh media convenor Manish Dixit told PTI that State party president and Union Minister of State for Finance Pankaj Chaudhary and the party's State in-charge Vinod Tawde welcomed Mr. Nabin at the helipad upon his arrival on Tuesday (November 17) afternoon.
In a post on X around 1:55 p.m., Mr. Chaudhary said he had welcomed Mr. Nabin at the brainstorming meeting in the land of Lord Krishna.
He added that he subsequently paid floral tributes to the statue of Pandit Deendayal Upadhyaya, describing him as "the proponent of Integral Humanism and Antyodaya".

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the fighting in the Middle East.
Iran has targeted an airbase inBahrainin the latest resumption of strikes since September, prompting public warnings and sirens to ring out in the Gulf kingdom this morning.

Bahrain, which lies directly across the Persian Gulf from Iran, is home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, and has been repeatedly attacked by Tehran during the course of the war, which has seen flare-ups in strikes amid long bouts of inaction.
There are fears Iran’s attacks this morning might signal a resumption of the war while US President Donald Trump has threatened but refrained from returning to major combat. Developments in the Red Sea this morning will add to further concerns for Gulf oil flows.
The Yemeni government forces supported by Saudi Arabia, fighting the Houthis, have retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb area, giving the Iran-aligned rebels even greater control over the critical shipping lane, which Saudi Arabia and other Gulf oil producers had been relying on to get their supplies out.
Elsewhere, Hamas has confirmed that a senior commander involved in planning the 7 October attacks was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Saturday.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards:
The US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force.
The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response.
Bahrain’s foreign ministry
Iran continues its systematic hostile approach through its sinful attacks targeting the Kingdom of Bahrain.
[Bahrain] rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks.
I’m yet to see a response from the US, but can expect Centcomm (which oversees all American military operations in the Middle East) to comment at some stage, like it did for Friday’s attack. Those strikes also targeted a radar site.

After two months of calm, the explosions have started again for Bahrain citizens.
Locals reported hearing blasts about 4am local time, and then a second round at 6.30am.
It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them”, Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told AFP news agency.
Another resident, Mohammed Abdallah, a shopkeeper in the capital Manama, which is just north of the air base targeted said:
I was hoping this period was behind us and wouldn’t happen again.
Bahrain’s Interior Ministry posted public warnings on X, telling “residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels”.
Iran had last launched strikes in the first week of September, when the regime targeted US military assets in Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they had launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base on Sunday morning, reported Iranian media.

US forces have been quietly carrying out a series of strikes on Iranian sites in recent weeks, including on the key Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, where there’s a major IRGC presence. Trump has called them minor strikes.
Bahrain officials this morning have accused Tehran of continuing a “systematic hostile approach” to the kingdom.
The drone flurry this morning comes just 48 hours after Iran launched drones on Friday, the first escalations targeting Bahrain in two months.
That attack targeted an American radar facility. US Central Command said it had shot down the two drones without any injury or damage.
Bahrain officials hadn’t issued any warnings for that attack, but were forced to send out public alerts this morning telling residents to seek shelter. The Interior Ministry told locals to remain calm but proceed to to the nearest safe location.

Is India rethinking its short-term military recruitment scheme?
- Published
For generations of young Indians, joining the armed forces offered something few other jobs did - a steady career, financial security, the promise of a pension after retirement and the pride of serving their country.
In 2022, the government upended that arrangement, announcing a new reform scheme under which young men and women entering the military would serve for just four years. Only a quarter would be allowed to stay on permanently. The rest would return to civilian life with a lump-sum payment, but without the pension and other benefits that had long made military service an attractive career.
Now, as the first batch of recruits prepares to complete its four-year term, the government is offering them a chance to stay longer, in a significant shift in a policy that has been fiercely debated since its introduction.
On 4 November, Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani announced that recruits who failed to secure permanent positions under the Agnipath, or "path of fire", programme would be offered another two years of service at higher pay. They would then get a second opportunity to join the regular forces, provided they met the selection criteria.
Gen Subramani said the decision followed feedback from the forces and insisted that Agnipath would continue.
But the timing is significant. More than 18,300 recruits from the first batch are due to complete their initial tenure by the end of 2026. Officials say the new arrangement will be offered to more than 300,000 Agniveers - as recruits under the scheme are known - currently serving across the army, navy and air force.
Whether future batches will also be covered remains unclear. The BBC has contacted the defence ministry for clarification.
The ministry has defended , externalAgnipath, saying internal assessments found the recruits to be physically fit, motivated and technologically adaptable. It also said the scheme had widened recruitment across districts and made the process more standardised.
But the extension has brought renewed attention to the trade-offs at the heart of the policy - and whether its original ambitions were realistic.
When the government introduced Agnipath, it argued the scheme would reduce the average age of the armed forces, lower long-term salary and pension costs and create a younger, more technologically adaptable fighting force.
But military experts and opposition leaders have questioned whether a four-year contract could replace what had traditionally been a coveted, long-term career in the armed forces.
"Being a soldier in the armed forces was a chance for these young men to make a life for themselves, to get their families out of poor or lower-middle-income conditions," says retired Maj Gen Yash Mor, a vocal critic of the scheme.
These concerns were also amplified by the timing of Agnipath's launch. Recruitment had been suspended for nearly two years during the Covid pandemic, leaving thousands of aspirants waiting for vacancies to reopen.
The changes were greeted by massive protests across the country, with many saying the career path they had spent years preparing for had fundamentally changed.
This sentiment was felt most in states and cities that have traditionally been major recruitment hubs, where military service has been a family tradition for generations.
Kulbeer Singh Chaudhary, who runs a recruitment training institute in Dehradun city, says interest in joining the armed forces fell sharply and he stopped conducting Agniveer training batches.
The latest announcement, he hopes, would reverse that trend.
"The possibility of a longer engagement and eventual absorption into the forces may offer young candidates greater assurance," he says.
The changes also come at a time when the armed forces are facing personnel shortages. In November last year, The Indian Express reported, external that the army alone faced a shortfall of nearly 180,000 soldiers and was considering increasing recruitment.
But the debate over Agnipath goes beyond what happens to recruits after four years. Critics also question whether that is enough time to turn them into experienced soldiers.
Sanjiv Krishan Sood, a former additional director general of the Border Security Force, has argued, external that the shorter training period is particularly problematic for technical roles requiring specialised skills.
Retired Maj Gen Mor says military effectiveness depends on experience and trust built over years.
"It takes eight-to-nine years to turn a raw recruit into a dependable, seasoned soldier - someone capable of handling a tank crew, an artillery gun crew or a small detachment," he says.
"Over those years, a soldier develops the ethos, camaraderie, brotherhood and fighting spirit that bind a unit together. These qualities cannot be built overnight."
Sood says the additional two years could help improve recruits' skills, particularly in handling specialised equipment.
Senior military leaders have also welcomed the extension. Air Vice Marshal Shekhar Yadav told news agency ANI, external it would allow the forces to retain trained personnel for longer.
But the change could create fresh challenges within military units.
Regular soldiers, Agniveers on four-year contracts and those serving an additional two years could find themselves working alongside one another despite differences in pay, promotion prospects and post-service benefits.
Experts warn that these disparities could affect unit cohesion.
There is also the question of whether the changes will undermine one of the government's central objectives: reducing spending. Almost half of India's defence budget, external goes towards salaries and pensions, leaving less money for modernisation and new equipment.
By limiting the number of personnel eligible for long-term benefits, Agnipath was expected to ease that burden. But critics argue that savings should not come at the expense of military effectiveness.
"We are not against making changes, but there are ways and means to go about it," says Mor, adding that the government could instead reduce annual recruitment while retaining soldiers for longer periods.
He also points to India's tense borders with Pakistan and China, where troops remain deployed year-round, placing sustained demands on manpower and operational experience.
Retired Major-General Birender Singh Dhanoa, meanwhile, questions whether shorter service makes financial sense when the military is investing in training to operate increasingly sophisticated equipment.
"The amount of time it takes to train, and the financial outlay for training, is much higher for modern equipment. So shouldn't you get the best bang for your buck?" he asks.
Many retired officers had proposed a different approach when the scheme was announced, he says.
"We suggested that if you want to reduce your financial burden, you increase the terms and conditions of service. Take these guys for eight-or-nine years and retain a larger number after that."
The announcement also comes at a politically sensitive time. Elections are due soon in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - states that have traditionally supplied large numbers of soldiers and where military recruitment remains an important source of employment.
The opposition Congress party has called the revision a "u-turn", alleging that the government is responding to fears of losing votes.
For young recruits approaching the end of their contracts, the changes offer some reassurance, but few guarantees. Two more years of service could mean more money, greater experience and another chance at a permanent career.
But for many, it also means putting their futures on hold, without knowing whether they will eventually be allowed to stay.

Rosemary Nyirumbe became a nun when she was just in her mid-teens – and she felt her true vocation lay in rehabilitating children who had been through some of the worst trauma imaginable. So that’s what she did. In this episode Mike Wooldridge hears Sr Rosemary’s astonishing story. In many cases, the LRA forced them to commit atrocities, leaving them deeply traumatised. Many of the girls also bore the children of rebel leaders. As they started to return home, these children were often rejected by their families and communities, says Sr Rosemary. More than once, Sr Rosemary put herself in enormous danger in order to fulfil her mission. But, she says, she also learnt that small acts of kindness can touch the hearts of even battle-hardened rebels.

Lindsay Clancy to face a new trial in spring of 2027 over children's killing
Prosecutors are seeking a new trial for Lindsay Clancy in the deaths of her three children. The trial is scheduled to begin on March 29, 2027.
There had been speculation that the mistrial of her first trial might spur prosecutors to consider lesser charges that wouldn't require a jury, such as manslaughter or second-degree murder. But no changes to the charges were made in Monday's court hearing.
"Given what the charges are, it requires a jury trial," Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague told Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Mass.
In response, Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington stated, "I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments."
Judge Sullivan is expected to preside over the new trial. He oversaw Clancy's murder trial that ended in a mistrial two months ago.
The decision to retry Clancy emerges after the judge denied a request from Clancy's defense team to dismiss the criminal charges against her on double jeopardy grounds.
Clancy's defense has argued that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for killing her young children because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.
Clancy was initially tried on three charges of first-degree murder, one for each of her children. Her case has drawn intense media interest, due to the shocking killings of her young children. And as WBUR has reported, the trial has also sparked conspiracy theories online.
Read WBUR's coverage of this case here.
Mistrial sparked defense motion to dismiss
Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4, after five weeks of testimony and seven days of jury deliberations. The jurors, nine women and three men, repeatedly told Sullivan they were deadlocked, unable to reach a unanimous decision. Jurors said a lone juror refused to join 11 others in finding Clancy not guilty of murder.
Clancy's defense filed several motions after the mistrial. The first asked the court to issue a "required finding of not guilty," a Massachusetts state law term for instances where judges determine there's insufficient evidence to sustain a conviction. Another focused on the holdout juror, asking the court for an inquiry and to examine their responses to a juror questionnaire and other records. Sullivan denied both of those motions.
When deliberations were dragging out at the end of the trial, Reddington had asked the judge to remove the holdout juror, saying the jury foreperson reported one juror refused to follow the law in regards to reasonable doubt. Sullivan declined to dismiss the juror, saying he reaffirmed his instructions with all the jurors about the law.
Tragic case highlights postpartum mental health
Clancy, 36, did not testify during the trial. But her attorneys didn't deny that she killed her three children in January of 2023. Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, were found strangled in the basement of the home Clancy shared with her then-husband Patrick in Duxbury, Mass., south of Boston.
In court, Clancy's defense argued that she can't be held criminally liable because of her mental state at the time of the killings. Her attorney said Clancy was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis, and didn't get adequate mental health help when she sought it out.
"I'm appalled and disgusted," Reddington said of Clancy's medical care, as NPR and WBUR reported. "It's repulsive what happened here."
But prosecutors argued Clancy was mentally capable of committing a premeditated crime, accusing her of sending her husband out on errands so she would be alone with their children. And they raised doubts about Clancy's claims that a voice told her to kill them.
"This case is not about our mental health system or how it treats women," Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said in her closing statement. "That's a distraction to get you angry and passionate about an important issue, but an issue that's not on trial here."
During the trial, the jury visited the house where the Clancy children died. Their bus route also took them past two places Patrick Clancy visited that evening — a CVS and a takeout restaurant -- before returning home to a horrific scene. Sullivan told the jurors that the visit, called a "view" under Massachusetts state law, was meant to "help you better understand the evidence" by seeing the locations and the house's layout.
Clancy remains in the custody of a state psychiatric hospital where she's been held for more than three years. She was severely injured by attempts to end her own life, and she used a wheelchair during the trial.
Massachusetts' highest court recently reversed a conviction in a separate case involving a mother killing her children – a case that both Cruz, the prosecutor, and Sullivan, the judge, also worked on.
In August, the state Supreme Judicial Court ordered a new trial for Latarsha Sanders, saying Sullivan committed an error in not allowing the jury to see medical records documenting Sanders' mental illness after she was arrested. Sanders was convicted of murder in 2022; she had argued that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible because she suffered a psychotic episode.

A new generation of disability rights activists carry on Judy Heumann's legacy
Judy Heumann is known as the mother of the disability rights movement — yet she is lesser known than many of the other civil rights activists of her time. Now, a new film seeks to change that.
Being Heumann, the latest movie from Oscar-winning director Sian Heder, tells the story of the young woman from Brooklyn who led the movement to win the first civil rights protections in the country for people with disabilities.
Before the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was passed in 1990, there was Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973. It was a single sentence, written into the law, promising people with disabilities the right to fair employment and access to public life without facing discrimination.
But for years, there were no rules or regulations making the federal government actually enforce those protections.
Until the spring of 1977, when a band of activists with disabilities decided to do something about it. Led by Heumann and Kitty Cone, activists took over the former Department of Health, Education and Welfare building in San Francisco for nearly a month — widely considered the longest sit-in of a federal building in U.S. history.
People across disability groups — from wheelchair users to people with intellectual and health-related disabilities — camped out, demanding, and eventually winning the passage of rules that made Section 504 enforceable. The protests paved the way for federally funded institutions like schools, libraries, city buildings and other entities to be made accessible for disabled people.
"Judy always said, 'disability only becomes a tragedy for me when society fails to provide the things we need to lead our lives' — job opportunities or barrier-free buildings, for example," says former NPR correspondent Joe Shapiro, who covered disability and was a friend of Heumann's until she died in 2023.
Regarding disability rights as basic civil rights was a novel concept at the time, but has remained core to the movement today.
Shapiro says Heumann was fueled by the idea of a generation of young disabled people who would come of age under the ADA: "They see the ADA as a floor, not a ceiling, and Judy loved that there's this new generation demanding more."
With the film having opened in theaters this month and now streaming on Apple TV, NPR sat down with some members of the ADA generation to talk about Heumann's legacy, and the threats they see today to the movement she helped launch.
"It is our job to carry on her legacy and keep that fire burning all these decades later," says Kaleigh Brendle, who started a disability rights organization called Judy's League to push back against the Trump administration's efforts to roll back protections attached to Section 504.
Last month, a federal judge dealt a blow to disability rights activists by agreeing to strip out mentions of "integration" of people with disabilities from Section 504 regulations. This erased some of the very language Heumann and her movement had helped win 50 years ago.
As she watched Being Heumann, Brendle says she "felt simultaneously sad that we're here again because I know she would be hurting to see so much of what she fought for at risk. But it also strengthened my resolve."
Brendle, who is blind and has other disabilities, held a watch party of Being Heumann with four other members of Judy's League. They spoke to NPR about their impressions.
These are excerpts from that conversation, edited for length and clarity.
On what stood out most about Being Heumann:
Liam Holland, 25, Philadelphia: The very first line of the movie is Judy chanting "[Sign 504]!" That gave me chills right away, because almost 50 years later, 504 is the exact reason we founded Judy's League. Seeing her lead the chant hit home because we are still fighting those exact same battles today.
Cricket Bidleman, 27, Baltimore: Like Liam said, seeing history come full circle was not particularly encouraging. But we did it once, so we can do it again. We can save 504.
Kaleigh Brendle, 23, Berkeley, Calif.: What I loved seeing over and over on display was just the unshakable resolve that Judy showed, that fire that would not be extinguished … And I think right now we're seeing relentless challenges to our rights from this administration, from every direction. ... It really gave me hope and renewed what I feel we need to be doing right now.
Ellana Crew, 30, Baltimore: I feel I've never seen so many real disabled people on screen in one place ... They are laughing, they are swearing, they're telling dirty jokes … That was one of my favorite things, honestly, it was just like, 'OK, wow, I didn't expect that to be in this movie.' They are not shying away from disabled people as sexual and romantic beings, which is rarely something that society lets us talk about. And ... it's remarkable how many of the sentiments in the movie, based on this time in the 1970s, still feel so relevant today.
On what parts of the disability rights movement back then still feel relevant:
Ellana Crew: A lot of attitudes expressed by non-disabled people [in the film] felt fairly indistinguishable from the attitudes I hear today. Like some of the same sentiments, some of the same opinions of pity, charity-based mindsets of like, "Oh, well we feel bad for you, but we can't do anything about it, it's just too hard." I think people would be amazed how often that still happens today, or maybe they wouldn't.
Cricket Bidleman: It's amazing to see how in some ways we've made so much progress. I mean, now we have computers and technology that work for us, and autonomous vehicles and things like that. But the discrimination hasn't really changed that much.
Kaleigh Brendle: What really moved me was hearing Judy lead the "Sign 504" chant because I, along with several other people in Judy's league ... we were in Austin, Texas on the Capitol steps this July. And all these years later we were having to chant "Hands off 504."
On how the legacy of Judy Heumann and other activists has shaped the disability rights movement today:
Liam Holland: Every week, I roll a mile and back [in my wheelchair] by myself to get chicken for my dinner puree. That trip has a lot of curb cuts. Before 504, sidewalks did not have ramps, which stopped disabled people's access to sidewalks. The [1977] sit-in forced the government to mandate public access. So every curb I go over is directly tied to that fight. ... The people at the deli see me come in every week by myself. They fist-bump me, get my card from my wallet, put it back ... And then I roll home over curb cuts listening to music. So what Judy means to me, quite simply, is independence and normalcy.
Leigh White, 30, Galloway, N.J.: Unfortunately, history rhymes. And we're not right back where we started, but we are in the crucible, if you will, where we're kind of being fired at on all sides. And it's important to remember her grit and her tenacity and her true dedication ... Disabled individuals are the largest minority group in the United States. And it crosses all genders and all races and everything. So by fighting for the rights of people with disabilities, it kind of raises all boats.Kaleigh Brendle: I always say to other people that don't understand the disability experience: If you broke your arm tomorrow, you would expect that the world would accommodate you. You would expect to have the accommodations that you needed as you navigated that temporary disability. Why is it wrong for us to expect what you would expect in that situation?
Cricket Bidleman: We've made so many advancements because of people like Judy and because of … all these activists and advocates who came before us. And although I do have to struggle with people to obtain access to media or textbooks or the standardized testing to get into various education, it's still nothing compared to some of the things we saw in the movie
Leigh White: Us being part of the 'ADA generation,' we're able to reap the benefits. Where do you stand on Jensen?
That question is roiling Silicon Valley as it reckons with the tech titan's fall from grace.
Venture capitalists, tech founders, and Nvidia employees are rallying to his defense — and some are pushing to bring him back. But others see the rush to forgive him as a familiar Silicon Valley reflex: excusing a powerful man's conduct while minimizing the damage to the people and institutions around him.
The Nvidia cofounder and CEO resigned last week following reports that he had multiple affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy and a subordinate. To some, that's overshadowed by his achievements.
"Jensen is one of the great builders of our time. We cannot starve the future of his innovation and industrial breakthroughs," reads a comment from Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick on Stand With Jensen, an online petition with more than 186,000 signatures.
"To err is human," Kalanick — who said he is crowdsourcing "wild ideas" to get Huang reinstated — added.
Nvidia's board of directors is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter confirmed to Business Insider on Monday.
Kalanick joins a growing chorus of people in tech defending Huang, including Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, and Nvidia executives, all of whom have signed the petition.
For others, Huang's downfall was well-deserved given the ethical and national security implications of his conduct. Huang has long rankled some corners of tech because of his constant lobbying to sell powerful AI chips to China.
One notable venture investor privately disagreed with Huang's friendly approach to China, given the chronic chip shortage in the US.
The investor was frustrated that Huang had done little to address the industry's growing compute crisis, with some startups struggling to secure the resources needed to continue scaling. Nvidia had a lot of compute primarily reserved for research and development, the person said.
Huang's business tactics are being scrutinized more than ever given his relationship with one of Nvidia's biggest customers, who some in the US government believe was part of an espionage scheme.
That's without even mentioning his reported affair with an employee, executive Kimberly Powell, while he painted himself as a family man.
One woman VC said Huang's infidelity and potential national security implications have barely surfaced in her Silicon Valley women's group chats. Some women investors, she said, have expressed that they feel sorry for Huang's wife. But, she said, "The general sentiment is, 'He's such a great leader, who cares what he does in his private life?'"
Another woman VC said she and other women in venture were hardly surprised by the news, having grown accustomed to such conduct in the Valley. "Any time there is ego, power, and money, this is what happens," she said.
"The tech right and founder class is rallying behind Jensen against all reason," Zvi Mowshowitz, who publishes an influential AI Substack, told Business Insider.
At stake isn't just whether Huang gets back on top of Nvidia or not — an unlikely prospect — but the legacy of a key figure behind the AI boom.
The godfather of the AI boom
For years, Nvidia was best known for the graphics cards it sold to PC gamers. Huang was prescient in predicting that the high-powered chips would power the AI revolution.
In a fateful moment, he personally delivered an Nvidia supercomputer, the DGX-1, to OpenAI's office in 2016. It was signed by then-OpenAI researcher Dario Amodei, who now runs Anthropic — which is set for a trillion-dollar blockbuster IPO this week.
Huang's role in helping birth the thriving AI startup ecosystem is partly why so many venture capitalists are still Huang fans, industry insiders said.
Nvidia's rise has been lucrative for them, too. Nvidia often invested in AI startups at high valuations, boosting the value of their portfolio companies by the billions.
The funding also benefited Nvidia because it could be used to buy even more Nvidia chips. If the next Nvidia CEO takes a less aggressive investment approach, it could be the beginning of an AI industry correction, some investors cautioned.
Tatiana Koffman, a GP at Moonwalker Capital, said Nvidia's board should finish its investigation, and that Huang should be reinstated if it finds no credible proof of a security breach.
"We're painting Jensen with a moral brush for something leaders have done time and time again. He's one of the greatest engineers of the last two generations, and few people have done more for American innovation," she said.
A divided AI community
In the AI policy and safety world, Huang's push to sell Nvidia chips to China raised concerns about giving a US competitor powerful AI hardware.
As worries about AI going rogue reached a fever pitch, Huang's staunch defense of the technology also raised eyebrows.
"I would say Jensen's views have been at odds with a lot of the AI community," said former OpenAI employee Will Depue.
Huang's brash statements annoyed some of the most senior people in the industry.
After Huang said that Anthropic was trying to control AI through safety regulations, Amodei called Huang's claim "the most outrageous lie I've ever heard."
Lior Susan, founder and CEO of VC firm Eclipse — which has invested in startups that Nvidia has also backed, like autonomous driving company Wayve — said the industry will endure beyond any single man.
“Jensen was huge for the industry of AI and robotics, but the rise of robotics did not happen because of one person, and the rapid technological transformations we are witnessing will not slow down,” Susan told Business Insider.
“There is a world after Jensen, and there is still so much progress to be made.”

New Delhi: Brazil is looking to expand its energy partnership with India, from exploring for oil and gas in the Andaman basin to supplying more crude oil and sharing its experience in biofuels, Brazil’s ambassador to India, Kenneth Félix Haczynski da Nóbrega, told Mint in an interview.
Responding to a query, Nóbrega said the country’s state-owned oil company Petrobras is mulling a role in deepwater exploration in the Andaman basin. The potential partnership is timely, as India looks to reduce its heavy dependence on imported crude and strengthen energy security amid growing uncertainty over global oil supplies.
Petrobras, which had largely focussed on its home market in recent years because of financial pressures, is now in a stronger position to expand overseas, Nóbrega said in an interview. “The company is already more solid, financially solid. So, I think they are planning to go abroad again.”
Petrobras already has a technology arrangement with state-owned Oil India Ltd, but has yet to participate in India’s hydrocarbon block auctions.
The government has been inviting global players to participate in the auctions for the hydrocarbon blocks under India's open access licensing policy.
The timing is crucial for India, which imports 90% of its oil. The US-Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz have heightened concerns over the country's energy security.
- Petrobras is considering deepwater exploration in the Andaman Basin, Brazil’s ambassador to India says.
- Brazilian crude imports into India surged 653% in April-August to $3.21 billion.
- Petrobras, now financially stronger, is planning overseas expansion again, the ambassador says.
- India imports 90% of its oil; the closure of the Strait of Hormuz deepens energy security worries.
- The Andaman basin may hold 371 million tonnes of oil equivalent; viability unproven.
Brazil is now already a much bigger supplier of crude oil to India. Imports from the South American country surged 653% year-on-year to $3.21 billion during April-August, according to commerce ministry data, underscoring its growing importance to India's energy needs.
India's Andaman-Nicobar basin is estimated to have around 371 million tonnes of oil equivalent (including oil as well as gas), with Oil India’s recent test drills confirming presence of natural gas and good prospects for crude.
Queries mailed to Petrobras remained unanswered until press time.
Brazil has also boosted crude oil supplies to India, as the country looks to diversify its markets.
“I think this is multi-pronged (approach). One very simple idea of cooperation in energy is the fact that you have increased your exports from Brazil. Brazil is now the fourth or fifth largest supplier of crude,” said Nóbrega, adding that the country was, of course, only a distant fourth or fifth largest.
The Ambassador asserted that bilateral ties go beyond trade.
Indian firms are exploring for oil in Brazil, and Brazil could help India with deep-sea drilling in the Andaman and Nicobar waters, where most of the new oil and gas is expected to be found, he said.
Oil India as well as Oil and Natural Gas Corp (ONGC) Ltd are currently involved in hydrocarbon exploration in the Andaman basin.
Oil India has so far made two discoveries of potential natural gas presence in the basin. In June, Oil India discovered natural gas in the Sri Vijayapuram-3 well, about 15 km off the east coast of the Andaman Islands, at a water depth of 355 metres. In September last year, the company had discovered natural gas at the Vijayapuram-2 exploratory well in the Andaman shallow offshore block.
The Ambassador's comments come as India's 10th round of hydrocarbon block auctions under the Open Acreage Licensing Policy is underway. The deadline for submitting bids for the deep- and ultra-deepwater blocks is 10 December.
Nóbrega noted that in February last year, when the Petrobras chief executive officer, Magda Chambriard, visited India, she had spoken to the minister for petroleum and natural gas Hardeep Singh Puri and Indian energy firms about prospective technological cooperation in offshore deep-sea exploration.
Biofuel push
Beyond energy exploration, Brazil's experience in biofuels could also offer India a hand in its green fuel push.
The South American country, a top producer of sugar, is a pioneer in biofuel adoption by blending ethanol with petrol. Brazil had launched its Proálcool programme way back in 1975 to reduce its crude oil imports by turning surplus sugarcane into fuel. In August 2025, the country had hiked its fuel blending mandate to 30% (E30). And year later, the country raised the level to 32% (E32) for 180 days, a decision it is set to review.
And, as early as 2003, Volkswagen do Brasil, a subsidiary of the Volkswagen Group, introduced the first flex-fuel vehicle in Brazil on a commercial basis, allowing engines to run on any petrol-ethanol mixture, up to 100% ethanol, commonly known as E100.
On ethanol-blended fuel pricing, Nóbrega said there is a significant differential between ethanol-blended fuel and 100% ethanol-based fuel used in flex-fuel vehicles in Brazil. The price of petrol, or gasoline, in Brazil is currently around Brazilian Real (BRL) 6.47 ($1.14) per litre, while that of the 100% ethanol-based variant is BRL 4.17 ($0.73).
“First, regarding the price relative to the energy content of ethanol, in Brazil, this was solved by regulation. You know that, by law in Brazil, there must be a certain difference between the price of one litre of ethanol and one litre of petrol. So, this takes care of the issue of paying more for less,” he said.
Brazil was the co-founder of the Global Biofuels Alliance, along with India, Indonesia, the US and others.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

Rashmi Ramesh, 40, from Mumbai, has been managing Hashimoto’s thyroiditis for nearly two decades. And yet, she continues to experience hair fall and fluctuations in weight. Staying fit and managing her health require constant attention to sleep, diet and exercise, she says. “It is tough to stay fit. I have to work much harder than someone who doesn’t live with Hashimoto’s.” During pregnancy, she experienced substantial weight gain and water retention, along with puffiness. Managing her condition requires constant vigilance.
