One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built.
A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward.
Finding the centers
The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.
In a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category.
That fact also introduces some uncertainty in the actual power usage of these data centers. Relying on other research, they use a range—some conventional data centers run at an average of about 48 percent of capacity, while AI training loads have been running higher, at around 70 percent.
Putting that together, the total power usage for the year by these 403 data centers was estimated at 68 to 99 terawatt-hours. That amounts to 1.5 to 2.2 percent of total US electricity use, on par with the total used by Wisconsin or Indiana.

My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
- Published
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.
They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.
"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.
But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.
This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.
Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.
Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.
After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.
"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.
The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.
The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.
After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.
Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.
This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.
After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.
This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.
"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.
Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.
He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.
In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.
Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.
"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.
Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.
The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.
However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.
"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.
For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.
He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.
Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns.
"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.
They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.
Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.
After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.
"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."
During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.
But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.
Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.
"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".
He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.
But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.
Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.
He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."
He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing.
"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.
The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.
Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.
"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

- Contrary to a claim circulating via social media posts, there's no evidence that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries explicitly threatened to withhold committee assignments from House members and members-elect who don't support his bid for speaker when Democrats take control of the legislative body in January.
- This rumor stemmed from Ohio Democratic Rep.-elect Don Leonard's comments about a dinner with senior Democratic representatives who allegedly warned Leonard that his life could become a "living hell" if he didn't support Jeffries. Leonard later told TMZ that potential consequences could include withheld committee assignments, but he framed it as a possibility as to what that "living hell" may entail.
- Snopes will update this report if we receive replies to our queries from either Leonard or Jeffries.
After Democrats won control of Congress in the 2026 midterms, a claim spread online that U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries was threatening to withhold committee assignments for any of his caucus members who didn't support him for speaker of the House.
The rumor circulated on X and Threads, and Snopes readers wrote in to ask us to verify it.
This claim originated from Ohio Democratic Rep.-elect Don Leonard's comments about "friendly advice with very stark consequences" he allegedly received from senior House Democrats in regard to supporting Jeffries' bid for speaker. Social media posts appear to have taken Leonard's comments somewhat out of context. There's no evidence that Jeffries has literally threatened to withhold committee assignments from anyone who does not support him as speaker.
Jeffries and Leonard's offices did not immediately return requests for more information. Here's what we know:
Leonard's allegations
Leonard, an Ohio Democrat who flipped a Republican-held seat, posted a video on Nov. 9 claiming that top House Democrats said his life will become a "living hell" if he doesn't support Jeffries. 
Leonard says in the video that he will not support Jeffries as speaker without the New York Democrat's commitments to two issues: ending U.S. support for Israeli military actions, including the war in Iran, and a constitutional amendment that would reverse Citizens United, a Supreme Court decision that gives free-speech protections to corporate money in politics.
Here's the transcript from that video (emphasis ours):
Tonight, I met with — we'll call 'em senior members of the Democratic House — who told me in no uncertain terms that the decision as to whether or not I support Jeffries, regardless of his willingness to speak with me and meet the interests of my constituents on a couple of key issues: No. 1, getting a constitutional amendment to end Citizens United, and No. 2, ending U.S. support for the war in Iran, and the country, Israel, that led us into it — that that would basically mean both making my life a living hell for the next two years in Washington as well as being sure to lose my election in two years.
You know, we kinda knew this stuff was coming. It's part of the stuff you see in the movies. It's a whole 'nother thing when, you know, it's in person by people who actually care about you and are cheering for you, but expect you to wear the team jersey and, you know, be a good team player. You know, we're searching our hearts tonight as to how we can reach Leader Jeffries and help him be a better speaker. At the end of the day, the big "D" Democratic Party needs some little "d" democracy and I'm just a stubborn SOB, so we'll continue meeting with our fellow members of Congress and members-elect and try and see if we can build support for what we're trying to do here. Please wish me luck. It's getting real, y'all.
On Nov. 11, TMZ posted a video in which a reporter with the tabloid asks Leonard about his comments. In that video, Leonard expands on what "living hell" could mean and says committee assignments could be withheld. However, he also makes it clear that the conversation he was referencing did not directly involve Jeffries, nor was it meant to be threatening.
As such, it's unclear whether anyone actually told Leonard that Jeffries would withhold committee assignments from him or any other Democrat who does not support Jeffries as speaker.
Here's a transcript of the TMZ interview (emphasis ours):
TMZ: You're in a room with top-level Dem officials. They say to you, "Listen, if you don't fall in line, we're going to make your life hell." Walk me through what that experience was like, just on your first couple of days here.
LEONARD: It was so much less cinematic. It was actually a dinner with senior elected officials, and I let them know where my position was on the speaker, and they were offering very friendly advice with very stark consequences. It wasn't in leadership, it wasn't their position to do it. It was just, you know, friendly advice from future colleagues.
TMZ: It doesn't sound that friendly. You literally said — your words — you said it was out of a movie. It sounds like something out of like "The Godfather."
LEONARD: What's out of a movie is the consequences of it, right? And the consequences are very real. Committee assignments will be withheld. You know, The ability to get, you know, legislation on the floor for votes will be difficult. And, you know, the ability to get support for the re-election will be a difficult case to make.
TMZ: Is this not what people criticize Trump for? It sounds very similar.
LEONARD: Yeah, I know, I think, you know, well, welcome to Washington, D.C., right? I mean, it's — I'm not shocked, but I'm —
TMZ: Sounds a little shocking. I think you're a little —
LEONARD: — I'm disappointed.
TMZ: Yeah, well listen. We can say — you already said what you had to say. And it's gone viral. But I think we gotta go the next step further, here, just for Americans. Who were these people who said it to you?
LEONARD: Yeah, no, that's how we build relationships and sustain them going forward. But I appreciate it.
TMZ: You don't want to get in trouble, hey man, I appreciate it.
Axios reportedly asked Leonard about the conversation, per a Nov. 11 story, and he emphasized that it was a "friendly" and "well-intentioned" conversation with senior House Democrats. Here's how he described it to Axios:
"They let me know that while we all agree on a lot of this stuff … the leader is going to pursue his message and agenda as he sees fit, and [said], 'Don't be insane. How could you possibly stand in the way?'"
Leonard also said he met Jeffries for the first time, per Axios, and there's no indication it was a threatening meeting:
The Ohio Democrat said he got a chance to meet Jeffries for the first time on Tuesday and arrange for their staffers to work out a time to sit down and talk.
- "I shook his hand and I asked him for six minutes," he said, telling Axios he wants to "look him in the eye, let him know that [I] respect his capacity as a leader ... but I need something to take back to my district that shows that my party understands the magnitude of the crisis we face."
Politico reported that California Democrat Rep. Pete Aguilar, who is running unopposed for House majority whip, said he didn't know which Democrats Leonard was referring to.
"It's my belief that he will be overwhelmingly selected to lead this caucus. I don't lose any sleep over that," Aguilar reportedly said of Jeffries. "Members could have ideas and interests, and they could have asks along the way, but the outcome is not in question."
It's also worth noting that Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, an outspoken progressive, told TMZ that no one has threatened her over Jeffries' bid for speaker. Omar suggested that Leonard simply received "advice that seems intimidating" and said Congress was "like high school: If people see any weakness, they'll roll with it, they'll take advantage of you."

The iPhone Duo gets face unlock with the latest iOS 27 beta.
You won't need to wait for TouchID on your $2,000 foldable.
The lack of Face ID is one of the main complaints users have had about the iPhone Duo. And while rumors suggest that the company might add a TrueDepth camera to the second generation of its foldable phone next year, it seems that Apple has a more immediate solution to address these complaints. The second beta of iOS 27.3, released to developers on Monday, adds a new option to unlock the iPhone Duo with facial recognition using its front-facing camera.
The feature is called "Unlock with Front Camera" and can be enabled in the Touch ID & Passcode settings in the Settings app. Engadget confirmed that the feature works on an iPhone Duo running the beta — but how it works is quite intriguing. Unlike most modern iPhones, the Duo lacks a TrueDepth camera with the depth sensors that Face ID uses to map a face in 3D. Instead, it has regular cameras on both the outer and inner screens, which is likely the main reason it relies on Touch ID for unlocking.
And the new feature in iOS 27.3 beta makes this very clear — the setup screen warns users that the feature "provides convenience" but "isn't as secure as Touch ID or Face ID." It's still too early to tell, but Engadget's tests show that the feature works reasonably well. It unlocks faster than Touch ID and wasn't fooled when a photo of the user's face was pointed at the camera. It also seems to work in certain low-light conditions, though not when it's completely dark.
Of course, Apple has set some limits to ensure that malicious people don't take advantage of the new feature to tamper with others' iPhones without their consent. It only works to bypass the Lock Screen, and you can't unlock apps, view your passwords or use Apple Pay with your face — Touch ID is still required for more sensitive actions. Not using your phone for more than 45 minutes also temporarily disables Unlock with Front Camera. The feature doesn't work using the iPhone Duo's inner display either, but that's most likely because the under-display camera has a very low resolution.
The approach is very similar to what Apple did with the recently announced HomeView. It also lacks Face ID and relies on a simpler form of facial recognition to identify who is using the device in order to display personal content. It seems that Apple has now brought the same system to the iPhone Duo. In our review, we found the Duo's Touch ID accurate but a bit slower to unlock than expected. The same beta also adds a setting to lock the Duo when it's closed, instead of moving content to the outer display.
Apple hasn't said when iOS 27.3 will be released to the public, but the update is likely to be rolled out sometime mid-December. For now, only developers and beta testers have access to it.

Cast your vote for BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026
- Published
Voting is now open for the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026.
Fans worldwide can vote from the five-player shortlist of Temwa Chawinga, Ewa Pajor, Alexia Putellas, Alessia Russo and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw.
The vote closes on Wednesday, 18 November at 09:00 GMT.
For the first time in the award's history, the winner will be announced as part of the BBC's Sports Personality of the Year on Sunday, December 13 as well as on the BBC World Service and the BBC Sport website and app.
Contenders for the award - now in its 12th year - are nominated by coaches, journalists and former professionals. It covers the period September 2025-September 2026.
Cast your vote, and read more on the five contenders.
Temwa Chawinga
Age: 28 Country: Malawi
Club: Kansas City Position: Forward
Chawinga has established herself as one of the world's most prolific forwards.
Her impact on the National Women's Soccer League is clear. Her extraordinary form helped Kansas City Current clinch the NWSL Shield as the league's top team in the regular season.
Chawinga scored 15 goals in the 2025 season as she became the first player to be named NWSL MVP in back-to-back campaigns. She also won the Golden Boot for the second year in a row.
Those performances earned her a contract extension through until 2029.
Chawinga returned to international football with Malawi for the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations.
Alongside her sister Tabitha, she helped Malawi reach the country's first Wafcon final and - in doing so - qualify for the Women's World Cup for the first time.
Chawinga scored against Nigeria, Egypt, Ghana and Algeria at Wafcon, winning the tournament's Golden Boot with five goals.
Ewa Pajor
Age: 29 Country: Poland
Club: Barcelona Position: Forward
Pajor is widely regarded as a world-class number nine - and it's clear why.
Instrumental as Barcelona won four trophies last season, Pajor scored their first two goals in a 4-0 Champions League final victory over Lyon.
The goals meant she finished as the competition's top scorer, while the result meant she won the Champions League for the first time after losing in five finals - four with Wolfsburg and one with Barcelona.
Pajor also enjoyed an outstanding second season with Barcelona in Liga F, scoring 16 league goals in her 23 appearances and providing five assists. She was a key player as Barca won the domestic treble.
On the international stage, Pajor captains Poland as is the team's leading goalscorer.
Alexia Putellas
Age: 32 Country: Spain
Club: London City Lionesses Position: Midfielder
Putellas showed again this year why she is one of the most influential footballers in the world.
After 14 years with Barcelona, she delivered a spectacular final season with the club - helping them win four major trophies.
Her 14 goal contributions in 11 Champions League appearances helped her childhood club win the competition for the fourth time, and she remained a decisive figure bringing experience and leadership when it mattered most.
Putellas delayed announcing her move to London City Lionesses to avoid creating a distraction, but in July 2026 she completed that transfer, saying the club's "women-only identity and ambition" were important factors.
Internationally, Putellas was instrumental in Spain retaining the Women's Nations League in late 2025, scoring three goals against Sweden in the semi-finals before being named player of the finals as Spain defeated Germany 3–0.
Last month she was awarded a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or.
Alessia Russo
Age: 27 Country: England
Club: Arsenal Position: Forward
Russo has proven to once again be a trusted and integral attacking force for Arsenal, while remaining a key player for England.
She scored 13 WSL goals last season to finish second in the league's scoring charts, and also added six assists in her 22 appearances. In total, she registered 24 goals and eight assists across all competitions.
Among the highlights of her season was winning the inaugural Women's Champions Cup with Arsenal, beating Corinthians 3- 2 after extra time.
It was the first competitive trophy Arsenal's women's team had lifted at the Emirates, though they finished runners-up to Manchester City in the WSL.
Russo remains a first-choice striker for England and in April scored her 30th senior international goal to move into the top 10 of Lionesses goalscorers.
She was also nominated for the PFA Player of the Year award.
Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw
Age: 29 Country: Jamaica
Club: Manchester City Position: Forward
After a fine year, Shaw has positioned herself as one of the world's elite forwards.
The defining striker in Manchester City's Women Super League title-winning campaign, she scored 21 goals in 22 league appearances, won a record third consecutive WSL Golden Boot and was named WSL Player of the Season.
Her goals were central to City ending a 10-year wait for the league title.
They went on to complete the Double, with Shaw scoring the opening goal in their FA Cup final victory over Brighton at Wembley to finish the season with 26 goals in all competitions.
She also reached a major personal milestone in December 2025 when she became the first player in the history of City's professional women's team to score 100 goals.
Amid uncertainty over her future, Shaw announced at City's end-of-season celebrations that she had signed a new four-year contract through to 2030.

Actor Ranveer Singh and boAt cofounder Aman Gupta have teamed up to launch H.I.M (Handsome Indian Man), a men's personal care brand that says its products are formulated for Indian male skin, local climate, and biology. The brand has debuted with eight products across face, body and hair, priced between ₹299 and ₹899. It claims that each product is powered by IN·XT™, a proprietary molecule developed exclusively for H.I.M. The range is available on the brand's website, Amazon and Blinkit. The launch seems to be a part of Gupta's broader plans to build a portfolio of consumer ventures through his venture studio OFF/BEAT, which aims to back new ideas and emerging founders. OFF/BEAT raised ₹100 Cr in a seed funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners in April this year. According to the brand, men account for nearly half of India's population but contribute less than a tenth of the country's beauty and personal care spending. It said products for men have largely been adapted from formulations originally developed for other consumers. H.I.M aims to address this gap with products designed around Indian male skin and local environmental conditions, including heat, humidity, pollution and hard water. It said its formulations draw on research into Indian male skin, including an all-male research panel. Its proprietary molecule is designed to improve the penetration of skincare ingredients. Speaking about the launch, Singh said he realised that existing personal care products were not necessarily formulated for Indian skin, weather and water conditions. He added that he worked with scientists to develop the formulations and tested them from the initial samples through to the final products. Gupta said Indian men are increasingly becoming conscious of skincare, reading product labels and adopting personal care routines. He cited an 850% increase in searches for men's skincare routines over the past five years. H.I.M’s debut range includes a face wash, moisturiser, and sunscreen for face care, an exfoliating body wash, hydrating lotion, and exfoliating soap bar for body care, and a 2-in-1 shampoo and conditioner marketed for hard-water protection and a scalp serum for fuller-looking hair. With the launch, the cofounders are looking to tap into India's growing men's grooming market. Rising disposable incomes, growing awareness of personal wellness and appearance, and the expansion of ecommerce channels are among the key factors driving the market. According to IMARC Group, the country's male grooming products market is estimated to grow from $2.62 Bn in 2026 to $4.46 Bn by 2034.

How to put your iPad in recovery mode (with and without a home button)
A failed update or a forgotten passcode doesn't have to mean the end of your iPad.
Many iPad problems can be fixed with a simple restart, but sometimes that's not enough. Severe issues with the tablet's software can make it completely inoperable, and in these cases, putting the iPad in recovery mode might be your only option.
Recovery mode also lets you connect your iPad to your computer to update it, or in the worst-case scenario, restore it to its factory default settings. It's best to save recovery mode for when nothing else works, but when it's needed, it can mean the difference between a bricked iPad and one that works just like new.
There are a few situations when you might want to use recovery mode. Major software updates can sometimes fail, leaving you with a partially installed update that keeps your iPad from turning on. Your iPad might reboot itself continuously, or you might enter the wrong passcode too many times and get locked out. Your computer might also stop recognizing your iPad, or your iPad might show a screen prompting you to connect it to a computer.
Updating or restoring your iPad with recovery mode
To put your iPad in recovery mode, first connect it to your computer with a USB cable, and open Finder on Mac or the Apple Devices app on PC. From here, the process differs based on whether your iPad has a home button or not. If it does, hold the home and the power button down at the same time. Eventually, your iPad screen will go black and then show the Apple logo. Finally, it will show the recovery mode icon: an image of a USB cable connecting to a computer. Now release the buttons.
Newer iPads, like the iPad Pro, don't have a home button, so you need to use the power and volume buttons instead. First press and release the volume up button and then the volume down button. Next, press and hold the power button, and keep holding it through the Apple logo until the recovery mode icon appears. Then let go.
At this point, you can use the Finder or Apple Devices on your computer to find your iPad. If the process worked, you should see a pop-up explaining that the iPad needs to be restored or updated. It's best to start with the update option, which will allow your computer to reinstall iPadOS without affecting anything else stored on your device.
If this option is successful, you'll be able to use your iPad again without losing any data. If it doesn't work, though, you'll have to put it back in recovery mode and choose the restore option. This will restore the iPad to its factory settings, completely erasing your data in the process.
You can restore everything from your most recent backup (if you have enough iCloud storage), but it's a far more disruptive process that should only be used as a last resort. If your iPad still isn't working after trying both options or you can't get it to enter recovery mode, it may be time to get it professionally repaired or shop for a new iPad.

The searches targeted premises linked to Sanjeev Kumar Sharma in a disproportionate assets case, The Indian Express reported. Sharma is an assistant director at the Satpura Tiger Reserve. Teams from the Lokayukta’s Bhopal division searched three premises linked to Sharma. They searched his government accommodation and office in Narmadapuram district. They also searched his private residence in Chhindwara district. The Lokayukta obtained search warrants from a court after registering an FIR against Sharma, according to Express. The teams seized ₹26.36 lakh in cash and 2.5 kg of gold. Officials valued the gold at ₹3.5 crore. Gold accounted for nearly half the provisional value of the assets identified during searches. Officials estimated Ecotel Resort’s value at about ₹2 crore. They valued Serenity The Villa at an estimated ₹1 crore. Both properties will undergo formal valuation, Express added. They suspect some assets were acquired in the names of Sharma’s wife and other individuals. The FIR cites Sections 13(1)(b) and 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. This is the bikepacking version of Big Agnes's popular Copper Spur tent. The only difference, aside from color, is that the pole segments on this model are shorter (to make it easier to store on a bike). The Copper Spur line is very nearly the lightest freestanding tent around (it's just slightly heavier than the Hornet above), and if you happen to use it with trekking poles you get what I think is the best feature, the covered awning modification for the vestibule. While this is the best deal, the 2-person model is also on sale for 20% off.
Sleeping Bad and Sleeping Pad Deals
This is one of my favorite ultralight sleeping bags. There are lighter quilts out there, but when you need the warmth of a mummy bag on those colder nights, this is what I use. It also has the smallest pack size of any bag I've tested in this temperature range. With the included compression sack, this thing is truly tiny. The down fill is PFC-free, 850+ hydrophobic down. The zippers are on the small side, but they slide well and rarely (if ever) snag on the bag. I've slept in this bag down to 20 degrees and never been the least bit cold.
Closed-cell-foam pads like the Therm-a-Rest Z-Lite Sol are a must-have. They weigh next to nothing (10 ounces for the small), fold up small enough to lash to the outside of any pack, and double as a chair, extra padding on cold nights, table, you name it. I am too old and too soft to be the sort of ultra-minimalist who gets by with just a Z-Lite, but I still have one around on almost every trip I take.
Nemo's Tensor-insulated sleeping pads have the best R-value-to-weight ratio of anything I've tested. The Tensor All-Season featured here sports an R-value of 5.4 and weighs 18.2 ounces. That alone is impressive, but what I love about the Tensor is that it's thick, comfortable, and most importantly, nearly silent. The lighter Trail model is also on sale at REI. Its R-value is only 2.8 though.
Deals on Camping and Backpacking Gear
I don't usually bring a chair backpacking, I just sit on the ground, but for some reason I do love a chair when I'm bikepacking, which is where I've used this Nemo the most. It's quite pricey, but it's very light and packs down to a tiny package. The genius part of this chair is that the cover is also a mat that keeps it from sinking into soft ground.
The thing to keep in mind when you shop REI brand gear is the company's basic proposition: you get 90 percent of the designer item for 70 percent of the price. It's a strategy that works quite well and has generated some really great, affordable gear. This chair is a good example of that. It's not as nice as the Nemo above, but it's still comfortable (it does wobble a little, side to side when you move) and half the price.
I sincerely hope you never have any need for one of these Sea to Summit bug head nets, but if you do, boy do you. I once did not have one, and tried to go backpacking in Michigan's UP in early May. I lasted about two hours. When I got home I bought one of these and... still haven't ventured back to that marshy bog of hike, but I could, and possibly even retain some of my sanity thanks to this thing.
What I said about the chair above goes for this pack as well, it's an excellent value, especially on sale. I was surprised by how comfortable this thing is, especially because, to look at it, the straps are very lightweight and there's almost no padding. It still managed to carry loads up to 10 pounds without straining the shoulders, and the side stash pockets are fabulously large—big enough for a Nalgene bottle or rain jacket. The Flash 22 is made of 70-denier recycled ripstop nylon, which is on the lighter side, but mine has held up well, even coming through some rough canyon hikes in Utah without any more than mud stains.
These two pots are my go-to cooking vessels for larger group meals. I find they're just about perfect for boiling up enough water to re-hydrate four servings. I don't take the bowls and silverware into the backcountry, but they're handy for camping.
The Stash is our favorite all-in-one backcountry cook system. The heat diffuser design is what speeds up boil times (Jetboil claims 2.5 minutes, which I was only able to match indoors in still air), but the real appeal here to me is the way this kit all packs down into itself. For weekend trips, this is the simplest system I've tested when it comes to cooking for two.
These dry bags from Sea to Summit have double-stitched, tape-sealed seams that have held up well over the years. I also really like the external lash loops that make it easy to strap to anything with a tie-down anchor.
I like these dry bags for organizing things in my pack. They're not dry bags in the sense that you can submerge them and your gear will be fine, but the 30D silnylon with PCF-free DWR sheds a little rain no problem and makes finding your stuff easy, so long as you use different colors for each thing. I put all my cooking gear in a red bag (red for fire), all my water filtering stuff in a blue bag for, wait for it, water, and so on. I find the 3 and 5 liter bags the most useful, but you can get all the way up to 35L.
I've noticed that, when trying to lighten their load with a smaller, lighter weight backpack, people then struggle to fit all their gear. The answer for sleeping bags and clothing is this compression stuff sack, which takes my favorite sleeping bag (the Sea to Summit Spark above) and smashes it down to about half the size of the included stuff sack. You can do the same thing to clothing, especially puffer jackets, but also fleece and merino to some extent, to free up more room in your pack.
REI’s Big Haul duffel is a durable, water-resistant, gear-swallowing bag for carrying, well, just about everything. It's one of our favorite ways to schlep your gear when flying. It hits the right balance of robust build materials and pockets without being too heavy to lug around all day. The strap system is cleverly customizable, and you can convert it to a backpack.
Once upon a time, in a galaxy far, far away, I traveled around Southeast Asia with an early version of this Osprey pack, living out of it for almost a year. It stood up well to the abuse of overland travel—more than once, I watched a bus driver tie it to the roof of a bus by cinching it down with a rope, pulling with all his weight right down the middle of my pack, like a cheese cutter. The Farpoint survived, and my gear inside did as well, thanks in part to the thickly padded sides, which provide considerable extra cushioning.

I don’t go into any given week at WIRED assuming I’ll be thinking much about extramarital affairs. But last week, they were the only thing on my mind.
These thoughts, of course, were prompted by Jensen Huang. In the span of a few completely insane days, the billionaire CEO and cofounder of Nvidia went from being a globally influential Silicon Valley executive to a lesson in exactly what not to do if you want to keep your job, and the extraordinary power that comes with it. It’s a damn mess—for Huang and his family, sure, but also for Nvidia, the AI industry the company is instrumental in powering, and the entirety of the global economy.
WIRED’s senior correspondent Lauren Goode has spent years reporting on Nvidia and Huang, including interviewing the man himself on multiple occasions. She also spent last week breaking news about his downfall, despite being in Europe on vacation. (Sorry, Lauren. You can have those PTO days back.) So at the end of a very long week for WIRED’s newsroom, I called Lauren to talk about what she makes of Huang’s ouster, what it means for AI, and where this all goes next. We also made a bet about Huang’s future—one involving a meal he recently made semi-famous.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
KATIE DRUMMOND: Lauren, first of all, thank you for your tirelessness these past few days. The last time I saw you, we were both in Miami for WIRED’s big event, and you were getting on a red-eye that night to go to Europe for vacation, which didn’t exactly go as planned. When you saw that first story about Jensen’s affair on Sunday, what did you think? What went through your mind?
LAUREN GOODE: Oof. The story first started bubbling up a while ago because The New York Times, and a lot of credit is due to The New York Times here, first reported on Nvidia’s relationship, if you want to call it that, with this company Megaspeed, back in the fall of 2025.
It was a very unusual story. And for some reason it just didn’t capture the attention of people the way that more recent reporting that we and others have been doing has.
Anyone who’s sort of been paying attention to that story, or had some sources in the industry, were starting to hear things. But the fact that the affair with this person, who goes by Alice Huang, was confirmed, that’s the kind of story that always captures people’s attention in a different way.
There are few things people love to read about more than extramarital affairs, especially when they involve powerful people. The reason it wasn’t surprising to you, was it because of that previous reporting and what you had been hearing here and there? Or was there another reason that you saw that story and thought, “OK, actually some of this is not shocking to me”?
It was both. I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but in the fall of 2024 we were doing a WIRED outing, a few of us hanging out, and we started chatting about whether or not we thought a lot of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley had girlfriends or extramarital affairs or situations. Because there are some people in Silicon Valley who are actually quite open about that. I remember us talking about it at the time, and there’s part of me that always kind of assumes that there are elements of their personal lives that we’re never going to have a full window into.
Not that we were talking about Jensen that evening, but it’s always been in my mind. Then, yes, I think being on the ground in Silicon Valley, you often hear things. But a lot of times there’s a certain threshold that things have to cross in order for us as journalists to consider something reportable or something worth chasing down as reportable.
I think an important distinction is that people cheat, people have affairs all the time, Silicon Valley or otherwise.
Right.
What tips this over into newsworthiness is, A) the Chinese espionage of it all, and B) the affair with a subordinate.
You reported that Jensen’s resignation—which really, to be clear, is the board of Nvidia ousting him—probably had more to do with the alleged affair with a subordinate than this other extramarital relationship, which is tied up in espionage allegations. A source told you this. Can you explain why that affair would tip the balance for the board?
I just think it’s important to note that this doesn’t seem like it was simply a moral decision. Someone had posted on X that “I can't believe the board caved to moral pressure.” To me, this doesn’t seem like it’s a moral issue.
I think if you’re looking at the three things that could have led to serious scrutiny of Jensen Huang’s behavior, there’s: One, extramarital affairs. Two, alleged extramarital affairs with subordinates within his own company. And three, an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese operative, which puts Jensen Huang in this position where the board and the investigators who are looking into this are trying to determine what he knew and when he knew it, and basically whether he was aware of the fact that chips were making their way into China.
This isn’t just about the fact that someone had a girlfriend outside of their marriage. I think what is still to be revealed here could in fact be very, very serious in nature.
Now, you also reported on Monday, in a fantastic scoop for WIRED, that Jensen hired a crisis comms firm a year ago. In October 2025 he hired a fixer, Risa Heller, who is very well known for working with high-profile men who are facing allegations of sexual misconduct, among other things. I’m talking about Anthony Weiner, Mario Batali, writer Jeffrey Toobin. Tell us a little bit about that story and what you found out.
I really feel like with everything else going on this week, I could have gone without ever hearing about all of those stories again.
Oh, you don’t want to hear about Anthony Weiner all the time?
No, it turns out. I had kind of forgotten that. I was like, “I think I blocked that from my memory.” And Jeff Toobin—what a throwback.
Yes.
But this firm, it’s a really interesting firm run by this woman named Risa Heller. They have offices in New York and LA, and yes, they have this reputation for dealing with a lot of sexual misconduct cases, as well as other types of corporate and personal PR needs for high-profile people.
A source had told me a while ago, and I’m not gonna timestamp it, but a while ago that it had been rumored that Jensen Huang had hired this firm. So immediately my antenna went up, and I was like, “Wait, what?”
I thought it was curious, but I didn’t know exactly what the nature of the contract was or when they had been hired, and then eventually through more reporting, I was able to get confirmation of some of the details.
What we know is that this firm, Heller, started working with Jensen Huang sometime in 2025, and ostensibly, Huang and his family had hired Heller for their own personal PR outside of Nvidia’s walls. This is because when you’re someone like Jensen Huang, you have a lot going on. You have a family office. You do a lot of work with philanthropy. You’re hosting personal events. He’s also been grooming his adult children to take over these higher profile roles within Nvidia, so some of the PR might have ostensibly been to work on creating more of a public-facing image for his kids.
We do know, though, based on more reporting, that as of October 2025, and then closer to the end of the year, Nvidia’s internal teams had been instructed to start looping this outside crisis firm, Heller, into all press inquiries, all communications related to Jensen.
That was definitely a change from the prior terms of his working relationship with Heller, and also timing-wise coincided with that first New York Times story I mentioned. I think that it was published on October 9th, 2025, and first highlighted Megaspeed and what appeared to be a very close relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang.
I can’t decide if he should get his money back for hiring this crisis comms firm, because this crisis has certainly not been contained, or if the fact that this is now coming up a year later suggests that maybe they did their job quite well for a while.
Well, first of all, I don’t think he needs the money back.
I don’t know, depends on how …
… on how his assets get divided, yes. Or if maybe they won’t divorce. You know, it’s also a very Silicon Valley thing not to necessarily do that.
I also think it’s possible that Jensen himself was not totally upfront with this firm when he hired them. Or, if they knew something was up, they may not have known all of the details. So if that is the case, hypothetically, then you can’t necessarily do everything you would typically do in terms of reputation management. TL;DR, it didn’t work out so well for him in the end.
No, things are not going well for Jensen. Now, Nvidia has named an interim CEO to replace him. Surprise, surprise, to both of us and women everywhere, she’s a woman.
It’s a woman.
What do we know about Colette Kress, who is the interim CEO of Nvidia?
Well, we know that when we emailed Jensen this summer to say, “Hey, Jensen, who do you think the most powerful women in Silicon Valley are?” He didn't mention Colette. Jensen mentioned Dina Powell from Meta and Ruth Porat from Google, both really high-ranking women, presidents of those companies.
And then [SpaceX president and COO] Gwynne Shotwell, because I prompted him. But no Colette, and that struck me as interesting at the time, too, though I didn’t press him on that. And then we did end up giving Colette a nod in our big feature that we did about high-ranking women in Silicon Valley.
Colette has been with Nvidia since 2013. Prior to that, she worked at Cisco, Microsoft. She’s CFO. She’s a financial whiz. She’s the person who appears on earnings calls with him every quarter.
She actually does a lot of the speaking, because she’s a person who has really, really deep knowledge of Nvidia’s complex financials. She’s the person who gives guidance for the next quarter. She’s CFO of arguably the world’s most important company. I think it makes sense that she would be slotted into this role.
Nvidia doesn’t really have a traditional hierarchy. They don’t have a traditional chief operating officer, for example. You know, when Steve Jobs was at the end of his tenure and he was very sick, Tim Cook, who was the operations whiz at Apple for many years prior, was basically groomed to be the CEO.
Nvidia doesn’t have someone like that. So it makes sense for now that Colette is the person who would slot in, because part of Nvidia’s goal has to be, at this point, easing the stock market. I don’t know if you’ve been following, but, I mean, it’s pretty bad out there.
I would say that, against my will, I am seeing a lot about Nvidia stock not doing well. I have not looked at my 401(k). I try really hard not to because I’m a control freak, and I simply cannot control how many affairs this man is having and what impact that has on my finances.
These things, though, help paint a picture of Jensen’s character and the way he ran the company. The fact that Nvidia did not do succession planning. There was no hierarchy; he had dozens of direct reports. There was no successor waiting in the wings. What do those things combined tell us about Jensen and Nvidia?
As I understand it, Katie, even you have had to do a succession plan, right?
Yes, without revealing too many details, Condé Nast, like most normal companies, has people in senior leadership roles do succession planning. They take it really seriously. It’s an annual exercise that we do, and my understanding is that that is very par for the course at most companies, at any company, and particularly a company of Nvidia’s stature and importance on a global scale. The idea that there would not be a formal succession plan is shocking to me.
It is shocking, and it’s shocking not just from the perspective that Jensen perhaps didn’t do that or didn’t have a super well-formulated one, but that the board wouldn’t demand that. I’ve heard a few different theories floated as to why this is. One theory is that Jensen may have had a lot of the insecurities that come with being a cofounder, CEO, someone who’s been living and breathing this company, his baby, since 1993, and not necessarily wanting to stuff the ranks with people who are just as capable, if not more capable in some measures, than himself, right?
Like you don’t create an environment in which someone could theoretically replace you that easily. So that’s one theory. The other theory is that—and Jensen himself has said this, both to me and other people in interviews too—he truly believed that keeping a flat org was better for the flow of information, that once you start to create a structure that’s too hierarchical, then any kind of changes that happen in the company, any kind of new information that comes out, even in some kind of white paper, fundamentally changes the direction of the way the industry is going.
I mean, think about the way people inside the AI industry probably reacted when they first saw the famous Transformer paper in 2017 and said, “Oh my gosh, this is going to change everything.” If you’re a big, fat, bloated, slow organization, you’re probably five years behind on your AI strategy. If you’re lean at the top, you can basically say, “Let’s go. We’re going in this direction now,” and you won’t encounter a lot of barriers to doing that. So that helps explain the flat org. It doesn’t necessarily explain the lack of a succession plan.
The third theory that’s been floated to me is that maybe in some, I don’t know, alternate universe, he really did think that his children, one of his two children, who are both working within Nvidia, would one day be the inevitable successors.
You have met Jensen several times. You’ve corresponded with him, you’ve interviewed him, you published a cover story for WIRED that featured an excellent interview with him. You published an edition of our newsletter, Backchannel, at the end of last week with a little bit about this. In it you talk about one experience you had interviewing Jensen at a conference. You wrote, “Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me.” You describe him as obsessed with controlling the narrative.
Again, we’re coming back to this theme of control. I’m curious to hear a little bit more about that observation, this idea of Jensen as fixated on storytelling and the stories that were told about Nvidia and about AI.
That particular interview was July of 2024, and Nvidia had invited me to interview Jensen again at the SIGGRAPH Conference in Denver, which is this whole confab of computer graphics nerds. It’s a really fun conference.
During the preparation for it, when I got on the call with some Nvidia comms executives, Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter, appeared on the call and she basically took the lead and said, “Here’s this cluster of slides that when you’re on stage, Jensen’s going to be referencing, and he’s gonna have a lot to say about each slide, and it would be great if you could tee him up at this point.”
And I said, “Well, wait a second. This is not a standard journalistic interview. Like, what’s going on here?” The whole thing felt very strange, but I made it clear I planned to ask him the questions I really felt I needed to ask him as a journalist. It was just very clear he did not want to answer a lot of my questions, and that he was going to just own the stage and reference his slides. I remember that he talked about how he made a little Jensen AI of himself, and the crowd was all, “Ha! Jensen AI,” and I was like, “What is happening?”
It was so strange. Afterwards, he did this impromptu Q&A with the crowd. A bunch of people rushed the stage. I could see someone from his PR team being like, “What just happened? What is he doing?” Not standard operating procedure. I thought, wow. It felt to me like Jensen Huang was just riding high on this wave, this AI wave and this incredible success that Nvidia was experiencing and the way the AI industry was growing.
Right.
But it occurred to me that he was really, really obsessive with controlling the narrative, and it reminded me of something that he’d said the first time we’d ever spoken, which was that he really admired the CEO of Adobe because he felt that the CEO of Adobe was a very good storyteller, and that he never had a pitch deck when he first pitched Nvidia as a company because he just thought it was better to tell a story.
Storytelling is so important in terms of establishing the culture of a company. He was very good at creating his own story, his own image of himself as this founder CEO who was utterly obsessed with his own company and really passionate about everything.
I guess we know where some of that passion led him.
We do indeed. It’s interesting that you talk about Jensen as a crowd favorite, because he did very much become that. He’s incredibly charismatic. He’s a great public speaker. He can really own a room. He can spin a great yarn. You describe in the cover story about Jensen, that you were “Jensen-pilled” after spending time with him, because he is so compelling.
That was interesting to me this week, in seeing how many leaders in Silicon Valley came out in support of him, despite these very, very troubling allegations, which to be clear, again, go beyond having an affair. This is beyond moral decision-making. Regardless of that, everyone from Elon Musk to Jason Calacanis came out guns blazing for Jensen.
Do you think that speaks to how revered he is in the industry, or do you think that that speaks to the fact that he is mission-critical for the industry’s ongoing growth? Are these defenses of Jensen essentially self-interested on the part of industry leaders?
I don't think they’re all self-interested. There are at least three layers to this, and one is that there are executives and lower-level tech workers who have worked for Jensen directly, and who came away from the experience with not a great taste in their mouths. They left feeling uninspired, and they actually saw a more egotistical side of him that they didn’t like, an obsessive side. There have been stories reported by other outlets about how he has sometimes berated some of his top lieutenants in front of other people. There’s almost a Dr. Jensen and Mr. Huang narrative here. He’s got two sides to him. But he’s very smart and almost can come across as sort of mensch-y. I think people really admire him.
Then I think, yes, there are people who probably own Nvidia stock, they’re industry watchers, they’re tech enthusiasts, and they see him perhaps still as a kind of our generation’s rock star who also happens to be keeping the economy afloat with his company.
So there are varying levels of interest there in terms of people who just either wish this didn’t happen, or really wish in some alternate universe he would be reinstated, which would be shocking to me at this point.
I will say WIRED had a great scoop last week, much credit to our amazing journalists, of Nvidia employees who would like to see Jensen back. There is a great deal of reverence for him, in a way that I have to admit gave me acute flashbacks to 2023, when Sam Altman was ousted at OpenAI. Very different circumstances, but yet again, a woman was installed to clean up that mess, and employees revolted and called for Sam to come back. I mean, these allegations are much more significant and serious and consequential. That said, the jury’s still out on whether Jensen makes a comeback in two weeks.
Really? You think there’s a possibility?
I think there’s a possibility.
Wow. OK. I would be very surprised. We should make a bet.
I was gonna say we should bet.
A GPU?
Oh, Lauren. I was going to say dinner the next time I’m in San Francisco.
Dinner sounds good. Let’s do it. You know what? Whoever loses the bet has to buy dinner at Proposition Chicken, which according to, was it the Daily … ?
It was the Daily Mail.
The Daily Mail reported that Proposition Chicken, which is a slightly elevated fast food chicken place in San Francisco, was being delivered to Jensen Huang’s house in Pacific Heights the other day.
OK. I’m in. Two weeks from today, we will see.
Two weeks from today.
I want to ask you lastly about ripple effects. Nvidia has invested in or bought outright plenty of AI startups. It finances a lot of the build-out happening in this industry. I have been stomping around the New York office all week screaming things like, “The global economy, the global economy!” I mean, this is much bigger than just this company, right? So what are the industry effects that we should all be watching out for from here?
What I’ve heard so far from people is that in the short term—even though we’re seeing this dip right now—there’s still just such incredible demand for Nvidia chips, and they plan everything basically 18 to 24 months out in terms of producing those chips, that I don’t think we’ll see any really serious softness in Nvidia in the short term.
But I think that the long tail of Nvidia is going to be interesting, because another CEO could come in with a totally different approach to how Nvidia spends its capital and how it also makes investments in outside companies.
Would a new CEO come in right now and make the kind of investment in CoreWeave or Perplexity, for example, that Jensen decided to? Quite possibly no. Would the new CEO come in and decide to spend so much on, let’s say, Nvidia’s healthcare division? We don’t really know. Would the new CEO come in and be as much of an open source booster as Jensen Huang had become? We don’t really know.
It’s just hard to say. The guys at Hugging Face are probably quite happy that they got in when they did.
Another thing that Jensen had set Nvidia on the path of in the past couple years was really investing in what they’re doing with CPUs as well as GPUs, which is an area that Intel and AMD are in, as well as Arm.
Was that the right path to set the company on, to over-index a little bit on CPUs for now because of the ways that the AI industry is shifting from training on high-powered GPUs to inference computing on slightly lower-powered CPUs? I think it was a smart move, but let’s see how that shakes out.
I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but back in 2008, shortly after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, a venture capitalist at Sequoia sent around a pitch deck to all of that firm’s portfolio companies that became very famous in the industry, and it’s called “RIP Good Times.”
In that pitch deck, this very prescient VC basically laid out all of the things that they wanted their portfolio companies to do, which meant saving a lot of cash. Like, this is a gird-your-loins moment. I think if we see something like that kind of mentality start to develop in Silicon Valley in the coming weeks and months, then I think that’s a very big indication that people are genuinely worried about what this Nvidia tumble means.
I am going to ask you to make one final prediction.
OK. I’m very bad at predictions, by the way, but please.
Two years ago, you said, “Huang is the man of the hour. The year. Maybe even the decade.” I would argue that that decade has been cut short, but I also think that someone like Jensen doesn’t just go quietly into the night. If he’s not reinstalled at Nvidia, and I’m wrong, and I’m buying your chicken in two weeks, where does someone like that go? Where do you expect we will see Jensen pop up in a year, in two years?
There’s a glib answer and it’s either Jensen goes to jail, or Jensen starts a podcast. I’m sure he’s hoping right now it’s the podcast outcome.
Sounds great.
Realistically, let’s say that he’s not implicated in the end result of any kind of federal investigation. And let’s say he’s not reinstated. In either case, I don’t think this is the last we’re going to hear from Jensen Huang.

With the Air Quality Index (AQI) crossing 400 at some locations in Delhi, people whose work keeps them outdoors for long hours say they are experiencing breathing difficulties, persistent cough, headaches and burning eyes, often without adequate protection against pollution.
For traffic police personnel, domestic workers, roadside vendors, mechanics and gig workers, staying indoors is rarely an option.
Yogendra Kumar, a traffic inspector posted in outer north Delhi, said pollution-related health risks for traffic personnel persists throughout the year but increases significantly when air quality deteriorates.
“The impact on health is inevitable in the outskirts, as road dust also contributes to pollution alongside emissions. We have no safeguards apart from masks. Prolonged exposure causes breathing problems and a persistent cough,” he said.
Reena Chaudhary, a domestic worker in Palam Colony, said she began experiencing breathing difficulties on the night before Deepavali, with her symptoms worsening on the festival day.
“I leave home around 7 a.m. and return by 9 p.m. I began having headaches and burning eyes the day before Deepavali, particularly while passing through smoke-filled lanes between houses at night. On Deepavali, my condition worsened. I felt dizzy throughout the day, had a persistent cough and just wanted to lie down. But who would work if I did?” she said.
Ms. Chaudhary said she had to walk through smoke on Deepavali night with her dupatta wrapped around her face. Since then, she has been taking her daughter along in case she falls ill and is unable to work.
Ravi, a 21-year-old gig worker who attends college during the day, said he works through the night, picking up rides across the city to support his family.
“Even at night, I can see that the air is dense and heavy. At times, I have to stop near a green area, such as Vande Mataram Marg, just to be able to breathe,” he said.
Mukesh Yadav, an e-rickshaw driver in Palam, said road dust remains a problem throughout the year, apart from smoke from firecrackers and vehicular emissions.
“The area remains dusty even on normal days. Since Deepavali, I have been tying a towel around my face,” he said.
Mr. Yadav works eight to 10 hours a day, making several trips between Palam metro station and Kailashpuri, a one-kilometre stretch that witnesses heavy traffic.
“The only time I am not outdoors is when I am charging my e-rickshaw. I thought my cough was due to the cold, but everyone seems to be coughing, even the passengers. It could be due to pollution,” he said.
‘Pollution higher this year’
An analysis by the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) found that Delhi’s average PM2.5 concentration in the week preceding Deepavali reached 236 micrograms per cubic metre, the highest in three years. This was 97% higher than the 120 micrograms per cubic metre recorded in 2025 and 32% above the 179 micrograms per cubic metre recorded in 2024.
The study also found that time-bound restrictions on vehicles had failed to ease traffic congestion, with nitrogen dioxide, a marker of vehicular pollution, accumulating during the evening and remaining elevated until midnight, even after traffic had eased.
“Deepavali pollution is an annual tipping point, but elevated particulate levels before the festival this year show that baseline pollution is higher than in previous years,” said Anumita Roychowdhury, executive director (research and advocacy) at the CSE.
She said cleaner air ahead of winter and measures to contain episodic pollution spikes from farm fires and firecrackers could have prevented such severe pollution during seasonal weather changes.

Federal officials on Thursday announced new funding to explore the medical potential of ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic drug championed by veterans, conservative lawmakers and podcasters aligned with President Donald Trump.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said his department is awarding up to $4.9 million to prepare for the first U.S. studies of ibogaine for post-traumatic stress disorder, a hard-to-treat condition linked to higher suicide and substance abuse rates among veterans.
The money will not go directly to patient research, Kennedy said, but to lay the groundwork needed to manufacture, dose and design studies of the drug.
Ibogaine is made from a shrub native to West Africa. It can cause intense hallucinations, nausea, vomiting, tremors and sometimes deadly irregular heart rhythms. Ibogaine is currently illegal, in the same ultra-restrictive class as LSD, ecstasy and most other psychedelic drugs.
Veterans organisations and psychedelic advocates contend that ibogaine has great promise for intractable conditions such as PTSD, severe depression and opioid addiction. U.S. research on the drug has essentially been frozen for decades due to ibogaine's restricted status.
Kennedy said the government will receive data and treatment guidance from Beond Inc., a Texas-based company that has treated more than 3,000 patients with ibogaine in Mexico, where the drug is not illegal.
“That is going to allow us to dramatically accelerate the clinical trial process,” Kennedy said. “We’re going to have, I think, a record drug approval process.”
Additional funding awards may explore ibogaine's use for addiction, he said.
Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins, who joined Kennedy for the announcement, said the collaborative effort would focus first on safety and “best-in-class research.”
“For veterans living with PTSD, we owe them both urgency and the best science we can produce,” Collins said.
Kennedy and Collins have previously voiced support for the potential of psychedelics, citing the experiences of veterans who have traveled abroad for therapy with ibogaine and other mind-altering substances.
Thursday's announcement was previewed in April, when Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to speed up review and research of psychedelics that could help with mental health conditions.
Three applications for psychedelics are pending review at the Food and Drug Administration. They include the first potential medicines made from psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, and MDMA, also called ecstasy. Decisions on those drugs could come within weeks or months.
Because of its safety risks, ibogaine research has moved more slowly.
The little data currently available mostly comes from patients who have traveled to Mexico or other countries where ibogaine is not heavily regulated. Ibogaine clinics typically charge $10,000 to $20,000 for one course of treatment, which often involves monitoring of a patient's heart readings while emergency medical workers are on standby.
Trump's order on psychedelics came after podcaster Joe Rogan said he texted Trump about ibogaine, which he repeatedly has discussed on his show. According to Rogan, the president quickly responded: “Sounds great. Do you want FDA approval? Let’s do it.”

Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has agreed to pay a quarter-of-a-billion dollars to begin the clean-up of the toxic Panguna mine site it abandoned more than three decades ago.
Panguna, once one of the world’s most profitable gold and copper mines, was shuttered in 1989 after violent protests over environmental damage and the inequitable division of the mine’s profits sparked a decade-long civil war on the Papua New Guinean island of Bougainville.
But the sprawling mine pit, once a mountain, remains a scar in the middle of the island, with vast pillars of rubble at risk of collapse, and polluted rivers running bright blue with toxins.
Rio Tinto was forced from the island and has never returned, but in recent years has been part of a detailed consultation process with landowners and government. It has now agreed to voluntarily contribute US$250m (A$370m) towards the remediation of the mine site.
Theonila Roka Matbob, a cabinet minister in Bougainville’s autonomous government and Panguna community leader, said the fund was a vital contribution towards repairing the “devastation left by the Panguna mine”.
“We have a lot of work still ahead of us, but the establishment of this fund gives us the chance to find solutions to the huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation.
“No amount of money will restore the damage caused to the environment in Panguna, but this sets a foundation for us to invest in addressing the environmental issues and invest in our children’s futures as well.”
Roka Matbob said the most fundamental remediation was to improve “accessibility” for the people living around Panguna – “accessibility to clean drinking water that is safe and secure … and infrastructure, in bridges that makes people’s access to trade, to school, to health[care], much easier. This is one critical area that immediately needs attention.”
The president of Bougainville, Ishmael Toroama, seeking to become the world’s newest head of state at the forefront of a long-running independence movement on the island, said the money would make a “meaningful difference” to villages and communities that had suffered from the impacts of the mine’s pollution.
“This work will deliver benefits not only for people today, but for future generations. Continued engagement with our communities will be essential to ensuring the work responds to local priorities and delivers lasting outcomes.”
The Rio commitment has emerged from the Panguna Mine Legacy Impact Assessment consultation process, which was initiated in response to a human rights complaint brought by the Australian-based Human Rights Law Centre, with Roka Matbob as the lead complainant.
Keren Adams, the HRLC’s legal director, said establishing the fund had taken years of work.
“It is a testament to the courage and persistence of community leaders, and the willingness of all parties to engage in difficult but constructive dialogue,” she said.
“The significant funding contributed by Rio Tinto creates a real opportunity to now address an environmental disaster that has remained unresolved for decades.”
Mark Davies, Rio Tinto’s chief safety and technical officer, said the establishment of the fund was an “important milestone … intended to support the transition from the assessment to practical remedy implementation”.
“Community engagement is an important next step to identify priorities and we remain committed to working with communities to shape the activities supported by the fund.”
The quarter-of-a-billion dollars will not be sufficient to entirely remediate the mine site, but it is being seen as a major step towards rehabilitation.
The funding commitment for Panguna comes at an acutely sensitive time for the restive Bougainville island.
The mine has become inextricably linked with the Bougainville’s political future: restarting operations at Panguna – believed to still hold at least $60bn in unrealised reserves – is seen by many, including the president, as the fundamental financial basis for the island’s independent future. Indian miner Lloyds has been granted a 25-year large-scale mining lease, but any future mining is years from starting.
Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly $2bn from Panguna over 17 years of operation from 1972. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands were destroyed by it.
Disaffected landowners ran a sabotage campaign that forced Panguna’s closure in 1989. The PNG government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war – known as “the crisis” – that ran for a decade. Between 15,000 and 20,000 people were killed, roughly 10% of the island’s population.
A recent environmental impact assessment found the abandoned mine remains an acute threat to people’s lives, including from landslides, levee collapses and floods. Untouched, the river delta will stay polluted for a century.
The future of Bougainville’s independence campaign is now before the PNG parliament, which will decide whether or not to recognise a UN-backed independence referendum held on the island in 2019, in which 97.7% of voters were in favour of Bougainville seceding and becoming an independent country.
The PNG parliament, which heard lengthy and impassioned debate over Bougainville last month, appears almost certain to vote against recognising the referendum result.
But Toroama, who has staked his presidency on achieving political independence, has said, regardless of the parliament’s decision, Bougainville will enter a period of “self-government” from September next year, before seceding, breaking away from PNG as a fully fledged independent nation, by 2030.
