Formula 1's one-race wonders
- Published
You've been handed the chance of a lifetime.
A chance to sit in the cockpit, on the grid, at motorsport's top table: Formula 1. The very pinnacle of everything you've strived for in your whole life.
What would you do?
"I sang the Grand Prix theme tune while I was sat on the grid. I thought I was watching it on telly," says Tiff Needell - one of 166 lucky or unlucky drivers, depending on your standing in motorsport, who graced an F1 race only once.
There are many reasons why a driver may only get one chance to race elite sport's fastest and most sophisticated machines, and, although F1's super subs were more of a feature in the 1960s and 1970s, the helmet-for-hire phenomenon is alive and driving in ultra-professional, modern F1.
Just ask Japan's Ryo Hirakawa, who only last month achieved his "dream", external when he got behind the wheel of a Haas at the Mexican Grand Prix following Esteban Ocon's controversial departure from the team.
"I just need to taste this moment. I'm really happy," Hirakawa said after scoring a point - admittedly, following a few demotions for others. "Just enjoy this moment and see what we can do."
Within a week there was nothing the Toyota factory driver could do as Haas' 2027 driver Rafael Camara was drafted in for the American team early, for the rest of 2026.
Hirakawa is a reserve driver for Haas as a result of the team's association with Toyota - the Japanese being in the right place at the right time.
The percentage of F1 test and reserve drivers who make it to the grid is typically low, and those who do tend to be drafted in for one shot at very unlikely glory.
The days of the aristocrat who fancies a pootle around the track are gone, and years of preparation are required even to be standing in the pit garage.
Injuries, sponsorship fails and outright cheating are just some of the reasons why it does not work out for some hopefuls.
Needell, known better for his time behind the wheel on Top Gear and other auto TV shows, got his big break at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. But his journey to the paddock was initiated a few years earlier - in the media.
"I won a car in a magazine competition," he says. "I was the kid on the terraces, on the fences - and made it on to the grid. We had no money at all in our family, so I was a working civil engineer five days a week and a mechanic in my garage five nights a week. At the weekend I was the van driver, the mechanic and the racing driver.
"I bumbled my way up to the top of the national scene and then got offered a professional drive in Formula 3. And after two years of that I moved up into the [long since defunct] Formula 1 British championship.
"I was out at the Nurburgring trying to get an F1 drive when I got the call. I was hanging around the paddock trying to chat up an F2 team, trying to say I had a sponsor, which of course I didn't.
"Ensign called me and said: 'This weekend would you like to drive?' I rushed home from the Nurburgring in my orange Ford Capri, had half a day's test at Donington and on to qualifying for the Belgian GP at Zolder.
"I got my chance because Clay Regazzoni crashed and hurt his back at Long Beach.
"A lot of that in the olden days was due to injuries - chances would come up when someone had crashed and got injured. It was dangerous back then."
Needell was in, but this was old-school F1 where you had to pre-qualify to show you were fast enough to qualify for the Grand Prix itself.
"There was something like 30 drivers trying to pre-qualify, and somehow I made it to the back of the grid - 23rd in the Ensign. It was so much cheaper then - aluminium chassis and a Cosworth DFV engine and away you go."
While the back of the grid beckoned, a 29-year-old Needell was in very good company in the form of double world champion Emerson Fittipaldi, who was having a bad weekend in his Skol Fittipaldi car.
"I found myself on the back row of the grid, sitting by one of my big heroes. It was all a bit of a dream," says Needell.
In contrast to today's VIP treatment, Needell's parents and his girlfriend (now wife) drove to Belgium in the family car and watched from the crowd as he lined up on the grid.
"When the mechanics started the engine and left me sitting there - me and Emerson - I actually started humming the theme tune [to Fleetwood Mac's The Chain]," Needell says.
"For 12 laps I battled with Emerson for the honour of being last place at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. Then the engine broke."
A failed attempt to qualify for Monaco a week later put the brakes on his F1 dream and eventually resulted in Needell pursuing a career as a Le Mans racer and TV presenter.
Often the reason F1 careers could be so fleeting would be of a driver's own making.
Hans Heyer did not qualify for his one and only race - the 1977 German Grand Prix at Hockenheim - but he thought he would contest it anyway, starting from the pit lane for the ATS team in a car that was never supposed to be there.
The German may have achieved his dream at his home race, but it came with disqualification after he had already retired with gearbox failure on lap nine.
And what of Marco Apicella? It has taken 73 years, since Alberto Ascari triumphed, for Italy to celebrate one of its own F1 world champions in Kimi Antonelli as he secured the 2026 title in Mexico last month.
For a country and a Ferrari team so important to the sport, that is a long time to wait - and Apicella was a good example of why it may have taken a while.
Rushed in at the last minute after only two hours of testing to replace a disgruntled, if experienced, Thierry Boutsen in the underwhelming 1993 Jordan, Apicella lasted approximately 800 metres of his home race after a multi-car collision during the first lap of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.
That was the end of Apicella's F1 career and he would end up embarking on five unsuccessful attempts to win Le Mans.
1 of 5
So what's the best any of the one-hit wonders have done in their first and only grand prix?
There have been a smattering of points finishes over the years, and Dorino Serafini's shared second place on the podium with legend Ascari at Monza in the final race of F1's maiden season is difficult to top for an F1 one-shot.
But Germany's Markus Winkelhock is surely up there as one of sport's super-sub icons of the modern era.
A last-minute replacement in the newly acquired, yet painfully slow, Spyker team's car at the 2007 European Grand Prix at the Nurburgring, the touring car driver took up the F1 super sub's favoured qualifying position on the grid: last place.
F1 ran in Winkelhock's family - father Manfred contested 56 grands prix in the eighties before his death from a crash during a sportscar race in 1985.
But Markus went one better than his uncle Jo, who never contested an F1 race despite trying to qualify seven times.
But, by his own admission, Winkelhock was a long way from ready. "I had one day testing in Silverstone and one day in Paul Ricard," Winkelhock told Motorsport magazine., external
"The first couple of laps it felt like a PlayStation - so unreal, everything was so fast. You're accelerating till you reach the braking point.
"But after all the [practice] sessions I could feel my neck already.
"I told my mechanics to put some beddings on the side of the headrest, in case the neck is completely done, to lean on with the helmet."
Then came some early rain from the Eifel mountains and an inspired decision from the pitwall of a team with very little to lose.
Winkelhock was on exactly the right tyres, at exactly the right time, as the rain came down, and Lewis Hamilton and Jenson Button slid helplessly into the gravel trap along with several others.
Winkelhock's orange Spyker simply danced through the rivers of rainwater flowing across the tarmac, sitting 33 seconds ahead of the field - a country mile for F1.
He said: "I didn't know it was for the lead. I was just driving. At the point they told me, 'You're P1'. I really didn't understand anything that was going on because this race was really crazy."
But when the rain stopped, so did Winklehock - first swallowed up by the faster cars on a drying track, and then by a hydraulic issue on lap 15, having led for six laps.
Make no mistake, a lost F1 career is very often a driver's glittering career in the making in sportscars at Le Mans, or on the ovals of American Indycar.
But even back in the day when other sporting codes, such as rallying's frighteningly fast Group B, were at the height of their popularity, F1 was the pinnacle for most.
"Being a grand prix driver was where you wanted to go," concludes Needell. "But I always had my eye sideways for any other drives.
"Single-seaters are the best cars to drive and they are made and designed to race. And the ultimate is the grand prix car. Everything else is second best.
"I was so proud I got there on no sponsorship and no money. I suppose I was a bit annoyed I couldn't stay for longer.
"But as I always say, 'unluckier than a few, but luckier than millions'."

On 11 November 2026, terrorists reportedly opened fire on a CRPF checkpoint near Mir Bazar in the Kulgam district of Jammu and Kashmir, injuring three personnel. The attackers fled after the firing, and security forces launched a search operation to track them down.
In this context, a video (here & here) is being shared on social media claiming that former Army officer Pravin Sawhney referred to the Kulgam terrorist attack as another “false flag” operation, similar to the Pulwama and Pahalgam attacks. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video depicts genuine footage of former Army officer Pravin Sawhney describing the November 2026 Kulgam terrorist attack as a “false flag” operation.
Fact: The video is an AI-generated deepfake and does not feature Pravin Sawhney. The original footage actually stems from a March 2025 interview on The Wire, where journalist Sushant Singh discusses the 2019 Balakot air strikes. Furthermore, Singh has made no such statements regarding the recent Kulgam attack. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
First, we observed that the interviewee in the video is not ex-Army officer Pravin Sawhney but rather journalist and author Sushant Singh. Next, a reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the original, full-length video uploaded on The Wire’s YouTube channel in March 2025. This video was published 20 months before the Kulgam attack and features journalist Ashutosh Bhardwaj interviewing Sushant Singh to critically assess the February 2019 Balakot air strikes, six years after the event. Singh made no such statements as those heard in the viral video.
Further, we ran the video through AI detection tools and found that the audio has been manipulated using artificial intelligence.
Furthermore, both Sushant Singh and the host, Ashutosh Bhardwaj, have publicly stated that the video is AI-manipulated and completely fabricates their past conversation.
To sum it up, an AI-manipulated video is being falsely shared to claim that an ex-Army officer called Kulgam attack a false flag operation.

Maverick. Loose cannon. Unmanageable.
Mario Balotelli heard it all.
Perhaps better known for off-field antics than his undeniable - yet arguably wasted - talent with the ball at his feet, the Italian has always attracted headlines.
Fifteen years have passed since his famous 'Why always me?' Manchester derby T-shirt celebration, which came just days after a firework was set off in his own bathroom, causing a house fire.
The 36-year-old is still playing, now in the United Arab Emirates first division with Al-Ittifaq alongside his biological brother, Enock Barwuah.
Here, BBC Sport looks at a career that has included 13 clubs, six countries - and an assist for arguably the most famous goal in Premier League history.
Mancini to Mourinho - cracks begin to show
Typical of his unconventional footballing life, Balotelli's career did not begin in an elite club's academy.
Instead, by his mid-teens he was turning out for Italian third-tier side Lumezzane, close to the family home in Concesio.
A trial at Barcelona did not lead to a long-term stay, and instead he was picked up by Inter Milan in 2006.
It was at Inter that Balotelli first came across his great mentor - Roberto Mancini.
The relationship between the two has been likened to that of a father and son. Under the Italian coach's tutelage, Balotelli flourished.
Aged 17, Balotelli helped Inter win the 2007-08 Serie A title and reach the Coppa Italia final, memorably scoring twice against Juventus to send his side into the semi-finals.
Life changed for Balotelli with the arrival of Jose Mourinho in the weeks after that campaign ended.
There would be disagreements, disciplinary action and accusations that Balotelli's attitude was not up to scratch. Mourinho said Balotelli was "unmanageable" and described one performance as "close to a zero rating".
The relationship with Mourinho was fractious - a rare occasion when the Special One was confounded by a player.
Balotelli still won three Serie A titles and one Champions League with Inter, but his reputation as a supposed loose cannon was already beginning to overshadow his feats as a player.
Hitting the headlines in England
Logic dictated that Balotelli's next step should be to reunite with mentor Mancini. That happened in August 2010 when the 20-year-old joined Manchester City.
Mancini set out to show that the unpredictable ways of Balotelli could be harnessed for the team's good, aiming to get more out of him than Mourinho could.
A hardline stance on discipline often appeared to soften when Mancini dealt with Balotelli, who by spring 2011 had garnered a reputation in England as a fantastic footballer who could not stay away from controversy.
Having already been sent off twice for City and been involved in a car crash - not in his famous camouflage Bentley but an Audi R8 - the striker threw a dart at a youth-team player, an act that showed a level of immaturity.
After helping City to win the FA Cup in 2011, ending their 35-year major trophy drought, Balotelli came under scrutiny after attempting a backheel trick shot when through on goal during a pre-season friendly against LA Galaxy.
Mancini swiftly hooked him, later questioning his mentality by saying: "If you are serious, you can play 90 minutes. If not, you can come and sit by me on the bench."
Sometimes the audacity paid off - like the famous shoulder goal and subsequent nonchalant celebration against Norwich.
On other occasions, not so much.
In October 2011, emergency services attended his Cheshire home to deal with a firework lit in his bathroom. Balotelli said a friend had been responsible.
BBC Sport reported at the time that four firefighters used two hose reel water jets to douse the flames, with a large fan deployed to clear smoke.
Days later he was in the spotlight for the right reasons as he scored City's opener in a 6-1 win over Manchester United, celebrating with the 'Why always me?' T-shirt.
There were other stories - that he had given a homeless person £1,000, that he had turned up to a young boy's school to confront the headmaster about the child being bullied, that he drove around Manchester handing out presents while dressed as Santa.
True? Perhaps only Balotelli knows and he has often denied such rumours. But such was his reputation at the time that the stories became plausible.
A chant City fans coined made reference to his ironic allergy to grass - which kept him out of a Europa League match in 2011 - and driving around Moss Side with "a wallet full of cash".
Was the 'nonsense' worth it?
On the pitch, Balotelli was sent off against Arsenal in April 2012 in what, at the time, seemed like a season-defining moment that could end Manchester City's title bid.
But one month later he assisted Sergio Aguero's last-gasp goal against Queens Park Rangers that gave City a first Premier League title. It was his only Premier League assist that season.
Micah Richards, who was a team-mate and friend to Balotelli at City, said: "He was crazy in a good way. He was brilliant to have around the squad - a cult hero not just for the nonsense he did off the field but on it as well.
"The best thing about him is he's a lovely guy - he's not arrogant or how the papers try to perceive him, he's just a bit mad."
But did the moments of brilliance make the "nonsense" worth it?
Despite once insisting his patience with Balotelli was "limitless", Mancini ultimately had a rethink.
The final straw came in January 2013 when the pair had an argument at the training ground. Balotelli left for AC Milan later that month.
Mancini said: "He is not a bad guy, and a fantastic player, but I'm very sorry for him as he continues to lose his talent and his quality. I don't have any words for his behaviour.
"I hope for him he can understand he is in a bad way for his future."
Affection remained on both sides, but the relationship had become too fraught.
"Once upon a time, Mario did genuinely believe he was one of the best players in the world," said Nedum Onuoha, another former City team-mate.
"There are lots of stories about him from his time at City, but the one I remember is at our old training ground in Carrington when someone was talking about Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, and Mario said he was as good as them - and he was deadly serious.
"It obviously hasn't worked out that way, but he still has done so much more with his career than most players could even dream of."

  - Published3 January 2013
- 'Balotelli to Barnsley? Now that is one Mario story I don't believe' 
  - Published23 November 2020
Highs and lows with the Azzurri
Balotelli never threatened to have an international career to rival Ronaldo or Messi.
But there were still moments that linger in the memory.
He became the first black player to feature for Italy at a major tournament when he starred at Euro 2012.
And, more than that, he hit three goals to finish as the tournament's joint top scorer - with five others - as Italy lost to Spain in the final.
An abiding image is that of a shirtless Balotelli flexing his muscles after scoring the goal that sent the Azzurri to the final, with a 2-1 win against Germany.
Yet that tournament proved to be the peak of Balotelli's international career.
Italy's national team took a downward turn, and so too did his club career. By 2015, Balotelli had more or less became an Azzurri afterthought.
While Balotelli enjoyed some big moments in an Italy shirt, he did not always feel the love reciprocated from his country of birth.
Before Euro 2012 he threatened to leave the pitch if he was subjected to racist abuse and spoke openly about the vitriol he suffered while playing for Inter.
In fact, racist abuse has followed Balotelli throughout his career and he has commendably refused to tolerate it.
Born Mario Barwuah in Palermo to Ghanaian parents, Balotelli was placed into foster care aged three.
Initially, he stayed with his foster parents - Silvia and Francesco Balotelli - in Brescia during the week, then returned to his biological parents at weekends. He was eventually fostered on a full-time basis and took on the Balotelli surname.
Balotelli identifies with both parts of his heritage - Ghana and Italy - and he struggled to reconcile his love for a nation with the people who aimed verbal abuse his way.
The good times were all too brief: 36 caps and 14 goals has been his tally since 2018. He wanted more and has often made it known.
Onuoha said: "Playing for his country was always so important to him and that's another really positive thing about him, that he had that drive and ambition."
From freefall to fulfilment
Mancini told AC Milan that Balotelli could become one of the world's best while in Serie A.
A glut of goals followed the striker's return to the San Siro in January 2013, before a surprising move back to the Premier League followed 18 months later.
Liverpool had been impressed, but Balotelli's spell on Merseyside would prove forgettable for all. One goal in 16 Premier League games under Brendan Rogers was not what was expected from the £16m buy.
The failed transfer sparked a loan move back to Milan, where injuries hampered his progress. When it was time for Balotelli to return to Merseyside, Jurgen Klopp had arrived and said the striker would not be part of his Liverpool plans.
Balotelli later called the move to Anfield "the worst mistake of my life".
Was it that Liverpool move that sent Balotelli's career spiralling into freefall?
Spells in Nice, Marseille, Brescia and Monza followed - each to varying degrees of success but never with a feeling of stability.
Then came Turkish club Adana Demirspor, Swiss outfit Sion and Italian side Genoa. He spent no more than one season at a time with any of these clubs, although he did return to Demirspor for a second stint.
And so to the present day, with Balotelli aged 36 and plying his trade in the UAE.
It is easy to wonder what might have been had Balotelli stayed in Manchester, had he managed to settle enough to entirely fulfil his potential.
But, after so much media attention and a career that has spanned more continents and leagues than most, it is perhaps also understandable that Balotelli has settled on fulfilment through simply playing the game he loves with his brother.
"Playing with a family member like he is will give him that happiness," said Onuoha.
"And yes, it is not Serie A, La Liga or the Premier League, but Mario is on a field sharing it with his brother - for him that will mean everything.
"At this point there aren't many people that would hold much against him. I think when he was younger, some people would.
"But now I think it is more a case of almost allowing him this happiness, and enjoying seeing him finish off the last days of his career in a place that makes him happy.
"So many people end their careers on a sour note, but for him he is going to be ending it doing exactly what he wants to do."

The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo.

The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild.
Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”.
Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals.
This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species.
The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara.
Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space.
“The [Jio World Convention Centre] was selected because it allowed us to host the event in Mumbai while meeting the practical requirements of an event of this size. It offers world-class facilities, technical infrastructure and experience of hosting major international events, including environmental ones,” Swift said. “In February this year, JWCC hosted the first ever Mumbai climate week.”
Vantara, Kensington Palace and JWCC have been approached for comment.
Vantara has previously denied allegations of wildlife trafficking and says its purpose is “to rescue wild animals in distress, provide treatment along with lifelong care, and rehabilitate those fit for the wild”.
“With regulatory approval, we also breed select endangered or extinct-in-the-wild species, serving as a modern Noah’s Ark to ensure their survival under human care and restore wild populations through reintroduction,” Vantara says on its website.
Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo of allegations that animals had been acquired illegally or mistreated.
A later Cites fact-finding mission raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.
Susan Cheyne, the vice-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s small apes section, said that Vantara’s model has not yet been shown to support conservation and “may be driving demand for wild animals in trade”.
“For gibbons and other primates, this matters a great deal. Moving animals out of their range countries into a private facility does nothing for wild populations unless there is a transparent, credible plan for those animals: for welfare, for any conservation breeding with clear goals, and for return to range states where that is possible. Real rescue and sanctuary work for primates is done by underfunded centres in range countries,” Cheyne said.
Daniela Freyer, co-founder of the German NGO Pro Wildlife, added: “Our planet is increasingly threatened by the overexploitation of wildlife and by climate change driven by fossil fuels. This week, the Cites Standing Committee, which oversees international wildlife trade, decided to keep India under its compliance procedure, as questions remain about the origin of some of the world’s rarest animals imported to Vantara. A prize whose goals include protecting nature and fixing our climate should be careful not to lend its reputation to these questions.”
Vantara had sought to lobby the UK, the chair of this week’s Cites meetings, attempting to persuade officials to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara, the Guardian and Mongabay reported earlier this month. Ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, internal documents revealed.
The Earthshot prize, founded by Prince William in 2020, is billed as the most prestigious environmental award. William appeared on the BBC’s Graham Norton show last month to promote the prize, saying it was designed to “talk about urgency and optimism together”.
Swift said that it was vital to host an edition of the Earthshot prize in India.
“Mumbai is the sixth largest city on earth. It is home to exceptional environmental solutions and the people behind them, with an impact felt in India and around the world. Spotlighting progress like this, to the largest possible audience, is why the Earthshot prize exists,” Swift said.

Musk and Sweeny are among the more than 175,000 who have signed the open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by a make up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.

Indian security personnel carrying batons and shields and accompanied by riot control vehicles surrounded the site of a planned opposition protest in Delhi on Sunday that is set to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Authorities warned of traffic diversions ahead of the protest march and rally that will be led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi. The opposition says it expects hundreds of thousands of people to participate in what it says will be a major challenge to the prime minister, Narendra Modi, and his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
Opposition parties, student organisations and the youth-led Cockroach Janta party have held near-daily demonstrations since last month demanding that the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, step down over the voter list revision that critics say favours the BJP.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol, while the BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029.
The opposition parties have announced they will hold a nearly 1.5km march on Sunday from central Delhi to the Ramlila Maidan, a ground that is the designated site for their protest rally.
Visuals from news agency ANI showed riot control vehicles and dozens of security personnel armed with batons and shields outside the rally venue, where announcements were being made urging people to ensure smooth traffic movement and cooperate with police officials.
Delhi traffic police said a “large gathering” was expected at the venue, and traffic regulations and diversions would be implemented “as required”.
“People have started coming to participate in this rally ... we have ensured proper arrangements at the venue, and arrangements are also planned on the route of the march that will happen in a few hours from now,” senior police officer Rohit Rajbir told ANI.
The protests demanding Kumar’s resignation erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported in September that his two deputies had raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The change, which began last year, removed over 130 million names from voter lists, including 28 million who died, 63 million who relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
Opposition parties allege the deletions disproportionately affect Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party – allegations the poll panel and BJP reject.

Lula to govern Brazil for fourth term but faces challenges. Here’s what to know
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a surprise reelection victory but faces significant challenges
RIO DE JANEIRO -- Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a surprise reelection victory in late October, but he faces a multitude of challenges on issues ranging from the economy and public security to relations with the United States.
While Lula ultimately bested challenger Flávio Bolsonaro by 4.4 million votes after trailing him in the first round, the country remains deeply divided and many voters expressed dissatisfaction with the leftist president's most recent term, which began in 2023.
Bolsonaro refused to recognize the result of the election, declared himself the victim of electoral fraud without providing evidence and fled to Miami. He has vowed to lead a fortified opposition from the U.S.
As Lula prepares to begin his next term, here is a look at challenges ahead.
Lula is facing pressure from investors who had counted on Bolsonaro winning the election after the far-right candidate received more votes than Lula on Oct. 4. Markets did not react well to his loss. Brazil’s currency, the real, dropped by 12% against the dollar the day after the election, while the stock market tumbled nearly 14% and has not rebounded since.
Investors believed a Bolsonaro victory would rein in government spending and are concerned about Lula’s future fiscal policy, said Sergio Vale, chief economist at consultancy firm MB Associados.
“Lula and the government have vowed not to touch spending while keeping all the promises made these last few years,” said Vale. “Unfortunately, they’re not compatible with fiscal responsibility.”
Lula’s government recently unveiled plans to save up to 60 billion reais ($10.6 billion) in public funds through curbs on tax breaks and spending caps — a proposal that is currently moving through Congress.
During Lula’s third term, Brazil’s public debt grew from around 7.2 trillion reais ($1.3 trillion) in 2022 to 11.1 trillion reais ($2 trillion) this year, which analysts say spurred inflation and contributed to high interest rates ultimately remaining unchanged from 13.75% despite variations over the course of the term.
The high cost of living also left many Brazilians unhappy with the state of the economy despite record-low unemployment.
Lula will face a Congress that shifted further to the right in October's legislative elections. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party secured the largest blocs in both houses, gaining an extra 23 seats in the lower house and nearly doubling its Senate seats, mostly at the expense of centrist parties.
Despite Bolsonaro’s departure for Miami, his party will remain a force to be reckoned with, retaining instruments to block governmental proposals and even challenge judicial authorities.
Bolsonaro’s congressional allies want, above all, to impeach Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who chaired the investigation that led to President Jair Bolsonaro serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup.
Their efforts would be helped if Rogério Marinho, Bolsonaro’s campaign coordinator, becomes Senate president. He announced his candidacy last week, promising not to focus solely on impeachment. But, he said, “we will not turn a blind eye, because no one is above the law.”
Brazilians cited crime as a top concern ahead of the election and insecurity featured prominently in the election cycle.
While Brazil's homicide rate last year fell to its lowest level since 2012, the country continues to face the expansion of criminal activities that use digital technology and online platforms, violence against vulnerable groups — including people of color, women and children — and the need to modernize security and justice institutions, according to this year’s annual report from the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety.
Drug-trafficking gangs have expanded their reach in recent years and are now present in large swathes of the country, including parts of the Amazon rainforest, while paramilitary-type militias have entrenched their power in Rio and other states.
Brazil’s Senate recently approved legislation that strengthens the government’s power to fight criminal gangs. Lula has touted the changes as key to tackling one of his nation’s biggest problems.
Navigating the rivalry between the U.S. and China will be key in Lula’s fourth term, said Ana Garcia, an international relations professor at the Rural Federal University of Rio de Janeiro.
Relations between Brazil and the U.S. fell to an all-time low during Lula’s third term, after the Trump administration imposed several rounds of tariffs. Meanwhile, ties with China deepened, displeasing the U.S., analysts say.
But Democrats' sweeping gains in the midterm election also reflected a repudiation of Trump’s tariffs, and pressure to reduce them — including those targeting Brazil — is likely to increase, Garcia said.
Garcia expects Flávio Bolsonaro and his brother Eduardo, who lives in Texas, to continue lobbying Trump administration allies against Lula’s government. But Democrats may increase scrutiny of Trump's policies abroad. In September, 31 Democratic members of Congress sent a letter to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio accusing the Trump administration of “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s election.
“The midterms were a rude awakening for the Bolsonaros,” Garcia said.

Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice.
The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars.
The missing ice
Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It’s what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets.
The outer parts of the disk are far enough from the star that water and other volatile molecules should freeze into solid ice. The disk holds a large reservoir of carbon monoxide gas, which ultraviolet light from the star should destroy within 50 to 300 years. For that gas to still be there, something must keep replenishing it—most likely it’s released from ice when volatile-rich comets collide. The properties of the planet Beta Pictoris b also suggest it formed from ice-rich material.
Yet despite plenty of reasons to suspect the system is full of ice, earlier searches have failed to find it. Attempts to detect water vapor found nothing, and a search for the telltale dip that water ice leaves in starlight at a wavelength of 3 micrometers also failed.

Jio Platforms has begun talks with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), Skyroot Aerospace, and other Indian launch providers to deploy satellites for its proposed 1,600-satellite low Earth orbit (LEO) constellation. The company wants to explore domestic launch options first and is also considering SpaceX, Mint reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Jio is evaluating whether it can carry out the entire programme from satellite design, engineering, integration, and testing to launch, deployment, and operations in India. Inc42 has reached out to Jio and Skyroot for comment. The story will be updated on receiving a response. Jio’s Satellite Rollout Jio is targeting a September 2027 test launch involving a handful of satellites to evaluate the network’s hardware, software, and other technologies. It plans to begin mass deployment in early 2028, put around 400-450 satellites into orbit by 2030, and complete the constellation by 2035. The company plans to launch an initial batch of about 390 satellites in phases and establish 23 ground stations across India. It is in talks with multiple operators to line up launches over the next two years, according to Mint. Reliance Industries outlined plans for an Indian-owned LEO constellation at its 49th annual general meeting in June. Jio Platforms MD Akash Ambani said the company was evaluating whether to develop its own constellation while exploring partnerships with global satellite operators. Leasing capacity from these operators could help Jio offer services sooner. The company also plans to build ground stations that can support both partner networks and its own satellites. ISRO’s heavy-lift LVM3 rocket put 72 OneWeb satellites into orbit across two missions in 2022 and 2023. Skyroot Aerospace and Agnikul Cosmos have flown privately developed rockets, while startups such as EtherealX are developing their own launch vehicles.

MUMBAI: For years, the United States was the destination of choice for Indian students looking for a foreign degree and, perhaps, a career to follow. That promise is beginning to look less certain. Indian student numbers in American universities fell 6% to 3,39,435 in 2025-26, while those from China declined 4% to 2,54,458, as visa uncertainties, a difficult employment market and shifting immigration policies complicate decisions about studying in the US.
The more revealing figure is the number of students entering American institutions for the first time. New international enrolments fell 18% to 2,28,123 in 2025-26. Unlike total student numbers, which include those admitted in earlier years, fresh enrolments provide a clearer indication of whether students are still choosing the US.
And the Fall 2026 Snapshot suggests the weakness will continue. Participating institutions reported a 15% fall in graduate students, a 3% decline in undergraduates and a 6% drop in OPT numbers. New international enrolments were down 15% compared with the previous fall.
The decline is part of a wider retreat. International student numbers across American higher education institutions fell 3% to 11,46,163 in 2025-26, according to the Open Doors 2026 report released on Nov 16 by the Institute of International Education (IIE). And the slide may not be over. A separate Fall 2026 Snapshot survey of more than 800 institutions has recorded a sharper 9% fall in international student numbers in the ongoing academic year, with new enrolments dropping 15%.
From record highs to a sharp retreat: The India story
For India, the reversal is particularly striking. Just a year earlier, in 2024-25, the country had sent a record 3,63,019 students to the US, a 10% increase over the previous year. India remains the largest source of international students for the third consecutive year, ahead of China, but the momentum that carried it to the top appears to have weakened. Together, the two countries still account for nearly 52% of all international students in the US.
The steepest fall has come at the graduate level, traditionally the strongest draw for Indian students, particularly those pursuing engineering, technology and management programmes. Indian graduate student numbers plunged 34% to 1,16,609, while undergraduate enrolments slipped just 1% to 39,711.
The distinction is telling. For many Indian families, a master's degree in the US is not merely an academic investment. It is also a route to professional experience, better earnings and, potentially, a longer-term career abroad. That calculation becomes harder when the cost of an American education remains high but the prospects of securing a job afterwards are uncertain.
The overall fall in Indian student numbers would have been much sharper had it not been for those already working in the US, said study-abroad. The number of Indians on OPT rose 27% to 1,82,201, accounting for more than half of all Indian students counted in the report.
China, meanwhile, also recorded a more moderate decline. Its graduate student population fell 5% to 1,14,043, undergraduate numbers dropped 5% to 74,594, and OPT participation declined 1% to 61,545.
Across nationalities, graduate enrolments fell 13% to 4,23,078, largely because of a 22% contraction in master's students. Doctoral numbers, however, rose 3%, while undergraduate enrolments were virtually unchanged at 3,56,165.
American campuses feel the pinch
The OPT figures are particularly noteworthy. In 2025-26, participation had risen 14% to 3,35,785, supported by the large number of international students who had graduated in previous years. The latest survey suggests that even this segment, which had helped cushion the overall decline, is beginning to contract.
For American universities, the implications extend beyond admissions. International students are an important source of tuition revenue, research talent and skilled graduates. According to the US Department of Commerce, they contributed nearly $56 billion to the American economy in 2025.
Yet the appetite for recruiting them remains strong. In the Fall Snapshot, 75% of institutions cited the value of international perspectives on campus, while 60% acknowledged the financial contributions of international students. As many as 91% said recruiting international students in science, technology, engineering and mathematics remained a priority.
Computer science was identified as a recruitment priority by 75% of institutions, followed by engineering and biological sciences at 59% each. In 2025-26, STEM disciplines accounted for 57% of international students, with mathematics and computer science drawing 2,86,168 students and engineering another 2,14,193.
Some countries buck the downtrend
Not every country, however, has seen its numbers fall. Nine of the 25 largest source countries, including Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan, Vietnam and Italy, reported record-high student populations. The divergent trends suggest that the slowdown is not uniform and that the international student landscape is changing in ways that cannot be explained by a single factor.
Jason Czyz, president and CEO of IIE, said international education continued to strengthen American institutions and foster relationships that extended beyond students' time on campus.
The report also recorded a 5% increase in American students studying abroad for academic credit, with 3,13,824 doing so in 2024-25. Italy, Spain and the United Kingdom were the leading destinations.

A group of around 40 men allegedly ambushed a house church in Rayan village in West Bengal’s Purba Bardhaman district on November 1, and physically assaulted the pastor and several Christian worshippers during a Sunday prayer service. The attackers accused the congregation of converting Hindus by luring them with incentives, and also accused them of running a ‘honey trap’.
Survivors told Alt News that they were forced to chant ‘Jai Sri Ram’, and were told, “This is a Hindu area; worshipping Jesus will not be tolerated”.
Several worshippers sustained severe injuries after the attack. Survivors said they were left traumatised without administrative protection or assurance. A written complaint was submitted at Burdwan police station. However, the survivors alleged that they were forced into withdrawing the complaint as attackers entered the police station and threatened to kill the complainant.
Alt News spoke to pastor Chottu Ruidas, who was leading the Sunday prayer service, and other survivors of the attack. Recounting the incident, Ruidas said the congregation had assembled at Sushanta Majila’s house around 10 am, and the service was nearing its conclusion, with the worshippers participating in communion, when a group of approximately 40 men descended on the house church, raising ‘Jai Sri Ram’ slogans.
According to Ruidas, Bisweshwar Choudhury, an influential and wealthy resident of the village who is known for helping people in need, was part of the group. He approached Ruidas during the prayer service and allegedly slapped him.
“Thereafter, the goons accompanying Choudhury started beating us mercilessly,” Ruidas told Alt News. “They slapped us, kicked us and beat us with the bamboo sticks they were carrying. They even took off their belts and whipped us.”
Ruidas said a 17-year-old boy sustained a severe head injury, leaving him bleeding profusely. “The goons told him, ‘We have treated you. Now go to a doctor and get it fixed,” he recounted.
The attackers allegedly dragged worshippers out of the house and beaten up. Those who attempted to seek refuge in neighbouring homes were pursued and assaulted, Ruidas said.
“After the goons beat us, the other attendees locked me inside a kitchen to keep me safe. But they broke open the door and dragged me out. My elder sister hugged me and fell to the ground while trying to protect me. But they continued kicking us. My sister eventually fell unconscious, and I had to take her to a nearby dispensary,” he said.
Ruidas told Alt News that he had attempted to contact police while hiding inside the kitchen but could not get through. He subsequently informed Pastor Jose Bernard, who then contacted the cops.
Bernard told Alt News that he called the Burdwan police station two to three times, but the police allegedly did not take the matter seriously. He eventually dialled the emergency helpline, 112, following which police personnel reached the village.
Bernard said his wife and minor daughter were also among the worshippers present at the congregation. By the time police reached the location, several miscreants had fled the scene. He claimed that when police entered the premises, the remaining miscreants accused the worshippers of having picked a fight with them.
Then, according to the pastor, instead of taking action against the attackers, police detained 20 women, three minors, and eight men from the Christian congregation.
Bernard categorically denied allegations of forceful conversion or conversion through inducement.
Worshippers Detained, Threatened by Accused inside Police Station
The detainees were first taken to Bardhaman Medical College and Hospital, where a doctor examined them inside the vehicle. Then, they were taken to the police station and kept in two separate rooms.
Pastor Jose Bernard subsequently submitted a written complaint at the police station. He alleged that this happened in the presence of police personnel.

Sometimes new species evade detection because they’re tiny and thus easy to miss—not this giant fungus. Shaped like a hand reaching out of the ground, this new species of fungus was discovered deep in the forest in China’s Yunnan Province. A research team from the Kunming Institute of Botany, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, reported it as a new species they named Dianjunus rex.
The name comes from the region’s ancient Dian Kingdom and the Chinese pronunciation of the word “fungus.” D. rex is a type of Ascomycete, which is the largest phylum of fungi with over 64,000 known species, and among them, this new fungus produces the largest masses of mushroom recorded. Unlike what we typically think of as a “mushroom,” Ascomycetes don’t form caps and stems but produce structures called fruiting bodies, which release spores to reproduce. And growing up to 20 inches and weighting nearly five pounds, D. rex’s are huge.
Within the Ascomycetes, the giant fungus constitutes an entirely new biological family (the broader classification of genus and species), meaning that it has no close relatives—at least that we know of. While 6,000 fungal species have been documented in Yunnan, mycologists believe the province known for its biological diversity could easily harbor 100,000
“The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests,” Indunil C. Senanayake, an associate professor at the Kunming Institute of Botany and the lead author of the paper, said in a press release.
Senanayake and his research team conducted surveys in the Nanban tropical rainforest, where they came across large, whitish fruiting bodies growing in the soil near the roots of dying trees. They documented and collected fungi growing in a wide variety of shapes like cylinders, spindles, and cupped palms. The fruiting bodies appeared to develop finger-like branches upon maturity. They found that the above-ground portions are covered with white, powdery fibers that turn dark yellow as the fungi mature while the portions buried in the soil are black and smooth.
The fruiting bodies dried rapidly when the scientists took samples back to the lab. They found that the interiors were dense and sponge-like, appearing white or yellow with no strong odor or taste. (Don’t try this experiment at home.)
Analyzing the DNA of these fungi, the researchers reconstructed a “molecular clock,” which revealed that D. rex diverged from other species approximately 65 million years ago. This is the end of the Cretaceous period, immediately following the mass extinction that is believed to have wiped out three quarters of all plant and animal species, including the dinosaurs. That means D. rex and T. rex never met, but this era was likely a boon for fungi. Large quantities of dead plant material became available following the die off, which could have provided new ecological opportunities for fungi and other organisms that decompose such matter.
Genomic analyses, however, indicated that D. rex doesn’t have nearly as many decomposition-related genes as the scientists expected. Compared to some of its closest relatives that also feast on plant matter, the huge fungus has only about half the usual number of decomposition-related genes.
Senanayake has a theory about this. Though, so far, they have only found the fruiting bodies around dying plants, the fungus may be leading a “double life”—living inside healthy trees and then feeding on dead plant material when the hosts die. That could perhaps explain how D. rex is able to store enough energy to build the massive fruiting bodies.
This is just a theory for now, but the giant fungi undoubtedly do need a surplus of energy to grow so large. Senanayake hypothesizes that the benefit of these large fruiting bodies is that they tower higher than the surrounding plants and fallen leaves, which could be advantageous for wind-mediated spore dispersal in a dense forest. “However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs.”

The High Court of Karnataka has advised the security and police organisations to prioritise the mental health and well-being of personnel entrusted with firearms while asking the authorities to examine existing policies and take appropriate steps to strengthen the mental health and welfare measures for their personnel.
Justice Suraj Govindaraj passed the order while quashing the criminal proceedings against a 37-year-old CISF Sub-Inspector for attempting to kill herself in 2022 by using her service pistol while on duty in Mangaluru. She had attempted to end her life following years of severe mental distress over her inability to conceive a child due to a blocked fallopian tube.
Allowing her petition, the court set aside the lower court’s order and discharged her from the offence under Section 309 of the IPC (attempt to commit suicide). The court ruled that Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, creates a mandatory presumption of severe stress, placing the burden on the prosecution to prove otherwise. Since no such evidence was produced, the court held that continuing the trial would be an abuse of the judicial process.
‘Grief and anxiety’
“Personnel serving in these forces are also human beings. They have families, relationships, responsibilities and personal problems. They experience grief, anxiety, financial difficulties, marital discord, illness in the family and other difficulties common to human life. Wearing a uniform or undergoing rigorous training does not make them immune to such problems,” the court said.
Further, the court said that “the expectation that they must remain available for duty at all times and discharge their responsibilities, come rain or shine, irrespective of their personal circumstances or mental condition, requires a change in institutional thinking.”
The concerned organisations must ensure that accessible and confidential counselling, professional mental healthcare and timely treatment are available to personnel at all levels, including those posted in remote and difficult locations, the court said.
Signals of distress
Commanding and supervisory officers, the court emphasised, must be sensitised to recognise signs of distress and facilitate appropriate assistance, and personnel who undergo treatment or experience mental health difficulties must also receive suitable support for rehabilitation and return to duty, based on professional assessment.
“The welfare of personnel and the security of the public are not competing considerations. A force which looks after the mental and physical well-being of its personnel is better equipped to maintain discipline, operational readiness and public safety, the court said.

Why sleep matters when it comes to weight gain and loss
If you want to maintain a healthy weight, you probably know you should watch what you eat and get some exercise, maybe hit the gym. But what about hitting the hay?
There is a lot of evidence linking lack of sleep to overeating and an increased body weight. But does that mean that getting more sleep could also boost efforts to lose weight?
"That's a good question," says Seth Creasy, an associate professor of medicine at the University of Colorado Anschutz who studies the interplay between weight management and lifestyle behaviors like sleep, diet and physical activity. "It's actually still an active area of research."
Creasy says the best evidence so far comes from a randomized clinical trial involving 80 overweight adults who were chronically short on sleep. Researchers randomly assigned half of them to get counseling on how to extend their snooze time.
"They got them to sleep a little over an hour more per night," Creasy says. "And they saw that, without intervening on food, these people started to eat less by about 270 calories per day. So once they were getting adequate sleep, they ate less."
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Other research has found associations between better sleep and weight loss. For example, one study found that people enrolled in a year-long weight loss intervention program who had good sleep health lost more weight and more fat mass compared to poor sleepers.
The poor sleepers in that study were also much more likely to report having trouble sticking to their diet and exercise goals, says Christopher Kline, the study's lead author and an associate professor of health and human development at the University of Pittsburgh.
And good sleep health doesn't just mean how long you sleep, Kline says. He says that factors like sleep timing, regularity and satisfaction also play a role.
"A good analogy I like to make is if you get your eight hours of sleep, but those eight hours are between 4 a.m. and noon, that might not be as healthy as someone who regularly obtains their sleep between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.," says Kline, whose research focuses on how physical activity, sleep and cardiometabolic risks are related.
The links between sleep loss and weight gain
Researchers say right now, the evidence that more sleep can boost weight loss efforts is still scant, but the science is much more consistent when it comes to linking insufficient sleep to weight gain.
When researchers restrict people's sleep, they eat more — by an average of around 300 calories a day if you look across studies, says Creasy, who recently published a review of the research on sleep and weight management.
Most of those studies required participants to severely curtail their sleep, usually to around four or five hours a night. That's much less than the seven to nine hours of sleep that adults are supposed to get.
But Creasy worked on a recent study that found even milder sleep loss can result in weight gain. In that study, people who were assigned to sleep just 90 minutes less than usual gained an average of one pound over six weeks. While that may not sound like much, "over time, it adds up," says Marie-Pierre St-Onge, the study's senior author and a sleep and nutrition scientist at Columbia University.
Imaging studies from St-Onge and other researchers have found that, when we're short on sleep, activity ramps up in areas of the brain involved in pleasure and reward. In other words, it becomes harder to make good food choices.
"Our brain is less able to inhibit our desires for those sweet and salty foods" — especially later in the day, Kline says. The result is we end up overeating when short on sleep.
Kline says he experienced this phenomenon first-hand when he was still a doctoral student working the overnight shift in a sleep study lab. Once a week, every week, one of his fellow lab workers would bring in glazed donuts from Krispy Kreme.
"I can tell you there was no chance I was going to end a shift without having at least one or two of those donuts. And I don't even really like glazed donuts," Kline says ruefully.
Skimping on sleep can also disrupt our circadian rhythms and impair our sensitivity to insulin, which may promote fat storage and make it easier to gain weight.
Creasy says early studies suggested poor sleep also affects hormones that regulate appetite, but newer research hasn't always borne that out. "Some studies have shown an effect on them and some have not. So it's just been inconsistent," he says.
Better sleep through food?
St-Onge says the relationship between sleep and food goes both ways. "As we find that how we sleep influences our food intake, we also find that what we eat during the day also influences our sleep at night," she says.
Research from her team and others has linked eating added sugars and saturated fat to more sleep disturbances and less deep slumber. Meanwhile, fruits, vegetables and fiber were associated with better sleep and fewer awakenings at night, she says.
If you want to eat better to sleep better, St-Onge says you can start with small, easy changes. "As a first step, cut out foods that are higher in added sugars and sweetened beverages," she says.
Switching to whole grains instead of refined carbohydrates is also a good idea. Her research has linked added sugars and refined carbs to a greater risk of insomnia.
And she says look for opportunities to eat more fruits and vegetables throughout the day.
"I always put a ton of leafy vegetables in my dishes, like stews and soups and stir fries," St-Onge says.
And of course, don't forget good sleep hygiene, says Philip Cheng, a sleep and circadian rhythms researcher and professor of medicine at Henry Ford Health in Michigan. That means things like keeping your bedroom cool and dark, and sticking to a regular schedule for going to bed and waking up as best as you can.
"That's going to stabilize your sleep in the long run," Cheng says.
But if your poor sleep lasts months or even years, he says it's time to see a medical provider for help.

A rumor spread in November that a "hovering orb" shut down a section of Interstate 80 in southern Wyoming.
For example, a Facebook page called Casper Planet said on Nov. 11 (archived):
A section of Interstate 80 in southern Wyoming has been closed early Wednesday morning following multiple reports of a large unidentified orb hovering above the highway. The first reports began coming into dispatchers at approximately 2:45 a.m.
Several truck drivers traveling east of Rawlins reported seeing a bright spherical object hovering motionless approximately 30 to 40 feet above the interstate. Within minutes, additional motorists began reporting the same object. Authorities initially believed drivers were seeing a drone or possibly equipment suspended from a helicopter.
The post includes two images purportedly showing a large, white orb hovering above a highway.
The claim spread elsewhere on Facebook (archived), and Snopes readers contacted us to investigate its legitimacy.
Searches on DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo (archived, archived, archived) uncovered no examples of reputable local or national news media outlets reporting on such an incident. If a hovering orb had really closed Interstate 80 in Wyoming, news outlets would have covered it.
The original source of the claim is the Casper Planet Facebook page, which describes its content as satirical. Snopes frequently investigates such claims originating from this account.
Casper Planet first mentioned the rumor on Nov. 11 and subsequently posted two follow-up posts about the same fake incident (archived, archived), both of which jokingly claim agents in black went around convincing people they had seen no such object floating above the highway.
The account's page description reads: "Delivering the Snews that doesn't matter directly to your Snews feed. Did we say this is satire? Well it is, names/locations are made up."
According to SynthID.com, a Google website that detects digital watermarks in alleged photos, both of the pictures Casper Planet used in its Nov. 11 post were created using OpenAI's image-generation tool.
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' descriptions of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

In November, a claim (archived) circulated online that the U.S. Air Force had held Maj. Jason Watson, an active-duty airman who publicly called for the impeachment of President Donald Trump, in solitary confinement for more than 80 days while he awaited court-martial.
CNN reported that the Air Force ordered Watson into "pre-trial confinement" on Aug. 18. Two days later, on Aug. 20, Watson's lawyer Christopher Mutimer told CNN that Watson was "basically in solitary confinement." He repeated this claim in early October, telling CNN (at 1:46, archived) that Watson was "still in solitary confinement."
One X user who claimed Watson remained in solitary confinement in early November — 84 days after the Air Force first ordered him into pretrial confinement — wrote:
Maj. Jason Watson has been in 24-hour solitary confinement for 80+ days & has reportedly lost 20 pounds, all before any trial. UN experts consider solitary beyond 15 days to be torture. He offered to resign, give up all his benefits, & the Air Force said no. Because he protested.
The claim also circulated on Facebook and Threads (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
Speaking to Snopes on Nov. 10, Mutimer confirmed Watson had been detained at Maryland's Calvert County Detention Center since Aug. 18 and described conditions that he said met generally understood definitions for solitary confinement.
Mutimer said Watson "is in a room by himself 22 to 23 hours a day. No one stays in there with him, he is not allowed to have any interaction. When he's let out it's to shower, make a phone call, get some time in the yard by himself." He described Watson's cell as a "pen" where "the light is on all the time."
Mutimer added, "Because he's an officer, he is in the military, that contract says he is not allowed to be with anybody who is not in the military."
A spokesperson for the Department of the Air Force said in a statement on Nov. 13:
The Department of the Air Force can confirm that Maj Watson is not being held in solitary confinement. Maj Watson is held in administrative protective segregation—not punitive solitary confinement—at the Calvert County Detention Center (CCDC) pursuant to an official Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) between CCDC and the 11th Wing Security Forces Squadron (11 SFS) at Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling (JBAB).
Maj Watson is physically separated from CCDC's civilian general inmate population to comply with military policy and statutory segregation mandates. While separated from civilian detainees, Maj Watson does have regular access to standard institutional amenities and programs, including the facility library, religious services/chapel, and physical fitness time. He also retains normal access to defense counsel, military leadership visits, medical care, and personal visitation.
Because of the opposing descriptions of Watson's confinement from his lawyer and the Air Force, we leave this claim unrated. we leave this claim unrated.
By November, the docket of the Air Force's military justice branch showed Watson was due for general court-martial in February. Mutimer said he would argue a petition for Watson's pretrial release on Nov. 17.
Mutimer also confirmed the claim some social media users made that Watson had attempted to resign after his July 1 arrest but said officials had denied his resignation and instead pressed ahead with the court-martial, a move that Mutimer described as "absolutely unheard of."
Tracking Watson's case
Capitol Police arrested Watson on July 1 on after he publicly called for Trump's impeachment while wearing his Air Force uniform. A live stream (at 50:56) of the arrest showed Watson standing on the Capitol steps in uniform while holding a sign that read "Impeach Convict Remove."
Watson said at a news conference earlier that day that he was calling for Trump to be impeached because he thought the president and Vice President JD Vance had governed in an unconstitutional way throughout their administration.
Watson highlighted the war in Iran, Elon Musk's sweeping cuts to federal government and the Department of Homeland Security's immigration crackdown and killings of protesters as "high crimes and misdemeanors" (at 28:28) for which "the president and vice president must be impeached, convicted, and removed."
The Air Force major repeated his call for Trump and Vance's removal while speaking to CNN's Erin Burnett (at 1:52) on Aug. 17. Burnett said (at 2:41) during the interview that the military had placed a "gag order" on Watson after his July 1 protest and that he was "under investigation."
According to a later CNN report, the Air Force took Watson into pretrial confinement days after he spoke to the network.
CNN reported that the Air Force charged Watson with 10 violations of three articles of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the military's legal framework, on Aug. 20. Mutimer reportedly spoke to Watson on that date and reported that he was "basically in solitary confinement."
On Sept. 29, The New York Times reported that an Air Force investigating officer had recommended Watson's case for general court-martial, the military's highest level of trial court.
According to the Judge Advocate General's Corps Department of the Air Force, which investigated and charged Watson, the major faced charges of four violations of articles 88, 92 and 133 of the UCMJ.
Article 88 (Page 34) of the UCMJ states that any commissioned officer who uses "contemptuous words" against certain public officials, which includes the president and vice president, should face a court-martial. Article 92 (Page 35) states that a person subject to the code that fails to obey an order or regulation can be subject to court-martial. Article 133 (Page 48) states that "Any commissioned officer, cadet, or midshipman who is convicted of conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman shall be punished as a court-martial may direct."
The code does not explicitly define what "conduct unbecoming an officer" means.
An Air Force spokesperson reportedly told Military.com in October that the Air Force had acted in accordance with the Rule for Court-Martial 305 when it took Watson into pretrial confinement in August. That rule says someone can be placed in pretrial confinement if there is probable cause they committed "an offense triable by court-martial."
That rule also says that someone taken into pretrial confinement can ask a military judge to review the "propriety" of the confinement, meaning whether it is appropriate. Mutimer said such a review for Watson would happen on Nov. 17.
According to the UCMJ's Article 13 (Page 5), it is prohibited to punish a service member awaiting trial. Any confinement before trial must not "be any more rigorous than the circumstances require to insure his presence, but he may be subjected to minor punishment during that period for infractions of discipline."
At the time of this writing, Watson had not been convicted or sentenced. Punishments for service members convicted by court-martial range from reprimands and salary reductions to dismissal or discharge.
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated whether an active-duty soldier took part in an anti-immigration-enforcement protest.

Injured Australian lawmaker Helen Haines leaves hospital after alleged SUV attack
An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack has thanked well-wishers around the world
MELBOURNE, Australia -- An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack thanked well-wishers around the world Monday and revealed she had been discharged from a hospital where she spent the past month.
In her first public statement since being struck by a SUV on Oct. 19, Helen Haines said she was “very pleased to confirm” she had left Melbourne’s The Alfred hospital.
Witnesses said she was repeatedly rammed by the vehicle outside her electorate office.
The 65-year-old independent lawmaker said she would remain in Melbourne for the “rehabilitation stage” of her recovery. Her staff would not disclose where her rehabilitation would take place for privacy reasons.
“This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage,” Haines said.
“I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across (my electorate) Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing,” she added.
Haines was in critical condition hours after she was struck when she was flown to Melbourne by helicopter from her hometown of Wangaratta, 236 kilometers (147 miles) to the northeast.
Surgeons amputated both her legs within a few days.
The hospital listed her as critical until Oct. 24 when her condition was downgraded to serious but stable. She had been listed as stable since Nov. 6.
Haines' family asked well-wishers to make donations to the international charity Save the Children instead of sending flowers. The appeal has raised more than 1.4 million Australian dollars ($950,000), Save the Children Australia said Monday.
Haines was “overwhelmed by the generosity of Australians” through their donations and looked forward to working with Save the Children to use the money to “improve the lives of children,” she said.
Her shocking injuries renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers. However, public incitement against officials is growing.
Security at several lawmakers’ electorate offices has been enhanced in response to the alleged attack.
Within hours of Haines being struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser Troop Carrier, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told a news conference her catastrophic injuries were not an accident.
“All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery,” Albanese said in a statement Monday in response to her hospital discharge.
“I have been in regular contact with Helen and her extraordinary family. We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation,” Albanese added.
Police have yet to disclose a motive for the alleged attack. Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old man who lived in the Wangaratta area, has been charged with offenses including intentionally causing serious injury.
Nugent has been in custody since bystanders dragged him from his SUV and rendered first-aid to Haines at the scene.
His father, Rod Nugent, released a statement a day after Haines was hospitalized describing the lawmaker as a “friend for more than 20 years” and the circumstances of her injuries “unfathomable.”

New Delhi- Recent developments in India-Pakistan relations, reforming the United Nations and India’s bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council (UNSC) are among the subjects selected for examination by the parliamentary standing committee on external affairs for 2026-27.
In a bulletin issued on Monday, the Lok Sabha Secretariat listed the subjects selected by the Committee on External Affairs for the year.
“Committee on External Affairs: Selection of Subjects for the year 2026-27 — India-Europe Relationship: Opportunities and Challenges; Performance of Passport Issuance System including issuance of e- Passports and review of the Indian Passport Act and Rules; Understanding India-China Relations and the way forward,” the bulletin read.
Other subjects include recent developments in India-Pakistan relations; India-US relations, including the role of the Quad, challenges and opportunities; and India’s relations with West Asia.
The panel will also examine reforming the United Nations and India’s bid for permanent membership of the UNSC; the country’s Act East Policy and its partnership with ASEAN; the India-Africa strategic partnership; India’s engagement with BRICS; and its soft power and cultural diplomacy.
The functioning of Nalanda University and the South Asian University, including governance, international participation and their contribution to knowledge diplomacy, as well as the functioning of Indian missions abroad, are also among the subjects.
Other subjects include issues relating to emigration, international mobility of skilled professionals and the welfare of the Indian diaspora; India-Bhutan bilateral relations; and strengthening the Indian Foreign Service to meet India’s expanding global responsibilities.
The committee will also examine the role of states and Union Territories in external engagement, including diaspora outreach and investment promotion, as well as the Ministry of External Affairs’ engagement with think tanks and academic institutions.

OpenAI sued by California over Hugging Face attack

In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.
Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".
Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.
But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.
Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.
The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.
Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.
"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.
OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.
"We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said.
The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents.
Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about".
"OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said.
