A video showing Akhilesh Yadav speaking to the media is being shared (here, here, here) with the claim that he was drunk while addressing reporters. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video shows Akhilesh Yadav in an intoxicated state while addressing the media.
Fact: The viral video is altered. The original video shows him speaking normally, and the audio has been altered to make his speech sound unclear. When the original video is heard at 0.75x speed, the audio matches the viral video. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to the same video, uploaded on 19 August 2026, on the official Facebook account of the Samajwadi Party. In this video, Akhilesh Yadav speaks in his normal tone. From the 50-second mark, he makes the same remarks heard in the viral video, but without the slurred tone.
Further, when we listened to the original video at 0.75x speed, we found that the audio matched the viral video. You can watch and listen to our edited video below.
We also found videos of the same interaction uploaded on 19 August 2026 by news agencies Bharat Samachar, IANS, and PTI. The microphones of these news agencies are also visible in the viral video. These videos show Akhilesh Yadav speaking to reporters after attending a Bhagwat Katha in Lucknow. He is seen speaking normally, without the slurred tone heard in the viral clip.
To sum up, this video claiming to show Akhilesh Yadav addressing the media in an intoxicated state is doctored.

Jensen Huang's dramatic departure from Nvidia may be the best thing to happen to Anthropic just as the AI startup prepares to go public this week.
Under Huang, Nvidia was investing heavily in cheaper, more open AI models that compete with Anthropic's offerings. The chip giant was also backing startups developing these alternative models and helping make them widely available.
That threatened Anthropic's business model, which involves spending heavily to develop closed AI models and charges customers to use them, often at higher prices than open alternatives.
"People really need to understand that the 'Cold War' going on here is that Nvidia was on a titanic collision course with the labs," the CEO of a leading AI startup told Business Insider. This person asked not to be identified while discussing sensitive topics.
The executive, who supports the open-source AI community and is sympathetic to Huang, described an ambitious Nvidia strategy to develop its own AI models, invest in rival startups, and build an ecosystem that could challenge not just Anthropic, but OpenAI too.
This strategy was just beginning to come together. But with Huang gone, the threat has diminished considerably.
The timing is extraordinary. Anthropic is preparing for a stock market debut this week that could value it at $1.4 trillion.
Investors are being asked to make an enormous bet on the future profitability of its AI services. Huang was helping build a world in which companies wouldn't necessarily have to pay Anthropic for that intelligence.
Nvidia's open AI push
The strategy centered on "open-weight" AI models. Unlike Anthropic's Fable and Opus offerings and OpenAI's top GPT models, these alternative systems can be downloaded, modified, and operated independently.
That makes them attractive to businesses that want greater control over their AI systems without paying a leading AI lab every time someone uses the technology.
Nvidia was pursuing this aggressively.
It developed its own family of open models, called Nemotron. It also backed startups including Reflection AI, Thinking Machines Lab, and Poolside, while moving to acquire Hugging Face, a major platform for sharing open-weight AI models.
Replit CEO Amjad Masad called Jensen Huang's ouster "an attack on open models" at a Silicon Valley conference on Monday.
"Jensen is the premier champion of open models," Masad said. "If it wasn't for Jensen, there wouldn't be a lot of funding going into US open model companies."
Fireworks
On November 3, I watched Huang evangelize this strategy at a Fireworks AI conference in San Francisco.
He acknowledged the value of closed AI models from companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI, but argued that businesses shouldn't have to rely on them. Instead, they could take open-weight models and adapt them to their specific needs, creating AI systems that could be even more powerful.
"By taking an open frontier model, adapting it and providing it with your domain knowledge, your access, your specialized tools, and the proper evaluation, you should be able to create essentially a super intelligence," Huang told Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao on stage.
"And I think those times are here," he added.
Nvidia's worst nightmare
This strategy made business sense for Nvidia. More open models running on its chips meant more potential customers.
It was becoming increasingly important as Anthropic and OpenAI sought alternatives to Nvidia's expensive hardware.
In fact, Anthropic has developed a system that could be Nvidia's worst nightmare, as Business Insider reported in October.
Anthropic disclosed in its IPO filing that it has spent years developing software that allows it to shift AI work between different types of chips from Nvidia, Google, Amazon, and AMD. That gives Anthropic more flexibility to choose the cheapest or most effective chips for a particular task, reducing its dependence on Nvidia and potentially weakening Nvidia's ability to charge premium prices.
The shift is already significant. A November 14 analysis by Michael Cembalest of JPMorgan Asset Management estimated that Nvidia accounted for just 39% of future computing commitments by leading AI labs, down from more than 80% of AI chip revenue in recent years.
The China battle
There was another key area of AI where Nvidia and Anthropic clashed.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has advocated for very strict limits on advanced US chip sales to China, arguing these restrictions are essential to maintaining America's technological lead.
Huang fought against those restrictions, warning that shutting China out would encourage Chinese companies to develop competing technology.
How he's gone, Anthropic's worldview is prevailing. On Monday, the US government rolled out new restrictions that close a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to use Nvidia GPUs by renting them from data centers outside China.
It's a win for China hawks within the administration and a huge victory for Amodei, arguably the biggest China hawk of them all.
There are caveats. For instance, Nvidia's interim CEO could continue Huang's strategies. Still, the immediate strategic implications are striking.
Anthropic is about to ask investors to bet on its future dominance of AI. Just days before that moment, one of the industry's most powerful figures pushing an alternative vision has been forced out.
For Anthropic, that's enormous.

Gadi Eisenkot sharply criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu days after the Israeli leader attacked Arab lawmakers in a divisive speech.
Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who is trying to form the next Israeli government, accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fueling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab citizens, in some of the strongest public criticism of his rival’s attacks on the community.
The comments were made days after Mr. Netanyahu delivered a divisive speech to the opening session of Parliament, or the Knesset, in which he referred to Arab lawmakers as “terror supporters” and “haters of Israel.” Diplomats and analysts condemned the remarks as a brazen display of hatred and incitement against Arab citizens, who make up about 20 percent of the overall population, and voted in massive numbers in inconclusive elections last month.

“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” he said, adding that it was wrong to malign an entire community.
“The attempt to marginalize them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of statesmanship,” Mr. Eisenkot said. “It dishonors Israel’s Declaration of Independence and the values we take pride in as a Jewish and democratic state.”
The Declaration of Independence says all citizens have equal social and political rights “irrespective of religion, race or sex.”

Bessent Takes Hawkish Turn in White House Debate on China
The Treasury secretary who sought to de-escalate tariff wars is taking a tougher approach to exports of sensitive U.S. technology.
President Trump heads to Asia on Monday for high-stakes meetings with foreign leaders aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine and smoothing over trade frictions with China. But the most tense meeting could take place aboard Air Force One.
Sequestered together on the journey across the world will be Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, whose long-running rivalry has recently spilled into the open.
Mr. Lutnick is under fire for slow-walking several measures aimed at clamping down on the supply of Nvidia chips to foreign data centers that serve Chinese clients. The controversy has put Mr. Lutnick at odds with Mr. Bessent, who has increasingly taken a hard line on China. The Treasury secretary traditionally manages America’s economic relationship with China. The internal clash over China policy has echoes of Mr. Trump’s first term, when the president’s economic advisers regularly argued about how forcefully to confront China over its trade practices. But in recent months, the Trump administration has been frustrated that China has not lived up to its commitments for purchases of American farm products and to accelerate exports of its critical minerals, which are needed for making high-tech electronics and military equipment.

49ers stun Cowboys, Chiefs and Bengals impress - NFL week 10
- Published
The NFL's brightest stars lit up week 10 of the 2026 season with some astonishing plays on Sunday.
The likes of Brock Purdy, Christian McCaffrey, Patrick Mahomes, Jahmyr Gibbs and Ja'Marr Chase showcased their skills with some explosive action to help their teams to victory.
The San Francisco 49ers produced a historic display in Dallas while there were also big wins for the Kansas City Chiefs, Detroit Lions and Cincinnati Bengals.
It means the 49ers and Buffalo Bills continue to share the league's best record (8-1), while five teams moved to 7-2, including the in-form Jacksonville Jaguars.
Purdy shines for free-scoring 49ers
The San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys have a fierce rivalry stretching back to the 1990s and they delivered another classic with a shootout in Texas.
Brock Purdy showed why he is among the leading contenders for the Most Valuable Player award as the 49ers won 46-40, racking up 584 yards of offence - the most Dallas have ever allowed at home.
San Francisco had three touchdowns of more than 65 yards, while Purdy threw for a career-high 389 yards and three touchdowns. The quarterback even blocked for one of the 49ers' other three scores, a 70-yard run by Deebo Samuel on a reverse trick play.
The highlights were two Purdy passes to Christian McCaffrey. The first saw Purdy show remarkable poise as he scrambled out of the pocket before finding McCaffrey for a 74-yard score, while the second was a perfectly-executed play over the middle that saw McCaffrey sprint in untouched from 66 yards.
Dual-threat running back McCaffrey finished with three scores and 223 total yards, including a career-high 161 receiving yards.
Purdy's MVP rival Josh Allen had a relatively quiet game as the Buffalo Bills won 31-12 at the New York Jets, while the Jacksonville Jaguars won 40-23 at the Tennessee Titans.
Including the end of last season, the Jaguars have won 15 of their past 17 regular-season games and must be considered Super Bowl contenders, especially after bringing in three key defensive players before the trade deadline on Tuesday.
Burrow keeps Bengals run going
Joe Burrow became the new MVP favourite last week and continued his superb form as the Cincinnati Bengals romped to a 38-18 win in their divisional match-up against the Pittsburgh Steelers.
New Manchester United boss Mauricio Pochettino was among the crowd as Burrow was involved in four touchdowns for the fifth straight game, tying an NFL record.
The Bengals quarterback had 300 passing yards before half-time and finished with 409. Most of them were to Ja'Marr Chase, who claimed 231 yards from just 11 catches for the 7-2 Bengals.
Their divisional rivals, the Cleveland Browns, pulled off another comeback as they recovered from 17-0 down to beat the Houston Texans 27-24.
The Browns have won their opening four home games for the first time since 1963 and are now 6-4.
Quarterback Deshaun Watson led the Browns to a game-winning drive in the fourth quarter of all six of those wins and he said this one was "definitely special" as it came against his former team.
Dream international trip for St Brown
Munich staged the penultimate international game of the season and just playing in Germany was a "dream come true" for the Detroit Lions' wide receiver Amon-Ra St Brown.
The 27-year-old's mother is German, and he and his two brothers speak the language fluently and have been regular visitors to their mother's homeland.
St Brown, who arrived wearing lederhosen and waved the German flag as he ran on to the field, scored two touchdowns as the Lions charged to a 35-10 win over the New England Patriots.
Yet St Brown was outshone by team-mate Jahmyr Gibbs, who had 99 receiving yards, 153 rushing yards and two touchdowns, taking him to 62 overall - a new NFL record in a player's first four seasons.
The Patriots lost Drake Maye to an ankle injury when he was sacked on the game's opening drive by Aidan Hutchinson, who injured his knee as he celebrated, and the Lions fear it is a significant injury.
Detroit, the Minnesota Vikings and Chicago Bears are now all 7-2 in the ultra-competitive NFC North, with the Vikings bouncing back after suffering back-to-back defeats.
Kirk Cousins returned to Minnesota before the trade deadline on Tuesday and the veteran quarterback led them to a 30-10 win at their other divisional rival, the 6-4 Green Bay Packers, with their defence claiming eight sacks - the most in a single game this season.
Seahawks spoil Mendoza's first start
The Las Vegas Raiders allowed Cousins to rejoin Minnesota as they felt Fernando Mendoza, this year's first overall draft pick, was ready to become their starting quarterback.
Mendoza's first start came against the Seattle Seahawks, the Super Bowl champions, and he managed to run in a 10-yard touchdown on the Raiders' opening drive.
But the Raiders' offence then struggled and Mendoza was sacked six times as the Seahawks won 21-13.
"It's good to get punched in the face because now it's a great opportunity to grow and learn," said Mendoza.
Seattle quarterback Drew Lock made two big touchdown passes on the run, one to Cooper Kupp and the other a 71-yard score by Jaxon Smith-Njigba.

Another milestone for Mahomes
The Kansas City Chiefs' run game has caught the eye so far this season, in particular new signing Kenneth Walker, but he was out injured on Sunday as Patrick Mahomes reminded everyone he has one of the best arms in the business.
For the first time since 2022, the three-time Super Bowl winner threw for five touchdowns, plus 348 yards, as Kansas City won 35-13 at the Atlanta Falcons.
Running back Emmett Johnson stepped up in the absence of Walker to claim 101 rushing yards, 70 receiving yards and two touchdowns.
Mahomes made explosive plays to Cyrus Allen and Andrew Armstrong for their first NFL scores, while fellow wide receiver Josh Downs scored on his debut after the Chiefs traded for him on deadline day.
That took Mahomes to 332 career touchdown passes, including the play-offs, putting the 31-year-old top of the all-time list for the most in a player's first 10 seasons.

His party’s deputy chairman, Shah Mehmood Qureshi, was also taken to hospital in the eastern city of Lahore from a jail in the same city on Tuesday (November 10). He remains in hospital.

AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast’s cable broadband service and Wi-Fi is “fiber-powered.”
“This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide,” AT&T’s lawsuit said. “At the center of that campaign is Comcast’s claim that Xfinity Internet and its associated Wi-Fi service are ‘Fiber-Powered.’”
While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds.
In contrast, fiber-to-the-home service can provide symmetrical upload and download speeds. Comcast has deployed fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory while advertising its service as fiber-powered in the majority of areas where cable makes the final connection.
AT&T’s lawsuit said that in describing its cable broadband as fiber-powered, Comcast “conveys to reasonable consumers the misleading impression that Xfinity Internet is a fiber-to-the-home service comparable to AT&T Fiber. In fact, the vast majority of Xfinity Internet runs over a hybrid fiber-coaxial (‘HFC’) network, where the critical ‘last mile’ connection to the customer’s home uses copper coaxial cable, not fiber.”
AT&T has its own history of ads that mislead customers about the nature of its network. It used to advertise 4G LTE service as “5GE” or “5G Evolution,” and displayed a 5GE network icon on 4G phones. AT&T claimed that its 5G Evolution ads “served to educate customers about the billions of dollars AT&T has invested to give customers an outstanding experience,” but the BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division found the term was likely to mislead consumers into thinking they had 5G connections.
AT&T: Fiber-powered is “literally false”
AT&T’s lawsuit said that Comcast’s fiber-powered claim “is literally false” because the cable firm’s HFC “architecture is fundamentally different from true fiber-to-the-home services like AT&T Fiber, which deliver fiber optic cables directly to the customer’s premises.”

Five European Countries Plan to Deport Migrants to Rwanda
Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark are seeking to establish a hub for rejected asylum seekers. Here’s what to know about their effort.
Five European countries announced a plan on Monday that would send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, an experiment that comes as governments across the continent toughen their stances on migration.
The joint push from Germany, Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece was pitched as a way to handle migrants who had no right to stay in Europe but who, for one reason or another, could not or would not return to their home countries.
The project, which is not yet finalized, shows how European leaders’ stance on migration has hardened since the arrivals of 2015-16, when countries like Germany admitted more than a million asylum seekers. With far-right groups like the Alternative for Germany rising in popularity, centrist leaders have gradually taken a less welcoming stance.
“For me, today marks a crucial step toward a new migration system,” Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister of Denmark, said at a news conference on Monday.
The pilot project is expected to start on a small scale, with perhaps 100 or 200 deportees. Critics are already worried both about the idea of sending people to a nation to which they have no connection, and about the risk that human rights will not be sufficiently protected in Rwanda.
Why Rwanda?
The country has a history of courting migration-related deals.
Britain developed a plan to send asylum seekers there in 2022, though judges in London ultimately ruled the effort unlawful and it was later abandoned. The United States has recently deported people to Rwanda.

A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
As retirees live longer, governments need to spend more on pensions. That makes it harder to fund other services, spurring protests like those planned this weekend in France.
Sébastien Ducros, a French data analyst who supports the widespread student protests in his country, has identified an obvious culprit for the lack of government funds for dilapidated schools.
“A huge portion of the money is going toward retirees, while many other things are being neglected,” said Mr. Ducros, 36. “I honestly think — even if it feels strange to say — that people like my parents are in a position where they should and could” surrender some of their pension payments, he added, saying that they were about to retire.
But Laurent Grinwald, 72, who retired recently after decades as a postal worker, isn’t eager for his pension to be reduced, particularly to pay for other state-funded services. Especially, he said, as rents and the cost of living have shot up.
“We’ve been working all this time,” Mr. Grinwald said, “and now, suddenly, the stance is, ‘Well, no, we’re going to start taking a bit more?’”
This disagreement embodies a broader question for Europe, one that is at the heart of mass antigovernment demonstrations planned for Saturday in France, as well as recent protests driven by frustrated young people in countries including Belgium, Germany, Greece, Italy and Portugal. As Europeans live longer, should the needs of the young be eclipsed by their parents’ and grandparents’ pensions, routinely the largest items in Europe’s national budgets?
“It’s a generational clash,” said Jorge Galindo, the director of EsadeEcPol, an independent think tank in Spain, which has some of the most generous pensions in Europe.

The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency. Stuck in a desert with little rain and abundant searing sun, these plants don’t just survive, they thrive—and in turn provide habitat for owls and other birds, and flowers for bats and other pollinators.
Yet cacti are in serious trouble, due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections. Now we can add worsening droughts to those woes, according to a new study in the journal Nature. Researchers modeled a future of not just relentlessly rising temperatures but also the attendant dry spells, finding that the majority of nearly 1,000 cactus species will lose habitat as the climate radically changes. More than a quarter of those species could lose at least 80 percent of that habitat by 2100.
“The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper. “In reality, cacti are absolutely amazing—and they’re my favorite plant group, clearly—but they’re not that different from other plants.”
That means cacti need water. In the deserts of the southwestern United States, for example, they rely on seasonal monsoon rains, which tend to make July or August the wettest month in a given year. Because this is still a desert, cacti have evolved a range of adaptations to survive, like a waxy skin that helps them retain that bounty of rainwater. “Just like other plants, they evolved under conditions that they’re used to,” Pillet said. “When you take them outside of those conditions, they might not be able to handle that.”
Think of these cacti like sick hospital patients. Someone might be admitted for heat-related illness, as their body struggles to cool itself. At the same time, though, they might be dehydrated. Cacti are dealing with the same stresses, as global temperatures rise and dry spells intensify. “When we consider drought conditions, then it turns out that they’re much, much sicker than we previously thought,” Pillet said. “These results really do change the outlook of cacti, and most likely plants more broadly under climate change.”
Instead of simply modeling these threats going forward, the researchers turned to the citizen science platform iNaturalist, where people upload photos of plants and animals. This provided 650,000 observations of cacti in the wild, helping paint a clearer picture of how species might be faring.
Really, this isn’t a simple matter of cacti withering and dying. Sure, if relentless droughts take hold, individuals can’t get water. But the stress could be temporally complex, too. “Now we can move towards questions of: What life stages are most affected?” Pillet said. “Is it the adults or is it the seedlings? But also, which processes? Is it reduced growth or is it increased mortality? Or are plants failing to flower?”
Put another way: Cactus species could be suffering from sublethal effects of drought—the lack of water may not kill them immediately but still interfere with their reproduction. And without procreation, populations shrink. In the Sonoran Desert, for example, the iconic, towering saguaro is reproducing less frequently during prolonged droughts, because they’re not always flowering.
Part of the problem is that while desert ecosystems may look tough and hardened overall, they’re in fact quite fragile. “They don’t recover quickly once they are disturbed, or once they are degraded, just because there’s so little water and such higher temperatures,” said Marcos Robles, the Nature Conservancy’s lead scientist in Arizona, who wasn’t involved in the research. “It takes multiple decades to recover, and in some cases, they don’t recover.”
Now drought is compounding with other stressors, like habitat loss and poaching, to drive cactus species to the brink. On the opposite end of the spectrum, too much water from rising seas has led to the local extinction of the Key Largo tree cactus in Florida. Higher nighttime temperatures are a problem, too, since that’s when saguaro and other cacti respire to avoid water loss. “If the nighttime temperatures are very high, they can’t do it,” said Rod Haenni, president of the nonprofit Cactus and Succulent Society of America, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Then if you water on top of that, the plants just rot.”
Still, some cactus species may persist by picking up and leaving. Well, not individual plants, but populations could creep into areas with climates that more closely match what the species adapted to all those millennia ago. A similar thing is happening in the Arctic, actually, where some plants are marching farther north in “search” of increasingly agreeable weather and more water.
In the end, the purpose of this sort of research is to better inform where conservation professionals might concentrate their efforts. They can’t stop droughts, of course, but they can evacuate enough cacti to establish populations in botanical gardens, where they can be cared for as the climate grows more unrecognizable to even the hardiest desert vegetation. Species can even be reintroduced to the wild in some cases, so long as drought and high temperatures don’t remain a threat to a population.
Governments, too, need to protect the lands where cacti are threatened, Haenni said. This new research, he added, could make that happen. “Hopefully, it’ll wake people up,” Haenni said. “But the problem is that a lot of the governments involved are indifferent to this. There are a lot of people in the countries who are not indifferent, but they’re not running the governments.”

U.S. tightens controls on remote access to AI technology amid Nvidia fallout
The U.S. government has announced a rule to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that could let adversarial governments access American AI technology through overseas data centers.
The move comes amid the fallout at Nvidia, the world's dominant producer of AI chips, following revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative. NPR has not independently verified the claims. Huang stepped down as CEO last week.
Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, is a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company. Jensen Huang has personally lobbied President Trump to loosen restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. It is not known if Alice Huang influenced this activity.
The rapid advancement in cloud computing and AI infrastructure has made it possible to access advanced U.S. computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions, the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday.
The rule is designed to reinforce existing restrictions on access to sensitive American AI technology through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in other countries, which could threaten national security
However, a loophole existed where Chinese companies could still access those chips remotely, despite U.S. restrictions on their physical sale to China.
"The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security," the BIS statement said.
The government refers to artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" following an executive order signed by President Trump in September.
Since October 2022, U.S. companies have typically needed a BIS export license to sell advanced computing chips meeting specified technical thresholds to China, including Hong Kong and Macau. These restrictions covered advanced Nvidia chips, some high-performance semiconductor components, and certain AI computing systems.
Megaspeed is based in Singapore and operates facilities in Malaysia.
"Megaspeed conducts legitimate and lawful business. The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," the company said in a statement emailed to NPR and other news organizations on Sunday.
Prior to the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration had resisted imposing additional regulations to prevent foreign access to American AI technology.
The Biden administration had written a framework designed to control worldwide distribution of advanced AI chips on January 15, 2025 – five days before Trump's inauguration. In May 2025, Trump's Commerce Department announced it would not enforce the rule and intended to rescind it, calling it "ill-conceived and counterproductive."
Biden's framework would have also limited access to AI chips by countries considered security risks, required licenses for certain chip exports, and created restrictions on the power of advanced models and computing infrastructure.
The New York Times reported that Trump was first briefed by intelligence officials about Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy in October 2025. Both Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are expected to testify before Congress this month and next month and there will likely be further investigations into what Trump knew about the affair when the Democrats take control of Congress in January 2027, Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-NY, told NPR.
"We need to get the facts investigated, bring in individuals to give us as much information as possible under oath, so that we can get to the bottom of why this happened, how it occurred, and how we could prevent this type of compromise from happening again," said Clarke.

VS Hospitals has introduced a new 2D digital mammography system to strengthen breast cancer screening and diagnosis.
The AMULET SOPHINITY system from Fujifilm uses a high-resolution detector with a pixel size of 50 microns, allowing detailed imaging of breast tissue, including tiny microcalcifications, which can sometimes be an early indicator of breast abnormalities.
Mammography uses low-dose X-rays to examine breast tissue and can help identify abnormalities that may not be detectable through physical examination. The new system has intelligent exposure control, which adjusts X-ray exposure according to breast composition while maintaining image quality. AI-based positioning support is designed to assist in accurate positioning and consistent image acquisition.
The equipment takes approximately five seconds for standard image acquisition and 12 seconds for high-resolution imaging. It also has features such as flexible positioning, intelligent breast compression and automatic decompression to help reduce discomfort during the examination.
Speaking at the launch, S. Subramanian, Chairman and Managing Director of V.S. Hospitals, said early detection was important in breast cancer care and that mammography played a key role in identifying breast abnormalities.
The hospital will offer free mammography screening to underprivileged people throughout November 2026. Those seeking to avail themselves of the screening can contact the hospital at 7448850500.

Direct-to-consumer (D2C) startups have been facing mounting cost pressures since the US-Iran conflict drove up global crude prices, making it increasingly difficult for them to protect their already-thin margins. Even as higher oil prices push up freight, logistics, packaging and raw material costs for new-age brands and manufacturers, revising price tags does not seem to be a viable option for them for their lack of scale and bargaining power, leaving them grappling for alternatives. Unlike established fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) companies, which can leverage bulk procurement, supplier bargaining power, and diversified portfolios to absorb cost shocks, smaller D2C brands have far fewer buffers. Absorbing the increase depletes their already unsure margins, while passing it on to consumers risks losing them and reacquiring them at a higher cost. It’s a catch-22 situation for them. The pressure is particularly visible in categories such as food, beverages and personal care, for which crude-linked packaging, agricultural commodities and imported ingredients account for a significant share of procurement costs. Higher shipping expenses and volatility in supplier availability have added to the challenge, making it difficult for startups to plan inventory and input requirements. The festive season did offer some respite on the demand side. Online festive sales grew 17% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹1.41 Lakh Cr in 2026, according to Datum Intelligence’s Festive Barometer. Elsewhere, ClickPost’s analysis of more than 80 Mn orders across nearly 400 D2C brands indicated that daily orders increased 27% YoY in the run-up to Diwali, while estimated gross merchandise value (GMV) grew 45%. The problem is that this has not necessarily translated into an easier operating environment for D2Cs. Brands are struggling now to sustain consumer demand beyond the festive period while managing the cost of acquiring customers, fulfilling orders and replenishing inventory. However, there’s some reason for optimism now. Brent crude, which surged to around $118 per barrel in late October, has since cooled to approximately $95 as of November 16, offering a possible reprieve to businesses grappling with rising input costs. For D2C brands, however, the relief may take time to materialise, as the impact of lower oil prices will take a while to filter through to supply chains, freight rates and packaging costs. For D2C startups, the bigger question is no longer whether input costs will ease, but how long they will have to absorb the pressure. How Brands Are Absorbing Cost Spikes The bigger challenge for startups is not necessarily the rise in input costs itself, but the unpredictability of procurement prices, which makes cost planning and margin management very difficult, said the founder of a large D2C beauty brand who preferred not to be named. “What bothers startups most is the variation. If a supplier does not stock one product because the price has gone up, the full production (line) might stop,” he said. For instance, a specialised ingredient may become unavailable because a supplier is unwilling to maintain inventory amid an uncertain price environment. Even if it accounts for a relatively small share of the final product’s cost, its absence can disrupt the manufacturing process altogether. “You cannot make any product with 99% ingredients. That one missing ingredient will hold the thing. Then you scramble and get it from somewhere at any cost,” the founder quoted above added. Brands that rely on imported ingredients or packaging materials feel the pinch harder. Shipping costs can fluctuate sharply, forcing them to choose between paying a premium to avoid production delays and waiting for freight rates to ease. Either way, higher procurement costs and the need to hold extra inventory strain working capital, leaving less money for scaling-up. Bharat Birla, executive director at Anand Rathi Investment Banking, said rising commodity and packaging costs have squeezed larger FMCG companies too, particularly in home care, packaged foods and personal care. But for smaller brands, which lack comparable procurement scale, the impact on operating margins can be far more pronounced, he pointed out. Food & Beverage Startups Face Most Cost Exposure The impact of input inflation varies depending on the product category. For several non-food D2C businesses, the cost of goods sold (COGS) may account for around 15-20% of the product price, and at most 30%, according to a large D2C beauty brand founder who did not wish to be named. Food businesses, on the other hand, can have a significantly higher COGS, sometimes reaching 40%. This makes food and beverage brands relatively more vulnerable to fluctuations in agricultural commodities, packaging and transportation costs. Crude oil is particularly relevant for beverage manufacturers because several packaging materials, including plastic bottles, preforms, caps and labels, are linked to petrochemical inputs. Nikhil Doda, cofounder of Lahori Zeera, told Inc42, “Most of our raw materials depend on crude. Our preforms, caps and labels are all affected. That hit was there.” The company did not raise prices specifically to offset the recent inflation, although it implemented selective hikes in April-May 2026 as part of its regular price revision cycle, he added. With Reliance’s Campa expanding and Coca-Cola and PepsiCo sharpening their pricing strategies, further hikes could risk weakening its competitive position. “You cannot increase prices when Coke and Pepsi have decreased their prices from ₹20 to ₹10,” Doda said. So, for emerging consumer brands, the pricing dilemma is sharper: with fewer buffers to absorb cost shocks, they must protect margins without pricing themselves out of the market. Why Cutting Discounts May Be Easier Than Raising Prices Unlike established FMCG players with decades of consumer loyalty, D2C brands rely heavily on digital advertising, promotions and discounts to acquire and retain customers, making price hikes risky in a market where consumers have plenty of alternatives. So, mid-sized and smaller companies are having to look at changes in product mix and pack sizes to manage inflation, Birla said. The room to raise prices, however, is narrowing for all. According to Sandeep Abhange, research analyst – consumer and midcaps at LKP Securities, large FMCG companies have so far absorbed roughly half of the input cost inflation. “HUL faced 8-10% material inflation but took only 2-5% price hikes, while Dabur took 4% against 10% inflation,” he said. Startups, Abhange said, could increasingly resort to calibrated price increases and changes in pack sizes, particularly at lower price points. Smaller packs may see grammage reductions, while larger packs could see more direct price increases. Also, brands should evaluate input inflation alongside marketing expenditure, said the beauty brand founder. “For D2C companies, the cost of goods has a relatively limited impact on overall prices in several categories. If some ingredients become twice as expensive, the cost may go up from, say, 18% to 22%, but marketing costs around 30%.” This means a reduction in marketing expenditure or discounting could sometimes have a greater impact on profitability than a marginal improvement in procurement costs. Brands with healthy gross margins, repeat customers and efficient marketing strategies may therefore be better positioned to absorb inflation. Those dependent on aggressive discounts and paid customer acquisition could face greater pressure. The challenge is particularly relevant after the festive season, when promotional activity begins to moderate and brands have to convert seasonal buyers into repeat customers. Abhange expects another meaningful round of price increases in Q3 and Q4 FY27, particularly across categories such as detergents, soaps, biscuits, noodles and packaged snacks, which remain exposed to crude-linked inputs and agricultural commodities. Crude Prices Have Cooled, But Will Startups See Relief? The softening of crude prices has offered some optimism. However, even as expectations of improved global supply have weighed on prices, geopolitical and shipping-related uncertainties continue to pose risks. For Indian startups, the transmission of lower crude prices into procurement costs is unlikely to be immediate. “Even if crude cools down, the effect on our procurement levels will take at least five to six months. It’s a process, and things should also remain stable,” Doda said. Suppliers may still be working with inventory procured at higher prices, while shipping and conversion costs can take additional time to adjust. Doda added that geopolitical uncertainty makes it difficult to predict when the situation will normalise. If global prices remain stable, he expects the impact to gradually reach procurement costs over the next five to six months. Birla too predicts a similar timeline. This means packaging-intensive businesses may have to wait until the first half of calendar 2027 to see a meaningful reduction in some input costs, provided the decline is sustained. The broader margin outlook, however, remains cautious. Abhange expects gross margins across FMCG companies to remain under pressure through Q3 and Q4 FY27, with stabilisation likely only from Q1 FY28 (April to June 2027) as lower crude prices and easing packaging costs gradually feed through. The timelines are not necessarily interchangeable for every D2C business. The pace of relief will depend on the category, supplier contracts, inventory cycles and the extent to which a brand relies on crude-linked inputs. Next Few Quarters Will Test Unit Economics For D2C startups, the next phase will be about managing growth without allowing higher procurement and marketing expenses to erode profitability. Lower crude prices offer a positive signal, but the relief will take time to reach procurement costs. For packaging-intensive businesses, the five-to-six-month transmission period cited by Doda and Birla suggests that meaningful cost normalisation may take until the first half of 2027, provided global prices remain stable. A broader recovery in FMCG margins could take longer, with Abhange pointing to Q1 FY28 as a possible turning point. In the interim, D2Cs will have to focus on supplier diversification, inventory planning, reducing avoidable marketing expenditure and improving gross margins rather than relying solely on price increases. The current cost cycle may not necessarily become a demand-side problem for the sector, but could reveal the difference between brands that have built resilient operating models and those whose growth depends on continuous discounts and external capital. For emerging consumer businesses, the festive season may have brought more customers through the door, but the bigger test now is whether they can retain those customers, fulfil demand and make money from every additional order.

Tokyo protests after two suspected Russian aircraft violate Japanese airspace
Japan said it has protested to Moscow after two suspected Russian warplanes temporarily entered Japanese airspace off the country’s southwestern coast on Tuesday as tensions escalate between the two sides
TOKYO -- Japan said it strongly protested to Moscow on Tuesday after two suspected Russian aircraft entered its airspace off its southwestern coast, the latest incident fueling escalating tensions between the neighbors.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told reporters the suspected Russian aircraft early Tuesday violated Japanese airspace for about five minutes near Fukuoka, long enough for the Air Self-Defense Force to scramble fighter jets and send warnings.
Japan's government has lodged "an extremely stern protest" and “strongly” demanded preventive measures be taken, Koizumi said. He did not specify the types of aircraft involved.
“The violation of the Japanese airspace by the Russian aircraft is not only a serious violation of our country's sovereignty, but also a threat to our safety,” Koizumi said. “It is absolutely unacceptable.”
The Russian aircraft flew across the Tsushima Strait, then headed south and flew above the waters between Taiwan and Japan's westernmost island of Yonaguni, Koizumi said.
Separately, South Korea’s military said several Russian military aircraft temporarily entered the country’s air defense identification zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan on Monday, though they did not violate South Korean airspace.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the military had detected the aircraft before they entered the zone and scrambled fighter jets. The South’s military did not disclose the number of Russian aircraft it detected or what types of planes they were.
Koizumi did not comment on why the violations took place but said Japan continues to closely monitor Russian military activity “with strong interest."
Japan has raised growing concern over growing joint military activity between Russia and China around the Japanese coasts.
The airspace violation was the latest sign of deteriorating relations between the two countries. Tensions have risen since Russian President Vladimir Putin visited Iturup in August, one of four Russian-controlled islands off Japan’s northern coast that Tokyo also claims.
Tensions escalated in mid-October after the arrest of a Japanese journalist in Russia on suspicion of spying. Despite repeated protests and demands for his immediate release, the journalist, who works for the Hokkaido newspaper, remains in custody.
Earlier this month, Russia placed several subsidiaries of Japan Tobacco Inc. under the temporary management of a Russian company following a presidential order issued by Putin. Japan protested and demanded the measure be withdrawn.
The Soviet Union seized the Kuril Islands from Japan in the final days of World War II. The territorial dispute has prevented the two countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending hostilities.

STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years.
The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase.
The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit.
When it came time for the first stage to return to the ground, it dropped like a rock. However, due to an unspecified issue, the vehicle was commanded to divert into the Gulf rather than return to the Starbase facility to be caught by the launch tower. It created a fantastically powerful explosion, even for observers more than 10 miles away.
Primary mission, a success
The primary aim of Friday’s launch was the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites from a narrow door at the base of the spacecraft. This occurred about 40 minutes into Starship’s flight, and all 26 satellites—which have solar panels that stretch 60 meters end to end when fully deployed—safely made it into orbit, where they will now use onboard propulsion to raise their altitude.
This means that Starship is now an operational, orbital rocket. It is the largest and most powerful machine humans have ever launched into space. The challenge for the company now is to make Starship reusable and dramatically increase its flight rate.
In that sense, the first part of Friday’s mission was not a success. SpaceX had hoped to return the first-stage booster, refurbish it, and fly it again. The company has previously landed and reflown Starship boosters but has yet to do so with the latest iteration of the vehicle, version 3.

Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back - and it cuts deep in a 'nation of good sports'
- Published
As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.
Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.
But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.
"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."
A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.
Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.
His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.
Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."
"I'm a bit bored of it," one woman watching the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.
Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.
There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.
There's a sense of injustice that Australia can't escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.
"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.
"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."
Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.
David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja was telling the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".
Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Cameron Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.
But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.
And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.
Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".
"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.
"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."
He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.
He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.
"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.
Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.
Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.
But he was also frank - using strong words to reject Khawaja's claims and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."
As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioning Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.
"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."
Few people think he'll get his wish.
"It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said.
"I don't know what the outcome will be."

The successful global run of Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana: Part 1, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, has turned a quiet, rocky hilltop in Kerala's Kollam district into one of India’s most sought-after travel destinations.
The film's dramatic depiction of the mythical bird Jatayu fighting Ravana to protect Goddess Sita has sparked a renewed cultural interest, drawing thousands of tourists to the Jatayu Earth's Center in Chadayamangalam—home to the world's largest bird sculpture.
At the heart of this architectural marvel is a decade of dedication by a visionary artist, Rajiv Anchal.
Rajiv Anchal is a renowned Malayalam film director and sculptor, best known for directing the 1997 Mohanlal-starrer Guru, which was India's official entry for the Academy Awards.
Anchal is the mastermind and chief sculptor behind the Jatayu Earth's Center. For nearly ten years, he trekked up the massive 1,000-foot-high rock every day to oversee the conceptualisation and construction of the monument. His vision was to create a colossal work of art while preserving the rocky landscape's natural ecology.
The result is a staggering concrete sculpture measuring 200 feet in length, 150 feet in width, and 70 feet in height, built to symbolise women's safety and honour.
Inside the sculpture, Anchal also designed a multi-level audio-visual museum and an immersive theatre.
The recent cinematic retelling of the epic has transformed the site of Chadayamangalam into a bustling tourist hub.
According to media reports, the centre is currently attracting around 3,200 to 4,000 visitors a day, with weekend numbers expected to exceed 5,000.
Local executives note a massive influx of tourists from North India, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka, driven by the emotional resonance of the film's Jatayu narrative.
Acknowledging the trend, Kerala Chief Minister VD Satheesan and the state's tourism department recently invited film enthusiasts to visit the site, positioning it as a prime destination for both spiritual seekers and adventure tourists.
The Jatayu Earth's Center operates daily from 10:00 am to 5:30 pm (timings often extend to 6:00 pm on weekends and holidays).
Visitors can choose from multiple entry packages based on how they wish to ascend the hill:
Note: Adventure sports like rappelling, zip-lining, and paintball incur additional charges, with full-day packages ranging from ₹1,500 to ₹3,500.
Located in Chadayamangalam, the destination is highly accessible for travellers:
By Air: The nearest airport is Thiruvananthapuram (Trivandrum) International Airport, located approximately 50 km away. Taxis and buses are readily available from the airport.
By Train: The nearest major railway station is in Kollam city, roughly 38 km from the site. Varkala railway station is also a convenient transit point.
By Road: The centre is situated right off the Main Central (MC) Road (State Highway 1), making it an easy drive from both Trivandrum and Kochi.

Quick Answer
You can upscale low-resolution photos for free using offline AI tools. Use Upscayl on Mac and Windows, Upscal on iPhone, or Offline AI Image Upscaler on Android. These apps enhance image resolution up to 4x without uploading your photos to the cloud, keeping them private.
If there is one area where AI has truly revolutionized, apart from writing and coding, it is image upscaling. Whether it’s your old photo taken on a Sony Cyber-shot or one that’s completely distorted, you can give it to AI and you can get a clean, high-resolution version without changing its original form.
Not just your old photos, you can also upscale any standard photo taken on modern phones to the highest resolution possible.
However, one downside of using AI to upscale images, especially if you care about privacy, is that your images need to be uploaded to the cloud for any AI provider, processed there, and then sent back to your smartphone.
Although those images won’t be public, some companies use them to train their AI models. This is the reason why many users, even we, think twice before uploading sensitive photos to AI models for upscaling
Fortunately, tools like Upscayl let the AI model run locally on your device and upscale images to the highest possible resolution without your data leaving your device. Although it has specific hardware requirements, most modern PCs and smartphones support it, and it’s faster too.
It also supports batch processing, where you can upscale multiple images at once. The quality is pretty good too. In this guide, I will show you how to set up Upscayl, a local image upscaler on your Mac, Windows, Android, and iPhone.
Table of Contents
How to Upscale Low-Resolution Photos Locally for Free
Please note that the original Upscayl is only available on desktop platforms like Windows, Mac, and Linux; there are also free apps that use similar technology and work well. I will cover everything in this guide together and help you set up a free image upscaler locally on your device. This guide is designed for beginners, so every step is comprehensive and detailed.
You don’t need much setup to upscale images locally. Since everything comes in one package, the process is very straightforward. You can download the upscaler app; it installs the upscaler model locally and includes a beginner-friendly interface, making it even easier for first-time users.
Below are the steps for each device.
How to upscale photos on a Mac with Upscayl
Step 1: Open Safari or any browser, visit upscayl.org in the address bar, and press Return. On the page, click on the Download button at the top right
Step 2: Now, on the download page, you can see download options for various platforms, including macOS. However, do not click on the macOS button. It opens the Mac App Store, where Upscayl is a paid app. The same app is available for free from Upscayl’s own website.
Step 3: Tap on the alternative download option below and select the DMG version of the app
Step 4: Once downloaded, install the app on your Mac
Step 5: Open the app and complete the onboarding steps. They’re straightforward and easy to follow.
Step 6: Now using Upscayl is easy. In the sidebar, under Step 1, tap Select Image, or drag and drop the image into the right pane.
Step 7: Next, once the image is uploaded, under Step 2, choose an AI model. Upscayl Standard is the best choice for most images. You can also select a different model based on your preference.
Step 8: Now set Image Scale to 4x. This setting makes the image width and height four times larger, so a 480 by 320 photo becomes 1920 by 1280 pixels. You can also drag the slider to change it.
Step 9: Next, under Step 3, you can set where Upscayl saves the new upscaled image. To save it in a preferred location, click Set output folder and choose a folder.
Step 10: Finally, under Step 4, click Upscayl. Depending on your settings and your hardware, it can take a couple of seconds to a minute to upscale images.
Step 11: Once it is done, you can compare the changes. Drag the slider in the middle of the picture to compare the original (left) with the upscaled version (right). The upscaled image will be saved in the folder you set in step 9, or next to your original image file on your Mac.
How to upscale photos on Windows with Upscayl
Next, let’s see how you can upscale images on Windows using Upscayl. The process is very similar to the Mac.
Step 1: Open Microsoft Edge or any browser, go to upscayl.org, and click Download in the top-right corner of the header.
Step 2: Now, on the download page, click the Windows button to start downloading (about 250 MB)
Step 3: Once downloaded, click the file to open it and go through the setup process. If Windows prompts you to allow this app from an unknown publisher, click Yes to start installing.
Step 4: Now select the installation folder; I recommend you keep the suggested installation folder and click Install.
Step 5: Finally, once installed, click Finish to complete the installation on your Windows.
Step 6: Now open the app and go through the setup process. It is very straightforward and easy to follow.
Step 7: Using Upscayl is easy; in Step 1, select an image. If you want to upscale multiple images, turn on the toggle that says ” Batch upscale above Step 1
Step 8: Select the image you want to upscale and tap on Open
Step 9: Now select the upscale model. The Upscayl Standard is best for most photos. Tap it and change it based on your preference. You can also increase the image scale to 4x. By default, it is 4x.
Step 10: Now, in step three, select the desired folder where you want to store the upscaled images, or keep the default, which stores the upscaled version right next to the original file, and tap the Upscayl button to upscale your images
How to upscale photos on iPhone with Upscayl
Upscayl.org is not available for mobile phones. However, free apps let you upscale images locally on your device. Some apps also offer an optional paid plan, but most features are free. Here are the two best upscaling apps.
Step 1: Download the Upscal Enhance Video and Image app on iPhone. Use this link.
Step 2: Once the app is installed, open the app and switch over to the image option
Step 3: Now you can select images from Photos or Files. In this case, I’m choosing the image from my files.
Step 4: The app shows your photo’s current resolution and how much you can upgrade it. In my case, my 480 by 320 photo can be upscaled to 1920 by 1280. Next, tap the settings bar just above Start upscaling. It shows the current model, scale, and format. You can tap the settings icon to customize the model, Upscaling methods, and more.
Step 5: Once you’ve made your changes, tap the Start Upscaling button and wait for the image to upscale. Once complete, you will see the completed status; tap Save to Photos to save the upscaled images to your Photos app.
How to upscale photos on Android with Offline AI Image Upscaler
Similar to iPhone, you can download the Offline AI Upscaler app by Bytesweavers to upscale photos locally on your Android
Step 1: Open the Play Store and download the Offline AI Image Upscaler app by Bytesweavers on your Android phone. You can use this link.
Step 2: Now open the app and tap on Choose photo, then select the image you want to upscale
Step 3: The app shows your photo and the resolution it will make. In my case, it’s 1920 by 1280. To edit the model, you can find the model settings below the photo. The default model is set to Photo AI, which is recommended. However, you can also choose a different model based on your needs.
Step 4: Once you’ve customized it, click Enhance Photo, and that’s it. The app will enhance your photo for a few minutes and when it’s done, drag the slider on the photo to compare the original with the enhanced version. Once you’re done, you can save the photo in different formats.
Give Your Old Photos a New Life With AI
This is how to set up an offline image AI upscaler on Windows, Mac, Android, and iPhone. This setup works completely offline, and many of these methods also support batch processing to upscale your images.
However, for local AI image models, Upscayl is currently the best option. However, it is not as good as any online model. Although it reduces pixelation, it adds softness; if the original image is too distorted and has fewer details, it can soften the image. In most cases with decent images, though, the upscaled version works well. But again, it all depends upon the quality of the original image.
Also remember that upscaling an image multiple times doesn’t improve its quality. Only the first output is the highest quality you can get. Exposure to extreme heat during pregnancy can lead to severe outcomes, including preterm birth, stillbirth and congenital abnormalities in newborns, prompting experts at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) to highlight maternal health risks and call for targeted adaptation strategies.
The issue comes into focus as countries at COP31 prepare to discuss progress towards the Global Goal on Adaptation, a framework to help nations develop key adaptation measures, including those needed to address the health impacts of climate change.
However, translating growing recognition of climate-related health risks into action remains a challenge, particularly in the absence of adequate financial support.
According to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), only about one per cent of formal climate finance under its financial mechanism is currently directed towards health.
The broader issue of adaptation finance for developing nations is also expected to feature prominently in discussions in the coming days.
Speaking to PTI on the sidelines of COP31, Alan Dangour, Director of Climate and Health at the Wellcome Trust, said the foundation is seeking to highlight the evidence of heat-related impacts on pregnant women through three key areas -- elevating the issues as a risk for women, developing guidelines and preparing health systems.
“We have three key points: recognising that pregnant women are a particularly vulnerable group when it comes to climate-driven extreme heat, developing guidelines to help nurses, midwives and doctors respond to the challenges pregnant women face during heatwaves, and prepare health systems for a new world shaped by climate change, and identify the most vulnerable people so they are protected,” Dangour said.
He said pregnant women were not always recognised as a particularly vulnerable group and stressed that health systems must specifically account for their needs and risks during heatwaves.
“At the moment they are not recognised as such, and they need to be included in clinical guidelines. When it comes to data, we are keen that countries record the impacts of climate change on pregnant women and then work out how their guidelines and processes can protect them,” he said.
“That evidence is important because we can see what works and what doesn’t in different parts of the world, and share that knowledge,” he said.
Former World Health Organisation (WHO) chief scientist Soumya Swaminathan stressed the importance of highlighting the issue at COP31, saying the health impacts of climate change were already being felt and required immediate action.
“It is good that for the last three COPs or so we have had a day focused on health and climate, because everyone is increasingly recognising that the health impacts of climate change are already happening and need immediate action. They are also hitting certain vulnerable groups disproportionately, and pregnant women are one of them,” Swaminathan told PTI.
Citing studies showing that exposure to extreme heat can affect pregnant women's health, pregnancy outcomes and the health of newborns, she said the WHO had recently released a document identifying pregnant women as a high-risk group and recommending measures countries should take to protect them.
She also stressed the need to integrate climate and health data, saying policymakers must urgently begin linking exposure to extreme heat and air pollutants with their effects on human health.
“When heat and air pollution occur together in the same place, the impacts are three times as high as from either risk factor alone. India has many places with both heat and bad air pollution, so we must start looking at these data and correlating exposure to climatic and weather variables, such as heat and pollutants, with health outcomes,” the former WHO chief scientist told PTI.
Swaminathan said there was an urgent need for a research programme to address the issue, adding that sufficient evidence was already available to warrant action. She also called for the government's and states' Maternal and Child Health Programme to factor in heat exposure and take proactive and preventive measures to minimise its impact on pregnant women.
Youssef Nassef, Director of the Adaptation Programme at UN Climate Change, said the first 1,000 days, from conception until a child turns two, were considered the most critical period, as climate-related harm could begin even before birth.
“A lot of what we're talking about in terms of climate impacts generally, but heat in particular, has a severe impact on maternal health, on newborn babies. Unfortunately, in climate finance, about 1 per cent of formal climate finance under the financial mechanism goes to health. There is an incongruence between the needs, the demand and the supply,” he said.
Bhavreen Kandhari, an environmentalist and the co-founder of the ‘Warrior Moms’ movement, underscored that heatwaves have had a significant impact on pregnant women, particularly those living in more vulnerable areas or working in more vulnerable occupations, such as daily-wage workers, construction workers and farmers.
“Daily-wage workers, for instance, have to earn a living. They have to continue working because they simply cannot afford to stop. There is no looking back for them. Vulnerable mothers and other at-risk groups are not thinking about the future, but simply trying to survive this particular season, or, at most, looking ahead to the next one,” she said.

Good morning and happy Monday! Today’s newsletter features some pretty saucy tidbits. We’ve got a doctor on why hot baths and “wellness modules” can’t cure the profession’s burn out, two medical school professors on why med school just isn’t working, and a (well-placed? wildly cliche?) Charles Dickens reference. Thanks for reading!
WH Chief of Staff Stephen Miller has Kennedy ready to go hard on MAHA
“It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.”
That line was written to describe the sprawling complexity of 18th century Europe. But it could just as easily apply to the Department of Health and Human Services. Sure, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is facing an oppositional Democratic Congress, a growing measles epidemic (with two more deaths recorded, bringing the total to 10), and a weakened MAHA movement.
And yet, sources told STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo that Kennedy has new pep in his step, thanks to recently-appointed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. Miller is purportedly a MAHA superfan, with a particular interest in vaccine schedule shakeups and redefining ultra-processed foods. And one week into the job, he’s already handed message control back to cabinet secretaries.
Kennedy and his team are preparing to charge hard at major MAHA targets. One close aid is even telling staff that it’s go time for MAHA. Read more here.
Meanwhile, Democrats have been preparing plans on their own …
Democrats settle on a message: ‘Medicare for More’
It doesn’t have quite the same ring to it as “Medicare for All.” But coming out of a retreat, House Dems have coalesced around a top health policy priority — bringing government-run health care to more Americans by allowing people to access Medicare earlier in their lives. A related proposal, ‘Medikids,’ would provide coverage from birth to 26 years old.
“I think we’ve got to lower the age of eligibility as it relates to Medicare,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) told reporters after the Denver gathering. “I think we gotta make sure we cover hearing, vision, and dental. And we’ve got to make sure that every child in America can be able to see a doctor with high-quality, affordable health care.”
STAT’s John Wilkerson writes that this unified message is new territory for a party once split between “those who support Medicare for All and those who prefer incremental changes.” But the comity could obscure deeper differences down the road. Find out more here, and read to the end for a crystallizing boat metaphor from New York Times columnist Ezra Klein.
The biggest biotechs in China
China’s ascendant drug industry is no monolith, despite the way it’s often described by Western competitors, pundits and policymakers. The country is home to scores of companies with diverging ambitions, founded last year or last century, each vying for attention and capital amid a domestic scientific renaissance and a geopolitical standoff.
It’s complicated. To help make sense of it, STAT and the risk intelligence platform WireScreen on Monday published China’s Biotech Powerhouse 25, a ranking of the country’s most valuable publicly traded firms that tracks the varying strategies — and fortunes — of the world’s rapidly growing new medicine chest. — Damian Garde
Stop telling burned out doctors to take walks and breathe deeper
As a physician on the edge of burnout, Frances Mei Hardin heard all the tips. Light some candles. Pop over to the doctor appreciation pizza party. Complete these mindfulness worksheets.
“The advice to take a warm bath for respite particularly appealed to me, although before long one bath per day became two,” she writes. “That yielded a yeast infection, which does not exactly help one unwind.”
The problem with all of these suggestions, Hardin writes, is that they put the onus on the physician rather than on the increasingly broken system many doctors operate in: “We already know what works for physicians, and it isn’t any of that level one relaxation stuff. A meta-analysis from 2017 found a 2.5 times greater effect from measures such as workload reduction and schedule changes than stress management and mindfulness education for physicians on an individual basis.” Read her column here.
New guidance on how to help patients who’ve taken a powerful sedative
Increasingly, the tranquilizer medetomidine is making its way into the U.S. drug supply, almost always laced into opioids.
Medetomidine is a powerful sedative, and standard overdose treatments like naloxone won’t always reverse all of its effects. Now, the American Society for Addiction Medicine has released new guidance on how to treat patients who’ve taken the drug. A key piece of advice — providers need to know whether medetomidine is in their local drug supply, since its symptoms can mimic other conditions, including sepsis. Read the full writeup here.
Medical school needs reinvention. Here’s one idea
Nearly as soon as doctors-to-be reach medical school, they begin to prepare for the U.S. Medical Licensing Exam Step 1. Step 1 is a bear of a test, and the first two years of medical school are theoretically meant to prepare students to pass.
But a lot of students have concluded their courses just aren’t that useful for this purpose. Many (50 percent, by some estimates!) skip lectures, instead spending thousands of dollars on top of tuition for commercial prep material.
This has created an untenable situation, two medical ethics professors write. Their solution: Break medical school apart. Let students prepare for Step 1 by any approach that makes sense for them — on their own, through an online course or one-year program, as part of pre-med. Once they pass, they can apply for a shortened medical school focused on clinical experience, professional identity formation, and deeper dives into ethics and population health.
This could help lower the cost of medical school attendance, the authors write, while also diversifying the pool of candidates who apply to school. It would also let medical schools refocus their resources on the training that matters. “We strongly believe that medical school should be about learning how to be a doctor, not how to pass a test,” they write.
