Has Trafford replaced Pickford as England No 1?
- Published
It was some night for James Trafford.
As he was mobbed by his England team-mates for a late double save that secured a memorable 3-2 win against world champions Spain, the debate that followed about who the country's number one is was inevitable.
The Leeds keeper was given his chance to show England boss Thomas Tuchel what he could do again - and he absolutely took it.
On his fifth England cap the 24-year-old enjoyed a magnificent performance in Madrid as his side handed the hosts their first loss in 43 matches.
Trafford made four key saves in the final 12 minutes of the game, including an incredible double stop to first deny a Lamine Yamal curler and then dive again to his right to keep out Fermin Lopez from close range.
Last week Tuchel had made it clear that Everton goalkeeper Jordan Pickford was his number one.
But after full-time in Spain Tuchel told ITV Sport "there's no number one" and Trafford had "a brilliant match".
So, following his performance on Sunday night, is Trafford now likely to oust Pickford as England's go-to goalkeeper?
The case for Trafford
Despite being just 24 years old Trafford has already been England's most expensive goalkeeper by transfer fee... twice.
Trafford returned to his boyhood Manchester City from Burnley for a £31m fee in 2025 and then left the Etihad for Leeds for £45m this summer - having been limited to being Pep Guardiola's 'cup goalkeeper'.
Given the downturn in form of their current goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, many City fans may well be wishing Trafford had stayed. Their loss is Leeds' - and maybe England's - gain.
At Leeds he has found his form and this season ranks first among the 52 goalkeepers who have played at least 10 games in Europe's big five leagues by save percentage (81.4%).
He has made five appearances for England, all of them in 2026, and has rotated with Pickford across the Three Lions' five matches since the World Cup.
Pickford has started against Czech Republic and Croatia twice whereas Trafford has played against Czech Republic and started both England's matches with Spain, home and away.
After England's win in Madrid, which was the first time Spain had lost in the city in 39 years, Trafford's double-save was praised by his Three Lions team-mate Declan Rice.
"Everything happened so quick so for him to make two in the space of two seconds is massive," he told ITV. "A massive night for him."
Spain manager Luis de la Fuente agreed. He said: "We did generate some chances but England's goalkeeper has produced a fantastic performance and stopped two or three potential goals in the last 10 or 15 minutes."
After the double-save several England players ran over to celebrate with Trafford.
And on Tuchel's decision to rotate between his two keepers former Manchester United captain Roy Keane told ITV: "I think it's smart management.
"This is the perfect time for Trafford to come in, against top players, and show what he's capable of doing."
Social media has been full of the 'England number one' debate since, with many suggesting this was a moment that marked the changing of the guard.
Could Tuchel really now not start with Trafford for England's Nations League quarter-finals? Only time will tell.
The case for Pickford
What about Pickford though? England's undisputed first choice for almost 10 years has rarely let his country down.
The 32-year-old has won 94 caps for England since making his debut in a 0-0 draw with Germany in 2017 and during his time as number one England have reached two World Cup semi-finals and two Euros finals.
According to Opta stats, Pickford has only made two errors leading to goals across his England career, with 46 clean sheets and a 74.3% save ratio.
And since the start of the 2024-25 season, only Arsenal's title-winning keeper David Raya has more clean sheets in the league than Pickford at Everton.
"We saw the last selections and all thought Jordan Pickford's place is under threat and James Trafford is going to be the next number one. I don't think Thomas Tuchel saw it as starkly or simply as that," said former England number one goalkeeper Paul Robinson to BBC Sport before England's win against Spain,
"It's a conversation that will definitely take place down the road, but not now. Jordan is England's first choice, in my opinion, rightfully so given his consistency and performances over such a long period.
"This is a debate and conversation for the future definitely because Father Time catches up with everyone eventually and the manager needs to have a contingency plan, but Jordan Pickford very much remains number one and Thomas Tuchel has said as much.
"I don't think Jordan Pickford is under threat for his jersey on a permanent basis any time soon, irrespective of the next selection."
This isn't a debate that is going away any time soon. But having two goalkeepers genuinely competing for that number one shirt can only be to England's benefit.

Ukraine and Russia trade strikes on key bridges
- Published
Russia and Ukraine traded attacks on key bridges overnight, with reports of significant damage to a symbolic bridge linking occupied Crimea and Russia.
A former adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky shared images purporting to show that a section of the Crimea bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - had collapsed into the water.
Meanwhile, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, important routes over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Those attacks came a day after Ukraine began its most recent attempt to disable the Crimea bridge, a prized Kremlin asset which has been seen as a symbol of Russia's occupation of the peninsula.
Two people were killed in that strike overnight on Sunday, the Russian-installed governor of Crimea said.
Former Ukrainian adviser Anton Gerashchenko shared images and video footage appearing to show extensive damage to the bridge from the latest strike, with a support arch and road section seen collapsed in the water. BBC News has not independently verified those images.
The bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014.
Russian President Vladimir Putin personally opened the bridge in 2018.
The severity of the latest strike on the route, which is protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences, is still not fully clear.
Crimea's Moscow-backed governor Sergei Aksyonov said on Telegram that traffic over the bridge had been suspended.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between the Chinese, US and Russian leaders in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems".
"Some areas are experiencing disruptions to water and heating supplies", he added.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services were damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Residents of Kyiv typically shelter in the city's underground stations during air raids.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv. An estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Several of the capital's major bridges were also targeted by Russian drone strikes in October.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials.
Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said.
The latest round of tit-for-tat strikes came after US, Ukrainian and European officials held talks on ways to facilitate "direct engagement" between Russia and Europe to end the war.
Following Monday's meeting, US envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, said the US was committed to providing Ukraine with a "strong, credible security guarantees", as well as a path towards EU membership.
He added that Nato "will remain a critical pillar of European security", and that preparations are underway for a further multilateral meeting "in the near future".
Zelensky said that the meeting was "difficult", adding that more needed to be done to support Ukraine's defence against Russian ballistic missile strikes.
The Ukrainian president has long called for European nations to be included in any peace talks, which he argues is necessary because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the EU.
He also used his address to say Moscow is receiving "dozens of missiles per month" from North Korea.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials said that the final death toll from a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian village of Kamyshuvakha earlier this month had reached 72.
Four people are still considered missing after the bombing, which Ukrainian officials say is one of the deadliest individual attacks since the start of the war in 2022.
Footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, showed residents going to an underground shelter after the initial attack on 2 November. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit.
Ukrainian police said of those killed were police officers, "staff of the gymnasium, utility workers and medical personnel".
Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

A JPMorgan Chase software bug is wreaking havoc on online banking services on Monday, leading to delayed transactions.
The company said it was working to resolve the issue — which impacted transactions with other banks — by the end of the day.
"JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems — there is no evidence this is cyber-related," the bank said in a statement posted online. "It is taking longer than usual to service some customers."
"Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue," it added. "Customers still have access to their accounts and funds."
Customers of Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and US Bank reported thousands of combined issues as of the afternoon, according to the third-party website DownDetector.com. Some customers reported issues with being unable to access information on their accounts. DownDetector also showed reports of issues with Zelle and Capital One. Other US banks said the issue was not on their end.
"Capital One has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time," a spokesperson told Business Insider.
A spokesperson for US Bank said its systems are not directly impacted. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the spokesperson added.
A Zelle spokesperson said that the payments app is not down and is operating as it should. "An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers," the spokesperson said.
The bank disruptions follow a tumultuous few days of high-profile disruptions, including a massive Microsoft outage and an FAA technical failure that sparked a nationwide ground stop and thousands of flight delays and cancellations.
While some online have questioned whether the crop of incidents in the last week could be connected, there is no evidence at the moment to suggest that.

Apple adds new disk controls to prevent AI agents from running amok
Mac users will be warned of the risks of granting AI full disk access.
After sounding an alarm about the issue last month, Apple is taking steps to limit Mac disk access to AI agents, the company announced on its developer blog. In its latest macOS beta, Apple introduced controls to ensure that users will need to take "very explicit" actions to grant apps like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini "this extraordinary level of [full disk] access."
The issue rose to prominence in September, when Inc. columnist Jason Aten noticed that Meta's Muse Mac app was able to access his messages even though he thought he had denied that permission. Meta argued that Aten must have granted access, saying the feature is entirely opt-in, but the incident caught Apple's eye. "Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems — including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history — without users' full knowledge and understanding," Apple wrote.
Apple vowed to address the issue with new disk controls. As screen grabs from X user @madeby_ldt show, Apple's Full Disk Access setting now requires explicit permissions to be granted from a scary-looking pop-up screen. It states, "Your Mac will not be able to protect your data from [your desired AI app]," and forces you to review and OK the actions it will be able to take. Those include "Read, Change, Delete and Export all your Data," "View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos," and "View History and Browser as You."
The new controls won't stop users from granting AI agents access to your files, but it should give them pause. If one of those AI agents goes rogue — which is something we've seen before — they could potentially leak or misuse your private data. Stopping this is key for Mac models like the Studio that Apple is specifically marketing for local AI models and agents.
"As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy," Apple said last month. The new feature is now out on macOS 27.3 beta 2, but there's no word on when it will be released to all users.

Instagram announced a change on Monday that may spell the end for users being nudged to visit a creator’s “link in bio.” At least when they’re promoting products sold on Amazon.
Starting today, creators and businesses can attach multiple Amazon affiliate links to their Instagram content—up to 30 per video or 20 per regular feed post. (Affiliate links let creators earn a commission on any resulting sales.) To participate in this Amazon program, creators must be US-based adults with a professional account that has over 1,000 followers.
Instagram’s parent company, Meta, dropped this shopping-focused change right before the holiday season really kicks off. As creators look to cash in on Amazon's sales, you might expect an avalanche of affiliate posts as you sip hot cocoa and scroll through Reels. But Instagram claims this won’t be the case.
“We don’t expect a sudden influx of shopping content from this launch,” Instagram spokesperson Megan Buckley tells WIRED. “Instagram’s recommendation systems will continue to recommend content based on people’s interests and what we think they’ll enjoy and find valuable. This update makes creators’ product recommendations easier to shop.”
For years, Instagram users could attach a single external link to their bio information. This led to the rise of bundlers like Linktree, where creators could create simple one-page sites with multiple links to content, like shopping recommendations or news articles. In 2023, Instagram expanded the number of links allowed in profiles to five. This most recent update could change how it feels to scroll Instagram, moving more shopping nudges from Amazon storefronts hidden in the bio to direct links on the viral videos.
In an example shared by Meta, a woman recording a Reel leans into her camera as she applies makeup. The caption reads: “My favorite lip tint these days!” Above the creator’s name, a small image tile pops up with the Amazon product. Tap the product and a page opens inside Instagram with the price. Tap one of the listed items, and Instagram will bump you over to the Amazon app or website to complete your purchase.
This change comes as social media shopping habits continue to expand and evolve. TikTok, one of Meta’s primary competitors, has been quite successful in expanding users’ purchasing habits through the app. Around this time last year, an analytics firm estimated that $19 billion worth of products were sold globally through TikTok Shop, putting it at roughly the same size as eBay. Unlike TikTok, however, Instagram will not take a cut of the sales (at least for now). Reddit is also experimenting with how users shop, heading into this holiday season, recently announcing Reddit Reviews, which uses generative AI to summarize user sentiment about products.
For over a decade, Instagram developers have searched for ways to streamline how users spend money through the app. In 2016, WIRED wrote about how the social media app added select commerce links from brands like Warby Parker, a fairly novel attempt at the time to get people to buy stuff through social media. A few years later, the Instagram experience morphed into something like a “digital mall” with in-app checkouts.
This latest attempt moves links from creator bios and places them directly in users' feeds. While this could be a boon for creators, the platform’s implementation could annoy users, who are already inundated with ads online. We’ll see if this change clicks.

Following the inconclusive legislative elections held in Israel on 27 October 2026, President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, with forming the next government. Against this backdrop, a video showing people clapping and chanting “Free, Free Palestine” is going viral on social media (here, here, here), with the claim that it shows a recent scene from the Israeli parliament. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video shows people clapping and chanting “Free, Free Palestine” inside the Israeli parliament recently.
Fact: The viral video shows Birmingham City Council councillors celebrating after voting on a proposal to review financial investments linked to Israel. It is not from the Israeli parliament. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to a similar video on Yahoo News, shared by Birmingham Live, titled “Councillors cheer after voting for proposal to seek to withdraw from Israel-linked financial investments.”
Further, a relevant keyword search led us to several media reports about the incident. According to these reports, independent councillors Nosheen Khalid and Jamil Khan moved the proposal. Birmingham City Council voted to examine its financial investments and banking ties with organisations linked to Israel, with the possibility of withdrawing these investments on human rights grounds (here, here, here, here). Moreover, we found no verified recent report of a group chanting “Free Palestine” inside Israel’s parliament, the Knesset. 
To sum up, this video of Birmingham councillors chanting ‘Free Palestine’ is falsely shared as Israeli Parliament footage.

Pope bids 'hasta luego' to his second homeland of Peru as he wraps up marathon South American trip
Pope Leo XIV has bid farewell to his beloved homeland of Peru
LIMA, Peru -- LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV bid farewell to his beloved second homeland of Peru on Monday with an “hasta luego,” after a marathon 12-day South American tour that tested his stamina after lung cancer surgery.
During the traditional popemobile ride before Leo's final Mass, someone threw an apparent rosary toward the pope that seemed to hit him in the face. The pope winced and touched his temple, but he proceeded on and the Mass began as planned. The Vatican said some 1.5 million people attended.
The faithful often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items towards the popemobile and Leo has often wowed the crowd with his quick reflexes in catching them. His bodyguards, though, have lamented that such tossed objects are among their chief concerns in protecting the pope when he is out in public.
For the Chicago-born Leo, who spent two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop, the trip was an emotional homecoming to a place that he has credited with teaching him how to be a shepherd. Upon arrival, he declared that Peru was his “patria” or homeland, and he sang the national anthem alongside President Keiko Fujimori. Leo has American and Peruvian citizenship.
“It was here that you taught me how to be a bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter,” Leo said at the end of Mass.
Over the course of the trip, it became clear that Leo modeled his ministry in Peru and now for the universal Catholic Church on the figure of the first archbishop of Lima, St. Turibius of Mogrovejo.
“I have felt at home, and you have reminded me that the Church truly is a family. It was here that you taught me how to be a bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter,” he said at the end of Mass.
Mogrovejo, who lived from 1538-1606, is revered for having denounced abuses against Indigenous and enslaved people by Spanish colonizers. He is also remembered for having crisscrossed his vast diocese on foot and horseback to minister to his flock, learning Quechua and Aymara to better preach to its Indigenous members and overseeing the translation of church teachings so they could understand.
Following his example, Leo traveled across Peru to where the Catholic hierarchy rarely goes to minister to his flock, going high up in the Andes mountains and deep into the Amazon rainforest and points in between. On his final full day in Peru on Sunday, Leo went from his former diocese of Chiclayo on the north Pacific coast to the southeastern Andean city of Cusco, to the northeastern Amazonian city of Pucallpa and back to Lima on the coast.
The climatic and altitude changes alone were exhausting — from hot, humid Chiclayo to chilly and rainy Cusco (at an oxygen-challenging altitude of 3,400 meters or about 11,150 feet) to the steaming heat of the Pucallpa rainforest and back to the gray humidity of Lima.
It was a daylong lesson in what it means to be a shepherd. But it also served to say “So there!” to the nay-sayers, including some in the Vatican who had questioned whether Leo would have to change the course of his pontificate given his lung cancer diagnosis.
On Monday, Leo proceeded with his program as planned and made clear he wasn't saying “adiós” or goodbye forever to Peru.
Speaking to the crowd outside the Vatican residence, Leo thanked Peruvians for having accompanied him on his trip. “Have a good day, thank you very much, and until later!” he said.
At the home for the elderly in Callao, where Leo visited with residents, Leo bid farewell again saying “hasta pronto, hasta luego,” another way of saying “see you soon.”
Callao Mayor César Pérez told The Associated Press that Father Roberto, as he is known to the Peruvian people, would drive approximately 12 hours from Chiclayo in northern Peru to Callao during the pandemic because he wanted to ensure the well-being of older residents.
Leo delivered food and other supplies to the home but didn't enter the facility in order to protect the residents from the virus, Pérez said.
The Peru stop capped a visit that began on Nov. 6 in Uruguay and proceeded on to Argentina, the homeland of Leo’s predecessor Pope Francis, who never returned during his pontificate.
The trip itself was in doubt after Leo underwent lung cancer surgery Oct. 13 in Rome. But Leo said as the visit began that he had “no doubt” that he would make it.
Rosa María Flores, who was attending Leo's final Mass, was glad he did. She said the most important thing about the pope’s visit was that he brought faith to the people of his homeland of Peru.
“We have so much crime, so many deaths; we’re in great need of peace, reconciliation and faith,” she said. “I know that he’s pouring blessings on Peru and that things will get better for all of us.”
One of the most meaningful visits for Leo was to the sanctuary of Mogrovejo in the city of Zaña in the diocese of Chiclayo. Leo revealed that he had come there the night before he was ordained a bishop to pray, so important to him was the saint who died there after falling ill during one of his own missionary visits.
“This is a kneeling place for Robert Prevost,” the Rev. David Farfan, the parish pastor, told AP. Many of the pope’s actions, he said, “helping people in the world, as a peacemaker, he did them while also kneeling in this sacred place because a saint passed away here.”

Pilots Kept Contact With Controllers During Nationwide Halt to Flights
Pilots were generally able to maintain contact with air traffic controllers and airline staff on the ground despite an outage that caused a nearly five-hour halt to departures.
Pilots were able to maintain communications with air traffic controllers and airline dispatchers during the nationwide halt to most departing flights imposed by federal officials for nearly five hours on Friday.
A representative of the union that represents about 17,000 pilots at American Airlines said on Monday that it had received no reports of crews losing radio contact with controllers. Some pilots noticed radio static, but that isn’t uncommon, said Dennis Tajer, a spokesman for the union, the Allied Pilots Association.
Even so, the union said it supported the hourslong ground stop called by the Federal Aviation Administration, a part of the Department of Transportation.
“Just because the national shutdown happened without incident, let that not be the catalyst for doubting if the right call was made,” said Mr. Tajer, who is a Boeing 737 captain and was stranded near Newark Liberty International Airport on Friday night. “You just don’t know what would have happened had you said, ‘Well, let’s take a chance and see.’”
Southwest Airlines dispatchers, who help to plan and guide the carrier’s flights, also reported no disruption of direct communications or data before the ground stop was ordered.
“Dispatchers did not experience any loss of communication with our flight crews or F.A.A. control facilities, and our tools and data feeds did not show any signs of disruption,” said Kevin Thurston, the president of Transport Workers Union Local 550, the union that represents dispatchers and meteorologists at the airline.
The F.A.A. has said that the technical outage was intermittent and not a blackout, noting over the weekend that some radio frequencies and radar feeds remained reliable.
The agency said the problem began when data began flooding an agency telecommunications network. An initial investigation identified two possible sources: a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Ark. An investigation is ongoing.
“Throughout the disruption, certain radio frequencies and radar feeds remained operational, allowing air traffic controllers to maintain communication with and track aircraft,” the agency said in a statement.
Even if primary communications had gone dark, aircraft are equipped with backups. Pilots can use emergency frequencies to speak with nearby planes and ground facilities. Aviation professionals can also use other tools to communicate with dispatchers, including text-based systems.
“We have plenty of knives in our boot,” said Mr. Tajer. “It doesn’t mean we want to use them.”
Niraj Chokshi is a Times reporter who writes about aviation, rail and other transportation industries.

If you were planning to do any banking today, good luck.
Customers of many major financial institutions experienced unspecified technical issues on Monday as thousands of reports flooded the uptime-tracking website Downdetector.com from people saying that they had issues using their banks in some way.
It is currently unclear which systems are having issues. However, the problem may stem from technical difficulties at JPMorganChase, the top retail bank that holds over 10 percent of all US deposits, did identify a specific issue.
“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems—there is no evidence this is cyber-related,” says JPMorganChase spokesperson Pablo Rodriguez. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.”
Rodriguez adds that the bank is not experiencing a “systemic issue” but that “other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.” The spokesperson adds that customers “still have access to their accounts and funds” and that the bank is working to resolve the issues.
Apparent issues with the banks, credit unions, fintech apps, and credit card companies appear to begin around 9:30 am ET and peaked at around 2 pm ET. Many people also reported issues using Zelle, the peer-to-peer money-transfer system adopted by major banks. However, in a statement, Zelle denied its systems were the cause of the reported outages while acknowledging that issues at banks may impact people’s ability to use Zelle.
“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” a Zelle spokesperson says in a statement. “Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds.”
US Bank spokesperson Jeffrey Shelman also says the financial institution’s systems “are not directly impacted.” Shelman adds, however, that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
Seth Eisen, senior vice president of communications at MasterCard, says, “Our network is operating normally.” A Visa spokesperson says the company is aware of the ongoing payments issue, but that Visa’s systems are operating normally too.
According to reports on Downdetector, which is sourced to user reports rather than official statements, the issues on Monday also impacted customers of Bank of America, Capital One, Wells Fargo, TD Bank, Navy Credit Federal Union, and more. These companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Eisen, the Mastercard VP, says that DownDetector was “not correct” in the case of his company.
Whatever the cause, the timing of the issues may as well have been designed to get people looking for broader patterns. Last Thursday, Microsoft 365 experienced an unprecedented 24-hour outage that impacted millions of people, governments, businesses, and other institutions globally. Microsoft executive vice president Charles Lamanna said in a post on X on Monday that the outage, which impacted Outlook, Teams, and many other Microsoft cloud services, was related to an update that started rolling out in July but only began causing problems last week.
Soon after Microsoft resolved its outage on Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop order. This time, the issue was related to a problem with Air Traffic Control’s communications systems. “The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” the agency wrote in an FAQ explaining the outage. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.”
The FAA’s five-hour ground stop resulted in thousands of canceled flights and otherwise disrupted travel for countless travelers. The impact of Monday’s banking outage remains unclear.

Prince William praises India for balancing growth and sustainability: ‘Rang birangi duniya’
In Mumbai, the Prince of Wales said India offered a picture of “colour, complexity and possibility”.
Britain's Prince William on Monday praised India's efforts to balance economic growth with environmental protection, saying the country had shown that emerging economies can achieve both prosperity and sustainability.
Addressing the Earthshot Prize 2026 Impact Assembly in Mumbai, the Prince of Wales said India offered a picture of “colour, complexity and possibility”. He spotlighted the country's achievements in renewable energy and the work of Indian organisations developing practical solutions to environmental challenges.
"Too often, the world's emerging economies are presented with false choices -- growth or the environment, prosperity or protection. But India shows us a different picture," William said.
Deep Dive
Invoking the Hindi phrase "Rang Birangi Duniya", meaning a world full of colour, he called for a future that moves beyond the idea that economic development and environmental protection cannot coexist.
"There is a phrase in Hindi: 'Rang Birangi Duniya'. A world full of colour. Perhaps that is how we should see the future. Not in black and white, and not presented as a series of false choices between people and the planet, prosperity and nature, but in all its colours. A world in which solutions can come from anywhere," he said.
William highlights India's renewable energy progress
Pointing to India's achievements in the clean energy sector, William noted that the country had reached its target of sourcing 50% of its installed electricity capacity from non-fossil fuel sources five years ahead of schedule. He also said that India's solar capacity had increased more than 50-fold in little over a decade.
"But this transformation is about more than energy. It is about people finding better ways to live," he said.
William also noted that India produced more Earthshot Prize winners and finalists than any other country.
Prince William praises Indian Earthshot finalists
The Prince spoke of the work of Delhi-based social enterprise Takachar, which became the Earthshot Prize's first-ever winner in the 'Clean Our Air' category in 2021.
Takachar developed portable, tractor-mounted technology that converts agricultural and forest waste, which would otherwise be burned, into marketable products such as fuel and fertiliser.
William said the innovation had helped reduce smoke by 98 per cent while also increasing farmers' incomes.
He also drew attention to two Indian organisations among the 2026 Earthshot finalists -- Mahila Housing Trust and Mahindra Last Mile Mobility.
"Mahila Housing Trust are empowering low-income women to cope with extreme heat through practical solutions such as cooler roofs and affordable insurance. And Mahindra, Last Mile Mobility, is making electric rickshaws an affordable choice whilst cleaning the air for people living in big cities across the country," he said.
Describing these initiatives as solutions that directly improve people's lives, William said that environmental action could not be the responsibility of one country alone. "These are not distant environmental ambitions. They are solutions that improve lives. But this is not India's responsibility alone," he said.
Calls for global cooperation on climate action
William asked countries, businesses and communities to learn from one another and support innovations that could be expanded across the world. Referring to the finalists working in areas ranging from cleaner transport and agricultural insurance to renewable energy and tackling dangerous chemicals, he said no single country or organisation had all the answers.
"We must learn from one another. Because when a solution works, others must follow. It took the world almost 70 years to install its first terawatt of solar power. The second took just two years. That is how change gathers momentum -- one breakthrough makes the next easier, until what once seemed impossible becomes inevitable," he said.
Acknowledging that significant environmental challenges remained, the Prince said countries could not afford to wait for universal agreement before taking action.
"But we cannot wait for everyone to agree before we act. We all want clean air to breathe, a chance to build good lives, and a natural world that endures for our children and grandchildren. These are not ambitions that divide us. They are ambitions that unite us," he added.
What is the Earthshot Prize?
Founded by Prince William in 2020, the Earthshot Prize is a 10-year initiative aimed at accelerating environmental recovery by identifying and supporting solutions to some of the world's biggest environmental challenges.
It focuses on five areas: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-free World and Fix Our Climate.
Each year, five winners are selected from 15 finalists, with each receiving GBP 1 million to help develop and expand their solutions.
The 2026 edition marks the first time the awards are being held in India. Mumbai will host the sixth Earthshot Prize Awards Night on November 17.
According to the British High Commission, Prince William and Princess Kate are scheduled to attend the awards ceremony on November 17-18. The visit marks their second official trip to India.

It’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.
Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.
As Nobel laureate economist Amartya Sen once wrote, Tagore was “a towering figure in the millennium-old literature of Bengal”, whose songs resonate across eastern India and Bangladesh, while his ideas on education, nationalism and freedom of the mind remain relevant today.
Yet his work also made a deep impression on the literary world far beyond the shores of India. WB Yeats is said to have described Tagore as “greater than any of us”. Gitanjali, the collection of poems that won Tagore the Nobel prize that same year, was praised by the committee for its “profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse”. Tagore’s English translation was published in London that March and reprinted 10 times by the time the prize was announced in November.
Tagore’s life and works have, of course, been well documented, but a collection of material preserved in a private family archive is now being brought into public view for the first time at an exhibition by Christie’s, opening in Mumbai this month. The archive draws from Tagore’s visits to the family home of his protege, Maitreyi Devi, in the bucolic village of Mungpoo in Darjeeling between 1938 and 1940. He died in 1941.
The collection on display – artworks, manuscripts, letters, photographs and personal effects – offers an intimate glimpse into Tagore’s creative process and personal world in his final years.
I spoke to the exhibition curator, Nishad Avari, head of south Asian modern and contemporary art at Christie’s, about the stories behind the archive.
One instructive document Avari points to is a manuscript from 1940. It appears to be a draft of Tagore’s memoir Chelebela or My Boyhood Days, in which he reflects on his life – from growing up in a large family in Calcutta (modern-day Kolkata) to the rapidly changing world ushered in by electricity and the motorcar.
For Avari, what stood out was how the ideas in the document echoed the educational philosophy Tagore put into practice in Santiniketan (or Abode of Peace), the experimental school he set up about 100 miles from the state capital.
“He speaks about how education is like being in prison and that it should be open and free … about the idea of wonder and even fear as inspiring creativity,” Avari told me.
“That’s a direct relationship to Santiniketan and the open model of the school where people sat under trees with their gurus and learned in the open. Education didn’t feel like a restriction, prison or imposition,” he added.
Avari points to another detail that makes this particular document valuable. Of the 10 complete manuscripts in the exhibition, it is the only one dictated to Devi, whose father was a close friend of Tagore’s. For Avari, this speaks to their close relationship and the trust he placed in her.
“If you look at the collection as a whole, she has copies of almost every single one of his publications signed to her by him,” he says. The collection includes hundreds of letters, too: first between Tagore and her father, and later between Tagore and Devi herself.
There are doodles among corrections, Avari explains, which show how his literary practice fed into his artistic practice. Alongside the manuscripts and correspondence are vintage photographs and personal effects, including a kurta and a lungi that Tagore left behind at the family home.
Among the artworks in the collection is a portrait of Devi, particularly notable because Tagore’s figure studies were not generally attributed to specific individuals in the way that portraits by his nephews, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath, often were, Avari said. There is also a landscape depicting the forests of Mungpoo, which Tagore embraced as a retreat.
On the international art market, Tagore’s paintings command significant prices. This year, Sotheby’s sold one of his watercolours for £1.02m (Rs 12.97 crore), nearly four times its low estimate.
Institutions such as Visva-Bharati in Santiniketan and the National Gallery of Modern Art hold much of Tagore’s archival materials, making the discovery of a private archive particularly rare.
He hopes that making these materials public will offer historians, scholars and admirers alike additional perspectives on Tagore. “We hope to add to the understanding of the artist, their career, and in this case, of course, our understanding of the man beyond his art as well.”
Rabindranath Tagore and Mungpoo runs between 10 November and 18 December at Christie’s space in south Mumbai.

An organ transplant controversy tests 'the dead donor rule'
The U.S. organ transplant system has approved the first national policy for a controversial procedure used to remove organs from hospital patients. The guidelines are designed to protect potential donors. But critics say they do little to improve safety and fail to address deeply troubling ethical concerns.
The procedure is called normothermic regional perfusion, known as NRP. It can be used after a family has decided to withdraw care because there's no hope of meaningful recovery for the person. To perform NRP, doctors attach an external pump to a donor minutes after their circulation has ended and they've been declared dead. The pump restores blood flow to their hearts, lungs, kidneys, liver and other organs to keep them from deteriorating.
"The hope with NRP is that it increases the supply of organs and it increases the quality of the organs," says Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at the Health Resources & Services Administration, the federal agency that oversees the organ transplant system.
NRP could help solve the chronic organ shortage, Lynch says. More than 109,000 Americans are waiting for an organ transplant, according to HRSA. About 12 die every day because of a chronic organ shortage.
Critics, however, say NRP is unethical because it violates the Dead Donor Rule, which is the most important rule protecting potential donors. The rule says transplant surgeons can only take organs from patients after they are dead because of brain death or circulatory death. But because NRP restarts circulation, critics say the procedure reverses the very condition upon which the person has just been declared dead.
"In order to be dead by circulatory criteria it means we're not going to attempt to reestablish circulation. But that's exactly what they do in NRP," says Dr. Lainie Friedman Ross, a University of Rochester bioethicist. "So, yes, I have a real problem with NRP. I think it violates the dead donor rule. It's taking organs from people who are no longer dead."
The other aspect of NRP that troubles critics is what surgeons do to try to make sure the donor is also brain dead, after circulation has been restarted by a mechanical pump. They clamp off blood vessels that supply the head. But alarm bells started going off for organ retrieval teams when blood appeared to get restored – or "reperfused" – to the brain during some NRP cases.
"We have seen signs of life in NRP when the brain has been reperfused," says Dr. Claire Morgan, a transplant surgeon who serves on the transplant network's Patient Affairs Committee and was the first to report such cases to HRSA. "It's extremely disturbing."
Those cases prompted HRSA to instruct the Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network (OPTN), which runs the organ system, to investigate and develop a response. On Nov. 6, the OPTN board of directors approved the first phase of the first uniform national guidelines for how to perform NRP.
The new guidelines, which will go into effect Dec. 6, call for surgeons to do more than just clamp the blood vessels to the brain. They should also cut holes in them, according to the new policy.
"Clamping the blood vessels should stop blood flowing to the brain," says Lynch. "Cutting or venting above the level of the clamping is a second safeguard to make sure that if the clamping is insufficient that it immediately drains out of the head and is not supplying warm oxygenated blood to the brain."
The new policy also includes other protections, including recommending against giving donors drugs that would paralyze them and mask any movements.
But critics say the new safeguards are insufficient. Most surgeons already both clamp and vent blood vessels to the brain, for example, they say.
"I honestly don't believe they have created a policy that creates much or any more protection than these donors already had," says Morgan, who also disagrees with the decision to implement the first phase of the new guidelines on an emergency basis before the public had a chance to weigh in.
Critics also say the new policy doesn't begin to address the bigger concerns that NRP donors are not technically dead when surgeons remove their organs. They worry the adoption of the policy could speed the use of NRP before the troubling questions have been fully aired.
"I really think the policy is the cart before the horse," says Dr. Matthew DeCamp, a University of Colorado bioethicist. "The fundamental issues around NRP still remain unresolved."
Lynch, however, argues the new guidelines will protect donors and that NRP is ethical.
"This is an important first step to make sure NRP care is available but that the safety of the family's loved one is always at the forefront," Lynch says. "This is life-saving care that will extend the supply and improve the quality of organs that patients can get in transplant. And if it is done properly, it is safe."

Kochi- A 36-year-old homemaker from Mulavukad here has allegedly lost Rs 89,904 after falling victim to a cyber fraud in which a caller posing as a bank representative offered to help her activate a credit card, police said here on Tuesday.
The Kochi City Cyber Crime Police have registered a Zero FIR in connection with the incident.
The victim, Linu K J,received a phone call on November 2 from an unidentified person who claimed to be assisting her with the activation of a YES Bank credit card.
When she reportedly faced difficulties in activating the card, the caller persuaded her to use her existing State Bank of India (SBI) credit card to complete the process.
Trusting the caller, the woman shared the OTPs received on her mobile phone.
This resulted in an unauthorised withdrawal of Rs 49,440 from her SBI credit card, police said.
The fraudster contacted her again on November 4, claiming to help recover the amount lost in the first transaction.
The woman was persuaded to share another OTP, following which Rs 40,464 was debited from her card.
She later realised that she had been cheated and approached the Cyber Crime Police with a complaint.
A Zero FIR has been registered under Section 318(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which deals with cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property.
The incident comes close on the heels of another major cyber fraud reported in Kozhikode last week, in which a 45-year-old woman allegedly lost Rs 49.2 lakh in an online trading scam.

Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (H5N1) has been confirmed in chicken samples collected from a poultry farm at Kattiyankuppam village in Kurinjipadi taluk of Cuddalore district.
“The National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD), Bhopal, had confirmed the H5N1 avian influenza virus in samples collected from a poultry carcass on November 5, 2026,” District Collector Sibi Adhithya Senthil Kumar told The Hindu.
The confirmation has triggered a full-scale containment operation, with the Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Services Department culling all birds in the affected farm and within a one-kilometre radius of the epicentre.
According to Mr. Senthil Kumar: “As many as 35,647 bird deaths were recorded in the affected belt till November 13, since the first case of sudden mortality was reported from a farm at Thamanampatti village in Thiyagavalli Panchayat on October 30.”
Samples sent to four laboratories
He added, “Veterinary teams that visited the farm on the day of the first report collected samples and sent them to the Poultry Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (PDDL) in Namakkal.”
As deaths mounted in neighbouring farms, further samples were routed to Poultry Disease Diagnosis and Surveillance Laboratory (PDDL) Erode and the Central University Laboratory (CUL) at Madhavaram in Chennai.
On November 5, a carcass sample was despatched to NIHSAD Bhopal, which confirmed H5N1 on November 13, he said.
Following the standard operating procedure under the National Action Plan, the district was divided into compartments to restrict the spread of the disease.
Culling and disposal
“Initially, we sent only one sample. But a total of 15 farms are affected, of which all the birds in 10 farms have already been wiped out. So only five farms remain, and we are going to cull all [the birds] anyway. As many as nine Rapid Response Teams have been deployed for this purpose,” the Collector said.
So far, 1,550 birds have been humanely culled, and the department is working to cull 100% of the birds in the epicentre farm and within the 1-km radius, in accordance with the Government of India guidelines, 2021.
The carcasses are being disposed of through deep burial in designated pits, with bleaching powder applied and biosecurity measures in place.
An official said that movement of birds to and from the affected farms has been strictly restricted.
All poultry farms in and around the affected area have been brought under intensive surveillance, and disinfection using VIRKON-S — administered orally to live birds and as a farm-level spray — has been carried out as a precautionary measure. Cleaning, disinfection, and fumigation of the affected premises are in progress.
The Cuddalore district administration has asked the public not to panic, stating that the outbreak has been confined to the Cuddalore compartment and that no confirmations have been reported from the other compartments so far.
Pamphlets have been circulated and residents have been advised to report any unusual bird mortality immediately to the nearest veterinary institution.
In the affected area, an advisory has been issued prohibiting restocking of poultry for three months. To monitor this, the Revenue Department and local bodies are involved at the village level, the official said.
Poultry farmers have been asked to strictly follow the prescribed protocols and cooperate with the containment efforts.
The situation is being continuously monitored by the Animal Husbandry Department under the supervision of the District Administration.

Few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.
The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)
Belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.
Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, it also caused a rift within the family.
Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi.
Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.
Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years
Gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.
For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.
Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents.
It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians
India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.
In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.
Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.
Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press
Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.
In 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes.
And it’s not just media …
The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be said, written and published.
Penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and said it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.
The book, released in the US by Alfred A Knopf, is being published in India by HarperCollins.
In June, Penguin had also pulled out of plans to distribute graphic journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot, about the 2013 Muzaffarnagar communal violence. The publisher cited an inaccurate map of India and unresolved citation issues. Sacco, however, blamed the decision on the “current political climate in India”.
She’s had quiet fallouts with the ‘thoroughly dishonest’
Western political memoirs, particularly by former heads of government or senior politicians, are often forthcoming in naming political adversaries, recounting private exchanges and offering candid assessments of colleagues. David Cameron’s 2019 memoir, For the Record, took aim at his former friend, Michael Gove, describing him as “mendacious” and a “foam-flecked Faragist”.
Gandhi, in contrast, is restrained. She writes warmly of the closeness between the Gandhi family and that of Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan, whose parents she lived with when she first moved to India, but she makes no mention of the subsequent estrangement between the two families. In another instance, she does not name the political leader she describes as “thoroughly dishonest” and who she says she trusted in 1999, when Congress unsuccessfully attempted to form a coalition government.

Whatever happened to the diamond that went missing in F1 crash?
- Published
Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?
If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.
A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.
Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?
Someone, somewhere, knows something.
The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.
Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport.
"My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport.
"It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."
His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.
They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie.
"I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says.
"One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."
Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.
The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.
Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.
What happened next, though, was not part of the script.
While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.
The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.
Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.
Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.
Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.
In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.
Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.
It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back.
"I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.
He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage.
"I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says.
"That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."
By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.
But there were plenty of theories.
Theory: it was not a real diamond
Sidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond.
"I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says.
"Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk.
"There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."
Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth.
"David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell.
"Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car.
"I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."
Theory: someone pocketed it
"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell.
"I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit].
"Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer.
"It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."
There would have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people in the area because within an hour or so of the end of the race the circuit would have been returned to public roads.
Sidhu is pretty certain about what happened to the diamond: "Someone's picked it up.
"What people tend to do is, believe it or not, pick up bits of tyre rubber, you know, claim that as Michael Schumacher's front tyre rubber or whatever they can find.
"Somebody may have picked it up not having any idea it came off a car.
"There's a lot of diamonds in Monte Carlo. There's a lot of people walking around Monte Carlo with a lot of jewellery and a lot of stones.
"Somebody dropped a diamond in Monte Carlo. Well, they're not going to miss that, are they? Probably not."
Theory: Klien crashed on purpose
Sidhu says the cost of the damage to the car was more than the cost of the diamond, which reports at the time said was uninsured.
And points and a good result in the race were more valuable to the team and individuals than a diamond or the publicity a crash would bring. It was simply not worth crashing on purpose.
"For us, bringing two cars home, ideally in the points, had far bigger commercial benefits to us in terms of constructors' points, broadcast money, and more importantly, trying to retain our sponsors and trying to protect the integrity of the team," Sidhu explains.
Klien drove straight into the barriers right in front of the marshals so would not have had the chance to start looking for a diamond or picking it up even if he had wanted to.
"Christian didn't try and say all the brakes failed or anything like that, he's just said 'I made a rookie mistake'," says Purnell.
"He was a young guy, first time, made a mistake, it happens. Doesn't usually happen with a $300,000 diamond flying into the crowd or wherever it went, but I'm sure Christian wasn't really aware of the diamond.
"No amount of money would have got Christian to do that [crash on purpose]. He wanted to make a success of what he was doing."
While events were unfolding, Purnell had not really been thinking about the diamond.
His main concern that day was that one of his drivers had crashed and the other also did not finish, and that this was not a good look in terms of pleasing current backers or attracting potential buyers.
"When Christian went into the wall and then later Mark retired, my entire thinking was 'Oh God. What am I going to say?' The chairman of HSBC [Jaguar's then sponsors] was there, Sir John Bond. Jackie [Stewart] was there.
"It was all about 'how am I going to explain another bad performance? How am I going to say 'just stick with the plan? We know what we're doing, it will take time' because sponsors don't have time. They want success."
In the end, the missing diamond came to the rescue.
"No-one mentioned Jarno Trulli winning the Grand Prix, no-one asked how the Jaguars did. No-one was interested that Mark Webber's car broke as well. It was, 'where's the diamond?'" says Purnell.
"I remember talking to somebody in Detroit saying, 'fantastic publicity over here, you know we never hear anything about Formula 1 but it's on the newscasts, it's in the papers - fantastic'."
Asked if the diamond mystery had helped the eventual sale of the team to Red Bull six months later, he replies: "I think that helped quite a lot because it buzzed the Jaguar team and showed that huge publicity was possible even if you weren't doing so well."
Red Bull went on to become hugely successful, winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' championships since joining F1.
"You couldn't design a better PR weekend," says Purnell.
Even if it was not quite how it was planned and there is still the small matter of a missing diamond.
