The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.
The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.
The international court of justice (ICJ) has never found a state responsible for genocide, a crime defined after the Nazi-led Holocaust. The ruling will have implications for a separate high-profile genocide case against Israel.
Nearly a decade after a military campaign forced hundreds of thousands of Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border, the ICJ in The Hague will deliver its judgment on Thursday morning.
“The ICJ ruling will be historic for Rohingya survivors and their families around the world,” said Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar.
“The international community failed to prevent Myanmar military atrocities against the Rohingya nine years ago. It must seize this opportunity to finally secure justice for the Rohingya and begin to reckon with these failings.”
ICJ judges have spent seven years weighing accusations by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN genocide convention.
A key issue in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Antonia Mulvey, the founder of Legal Action Worldwide (Law), a group that represents hundreds of Rohingya survivors, said she was “cautiously optimistic” the court would hold Myanmar fully accountable.
Government actions showed “patterns of conduct” that proved clear attempts to destroy the group, she said.
“The attacks on the villages took place the same way,” she said. “They would attack the civilians, burn the villages, separate men and women, conduct sexual violence … and then as they fled, they would continue to kill them.”
Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the Balkans fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica.
Mulvey said a key part of the upcoming judgment will be how it handles the issue of rape and sexual violence as an act of genocide. Her team has collected accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals and biting their faces. “That’s to mark people, to brand them … it is also to stop reproduction,” she said.
“Yes, we would say sexual violence is a critical part to show their intent to destroy the group,” she added.
“You don’t need to gang-rape people. You don’t need to kill their children in front of them. You don’t need to mutilate them. You don’t need to do it in public. What is the purpose of that? The purpose is to destroy the group.”
In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear directly from Rohingya survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. One witness said her child was taken from her arms, stabbed and thrown into a fire, according to Law, while another described seeing piles of bodies in a mass grave.
During hearings, Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.
“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents.
For decades, Rohingya people have been stripped of their citizenship and targeted by increasing discrimination, amid a backdrop of communal violence with Buddhists in the country’s western Rakhine state.
The crisis reached a climax after a Rohingya militant group conducted guerrilla-style attacks in the summer of 2017. The Myanmar army responded with massive “clearance operations”.
Refugees who fled into Bangladesh in 2017 told the Guardian of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, including the drowning of children in a river.
This testimony from Tula Toli – which satellite footage later showed had been razed – added to dozens of witness accounts collected over the years to build a case for genocide.
A ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would add international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks and later overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead.
The former general is separately being investigated by the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has made efforts to rebuild diplomatic ties.
For many onlookers, the ICJ decision will hold relevance far beyond Myanmar, as it will provide the strongest hint of how judges might assess the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.
The cases have much in common, with an ethnic group targeted by a powerful military, although Israel has far stronger diplomatic backing from the US.
The judgment comes as Washington has been on the offensive against international human rights bodies, including sanctioning the ICC. Washington technically already considers the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration.
However, Trump’s UN ambassador, Mike Waltz, warned that the ICJ “must not be allowed” to establish a standard for genocide that could be used against “allied soldiers”, a statement that will be relevant for Israeli troops.
Supporters of the Myanmar case say the judgment should compel states to block arms transfers and jet fuel supplies. While the court does not have the means to enforce its decisions, they have been respected in the past, and the UN security council could give it strength, although divisions, especially between the US and China, make this unlikely.
More than 1 million Rohingya remain in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement. Fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Myanmar.
A displaced Rohingya living inside Myanmar told the Guardian he hoped the judgment would “help end decades of persecution and discrimination”.
“We are not asking for sympathy alone,” he said. “We are asking for justice, recognition, equal rights and a future in which our children can live safely and with dignity in their own homeland.”

Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack
- Published
Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked with a car and left a double amputee.
The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, an incident which horrified Australia.
Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He has yet to enter pleas.
In her first public comments since the attack, Haines, 65, said she had moved into the rehabilitation stage of her recovery.
"This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Haines said.
"I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing."
She added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the generosity of well wishers who had donated to Save the Children in her honour.
Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.
Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.
The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate.
Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had been in regular contact with Haines and her "extraordinary" family.
"All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery," he said in a statement.
"We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation."

India has seen a 38% reduction in tuberculosis (TB) mortality since 2015, compared to a global average of 35%, and a 94% treatment success rate among patients with drug-susceptible TB, according to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Global Tuberculosis Report 2026.
Last year, the South-East Asia Region recorded the largest number of new TB cases (35%), followed by the Western Pacific Region (27%) and the African Region (25%).
Around 88% of new TB cases occurred in 30 countries. India, Indonesia (10%), the Philippines (6.8%), China (6.5%), Pakistan (6.4%), Nigeria (4.9%), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (3.9%) and Bangladesh (3.7%) accounted for about two-thirds of the global total.
The top five countries made up 55% of the total.
Globally, about 50% of people treated for TB and their households face total costs (direct medical expenditures, non-medical expenditures, and indirect costs such as income losses) that are catastrophic (greater than 20% of total household income).
People with compromised immune systems, such as those living with HIV, undernutrition or diabetes, or people who use tobacco have a higher risk of falling ill. An estimated 9.6 lakh new TB cases were attributable to undernutrition, 9.2 lakh to diabetes, 7.3 lakh to alcohol use disorders, 6.9 lakh to smoking and 5.5 lakh to HIV infection.
The report showed a total of 1.13 million people died from TB in 2025. Globally, TB is the world’s leading cause of death from a single infectious agent. Last year, an estimated 10.6 million people fell ill with TB worldwide, including 5.7 million men, 3.7 million women and 1.2 million children.
Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) remains a public health crisis and a health security threat. Only about two in five people with drug-resistant TB received treatment in 2025. Global efforts to combat TB have saved an estimated 86 million lives since 2000.
Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by bacteria that most often affects the lungs. It spreads through the air when people with TB cough, sneeze or spit. TB is preventable and curable.
Between December 7, 2024 and November 8, 2026, the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan achieved significant progress, identifying and bringing over 25 crore individuals within the scope of screening activities.
“India’s reduction in TB mortality has been the result of interventions under the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP), including proactive case finding including use of AI-enabled X-rays, rapid diagnostics, prompt treatment initiation, differentiated TB care, and nutritional support through the Nikshay Poshan Yojana and Nikshay Mitra initiative. These interventions were supported by AI tools for identification of hotspots, prediction of high-risk TB cases prone for adverse outcomes, Khushi – AI Chatbot & Avatar Videobot, etc.,” the Union Health Ministry statement said.

In the days surrounding the U.S. midterm elections, people shared a rumor warning against opening a text message claiming President Donald Trump "was arrested" (or "got arrested") because it would attack their bank accounts.
For example, the matter primarily circulated among Facebook users who posted the following text:
FYI... Just sharing, idk how true this is but just in case....if you get a text that Trump was arrested don't open it ,because it will attack your bank account. Tell all your family, & friends. Too much going on! Please forward to family, followers and friends ASAP!
Do not open any text msg about Trump.
Snopes readers emailed us to ask if such a dangerous message truly existed.
In short, our research concluded the warning was a hoax. Snopes did not locate screenshots or transcripts of the alleged text message when the warning apparently first started circulating in November 2024 — or again in January 2026 — nor could we determine who started the rumor.
People appeared to begin sharing the hoax warning shortly after the Justice Department indicted Trump in 2023 on charges related to election interference in the 2020 presidential election and around the time voters elected him to a second term.
Similarly, in 2016, we reported on another hoax that falsely claimed a virus would infect people's devices when they click on a photo supposedly showing Trump's "arrest."
Searches — including of Reddit's r/Scams community — produced no credible discussions about the purported scam.
What to know about text scams
Despite what some users claimed, consumers can't get scammed simply by opening and reading a text message. For a scam to succeed, scammers typically first need recipients to respond to a message or click on a link.
After that, scams typically require of users to fill in login details, personal information or financial data for the scammers' fraudulent attempt to achieve success. For example, a text message link might lead to a scam website posing as a specific bank's login page, or perhaps a fake Amazon.com login page — nothing more than an effort to steal usernames and passwords out of users.
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) published a full guide on text message scams, primarily that scammers attempt to steal consumers' personal and financial information. If any readers provided personal or financial details to scammers, we recommend reporting the text messages to the FTC using the instructions at the bottom of their guide. Additionally, we advise contacting the associated bank or credit card company — either by visiting a branch or calling an official number (not one provided in the scam text) — to address the issue.
Victims of internet crimes can also file a complaint with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center on IC3.gov.
For further reading, we previously reported about other claims involving Trump. For example, we investigated if an image truly showed Trump being carried by Secret Service agents after fainting at the White House.

Ente Photos is a privacy-focused Google Photos alternative offering 10GB of free storage, end-to-end encryption, open-source code, selective album backups, cross-platform access, easy photo imports, collaborative sharing, and on-device AI features like face recognition and Magic Search.
When we think about a dedicated photo app, we instantly remember Google Photos or the default gallery on our phone. We do not have many trustworthy options. That’s when I came across Ente. Ente is a dedicated photo app available as a standalone app to install on Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, and Linux operating systems.
Is Ente the real challenger to the Google Photos app? Can we replace the gallery on our phones with Ente? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
Features That Make Ente a Worthy Photo App
Ente has some exciting features that really make it stand out from the few others available. Here’s what makes it worthy.
Generous Free (Forever) Storage Plan
Ente offers a 10GB free storage plan for your photos and videos. Ente claims the plan is free forever. 10GB of free cloud storage dedicated to photos and video backup seems a good deal. That too without any ads.
Google offers 15GB of free storage space for each Google account. There is no dedicated storage space for the Google Photos app. As Google’s free storage is tied to all Google products as a whole, Ente’s 10GB looks big.
If you exhaust the generous free space on Ente, you can upgrade to a paid plan that offers storage starting from 50GB to 2TB for a monthly or annual subscription.
End-to-End Encrypted Backups
The photos and videos you back up on Ente are end-to-end encrypted by default. Ente claims they never use our data to train their models or spy on us.
The photos we back up via Google Photos are not end-to-end encrypted. Google may use our data to train their AI models, serve us customized ads, etc. You can prevent Google from using your data to show you personalized ads, but they can read your data. That’s where Ente succeeds.
The backup is end-to-end encrypted with keys before it leaves our device. The encryption keys are derived from our password using advanced key derivation functions. That means only the password you set can decrypt the data.
As the source code of Ente is publicly audited, the trust factor improves. When I tried to sign up on Ente, it provided me with a recovery key or the master key that I can use in case I lose my password.
The encryption process involves only us, the users, and they can never access the data. Even in the unfortunate event of a data breach, our data can remain safe as it is end-to-end encrypted.
Fully Open-Source Platform
Ente’s entire codebase for photos and its other apps is available for public audit on GitHub with more than 29k stars. The stars do not necessarily mean the project is good, but they give some form of trust.
The internet rewards the sensation. If someone had found a mismatch between Ente’s tall claims and the code, they surely would have flagged it and made an issue out of it.
Backup of User-Selected Albums
When you give permissions for Google Photos on our device, it backs up all the available albums, photos, and videos. We cannot select or ignore certain albums.
Ente, on the other hand, gives users the option to select which albums to back up. The albums that we choose not to back up are ignored by Ente as well. I loved this feature personally, as a lot of unnecessary data gets uploaded and wastes storage space. We can also customize the albums for backup anytime.
Easy Accessibility on All Platforms
Ente Photo has an app for every major operating system. We can install its app on Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. If we do not want to install the app, we can use it on the web through Ente.com.
Import Data From Google and Apple
Just download the Google Takeout that only has Google Photos data, import it into the Ente desktop app, and you are all set. It’s that simple to import data from Google Photos.
If you are an Apple user, just install the Ente app on your mobile device. Ente will read the data directly from your iCloud library and import it.
If you have iCloud shared albums, select the photos you want to import into the Ente app, and then save them to your device library for Ente to read them automatically.
Better Sharing and Collaboration Features
Ente Photo app provides us with three ways to share albums with others. You can share with a person on Ente, create a public link and share it with non-Ente users, or create a collaborative link to let non-Ente users add photos without an Ente account.
This does not put pressure on non-users to create an Ente account before collaborating with Ente albums, unlike the Google Photos app.
On-Device Machine Learning Features
There are a few machine learning-based features, like Magic Search, where you can search for photos with descriptions of how you remember them, Face Recognition, Memory Lane, Map and Location, and Jump to Date. These are all the latest advances in AI features.
To protect and maintain your privacy, all the machine learning happens on your device itself and is never sent to Ente’s servers. The machine learning feature is not enabled by default. You have to enable it manually and choose to disable it whenever you need to do so.
Is Ente Photos safe to use?
Yes, the Ente Photos app is safe to use to back up your photos and videos. It provides end-to-end encryption based on your password, and only your password can decrypt the data. Once you forget your password and also lose the recovery key they provided, you may never get to access the backup. The entire codebase of the Ente Photos app is available for public audit on GitHub.
How do I transfer photos from Google Photos to Ente?
You can transfer photos from Google Photos to the Ente Photos app in two ways. You can either download Google Photos data from Google Takeout, or download the entire library from the Google Photos app and drop it into the Ente Photos desktop app. It will read the data and import it to back it up safely.

The Union of European Clubs lodged a formal complaint with the European Commission on Monday, alleging that the memorandum of understanding between UEFA and European Football Clubs breaches the European Union’s competition regulations.
The UEC claimed the agreement violates Articles 101 and 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.
The body argues that UEFA’s recognition of EFC as the sole representative of clubs across Europe excludes hundreds of smaller clubs from major governance decisions, including revenue allocation, match scheduling, and competition structure.
“Today one association holds that mandate for all of Europe’s clubs, while most clubs have no effective voice in it,” UEC general secretary Dennis Gudasic said.
“We are asking the Commission to examine whether that is compatible with EU law.”

UEFA and EFC did not respond to requests for comment.
The memorandum was originally signed in 2023 and later extended in 2024 to last until 2033. Currently, EFC nominates 16 of the 20 members of UEFA’s Club Competitions Committee, which reviews proposed changes to key governance within European club football.
Three members are chosen by UEFA from its executive committee, and there is one representative from European Leagues, which represents 53 leagues across the continent. EFC also nominates two members of the UEFA executive committee.
EFC approved its own governance reforms in September, expanding its board to 33 members, of which five to seven seats are reserved for representatives of member clubs.
All board members have voting rights, but it is not stated how the remaining seats are selected.
The UEC said it is open to discussing the matter with UEFA, as it seeks “binding and practical” changes to the memorandum.
“Our partnership with the ECA is the foundation of an inclusive, sustainable and dynamic ecosystem that benefits the entire European football pyramid,” said UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin, after the memorandum was extended in 2024.
EFC, formerly known as the European Club Association, is an organisation consisting of more than 900 member clubs.
The UEC consists of 138 member clubs across 22 countries and was founded in 2023 to “promote a fair, sustainable and balanced football ecosystem.”

Clothing factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike over pay
- Published
Dozens of factories in Bangladesh's main clothes-producing area have been shut by workers striking over a higher minimum wage.
Nearly 150 sites across the country have been closed in the textile hubs of Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur this weekend.
The garment industry is big business for Bangladesh, generating nearly $40bn (£30bn) in exports every year and making up 10% of the country's total GDP.
Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month. The minimum monthly wage in Bangladesh is currently 12,500 taka but employees say this is not enough to deal with the cost of living crisis.
On Sunday morning workers massed on the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur to block the road. Traffic was stopped by the protests for about an hour before police stepped in.
A "No Work No Pay" provision of labour laws allows owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.
Police Supt Mohammad Amjad Hossain told the BBC officers shut factories in the city after the workers walked out.
He said 13 factories were closed on Saturday night and "sixteen factories were closed during the morning unrest".
- Wage protests force hundreds of Bangladesh garment factories to close 
  - Published3 November
The garment industry in Bangladesh employs about four million workers making clothes for big brands including H&M, Primark and Zara.
Bangladesh is the world's second largest exporter of ready- to-wear clothes after China and it is feared that the current unrest could have a knock-on effect for international buyers if it carries on for substantial amount of time.
The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) is calling for protection for factories.
"BGMEA and BKMEA have questioned the justification of continuing to participate in wage board negotiations without any assurance that the factories will be protected," BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said.
"Garment factories that have been unable to continue production due to the ongoing unrest will remain indefinitely closed from tomorrow under... Bangladesh's labour law."
On 1 November the government formed a minimum wage board to recommend a revised pay structure for workers.
The board, chaired by a senior district judge, said at its first meeting it would finalise any recommendations by the end of November.
Once it is put in place, the revised pay structure is expected to take effect from 1 December.

“Light it up like a Christman tree,” the man, an Iraqi named Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, urged the 17-year-old, according to U.S. prosecutors. The teen climbed over a wall and tossed a bomb through a broken window. “J’s mic is muted,” read the text on Mr. al-Hassani’s computer screen.
The synagogue arson in April was a small, violent part of Iran’s efforts to force an end to the bombing campaign that was pummeling the country, according to American investigators.
The attack was described in a federal indictment filed in New York this week. It revealed extensive new details about a wave of violence against Jewish institutions in Europe and U.S. targets, including a British air base used by American bombers. Prosecutors hold Iran’s agents responsible for the assaults.
Within days of the war starting, Mr. al-Hassani and at least two associates, including an operative for Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, began plotting the attacks in Europe, prosecutors said. The men talked about procuring drones and missiles from contacts in Iran. They pored over a map of London, with one saying they should “get focused” on targeting the British capital. Soon after, attacks hit temples and other Jewish sites in London.
In the fight against much stronger conventional forces, Iran has found ways to impose costs on its adversaries without inviting a full military response. One major aspect of Iran’s strategy is its embrace of small-time criminals to conduct low-cost assaults against vulnerable targets that are part of everyday life.

After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty
- Published
Cheers erupted at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in July as news broke that Gen-Z protests had forced federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign.
One protester turned to me, beaming: "This is the youth's victory."
Just over three months later, the mood has shifted dramatically. Student protesters are now struggling even to assemble. Demonstrations by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) last month over voting rights were met with sweeping restrictions and thousands of peaceful protesters were detained.
The summer had seen a new wave of dissent in India, driven by deep frustration among the youth and fuelled by irreverent online satire.
The movement spread across the country, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a leader with a strongman image, unaccustomed to open criticism or mockery, struggled to contain it. But the government's increasingly forceful security response suggests it has learned from its rare concession to protesters, invoking public order to curb dissent.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam rejected accusations of heavy-handedness and told the BBC: "The right to protest and freedom of expression is mandated by the constitution, but it has to be done within the law. It cannot override the rights of others, at the cost of public security".
This is by no means the first time the Modi government has faced large-scale protests.
But the breadth of them pose a challenge for the BJP, according to Yamini Aiyar, former president of the Centre for Policy Research and visiting professor at Brown University.
"They are not defined by caste, gender or economic class," Aiyar said. "Even some of the core BJP base, the upwardly mobile, lower-income classes, were attracted by the movement."
The scale of the youth protests is also magnified by its online presence. Protesters have broken a longstanding political taboo, openly mocking the prime minister online.
"It's more than just laughs," said Sakhi, a student protester who identifies as they/them and affiliated with one of Delhi University's left-wing student organisations.
"The fear of repercussions in other generations isn't felt as much in ours," they said. "Comedy is a new language to challenge authority."
Previous protest movements posed serious challenges to Modi but were easier to dismiss as representing narrow sections of society or to label "anti-national", according to Aiyar.
In 2020, farmers protesting against controversial agricultural reforms were blocked from entering Delhi, leading to months of demonstrations and, at times, clashes on the capital's borders. After a year of protests, the government abandoned the reforms.
Protests against a contentious citizenship law in 2019 and 2020 are a stark reminder of the powers of the judiciary should anyone be deemed a national security threat.
Student activist Umar Khalid was arrested under anti-terror laws after violent clashes in Delhi that killed 53 people, mostly Muslims. He was accused of being a "key conspirator". He has now spent more than six years in jail without his trial having begun.
His partner Banojyotsna Lahiri told the BBC they have no regrets, but that the situation instilled "a kind of fear that has prevailed".
"We are just looking at a very dark mesh of empty space, because we don't know when the endpoint is," Lahiri said. Khalid's latest appeal was lodged this month.
Aiyar believes opponents are using a familiar "playbook" today to "de-legitimise" protests, but that it isn't resonating as convincingly.
Nevertheless, the youth protests have struggled to recapture this summer's momentum.
CJP leaders, including spokesperson Saurav Das, have faced repeated detentions and legal action. Das and fellow leader Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Delhi's Tihar jail after being accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar.
The site of their summer victory has since been struck off the list of authorised protest venues, a decision being challenged in court.
Protesters from other groups, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (Aisa), have also faced police action over allegations of defying orders.
"We were expecting some kind of crackdown," said Das. He added that "the government has learnt a lot" since the summer.
Legal experts warn the proceedings themselves can have a chilling effect.
"A lot of cases can lead to acquittals, but it can take years. The process is the punishment, and that can deter protesters," said Ali Khan, an assistant professor at Lloyd Law College.
The restrictions on demonstrations have become excessive, according to constitutional lawyer Vrinda Grover, who is advising the CJP.
"Those who are organising the protests have repeatedly emphasised that this is non-violent," she argued. "Rights have been whittled down in the name of law and order."
The BJP has rejected suggestions it is suppressing peaceful dissent.
Islam told the BBC that demonstrations "cannot override the rights of other citizens just because a handful of people want to protest and be responsible for violence".
Even dissenting online carries risk. Sakhi's viral social media posts have attracted targeted abuse and transphobic attacks. The BBC has seen posts threatening them with violence and rape.
Sometimes, it can deter Sakhi from protesting or even make them change the way they dress.
"Making people laugh can turn into being called anti-national," Sakhi said. "They want me to feel damaged," they added.
They claim some of their content was removed after getting millions of views.
Under India's information technology laws, the government can order platforms to block content on national security grounds. Notices on X and Instagram have shown accounts being withheld in India.
CJP leaders have likened the crackdown to the 1975 Emergency, when then prime minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and jailed political opponents.
Yet dissent has not been stamped out.
Opposition parties have, in part, filled the void. Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi on 1 November for a rally organised by INDIA bloc, an alliance of opposition parties led by Congress, and permitted by the authorities.
CJP leaders, meanwhile, insist the movement is bigger than their organisation.
When Das walked out Delhi's Tihar prison on 21 October, photographs showed him smiling.
"I would just say wait and watch," Das told us. "Time is on our side. We are a very young generation."

A video is going viral on social media, where a young man is heard saying in Bangla, “We won’t allow any Hindutva aggression or Indian aggression in Jagannath University.”
The video wad shared by X handle Voice of BD Hindus (@HinduUnityBD) on November 7 with the claim that Muslim students of Jagannath University in Bangladesh had declared Diwali as a form of Hindutva aggression. (Archive)

In the 25-second-long clip, the man states, “We won’t allow any Hindutva aggression or Indian aggression in Jagannath University. This university is situated in a country of 92% Muslims, and the university claims that it runs by nurturing the culture, ethics and heritage of the Muslims. If anyone wants to make things work differently, the people of Bangladesh will give a befitting reply. Inshallah”.
The video was also shared by X user Monica Verma with the claim that “Muslim Students in Bangladesh are calling Deepawali celebrations as “Hindu aggression” warning the Hindu students of consequences if they celebrate it.”
Muslim Students in Bangladesh are calling Deepawali celebrations as “Hindu aggression” warning the Hindu students of consequences if they celebrate it.
Indian as well as the global Media will never show you this side of the F*cked Up Bangladeshi Gen Z. https://t.co/wij366yQtp
— Monica Verma (@TrulyMonica) November 7, 2026
Several other prominent Indian social media users shared the same video with similar claims.
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the claim, we conducted a reverse image search using key frames from the video in question.
This led us to a video published by Bangladesh-based media outlet ‘Desh Somoy News’. The video is identical to the one currently going viral and was published on October 16 in connection with the beef festival controversy at Jagannath University in Dhaka.
The controversy at Dhaka’s Jagannath University began on October 12, when students of the department of Islamic history and culture organised a beef feast near the university’s central temple. Hindu students objected to the proximity of the cooking arrangements to the temple and the alleged use of temple bricks to build a makeshift stove. Protests followed, triggering a wider dispute on campus.
On October 14, the university administration issued a notice prohibiting animal slaughter on campus, prompting further student protests.
Protesting against the administrative decision, students led by the Jagannath University Central Student’s Union organized a rally in the campus on October 14 itself, and held an impromptu press conference after the protest rally. The video in question is from that press conference.
Bangladesh-based online news portal Bd24report covered the press conference on its Facebook page on October 14. The live video is 17 minutes long, and from 5:13 minute mark, the press conference can be seen. At the 8:39-minute mark, the social work secretary of the Student’s Union, Mustafizur Rahaman, addresses the press. Rahaman is the same person seen speaking in the viral video.
Rahaman spoke from 8:50 till 10:56 minute mark, and the viral snippet is from 10:22 till 10:47. There was no mention of Diwali in the entire programme. The students spoke in protest against the University administration’s decision to ban animal slaughter within the campus.
Although the administration subsequently softened its position, students led by the Jagannath University Central Student’s Union slaughtered a cow on October 16 and organised a beef feast. The student’s union is run by Jamaat-e-Islami Bangladesh’s student wing Islami Chatra Shibir backed candidates.
On October 17, Bangladesh Khelafat Chatra Majlish held a similar feast, slaughtering a second cow and organising a Qawwali programme.
It is also important to note that Diwali celebrations and Kali Puja were organized on the Jagannath University campus this year. A pandal was set up for Kali Puja and students were seen creating ‘alpona’, a traditional Bengali art form drawn on floors, which is considered auspicious.
To sum up, a video related to the controversial beef festival on Dhaka’s Jagannath University campus in October is viral with the false claim that Jamaat student leaders objected to Diwali celebrations at the university. The statements made in the clip have got nothing to do with Diwali. Besides, Kali Puja was held on the campus like previous years.

In early November, social media users shared a claim that Japanese intelligence uncovered an Israeli plot to detonate radioactive "dirty bombs" in two American cities before Christmas. Some posts claimed Iran would be blamed for the attacks and that the Pentagon was involved in the supposed operation.
For instance, one Facebook post (archived) claimed:
This is very serious news coming in. Japan warns an Israeli intelligence is planning to detonate dirty bombs in two American cities before Christmas, with the attacks supposedly being blamed on Iran. The viral reports claim Japanese intelligence uncovered the alleged plot, with further accusations involving the Pentagon, America's power grid and a secret plan to reshape the world order. Spread the word and follow for more.
Similar claims circulated on Instagram and X. We also received reader inquiries asking whether the supposed warning was real.
But we found no credible evidence that Japan ever issued such a warning or that Israel was planning the alleged attacks. A warning of this scale would likely receive widespread news coverage, but we found no such reports. The claim appeared to come from The People's Voice, a website with a history of spreading false information. Japan did urge its citizens to prepare for emergencies in early November, but the announcement concerned natural disasters, including major earthquakes — not attacks on U.S. cities.
Snopes contacted the Japanese Embassy, CNN and The People's Voice for comment. We also reached out to the Pentagon, which told us, "We don't have a comment to provide."
How the rumor spread
One Facebook page sharing the rumor was called "The Pentagram" and described itself as:
Pentagon News | Strategic, Global, Unbiased.
We navigate the complex landscape of global events, defense, politics, and breaking news to bring you the facts that matter. 5 sides to every story, one trusted source.
(The Pentagram Facebook page)
However, despite its name, the page was not affiliated with the Department of Defense.
The post featured what appeared to be a CNN headline attributed to journalist Lauren Kent, reading, "Japan warns an Israeli intelligence is planning to detonate dirty bombs in two American cities before Christmas." However, we did not find any such article on CNN's website. A Google search for the headline returned solely social media posts repeating the allegation, and the purported article did not appear on Kent's CNN author page.
We traced the rumor to a Nov. 1 article published by The People's Voice, titled "Japan Warns Israel Planning to 'Nuke 2 American Cities' Before Christmas." The website, formerly known as NewsPunch, has a long history of publishing false information. Over the years, fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked claims published by the outlet.
The article began:
This is an emergency broadcast. Japanese intelligence has issued an urgent warning to the West… and we need to listen.
Israel is planning to destroy two American cities with devastating radioactive dirty bombs. Tens of millions dead within minutes. Millions more lives shattered in the blast zone. The toxic radioactive cloud will spread across the country, across the world, leaving nothing but devastation in its wake.
And as the global order crumbles, the nations will regroup under one government. The New World Order will be born from the ashes.
According to Japanese intelligence, the plan is already in motion. And the worst part? The US military is part of the plan. The moment the US military merged with the IDF—that was the moment the false flag was finalised.
Now, Israeli citizens are being told to leave the US. It's not coming. It's here.
"Last week, the Japanese government issued an urgent nationwide emergency request, urging citizens to stockpile survival essentials. Then, highly placed Japanese intelligence agents blew the whistle, revealing that Israel is preparing to attack two American cities with radioactive dirty bombs," it further claimed.
But the article didn't provide any evidence to support its claims. It did not name any Japanese intelligence officials who supposedly uncovered the plot or provide any verifiable information. The article's description of dirty bombs was also misleading. According to the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, dirty bombs combine "a conventional explosive, such as dynamite, with radioactive material." They do not cause nuclear explosions or mass destruction as described in the article.
Moreover, next to the dramatic warnings of a supposedly planned attack, the article promoted a VPN service, claiming it could protect users from Israeli surveillance:
But first, ask yourself: how do you survive the chaos they intentionally create? For me, there's only one option — stand and fight, for freedom and liberty. And to do that, you have to protect yourself by removing yourself from their battlefield.
I protect myself with the only VPN that hasn't been infiltrated by Israel, with next gen privacy tech that makes it mathematically impossible for them to spy on me. It's a life saver, literally, and I recommend it to every one of you. Do yourself a solid. Check out [URL].
The allegations were later repeated in an X post by Sean Adl-Tabatabai, the founder of The People's Voice.
What did Japan actually warn about?
Around the time the rumor began spreading, the Japanese government did issue a real warning urging people to prepare for emergencies. On Nov. 2, Japan's newly established National Disaster Management Agency issued a request urging residents to prepare for natural disasters:
(bousai.go.jp)
The announcement didn't mention Israel or any planned attacks on the United States.
Moreover, during an Oct. 30 news conference, Japan's disaster management minister, Goshi Hosono, addressed rumors that the government knew of an upcoming war or another major crisis. He said this was not the case and explained that the warning was simply meant to encourage people to prepare for natural disasters.
All in all, the rumor had no credible evidence supporting it, but its alarming claims could easily raise unfounded concerns. That's why it's important to check the source of such stories before sharing them with others.

Fitness obsessed & 'control freak' - what can Man Utd expect from Pochettino?
- Published
Mauricio Pochettino heads to Old Trafford with a reputation for "brutal" pre-seasons, an obsession with fitness and a no-nonsense approach.
Manchester United confirmed on Friday that Pochettino will become their manager on 18 November - replacing Michael Carrick - and has signed a contract until June 2029.
So what should the players and staff expect when the Argentine takes control at the end of next week?
BBC Sport spoke to Toby Alderweireld, who spent four years playing for Pochettino at Tottenham during a successful period where they reached the Champions League final and finished second in the Premier League.
- How Ferguson-inspired Pochettino can succeed where Carrick failed at Man Utd 
  - Published11 hours ago
- Pochettino a decade in Man Utd's making - but Carrick deserves better 
  - Published2 days ago
'The main man'
Alderweireld, 37, says Pochettino has a no-nonsense approach to management and that he can get the best out of a squad, as long as you do it his way.
"He is very approachable but you need to follow his plan. If you don't follow his plan, you go on the side and you're not coming back any more.
"You need to think about team, team, team. If you're thinking about yourself, you're gone.
"As a player you have your own life, your own situation but he says 'look, I understand and you can talk to me about it but the team is number one' - that's the way it is and if you're not following it, he'll put you on the sideline.
"He's straightforward, has his own ideas and maybe you agree with them or don't, that's up to you. But you need to follow him and I think that's something Manchester United need - a big character, everyone in the same direction, following the plan and if not, no problem, you can go. He's the main man.
"He's a very smart man, knows how to talk to the press and what to say. He will create an environment like 'it's us against the world' - we are getting fit, we are together as a team. It doesn't matter what people say, let's work together and get results together.
"At Spurs there was coaching staff but he will be there. He knows everything. If he's not there, he's looking at video and data. He knows everything about the players on and off the pitch - the players will be watched.
"He is, in a positive way, a control freak because he says your body is your weapon and it needs to be ready to perform."
'The basic is to be fit'
Manchester United have been criticised this season for an apparent lack of fitness and for not running enough in games - they rank in the bottom five in the league for distance covered and most high-intensity runs.
Alderweireld says Pochettino's number one demand is fitness and running.
"First of all he made us very fit. Pre-season was brutal.
"The way he wants to play - on the front foot, putting people under pressure, a high line, very dynamic play - you need to run. You need to be capable of running and be capable of high intensity runs - the basic is to be fit.
"Every manager wants a good pre-season and time to give the players their ideas and the fitness. But the players are going to feel straight away that it's a different level.
"This is every day at the training ground, it's 100% - that's what he asks, what he demands. It will be a big difference for the players and they're going to see results there straight away.
"In the Champions League semi-final, we were 3-0 down [against Ajax] and he didn't have a tactical half-time talk. He just said 'you're going to be physical, you're going to fight, you only need one goal to be back in the game, believe that everything is possible'.
"That was a big moment because we were nowhere near Ajax at that time, especially in that game. But we changed everything by intensity, by duels. I remember the long ball to [Fernando] Llorente and just fighting and asking 'how badly do you want it?' It changed from that moment."

Excellent design feels more like a “real” handheld console. Improved battery life. Bright, colorful, smooth screen. Thumbsticks pave the way for even more retro games.
TIRED
No meaningful, powerful boost to previous Evercades. No more HDMI out. D-pad sits too high.
Specialist hardware manufacturer Blaze Entertainment has spent the 2020s quietly carving out a niche for itself as the go-to option for retro gaming. With a stable of reliable hardware, from the original Evercade handheld to the Evercade Alpha bartop arcade cabinet, it offers numerous ways to play, all built around an ever-expanding library of physical cartridges. Each brings a curated selection of classic titles and lost curiosities to modern players.
The Evercade Nexus is more than just the latest addition to its console lineup. While it retains compatibility with every previously released Evercade cartridge, it’s also the biggest leap forward the line has taken so far, both in hardware and in what it might offer with games going forward. It’s a real level up—and it’s rather brilliant.
Bigger and Better
The most obvious change is the sheer size. Where Blaze’s previous handhelds were about on par with the original Game Boy Advance, aimed at pocketable play, the Evercade Nexus is closer in scale to a Nintendo Switch Lite. It measures 215 x 111 x 34 millimeters and weighs 410 grams—still easily portable, but more in the “buy a protective hard case and throw it in your bag” kind of way.
The size increase works in its favor, though. The larger design feels more substantial, with more real estate for your hands for better comfort. The control layout remains broadly the same as the Evercade EXP—a D-pad, ABXY face buttons, shoulder buttons, and triggers all return, with a few beneficial tweaks. Notably, the triggers are now chunkier and curved to meet your fingers, while all four shoulder inputs and the rear of the device are now nicely textured for better grip.
Photograph: Matt Kamen
The big change is the addition of twin symmetrical thumbsticks. This has implications for Evercade going forward—more on that later—but it also improves Tate Mode (pronounced tah-tay, meaning vertical in Japanese), a returning feature from the Evercade EXP. As on that model, tapping the dedicated mode-shift button rotates the screen 90 degrees, letting you play vertically scrolling arcade games in the intended orientation, rather than crammed into a tiny pillar-boxed view on the widescreen display.
On the EXP, you’d hold the console on the left to use the D-pad for movement, which required duplicate A+B buttons on that side and cluttered the inputs. On the Nexus, Tate Mode rotates in the opposite direction, letting you use the right-hand thumbstick and the default ABXY buttons. It feels much better—again aided by the increased overall size—and keeps the device's design looking much tidier.
Whichever orientation you play in, the screen is bigger—a 5.89-inch IPS panel with an 840 × 512-pixel resolution for a 167 pixels-per-inch density, versus the original's 4.3-inch LCD—and brighter, now boasting 500-plus nits. It’s clear and colorful, and games look fantastic on it.
The only minor build-quality demerits are the D-pad, which feels a little too raised and prone to rocking—a slightly more flush fit would have been better—and the glossy finish under the face buttons and around the front trim. These accents are aesthetically pleasing, standing out from the matte plastic of the rest of the unit, but they attract micro-scratches far too easily. Those small gripes aside, the Nexus is a huge improvement on its predecessors, feeling less like a quirky gadget and more like a serious, modern gaming handheld.
Up and Downgrades
The Nexus doesn’t actually see any boosts in processor power or memory. It still uses the 1.5-GHz quad-core chip in the EXP with 512 MB of RAM. That may not sound like much in 2026, but it’s significantly more powerful than the original hardware it emulates, and it ensures Evercade’s universal cross-device compatibility for every cartridge.
The downside is that the Nexus still feels slow at the system level. Booting it up takes about 35 to 40 seconds on average, and it can take about the same to load up a cartridge. Games don't have any performance issues, but getting there is sluggish. Disappointingly, there’s also no quick-suspend feature, forcing you to power off fully and back on between play sessions.
Photograph: Matt Kamen
There are some upgrades to the underlying tech, though. One material improvement is the battery, which jumped to a 5,000-mAh cell from the EXP's 3,000 mAh. Even with that bigger, brighter screen sucking up juice, the Nexus offers around five hours of play between charges, roughly an hour longer. On the audio front, the integrated front-facing stereo speakers are solid, offering louder, clearer output. Even better, the Nexus now supports Bluetooth, finally allowing you to connect wireless headphones, while still offering a 3.5-mm jack for wired headsets.
Bluetooth isn’t the only connectivity upgrade. The Nexus now supports the Wi-Fi 6 standard and can connect to 5-GHz networks (previous models could only use slower 2.4-GHz ones). That’s useful for downloading console updates and Evercade’s free Game of the Month. It also enables the new EverSync feature, unique to the Nexus, which allows multiple units to communicate wirelessly. Much like Nintendo’s GameShare, it’s set to allow multiplayer across devices even with only one cartridge, although I haven't been able to test this feature yet.
The underlying OS also gets a refresh. Hop into the settings menu and you'll find new customization tools. These let you adjust the color palette for the menu background and the glowing LED Nexus logo, select onscreen borders for non-widescreen games, and even tweak aspect ratios and virtual scan lines—all nice ways to personalize your device.
The glaring omission is any form of TV connectivity. Previous handheld Evercades featured a mini-HDMI out port, but that’s removed entirely here. It was always a nice-to-have rather than a major selling point, but it’s disappointing to lose a feature. Evercade players wanting TV play will have to opt for the Evercade VS-R set-top console.
A New Era for Old Games
While the Nexus hardware is a significant improvement, more exciting is where the games themselves may be heading. Almost every game on Evercade to date has been from the 8-bit or 16-bit era, if not earlier, a period that near-universally consisted of 2D titles. Adding thumbsticks opens the door to an entirely new generation of 3D games. Blaze says the Nexus works with 32- and 64-bit games, which dramatically expands possibilities for future releases.
Photograph: Matt Kamen
More impressively, the first two cartridges to benefit from this generational leap also see Evercade step beyond emulation for the first time. Both the Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie double-pack and the DOOM and DOOM II collection are natively ported. That means improved performance, intentional widescreen aspect ratios to match the display, higher resolutions up to 60 frames per second, and on-cartridge save slots rather than virtual quick saves.
The Banjo duology is the real standout so far, with the colorful worlds of Rare’s classic 3D platformers shining on the Nexus’ superior screen while taking full advantage of the dual thumbsticks (something the N64 controller lacked) to offer smoother camera controls alongside free movement. These are authentic and accessible versions of 64-bit gaming greatness, without compromise. This might be the best way to play this pair of games, period, and all the better for being able to do so portably. (For anyone who’s looked up the price of a Banjo-Tooie cart on the secondary market, a bargain, too.) The DOOM collection also holds up well, with classic boomer shooters and a stack of bonus missions and map packs, but as some of the oldest examples of first-person shooters, they show their age more.
The ports are to Evercade as an ecosystem, meaning the cartridges will still play on existing hardware—even Blaze’s budget Super Pocket devices—with camera controls mapped to shoulder buttons, albeit with a slower rotational view. It also partly explains the lack of power upgrades for the Nexus, as cross-device compatibility is a signature of the collection. Still, as Blaze works its way through gaming history, it feels as though a future Evercade will inevitably have to make a break to offer more power and support more recent games.
For now, though, the Nexus is hands-down the best way to play both Evercade’s vast library of games and this new pseudo-generation of native releases. With its better screen, bigger form, and added controls for 3D games, it’s a delight to play on. If Blaze can keep up the momentum with more dedicated ports, this will be a bright new age for the best old games.

Quick Answer
LastWave, Musify, Convx, Spotube, and SimpMusic are free open-source clients for YouTube Music and Spotify. They unlock premium perks without subscription fees or ad tracking, offering background playback, offline downloads, time-synced lyrics, lossless audio, and customized interfaces without locked controls.
Subscription prices are going through the roof. And when you stack multiple subscriptions together, it can put a big hole in your pocket. For listening to music, we usually depend on Spotify and YouTube Music. They are the default music streaming sources for millions across the globe. Though there are alternatives from which you can hear high-quality audio, they just can’t match the ease of popular apps. But you are bombarded with ads, and several features are locked behind a paywall unless you pay.
Thankfully, you don’t have to search the internet for free options. Developers around the world have built free apps that give you many of those perks. Below are five of the best, what each does well, and what to watch out for before installing.
Table of Contents
Why are open-source music apps worth a look?
To be clear, most of these apps are clients. This means that they don’t store any music themselves. They plug into a service like YouTube Music and show it in a cleaner, ad-free interface with extra features on top, which you’d usually get after paying for a premium subscription. For me, Spotify has been the go-to music streaming app, but slowly the app has become quite greedy.
After a few times, the next and previous song buttons get locked, and it asks you to pay to unlock them. I mean, what is wrong with companies today? Thankfully, I have now ditched Spotify and have picked one of the below open-source music options.
That has three practical effects:
- No ads and no subscription fees. Everything below is free.
- Most of these apps have no ad trackers or tracking SDKs.
- New features are constantly added, and some of them aren’t even available in paid apps.
The catch is that these apps rely on unofficial methods to fetch music, so they can break when YouTube or Spotify changes something. Treat them as great free alternatives, but not as rock-solid replacements. Let us take a look at the free alternatives.
Best free open-source music apps
LastWave
If you care about how your music sounds, LastWave is the one to install first. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. Most of us would care about the free music that we get with LastWave, but you will soon appreciate the quality of music that it offers. And since it is a YouTube Music client, you are getting access to almost every song that is available on YouTube.
The headline feature is lossless FLAC audio, up to 24-bit/192 kHz. When you press play, the song starts playing right away on the fastest available stream, and while you listen, the app fetches the lossless version in the background and switches over once it’s ready. On compatible phones and headphones, LastWave also plays the Dolby Atmos version of a song automatically. For those who own a USB DAC or a pair of IEMs, there’s a bit-perfect mode that sends raw, unprocessed audio straight to your device.
The app is packed with features that normally sit behind a subscription. The lyrics are synced word-by-word and pulled from sources like Apple Music, Musixmatch, and LRCLIB. There’s a 10-band equalizer with presets for thousands of headphone models, and smart playlists that build mixes from your listening history. Plus, you have the option to import playlists from Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube Music in seconds, and even sync your Spotify liked songs.
Musify
Not everyone wants a hundred settings and toggles. Some people just want to listen to their favorite music without having to deal with ads and a hundred pop-ups about purchasing the subscription between two songs. Musify is for people who just want to open an app, search for a song, and press play. It’s a lightweight Android app built around Material You, which means its colors automatically match your phone’s theme and wallpaper.
Using it is fairly easy. You search for songs, albums, artists, or playlists and start streaming over Wi-Fi or mobile data. If you want to save data or listen on a flight, you can download tracks and play them offline. It lets you create your own playlists, rename and reorder them, or import existing ones from online sources. The player shows lyrics so you can follow along. You can also control the quality of the audio.
There are no annoying banner ads, no audio ads, no sign-up, and no tracking inside the app, and the interface is translated into dozens of languages by the community. I found this to be a great choice for older phones, or for a parent or sibling who finds complicated apps annoying.
Convx
While most open source music apps work well, there are only a few that also feel nice to use. Convx comes in the second category. If you like iOS’s “Liquid Glass” design, then you would love Convx. It brings iPhone’s Liquid Glass design to Android, with frosted, see-through menus, floating controls, and album-inspired colors that change with whatever you are playing.
Under the pretty surface, Convx is a complete music player. You can browse and stream music, save songs for offline listening, build queues and playlists, set a sleep timer, change playback speed, and tweak the sound to your taste with an equalizer. What makes it stand out among the heavy hitters is its DJ-style playback. You also get automix, crossfade, and smooth transitions between one song and the next. Lyrics are synced word by word and come from several providers, plus it gets animated artwork.
Convx can play local files and even songs stored on a home server or NAS through SMB and WebDAV. You can choose the option to import your Spotify playlists, show what you’re playing on Discord, scrobble to Last.fm, recognize songs playing around you, and use Listen Together to sync playback with friends.
Spotube
Spotube is the veteran here, with over 46,000 stars on GitHub, and it works differently from the rest. Instead of being locked to one service like Spotify or YouTube, it runs on plugins. You choose your own music sources, metadata, and playlists through plugins made by the community, or if you’re good with it, you can write one yourself.
The biggest advantage is that it works everywhere. Spotube runs natively on Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. This means you can use the same app on your phone and your laptop. It’s small, fast, and light on data. You can import and sync playlists from popular music services or manage them locally. It gives time-synced lyrics from public lyric databases no matter which source you use. Offline downloads are supported, with proper metadata and ID.
Privacy is one of the biggest highlights of Spotube. It collects no telemetry and no user data. Installing it is also easy, because you can download it through winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, Homebrew, Flatpak, and F-Droid.
SimpMusic
SimpMusic is that one app that does everything. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android and desktop that borrows many of Spotify’s best ideas. You can play music from YouTube Music or regular YouTube without ads, and it gets you background playback. You can browse the home feed, charts, podcasts and moods, search everything on YouTube, cache songs for offline playback and use Android Auto.
SimpMusic Wrapped gives you a year-in-music recap just like Spotify’s. Then there is monthly recap playlists and listening charts that stay on your device. There are three Now Playing styles, including one that looks like Apple Music, and the lyrics are synced in 12 languages. You can even share lyrics as an image.
You can switch to 1080p video with subtitles, skip sponsor segments with SponsorBlock, see dislike counts with Return YouTube Dislike, and use a 10-band equalizer with AutoEq headphone profiles.
Which one should you pick?
If you care most about sound quality, I would suggest LastWave. If you want something simple, pick Musify. If design matters to you, try Convx. If you want plugins and an app that runs on every device you own, choose Spotube. If you want the most features in one place, install SimpMusic. The best part is that all five are free and can be installed side by side, so you can try a few and keep your favorite. You will get access to unlimited songs from the best sources in good quality. Let us know which one you chose, and comment below if you have a different app that you use for listening to music.

October has rolled around, and that means only one thing: Spooky season is here! And what better way to celebrate Halloween than with some of the finest fright fests of the last 50 years?
We’re bringing you a more retro-tinged selection of the best films on streaming this month, but the mix of crowd-pleasers and cult classics offers something for horror fans of all tastes. For instance, David Cronenberg’s grotesque revamp of The Fly, buzzing onto Hulu, and Ken Russell’s Altered States materializing on The Criterion Channel, both bring uniquely visceral takes on body horror to your screens, while sleeper hit Under the Skin on Netflix offers slow-burn sci-fi scares, and Midsommar on Prime Video takes to the hills for a sun-drenched approach to folk horror.
If you fancy something a bit newer, fear not. Well, fear lots actually—Zach Cregger’s shockingly original horror debut Barbarian smashes its way onto Hulu, while Netflix brings the final chapter in the sumptuously scary Mononoke trilogy, an anime extravaganza that looks like nothing else. Plus, there’s even one post-credits stinger of an entry that’s too scary to mention here …
Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.
Barbarian
When Tess (Georgina Campbell) finds her Airbnb in a sketchy neighborhood double booked with Keith (Bill Skarsgård), you’ll probably think you know where Barbarian is headed. You don't—and you should brace yourself for everything that follows. Written and directed by Zach Cregger (in a seismic departure from his early comedy background), Barbarian constantly flips the script, regularly subverting viewer expectations of horror movie clichés at every turn.
Smartly written, brilliantly shot, and psychologically disturbing on multiple levels, Barbarian is a genuinely terrifying entry in the modern horror canon. If you’ve discovered Cregger’s work from the Academy Award–winning Weapons or his recent horror-comedy reboot of Resident Evil, this is where he first made his mark on the silver screen.
Under the Skin
Under the Skin almost defies explanation. Scarlett Johansson plays an alien in human form, roaming Glasgow and the Scottish Highlands, luring isolated and lonely men to their doom, drowning them in an inexplicable oily abyss that seems to exist in a null space. All the while, she’s observed by a motorcyclist, trailing her from victim to victim.
No names are given, no purpose explained (not even to the cast; director Jonathan Glazer shot many of the alien’s initial encounters with humans using hidden cameras, only explaining and asking for their involvement afterward), but it’s far better to watch this blind and make your own mind up. Be warned, though—Johansson’s performance is truly unearthly, and in conjunction with Glazer’s bizarre imagery and a soundscape that maddeningly claws at your nerves, this is a deeply unsettling slice of sci-fi.
Midsommar
This acclaimed indie horror movie stars Florence Pugh as Dani, an American student struggling to deal with a family tragedy, who joins her boyfriend Christian (Jack Reynor) and his friends on a trip to Sweden. The vacation sounds like the perfect escape—nine days of communing with nature at a festival held only once every 90 years; a true once-in-a-lifetime experience. The problem? The festival is a front for a pagan cult, and things get rapidly, wildly out of hand.
Midsommar is a deeply effective and distressing folk horror film, with none other than Jordan Peele, director of the smash hit Get Out, declaring it has "the most atrociously disturbing imagery I've ever seen on film." Perfect date night material for Halloween season, then.
Train to Busan
South Korean cinema seems to love combining the end of the world and trains. Bong Joon Ho’s Snowpiercer got things on track in 2013, but director Yeon Sang-ho really left the station with this 2016 zombie horror masterpiece.
Seok-woo (Gong Yoo) starts his journey on the express train from Seoul to Busan just wanting to drop daughter Su-an off with her mother. Unfortunately, the last passenger to board might be a teensy bit infected with the zombie plague that’s kicking off outside, turning the ride into the express train to hell. The tight confines allow for some incredibly inventive action choreography, while genre fans are treated to a revolting twist on the undead themselves, a misshapen, juddering, ravenous horde that moves like a liquid mass of corpses.
Like all the best zombie films, though, it’s the social commentary that really elevates Train to Busan, with its exploration of class and status standing alongside Romero’s work at his peak. A decade on from release, this is still one of the freshest takes on zombies you’re likely to find—look up animated prequel Seoul Station and stand-alone sequel Peninsula if it leaves you wanting another bite.
Altered States
A bit of a deep cut, but director Ken Russell’s 1980 outing will really mess with your head. No, really—this tale of psychological horror and transformational terror is loosely based on real-world tests of the effects of psychoactive drugs and sensory deprivation on the human brain. The film sees researcher Eddie Jessup (William Hurt) subjecting himself to highly questionable experiments with hallucinogenics and isolation in an effort to tap into other states of being. Unfortunately, he’s wildly successful, not only opening his mind to genetic memories and shared consciousnesses, but seeing his physical body horrifyingly warp and devolve beyond recognition with each trip.
And what a trip—Russell masterfully creates a sense of psychedelic overload with a pioneering use of bizarre imagery and sound, the film shifting with each of Jessup’s transformations until you feel you’ve taken mind-altering substances yourself. An uncomfortably weird experience, Altered States will stay on your mind long after the credits roll.
Colossal
Anne Hathaway is literally a monster—at least she is in this darkly comedic crossover between kaiju flick and character study. After her life in New York falls apart, Gloria (Hathaway) moves back home to New Hampshire. At the same time, a giant monster starts rampaging across Seoul, destroying buildings and causing mass panic. Yet these two incompatible events aren't unrelated, as Gloria starts to realize that she can somehow control the beast from half a world away—but her heavy drinking and constant bad decisions may get in the way of saving the world. Director Nacho Vigalondo lovingly pastiches the likes of Godzilla, Gamera, and King Kong in this quirky film festival favorite.
Mononoke The Movie III: The Curse of the Serpent
A nameless Medicine Seller (Hiroshi Kamiya in Japanese, Crispin Freeman in English) traveling Edo period Japan may seem a humble figure, but his strange tinctures and concoctions make him one of the few capable of tackling mononoke—powerful spirits corrupting places and people alike. This trilogy-capping third movie takes the enigmatic traveler back to the cursed Imperial Palace visited in predecessors Phantom in the Rain and Ashes of Rage, seeking to uncover once and for all why it seems to attract so many dangerous monsters.
A master class in tension and otherworldly horror, Mononoke maintains its stunning visual approach of kaleidoscopic watercolors swirling on parchment, making for one of the most sumptuous and visually striking pieces of animation you’ll ever see. It’s worth noting that there is some real-world controversy over a returning voice actor embroiled in a scandal in Japan, so this might be a rare case where the English dub is the better option.
The Fly
Despite being a remake, David Cronenberg’s quintessential slice of 1980s body horror has almost completely supplanted the 1958 original in the public consciousness (although the original stars Vincent Price and is definitely still worth checking out on Prime Video).
This wholesale reimagining twists expectations away from mad science clichés—it almost feels like a superhero origin movie to start, with scientist Seth Brundle (Jeff Goldblum) accidentally splicing his genes with a fly during a teleportation experiment, and emerging with enhanced physical prowess in every respect. But with great power comes great personality shifts, wiry black hairs growing along his back, and the need to vomit acid onto his food before eating. And, as animal instincts take over, the self-proclaimed “Brundlefly” starts looking at science reporter Ronnie Quaife (Geena Davis) very differently.
The groundbreaking effects work that marked Brundle’s slow metamorphosis into a repulsive hybrid monster won the film the Oscar for Best Makeup, but its ability to pack in some genuine emotion alongside the scares make it easy to see why this is the de facto iteration of The Fly.
The Social Network
Oh, you think this isn’t horror? Ask yourself: What could possibly be scarier than the deleterious impact social media has had on the human condition? Director David Fincher and writer Aaron Sorkin’s biopic telling of the rise, and rise, and rise of Facebook, is the kind of film you watch through your fingers, too.
There’s an almost predatory hunger in Jesse Eisenberg’s Mark Zuckerberg, as he goes from a Harvard student whose hotness-ranking website was popular enough to crash the college’s whole network to a Silicon Valley darling attracting unheard-of sums of investment and power. Like most “based on a true story” horror films, it’s not entirely historically accurate and, true to genre norms, there’s a not-as-good sequel, with Sorkin returning to write and direct the newly released The Social Reckoning, but if you’ve been paying attention to reality the past few decades, this will definitely chill you to the bone.

Mozambique opposition leader faces trial over deadly 2024 election unrest
- Published
Tensions are running high in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, with a heavy police deployment as a prominent opposition leader goes on trial over deadly protests that followed the country's disputed 2024 elections.
Venâncio Mondlane faces several charges, including incitement to terrorism and civil disobedience, over protests that left hundreds of people dead. He denies any wrongdoing.
Security has been tightened around the Supreme Court, where Mondlane is due to appear on Tuesday, with authorities fearing a fresh wave of demonstrations by his supporters.
Police have appealed to citizens to follow the proceedings calmly and avoid actions that could threaten public order.
The trial is widely seen as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after disputed elections triggered some of the country's deadliest political unrest in decades.
"The trial is a real test for Mozambique. It is is an important opportunity to demonstrate that the rule of law applies equally to everyone," said Luis Nhachote, a political analyst.
Mondlane, who challenged the presidential election results that declared Daniel Chapo of the ruling Frelimo party the winner, accused the authorities of widespread electoral fraud and called for nationwide protests and work stoppages.
- Children shot dead after joining pot-banging protests in Mozambique 
  - Published23 November 2024
The demonstrations continued for months, with rights groups accusing security forces of using excessive force against protesters.
Amnesty International, citing local civil society organisations, said more than 300 people were killed during the unrest, which was one of the country's worst post-election crises since independence.
Mozambican police put the death toll at 96, including 17 police officers.
European Union election observers also reported irregularities in the October 2024 vote, raising questions about the credibility of the results.
Prosecutors accuse Mondlane of encouraging demonstrations that disrupted public services, damaged property and threatened public security.
The charges include publicly glorifying criminal acts, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to commit crimes and offences linked to terrorism.
He could face up to 24 years in prison if convicted of the most serious charge.
Mondlane has rejected the accusations, insisting that his calls for demonstrations were aimed at demanding electoral transparency rather than encouraging violence.
His party, the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), has described the prosecution as politically motivated.
The Supreme Court has denied allegations of political interference in the proceedings.
A heavy deployment of police has been seen patrolling around the Supreme Court and major streets in Maputo ahead of the trial.
In a statement issued on Monday, Mozambique's police appealed to citizens to "preserve tolerance and peaceful coexistence," adding that the right to demonstrate must be exercised strictly within the limits of the law.
Police also pledged to protect people and property while acting preventively and proportionately in accordance with the rule of law.
The court has only granted access to selected media organisations, sparking criticism from journalists and press freedom campaigners.
Court officials say the restrictions are necessary because of limited seating capacity in the courtroom, but critics argue they undermine transparency in a case of significant public interest.
The proceedings are expected to be heard by five judges, with witnesses called by both the prosecution and defence.
Political observers warn that the trial could reignite tensions in a country still struggling to recover from the violence and deep political divisions that followed the 2024 elections.
