Fremantle‘s revenue climbed 7.8% to €482 million ($541 million) in the third quarter, driven mainly by delivery of the thriller series “Kill Jackie.” The gain gave parent company RTL Group a lift while its TV advertising business continued to shrink.
The figure compares with €447 million ($501 million) in the same quarter of 2025, and it made up for a slow start to the year. Across the first nine months of 2026, revenue at the “America’s Got Talent” producer fell 2.6% to €1.32 billion ($1.48 billion), down from €1.35 billion ($1.52 billion). RTL Group put the dip chiefly down to timing effects at Fremantle’s drama and film division in the first half. Its entertainment and documentary units held roughly level.
Several Fremantle titles did well on streaming over the period. Reality competition “Wonka’s The Golden Ticket,” which bowed on Netflix in the third quarter, is the streamer’s top reality competition launch of the year so far. Documentary series “Death of the Pastor’s Wife” spent two straight weeks as Netflix’s No. 1 TV series worldwide and became the platform’s strongest nonscripted launch of 2026 to date. “Minerva Academy” made the Netflix Top 10 in 62 territories.
On broadcast, “America’s Got Talent,” now in Season 21, led NBC’s entertainment lineup for 2025/26 and topped the U.S. summer schedule.
“Kill Jackie” has also traveled. In July, Warner Bros. Discovery picked up the thriller for HBO Max in key European markets, adding to earlier deals with Prime Video and AMC+. The show opened as the No. 1 title on AMC+ in the U.S. In August, Fremantle and Prime Video unveiled a multi-territory distribution deal covering the “Baywatch” reboot as well as older seasons of the franchise.
At group level, RTL Group’s revenue for January to September rose 15.1% to €4.74 billion ($5.32 billion), helped by its June 2026 acquisition of Sky Deutschland and by streaming growth. Adjusted for portfolio changes and currency effects, revenue grew 1.6%. Third-quarter revenue jumped 38.4% to €1.85 billion ($2.08 billion), or 4.8% on an organic basis.
Streaming revenue rose 27.9% to €449 million ($504 million) over nine months. Paid subscriptions to RTL+ in Germany and Hungary and M6+ in France reached 9 million at Sept. 30, up 18.4% year on year. That already hits the group’s full-year target.
“Despite further headwinds in the linear TV advertising markets, our operating profit – Adjusted EBITA – also increased organically in the first nine months of 2026, thanks to our streaming business and Fremantle,” said Clement Schwebig, CEO of RTL Group.
TV advertising revenue fell 5.2% over the nine months and 8% in the third quarter. Because fourth-quarter demand for linear TV advertising is weaker than it expected, RTL Group now sees full-year revenue of around €7.1 billion ($7.96 billion). That is the bottom of the €7.1 billion–€7.2 billion ($7.96 billion–$8.08 billion) range it gave in August. It also expects Adjusted EBITA of around €700 million ($785 million), against August guidance of €725 million ($813 million), plus or minus 3%. The company kept its medium-term Adjusted EBITA target of €1 billion ($1.12 billion).
Fremantle produces more than 11,000 hours of programming a year and has teams in 28 countries. It remains on track to reach its 9% margin target in 2026, RTL Group said.

Srinagar, Nov 16: Commuters passing through the busy Bemina crossing on the Srinagar–Baramulla Highway faced severe hardship on Monday evening as a massive traffic jam brought vehicular movement to a standstill for over two hours.
Commuters claimed that no traffic police personnel were visible on the ground to regulate the chaos.
The bottleneck, which began building up around 5:00 PM during peak evening rush hour, quickly spiraled out of control as vehicles from Batamaloo, Qamarwari, and the Parimpora stretch converged at the intersection. Bumper-to-bumper traffic stretched for nearly two kilometers on all approaching roads, trapping office-goers, students, and daily wage earners in the evening chill.
Frustrated motorists alleged that the complete absence of traffic cops at one of Srinagar’s most critical junctions worsened the situation. “There is not a single traffic policeman here to manage the flow. Everyone is trying to squeeze through from the wrong side, which has completely locked the intersection,” said Bashir Ahmad, a daily commuter stuck near the Bemina bypass for over an hour.
Witnesses said Emergency vehicles, including ambulances heading toward SKIMS Medical College in Bemina, were also caught in the snarls, forcing local shopkeepers and pedestrians to step onto the road to manually clear a narrow passage.
Residents and transporters pointed out that haphazard parking of passenger cabs and sumo vehicles near the crossing, combined with ongoing road work bottlenecks, frequently triggers congestion in the area. However, the lack of enforcement during peak hours left commuters entirely at the mercy of undisciplined driving.
Officials from the Traffic Police City Srinagar stated that a team had been dispatched to the spot to clear the backlog and restore normal movement.
By late evening, vehicular movement began inching forward slowly after local volunteers and a few arriving personnel intervened. Commuters demanded permanent deployment and strict action against roadside encroachments to prevent daily recurrences.

Eurovision’s organisers have said they are “surprised and disappointed” that the first Eurovision Asia was altered when it was broadcast in Malaysia, apparently removing LGBTQ+ imagery and people from the show.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), the alliance of public broadcasters that owns Eurovision, said it would write to Voxovation, the company producing the Asian contest under licence, and ask it to establish with the Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why it happened.
Footage circulating online of the contest, which was won by the Philippines’ Carmelle, showed the first of two cuts during the voting in Saturday’s final in Bangkok, when the Philippines’ spokesperson, Vice Ganda, awarded the Philippine jury’s points.
Vice Ganda is gay and identifies as non-binary. The comedian is among the biggest stars on Philippine television, has fronted the country’s most watched daytime show, and has campaigned for LGBTQ+ acceptance at home.
Announcing a national jury’s points is one of the most visible roles in a Eurovision final. Each country’s spokesperson appears in turn to reveal how their jury has ranked the other entries.
While the international feed showed Vice Ganda announcing that the Philippine jury had given its 12 points, the maximum, to the Malaysian entrant, Aina Abdul, TV3 viewers saw only the scoreboard.
Separate footage shows part of the show’s opening number showcasing Thai culture, in which drag performers appeared on street food carts, replaced with a wide shot taken from rehearsals.
Eurovision fans accused the channel of “censorship”. The Guardian has not been able to review TV3’s broadcast independently as its livestream is no longer available online.
Martin Green, the director of the Eurovision song contest, said: “We are surprised and disappointed to learn that the broadcast of Eurovision song contest Asia was altered in Malaysia.
“We take this matter seriously and will be writing to Voxovation, the producers of the show, to seek clarification and ask them to establish with Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why this happened.
“This appears to be isolated to the Malaysian broadcast of the show, and all other transmissions were not altered.”
Voxovation said in a statement that it was aware of the concerns raised and was “looking into the matter with the broadcaster to establish the circumstances … We are working with the Malaysian broadcaster to make sure this doesn’t happen again.”
Neither the EBU nor Voxovation said whether the contest’s participation agreement required broadcasters to carry the show unedited or what the consequences would be if one did not.
The Guardian has asked Media Prima, Malaysia’s largest media group and TV3’s owner, for comment.
This is not the first time the wider Eurovision song contest has faced allegations of censorship. In May 2018 the EBU terminated its partnership with the Chinese streaming service Mango TV after it dropped the Irish and Albanian entries and blurred a rainbow flag in the audience, saying such censorship was not in line with its “values of universality and inclusivity”.
Asked before Saturday’s final how the EBU’s commitment to its values squared with the laws in Malaysia and Bangladesh, the other competing country where same-sex relations are criminalised, the EBU’s head of communications, Dave Goodman, said the contest’s values were “non-negotiable”.
Malaysia has some of the harshest anti-LGBTQ+ laws in Asia, with oral and anal sex being punishable by up to 20 years in prison.
Rights groups have warned of a hardening climate. In November last year, authorities raided a men-only spa in Kuala Lumpur and detained more than 200 men, though no charges followed. And in 2022, police raided an LGBTQ+ Halloween party in the capital and arrested 20 people.
In 2023, a festival appearance by the British band the 1975, whose singer criticised the country’s homophobic laws and kissed a male bandmate on stage, led to the event being cancelled and prompted tighter entry rules for foreign performers.
TV3 has faced pressure over LGBTQ+ visibility before. In February 2025, it apologised after male guests arrived at a red carpet event in clothing resembling women’s dress.

The original Blue Yeti microphone was first released in 2009, and it remains the most ubiquitous microphone for home recording 17 years later. Chances are, if you’ve watched a YouTube video, Twitch stream, or listened to a podcast, you’ve heard (and probably seen) this microphone at least once.
Long after absorbing Blue and phasing out the brand name, Logitech has finally released its highly anticipated successor: the Yeti 2. The follow-up maintains the same general shape and look but drastically changes the microphone’s functionality. Instead of simply recording audio, the Yeti 2 has a handful of features to monitor and manipulate the audio passing through it, seamlessly recording production-quality audio with zero delay. While some of the design feels a bit underdeveloped, the Yeti 2 is a deserving sequel to the iconic original model and an easy shoe-in as the best USB microphone you can buy.
Intuitive Interfaces
The Yeti 2's biggest upgrades stares you directly in the face after taking it out of the box. The built-in screen and dial allow for on-the-fly adjustments right on the microphone. No software required. While I was a skeptic at first, I quickly found this little screen to be significantly more convenient than the alternative. It can be used to adjust gain, enable different post-processing settings, and configure the sound profile of the microphone.
More importantly, the screen can quickly provide insights into audio quality at a glance. The main screen shows a graph of the gain-adjusted input volume, which is what the microphone is sending to your computer. It can also display a histogram of volume over time, a pattern to show what direction input is coming from, or … a pixel-art Yeti. This little guy looks confused when you’re quiet, happy when you’re talking at a normal volume, and alarmed when you’re too loud for the microphone to handle. Within the G Hub app, the icons can be swapped out with any of Logi’s other premade avatars (a dragon, flower, frog, or jellyfish), or freely customized with your own images using a simple drag-and-drop menu. This is the least functional feature of the microphone, but it’s an endearing and intuitive way to indicate audio quality at a glance.
The screen also has quite a few adjustable menus for different features, including a de-noise function with four levels, five EQ presets, a pattern customizer with eight default options, and a multitude of toggleable settings to clean up and improve recording quality. While the settings can’t be customized using the screen, the G Hub application provides more in-depth adjustments for how intense each of these settings are, along with explanations of how they work and when to use them.

Samsung and Xiaomi have increased smartphone prices by up to ₹4,000 across 48 variants in India amid rising memory chip prices and subdued consumer demand. Prices for about 30 Samsung phones as well as 19 Xiaomi phones have been increased in a range of ₹1,000-4,000 between November 15-16. Samsung's latest revision covers 14 variants across its Galaxy A07 5G, A17 5G, A36, A37, A56, A57 and F17 5G lineups, with most models becoming costlier by ₹2,000. The Galaxy A57 saw the steepest hike of ₹4,000, taking the 8GB+256GB and 12GB+256GB variants to ₹66,999 and ₹76,499, respectively. Its November 15 revision also raised prices of seven Galaxy M17 5G, M17e and F70e 5G variants by ₹2,000 each. Xiaomi, meanwhile, revised prices across 19 Redmi variants. Hikes ranged from ₹1,000 to ₹4,000, with the Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G seeing the steepest increase. Its 8GB+128GB and 8GB+256GB variants now cost ₹40,999 and ₹43,999, respectively. This adds to an ongoing trend in the smartphone market where higher average selling prices have led to a weaker consumer demand. Damp demand during the recently concluded Diwali sales, one of the major occasions for such purchases in India, is evidence to that. Smartphone sales volumes dipped as much as 20% year-on-year (YoY) during the four-day festive period between November 6-9, as per data from All India Mobile Retailers Association (AIMRA). While overall sales value remained broadly in line with the previous year due to higher average selling prices, the contraction in volumes squeezed retailer margins and store profitability. AIMRA also reported that offline smartphone sales volumes fell nearly 40% in the seven days preceding Dhanteras (November 6), as consumers delayed purchases in anticipation of festive offers. Financing constraints further affected demand, with only 60-70% of logged loan applications receiving approval during the festive period. Against this backdrop, the latest price increases could add to the affordability concerns, particularly in the price-sensitive budget and mid-range segments. AI Data Centre Demand Adds To Memory Chip Supply Constraints The price revisions come amid a broader surge in memory chip prices at the behest of sharper demand from AI infrastructure and data centres. AI infra particularly relies on DRAM, which provides the high-speed memory GPUs needed to process AI workloads, and NAND flash, which enables cost-efficient storage of the massive datasets that enable AI model training. These chips are also essential components in smartphones, laptops, gaming consoles and other consumer electronics. Thus, the rise in AI development globally is now creating tightened supply chains for manufacturers and pushing up procurement costs. The impact extends across consumer electronics, with smartphone, PC and gaming console makers facing higher component costs. This was also highlighted by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who recently flagged the growing competition for memory resources during a podcast. He argued that while large amounts of DRAM in personal computers often remain underutilised and could be put to better use in cloud infrastructure. He also pointed to supply constraints in the memory market and said its usual price correction mechanism was not working effectively. Meanwhile, expanding semiconductor manufacturing capacity remains challenging, as setting up new facilities requires significant investment and time.

Bulk Crap Uninstaller (BCU) lets you uninstall multiple Windows apps at once for free. Select unwanted apps, remove them in batches, and clean up leftover files to reclaim storage. It also supports quiet uninstallation, but review your selections carefully before deleting anything.
An easy way to free up storage on your Windows PC is to remove unnecessary apps — ones you no longer need. You identify the apps and delete them one by one. It’s pretty straightforward as long as you’re dealing with a couple of apps. If the number is higher, the method starts to feel tedious.
This is where a one-click uninstaller comes in handy, allowing you to delete multiple apps at once. Bulk Crap Uninstaller (BCU) is one such app. Here’s how it works and how to use it to bulk uninstall Windows apps on your PC.
What Is Bulk Crap Uninstaller, and What Makes It Better Than Other Tools?
Bulk Crap Uninstaller (also called BCUninstaller or BCU) is a bulk uninstaller that makes uninstalling multiple apps on your Windows PC at once incredibly easy. It can scan your computer comprehensively and find everything from Windows Store apps (pre-installed by Microsoft) and third-party apps to Steam games, portable apps, and Chocolatey packages. You can then select what you want to remove. This adds them to a queue, and the app handles uninstallation for you.
Bulk Crap Uninstaller stands out from other bulk uninstallers, including some paid alternatives, in a few ways. First, it can find broken or un-uninstallable programs and force uninstall them. Second, it can scan your file system and find leftover or orphaned items (files, folders, registry keys) left behind by apps you deleted manually. That way, you can safely and easily delete them and reclaim storage space. And third, it offers a “quiet uninstallation” mode that eliminates the need to click through dialog boxes and instead uninstalls the selected apps silently in the background.
How To Use Bulk Crap Uninstaller to Bulk Uninstall Windows Apps on Your PC
Bulk Crap Uninstaller is free to download and use. Go to the Bulk Crap Uninstaller website, and you’ll see multiple ways to download the app there. You can choose any method; the easiest is to download the installer from SourceForge. Next, run the installer and follow the on-screen instructions to complete it. Once installed, the app will require configuration. Configure it per your preference; you can change the settings later if you don’t like them. I recommend enabling the Select using checkboxes and Show items in groups options.
Once configured, Bulk Crap Uninstaller will scan your computer and populate a list of all installed programs, including hidden apps, Windows Store apps, Steam games, portable apps, orphaned shortcuts, and leftover registry keys. You’ll see additional details, such as size, version, publisher name, installation date, and certificate, next to each listing. You can use filters and sort options to filter out and sort items in a specific order.
Go through the list and tick the checkbox next to the apps you want to uninstall. The status bar at the bottom will show how many items you’ve selected and how much space deleting them will free up. Finally, click the Uninstall button at the top. The app will open a dialog box showing your selection. Hit Continue while checking (and changing, if required) the settings, and click Begin Uninstallation.
You’ll see a prompt asking if you’d like to create a Restore Point. Select accordingly, and the app will uninstall the selected apps. While it deletes apps, you’ll see the uninstallation status in a dialog box. At any point, if you want to cancel the uninstallation, click the Cancel button.
Once Bulk Crap Uninstaller finishes uninstalling the selected apps, it will ask if you want to delete the leftovers too. Review the listed files carefully, uncheck the ones you don’t want to delete, and click the Delete selected button to get rid of them. Be sure to back up your registry if you’ll be deleting leftover registry keys.
When you uninstall apps this way, you’ll need to click through multiple dialog box menus to complete the uninstallation. You can save yourself this hassle by clicking the Quiet Uninstall button instead of Uninstall after selecting apps for deletion. Bulk Crap Uninstaller will try — wherever possible — to uninstall apps silently. You won’t see visual confirmation in this mode.
Other Bulk Crap Uninstaller Features You Should Know About
For most people, the standard uninstallation process we checked out above is enough to get the job done. However, Bulk Crap Uninstaller has a few advanced features that can help you get the most out of the app.
For example, Bulk Crap Uninstaller offers a CLI version called BCU-console. It’s a great option for those who want to clean up their PC without dealing with multiple windows. Similarly, it lets you run an uninstallation script with your selected apps to automate deletion. This can be useful for cleaning up new PCs, too. Just feed the app a list of all the pre-installed apps from Windows, and it will remove them. You can go through Bulk Crap Uninstaller’s documentation to learn more about using scripts.
Bulk Crap Uninstaller can also run portably. So, you can put it on a USB flash drive and run it directly. This is handy when you want to uninstall apps on a PC running very low on storage space or one that isn’t connected to the internet and can’t download the Bulk Crap Uninstaller app.
Last but not least, Bulk Crap Uninstaller is highly configurable. As such, you can configure its behavior per your preference. Click the gear icon in the top toolbar to access the app’s settings. Here, you can change things like where to look for apps, which items to show/omit, and how the list appears. You can also configure the default behavior of quiet uninstallation and how many concurrent uninstalls the app can perform, among other things.
What I’m Not a Fan Of
I’ve used Bulk Crap Uninstaller on my PC for a while, and although it does its job well, there are a few aspects that I’m not a fan of and wish were better. The biggest one is that the app’s interface can seem intimidating, especially to first-time users. In other words, it looks more like a developer tool than a regular consumer app. It’s best to spend some time exploring different menus and options the app offers before jumping straight into uninstalling apps.
Then, there’s the risk of over-cleaning. Because Bulk Crap Uninstaller can scan deep system components, too, it’s important to double-check the selection — and not blindly trust the populated list — before uninstallation. You can configure the settings to minimize the risk. Another thing I’ve noticed is that the quiet uninstallation mode sometimes doesn’t work: some apps don’t obey it and keep popping up dialog boxes that require confirmation before uninstallation. Although rare, some users have complained about aggressive registry scanning, wherein Bulk Crap Uninstaller highlights shared keys (those used by other apps too) for removal. You can avoid this by reviewing the registry keys highlighted for deletion.
These aren’t drawbacks of Bulk Crap Uninstaller, though; they’re just a trade-off for its advanced capabilities. For this reason, it’s important to configure the app before you start using it and be completely sure about the actions you perform using it. You should also create a Restore Point when dealing with apps with broken uninstallers or stubborn leftovers. This way, if the cleanup goes wrong and renders your PC unusable, you can roll back to the last working state and undo the action.

How Sen. Chris Van Hollen plans to flex Democratic power on the foreign aid front
"We need new leadership," says Senator Chris Van Hollen, who on Thursday announced he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Democratic majority leader. Van Hollen has garnered support among Democrats for his sharp criticism of the Trump administration, including their upheaval of U.S. programs to promote health and end poverty around the world.
In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, two days before his announcement, Van Hollen spoke to NPR about his plans to "shine a light on all the harm and damage the Trump administration's done to our country and our interests around the world" — and what the Democrats hope to accomplish with foreign aid.
As the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee, which oversees the State Department and what's left of the United States Agency for International Development, he could have considerable sway over how Congress investigates and legislates on foreign aid.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length. NPR reached out to the State Department for comment but did not receive a response in time for publication.
You've taken a strong stand against the Trump administration's shakeup of foreign aid. You led protests against the dissolution of USAID and in a hearing last year told Secretary of State Marco Rubio that "People died because of those actions, mothers, fathers and children." You've also authored statements condemning a range of actions, including tying health aid to mineral deals. In the majority, what's the first step you'd take on the aid front?
Priority number one is to do an analysis of all the harm the Trump administration has done.
There have been very credible analyses showing that over 700,000 people around the world died between January 2025 and January 2026 because of cuts to USAID. If these trends continue, you're talking about millions of people dying in the coming years.
One of the great benefits of being in the majority, is you actually have a gavel and can call a public hearing, and use that as a spotlight to help educate people around the country.
We can do that to show the consequences of Elon Musk taking a chainsaw to USAID. I remember to this day a scene at the White House [in February 2025] when Donald Trump was at his desk and Elon Musk was standing behind him, and a reporter asked Elon Musk about the cuts to fighting Ebola, and Elon Musk's response was essentially, "Whoops, yeah, we missed that." And then he claimed that they'd restored it. Well, we know that they've not restored it adequately — there's good evidence that the current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo could have been better contained if the United States had not made big cuts to public health.
We can investigate what they did, not for the purpose of putting it back exactly as it was but understanding the damage that has been done, fully, with an eye toward reforming it.
You've already been speaking out against a lot of this in the minority. What kinds of actions can Democrats take as a majority that they couldn't before?
Being in the majority makes a big difference. Now we have many more tools available, specifically through the power of the purse.
One of the things the Trump administration has done is essentially sit on funds appropriated by the Congress for public health here at home but also for international health programs. So there's an example where we can much better safeguard the will of the Congress now that we're in the majority.
Can you give an example?
One of the things the Administration did was to rescind over $500 million in funds for global health. In other words, they cut it, and you had a rubber stamp majority in the Congress. Republicans, go along with that. You would never get Democrats to agree.
There's another ongoing example right now, which is a number of years ago, we passed about $1.5 billion in funds for [global] public health, and it appears that they're using those funds not for public health but to wind down USAID. So this is an area where we could say no, you may not use these funds to wind down USAID.
The administration has been ignoring a lot of these "no's" so far. What gives those "no's" more weight in the majority?
When we in Congress provide a sum of money, for say public health, we say this money should be spent on these specific items, like vaccinations or clinics. That's guidance, that's direction. It's technically called report language, and this report language used to be respected by Democratic and Republican presidents.
The Trump administration has ignored report language because it's not technically legally binding, and Republicans in the Congress have let them get away with it. And the more they let them get away with it, the more they do it.
So we're going to have to convert what used to be report language into real law to prevent this administration from taking those actions. We Democrats have been trying to do that, but since we've been in the minority, we haven't been able to get that passed.
What if the administration still tries to hold up funds or ignore or veto Congress' actions?
This has been a lawless president, and he's still in the White House. But being in the majority will give us more leverage. If we're able to codify the safeguards that would prevent the Trump administration from diverting funds from their intended purpose to something else, that would be legally binding. Then you can go to the courts and say, you know this isn't simply report language. This is not just guidance. This is legally required, and so that does provide the safeguards that we would need.
Now we may have a back and forth and fight with the administration over providing those safeguards, but we're in a much stronger position now than we have been.
If the Democrats win the presidency and keep control of Congress in 2028, would the fate of USAID be revisited? Might the agency return? Or are there parts of the Trump administration's global health policy that you think are worth preserving or building on?
I don't think there's anything the Trump administration has done that's worth preserving or building on. That does not mean that I'm in favor of simply returning to the status quo prior to this administration.
I am a big believer that the role that USAID performed was both helpful to protecting the health of Americans but also helpful to developing good relations with other countries and the people of other countries. I think we need to develop our plan for how we perform this very important role as part of our foreign policy and as part of our health policy. But I'm not saying we would just go back exactly to the way USAID was.

If you’re still sporting an Apple Watch that launched five or so years ago, now is a good time to upgrade. Apple’s latest smartwatch, the 42mm Apple Watch Series 12 with Wi-Fi and GPS connectivity, has dropped to a new all-time low of $329 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, beating the October Prime Day price by $20. If you prefer a larger size, the 46mm model is on sale for $379 ($70 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, which is also $20 lower than the previous best price.
The Apple Watch Series 12 is cheaper than ever ahead of Black Friday
Apple’s latest smartwatch introduces AI-powered audio features, redesigned health sensors, and faster charging.
The Series 12 stands out compared to previous models with its new AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, which are made possible by Apple’s new S11 chip. For example, the watch can alert you when it detects sounds like a doorbell, alarm, or even a baby’s cry, while other upcoming features like Live Rewind and Siri Recap lets you look back at a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of conversation and get a high-level overview of the conversations you had that day. The new chip also makes Siri more responsive, so you can get answers to questions with less waiting around.
It’s not all about AI, though. The Series 12 also features redesigned health sensors that can now track your heart rate every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, which is particularly help if you have a chronic condition and need to keep a closer eye on your heart rate. It also introduces a new readiness score to help you decide how prepared your body is for the day. Other highlights include easier navigation with simple pinch gestures, and faster charging, which helps to make up for the fact that battery life is rated at up to 24 hours on a single charge, just like the previous-generation model. In our testing, the watch went from 20 to 64 percent charge in just 20 minutes, making it relatively easy to top up while showering or getting ready for the day.

60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages
- Published
Thomas Tuchel went with bold words when reminded about the caution that sabotaged England's World Cup hopes and left them with so much to prove against Spain in the Nations League on Sunday.
In a media theatre at the Metropolitano in Madrid, head coach Tuchel's sixth sense led him to go public with what he was convinced England would produce against the world champions.
Tuchel looked his inquisitors in the eyes and declared: "We are up for something spectacular."
To say Tuchel and England kept their word was a masterpiece of under-statement after the finest night of the head coach's reign resulted in a 3-2 victory that was large parts magnificent, some parts madness - and all parts spectacular.
It also ended Spain's 43-game unbeaten run - setting aside their penalty shootout defeat by Portugal in the 2025 Nations Cup final.
If England and Tuchel could be accused of being cowed by pressure when they led Argentina in the ill-fated World Cup semi-final, they were thrillingly positive in this unforgiving Madrid environment.
The question being asked when England held a one-goal advantage through Harry Kane's penalty at half-time was 'what would theirs and Tuchel's reaction be?' Stick or twist?
Would Tuchel tell England to press their foot on the pedal for acceleration? Or would he take the approach of going into reverse gear, as he did to ill-fated effect against Argentina?
The answer was delivered when they added goals from Arsenal duo Ezri Konsa and Ben White in the first 12 minutes of the second half.
Not a backward step was taken.
This being England, they then created a mess for themselves when Elliot Anderson was sent off for fouling Lamine Yamal in the area after 65 minutes, although the main culprit was Jarell Quansah for initially conceding possession.
Mikel Oyarzabal scored from the spot and, when Yamal set up Nico Williams for Spain's second with 15 minutes left, it looked like more than an hour of faultless England football might be wasted.
But not a bit of it, as goalkeeper James Trafford produced heroics and England defended with every fibre to close out this landmark win.
Was this the statement victory that was almost demanded of Tuchel as recompense for the World Cup disappointment, a performance to convince the doubters?
"We're fully aware what we put out there," said Tuchel afterwards. "What a performance we put out for 65 minutes to be deservedly 3-0 up.
"Of course, the red card and the penalty changed the momentum and the characteristics of the game... but we know, and the players know very, very well, what they put out there. That is the statement - and that is the significance of this victory."
England were in a different class to Spain - yes, you have read that right
Simple details of the game barely touch the sides of a night filled with quality and glorious chaos, vindication for Tuchel and England's positive approach.
Spain opened with an ostentatious parade of the World Cup in front of England's players as the teams lined up, perhaps a psychological reminder of the superiority that has seen them dominate international football.
What followed, at times literally, reduced Spain's supporters to stunned silence and their players to a shell-shocked shambles chasing the shadows that were overpowering them.
England's white shirts were everywhere but Spain could not get near them. The tormentors had become the tormented.
It was alien territory for a Spain side that has carried all before them, while England's fans tucked away high in a corner of this vast arena were equally unbelieving as a dream unfolded in front of them.
England, for 65 minutes, were in a different class to Spain. And, yes, you have read that right.
From the first whistle, employing a suffocatingly high press, England ran all over Spain.
When White crowned a superb move with the third goal four minutes after Konsa's second, it looked, remarkably, to be a case of how big England's victory margin would be.
In the end, the margin was narrow but the stature and significance of England's victory was huge.
Tuchel labelled this meeting with Spain as "proof of concept at the highest level".
There was no doubt the German manager and England were under fierce scrutiny after the manner of the collapse, mentally and tactically, against Argentina at the World Cup.
Here they delivered the proof they can match the best then beat them.
Tuchel got his big calls right
If the vital signs were being forensically examined for evidence Tuchel has learned lessons from a chastening World Cup, that England have improved after that harrowing experience, this game delivered these conclusions.
Yes. And yes.
Of course, England must do it again. Do it when the pressure and expectation in at its highest.
The Nations League is competitive but cannot be compared to a World Cup and European Championship, both titles currently in the possession of the team they beat here.
But England's world-class players delivered - Kane inevitably with his 93rd international goal, but Jude Bellingham was on a level of his own, the outstanding performer on both sides with an individual display simply confirming he is the player with everything.
And Tuchel got his big calls right, especially selecting Trafford, who responded superbly in a frantic closing phase. White, making a strong claim for the right-back berth, not only scored a goal but produced crucial challenges in the face of relentless, albeit belated, Spain pressure.
"This was the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness," said Tuchel. "It was on the highest level football wise in all aspects of the game. We did everything that needs to be done together.
"The deep build-up. The high press. The counter-attack. The tracking. The defensive phases. This was an excellent performance and of course a wonderful feeling for us in the dressing room.
"We overcame some difficult moments in the end. That's how it is. But we are very well aware which steps we took now through after the World Cup."
England's win means they top their Nations League group, but the importance spreads much wider than simply a league table.
The first 65 minutes were simply breathtaking. Spain wilting under attack after attack. Spain rattled until they shook as England refused to allow them meaningful possession.
After Anderson's dismissal, bad memories were revisited as England were forced into a rearguard action, but any other result than the one that was eventually delivered would have been a huge injustice.
England survived 29 nervous minutes, including added time, to make a powerful statement about their current status, which is much healthier than when recriminations about Tuchel's approach provided the post-World Cup narrative.
"I'm very impressed with the steps that we took after the World Cup", said Tuchel. "We wanted to get better, better in a deep build-up, get better in defending in a low block and, on top of it, we wanted always to impose our identity and the way we want to play against every opponent.
"I think this was clearly visible throughout the whole group phase. The results followed with an excellent group phase."
Was this the finest performance of Tuchel's time in charge? Most observers felt so, but the head coach was best placed to answer.
"Yes, given the circumstances," he said, "and the pressure, the quality, where we played in this building against the reigning world champions, unbeaten in 43 matches. Putting a performance out there in Madrid, and in this environment, was a very complete performance."
Tuchel will, of course, need repeat performances - but the outstanding ability and character England displayed here to beat the World Cup holders will deliver a huge injection of confidence and self-belief.

Before Clavicular and other manosphere streamers were introducing young guys to the concept of breaking their facial bones to become more attractive, there was an older generation of creators building massive followings with content focused on chemical biohacking. Were it not for steroid-obsessed influencers like Anthony “Tony Huge” Hughes launching YouTube channels over a decade ago, looksmaxxing might not have become such a prominent part of the digital media landscape in 2026. These creators became internet famous by presenting themselves as peak male specimens. But their larger-than-life online personas often concealed the truth about how sinister and toxic this kind of influencing can really be.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
Hughes is the gravitational center of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death — Hulu’s new three-part docuseries from director Stacey Lee. The series is both a deep dive into Hughes’ strange life and a fascinating exploration of how perilous the creator economy can be in the age of manosphere and looksmaxxing influencers. Through Hughes’ ever-expanding orbit of creators, Lee is able to highlight how lonely, impressionable men are all too easily radicalized by what they see and post online. And it makes clear that all these men are trapped in a deadly psychological prison of their own making.
Get Huge takes some time to touch on Hughes’ former life as a bankruptcy lawyer and supplement salesman who was investigated by the FDA for hawking unapproved performance-enhancing drugs. But most of the series takes place in Pattaya, Thailand, where Hughes spends his days producing content showcasing his extravagant life of nonstop partying and injecting substances that swell his muscles to huge proportions. Hughes takes pride in his image as a man with access to a harem of women, and the fact that his money gives him power over many of the people around him. He presents himself as the ruler of a small kingdom — and his entire brand is built on the idea that he can show people how to become more like him.
The men caught in Hughes’ aspirational fantasy aren’t just stateside fans who’ll never reach his muscle-y heights. He is also marketing himself to other established bodybuilding influencers who might be interested in joining his inner circle by following him to Thailand. These include a menagerie of biohacking / manosphere influencers who became vital parts of Hughes’ operation over the years. Leo Longevity (legal name Laith Abdallah Algaz), Elon Muscular (his legal name isn’t revealed), and Connor Murphy all built sizable social media presences of their own. But they were each compelled to move to Pattaya and join Hughes’ entourage by a powerful desire to feel connected to something larger and more fulfilling than their individual followings.
As Get Huge features clips of Hughes’ videos — the bulk of which are now only featured on Rumble and X following multiple account bans on YouTube and TikTok — you can see that he’s trying to sell his audience on his highly specific way of life. Hughes’ own videos make it seem like he’s living his dream surrounded by people who revere him. But with each interview, Get Huge makes it clear that for all of his posturing, Hughes has been living in something of a nightmare — one where many of his disciples have died under mysterious circumstances.
As these men explain why they were drawn to Hughes, you get the sense that looksmaxxing culture is a direct response to the widespread disaffection that followed the last decade of interconnected societal shifts, from the #MeToo movement to Donald Trump’s presidencies. Hughes seems very much like an entrepreneur profiting from men’s loneliness by convincing them that their lives would be better if they were part of his community. As Get Huge first maps out Hughes’ friendships, they all appear to be anchored by an odd, sometimes envious, but genuine kind of intimacy. But as the documentary digs deeper into its subjects’ lives, it becomes hard to see them as anything but emotionally stunted men who perform cartoonish masculinity for one another in ways that are psychologically unhealthy and, at times, physically dangerous.
Part of what makes Get Huge such an unsettling watch is how relatively calm and collected Hughes and the other interviewees are as they begin to discuss how many people in their circle have died in recent years. Hughes and Murphy grow closer as friends following Algaz’s death in 2023, but they seem to bond by making Algaz the butt of the joke in content produced after his death. Simply by letting these men speak frankly about their social dynamics, Get Huge reveals the manosphere as a space in which connections built on mogging and the objectification of women can quickly deteriorate into infighting and petty jealousy. Elon Muscular readily speculates that Murphy might have had something to do with Algaz’s death because Murphy openly jokes about it. And the entire situation becomes that much stranger and more grim when Get Huge reveals that Murphy drowned shortly after the series initially wrapped filming.
Though the deaths in Hughes’ circle bring a dark whodunit energy to Get Huge, the documentary emphasizes how much peril comes as a part of existing in the looksmaxxing space. Rather than trying to solve the mystery of how Algaz died, the docuseries presents his story as a cautionary tale. He’s an object lesson in how this lifestyle can warp a person’s perception of reality in a way that ultimately cuts them off from the kind of help they really need.
What might be most disturbing about Get Huge is the way it ends. The series follows Hughes to a youth bodybuilding event where he talks up his less-than-legal products to a new group of boys — some as young as 13. To keep his momentum going, Hughes has to appeal to a new, younger audience that doesn’t understand how everything about looksmaxxing is a performance. Though the docuseries gives you the distinct impression that people like Murphy and Algaz felt a true belonging with Hughes, its closing shots call into question how genuine any of his connections with other bodybuilders really are. By juxtaposing the deaths of Hughes’ adult acolytes with his focus on turning children into fans, Get Huge paints a clear picture of how the manosphere’s promise of emotional connection often ends in a twisted kind of exploitation. And that extractive energy feels foundational to a culture that runs on people turning every aspect of their lives into content.
All three episodes of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death are now streaming on Hulu and Disney Plus.

Britain's Prince William and Princess Catherine arrive in India for 3-day visit
Prince William and Princess Catherine have arrived in India for a three-day visit
MUMBAI, India -- MUMBAI, India (AP) — Prince William and Princess Catherine arrived in India on Monday for a three-day visit, the first overseas trip together since she was diagnosed with cancer in 2024.
The U.K. royal couple began their visit in Mumbai and will attend the Earthshot Prize awards ceremony on Tuesday. Founded by William, the annual environmental prize awards five winners $1.3 million each to expand solutions addressing climate change.
The ceremony, expected to be the biggest since the prize was established in 2020, will feature several prominent guests including Indian cricket great Sachin Tendulkar, actors Alia Bhatt and Rami Malek and British pop group Take That, which will make its debut performance in India.
“India has made an extraordinary contribution to Earthshot over the past six years and is home to more Earthshot finalists and winners than any other country,” William posted on social media.
Shortly after their arrival, the royal couple took part in a game of street cricket in an alley in Ballard Estate, a neighborhood in Mumbai. Street cricket, a common sight across the city, is an integral part of everyday life in Mumbai.
The couple also will attend events highlighting India’s cricket, fashion and film industries before traveling to New Delhi, where they were scheduled to meet with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.
The couple met with Modi on their previous trip to India a decade ago before William, the eldest son of King Charles III, became the heir to the U.K. throne.
The trip marks a significant return to overseas royal engagements for the Princess of Wales, commonly known as Kate, who announced in March 2024 that she was undergoing treatment for cancer following major abdominal surgery. Kate disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission and has gradually resumed her public duties.
She traveled to Italy without William in May, marking her first overseas engagement since her diagnosis.

While Indian employees enjoy several leave entitlements, many struggle to avail themselves of them. An employee has taken to Reddit to express frustration over constantly having to follow up with his manager for leave, only to have his requests denied. The employee, whose username remains anonymous, shared on r/IndianWorkplace that he had applied for leave on Dhanteras, but his manager denied the request. When the employee pointed out that he had a substantial number of pending leaves, his boss said there was a lot of work pending and that they could not grant him leave at that time. "When I insisted, she got annoyed. And when I said I would use my privilege leave (PL), she said I couldn't use my PL. But why? Can't I? "And now she's angry about how I can even ask for leave. And FYI, I haven't used any PL yet. In the last week of October, I asked for four days' leave, and she emotionally said, 'Yaar, itna kaam hai, abhi mat lo leave. Kaise hoga kaam?' So I didn't take leave at that time, and now this," the employee shared. The employee stated that he had been completing all his work efficiently and had also been handling projects that were not mentioned in his job description. However, his leave request was still not considered. "And since joining, I've been doing work that isn't even mentioned in my offer letter. I did all that thinking that the company was at its starting stage, but now I think I was a fool," he wrote. He further shared that the company was making profits, but his salary had not increased despite him handling all the clients. "And for the past few months, the company's revenue has been growing. I am visiting clients and attending meetings, but my salary hasn't increased, nor has my workload decreased. I am handling tasks from all departments alone," he said. The post quickly went viral, evoking a range of reactions from Reddit users. Here are some of the comments: One user wrote: "So, I take it that you do a lot of work — basically, you're someone whose replacement would take some effort to find. If this is true, just take the leave anyway. Your boss isn't going to risk losing you just because you took a few days of well-deserved break." Another user said: "Complain to HR. You are entitled to leave." A third user commented: "Since you have been doing more work than your assigned responsibilities, they are taking you for granted. It's better to do only the work that was originally mentioned in your job description. If your boss says anything, just submit your resignation. "He will immediately grant you leave. Also, demand a salary hike or threaten to leave in the middle of a project." (Disclaimer: This report is based on user-generated content from social media. The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) has warned of penal action against those failing to comply with the revised prices of 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs
The authority, which functions under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, has asked State drug controllers (SDCs) to strictly monitor the prices and submit their action taken reports by November 16, according to an official release on Friday (November 13, 2026).
The revised prices for the 137 anti-cancer drugs came into effect on November 9, 2026, following a gazette order issued on October 17, 2026. The order capped the trade margin on these medicines at 30%.
Based on submissions received from pharmaceutical companies up to November 11, the latest revised price lists have been uploaded on the NPPA website as well as the Pharma Sahi Daam app and portal, the Chemicals and Fertilizers Ministry said.
All manufacturers, stockists, dealers, retailers, hospitals, and medical institutions have been directed to comply with the revised prices and prominently display the updated price lists at their premises and on their websites.
The SDCs have been instructed to strictly monitor compliance across the supply chain and healthcare facilities to ensure that the benefits of the revised maximum retail prices (MRPs) are passed on to patients.
Any violation of the directive may attract overcharging proceedings under the provisions of the DPCO, 2013, the release noted.
Complaints regarding overcharging, shortage, or non-availability of medicines can be reported through the Pharma Sahi Daam app or portal, the NPPA helpline (1800-111-255), or via email at monitoring-nppa@gov.in, it added.

Ukraine’s Starshield Access Is Being Restricted Again, Zelensky Says
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the system, which Ukraine uses to guide drones, was being throttled over Russian-occupied territory. SpaceX, its developer, has denied the claim.
Ukrainian military operations were disrupted again this week along the front lines because of restrictions on Starshield, the satellite internet system developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and controlled by the U.S. government, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday.
Mr. Zelensky told reporters that speed limits of about 100 miles per hour were being enforced for Ukrainian devices connected to the system. It would be the second time in recent weeks that Ukraine’s Starshield connectivity had been throttled. The previous restrictions caused Ukrainian drones to lose their connection to the system if they flew above certain speeds.
Mr. Zelensky said that the latest speed limits took effect on Monday and were being enforced over Russian-occupied territories, not over all of Ukraine. That hurts Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian troops with drones in those territories.
Imposing restrictions on occupied territories is “very dangerous, because it already has political implications,” Mr. Zelensky said. “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” he added.
Mr. Zelensky said separately in his nightly speech that the Starshield limits hurt Ukraine’s ability to use newly developed interceptors to protect its cities from Russia’s jet-powered drones. It is likely, however, that those limits would not affect interceptors in Kyiv, the capital, which is being battered by jet-powered drones but is far from the front lines.
Mr. Musk and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment on Friday evening. SpaceX had earlier told Axios that the Ukrainian claim about throttled connectivity was false.

Cape Verde’s president is reelected for a second 5-year term, provisional results show
Cape Verde’s president, José Maria Neves, has been reelected for a second term, defeating five challengers, including the country’s first female presidential candidate
PRAIA, Cape Verde -- PRAIA, Cape Verde (AP) — Cape Verde ’s president, José Maria Neves, has been reelected for a second five-year term, beating five challengers, including the first woman presidential candidate in the country’s history, provisional results show.
Neves called his reelection as president of the Atlantic island nation off West Africa “a great victory.” The election was dominated by high unemployment and the high cost of living, which has fueled emigration.
Provisional results showed Neves comfortably edged out his opponents, garnering 64% of the vote while Joana Rosa, the main opposition candidate, won 31.4%.
Rosa called Neves to concede defeat.
The small country has a history of smooth transfers of power and is one of the most stable in a region fraught with tense elections.
“The president of the republic does not have a majority; the president of the republic belongs to everyone,” Neves said in his victory speech.
Turnout was low, with only 31.7% of the 418,000 registered voters casting a ballot.
Neves said the low turnout could be explained by high emigration, population movements within the country and outdated voter records. He promised a study to examine the issue.
Under Cape Verde’s parliamentary system, the prime minister directs policy and holds most executive power. The directly elected president’s role is largely ceremonial, although the president can veto legislation.

U.N. Starts Uncertain Effort to Regulate Lethal Autonomous Weapons
Delegates met in Geneva to discuss guardrails for such systems even as their development grows. Russia and the United States have resisted the efforts.
Global efforts to limit the use of lethal autonomous weapons reached a crossroads this week as countries gathered to decide whether to negotiate binding restrictions on the technology, despite strong resistance from the United States and Russia.
Delegates of 128 states met at the United Nations in Geneva on Monday for a weeklong conference to determine whether to draft a treaty that would ban lethal autonomous weapons and require meaningful human control of such systems.
“The longer the international community waits, the more difficult it will become to establish meaningful safeguards — and it may be too late,” Volker Türk, the U.N. human rights chief, said before the conference.
Artificial intelligence and its military uses are developing at breakneck speed, as seen on the battlefields of Ukraine and the Middle East. That has deepened international alarm and prompted calls for action by many countries, global leaders and activist groups, even as top military powers balk at attempts to curb their ability to develop new weapons.
“Decisions affecting human life, freedom and the use of force must always remain subject to effective, informed and responsible human oversight,” Pope Leo XIV said in a statement last month that urged those at the Geneva conference to take “concrete “steps” to ban lethal autonomous weapons. Artificial intelligence, he said, “must be ‘disarmed.’”
Russia and Ukraine have already deployed fully autonomous drones to carry out attacks. Disarmament experts fear that the low cost and easy availability of such technology could lead to its rapid spread to law enforcement, nonstate armed groups and organized crime.

Leo XIV returned to the city in Peru where he served as bishop for eight years, drawing large crowds who remembered him before he was pope.
It was hard to believe that anyone who lived in Chiclayo, Peru, was not lining its streets on Friday.

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

State-owned Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) has secured government approvals to commercially supply sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from its Panipat refinery in north India, with the facility capable of producing enough fuel to meet the country's 1 per cent blending target for international flights in 2027, Chairman A.S. Sahney said on Tuesday (November 17, 2026).
The State-run refiner plans to enter into supply agreements with airlines before committing investments to additional SAF projects, Mr. Sahney said at an industry event, signalling a demand-led approach to expanding production capacity as India prepares to introduce low-carbon fuel requirements for international aviation.
IOC's Panipat facility is positioned to meet the initial blending mandate, Mr. Sahney said, although he did not specify the volume of fuel covered by the government approvals or when commercial supplies would begin.
In August, an IOC executive had said the company expected to begin operations at its first SAF plant at Panipat within two months and was looking to take an investment decision on a second facility within five to six months.
The refinery, which has a crude processing capacity of about 301,000 barrels per day, received India's first International Sustainability and Carbon Certification (ISCC) CORSIA certification for SAF production in 2025, enabling it to produce fuel meeting internationally-recognised sustainability requirements for aviation.
IOC has planned to produce about 35,000 tonnes of SAF annually from used cooking oil at the facility, sourcing feedstock from large hotel and restaurant chains. The company has also signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Air India for SAF supplies, although the agreement did not specify a commencement date or volumes.
The Panipat project forms part of India's broader effort to introduce sustainable fuels into aviation, a sector seeking to reduce its carbon footprint while accommodating growing air travel demand.
India is targeting a 1 per cent SAF blending requirement in fuel supplied for international flights from 2027, rising to 2 per cent in 2028. The targets are aligned with the global push to reduce aviation emissions under the International Civil Aviation Organization's Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA).
SAF can be produced from non-petroleum feedstocks such as used cooking oil and agricultural waste and can be blended with conventional jet fuel. It offers airlines a way to lower lifecycle carbon emissions without requiring wholesale changes to existing aircraft or airport fuelling infrastructure.
IOC is also developing a separate SAF production facility using alcohol-to-jet (ATJ) technology, with planned annual capacity of 86,800 tonnes. The project, being developed with US-based LanzaJet, will use ethanol as feedstock and is targeted for completion by March 2028.
The expansion would diversify IOC's SAF production beyond used cooking oil and add capacity as blending requirements increase. However, the availability and cost of sustainable feedstocks, alongside long-term purchase commitments from airlines, will be important factors in determining the pace of investment and commercial adoption.
IOC's Panipat refinery is also undergoing an expansion to increase its conventional oil-product processing capacity by 200,000 barrels per day by 2027.
