Quick Answer
Concat is a free, open-source CapCut alternative with offline AI captions, voice cloning, background removal, 100+ effects, and 4K exports. It runs locally, needs no account, and adds no watermarks. Available across major platforms, it’s promising but still in beta, with some rough edges.
When you think of video editing, CapCut is a popular name that would pop up. It has made short-form editing painless. However, it has now started to put more of its tools behind a paywall, and a few of them need an internet connection to work.
If you are looking for a way out, you have probably already seen OpenReel, the browser-based open-source editor, or gone through our list of the best free video editing software. This time we have something different. Concat takes a different route. It is a free, open-source editor that runs on your own computer and is loaded with features like captions, voiceovers, and background removal built in.
Table of Contents
What is Concat?
Concat is a video editor that is currently in beta. The idea behind its development is easy to understand: It wants to give people stuff that CapCut offers but for free, like auto-captions, text-to-speech, background removal, keyframes, effects, titles, and 4K export. Everything Concat has on offer comes without strings attached. You don’t need to sign up, no watermark stamped on your exports, and no premium tier waiting around the corner.
The other big difference is where the work happens. Concat does everything locally, on your machine. It is built on a native Rust engine with a GPU compositor, and the AI models it uses (for captions, voices, and cutouts) are downloaded once from the settings and then run offline. This means the raw footage that you upload never gets uploaded anywhere.
CapCut is still a great editor, and nobody is pretending otherwise. When we compared it with Instagram Edits, we pointed out that CapCut has the richer feature set, but also that some of its tools need a connection and that its template and music ecosystem is tied closely to TikTok, which owns it. And if you are in India, you already know CapCut is banned here. So, you have to download the modded version or depend on some ad-filled alternatives.
That is the gap Concat is trying to fill. Not a “lite” version of a big editor, but a free one that keeps the stuff you reach for every day and keeps it on your own PC.
Concat features that matter
The feature list is long. But here are the parts that stand out.
Auto-captions that work offline
Captions are quite important nowadays, as content is reaching every part of the globe. But it is a chore every Reels and Shorts editor knows too well. Concat handles them using Whisper, a speech-recognition model that runs locally. You pick a model size (you can choose larger models, which are more accurate but require a stronger machine), and styled captions appear straight on your timeline. No upload, no waiting on a server, and it keeps working without internet.
Text-to-speech and voice cloning
Concat gives you free voices for narration, which is handy for tutorials or faceless channels. You can also clone a voice from just a few seconds of recording. That’s nice to edit a flubbed line without re-recording a whole take.
Background removal
You might have removed people or objects from your images. For videos, most of the editors ask you to pay. But Concat lets you edit out people or objects from a clip for free. If the automatic cutout misses a spot, you can paint the mask manually.
Keyframes with a curve editor
With keyframes, you can animate almost anything over time: position, scale, rotation, opacity, volume, and the settings of effects. There is a built-in curve editor too. You can use this to make a zoom feel smooth instead of mechanical, something that a paid video editor offers.
100 effects, filters and transitions
Concat comes with about 100 effects, filters, and transitions. They are rendered by your GPU and show up live in the preview. This way you can see what you are doing instead of waiting for an export to find out.
Fast cutting and a proper timeline
You get everything like split, trim, ripple delete, merge, freeze frame, and speed changes. If you like clips snapping together without gaps, you can switch on a magnetic timeline. Additionally, you can stack as many tracks as you want for overlays and picture-in-picture, keep several timelines inside a single project, and use blend modes like screen, add, and multiply. Crop and flip tools are there as well.
Titles with real styling
You can change fonts, add strokes and shadows, and drop in a background plate behind the words. If you don’t have any ideas, you can start from the already available presets.
One-switch audio cleanup
If your video has bad audio because of a faulty microphone or nearby noise, it can spoil a good video more than bad lighting does. Concat has a simple toggle for noise reduction, voice enhancement, and loudness leveling. You can also change voice effects to chipmunk, robot, and telephone.
Export and performance
Now, the best part is that with Concat, there is no limitation on export. It supports H.264, HEVC, and AV1, up to 4K at 60 frames per second with 10-bit colour.
Which platforms does Concat support?
Concat is versatile and supports multiple operating systems:
- Windows
- macOS
- Linux
- Android
- iPhone and iPad
Moreover, the editor is available in 26 languages. Downloading and setting up Concat is simple. Here’s what you need to do:
- Open the official download page, which picks the right build for your device. You can also grab any version from the GitHub Releases page.
- Install it like any other app on your device.
- On Windows, your system may warn you because the builds are not code-signed yet. Click More info, then Run anyway.
- On macOS, if the system refuses to open the app, the project suggests running xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Concat.app in Terminal.
- Open Settings and download the AI models you want (captions, voices, cutout). After that, they work offline.
Concat vs CapCut
| Feature | Concat | CapCut | 
|---|---|---|
| Price | Free, no subscription | Freemium | 
| Who is behind it | Open-source project (AGPL-3.0) | ByteDance | 
| Internet needed | Only to download AI models once | Some tools need a connection | 
| Templates and music | Limited | Large library tied to TikTok | 
A few things to keep in mind
Concat is promising and has all the features you would need from a video editor that is trying to be an alternative to CapCut. But don’t forget that it is young, and there are a few caveats that you should know about.
- It is a beta. The repo had over 200 open issues at the time of writing this article. So, you may come across some rough edges. We would advise you not to trust it with a client deadline until you have tested it on your own projects.
- Unsigned Windows builds and the macOS quarantine step can feel sketchy to newcomers. But it is safe, even though they are expected for now.
- You do not get a stock library to lean on. You will need your own assets.
- iPhone users have extra work because you have to sideload it, and sideloading is not for everyone.
Once you have the clarity, you should give Concat a try and let its output help you decide if you should keep using it or not. Let us know in the comments below which editor you are currently using.

Ramoji Rao had qualities to advise country on complex issues, says Amit Shah
Shah said he was particularly impressed by Ramoji Rao’s comprehensive understanding of the state despite not being directly associated with its political
Union home minister Amit Shah on Sunday described late media baron Ch Ramoji Rao as an intellectual with all the qualities of a national advisor, as he could offer insights into even the most complex issues confronting the country.
Addressing the Ramoji Excellence Awards Ceremony 2026 organised in Vijayawada, the home minister said Ramoji Rao had extraordinary understanding of national and international issues and his ability to suggest clear and sustainable solutions to the country’s problems.
“I met Ramoji Rao on four occasions. Every time I met him, I was amazed by his extraordinary knowledge of almost every subject in the world. He would not merely suggest solutions to problems but also ensure that his ideas had clarity and stability. He firmly stood by what he believed in,” Shah said.
Recalling a discussion about Uttar Pradesh, Shah said he was particularly impressed by Ramoji Rao’s comprehensive understanding of the state despite not being directly associated with its political and administrative affairs.
“I had travelled to every remote corner of Uttar Pradesh. Yet, I was surprised to see how a person whose mother tongue was Telugu could speak so comprehensively about the state’s affairs. He could easily predict the possible political developments in Uttar Pradesh during elections,” he said.
Shah said Ramoji Rao had an in-depth understanding of several complex national issues, including the abrogation of Article 370 and the roots of separatist movements in the northeastern states.
“At that time, I felt that if the country needed an adviser capable of identifying solutions to its numerous problems, Ramoji Rao was the person who could fit that role,” he said.
Reflecting on Ramoji Rao’s 90-year journey, Shah said his achievements should be viewed in the context of the hardships he overcame and his contribution to the overall development of the country.
Born in a remote village in Krishna district, Ramoji Rao had neither inherited wealth nor privileged opportunities. He did not even possess a degree in journalism, but had extraordinary vision and an immense willingness to work hard, Shah said.
Through determination and relentless efforts, he worked towards bringing the truth to Telugu people every morning, he added.
“He experimented with several innovations in journalism. He launched a 24-hour regional-language news channel and subsequently inspired the launch of news channels in other regional languages, enhancing their stature across the country,” Shah said.
Referring to the Padma Vibhushan conferred on Ramoji Rao, Shah recalled that a Gujarati newspaper had described the honour as recognition of Telugu pride and the entire journalistic fraternity. He said Ramoji Rao built an institution founded on strong values and ensured that it would continue to serve society.
Ramoji Rao also made significant contributions to the film industry, Shah said, recalling a conversation with a Gujarati film producer who told him that a film could be made at Ramoji Film City if one had the money, a story and artistes.
Andhra Pradesh chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu and deputy chief minister Pawan Kalyan also recalled the contribution of Ramoji Rao to the field of journalism and his philanthropic activities.

People with diabetes could be at a 53% higher risk of Alzheimer's disease, compared to those living without the metabolic disorder, a review of studies has found.
Researchers, led by those from Australia's Curtin University, conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies. They found that if 1,000 people living with type 2 diabetes were followed for a year, an estimaated average of 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder in which memory and thought processes steadily decline with age.
Cognitive risk prevention should be integrated into diabetes care, they said.
"Individuals with T2D (type 2 diabetes) experienced approximately five AD (Alzheimer's disease) cases per 1,000 person-years and a 53 per cent higher risk of AD, supporting the rationale for integrating cognitive risk prevention into diabetes care," the authors wrote in the study published in the journal Alzheimer's Research and Therapy.
Study author Emmanuel Adewuyi, an investigator fellow at Curtin University's school of population health, said the review was important as it quantifies the relative risk and incidence of Alzheimer's in people living with type 2 diabetes.
"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred," Adewuyi said.
"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes," the author said.
Databases including MEDLINE, CINAHL and Embase were searched from for publications since inception until April 2026. Forty studies, involving 27,102,559 data points, and looking at the incidence of Alzheimer's disease among people with diabetes or link between the two disorders were analysed.

Pope Leo XIV has demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging and illegal mining.
On the penultimate day of his South American tour, Leo on Sunday travelled into the Peruvian Amazon and channelled one of Pope Francis’s core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.
“The cry of the Earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered along the Ucayali River in the north-eastern city of Pucallpa.
He said he came to Pucallpa to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to what environmental groups estimate have been 57 murders of environmental defenders between 2010 and 2024.
“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice,” Leo said to applause from the crowd, many of whom were wearing traditional feathered headwear and face markings of the region.
In addition to deforestation, illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Illegal mining and coca production has also driven deforestation.
Leo addressed the combination of threats in one of his most forceful speeches to date, drawing on his years of experience as a Peruvian bishop and Francis’s constant preaching about the environment and the plight of Indigenous groups.
During the encounter and a subsequent mass in Pucallpa, he demanded a different model of economic development that respects the Earth and the Indigenous peoples who care for it, rather than the “irresponsible exploitation” by outside actors.
“Very little has been done – and very slowly at that – while the means to exploit and pollute creation have accelerated,” he said at mass. “In the face of these evils, let us not bury the Lord’s gifts, for he gives us the strength to repair and heal the suffering caused by an insatiable thirst for domination.”
In Peru, most murders of environmental defenders go unpunished; only a few have resulted in convictions.
The most recent conviction came in the case of Kichwa leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado, who was murdered in 2023 when he was ambushed by hitmen on a river in the San Martín region, the Amazonian territory he was defending.
Leo also referred to a notorious rise in sexual violence against Indigenous Awajún and Wampis schoolgirls in the northern Amazon, and blasted the “impunity” and “corruption” surrounding them.
The Awajún and Wampis Women’s Council has recorded 370 cases of sexual violence in the Condorcanqui province between January and July.
Julio Cusurichi, an Indigenous leader, handed Leo a letter during his visit to Pucallpa, asking him to help protect the rights of uncontacted Indigenous relatives.
“The Peruvian state is weakening the mechanisms that should safeguard their territories,” said the letter from the Indigenous rights organisation Aidesep, on which Cusurichi is a board member.
“We cannot allow economic interests to take precedence over the lives and rights of these vulnerable peoples. Therefore, we ask Pope Leo XIV to raise his voice and support this urgent call for their defence.”
Cardinal Pedro Barreto praised the pope’s decision to meet with Indigenous peoples. Barreto, a former Peruvian archbishop who helped win a multimillion-dollar pollution payout for an Andean town, said: “[Leo] is well aware of all the historical suffering … corruption, illegal mining, deforestation, and the contempt shown by politicians.”
Luis E Fernandez, co-founder of Cincia, a scientific research centre in Peru, also hailed the pontiff’s power to raise awareness. “Pope Leo’s recognition of pollution from illegal mining brings much-needed attention to a crisis affecting Indigenous and riverine communities across the Amazon,” he said.
Fernandez visited the Vatican in October and presented Leo with scientific evidence detailing the impact of illegal gold mining and associated mercury poisoning.
Leo’s last full day in Peru was also his most ambitious, crisscrossing the nation to minister to communities high in the Andes mountains. Peru’s air force released footage of the pope inside a helicopter and said it was “an unforgettable memory” to take Leo around the country.
His first stop was the mountain city of Cusco, where huge crowds greeted him.
“It is all worth it,” said Margarida Salomon, 63, who said she came from Sucre in Bolivia to see the pontiff, spending about $500 to take a bus and sleep in a tent. “I am still getting to know this pope, but the fact he is here in the Andes means a lot.”
The visit to Cusco, 3,400m (more than 11,000ft) above sea level, tested Leo’s stamina as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery last month. Leo sat in the chair of his popemobile during part of the ride around Cusco, but it wasn’t clear if that was to preserve his energy or to steady himself on the uneven streets.
In general, the 71-year-old Leo has seemed unfazed by the toll of the three-nation South American trip, the longest of his pontificate.

With so much going on all the time, you may not have thought about ransomware and data extortion attacks in a minute, even though they’ve been among the the biggest cybersecurity threats to institutions—and, by extension, people—over the past decade. But in the new era of AI-powered and automated cyberattacks, the danger posed by ransomware is only increasing as cybercriminals profit by combining established methods with new techniques made possible or more accessible by AI.
It is difficult to determine exact numbers of ransomware attacks, given that victims don’t always disclose incidents and attackers wildly inflate their claims. But researchers who specialize in tracking and attempting to de-duplicate the field agree that claimed incidents have spiked over the last few months. Some put the number of alleged ransomware attacks on leak sites—where groups post alleged victims—at nearly 3,000 attacks over the summer. This would mean a 20 to 40 percent increase since the spring by some estimates. And, crucially, researchers emphasize that while volume always fluctuates somewhat, ransomware attacks overall have been consistently and concerningly elevated in recent years.
“What we see is most of the recent increase was fueled by international attacks; the United States was a little more steady, but still high, still a lot of attacks,” says Cynthia Kaiser, former FBI cyber deputy director who now leads research for the anti-ransomware platform Halcyon. “Internationally we’re seeing a lot more attacks. That to me is the really new part, and I do think it is in part fueled by AI.”
Fully AI-powered ransomware attacks have yet to emerge, perhaps because the criminal business model already works so effectively. But cybercriminals do appear to be using LLMs for some of the more mundane aspects of their attacks.
“We are seeing AI relied on more heavily in certain aspects of the ransomware attack chain, such as creating better phishing emails and in the negotiation process, but the ‘successful’ ransomware groups are still largely human operated,” says Allan Liska, a longtime ransomware researcher and threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future. “But the fact that these groups are experimenting heavily with AI means that this could change going forward, and change quickly.”
Kaiser notes that broader trends in scamming are always relevant to ransomware, because attackers often use the same types of phishing and social engineering techniques to gain initial access to targeted systems. In Japan, for example, successful scamming has spiked drastically in recent months as AI enables foreign attackers to generate consistently convincing content in Japanese for the first time.
A few ransomware groups—namely, the Gentlemen, Qilin, and Akira—have emerged as some of the most prominent and stable operations in recent months. However, in their shadow is a range of smaller groups, emerging actors, and fragmentation of the ransomware ecosystem. In recent weeks, multiple new ransomware groups have appeared and quickly claimed to have attacked dozens of businesses. Halycon’s analysis says around 111 ransomware groups made claims of attacks between July and September this year.
One new group calling itself Global Secret Group claimed attacks on 48 victims, with more than half of these being listed on the same day, according to security firm ReliaQuest’s analysis. Another, called Storm, listed 71 victims in just 20 days. Not all of the attacks may be legitimate, but they still cause uncertainty for businesses.
“That growth has all happened because, in my eyes, this acceleration that AI has provided to these threat actors, essentially allowing for them to go out and start their own groups,” says Brandon Tirado, the director of threat research at ReliaQuest.
Instead of being beholden to traditional “ransomware-as-a-service” providers, all of the researchers Kernel Panic spoke to say they have seen more lone-wolf operators branching out. Tirado says his team recently managed to identify who is behind one new group and found that it is being run by an inexperienced teenager who has made more than $800,000 in under two weeks. He declined to name the teen publicly.
Halcyon’s Kaiser agrees that more actors are using AI to attempt to strike out on their own with expanded capabilities to trick targets, exploit vulnerabilities, check their code, and even compromise other groups’ remote-access tools to gain redundant access to a victim in case one avenue gets blocked. But she adds that it’s still not clear how successful these upstarts will be long-term. She suspects that many of them may surge initially and then burn out, because they don’t have the institutional knowledge and expanded resources of an established group.
While established attackers typically conduct “double extortion” attacks in which they deploy traditional ransomware that encrypts a victim’s systems while also exfiltrating a target’s data and then threatening to publish it online, those operating independently may be more likely to focus solely on data extortion to simplify their operations.
“The number of attacks that Recorded Future has seen this year already dwarfs the total number for 2025,” Liska says, “but the number of attacks involving encryption may actually decrease year over year.”

Real Madrid's Vinícius Jr sends surprise message to boy who lost his legs in Sudan's war
- Published
In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.
The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.
Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.
We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.
More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.
Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.
More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.
The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.
For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.
When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was Vinícius Júnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.
"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.
Vinícius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."
Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."
Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new Vinícius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.
"Tell Vinícius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".
Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.
Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.
Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck.
"I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.
She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."
Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.
Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection.
"I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time.
There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.
Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising £45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.
Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.
After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.
For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.
- 'I can't afford to save both twins': Sudan's war left one mother with an impossible choice 
  - Published16 October 2025
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through.
"He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."
His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.
As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.
He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.
For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.
The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.
Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine".
"I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.
Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.
Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.

Buying a used phone? Make sure to check the IMEI first
A phone's IMEI number can reveal whether the device has sketchy history, what networks it can connect to and more.
Smartphones are no exception to soaring tech prices and the pre-owned market has become a necessary respite for many. However, whenever you're buying a refurbished or generally pre-owned phone, you need to take a few precautions. In particular, you need to look out for the red flags of a potential scam and every mobile device has a special number that can help you.
Buying a pre-owned phone from eBay, Facebook Marketplace or a physical repair shop requires a good deal of prep work. You should properly clean and sanitize the secondhand phones you find while also making sure the phone you're getting doesn't have any obvious defects. When you're asking the seller about the device's condition and history, you should also ask about the phone's IMEI number — which can reveal whether a phone has sketchy history, what networks it can connect to, and more.
What IMEI numbers are for and how to find them
Every mobile device has a unique 15-digit number associated with it known as an International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) number. This number is used to register your phone with your network provider and can subsequently be used by that provider to identify your phone. If your phone is lost or stolen, you can contact your provider and have them blacklist your phone via that IMEI number.
If you want to find your phone's IMEI number, it can typically be found in the device's packaging or on any physical or digital receipts, as well as on your network provider account. Additionally, while you can generally find your IMEI number in your phone's settings, dialing *#06# into the keypad of any phone will reveal its unique IMEI code. You can also contact your provider's support team about finding this number if all else fails.
Why you should ask sellers for a phone's IMEI number
If you're in the position of buying a new phone, the device's seller should provide its IMEI code to you upon request — and you should definitely ask for this code. The IMEI number will help you confirm whether it's been stolen or whether it's compatible with certain cellular networks.
There are all too many scams to avoid when buying refurbished tech online and in person, so be on the lookout for sellers that refuse to provide the IMEI number as they may be selling fenced goods. An IMEI number can't be used to hack or track phones by itself but sellers should only share it with serious buyers through private messaging and buyers should keep screenshots of the conversation just in case.
Upon being provided with an IMEI number, you should proceed with checking its validity and whether it's been reported stolen or lost. There's quite the smorgasbord of sites to use if you want to check an IMEI number, many of which will ask for a small fee before checking the number. While many of the options are free, research whichever site you use first to make sure you're not about to fall for a phishing scam.

Intel is being sued by shareholders, who are accusing the chipmaker of misleading them about the impact of the PC sales slump that contributed to a drop of 28.6 percent in the price of Intel’s stock on October 30.

Delhi is looking to bring neighbouring states into a coordinated fight against air pollution, shifting from city-centric measures to a regional approach targeting emissions across administrative boundaries.
The Delhi government is in discussions with the World Bank to adopt an airshed-based approach, recognizing that much of the pollution choking the capital originates in neighbouring regions and cannot be tackled through measures within the city alone, according to three people aware of the development.
The discussions could pave the way for coordinated pollution-control measures across Delhi and neighbouring states, targeting specific emission sources rather than relying on fragmented interventions.
The need for such an approach is underscored by another severe pollution episode in the capital. On Diwali, 8 November, Delhi's 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) stood at 376, in the 'very poor' category, according to the Central Pollution Control Board. An AQI reading of 0-50 is classified as 'good'.
An airshed is a geographical region where pollutants circulate across administrative boundaries. Managing pollution at this level requires states and districts sharing the same air basin to coordinate action across transport, industry, agriculture and other emission sources.
The rationale, according to a person familiar with the discussions, is that pollution cannot be effectively controlled when responsibility for its sources is fragmented across central, state, district and municipal administrations. An airshed-based approach could offer an alternative to Delhi's reliance on emergency restrictions, which curb economic activity but have struggled to deliver sustained improvements in air quality.
Queries emailed to the World Bank and the Delhi government remained unanswered until press time.
Beyond Delhi’s borders
The scale of the challenge is evident from a World Bank presentation. According to its April 2024 presentation titled Improving Air Quality in East Asia and the Pacific, Delhi has direct control over less than a quarter of the pollution concentrations it experiences.
Restrictions on vehicles, construction and industrial activity within the capital may therefore have limited impact without parallel action in neighbouring regions.
“A city may regulate construction dust and traffic emissions, yet continue to experience high particulate concentrations from nearby industrial clusters, brick kilns, agricultural burning or regional transport,” said Aparna Roy, fellow and lead, Climate Change and Energy, at the Observer Research Foundation. Similarly, state-wide measures may establish common standards without accounting for differences in emission sources and enforcement capabilities across districts, she added.
“Delhi, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh are all part of the same airshed. If you intervene in only one geographical area, you may not achieve the full potential impact,” said Santosh Singh, managing director of Intellecap, the advisory arm of the Aavishkaar Group.
Singh illustrated the potential benefits with a hypothetical example: if Haryana contributed 30% of Delhi’s pollution during peak months, reducing emissions in Haryana could significantly improve Delhi’s air quality.
From city curbs to regional action
Delhi's discussions with the World Bank follow similar initiatives in Uttar Pradesh and Haryana, where the multilateral lender has approved nearly $600 million for clean-air programmes covering a combined population of approximately 270 million.
Uttar Pradesh plans to deploy 15,000 electric three-wheelers and 500 electric buses, while Haryana intends to help approximately 2,000 micro, small and medium enterprises adopt cleaner technologies, alongside measures to reduce crop-residue burning.
The initiatives point to a shift in India's clean-air strategy, from treating pollution as a municipal problem to recognizing its regional dimensions. Delhi's participation could strengthen this approach, but success will depend on translating state-level commitments into measurable emission reductions on the ground.
The economic cost
Delhi's recurring pollution episodes exact a heavy toll on both public health and economic activity.
Dr Vijay Hadda, a professor in the Department of Pulmonary Medicine and Sleep Disorders at AIIMS Delhi, described the city's toxic post-Diwali air in stark terms. “I am honestly surprised that we are still alive,” he told ANI.
The latest pollution episode brought another familiar round of restrictions. Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav announced a ban on construction and demolition activities across Delhi and the National Capital Region from 5 November to 20 November.
But blanket restrictions also carry significant economic costs, particularly when they are not targeted at the sources contributing most to pollution.
“We do not know whether shutting down all construction activity delivers the desired results. However, we do know that it adversely affects economic activity,” said Prof. Sachchida Nand Tripathi, inaugural dean of the Kotak School of Sustainability at IIT Kanpur.
Tripathi argued that better localized data and intelligent monitoring systems could help authorities identify pollution sources in specific areas. An airshed-based approach could make interventions more targeted, rather than relying on blanket restrictions across the capital.
Implementing it, however, will require more than inter-state coordination. Industrial clusters, agricultural districts, transport corridors and urban centres across the Indo-Gangetic Plain have different emission profiles. An effective strategy would need district-specific action plans, adequate funding and clearly defined institutional responsibilities, alongside common regional objectives.
“The real test for Uttar Pradesh and Haryana is whether an airshed-wide strategy, backed by empowered local institutions, delivers sustained improvements in air quality,” said Roy. “If successful, they could offer a model for other states across the Indo-Gangetic Plain.”

The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.
The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.
The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.
During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.
After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”
It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”
On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.
“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”
The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.
It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”
Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.
José Antonio Kast, a politician who spent a career railing against progressive issues, reproductive rights and welfare policies from the extreme fringes of right-wing politics, now finds himself with just 24% approval in the polls.
It is less than a year since Kast stormed to the presidency in December 2025 by avoiding all mention of his hardline stances on social matters, focusing instead on two hot-button issues whipped up in the national media: illegal immigration and public security.
But rather than pressing ahead with those at the top of his agenda, he has floundered. And as elsewhere around the Americas and worldwide, rising costs of living have come to hit him hard.
"Our salaries are maybe 20% of a European income, but with a similar cost of living – it's terrible," said Simón Echavarría, a 30-year-old architect, at a march in Santiago on Friday evening.
"We want to protest against the measures that have set us back on environmental issues, on human rights, even reducing the sentences of pedophiles – they are implementing things that nobody asked for," he said.
Behind him, heavily armed police blocked the streets and fired water cannons at protesters chanting and waving flags in the square.
Much of the recent ire stems from the revelation last month that Kast's government had signed decrees to cut the sentences of 56 prisoners whose crimes range from the rape of children to dictatorship-era human rights violations.
Kast has since admitted that this was an "error", but came out in support of the undersecretary who signed the decrees nonetheless.
But beneath the more egregious moves Kast has made in his first year in power is simmering discontent over affordability.
In July, Kast's government chose not to apply an anti-inflation tool available to the Chilean state to ease the rise in fuel prices brought about by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Protests exploded as prices shot up overnight and motorists joined long queues at gas stations to fill their tanks before the rise came into effect.
This week, Chile's formidable truckers' unions blockaded two major highways in an effort to exert pressure on the government and address high fuel prices.
On Friday, the strike was broken after the government backed down, sending a bill to Chile's congress which will reverse planned fuel price rises.
It is expected to be approved this month, but public anger continues to grow over the cost of living.
Politicians across the Americas who have enthusiastically aligned themselves with President Donald Trump are facing challenges similar to those confronting the U.S. administration, as rising fuel prices and the cost of everyday goods fuel public discontent.
In Argentina, far-right libertarian Javier Milei faces reelection in less than a year, with 60% of the country disapproving of his leadership amid spiraling inflation. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori is also facing growing discontent, with 53% disapproving of her government, according to a recent Ipsos poll.
At the march in Santiago on Friday, 30-year-old veterinarian Patricia Pereira said that she was concerned about cuts to science funding, but that her discontent ran deeper.
"Here in Chile, it was a hard-won victory for children to have free education, achieved through protests, and now even that's also being called into question," she said.
Protests are likely to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living. President Kast has shown little sign of doing so.
To the contrary, his budget proposal is making its way through Congress, with the government seeking cuts to education, culture, science and a host of social programs.

Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.
The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.
A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.
Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.
At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.
Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.
The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.
The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra with her mother Sonia Gandhi at the book release event
NEW DELHI: "And listen, if you want to fall in love, go to Varsity Restaurant in Cambridge. But never eat the chicken chasseur, okay?" Rahul Gandhi jokingly delivered this piece of advice at the launch of his mother Sonia Gandhi's memoir, 'Belonging: A Journey of Love', in Delhi on Monday. Years after hearing the story about his parents' first meeting in Cambridge, he recounted how he went to the Varsity Restaurant with his girlfriend to see where they had met.When Rahul told the man at the entrance that his parents had met there, the man said he knew exactly who they were and recommended the chicken chasseur from the menu. However, the meal did not live up to its romantic legacy. Rahul contrasts his parents' memories of the restaurant with his own experience. "They seem to remember that the food was fantastic. The food's horrible!" he said as the audience laughed.The anecdote was part of a series of family recollections the leader of the opposition shared after saying he had been instructed to avoid politics. However, many read a political subtext into the seating arrangements. In the front row was an array of opposition leaders such as Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav; Trinamool Congress MP Abhishek Banerjee; National Conference president Farooq Abdullah; Supriya Sule of NCP-SP; Jharkhand CM Hemant Soren; and Tamil Nadu CM C Joseph Vijay.
Also in the front row was former Punjab CM Captain Amarinder Singh, who left Congress in 2021 following a bitter falling-out with the Gandhis.Rahul name-checked Amarinder and mentioned that he had seen his parents fight only once. Rajiv Gandhi was speaking to Amarinder on phone when Sonia tried several times to tell him something. Rajiv was stressed and eventually got angry. "We saw them argue many times, but that was the only time we ever saw them fight," Rahul said.Sonia Gandhi too kept the conversation away from politics. Asked why she chose to write a memoir when she had guarded her privacy fiercely in the past, she said she wanted to set the record straight about her family amid "unreal stories" woven around them. "So much has been said about my mother-in-law, husband, son, daughter, and myself; and most of it is unreal. It has really nothing to do with the way we are. Stories are woven around you, untruths are woven around you, and hurtful things are said which are nowhere near the truth. And I thought, well, perhaps this was a way of bringing out my feelings, what I know of my family, and maybe people will be open to listening to my story too," the Rajya Sabha MP said.She recalled feeling like an outsider when she first moved to India, conscious of making mistakes. She connected that experience to Indian women who enter a new family after marriage and have to adjust to its ways. The memoir's title, she said, reflected "the effort to be accepted and to belong, to finally belong."While she recounted a story of how she and Rajiv would go to India Gate to have ice cream (she had a favourite Sardarji ice cream vendor), Rahul spoke of his parents' affection and a habit he had assumed was common in every home: "Every meal there would be Papa and on Papa's lap there would be Mama." He said he realised it was unusual only when he visited friends' homes.
But things changed after the assassinations of Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi, he said, "The fun-loving mother, the smiling mother disappeared." Sonia, once an extrovert, withdrew into herself.Rahul also spoke of his mother's resilience in the face of cancer, saying he had never seen her afraid or back down. He ended by telling her how proud he believed Rajiv would have been of her: "Mummy, Papa loved you. But I cannot even tell you how proud he would be of you."

Europe Agrees on a Team to Represent It in Talks With Russia
After coveting a seat in the Ukraine war discussions, Europe is poised to get one. The continent wants to fill it with a six-member team.
European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. They learned this week that they would get one, and simply needed to decide which official should sit in that chair.
Instead, they decided on six.
European Union leaders concluded in Dublin on Friday that they will tap a group of major nations — Britain, France, Germany, Poland, and Italy — along with a representative from the E.U’s leadership arms, the European Council and European Commission.
In some ways, the choice of a crowd plays into jibes Americans have made about the continent’s indecisiveness: “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and a U.S. envoy, said earlier this week.
Europe’s failure to pick one negotiator leaves open the possibility that its fragmentation will diminish its influence. Even so, Europeans have underscored that they are a democracy of many nations, though, and that many voices must be represented.
“We decide on who represents us, and that is what we have done today,” said Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission.
“We need to work as a team,” António Costa, president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, said at a news conference on Friday, noting that America itself has two envoys.

After the world’s hottest summer since records began in 1850, the death toll from extreme weather in 2026 is already in the high tens of thousands. That is a conservative estimate and is certain to rise much higher.
As Cop31 continues and scientists warn that climate breakdown may be accelerating, the Guardian looks back at a year of droughts, fires and floods as a reminder that, unless the world takes urgent action to cut emissions, this disastrous year will be one of the best of the rest of our lives.
January 
  
Fourth-hottest January on record
Extreme heat fuels wildfires in Australia 
  
As temperatures jump nearly 20C (68F) above average, Victoria and other southern states register new heat records, including 50C in Port Augusta and the tiny opal mining town of Andamooka. Melbourne hospitals report a 25% increase in heat-related illnesses, while authorities in many areas struggle with wildfires. Scientists say the supercharged climate has made the heatwave five times more likely. Heatwaves already cause more deaths in Australia than all other natural hazards combined.
February 
  
Fourth-hottest February on record
Mudslides kill 72 in Brazil after record rain 
  
The city of Juiz de Fora in Minas Gerais records its wettest ever month, triggering landslides that sweep away hundreds of homes in poor communities on unstable hillsides. Floods also disrupt Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. More than 10,000 people are displaced.
March 
  
Fourth-hottest March on record
Devastating floods across much of the world 
  
In Ethiopia, at least 131 people are killed in floods and mudslides that bury entire villages. Eighty die in Kenya and 18 in Tanzania. The Arabian peninsula is battered by fierce winds and heavy downpours that flood the streets of the desert kingdom. Hailstones the size of tennis balls fall in Oman and lightning storms leave cities in the UAE inundated with water. Many areas report record rainfall. At least 30 die in Afghanistan as heavy rains trigger landslides. Hong Kong is soaked in twice the usual monthly precipitation. Flood waters in southern Russia submerge homes and leave more than 300,000 without electricity. Huge tracts of farmland are left underwater in Argentina and Chile.
World’s energy imbalance accelerates rapidly 
  
The World Meteorological Organization reveals an alarming buildup of energy in Earth’s system. More than 90% is stored in the oceans, where warming has more than doubled over the past two decades compared with the average over the previous 45 years. This makes weather more extreme and threatens health and food supplies. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, says: “The global climate is in a state of emergency. Planet Earth is being pushed beyond its limits. Every key climate indicator is flashing red.” Guterres urges the world to cut fossil fuel emissions as rapidly as possible to minimise future risks. However, CO2 in the atmosphere continues to rise.
April 
  
Second-hottest April on record
Super typhoon tears through Micronesia, Guam and Saipan 
  
At peak intensity on 12 April, Sinlaku registers a wind speed of 295km/h (183mph) – roughly the same as a Shinkansen bullet train and the joint highest recorded by a storm in the western Pacific basin so early in the year. It is also the deadliest in decades, killing 12, leaving 43,000 without power, forcing mass evacuation and causing $1.5bn (£1.1bn) in damages. This will remain one of the most powerful storms of 2026, superseded only by Super Typhoon Champi that will strike Taiwan and Japan in October.
May 
  
Second-hottest May on record
Hundreds of millions endure deadly heat in south Asia 
  
At least 47 heat-related deaths are reported in southern Asia as temperatures soar above 45C in several Indian and Bangladeshi cities, and hit a peak of 52C in Pakistan’s southern province of Sindh. Scientists warn that the climate crisis is exposing hundreds of millions of people in south Asia to longer, deadlier pre-monsoon heat.
June
  
Second-hottest June on record
Ocean heat enters uncharted territory 
  
Sea surface temperature graphs begin to jag upwards and away from all previous highs on 21 June, starting a trend that will worsen over the rest of the year. This alarms scientists because oceans absorb more than 90% of the excess energy in Earth’s system. If the seas start to release that heat then the land and air will get warmer more quickly. This coincides with the emergence of the latest El Niño, which is confirmed on 2 June.
Arctic and Antarctic swelter in unprecedented warmth 
  
Instead of the usual winter snow and ice, scientists at the Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula of Antarctica are astonished to see rain and dirt outside their windows after an eight-day heatwave that peaked with a record temperature of 15C on 6 June. At the other end of the planet, the Arctic experiences its warmest ever June. Beliy Island, Siberia, registers 28.3C on 25 June, the highest temperature ever recorded that far north in the Eurasian Arctic.
West African deluge takes heavy toll 
  
Relentless rains claim almost 100 lives in west Africa from May to June. Record downpours of up to 140mm (5.5in) in a single day are made five times more likely and 23% more intense by the human-caused climate crisis. Floods and mudslides kill 59 in Côte d’Ivoire, 35 in Ghana and five in Togo.
July
  
Joint-hottest July on record
Fires choke Canada and Europe 
  
Almost 1,000 wildfires sweep across Canada, charring 3m hectares (7.4m acres) and sending a haze of smoke as far as New York. On 15 July Toronto registers the world’s worst air quality as a result of the haze. Smoke kills 4,000 people in Canada each year, almost four times as many as at the start of the century. Meanwhile, in Europe, prolonged droughts create tinderbox conditions for wildfires in Greece, Portugal, Italy, Norway, Germany, Spain and France. They burn 686,000 hectares in Europe, twice the average of the past 20 years.
Extreme weather disrupts US 250th birthday festivities and the World Cup 
  
Half of the US population is under a heat alert before 4 July independence celebrations, disrupting Donald Trump’s Great American State Fair on the National Mall in Washington and other events. Dozens of heat-related deaths are reported and thousands experience power cuts.
At least nine World Cup games are played in potentially dangerous heat and humidity, while fierce storms delay three matches by more than an hour, including Mexico v England.
August 
  
Hottest August on record
Nepal glacier collapse kills at least 1,300 
  
Lhende Khola river valley communities are swept away after a 2 sq km (0.8 sq miles) slab of rock and glacier ice falls 1,400 metres (4,600ft) in the Himalayas, triggering a flood of water and debris. More than 5,000 people are missing and 8,600 need medical attention. Scientists say unusually warm temperatures and long-term permafrost degradation owing to the climate crisis were among the likely causes of the catastrophe.
Europe’s murderous heat forces reactor shutdown
 
The UK and France are among a host of nations that swelter through the warmest summer (June to August) in European history. The heat kills an estimated 50,000 people in cities across the continent. Two-thirds of those excess deaths are attributable to the climate crisis. Many more are likely to have died in rural areas. As droughts spread, Romania is forced to shut down its only nuclear power station because the cooling system could not be replenished by low water levels in the Danube River.
September
  
Second-hottest September on record
Record heat and deadly storms lash Asia 
  
Hundreds are killed and millions evacuated as the world’s most populous continent experiences its hottest September and severe storms. Typhoon Dujuan kills at least 10 people in Japan, with violent winds of 144km/h and 832mm of rain in only 48 hours on the island of Izu Oshima. Three die in a mudslide in eastern China during Typhoon Saudel. At least 102 are killed in India and Nepal amid rain that is nine times the norm in some places. Eight die and half a million are affected by flooding in Bangkok, Thailand.
October
  
Hottest October on record
Governments warned to brace for peak El Niño 
  
The UN disaster relief agency urges countries to prepare for an unprecedented “wrecking ball” El Niño that is forecast to peak around the end of the year. UK authorities advise households to stockpile a few days of basic supplies. Climate scientists project more than 450,000 people globally will die by February as a result of the additional heat brought by the super El Niño.
Protests in Indonesia after deadly fires 
  
Demonstrators in Jakarta protest against Indonesia’s worst fire season in a decade, which has scorched almost 2m hectares of forest – more than twice as big an area as last year. The choking haze is estimated to have killed 3,560 people in one month alone.
Roads turn to rivers in Chile 
  
After the heaviest October rainfall in 76 years, the Chilean government declares the Santiago district of Las Condes a “disaster zone”, with more than 1,000 people evacuated from their homes, some by helicopter.
Drought and fire in the Amazon rainforest 
  
Months of drought leave some of the world’s mightiest rivers, including the Rio Negro, Madeira and Tapajós, close to record low levels, curtailing the water transport of essential goods. This coincides with a sharp rise in fire activity in the central and eastern Amazon region, releasing so much smoke that the city of Manaus registers the second-worst air quality in the world on 12 October.
November
2026 is forecast to be one of the hottest years in history
Global temperatures tie an all-time record of 2.04C above preindustrial levels, which was set in 2023. This year is forecast to be one of the four warmest years in history, along with 2023, 2024 and 2025. Sea surface temperatures are so high that the climate scientist Eliot Jacobson calculates the odds of being this far above the norm at 33tn to one. Meanwhile, the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere reaches a peak not seen in 2m years. On the plus side, global fossil fuel emissions are likely to fall this year thanks to a shift away from oil and gas owing to high prices after the US-Israeli attack on Iran, and ever cheaper renewable alternatives.
