- GTA 6 could score between 96 and 98 on Metacritic, according to current prediction markets.
- GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 both hold a score of 97, while GTA 4 leads with 98.
- GTA 6 reviews are reportedly expected on November 18, 2026, one day before launch.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is almost here, and apparently, launching one of the most anticipated games in history isn’t enough pressure for Rockstar Games. With the launch approaching, prediction markets are already placing their bets on the GTA 6 Metacritic score.
The reported GTA 6 review embargo is scheduled for November 18, 2026, just a day before launch. So, will Jason and Lucia deliver a 98-rated masterpiece, or will the weight of expectation finally catch up to Rockstar? Let’s learn all about that here.
Prediction markets such as Polymarket and Kalshi already suggest that expectations are sky-high for the Metacritic score for GTA 6. According to Polymarket figures tracked on November 17, the odds of GTA 6 crossing 96 on Metacritic sit around 76%, while the chances of crossing 97 are approximately 61%.
The 98+ threshold is considerably tougher, and the chances are around 32%. Well, the market has also recorded more than $108,000 in trading volume.
Things are slightly different on the Kalshi platform, where the odds of GTA 6’s Metacritic score crossing 96 sit around 57%, and the odds of crossing 97 are around 36%. Moreover, here the recorded trading volume is more than $125,000 at the time of writing this.
Looking at Rockstar’s history of making blockbuster titles, they’ve done a fabulous job with GTA 5 scoring 97, Red Dead Redemption 2 scoring 97, and GTA 4 still holding the studio’s record at 98 on Metacritic. So, beating these scores would naturally mean setting a new record with the GTA 6 release.
Despite these optimistic predictions, the GTA 6 critic review has yet to be published by Metacritic. The reported November 18 review embargo could finally give us an answer, although Rockstar hasn’t confirmed an exact time for that yet.
GTA 6 might have a bit to prove to the critics, but to the gamers, it’s a blockbuster game that everyone has been waiting for these 13 years. The release in two days will finally mark the community’s exit from Los Santos and the first long drive through the streets of GTA 6 Vice City.

Kashmir has no shortage of business associations, trade bodies or organisations claiming to represent civil society. Their numbers have multiplied over the decades, each speaking for a particular trade, profession, locality or economic activity. Yet our collective influence on public policy remains limited. We continue approaching governments separately, often repeating similar demands, while larger questions of economic development, employment, environmental protection and social welfare remain inadequately addressed.
Have we become so preoccupied with creating organisations that we have forgotten the purpose of getting organised?
This question returned to me at the ninth Annual General Meeting of the Nigeen Tourist Traders Association (NTTA), held on November 14, 2026. The gathering acquired wider significance when the Association highlighted environmental initiatives undertaken by the Nigeen Lake Conservation Organisation (NLCO).
Both organisations are headed by businessman and environmental campaigner Manzoor Ahmad Wangnoo, whose dedication, alongside his committed team, to restoring water bodies, promoting plantation and mobilising public participation deserves recognition.
Listening to environmental activists, government functionaries and business representatives, I initially wondered what a tourism association’s annual meeting had to do with environmental conservation. The answer soon became obvious. Governments may legislate and regulate, but society must actively participate in protecting the environment.
Wangnoo’s initiatives demonstrate what organised citizens can accomplish beyond their commercial interests. Why should hundreds of associations across Jammu and Kashmir not undertake similar initiatives, each assuming responsibility for its surroundings?
During my address, I reminded the gathering that when Maharaja Hari Singh’s rule ended in 1947, we inherited a Jammu and Kashmir endowed with extraordinary biodiversity, magnificent forests, pristine lakes, rivers and wetlands. Much of the subsequent devastation is our own handiwork, particularly the consequence of successive governments permitting or failing to prevent encroachments, deforestation and environmentally destructive development.
Sustainable tourism, industry and infrastructure cannot be pursued by sacrificing the natural resources upon which their future depends.
But the larger question is whether our business associations can unite not merely for environmental conservation, but to influence major issues confronting our economy and society.
I recalled a meeting convened years ago by former Chief Minister Mufti Mohammad Sayeed at Nehru Guest House, CheshmaShahi, where I counted more than 26 tourism associations alone. Numerous other trade and industrial bodies, including several claiming apex status, were also present. Representatives rose one after another, presenting largely repetitive demands.
After hearing the representatives, Finance Minister DrHaseebDrabu, who was conducting the proceedings, invited Chief Minister Mufti Mohammad Sayeed to deliver his concluding address before lunch.
During the break, they noticed me and the then FCIK President, Mohammad Ashraf Mir, and enquired why we had not spoken. The session was subsequently reopened to hear us. 
When my turn came, I questioned the Chief Minister’s observations about proposed tourism infrastructure in the Zabarwan range and other destinations. I argued that Kashmir certainly needed tourism development but not at the cost of forests, fragile mountains and ecological balance. The exchange became contentious, with another issue concerning Chenab Valley also provoking disagreement.
Drawing upon that experience, I posed a simple question at the NTTA gathering: What if all those 26 tourism associations, or even more, came together under one umbrella federation?Imagine their collective strength in presenting a comprehensive, evidence-based policy document instead of approaching government with repetitive, sometimes contradictory, demands.
Houseboat owners, hoteliers, travel agents, tour operators and other tourism bodies could retain their identities and autonomy while pursuing common policy issues collectively. Each could simultaneously undertake local initiatives in environmental protection, education, healthcare and social welfare, making the tourism fraternity a force for wider societal development.
The same principle should apply to agriculture, horticulture, handicrafts, manufacturing, trade, transport, fisheries, information technology and other economic activities.
District, area and sector-based associations established for common accomplishments could organise into representative federations, creating channels through which grassroots concerns reach policymaking institutions.
Kashmir already possesses examples of such representation.
The Federation of Chambers of Industries Kashmir (FCIK) brings together industrial estate, district and sector-based associations, enabling collective participation in industrial policy formulation. The Kashmir Traders and Manufacturers Federation (KTMF) has also been working towards wider representation through market and bazaar committees. Both could strengthen their representative character by ensuring inclusive participation.
The next logical step would be to bring these and other sectoral federations under one genuinely representative apex Chamber.
The Kashmir Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KCCI), established in 1934, represents a legacy Kashmir’s business community should cherish. It emerged just seven years after the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) was founded in 1927, and fifteen years after the International Chamber of Commerce in 1919. Few regional business institutions can claim such an early beginning.
At its inception, when Kashmir’s economy revolved largely around handicrafts, traditional trade and exports, KCCI could reasonably represent most organised business interests. But as manufacturing, tourism, horticulture, transport and services expanded, its representative structure failed to evolve sufficiently to accommodate them.
Consequently, emerging sectors established their own bodies, including FCIK for industry and federations for trade, tourism and other activities. Institutional rivalries subsequently encouraged parallel chambers, further fragmenting the business community without corresponding gains in collective influence.
The answer is not to dismantle these organisations, but to reunite their collective strength under a restructured KCCI while preserving their identities and autonomy.
Under its present constitution, KCCI’s executive leadership is elected principally by individual members, notwithstanding the affiliation of associations. This does not adequately reflect the representative character expected of an apex institution.
Constitutional restructuring could transform KCCI into a genuine federation of federations, with its governing body drawn from recognisedsectoral federations through transparent, democratic procedures. Constituent organisations would manage their affairs, while the Chamber would provide a united voice on major economic, developmental and public policy issues.
Such transformation would preserve KCCI’s legacy while restoring its larger representative purpose.
FICCI offers a compelling example. Established in 1927, it has evolved beyond trade representation into an influential research and policy institution. Its economic surveys, sectoral studies and pre-budget memoranda provide governments with evidence-based assessments and practical recommendations on industry, employment, investment and trade.
Its expertise receives serious government attention. The Union Ministry of Consumer Affairs even entrusted FICCI with studying internal trade reforms, whose recommendations were presented to a high-level group constituted by the Prime Minister’s Office.
FICCI’s strength lies not merely in whom it represents, but in the quality of research and solutions it offers government. Why should KCCI not aspire to similar institutional credibility?
Every affiliated federation could establish expert committees, collect grassroots information and document policy deficiencies. The Chamber could consolidate their findings, commission studies and prepare comprehensive submissions to the Jammu and Kashmir government, the Government of India and regulatory institutions.
Instead of competing delegations seeking appointments with ministers, we could have one institution presenting thoroughly researched policy documents backed by representative consensus and professional expertise.
Such an institution could help reshape Jammu and Kashmir’s economy by identifying opportunities for import substitution, indigenous manufacturing, employment and self-reliance. Its federations could develop evidence-based strategies for industrial revival, sustainable tourism, agricultural and horticultural development, value addition, entrepreneurship and rehabilitation of distressed enterprises.
Environmental protection would remain integral. Initiatives such as those undertaken by ManzoorWangnoo and NLCO could inspire similar efforts across Jammu and Kashmir. Collaboration with scientists, consultants, academics and civil society organisations could extend the Chamber’s contribution to education, healthcare, labour welfare and other societal concerns.
Government should welcome such an institution as a partner rather than an adversary. Policy papers prepared through extensive research, field evidence, scientific analysis and expert consultation effectively undertake part of the government’s own policy-development work. They deserve serious examination and reasoned responses, rather than ceremonial acknowledgement before disappearing into official files.
Such cooperation would strengthen governance while preserving the Chamber’s independence to question failures and demand accountability.
But who will take the initiative?
I make a particular appeal to my own generation of business leaders, former office-bearers, entrepreneurs, consultants, academics and professionals who have devoted decades to building enterprises, leading institutions and advising governments.
We have witnessed Kashmir’s economic struggles, squandered opportunities and institutional rivalries. Some of us have been part of these divisions and must accept our share of responsibility. But we also possess a lifetime of experience, knowledge and relationships. Should we allow this collective wisdom to fade with us, or invest it in building something greater than the organisations and positions we once held?
There comes a time when the worth of our public life must be judged not by the offices we occupied, but by the institutions we leave behind. The younger generation deserves more than memories of our achievements and failures. It deserves a credible platform capable of creating opportunities, nurturing enterprise and shaping its economic future.
KCCI has the legacy, federations have the grassroots strength, and our entrepreneurs and professionals possess the expertise. What we lack is not capacity, but the collective will to rise above individual ambitions and institutional rivalries.
I hope this proposal sparks serious debate across business chambers, professional institutions, academic circles and civil society. Let it be challenged, improved and translated into action.
If we can unite to seek concessions from government, why can we not unite to offer solutions, build a self-reliant economy and protect the future of our children?
This is an appeal to the conscience of my generation. Our greatest legacy would not be another association, another presidency or another memorandum, but an institution stronger and more enduring than any one of us.
Let us leave the next generation something to build upon, rather than compel it to begin all over again.
Shakeel Qalander, prominent business leader and a civil society animator.

Indian actress, director and social advocate Nandita Das and Syrian star Taim Hassan are set to be honored by the Doha Film Festival with Creative Excellence Awards during the event’s opening ceremony on Thursday.
Das has acted in more than 40 feature films, starting with Deepa Mehta’s “Fire,” which depicts a relationship between two women in an Indian household. She’s subsequently worked with top Indian directors such as Mrinal Sen, Shyam Benegal, Adoor Gopalakrishnan, Rituporno Ghosh and Mani Ratnam. Her directorial debut “Firaaq” — about the aftermath of the 2002 sectarian carnage in Gujarat, where 3,000 Muslims were killed — played at Toronto in 2008 and went on to travel widely and score many awards. She’s been a member of the main jury at Cannes Film Festival twice, in 2005 and 2013.
Hassan made his breakthrough playing young ruler Fatimid Caliph Al-Adid in Syrian director Hatem Ali’s historical epics “Al-Zir Salem” (2000) and “Saladin” (2001). He has led all five seasons of hit Arabic TV show “Al Hayba,” about a family of arms smugglers working the border between Syria and Lebanon, a role that has made him a household name across the region and reached international audiences on Netflix. Hassan’s more recent work includes the show “Taj” (2024), in which he plays a boxer resisting the French occupation of Syria; hit political drama “Under the Seventh Ground” (2025); and thriller series “Mawlana” (2026).
“Cinema transcends borders, challenges perceptions and brings us closer to our shared humanity. Nandita Das and Taim Hassan represent the very best of this power,” said Doha Film Institute CEO Fatma Hassan Alremaihi, who also heads the festival. “Their remarkable artistry, courage of expression and unwavering commitment to authentic storytelling resonates far beyond geographical and cultural boundaries.”
As previously announced, Yemeni-Scottish filmmaker Sara Ishaq’s timely drama “The Station” — which looks at the impact of Yemen’s civil war on the country — is set to open the revamped event’s second edition, which will run Nov. 19-27 in the Qatari capital.

The Telangana State Women’s Commission (TGSCW) has initiated an inquiry into an alleged illegal oocyte donation racket in Hyderabad, issuing notices to eight Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) centres and egg banks over suspected irregularities in their donor records and procurement practices.
The Commission examined representatives of the eight institutions on Friday, November 13, after directing their managements to appear before it. However, TGSCW Chairperson Nerella Sharada expressed dissatisfaction after some centres sent staff members and other representatives instead of senior management, despite being specifically instructed to attend in person. The inquiry was subsequently adjourned after the institutions assured the Commission that their management would appear at the next hearing.
During Friday’s proceedings, the Commission scrutinised reports, records and details of egg donors submitted by the ART centres and egg banks. “Several irregularities and suspicious elements have emerged from the records examined so far,” said Ms. Sharada.
She also questioned claims made by the institutions that nearly 90% of their egg donors came from other States and donated their eggs voluntarily without receiving any remuneration or financial compensation. She said the claims raised several questions and warranted further investigation.
Health Department’s investigation
Commissioner of Health and Family Welfare, Sangeetha Satyanarayana, also attended the inquiry, during which Ms. Sharada sought details about the progress of the department’s investigation into the alleged illegal egg procurement practices. The discussions also covered shortcomings in the existing Assisted Reproductive Technology Act and its implementation, particularly the challenges in regulating and monitoring ART centres and egg banks.
Ms. Sharada said she would soon meet Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha and Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy to inform them of the findings and discuss corrective measures, including possible legislative amendments to strengthen regulation of the sector.
More ART centres likely to come under scanner
Ms. Sharada further said that the Commission has also received information indicating the possible involvement of several other ART centres and egg banks in the alleged racket. It plans to issue notices to their management and summon them for questioning as part of the ongoing inquiry.
“The Commission will not tolerate illegal practices that compromise women’s health, dignity and rights. We will continue the investigation in coordination with the concerned government departments to identify those responsible and ensure appropriate legal action,” she added.

On 11 November 2026, terrorists opened fire on a CRPF checkpoint near Mir Bazar in Kulgam district of Jammu and Kashmir, injuring three personnel. The attackers fled after the firing, and security forces launched a search operation to track them down (here, here, and here).
Amid the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel, a video is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it shows defence expert Wing Commander (Wg Cdr) Praful Bakshi (Retd) alleging that the attack was a false flag operation orchestrated to divert public attention from mounting political pressure on the Narendra Modi government, including Congress protests demanding the Chief Election Commissioner’s resignation and the Arunachal Pradesh controversy. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) stating that the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel was a false flag operation.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) did not describe the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel as a false flag operation. In the original ANI video, he discussed the security situation in Kulgam, the presence of terrorist sleeper cells, and the need for better intelligence coordination and proactive security measures. The Indian Army’s fact-check wing also confirmed on 12 November 2026 that the viral video was digitally altered and falsely attributed remarks to him. AI detection tools, Hive and Hiya, also indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) made any such statement, we searched Google using relevant keywords but found no credible news reports or official statements corroborating it.
We noticed the viral video carries an ANI watermark. A keyword search led us to an ANI post on X (archived), dated 11 November 2026, featuring the same footage of Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd), wearing the same attire and speaking against an identical background. However, in the original video, he does not describe the Kulgam attack as a false flag operation or link it to the political developments mentioned in the viral clip. Instead, he expresses concern over the incident, noting that Kulgam has witnessed several such attacks in the past. He emphasises the need for a more proactive security approach, better intelligence coordination, and improved intelligence gathering in areas where terrorists operate and maintain sleeper cells. He also highlights the need to investigate how these groups receive logistical support, including accommodation, ammunition, and water.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated, suggesting fabricated audio was added to the original footage to make it appear that Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) was describing the Kulgam attack as a false-flag operation.
The Indian Army’s fact-check wing also debunked the claim in an X post dated 12 November 2026, stating that the video was digitally manipulated and falsely attributed remarks to Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd). It clarified that he did not make any such comments in the original video and had instead spoken about terrorist organisations and the need for offensive action and better coordination to prevent such attacks.
To sum up, this video of Wg Cdr Praful Bakshi (Retd) alleging that the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel was a false flag operation is digitally manipulated.

Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
- Published
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.
The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.
Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.
The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024.
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".
The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.
In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.
In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".
Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.
Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".
He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".
Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.
The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.
"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.
Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries.
Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.
"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."
The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.
The agency added that unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, which the Dutch government has confirmed will not take place.
According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.
In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

Here is a thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama from director Nitesh Tiwari, with music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman, based on the ancient classical poem about Rama, the avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu. It has often been adapted for live-action and animated movies in the past, though surely not on this scale, the current three-hour blockbuster being only the first half. (There are no musical numbers though.) The idea of aristocrats submitting stoically and yet playfully to exile in the forest has something Shakespearean about it, and if you are suffering from Homer-withdrawal after Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, a story about the noble Prince Rama finally vowing to wage war on a distant city where his wife has been abducted might just fit the bill.
Ranbir Kapoor plays the mythical Rama, a noble warrior and statesman who has been brought into being in the city state of Ayodhya as a bodily representative of Vishnu, and from the first his sense of destiny is overwhelming. But what exactly is that destiny? In broad terms, his fate is to face off with Ravana (Naveen “Yash” Kumar), king of far-off Lanka, a figure whose former slave status once triggered in him such a cosmically intense prayer for justice that Lord Brahma offered him the superpower of athletic strength and indifference to pain.
In Ayodhya, Rama marries the sweetly devoted Sita (Sai Pallavi), he enjoys an intense bond of comradeship with his brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey), and is the apple of his father’s eye; this is King Dasharatha (Arun Govil) who, careworn by affairs of state, is about cede the throne to Rama. But Rama’s stepmother Kaikeyi (Lara Dutta) furiously reminds Dasharatha that he promised the crown to Bharata (Adinath Kothare), the son they had together. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are banished to the forest.
Over in Lanka, a toxic stew of plotting against Ravana is being stirred by his slippery, smirking brother-in-law Vidyutjihva (played by Bollywood veteran Vivek Oberoi), whom Ravana ruthlessly slays in single combat; this man’s widow Shurpanakha (Rakul Preet Singh), who is Ravana’s sister, is banished to the same forest where Rama is humbly eking out his civilian existence. She falls in love with Rama, using her witchy wiles to trick and bamboozle the happily married man, and this is to lead to a cataclysmic confrontation between Rama and Ravana.
With its giant canvas and some truly beautiful sunset skyscapes, this very enjoyable film has a little of Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings and even Disney’s The Lion King (the latter surely influenced the animal-kingdom tableaux). The bizarre flying machine piloted by Ravana (who does not have the ability to fly as such) has something engagingly Gilliamesque about it. As so often with Indian cinema, this movie reminds you of the forthright, unselfconscious storytelling energy that popular Hollywood films had in the 1950s and 60s, the era of sword-and-sandal. It’s a rather amazing adventure.

Srinagar, Nov 16: Deputy Commissioner (DC) Srinagar, Akshay Labroo on Monday convened a comprehensive meeting of all executing agencies and line Departments here at Meeting Hall of the DC Office Complex to review the physical and financial progress of approved developmental works taken up under the District Capex Budget 2026-27 across the district.
The meeting was attended by Chief Planning Officer, Fayaz Ahmad Dar, IAS Probationer, Aakash Garg, Secretary SMC, Tahir Magrey, Assistant Commissioner Development, Tariq Ahmad Reshi, Chief Education Officer, Ghulam Mohi-Ud Din, Assistant Commissioner Panchayats, Bashir Ahmad Para, Executive Engineers of R&B, PHE, KPDCL, SMC, UEED, Block Development Officers and all other District and Sectoral Officers.
During the meeting, the Deputy Commissioner undertook an executing-agency-wise detailed review of the progress achieved in the tendering process, allotment of approved works, commencement of projects and completion of developmental works so far under the District Capex Budget 2026-27. He also took stock of the works taken up under the savings plan.
On the occasion, the DC was apprised that 99 percent of the works have already been allotted, with 87 percent works started on ground, while over 60 percent works have been completed on ground.
While appreciating the efforts of the Officers, the Deputy Commissioner directed all executing agencies to maintain the momentum and further accelerate the pace of work on the ground to ensure timely completion of projects.
The DC underscored the need to make optimal use of the ongoing working season to accelerate the physical execution and financial progress of developmental works. He further stressed strict adherence to prescribed technical standards and stipulated timelines to ensure quality execution, timely completion of projects and effective delivery of developmental benefits to the public.
Reviewing the status of developmental works approved under the savings plan for the current financial year, the Deputy Commissioner directed the concerned executing agencies to accord these works priority, expedite the execution process and ensure visible progress on the ground within the stipulated timelines, while maintaining the prescribed quality standards.

Every year in Delhi, the arrival of the winter months also signals the beginning of what residents widely call “pollution season”. A thick toxic smog shrouds the city, home to 30 million people who have no choice but to breathe the poisonous air as they go about their daily lives, often while suffering from wheezy coughs, nausea and itchy eyes. While successive state governments have brought in measures intended to improve air quality, the situation has remained the same for more than a decade. Delhi is widely regarded as the world’s most polluted city. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Pollution season usually begins around the same time as Diwali, the Hindu festival of light. Amidst the plummeting air quality, people still gather in the markets for festival shopping and at festivities outside. Diwali is also known to cause a surge in the pollution levels, due to the tens of millions of cars that hit the roads and the use of firecrackers for the celebration. In previous years, firecrackers were banned, but this year the state government has allowed “green” firecrackers”. However environmentalists argue that these are still highly polluting.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The causes of Delhi’s apocalyptic pollution are multi-faceted. In recent years, one of the biggest causes has been vehicle emissions, from the almost 10m cars, rickshaws, motorcycles and trucks on the city’s roads. It is also the season where farmers in the neighbouring states of Haryana and Punjab often burn their fields to ready them for the next crop. These fires are illegal but still occur. Factory emissions, dust from construction and rubbish burning also contribute to the toxic air quality levels.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
So far, the air quality index (AQI) has already soared above 650, more than 30 times the limit the World Health Organization (WHO) deems to be safe. Air pollution is linked to numerous serious diseases, particularly respiratory, and hospitals have already reported a surge in patients suffering from breathing difficulties.The pollution season is expected to last until January, when the weather warms up.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Millions of Delhi’s residents are poor families or migrant workers, who have no choice but to go out to work in the toxic air, often suffering long term impacts on their health. Doctors and campaigners have described the pollution as a “health emergency”. According to a study last year, at least 15% of deaths in the capital are linked to air pollution. Pollution now kills more people in Delhi than obesity of diabetes.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
As in previous years, the state government has introduced various restrictions to try and bring air quality levels under control. Coal and firewood have been banned as fuel. Construction has also been halted and so have older diesel and petrol cars. Offices have been instructed to get people to work from home to limit traffic on the roads. Trucks can often be seen spraying water on the roads. However, it is widely acknowledged that, so far, these restrictions have had little impact on the pollution levels. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
The pollution has been a problem for so long in Delhi that it has become normalised and people carry on with their daily lives in the toxic smog.Residents rarely wear masks outside and the parks will still be full of families and children and people exercising outside.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
While rich and middle class families will buy air purifiers for their homes, they are unaffordable for most poorer families who often live in makeshift tents or informal homes. As a result, breathing clean air during pollution season has become a luxury privilege in Delhi.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The pollution is not restricted to Delhi alone. All across north India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana, the air is also toxic due to coal-powered plants, vehicles and farm fires. Cities such as Amritsar in Punjab, on the border with Pakistan, also suffer from extremely dangerous air quality levels during the winter months. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images
Campaigners say more money needs to be invested into proper public transport and better vehicle emission regulation in Delhi to tackle the root causes of pollution. Every year, the number of cars on Delhi’s roads keeps rising, releasing more harmful pollutants, and yet few the percentage of electric vehicles remains very low.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Delhi has an extensive bus and metro network, but it is not sufficient to cope with the huge daily demand and still has poor connectivity in many areas. Most people still rely on polluting rickshaws, cars and motorcycles to get them to the bus stops or metro stations. Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
Delhi’s topography – a city built in a bowl-like valley, which has little breeze or rain in the winter months – means most of the emissions get trapped over the city as the cold weather hits and cloak the city in brown smog. Some call it Delhi’s “death shroud”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
In past years, the state and national government has been accused of manipulating the data to disguise how bad pollution levels are in the capital. Last year, it was found that water was being sprayed around the air quality monitors, allegedly to bring down the readings. Campaigners and opposition politicians have alleged that a lot of data from the air quality measuring stations has gone “missing”.
Environmental campaigners have argued that much more extreme measures are needed to bring pollution under control, similar to how Beijing successfully cleaned up its air in recent years. However, others have argued this would have an economic cost that India, as a developing country, can not afford.Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
One of the plans being prepared by the government this year is to experiment with “cloud-seeding”, to create rain which would clear the skies. But many residents and campaigners say that until the root causes are tackled, these plans are nothing more than a “gimmick”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

Grand Slam of Darts: Gerwyn Price produces controversial 145 checkout en route to routine victory over Sebastian Bialecki
Fourth seed Gerwyn Price hits controversial checkout in 5-2 win against Poland's Sebastian Bialecki; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports up until the final on November 22
Monday 16 November 2026 22:29, UK
Gerwyn Price produced a controversial 145 checkout en route to a routine Grand Slam of Darts victory over Sebastian Bialecki on Monday night in Wolverhampton.
Both players went into the contest with one win each after beating Joe Hunt, which made it a straight shoot-out with only the group winners reaching the knockout stage this year.
Price had opened his week with a 5-3 win over Hunt on Saturday, racing into a 4-0 lead before Hunt won three legs in a row. Bialecki needed a deciding leg to beat Hunt 5-4 on Sunday.

Price, the three-time champion in Wolverhampton came through 5-2 against Poland's Bialecki to book his place in the knockout stage.
However, there was controversy during the final Group E match as Price hit a 145 finish when he had 135 remaining in the fourth leg of the match.
'The Iceman' needed 135 to hold his throw, and he thought he had taken it out.
After hitting T19 he asked referee Charlie Corstophine what he had left and was told 88.
However, he actually needed 78.
With 88 in mind, Price incorrectly hit T16 and D20 to finish off the leg and was given the hold.
Of course, Price believed he had gone the correct route for what he needed and went on to set up a last 16 date with Ryan Searle.
"I didn't know until I just walked in," said Price in his press conference. "I hit the first treble and I asked what I'd got left and he said 88.
"So I went treble 16 double top and he said game shot. I swear to god I didn't know until I came back here!"

A Mexican Artist Sang Some of His Hits. Authorities Stopped the Show, Then Arrested Him.
A concert by the singer Gabito Ballesteros was suspended after he sang songs that supposedly glorify cartel culture. The action has renewed a debate over culture and free speech.
A popular Mexican singer’s concert was halted on Friday night because he performed songs considered to be glorifying cartel culture, making him the latest and most high-profile artist to be ensnared in a government crackdown on the genre known as narcocorridos.
He was later arrested by the federal authorities in relation to an unrelated investigation.
Gabito Ballesteros, 27, whose songs have billions of streams, was performing at a fair in Querétaro State in central Mexico when authorities escorted him off the stage.
Before the show, his set list was reviewed and approved by state officials and event organizers, according to a statement issued by the fair. Songs that glorified criminal activities were explicitly excluded, in accordance with state regulations, the fair said.
Last year, the state joined several other states and municipalities throughout Mexico that effectively prohibit the public performance of so-called narcocorridos, a version of traditional Mexican ballads that celebrate drug cartels instead of historic events and everyday life. Violations were punishable with fines or even jail time.
The actions — and the genre itself — have sparked much debate in Mexico, which has been wrestling with both the effects of organized crime, particularly amid pressure from the Trump administration to crack down on cartels, and its identity as defined through popular culture. The discussion also has became a referendum on free speech.
On Friday night, Mr. Ballesteros performed an unauthorized song and local authorities took him offstage to remind him of his prior agreement, the fair said. When he returned, the fair said Mr. Ballesteros started to perform another unauthorized song, “AMG.” The 2022 hit, which references the luxurious lifestyles and fancy cars of cartel members, has nearly one billion streams on Spotify.

Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
- Published
In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.
Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks.
The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades.
Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party.
This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.
The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false".
This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions.
Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account.
At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures.
A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency.
Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal.
Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership.
In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues".
He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time".
Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada's York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni's succession, often referred to as the "Muhoozi Project".
"Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason," he tells the BBC.
He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question.
Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general's forgiveness.
The detention of one of the country's most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu, has brought the crackdown into sharper focus.
The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region.
His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted.
"The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private," Kainerugaba wrote on X.
He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested.
The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post.
The army later confirmed Elwelu's detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations.
Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper.
They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda's most sensitive security operations.

  - Published30 October 2022
Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption.
He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had "forgiven" him.
Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor.
His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him.
Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications.
The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces.
Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge.
He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive.
"Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief," Egesa says, adding: "The arrests are not summarily done."
But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba's presidential ambitions are being targeted.
"The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi," he says.
He points to divisions between the elite Special Forces Command (SFC), which he says is largely loyal to the president's son, and army commanders who remain unconvinced about his succession.
The allegations against the officers are at different stages, with some facing charges, others in detention without publicly announced charges, and several having been released.
Bareebe also questions whether military trials can deliver independent proceedings.
"Many Ugandans regard the charges as politically motivated and therefore expect little justice," he adds.
He alleges that some officers have had charges dropped after closed-door negotiations with the president and his son, during which they were pressured to declare support for Gen Kainerugaba.
Government spokesperson Allan Kasujja dismissed the claims of a succession fallout as "hogwash".
Unlike his predecessors, who communicated through official military channels, Gen Kainerugaba frequently uses X to announce arrests, criticise public officials and comment on domestic and international affairs. Some have sparked diplomatic controversy.
On the night of 9 November, he turned his attention to Vice-President Jessica Alupo, demanding to take her job.
"Whoever is in that office should prepare to hand it over soon," he wrote, in posts that he later deleted.
He also questioned Alupo's loyalty and threatened her dismissal, adding that the government would operate "on military terms", if he became his father's deputy.
The following day, his X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, became inaccessible.
It was unclear whether he deactivated it himself, which he has done before, or the platform had suspended it.
Alupo remains in office and has yet to respond publicly.
Egesa says Gen Kainerugaba's controversial posts reflect his preferred style of communicating, but adds that security analysts are assessing their implications for Uganda's political and military stability.
Bareebe, however, sees them as part of a broader effort by the army chief to extend his influence into civilian politics.
He says the public confrontation with senior political figures illustrates how the succession debate was spilling beyond the army and into the ruling party.
Gen Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in March 2024, after previously commanding the SFC, which is responsible for protecting the president and strategic installations.
Under Uganda's military structure, he reports directly to Museveni, giving him considerable influence over the army.
Bareebe argues that the SFC's loyalty to the president and his son could prove crucial in any future transfer of power.
"The regular army remains important but has been sidelined by the SFC, which now functions as a personal army for Museveni and his son," he adds.
At the heart of the tension is the question of who will succeed Museveni, 82, who has ruled Uganda since 1986, when his rebel National Resistance Army seized power after a five-year guerrilla war.
He was sworn in for a seventh elected presidential term earlier this year, extending his rule into a fifth decade.
Gen Kainerugaba has been regarded as a possible successor and has indicated that he intends to seek the presidency in 2031, when his father's current term is due to end.
He also leads the Patriotic League of Uganda, a political movement that has mobilised support around his leadership.
But recent developments suggest that a transfer of power from father to son may be more complicated than his supporters anticipated.
At the recent meeting of the NRM leadership, one official reportedly urged Museveni to retire his son from the military and give him a civilian role to gain administrative experience, AFP reported.
Local media reported that some party officials consider Gen Salim Saleh, Museveni's younger brother, better suited for civilian leadership.
There is, however, no indication that he is interested in becoming president.
Others reportedly defended Gen Kainerugaba, pointing to his military leadership, anti-corruption campaign and grassroots political mobilisation.
Bareebe says opposition to the proposed succession has grown within the NRM, with both veteran figures and younger members concerned about what they see as an attempt to secure power through coercion.
He suggests Museveni's reluctance to move his son out of the military could reflect the importance of retaining control of the army during any transition.
"The underlying calculation appears to be that, so long as Muhoozi controls the SFC, he can use it to capture power even in an event of a contested transition," he says.
The military has been central to Museveni's hold on power, making the loyalties of senior commanders particularly important as succession questions intensify.
The family's military influence has also drawn attention to the possibility of a political dynasty spanning generations, with Gen Kainerugaba's son, Ruhamya, recently graduating from Britain's Sandhurst military academy.
The succession debate is unfolding against a backdrop of sustained pressure on the opposition.
Veteran opposition politician Kizza Besigye remains in detention on treason charges, which he denies.
Bobi Wine, who came second to Museveni in this year's presidential election, has gone into exile in the US, after being threatened by Gen Kainerugaba.
The government has consistently defended its security operations as lawful and necessary to maintain stability.
For now, Museveni remains in power.
But the arrests, his son's threats and competing accounts of divisions within the ruling party have intensified questions about how Uganda's next political transition might unfold, and what role his family may play.

Sydney Sweeney has great jeans. Who made them? (Psst: Workers)
KARACHI, Pakistan — In a slum dotted with shimmering pools of sewage, a garment worker nods in recognition as Sydney Sweeney slowly zips up her jeans in an American Eagle Outfitters advertisement playing on a smartphone.
But it's not Sweeney she recognizes — it's the jeans and jacket. This woman, a single mother, has worked on American Eagle production lines and seen those denim styles and similar models. "I know how all of them are made, because I have worked on them," she says.
When Sweeney's advertisement for American Eagle landed in July last year, with the tagline "Sydney Sweeney has great jeans," it triggered debate over whether it was a winking reference to eugenics because of Sweeney's va-va-voom beauty: thin, blonde, blue eyes, large breasts. Following the controversy, American Eagle said in a September 2025 statement that "'Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans' is and always was about the jeans." (Sweeney did not respond to NPR's request for comment.)
Missing from the debate over whether the advertisement was about jeans or genes was any significant reflection on who actually made the American Eagle jeans that Sweeney was wearing — as in, the workers. The majority of garment factories operate out of Asia, so most Americans will never meet the workers making their clothes or see the conditions they're made under.
The workers who make Sydney Sweeney's jeans
Workers like that single mother. She asks that we refer to her as S., the initial of her first name, because she fears her bosses at the garment factory where she works will fire her if she's identified. "If you raise your voice, they'll push you out," she says. "We are helpless."
S., a young woman, works at a factory run by a company called Artistic Garment Industries, where she says she's paid about $144 a month, a sum that supports her son and her mother.
She says the factory is "oppressively hot." It was 106 F outside when we met her, and she says the factory inside is even hotter. She says it's hard to leave her workstation to drink water because she has to meet her production targets. She says she has to check the quality of 1,000 to 1,600 pieces of clothing a day — and she's fainted three times this year. "I feel faint, and I can barely stand. I have no energy in my hands and feet," S. says. "They don't even let us sit down." But S. says she has no other options.
Artistic Garment Industries confirmed it makes clothes for American Eagle but tells NPR that it does not push out workers who complain about their working conditions. The company says it has a robust complaints system that workers can use and says it frequently checks on temperatures inside different parts of its factories.
In response to questions NPR sent to American Eagle, the company says it's "committed to working directly with our suppliers to protect the health, safety, and rights of workers. We take the concerns raised by workers — and those whom NPR interviewed — very seriously."
S. is one of around 20 workers we interviewed over the spring and summer in Bangladesh and Pakistan, two of the world's biggest global garment production hubs outside of China. Those men and women worked in five different factories. All of those workers asked NPR not to use their full names and to use only the initial of their first name, worried they'd lose their jobs or be blacklisted from future jobs if they were identified.
Inside the world of fast fashion
Although we focused on the American Eagle jeans worn by Sweeney for the 2025 campaign, the reporting led to a bigger issue: how fast fashion is made, because garment factories make clothes for multiple brands at once. Workers we met told us they made clothes for Levi's, Massimo Dutti, The Gap, H&M and American Eagle. They said it's common knowledge at the factories which brands they are making clothes for, in part because some workers are stitching on the labels.
The garment workers we spoke to offered strikingly similar accounts. And they echoed worker testimonies in multiple reports by labor and climate rights groups. The workers told us they're paid low wages, even as they're expected to reach what they say are unreasonably high production targets, often laboring in sweltering factories.
These are production targets like stitching 200 sleeves an hour or checking the quality of a thousand pieces of clothing a day. The workers we interviewed say they are unable to hydrate or cool down properly, even as extreme heat caused by climate change makes their workplaces and homes even hotter.
It can be four to six degrees hotter inside a factory, says Jason Judd, executive director of the Global Labor Institute at Cornell University, which researched heat inside garment factories and worker homes. "You've got all those bodies, all that material, all that machinery putting off heat. You've got ventilation problems."
"We're starting to see fainting, heat illness, exacerbation of chronic disease, even death," says Cara Schulte, a researcher at Climate Rights International. She authored two reports on the impacts of heat on garment workers.
Schulte says workers are put under that extreme pressure to reach production targets. A major reason is that brands demand their suppliers make enormous volumes of clothes on tight deadlines and on thin profit margins. And she says garment workers are vulnerable to the heat because they're clustered in countries like Bangladesh and Pakistan. She cites U.N. publications stating that those factories are "in areas that are warming faster than the global average, that are [already] incredibly hot and humid."
H&M, one of the brands that workers identified making, said it "put great effort" in ensuring fair payment to its suppliers and that labor costs are "excluded from the price negotiations of our product orders" to ensure that worker wages were not driven down.
Citing her own research, Schulte of Climate Rights International says garment workers are compelled to risk their health to survive. It's not a choice, she says. "Workers are not choosing to take these risks," she says. "They're being forced into them by poverty."
One worker's survival strategy
Like a woman who asks we call her R. When we met in February in the Bangladesh capital, Dhaka, R. said she was working six days a week, at least 12 hours a day, for $140 a month at a garment factory run by a company called MBM, which makes denim clothes, including for Levi's. Her job is to stitch 150 pieces of fabric per hour, which are assembled into jeans.
R. says she's considered old for a garment worker — around 40 — and says she's slowing down. She says she's berated by managers who tell her, "Why aren't you speeding up your work?" She says, "If you're short by even a single piece, you face a lot of harassment."
R. says she's managed to meet her targets so far. "Allah has kept me safe," she says. She says friends of hers who could not meet their targets were fired by the company. To reach her targets, R. says, she stays at her station throughout her shift. "Even going to the washroom has become extremely difficult."
So despite Dhaka reaching 98 F this summer, R. says she doesn't drink much water to avoid the need to take bathroom breaks. There's no AC on the factory floor, but R. says managers run ceiling fans and keep windows open.
R. says that if workers feel faint, their bosses will let them rest in a sick room for about 20 minutes. But, she says, management will terminate employment if workers say say they feel sick too often, so she pushes herself to keep going.
MBM did not respond to questions from NPR about worker allegations.
Despite the issues she raised, R. says she works in a good factory. She says the pay is higher than other garment factories. And if she's terminated, she says the company will pay the wages, including overtime, that she's owed. But she doesn't want to be let go.
Taking the heat
These garment factories are blazing hot in part because it's expensive to retrofit them with air conditioners. A manager for MBM, who asked that NPR not use their full name because they are not authorized to speak to media, says that the company needs a brand to commit to purchasing long term in order for retrofitting the factory to pay off. The manager says no brand had committed to that kind of long-term business.
Conditions in Bangladesh are still better than in other garment hubs, because of the scrutiny after a building collapse killed more than 1,100 garment workers in 2013. Just three weeks after that disaster, a legally binding commitment called the International Accord emerged between hundreds of brands, companies and trade unions in Bangladesh to protect worker health and safety. So far, 248 global brands and retailers have signed on, covering 2.8 million workers. A version of the International Accord was established in 2023 in Pakistan but has a smaller footprint.
There's meant to be more progress on protecting workers from extreme heat soon. Last December, the International Accord agreed to develop a protocol on heat stress. That means keeping workers cool will be an enforceable commitment for brands. For apparel companies in Bangladesh and Pakistan that have signed on to the accord, the International Accord staff will regularly inspect factories to ensure they're kept cool.
Judd, of the Global Labor Institute, says he believes there will be positive changes because the garment industry knows "they've got a problem — whether it's from a worker rights perspective, or from a business perspective, workers are slowing down, productivity is falling," he says. Either way, "you've got an interest in reducing the heat stress."
But for now, workers in Pakistan, in particular, described sweltering conditions, particularly in the port city of Karachi, one of the world's hottest garment hubs, according to the U.N.'s International Labor Organization.
In a dusty bazaar in Karachi, we met seven factory workers who mostly worked for two companies: Artistic Garment Industries — S.'s employer — and another called Artistic Milliners. Both produce clothes for big Western brands.
In their interviews with NPR, women who work, or worked, for Artistic Garment Industries described vomiting, fevers and fungal skin infections that they say were caused by the heat.
One young woman worker is I.
Her workday starts at 8:30 a.m. She says she is expected to work beyond her regular, nine-hour shift — often till 9 p.m. — and on Sundays as well, at some stretches. But she says she isn't paid all her overtime. I. also says supervisors on her floor berate workers if they leave their stations to drink water because it might cause them to miss their targets. So, I. says, "one person goes" to the water cooler and weathers the abuse, "fills a water bottle" and shares it with colleagues. I. says she gets about a glass full.
I. accuses the company of "eating" her money — and her health. "They exploit us," she says.
She says she suffers from dizziness and what she describes as a sense of fatigue and weakness. She pushes herself to work: "I can't lose my job — who else will support my family?"
Artistic Garment Industries contested these claims of unhealthful and exploitative working conditions. The company told NPR that it has a robust internal complaints system that workers could, and do, use. The company says it pays all overtime and does routine checks to ensure that the heat and humidity are not excessive on the factory floor. The company says it places water stations near workers to encourage them to hydrate and says it would not tolerate supervisors who pressure workers not to drink or use the bathroom.
Workers at Artistic Milliners described hot working conditions that badly impacted women and older male workers. One woman reported constantly feeling faint but said she pushed through. The workers said their supervisors let them drink water when they needed to, but they were pressured not to use the bathroom. Some workers said they were not paid for all the overtime they worked.
A 66-year-old former worker at Artistic Milliners, Sardar, said he was let go during the pandemic but had not been given compensation owed to him by the company. When NPR met him in June, he was homeless and relied on his children for meals. When we asked if he'd ever asked for charity, he began crying: "I'd feel ashamed if people thought I was begging."
Artistic Milliners did not respond to requests for comment about statements by Sardar and other workers. Parts of the company are certified through Fair Trade USA, a nonprofit organization that certifies companies that uphold high ethical standards for treatment of workers. NPR has sought comment from Fair Trade regarding allegations made by men and women who used to work for Artistic Milliners but has not received a response.
Answers from fast fashion brands
NPR also sent detailed questions to brands that workers said they made clothes for, alongside American Eagle.
Levi Strauss & Co. says it takes "allegations of worker rights violations seriously."
Inditex, the parent company of Zara and other labels, says Artistic Milliners, which makes clothes for one of its prominent brands, Massimo Dutti, was "subject to a corrective action plan." NPR contacted Inditex for clarification on what that corrective action plan entails but did not get a response.
Gap Inc. says it is "committed to supporting the rights and safety of workers."
H&M said in an emailed response that it has "required" AGI "to develop and implement corrective action plans to address the issues identified" by NPR: "Compliance with our requirements is a condition of our business relationship." H&M also said it recognized "the increasing risks associated with extreme heat" and is part of a pilot on heat stress in Pakistan conducted by the International Accord to develop "effective and sustainable solutions."
Those big brands partly ensure working conditions in factories are up to standard through regular audits. I. and other workers tell us they regularly saw auditors visiting their garment factory floors. They also tell NPR that supervisors give them advance warning. I. says that the supervisors "tell us to say that the working conditions are better than they actually are."
Anna Bryher is part of the workers' rights group Labor Behind the Labels, which published a report in July on the "clear mismatch" in the garment industry auditing system "between what the brands are saying and believing and hearing and what the workers report." Bryher says her findings suggest that the auditing system relied on by big brands is not working.
Artistic Garment Industries says workers may have confused regular updates informing workers of their rights with being told what to say at audits. The clothing brands that NPR reached out to did not comment on allegations regarding workers being told what to say during audits.
Some workers tell NPR that their supervisors warn them that if the workers were to criticize working conditions to auditors, the companies running the factories will lose business — and that they should paint a positive picture of their workplaces. "In other words," I. says, "they ask us to lie about everything."
With additional reporting by Hanan Biswas in Dhaka, Shahzaib Wahlah in Karachi and Abdul Sattar.

‘My father belonged to her’: Rahul Gandhi’s heartfelt tribute to Sonia Gandhi at memoir launch
Rahul Gandhi also narrated how the love story of his parents started at the Varsity restaurant in Cambridge, recalling visiting the same eatery.
"She belonged to my father, and my father belonged to her," Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said on Monday, talking about the bond between his parents, Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi.
"Mummy, Papa loved you, but I cannot even tell you how proud he would be of you," Rahul Gandhi said in a brief speech at the official launch of Sonia Gandhi's memoir, 'Belonging: A Journey of Love', published by HarperCollins India.
Rahul Gandhi also narrated how the love story of his parents started at the Varsity restaurant in Cambridge, recalling visiting the same eatery with his "girlfriend" when he was there.
"There are quite a lot of myths about my parents. One big story was their meeting at the Varsity restaurant, and how they met there. Many years later, I happened to be in Cambridge, and I told my girlfriend, 'Let's go to Varsity restaurant'. She had no idea what it was… So we went there. I wanted to see where my parents had met," the Lok Sabha leader of the opposition said.

"I still remember the yellow door. And the gentleman standing there said, 'How many people?' I said, 'Two'. And he said, 'Go and sit down'. I sat down, looked at the menu, and said, 'You know, my parents met at this restaurant'. And he just looked at me and said, 'Oh, I know them'," Gandhi said.
"And I was like, 'What do you know about them?' He said, 'Oh, those two – I know exactly who you're talking about'," Gandhi said, recalling the conversation.
The Congress leader added that when he asked what was good on the menu, he was told, 'chicken chasseur'.
"I said, 'Well, we will have two of those'. If you want to fall in love, go to Varsity restaurant. But never eat the chicken chasseur – the food is horror," he said to peals of laughter from the audience
Pointing out BJP leader Amrinder Singh, who was once very close to the Gandhis when he was in the Congress, Rahul Gandhi said the only time he saw his parents fight was when his father Rajiv was speaking with Singh on the phone and not listening to Sonia Gandhi.

Talking about the close bond between his parents, Rahul Gandhi said that at every meal, "there would be papa, and on papa's lap, there would be mama".
"Now, I thought this was a normal thing. So I would go to my friend's house, but their parents wouldn't be sitting on each other's lap, and I'd ask my friend, 'What is going on? Why is your mother not sitting on your father's lap?'" he said.
"This is what we grew up with," Rahul Gandhi added.
"And then we saw it all get smashed. Not over time – suddenly… We saw one of our anchors get shot, and then we saw our biggest anchor get blown to pieces," he said.
"So the book 'Belonging'... She belonged to my father, and my father belonged to her. When my father disappeared, she began another journey – the fun-loving mother, the smiling mother disappeared, and a new mother came. Why? Because the flame of her life had gone out, literally," Rahul Gandhi said.

Rahul Gandhi also said that Sonia Gandhi survived cancer four times, and not twice or thrice.
"She plays it all down. Not once in my life have I seen her scared, not once have I seen her back down," he said.
"Mummy, papa loved you; but I cannot even tell you how proud he would be of you," Rahul Gandhi said.

Geopolitics Looms Over Eurovision, but Not Its Asian Edition
So far, the contest’s organizers have kept politics offstage. The European edition shows how difficult that can be.
Geopolitics have long intruded on the Eurovision Song Contest. But they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia for the first time.
That was still true as of Saturday evening, when the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia took place in Bangkok.
Over the decades, Eurovision organizers have insisted that the contest is nonpolitical. Its organizers impose rules governing lyrics, political symbols and what can be broadcast. Even so, wars and diplomatic disputes have shaped who gets to sing, who stays home and what broadcasters are willing to air.
“Politics is why we watch Eurovision,” said Dean Vuletic, a historian of the show at the University of Luxembourg.
Here are some examples of geopolitics bleeding into the European edition of the contest:
- In 2009, less than a year after fighting a war with Russia, the former Soviet republic of Georgia planned to send a disco song called “We Don’t Wanna Put In” to Eurovision. Eurovision’s organizers said that the apparent dig at Vladimir Putin, then Russia’s prime minister, had to go. Georgia pulled out instead of changing it.
- In 2017, Russia pulled out of the contest in Kyiv after Ukraine barred its singer from entering the country. And five years later, after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Eurovision barred Russia altogether.
- In 2024, the war in Gaza triggered mass protests over Israel’s participation. A bitter dispute over government influence on voting followed in 2025, and there were boycotts of the contest by five countries in 2026, the biggest crisis in Eurovision’s 70-year history.
The 11 Asian countries that sent artists to Saturday’s show have plenty of offstage geopolitical friction.
Cambodia, for example, is set to sing in Thailand’s capital less than a year after a border war between the two neighbors killed dozens and displaced hundreds of thousands. As fighting picked up last year, Cambodia withdrew its athletes from the Southeast Asian Games in Thailand, citing safety concerns.
