How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
- Published
A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.
On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.
For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.
With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.
But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.
Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.
Megaspeed is a case in point.
It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
The city-state has had some success in policing this.
It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.
They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.
In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.
The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.
Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.
But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.
Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.
In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.
Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.
Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.
In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.
Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.
Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.
On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".
China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.
How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.
In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.
For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.
But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.
Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.
BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.
In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.
Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.
During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.
Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.
Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.
All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore.
"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.
Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".
But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.
With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.
Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said.
"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.
But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China".
"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."
Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.

I return to my room as my mother-in-law leaves for her office in the building adjacent to our home. I am about to start my bath when I hear a series of explosions, as of firecrackers, but different. I freeze. Someone comes pounding frantically on my bathroom door. It is Ongmu, the children’s nanny, crying hysterically. I fling open the door, my heart thumping. She is gesticulating wildly, speechlessly, towards the garden.
I run along the path leading to Akbar Road. I see the white Ambassador car slowly moving towards the same path. I hesitate. I stop, heart in my mouth. Dread, panic, fear. I feel suffocated. I can’t breathe. I am about to collapse. No, no, I can’t. I have to walk to the car. I see her being carried into it. I understand; I scream.
I’m in the car now, crouching on the floor, facing her … Blood – blood on her sari, blood on her chest. Her large eyes are wide open; her face wears a surprised expression. She doesn’t move. I attempt to speak to her, to call out, “Mummy, Mummy”, but no word comes out. I try again; she doesn’t reply.
Her aides are in the front of the car, screaming. Heavy, slow traffic, the car barely moves, it has no siren. One red light, then another. Then the hospital. The gate isn’t opening. Chaos. We are stopped; someone looks through the window in a questioning attitude. They let us in.
We reach the emergency department, teeming with people. We are stopped again, not allowed in, we have to wait for our turn. Someone calls out to the driver, signals him to move forward. They identify us; she is placed on a trolley. We are led somewhere – an operation theatre? They ask me to follow. I’m taken to a room nearby. No, no, I want to stay by her, I insist. I want to know. I have to see. They don’t reply; they are immersed in their emergency procedures.
I feel confused, lost … I don’t recognise anyone there. I’m shivering under my dressing gown. I feel scared, my mind is racing. Where is Rajiv? I try to remember. I can’t, I can’t. The children, yes, they’re in school; they must be brought home. Oh God, no, no. Let them be safe, let Rajiv be safe … Whom do I tell, whom do I speak to? I sense someone in the room. I don’t know who it is. I try to speak, to put some words together; nothing comes out. “There’s blood all over her clothes,” someone says. Some clothes are brought in for me. I am helped into them in a nearby closet.
Hours go by, agonising hours. More people come in and crowd around. I signal a question to the doctor; he shakes his head. I understand, yes, I understand. I break into sobs, uncontrollably. Someone tries to calm me. I feel numb, cold.
At two in the afternoon of 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was declared dead. I was driven home to collect some clothes for her body to be changed into. On the way, a group of men tried to stop our car, banging on its windows. They were angry, shouting something I couldn’t understand.
At home, the children, Rahul and Priyanka, rushed to my arms in tears. When they had been abruptly picked up from school by black-uniformed commandos, they sensed a catastrophe. Once home, they saw some of the staff sobbing. They asked question after question. “Where’s Mama?” “Why have we been brought home?” “Where’s Papa?” “What’s happened?” “Where’s Dadi?” “You aren’t telling us the truth!” My friends Nina and Sterre had been with them, trying to calm them down, not knowing what to say to them. I wanted to sit with them and hug them, to break the news to them gently, but I was unable to – I had to go back; Rajiv was coming to the hospital.
Rajiv had been in West Bengal at a political rally when his cavalcade was stopped by a police patrol. He was told there was a message from Delhi to say he should rush back – a serious accident had taken place. He was driven to the helipad, from where he flew to Calcutta and then to Delhi. He’d heard on a BBC bulletin that Mrs Gandhi was wounded and in a grave condition. Nobody told him directly that his mother was no more, but he understood.
He landed at 3.30pm and was driven straight to the hospital. He walked in with other people, and I remember longing to be left alone with him for a moment at least. We held each other, and as he spoke to me, it sunk in that he was saying something I didn’t want to hear. “I have been asked … They want me to be sworn in as prime minister.”
I felt as if a knife had been plunged right into my heart. I felt a pounding in my chest, a rage welling up deep inside me. I was about to explode. I attempted to hold it in. “You have been asked to? How dare they ask? How dare they? Who are they? Why you, why does it have to be you? Why did you allow them to ask you? No, it cannot be; this time it’s not going to be!” Seized by utter pain and anguish, soaked in perspiration, I felt like throwing up. I wanted to scream, to ask for help. “Someone please help me put an end to this.”
I burst out crying, pleading, begging him with folded hands, “No, no, you can’t think of it. You have to stop them, you must refuse, you must say no – for the children’s sake, for yourself. You can’t do this to us. They will kill you; they will kill you, too!” I cried out. He replied, “They will kill me anyway.”
We brought my mother-in-law home. The dining room had been emptied out, and we laid her body down on the floor, her feet pointing south as Hindu custom decrees. The same evening at around 6.30pm, Rajiv was sworn in as prime minister of India. I was too broken to even register what was happening around me. His mother lay there, her body pierced with more than 30 bullet holes. I knew, I knew it then in my heart: Rajiv’s path would lead to the same end.

A hidden defect in Microsoft’s cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company’s history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft’s report lists the incident’s final status as “a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents.”
Microsoft’s preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14.
The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft’s cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft’s incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company’s status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report, and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft’s service-health updates.
A perfect storm
Microsoft attributes the outage to three factors. A change deployed to Microsoft’s cloud gateway starting in July created a bug where, under certain conditions, CPU and memory resources could become exhausted and unresponsive. Microsoft contends that the defect was never discovered in pre-release testing because the hardware used was less powerful than some systems already deployed in production, where higher CPU core counts on newer machines apparently contributed to the lockout.
The second factor was server load. Microsoft said that “Traffic shifts during standard network maintenance and upgrades exposed a latent bug.” The company keeps two independent gateway systems in place to access Microsoft 365 for resilience. If one system encounters trouble and users can’t get through the front door, the other is opened to keep traffic flowing. According to the report, about 15 hours prior to the outage, traffic from Teams was shifted from the alternate gateway to the primary, where Exchange Online access is maintained. The switchover was a standard fail-safe, but it left the gateway handling more traffic, with a different mix of requests than before. As requests continued to pile up, affected servers exhausted their capacity and refused new connection requests.

About 65 million light-years from Earth, three galaxies don’t look quite right. They aren’t whirlpools bursting with light, but pallid objects dimly illuminated by a smattering of stars. “They have this ghostly appearance,” said Michael Keim, an astrophysicist at Yale University. And this isn’t even the weirdest thing about them.
Dark matter is the invisible glue that keeps the largest structures in the cosmos together. It draws ordinary, visible matter toward it, allowing stars to form and keeping the stelliferous limbs of galaxies from flying off. “Almost all galaxies are dominated by dark matter,” said Shyam Balaji, a theoretical physicist at King’s College London.
But these three diffuse galaxies, known as DF2, DF4, and DF9, have left astronomers stunned. After using a suite of telescopes to estimate their masses—using the motions of their stars as a proxy—the researchers found that all three have little dark matter. Instead, a pittance of ordinary matter alone must have forged their small selection of stars. How could these rule-breaking galaxies have formed?
A paper published in June 2026 in The Astrophysical Journal offers a potential solution. Once upon a time, two regular galaxies collided. Their ordinary matter—their gas and dust—swirled about and got clumped up. But the dark matter passed right through and continued on, like a specter passing through a wall. The cosmic pileup left behind three new galaxies, each bereft of dark matter, each left to struggle to form a new batch of stars.
It’s a convincing explanation for many experts—one that, crucially, may tell us something about the mystery of dark matter.
Some scientists have suggested that dark matter, which has yet to be directly detected, may not exist. Instead, they propose that a tweak to our understanding of the gravitational force might explain various features of the universe.
These bizarre galaxies pour cold water on that idea. “What this is showing is that dark matter is … not just a modification of gravity,” said Keim, who is an author of the new study. If you segregate ordinary matter from dark matter, you’d expect that the dark-matter-lacking galaxies would struggle to form stars—and that’s what DF2, DF4, and DF9 show.
That suggests, as many have suspected for some time, that dark matter is a physical thing. “The absence of dark matter is, in a way, some evidence of dark matter, which is ironic,” Balaji said.
What, exactly, is dark matter? Ever since it was formally proposed by the astronomer Fritz Zwicky in the 1930s—and built upon in the 1970s by the astronomer Vera Rubin—cosmologists and astrophysicists have been putting forward their best candidates. Could it be a stealthy type of neutrino? Might it be so-called weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs? Some have even opined that it could be primordial black holes as small as individual atoms and as old as the universe itself.
“We don’t know which dark matter candidate is the right one,” said Daniel Whiteson, a particle physicist at the University of California, Irvine. Whatever it is, it has yet to be detected. But “there’s a lot of independent lines of evidence that dark matter is matter.”
Dark matter, which makes up 27 percent of the universe—and 85 percent of all matter—interacts with gravity. If it were down to the gravitational pull of ordinary matter alone, stars on the edges of rapidly spinning galaxies would escape into space. Ordinary matter alone would struggle to clump together tightly enough to form stars. Dark matter also seems to warp space itself, bending light around objects in a process known as gravitational lensing.
“You wouldn’t get galaxies without dark matter,” said Chamkaur Ghag, a physicist at University College London. “Is there a way of evolving the galaxies without dark matter in the first place? Our understanding says no.”
So when DF2 was discovered in 2018, astronomers didn’t quite know what to make of it. The galaxy is roughly the same size as the Milky Way, but with 200 times fewer stars, it’s considerably dimmer. Suspicious, scientists used the Keck Observatory in Hawaii to track the motions of those stars to estimate the galaxy's total mass. They discovered that, even for such a star-deficient galaxy, it was lightweight: It seemed to contain, at most, 400 times less dark matter than they would expect, making DF2 the first dark-matter-deficient galaxy ever spotted.
In 2019, they observed DF4, another phantom galaxy with a dearth of dark matter. And in 2026, scientists announced that a third, DF9, had joined the club. It contains the mass of roughly 100 million suns, which is consistent with having only ordinary matter. If it were also packed with dark matter, it would be 100 times more massive.
That all three gossamer galaxies existed along a line, as neighbors, didn’t escape the attention of astrophysicists, who began to coalesce around an origin story.
Dark matter is only known to act with the gravitational force; there’s no compelling evidence yet that it interacts with other fundamental forces, like electromagnetism. If two typical galaxies met in a head-on collision, the dark matter would experience very little friction, or drag, and would keep on rocketing by. But ordinary matter, which interacts using all four fundamental forces, would get all tangled up.
“An analogy would be two knights jousting, where the knights and their lances collide and may be thrown to the ground in a heap, while their horses keep on running at full speed,” said Aaron Romanowsky, an astronomer at San Jose State University.
Several independent experts buy the tale spun by Keim and his colleagues. “It’s very convincing,” Whiteson said.
It’s reminiscent of the Bullet Cluster, two massive collections of galaxies 3.8 billion light-years away that also collided eons ago. This destruction derby, which was recently observed by the James Webb Space Telescope, has a messy distribution of mass that only makes sense if dark matter and ordinary matter got torn asunder during the collision.
Although this kind of segregation can be seen with greater clarity in DF2, DF4, and DF9, not everyone agrees on how the separation took place.
Kinwah Wu, a theoretical astrophysicist at University College London, noted that the triplet does not exhibit any of the fluid, wispy features that one would expect to see after a galactic collision. He suggests that, in this case, DF2, DF4, and DF9 were passing through a large group of massive galaxies. This outsize rabble then stripped the triplet of all their dark matter during their ill-fated voyage.
Stacy McGaugh, an astronomer at Case Western Reserve University and a longtime proponent of modified-gravity theories, is more skeptical. “It’s not clear to me what the formation mechanism is,” he said. An ancient collision “is a plausible origin story, albeit an exceptional one. If that’s what’s happened, then the rest follows.” In other words: If these galaxies were created when their dark matter was stolen away, then it makes sense that dark matter is a physical substance.
“But the question is: Is that what happened?” he continued. “And I’m not convinced that that’s the only way that can happen.” Without definitively knowing their origin story, McGaugh doesn’t think it’s possible to say anything about the nature of dark matter itself.
Most experts, though, cannot see how DF2, DF4, and DF9 could exist without dark matter being a physical thing, even if the trio’s genesis can be debated. “It’s hard to explain how you’d get something like this evolving by itself without something like dark matter,” Ghag said.
That makes this galactic trio bad news for MOND, or modified Newtonian dynamics, an alternative to dark matter proposed in 1983 by the physicist Mordehai Milgrom. “MOND says: What if there’s only visible matter, but its gravity works differently than we thought?” Whiteson explained.
MOND implies that, when objects are experiencing a very weak gravitational pull—for example, when two stars are separated by extreme distances—the gravitational force doesn’t dwindle as much as scientists think. That could explain why spinning galaxies can be held together without needing an extra source of gravity from dark matter, its proponents have argued.
Dark matter has long been the favored theory for cosmologists, as MOND “could never really explain everything,” Ghag said. He explained that MOND suffered a significant blow in 2015 when the US-based Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, or LIGO, detected gravitational waves—ripples in the fabric of the universe—for the first time. Scientists found that these waves move at the speed of light in all directions over huge distances, which implies that gravity works in a consistent, unmodified way throughout the cosmos.
DF2, DF4, and DF9 are also more elegantly explained by dark matter than by attempts to adjust the mechanics of gravity. “It’s easier to remove matter, cold dark matter, through something like a collision, than it is to turn off a law of nature,” Balaji said.
“I think it’s fine and healthy to have alternative theories and open debate,” Whiteson said. “But let’s also be frank about whether the theory fits the data. MOND does not.”
The identity of dark matter still eludes us. But these galaxies are arguably another nail in the coffin of its increasingly unpopular competitor.

Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of greenhouse gas emissions.
US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
The latest numbers are in on how much energy hyperscale data centers use and the carbon pollution they create.
The study homes in on hyperscale facilities — the massive structures spanning millions of square feet that developers are racing to build in large part to support generative AI. Researchers say the findings show that there’s a lot of work left to do to cut down pollution stemming from AI’s reliance on fossil fuels.
“We tend to discuss AI’s environmental footprint as though it were some fixed property of the technology, when in reality the same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it,” Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the new study and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, says in an email to The Verge. “I actually find that encouraging, because it means these impacts aren’t inevitable. We have choices about where we build and how we power this infrastructure.”
“The same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it.”
Guidi and his team used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated how much carbon pollution each data center would have produced if connected to the local power grid between May 2024 and April 2025.
Altogether, the 403 hyperscale facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity that year, about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption. That’s even more than the amount of electricity that about 148 nations — a majority of the countries in the world including Austria, Israel, and Venezuela but excluding the largest economies including the US and China — individually burn through each year, according to John Sterman, director of the MIT System Dynamics group and MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative.
Electricity demand from these data centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions, comparable to the annual carbon footprint of Denmark, according to the research paper. Sterman says that exceeds the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations. That’s because about 54 percent of the electricity the hyperscale facilities consumed likely came from gas and coal.
Sterman, who was not involved in the research with Guidi, disclosed that he used the help of Claude to compare the paper’s findings to electricity use and emissions of countries. “I think AI can be extraordinarily helpful,” Sterman says. “But we’ve got to figure out a way to limit the harms … Especially because those impacts are irreversible. Once you allow these data centers to emit the CO2, you can never undo that.”
Sterman says policymakers should require data center operators to bring new clean energy online. The study doesn’t account for local air pollution that can result from new gas infrastructure that’s being built to meet data center demand, or gas turbines that some AI companies have installed at their facilities to power themselves without connecting to the grid. And while hyperscale data centers encompass more than just AI-related computing, they also make up just a fraction of the thousands of data centers in the US — with more cropping up each year.
The study showed how big a difference the local electricity mix makes when it comes to the environmental impact of AI and data centers. Generating electricity in heavily coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon. “Two data centers consuming exactly the same amount of electricity can have dramatically different carbon footprints simply because of where they’re located,” Guidi writes.
Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University who was also not involved in the study, says the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in.” “Power plants and supporting infrastructure built to meet rapidly growing data center demand may operate for decades. Decisions made today could therefore shape emissions well into the future,” You says in an email to The Verge.
Both You and Guidi also pointed out how problematic it is that researchers have to go through such great lengths to estimate energy consumption because data center operators won’t disclose that information. To that end, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a website to track the environmental impact of individual data centers. A bipartisan bill making its way through Congress could also mandate greater disclosures nationally on data centers’ electricity use.
“Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step.” Gina McCarthy, former White House national climate advisor and EPA administrator, said in a statement shared by the research authors.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Mohan Yadav on Tuesday described the upcoming Cabinet meeting at Gandhi Sagar as distinct from previous meetings, saying the initiative aims to highlight the region’s development potential, promote tourism and create employment opportunities.
The Chief Minister also highlighted the Rs 11,474 crore 'pumped hydro storage project' with a proposed power generation capacity of around 2,000 MW, emphasising that the pumped storage project would enable the state to generate and supply electricity during peak demand hours by recycling water, providing significant economic benefits.
“The Gandhi Sagar Cabinet meeting is different from all the Cabinet meetings we have held so far. We are holding a Cabinet meeting at a location which stands to gain both in terms of recognition and the creation of employment opportunities, for a variety of reasons. A new method of power generation through our pumped storage system has been introduced, in which water is recycled. During peak hours, when electricity demand is high, power can be generated quickly and supplied immediately,” the CM said.
He added that it would provide significant economic benefits to the states, ensuring electricity availability at all times at nearly half the cost.
“When the pumped storage facility operates at almost full capacity during peak hours, it will generate approximately 2,000 MW of electricity. The project has a cost of Rs 11,474 crore. I hope that, just as the Prime Minister encourages innovation and promotes public welfare initiatives through new technologies, this project will also serve as a remarkable destination, particularly for those interested in science,” the CM said.
He further stressed that Madhya Pradesh is rich in natural resources and solar power will be used to fill the upper reservoir with water. After that, during periods of high demand, the stored water will be used to generate electricity immediately and efficiently.
Meanwhile, speaking about Gandhi Sagar’s tourism and historical significance, the Chief Minister said the ongoing Cheetah Project, ancient rock formations, inscriptions and prehistoric paintings made the region an important destination for tourism and archaeology.
“We hope that the Cheetah Project underway at Gandhi Sagar will further strengthen its position as an exceptional tourism destination. The region has ancient crystalline rock formations bearing inscriptions and paintings from the era of early humans. The entire area is significant from archaeological, tourism and religious perspectives. Through its vast water reservoir, several local fishermen will also benefit from fish production through cage culture,” Yadav said.

Cabinet Destination Meet Helps To Solve Area-Specific Problem: CM Mohan Yadav
“We have undertaken several initiatives to bring the information and importance of these places before society. The Italianization of Europe
Over more than a quarter-century, I’ve watched Europe’s politics become more like Italy’s, with all the resulting instability, as the far right came in from the cold.
When I first moved to Rome, I spent my time living in the past.
At the turn of the century, I drifted through a vintage postcard of postwar Italy: old women sitting around tables they had dragged into the street, old men playing cards in caps, cats arching their backs on the hoods of snub-nosed Fiats.
As newspapers filled with talk of Silvio Berlusconi, a media mogul with ambitions and appetites worthy of a Roman emperor, my meanderings inevitably took me toward Tiber Island, a sliver of land in the middle of the river that divides Rome.
An ancient bridge on the island’s left bank had a strange statue of weather-beaten faces positioned back-to-back as if they couldn’t stand one another. The heads rose out of the shared torso of a square pillar and represented Janus, Rome’s god of the past and future, the deity of transitions and change.
Back then, I didn’t see the change around me, but now, more than a quarter-century later, after spending decades reporting on Italian politics and changes across Europe, I have come to understand that I was living in the future.
In the time since, I have seen an Italianization of politics all around the continent, with coalitions of small parties resulting in instability, with fed-up voters desperate for new saviors. But more than anything, I have seen — in Britain, France, Germany — countries following the Italian model by allowing the far right into the political mainstream.

Happy World Kindness Day! Check out our kind photos of kindness to humans — and cats
Editor's note: Today, November 13, is World Kindness Day!
Kind-minded organizations from various countries came up with the idea and announced it on November 13, 1998. (And the date stuck.) The goal is kinda obvious — do something kind!
It doesn't matter if it's a modest action. One of the founding groups is the Small Kindness Movement of Japan. And no kind deed is too small to acknowledge. One year, the Japanese movement gave an award to a cabbie who pulled over to clear trash bags off the road lest they cause an accident. According to a report in the Christian Science Monitor, the cab driver humbly said it was "no big deal."
So on Friday, November 13, 2026, try a little kindness. To inspire you, we've talked to folks whose lives were changed by kindness — and asked the photojournalists of The Everyday Projects, a global network, to submit pictures that capture a kind moment. Animal lovers will be happy to see photos of kindness toward animals as well as an image of a support donkey — a reminder that animals can be kind to us humans, too.
Let's start with a simple yet profound story about a snack.
Back in 2004, Maymunah Yusuf Kadiri, a neuro-psychiatrist and mental health advocate in Nigeria, was a young doctor working in the emergency room at the Lagos State University Teaching hospital. One night sticks in her mind. It was chaos. There were accident victims everywhere. She recalls the blood, the cries and her own exhaustion.
"I hadn't eaten for over 12 hours, and my hands were shaking," says Kadiri, who was 28 at the time. "Then an elderly cleaner, one of those invisible heroes in hospitals, walked up to me with a small nylon bag." Inside was a biscuit and a sachet of water.
"Doctor," she said, "you need small strength to save people."
"It sounds simple, but I'll never forget it. That biscuit tasted like hope. Her kindness reminded me that healing isn't only about medicine, it's about humanity," says Kadiri. "As a psychiatrist, I've seen it over and over: People don't just heal in hospitals, they heal in human connections."
And while one isolated act of kindness may seem random, it can lead to much more.
Huguette Diakabana remembers when she had to drop out of school at age 10 — until a mysterious donor came to her rescue. Her family was planning to emigrate to the U.S. from Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of Congo) and couldn't afford school fees. They figured she'd make up the year later. She had a different idea: "I put on my previous year's uniform and sat outside under the street window of my would-be classroom." One day, the director invited her inside. Diakabana realized someone must have paid her school fees, but who?
Returning to the school years later, Diakabana discovered it was a school guard. She wanted to repay him. "He told me to help others when I could, so I launched a scholarship program," says Diakabana, who now lives in Switzerland and is co-founder of The Luminous Agency, which focuses on digital literacy.
Dr. Junaid Nabi, a physician-scientist who conducts research in health care technology at the RAND School in Washington, D.C. and is a senior fellow at the Aspen Institute, says he's come to realize that kindness isn't actually a trickle in the ocean. An act of kindness is more like dropping a stone that creates expanding ripples, he says.
"There are studies that illustrate how kindness spreads through social networks in measurable ways. When we are kind to someone, they don't just feel better — they become 25% more likely to help others."
One such investigation described how kindness can be contagious. It was sparked by reports of an outbreak of kindness on a cold December morning in 2012. A stranger picked up the tab for the coffee order of the next customer in the drive-through line at a Tim Hortons coffeehouse in Winnipeg, Canada. And that customer picked up the tab of the person behind him. In the end, 226 customers passed on this act of kindness.
The study authors, citing other examples of "pay it forward" kindness at fast food restaurants and their own experiments encouraging subjects to help others, write: "Why, in the absence of external sanctions and opportunities for reciprocation, do people help strangers? One possible explanation is that helping is driven by receiving or observing help. In other words, generosity towards strangers may be socially contagious."
Don't talk yourself out of it
It might sound contradictory, but researchers studying the psychology of altruism, kindness and giving have uncovered this curious paradox: Sometimes, people can be kind-hearted, have a genuine desire to help someone, but in spite of that, not give at all.
Marta Serra-Garcia, a professor of economics and strategy at the Rady School of Management in the University of California, San Diego, is one of the authors of the study Give Enough or Not at all.
"There's a growing body of work in economics and psychology trying to understand altruism. Altruism is a result of a feeling of empathy and the emotion of feeling warm and well when you help others. We know people are altruistic, but we're trying to understand when, why and how," she says.
The study, published in the September Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, revealed that people may prefer to give nothing rather than donate an amount they consider too small — even when those on the receiving end would welcome whatever they can get.
"It seems like an odd thing," Serra-Garcia says in an interview over a video call with NPR. "You're generous, but because you want to do the right thing, you might end up not giving at all, out of concern that your gift would be viewed as inappropriate or might even offend the other person."
In one experiment in the study, givers tended to overestimate the minimum amount recipients would consider acceptable.
"We tend to think there are givers and non-givers," says Serra-Garcia. "The people who give are the generous and kind ones, the non-givers are just not generous." But the study indicates otherwise.
"That perception of appropriateness makes them think, "I'd rather not give at all, although I'm a generous person," says Serra-Garcia.
Nature or nurture?
And where does kindness come from? Are you born with it? Or can you learn to be compassionate and empathetic?
Jeff R. Temple, a professor and psychologist with UTHealth Houston, says kindness is a central thread running through his studies on healthy relationships among adolescents and young adults.
"In our intervention work — including with the Fourth R program and other school-based curricula — we teach adolescents to practice perspective-taking, to express care even during disagreement and recognize the impact of their words and actions. These are essentially the behavioral expressions of kindness."
Such kids are less likely to bully others because they know what healthy relationships are like, he says.
A ripple effect
And let's not forget that kindness can change not only the life of the recipient of the kind deed but of the kind person, says Nabi, who offers this anecdote.
In the 2013 Savar building collapse in Bangladesh, more than 1,000 garment workers died and thousands were injured. Nabi arrived at the disaster site as a Red Cross volunteer, expecting to gain experience in trauma care. Instead, he says, the experience changed his psyche, teaching him about the nature of true kindness.
"In the midst of chaos, with bodies awaiting identification, kindness came down to being present during others' darkest moments," says Nabi. "I performed CPR on workers I knew wouldn't survive and when I couldn't save someone, I stayed by their side, holding their hand."
"Before Savar, I was mechanistic, rushing through clinical work like tasks," he recalls. "The image of workers who had embraced each other as concrete crushed them — that final act of human kindness in the face of death — shattered my callousness completely."
When he returned to the hospital, he listened to patients differently, giving them more of his time. He also urges doctors to volunteer for humanitarian causes to practice compassion.
"Kindness, I learned, is about showing up completely for another person's suffering," Navi reflects, "and letting that experience fundamentally change who you are."
So if you began reading this story with the thought that World Kindness Day is … a gimmick … it is a gimmick imbued with heart and hope.
It's a good reminder to practice kindness more, Dr. Kadiri says. "And here's the beautiful part: When someone receives kindness, they don't just feel better, they become better." They may be inspired to perform their own act of kindness. And that, she says, makes the world a kinder, better place too.
Your turn: Readers! Have you ever had a life-changing moment because of an act of kindness. Share your story with us by emailing globalhealth@npr.org. We'll consider all submissions for a follow-up story. Be sure to tell us how to contact you if we are interested in featuring your anecdote.

Fear, outrage grow as Quebec moves to ban religious symbols for elementary students
Experts say PQ's plan would cause harm, say it's 'misguided' and 'disrespectful'
Mehwaish Raja’s 11 year-old daughter surprised her during a conversation this past summer on the way to day camp.
“She shared with me during the car ride: ‘Mama, I will wear my hijab at the end of the summer,’” Raja said.
Up until that point, her daughter only wore the hijab for special occasions, and Raja had never insisted she wear it regularly.
“I just said, ‘OK.’ And by the end of the summer, it actually happened,” Raja said.
Her daughter now wears the hijab every day in her Grade 5 class in a public school in Montreal’s West Island.
Now, the new Parti Québécois government is proposing a law that would make that practice illegal as part of a series of measures announced on the campaign trail to strengthen secularism.
Raja is struggling to understand why.
“Honestly, I'm out of words. I'm out of words when I hear things like this,” she said.
She doesn’t think the government should be able to decide what her daughter wears to school.
“When we step out of our house, we leave as who we are. What part of us do we leave at home?” she said.
Religious symbols gradually squeezed out of schools
The previous CAQ government already introduced several laws restricting religious symbols in schools, preventing at first teachers, and then all school staff – even parent volunteers – from wearing them.
Generally, religious symbols bans in Quebec have targeted employees of the state considered to be in positions of authority, but the CAQ opened the door to targeting students by introducing a ban on full face coverings at school.
Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is opening that door wider, proposing a blanket ban preventing elementary school students from wearing "conspicuous" religious symbols while at school.
“Separating children through what they wear and through religious beliefs at such a young age is not helping cohesion and integration,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in September when announcing the measure, without providing any specific examples.
“We think it's a good policy in terms of letting children just be children, with no connection whatsoever to what their parents believe about religion,” he'd said.
When proposing the religious ban for elementary schools during the election campaign, PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said the symbols 'interfere with cohesion and integration.' (Ivanoh Demers/CBC/Radio-Canada)
Winning a minority government in the general election did not soften the PQ's resolve, with new Education Minister Joël Arseneau saying the measure was a "non-negotiable."
"It’s on this basis that we were elected, and it’s on this basis that we’re working,” Arseneau told reporters at the National Assembly in late October.
Mother says proposed law based on misconceptions
Asma Qureshi says the PQ's proposal comes from a place of ignorance.
Qureshi, who lives on Montreal’s South Shore, has four children. Her oldest daughter, now in high school, started wearing a hijab to school when she was in Grade 4. Her youngest daughter, currently in kindergarten, wore one to school a couple of times this year just to try it.
Qureshi – who wears a hijab herself – says in both cases, she didn’t ask or order her daughters to wear one.
"I told myself that I would never impose it on my kids," she said.
"There’s this narrative that goes around – and it's been there since I was a young kid – that children and women are being forced to wear the scarf."
Qureshi thinks that misconception is what’s feeding the gradual tightening of restrictions on wearing religious symbols in Quebec, particularly in schools.
She says she hasn’t yet discussed the proposed ban with her daughters.
“How do you tell a child it’s against the law for you to wear something that your mother wears?” she said.
Raja says her daughter's decision to start wearing the hijab regularly this fall convinced her to do the same. (CBC News)
For Raja, who up until now had been reluctant to wear a hijab in Quebec for fear of standing out, says her daughter's decision to wear one at school this fall convinced her to do the same.
“I'm really proud of her because at 11 years old, she decided to wear it, whereas I’m 40 and I hadn't been able to,” she said.
“My daughter truly inspired me."
Ban would cause harm, experts say
Experts in secularism and child development told CBC there is no justification for banning students from wearing religious symbols — and that the measure would be harmful.
Thomas Dee, an economist at Stanford University who specializes in how education policy affects student outcomes, disagreed with the notion of asking children to leave their parents' religious baggage behind.
“Parents are children's first and most impactful teachers, and to sideline their guidance and insights just seems misguided to me and disrespectful,” he said.
Dee testified as an expert witness in the court challenge to Bill 21, Quebec’s first secularism law.
Thomas Dee, an economics professor at Stanford University who studies the effects of education policy on student outcomes, says a policy that marginalizes parents' values in school is misguided and disrespectful. (CBC News)
Sivane Hirsch, a professor in the faculty of education at Université Laval who specializes in cultural and religious diversity in schools, believes the ban is a horrible idea.
“We don’t want children to feel they’re being taught in school against their parents, against their family,” Hirsch said.
Dee said such a conflict would also hurt students’ performance.
“Anything that makes students feel less welcome or less at ease will imply they're not able to bring their full attention and motivation to the realization of their academic potential,” Dee said.
Zeinab Diab, a religious studies researcher at Université de Montréal and author of Au nom de la laïcité, a book about Islamophobia in Quebec, said a secularism law that targets young children is inhumane.
“They are dehumanizing them and limiting their access to school. What kind of society allows that?” she said.
Author and religious studies researcher Zeinab Diab says targeting children for a religious symbols ban is inhumane. (CBC News)
Dee said the presence of religious symbols in the classroom could actually help.
“If you engage with people across difference, you no longer use simple rules of thumb to judge them, but rather you judge them as people,” he said.
Qureshi said that was her daughter’s experience.
She said no other students made negative comments or gave her daughter a hard time when she started wearing the hijab.
“It was just like she was any other regular person,” she said. “That's the beautiful thing – when people can recognize you for who you are rather than what you wear."
PQ needs support of at least 1 other party
In order to adopt the ban, the PQ will need support from at least one other party in the National Assembly.
Charles Milliard, leader of the Quebec Liberals and the Official Opposition, said last week his party wouldn’t support the measure.
“We're talking about children. I'm not going to do politics on the backs of children,” Milliard said.
Québec Solidaire also doesn’t support the measure.
That leaves the Conservative Party of Quebec.
On Monday, leader Éric Duhaime said his party generally supports secularism, but wanted to see more details before deciding whether to support the proposed law.
"I mean, what are we going to do with those kids if they don't respect the rules?" Duhaime told reporters.
"That's the kind of thing that I want to know before we move forward."
Education Minister Joël Arseneau says he's negotiating with other parties about the idea of banning religious symbols for elementary school students, and that their positions may evolve. (CBC News)
Last week, Arseneau said he was in negotiations with other parties about the bill, and that their positions may evolve. He declined CBC’s request for an interview.
Raja says if the ban does become law, her daughter would likely leave her current school.
“If the public system is really asking us not to practise certain values that we strongly believe in, I would choose another way of educating my children,” she said.
For her that would likely be private school, but she said some other parents might choose homeschooling.
Diab said not all families have either the money or the time for those options.
“Maybe they’re going to adapt, but no one should be always in fight and survival mode,” she said.
“This is exhausting.”

New Delhi: At COP31, India made a strong case for moving beyond all the talk about fair energy transitions and actually implementing them. Developing countries need the money, technology, and training to do it in their own way. COP31 is the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Environment minister Bhupender Yadav stated at a ministerial roundtable that a ‘just transition’ (a shift to cleaner energy that doesn’t leave workers and the most vulnerable behind) cannot be one-size-fits-all. Yadav was addressing the Fourth Annual High-Level Ministerial Roundtable on Just Transition under the UAE Just Transition Work Programme at the UN climate conference COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. India is in favour of a new body that would help countries translate what they learn from UN negotiations into action. Yadav said the member states themselves should steer the body, and it should not be the body’s function to provide sectoral pathways or impose any new obligations. The pressure is on as the poorer countries seek to strike a balance between climate action and their own needs for growth, energy security and poverty reduction. India has long maintained that the balance should be in accordance with each country’s level of development. The minister underlined the need for clearly defined and complementary roles for the UAE Just Transition Work Programme and the proposed Just Transition Mechanism. While the Work Programme should continue to provide a platform for dialogue and the exchange of experiences, the Mechanism should facilitate practical support through technical assistance, capacity-building, and cooperation, translating the lessons from ongoing discussions into action, he stated. The mechanism should build on existing initiatives, avoid duplication and improve access to the resources needed for implementation. It should not prescribe uniform sectoral pathways or impose new obligations on countries, but enable them to pursue transition strategies based on their national priorities, Yadav added. His remarks come amid broader discussions on how developing countries can balance climate action with economic growth, energy security and poverty reduction. Vijay C. Switzerland 4-0 Scotland: Andy Robertson breaks caps record as Scots fall to heavy Nations League defeat
Match report as Scotland lose to Switzerland in their final Nations League Group B1 match; Lewis Ferguson's own-goal put the hosts ahead; Winsley Boteli, Alvyn Sanches and Zeki Amdouni scored in the second half; Scotland will remain in League B for the next Nations League tournament
Tuesday 17 November 2026 01:09, UK
Andy Robertson created Scotland history, then delivered a scathing assessment of their Nations League collapse against Switzerland.
On the night he became the men's record appearance holder with 103 caps, Sebastien Pocognoli came under pressure with a bruising 4-0 defeat in St Gallen.
"That cannot happen in international football," he told BBC Scotland after the match.
"I don't think you've got time in international football, you have to do it. These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden, who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.
"We don't have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up.
"We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow."
The Scots were comfortable against the much-changed Group B1 winners until the 22nd minute when midfielder Lewis Ferguson put through his own goal.
The unforced error deflated the visitors, who lost wing-back Aaron Hickey to injury before the break, and there was more damage in the 47th minute when Samuel Ballet's drive was touched in by Winsley Boteli before Alvyn Sanches hammered in a third just four minutes later, with substitute Zeki Amdouni adding a late fourth.
The Scots finished third in the group behind Switzerland and Slovenia, with seven points from 18, missing out on a promotion play-off spot next year and a more favourable seeding for the European Championship qualifying draw next month.
The Belgian boss' first campaign as Steve Clarke's successor has been underwhelming to say the least with just two wins - both against bottom side North Macedonia - from six fixtures and Pocognoli now finds himself under the spotlight just months into his tenure.
The key moments from Berit Sitterstadion
2: SAVE! A comfortable save for Angus Gunn but Isaac Schmidt is given too much time to get a shot away. An early warning.
17: CHANCE! John McGinn hooks the ball over the bar as Scotland continue to pile on the pressure.
22: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Disaster for Scotland as Lewis Ferguson sticks out his leg and sends the ball into his own net.
24: CLOSE! Almost an equaliser from Aaron Hickey. He gets his head to Andy Robertson's cross, but it's just past the post.
36: INJURY! Hickey pulls up holding his hamstring and his night is over.
42: CHANCE! Nathan Patterson sends the ball in to McGinn but he heads straight at the goalkeeper. An opportunity missed.
44: CHANCE! That should be a second for Switzerland! Adrian Bajrami gets on the end of the cross but somehow heads the ball well off target.
47: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Samuel Ballet plays a one-two with Remo Freuler, and Winsley Boteli gets the last touch to put the Swiss two up.
51: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Alvyn Sanches gets on the end of a ball from Boteli and fires across Gunn and into the net.
66: SAVE! Gunn pulls off a save to deny Ballet a fourth for the hosts and Luke Graham is there to block Zeki Amdouni's follow-up effort.
72: OVER! Scott McTominay gets on the end of Kieran Tierney's cross and somehow blasts it over the bar.
85: SUB! Kristi Montgomery replaces Ferguson as he makes his Scotland debut.
89: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Amdouni's shot from the edge of the box takes a deflection off Graham as it goes past Gunn.
What now for Pocognoli?
Almost a year on from the elation of Scotland beating Denmark to reach the World Cup, it now looks like a struggle to reach Euro 2028.
Scotland will be in Pot 3 when the draw is made next month, and there is a lot of improvement needed before the qualifying campaign then kicks off in March.
In his first six games as Steve Clarke's successor, Sebastien Pocognoli has won just two. Both against North Macedonia.
They had a decent first 20 minutes in St Gallen, but this was not Switzerland's best team.
Murat Yakin was without Granit Xhaka, Dan Ndoye, Manuel Akanji and Johan Manzambi and they still made it look easy against the Scots who managed just one shot on target. A tame one.
How much time should the new Scotland head coach bet given? Following the man who led the nation to three major tournaments was always going to be a hard act to follow, but the team appears to have regressed.
Pocognoli positive about Scotland's future
Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli speaking to BBC Scotland:
"The score is heavy with the 4-0, but I don't think it's a reflection of the game, if I'm really honest and objective.
"I think we had some very good moments in the game, we started the game like we wanted, aggressive away from home.
"I think if we were in confidence, we would not produce the moments we produce in the game.
"I think we create good moments on the ball, on pure bravery decisions to play forward through the lines or the pressure.
"We create chances also for pressing, sometimes we should have to manage better the transition from pressing, but it is all the things we want to see.
"So the next step is to have the quality to just finish this action, and the more we have games together, the more we will try to fix these things.
"We have a lot of good response from this camp and it's good for the future as well."
Robertson: 'That can't happen, we've got to step up'
Scotland captain Andy Robertson speaking to BBC Scotland:
"First half we were in the game but lost a stupid goal. But I thought we had chances and should have made it one each at half-time.
"We talked about it at half-time, we told ourselves to keep going and the time you get to 50 minutes, you're 3-0 down? That cannot happen in international football.
"That's what happened tonight. We were playing against a good team. But while we were in the game in the first half, you have to do it for 90 minutes. Then you're 3-0 down, it's a tough place to come and that. A really tough night for us."
