On Nov. 10, the U.S. House of Representatives voted on articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has been the face of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran that began in February.
The impeachment effort failed in a 211-204 vote, which many Democrats blamed on 11 of their fellow party members who were absent from the voting chamber.
The 11 absent Democrats were Reps. Julia Brownley, Melanie Stansbury, Brittany Pettersen, Laura Gillen, Nancy Pelosi, Haley Stevens, Marilyn Strickland, Frederica Wilson, Jonathan Jackson, Steven Horsford and J. Luis Correa.
Social media users claimed some of those 11 missed the vote because they were attending an event related to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a powerful pro-Israel lobbying group.
The event in question was reportedly hosted by Elect Democrat Women. According to the nonprofit OpenSecrets, the top donor to the Elect Democrat Women-affiliated super PAC, EDW Action Fund, was the United Democracy Project — a super PAC affiliate of AIPAC.
Drop Site News, a nonprofit investigative news outlet, reportedly obtained an RSVP list of the event showing that three of the 11 Democrats who missed the vote were present at the event: Brownley, of California, Stansbury, of New Mexico, and Pettersen, of Colorado. As of this writing, the reported RSVP list was not publicly available and Drop Site News did not reveal how it sourced the list.
Two of the representatives, Brownley and Pettersen, reportedly acknowledged attending the Elect Democratic Women event. However, none of them had responded to our requests for comment by the time of publication. Until we hear directly from the representatives' offices or primary evidence confirming their attendance emerges, we've left this claim unrated.
On Nov. 11, USA Today reporter Zach Schermele posted that Brownley told him she "left last night's Elect Democratic Women event for the Hegseth vote with plenty of time to spare" and that "when the traffic jam made it clear she might not make it in time, she and other lawmakers started texting each other." He reported that Brownley, 74, then got out of her car and started running, missing the vote by "seconds" (archived).
According to Denver NBC affiliate KUSA, Pettersen acknowledged she attended the event, saying in a statement, "Last night, I was late to the floor and there is no excuse for that. I was at an Electing Democratic Women event."
Stansbury posted a video on Nov. 11 apologizing for her absence, saying, "I know I should've been there at that moment." She blamed rush-hour traffic on Independence Avenue for her absence. She did not mention the EDW event, though her comments were flooded with users accusing her of attending it.
Because the reported RSVP list was not publicly available and Drop Site News did not reveal where it sourced the list, we are unable to rate this claim. We can, however, break down Drop Site News' findings and any other publicly available information.
The document Drop Site News reportedly obtained also included a "Run of Show" listing the event's schedule, which read:
Run of Show:
- 4:30 pm: Event begins.
  - Mix and mingle
- 5:00 pm: EDW Chairwoman Lois Frankel to give opening remarks.
  - Thank everyone for attending, supporting EDW, and our historic wins.
- 5:10 pm: Acknowledge all new members in attendance and have them answer questions.
- 5:30 pm: Guests resume mingling.
- 6:00 pm: Event ends.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., publicly posted the voting schedule on Nov. 10, which indicated the vote on the impeachment articles he introduced would take place at 5:30 p.m. (archived).
According to Drop Site's reporting, the event took place at Goldfinch Social, a venue in Washington, D.C., about 2 miles from the Capitol.

On a summer day in 1992, a man dumped a cooler full of a fish called yellow perch into Lake Mary Ronan, in northwest Montana.
Why do people keep dumping buckets of fish into Montana’s lakes?
Guerilla ecology is incredibly easy. It also has disastrous consequences.
We know this because two teenagers saw him do it; they wrote down his license plate number and called in a tip to the Montana Fish, Wildlife, and Parks department (FWP), which immediately dispatched biologists to capture and kill the perch with nets and poison.
The teenagers got a reward of $500 each for their efforts, while the man was charged with illegally introducing non-native fish into the lake, slapped with a small fine, and sent on his way. The law changed soon after: Now, intentionally introducing a non-native, invasive species to Montana’s waters is a felony punishable by as long as two years in prison or a fine of up to $25,000, or both.
Why I wrote about this
I visited Flathead Lake Biological Station in October, and while I was there I heard from a biologist about this strange, totally avoidable, invisible catastrophe in the making. I was absolutely fascinated — as I looked at the lake, I hardly believed it could lose its signature clarity because of a bucketful of fish — and decided I had no choice but to open this can of worms.
But the perch? The yellow perch — at least two of them — survived, multiplied, and quickly went on to wreak havoc. They established dominance in the lake, wiping out its population of a native fish called the Westslope Cutthroat trout and causing other ecosystem disruptions. This hasn’t only happened here: Montana is filled with thousands of beautiful alpine lakes and rivers, nestled in the sort of rugged territory that sold people on the idea of the West. Yet, across the state, without permission, people keep dumping non-native fish into them.
The reason is simple: The introduced fish, according to some anglers, are more fun to fish than the stuff that’s already swimming around in Montana’s waters. But this guerrilla ecology — or “bucket biology” as some call it — risks upending delicate, longstanding ecosystems, harming not only native fish, but also animals that depend on them, like bald eagles, bears, and otters. It could turn Montana’s pristine waters into murky messes that also require millions of dollars in cleanup and additional maintenance every year.
And it’s not just a problem in Montana. Across the country, states are trying to stop people from filling lakes with fish that don’t belong. It’s a high-stakes issue with ramifications that can reach far beyond the underwater neighborhood of a single lake; efforts to stop illegal fish-dumping have now spawned everything from high-dollar bounties and dedicated fish forensics.
“A decision made by one person can affect an entire interconnected ecosystem,” said Craig Barfoot, Fisheries Program Manager for the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes (CSKT), which is based on the Flathead Reservation in northwestern Montana and oversees some of the most pristine aquatic habitats in the state. “It’s like an act of arson.”
The power of a bucket
Flathead Lake, about an hour’s drive south of Glacier National Park, is the sort of place postcards were made for. The 27-mile-long lake, half within the Flathead Reservation (and overseen by the tribes) and half managed by the state, is one of the cleanest, clearest lakes in the populated world — a survey last year found that the lake is clear down to about 36 feet — which draws all sorts of creatures to its shore. During a two-day visit in October, I saw a black bear ambling along the shore and a bald eagle sitting in a tree, tearing into a fish it had scooped out of the water.
This massive glacial lake “was ice about 15,000 years ago,” said Tom Bansak, associate director of the Flathead Lake Bio Station, a research station in the lake that’s run by the University of Montana. “Before western contact, there were maybe eight to 10 species of fish in the lake, which is not very many for a lake of its size.”
That changed starting in the late 1800s, when wildlife managers at the federal and state levels decided to start stocking lakes around the country with fish that were raised in hatcheries and released into the water for recreational fishing. For decades, states mostly made stocking decisions based not on local ecologies but rather on the kinds of fish people wanted to catch, filling them with nonnative fish like trout, bass, walleye, and pike. If you live in the United States, there’s a good chance the closest popular fishing spot is filled with stocked fish; at Flathead Lake, wildlife managers introduced around 30 different kinds of non-native fish, of which about a dozen established spawning populations, and today non-native fish outnumber native ones.
Eventually, state wildlife agencies began to realize that this sort of recreation-driven stocking can harm local ecosystems: In the 1970s, for example, Montana decided to stop stocking non-native fish in most of its streams and rivers. It still stocks plenty of fish, though, including a few non-native species, in some of its lakes and reservoirs, as do most other states.
For some people, however, that’s not enough. Some anglers believe the fish native to Montana, like bull trout, cutthroat trout, and sturgeon, just aren’t as fun to catch or as tasty to eat as, say, northern pike and walleye — both of which have been illegally introduced to the state’s waters in recent years.
Enter the bucket biologists. It can take as little as a bucketful of fish to alter the population of an entire lake, which means that if someone is bored of the fishing options at their local lake, they could unilaterally decide to spice things up with little risk of getting caught. Despite nonnative fish introductions now being a felony in Montana (and at least four other states), not a single person has been charged, let alone convicted there; that man the two teens saw at Lake Mary Ronan more than 30 years ago is the only person to have ever even been reported.
“People are mad at us, and they vocally say it.”
— Sam Bourret, FWP Fisheries biologist
But fish and wildlife officials know it’s still happening because they keep finding non-native fish in the state’s waterways, and the most likely way they got there is by someone illegally dumping them in.
”They’re obviously avid anglers, and we probably know them,” said Sam Bourret, a fisheries biologist at FWP based near Flathead Lake. Investigating illegal fish introductions is Bourret’s speciality: The Great Falls Tribune called him the “fish detective” for pioneering a forensic technique that looks at chemical clues inside otoliths, fishes’ stone-like ear bones, to figure out where they might have come from. He’s also used data modeling based on conditions like elevation and fishing pressure to figure out which lakes might be most vulnerable to future fish introductions, which could help steer resources towards them and stop would-be bucket biologists. From his time on the job, which has included many firsthand interactions with anglers, he can tell many of them are irked that they can’t stock the fish they want wherever they want them. “I do think some of these people are spiteful in their desire to move fish around,” Bourret said. “People are mad at us, and they vocally say it.”
Sometimes the culprit is less intentional. Non-native fish that are kept in ponds on private property (which technically require permits to build and stock but often slip by under the radar) can get into nearby rivers or lakes if the pond overflows during a storm, or by being picked up by a bird and then dropped into another waterbody. Earlier this year, FWP biologists on Bourret’s team removed 4,000 goldfish from a pond at a hotel on the edge of Montana’s Thompson River; the pond had been an attraction for families visiting the hotel with small children, who liked to scoop fish out of the water with nets. But goldfish can be disastrous for freshwater ecosystems, and the FWP wanted to be sure they wouldn’t slip into the adjacent river — and from there into a nearby lake.
But they often don’t get so far ahead of a potential problem. “Introduced fish probably go undetected often,” Bourret said. “We usually find out about them through a needle in a haystack catch. Once a population sets up in a lake, it’s already way too late.”
Fish-shaped dominoes
Monitoring species in the underwater realm of rivers, lakes, and streams is vastly more challenging than it is on land. “It’s a lot more obvious when a terrestrial animal doesn’t belong,” says Andrew Gilham, Fisheries Management Bureau Chief at FWP. “If you see a zebra in Montana, you’d probably think it’s weird. But if people see a brown trout, which is from Europe, it just doesn’t register in the same way.”
And that may even play into the general public’s understanding of just how much impact a few fish can have. “Some of it may just be that they don’t really understand the consequences that can follow illegal introductions,” he said.
Aquatic ecosystems are delicate balances, and in a healthy lake the populations of fish, predators, and small organisms like zooplankton and phytoplankton typically exist in a hard-won equilibrium. To simplify greatly, there are usually enough zooplankton to eat phytoplankton and prevent algal blooms, enough zooplankton-eating fish to prevent the zooplankton from eating all the phytoplankton, and enough predators to keep those zooplankton-eating fish in check — but not so many that the smaller fish get wiped out.
“If you see a zebra in Montana, you’d probably think it’s weird. But if people see a brown trout, which is from Europe, it just doesn’t register in the same way.”
— Andrew Gilham, Montana Fish, Wildlife, and Parks
Bucket biology, especially with voracious carnivores like pike, is a bit like tossing a fish-shaped grenade into the lake. If the newcomers establish a spawning population, they can compete for resources with the native fish or eat them directly, eventually causing something called a trophic cascade: a domino-like series of events that can upend an entire ecosystem.
What happens to fish in a lake can have huge effects on the creatures outside of it, too. In the Yellowstone region, Yellowstone Lake had long been home to a native fish species called the cutthroat trout. These fish would make long, winding spawning migrations through the Yellowstone lake and river system, where some four mammal species and 16 bird species — bears, otters, eagles, and pelicans, among others — would pluck them out of the water for meals. The migrating cutthroat were also important vectors for nutrients, which came from the fish’s poop and were important food sources for plants and algae growing in and along the waterways.
But then, in the 1990s, a non-native species arrived (likely through an illegal introduction): lake trout. Lake trout eat cutthroat, and without any predators of their own, they could feast on the smaller fish without anything to stop them. Once the lake trout appeared in Yellowstone Lake, they decimated cutthroat populations; according to a report from the National Park Service, by 1998, there were some 125,000 lake trout in the lake, and they ate somewhere between 3 and 4 million cutthroat that year.
Zooplankton in the lake, which the cutthroat used to eat, had a population boom, which led to a decline in phytoplankton. And the lake trout just stayed in the lake rather than migrating through the rivers and streams like the cutthroat did, which not only robbed those waters of the additional nutrients they brought, but also took a of a high-impact food source away from bears, otters, and birds. Bear and otter activity alongside the streams declined; while bears are opportunistic feeders and likely found another food source, the otters probably had a harder time finding something to supplement their diets. Bald eagle nests saw a sharp decline in their success rates after cutthroat disappeared, and osprey nest counts fell from 60 in 2001 to 3-5 from 2008-2015.
“We don’t want to just be moving things around willy-nilly,” said Niall Clancy, director of the Fisheries Lab at Salish Kootenai College. “Because one thing we learned is that we are bad at predicting the impacts — and there’s a good chance that something will go wrong that we didn’t think of.”
And, Clancy added, these sorts of introductions can cause financial cascades alongside trophic ones: FWP now spends millions of dollars each year to reduce invasive fish populations in the state’s lakes and boost native fish populations through hatchery programs. This, in turn, diverts money away from other programs.
Can the buckets be stopped?
Stopping illegal fish introductions is a nearly impossible task; catching someone red-handed would require vigilantly monitoring thousands and thousands of miles of shoreline in Montana. Instead, FWP and groups like the CSKT are investing in things like an educational outreach program and signs along popular waterfronts that exhort people not to dump live fish, warning that doing so is a felony.
FWP has also teamed up with groups like Trout Unlimited, a nonprofit that advocates for fish and waterway conservation, to offer massive rewards for information on bucket biologists. In 2017, for example, they offered a reward of over $35,000 for information related to the illegal introduction of walleye in Swan Lake, a lake about eight miles east of Flathead as the crow flies. But even the promise of a big reward hasn’t worked, and nobody has come forward yet. Instead, FWP declared open season on invasive fish like brown trout and walleye, requiring that anyone who catches one of the fish kill it rather than toss it back into the water, and then bring the entire fish into a FWP office so that biologists can study it. Biologists at FWP are also exploring other solutions like following the lead of Washington state in introducing sterile non-native fish to lakes. This would reduce the populations of non-native fish by tricking fertile ones into wasting their mating efforts on fish that will never be able to reproduce.
For the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, the issue goes beyond the science.
“We have stories about the native bull trout and the native West Oak cutthroat going back to before colonization,” said Rich Janssen, head of the CSKT’s department of natural resources. “They’re part of our heritage and our culture, and when they’re gone, they’re gone. It’s like losing our language.”
At Flathead Lake, the lower half of which is in the Flathead Reservation, the fish that were introduced through earlier federal and state stocking programs largely settled into a state of coexistence with the native fish. That doesn’t mean they were completely harmless, however: They competed for resources with the bull trout and cutthroat, which led to a reduction in those fish. Today, the CSKT has placed restrictions on bull trout and cutthroat fishing, banning people from taking those fish except for religious reasons, and has stepped up efforts to proactively monitor for new non-native fish at Flathead Lake. They’ve also removed fishing restrictions for smallmouth bass and northern pike in tribal waters. Both species were illegally introduced to the lake and can not only outcompete the bull trout and cutthroat but eat them outright, so anglers are now welcome to take as many of those non-native fish out of the water as they’d like.
“They’re part of our heritage and our culture, and when they’re gone, they’re gone. It’s like losing our language.”
— Rich Janssen, Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes
When I went for a swim in Flathead Lake this fall, the water was startlingly clear and calm, the surface broken every now and then by ripples from a passing fish or insect. But farther north, where the Flathead River meets the lake, a gauntlet of hungry pike lay in wait for bull trout making their way upriver to spawn. And as cold as the water was — it is a glacial lake, after all — it has also been warming with climate change, creating more pockets of warmer water for smallmouth bass to spawn in and shrinking the cold-water areas that the bull and cutthroat trout like.
I waved at a passing motorboat, which had a fishing pole stuck into a holder on its side. More and more people have been moving to Montana in recent years, attracted by the rugged nature and the allure of the West; new houses and docks have sprung up along Flathead Lake’s shoreline. But much like the pike and bass, their presence has been putting more pressure on the local landscape, and the newcomers could make the problem worse if they decide Montana’s fish aren’t as good as what they have back home. The future of the lake, and many others like it across the country, is murky. What it will look like depends, in large part, on what people decide to do with their buckets.

A video showing people vandalising and fighting inside a restaurant is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows an incident in West Bengal, where RSS workers allegedly created a ruckus and vandalised the restaurant when asked to pay for their food. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows RSS workers vandalising a restaurant in West Bengal after being asked to pay for their food.
Fact: The video shows an incident at Durbin Bangla Restaurant in Dhaka, Bangladesh, where a group of people vandalised the premises following a dispute over seating arrangements. The restaurant authorities alleged that students of Government Titumir College were involved in the attack. The incident has no connection to RSS workers or West Bengal. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple Bangladeshi media reports (here, here, and here) featuring the same video. According to these reports, the incident took place at Durbin Bangla Restaurant in Mohakhali, Dhaka, Bangladesh, on 13 November 2026. The incident reportedly began with an argument over seating arrangements between a customer and restaurant staff. According to the restaurant owner, a young man took a seat that a family was already waiting for. When a staff member intervened, the young man left but later returned with others and assaulted an employee named Khalil outside the restaurant. The group then vandalised the restaurant, damaging furniture and other items. The incident caused panic among customers and left several people injured. Police visited the spot and said they were examining CCTV footage to identify those involved and take legal action. The restaurant authorities alleged that students of Government Titumir College were involved, an allegation that police said they were investigating (here, here, and here).
The restaurant is located in the Mohakhali area of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Photos of the restaurant available on Google Maps match the visuals in the viral video, confirming that the incident took place in Bangladesh and not West Bengal.
To sum up, the video of a ruckus at a restaurant in Bangladesh is being shared as RSS workers’ hooliganism at a restaurant in West Bengal.

Mountains of scientific evidence support both the negative and positive effects of our eating habits on our health. Research shows that a healthy diet can help those suffering from chronic health conditions like Type 2 diabetes, heart disease and high blood pressure.
This is where “food is medicine” comes in. Food is medicine, also known as “food as medicine” and “food prescriptions,” is a movement dedicated to providing healthy food – fruits, vegetables and sometimes healthy proteins – based on a clinician’s prescription in order to prevent, manage or treat specific clinical conditions.
Prescribing food to patients is intended to convey that food is just as important as medication for health and wellness.
As researchers whose work focuses on food access and health in rural communities, we have firsthand experience running food is medicine programs in our local area in northern Mississippi. This experience has shown us the benefits and limitations of these programs in our community.
Fighting food insecurity
Food is medicine programs can be delivered through curated food boxes, grocery vouchers and medically tailored meals. Most programs are collaborations between nonprofit organizations, health clinics and healthcare providers. The goal of food is medicine is to improve patient health, especially for those with chronic conditions, while reducing healthcare costs.
Increasingly, food is medicine programs have become lifelines for people with food insecurity. In 2024, more than 47 million Americans, including 7.3 million children, lived in food-insecure households – meaning they were at some point uncertain of having, or did not have, enough food for everyone in the household.
Internationally, the number of people experiencing hunger rises to roughly 673 million. Rural populations are more likely to be food insecure due to the loss of local grocery stores and distance from urban centers. Unlike a food bank, food is medicine programs provide only healthy foods, which are often curated by a dietitian, to optimize patient health.
Forward momentum
Though food is medicine isn’t formally connected to the Make American Healthy Again movement, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has brought new energy and attention to the concept. In January 2026, the second Trump administration launched a campaign encouraging Americans to “Eat Real Food.”
But the food is medicine movement actually began more than 60 years ago. One of the early providers who prescribed food as medicine was civil rights activist and multiple Nobel Peace Prize winner Dr. Jack Geiger. In the 1960s, he co-founded community health centers in South Boston and the Mississippi Delta.
When government officials chastised him for prescribing food to patients in the Delta, Geiger responded, “The last time I looked at my textbooks, the most specific therapy for malnutrition was food.”
Since then, thousands of community organizations like Community Servings and Project Open Hand have provided healthy food to vulnerable community members.
In 2023, the president of the American Heart Association convened an advisory group of researchers and physicians to review current food is medicine research and suggest next steps for work in this area. This advisory has suggested that these programs could help prevent or manage chronic conditions, saving the U.S. healthcare system an estimated US$4.3 trillion annually.
Food is medicine has also started to gain international momentum. In 2025, the Rockefeller Foundation supported a meeting of international scholars, policy experts and practitioners that established the Food Is Medicine Global Alliance. This organization plans to help integrate, sustainably finance and routinely deliver food is medicine programs worldwide by 2030. So far, it has released several reports highlighting the current food is medicine environment and made resources available to providers looking to start their own programs.
Food is medicine in our local community
Food is medicine programs can use food from local farms or grocery stores, and the means of getting the food to patients varies. The four projects we have run to date have been relatively small and local.
One was a food box pickup program that supplemented fruits and vegetables for 55 households whose members demonstrated food insecurity. We followed the participants for two years and found statistically significant reductions in weight, waist circumference and triglyceride levels in the primary adult participants.
For two of our other programs, including one that is ongoing, we partnered with local farmers. One was a pilot test of a food box delivery program for housebound people. Both the recipients of the food and the farmers reported high satisfaction with the program’s delivery and felt the program strengthened community connections while also supporting local agricultural livelihoods.
What other researchers have found
One recent large-scale literature review identified 14 trials of food is medicine interventions and found that these approaches often positively influenced diet quality and food security.
Another review of food is medicine programs for people with diabetes found significant increases in fruit and vegetable intake and reductions in blood sugar levels. This data supports our own previous findings.
However, the effect of food is medicine programs on long-term health outcomes has been inconsistent, in part because many trials have been too small or not rigorous enough to determine causation. In some cases, the “dose” – that is, the amount of food provided – is limited by grant funding. Our food box pickup project supplemented only four to five meals each week, which may have been insufficient to significantly improve all health outcomes.
Moreover, it will be important for researchers to consider the logistics of making these programs work in various local food environments. Global factors like changing weather patterns and, more recently, delays in fuel and supplies from the Strait of Hormuz have increased prices of staple food products like cereals and vegetable oil and led to shortages of cooking oil in some countries.
Food is medicine can be appealing because it makes intuitive sense. But going forward, larger, high-quality studies are needed to adequately track clinical outcomes from the various types of food is medicine programming. If studies show food is medicine is beneficial, it could lead to a shift in how healthcare practitioners approach diet for patients with chronic illness. Access to healthy food would be considered as essential as medications for patients with chronic illness.
Meagen Rosenthal, University of Mississippi and Natalie Minton, University of Mississippi

Bill Ackman said there could be a case for reinstating Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO — that is, only if Huang is cleared of any wrongdoing related to putting his company's national security obligations at risk.
At a conference hosted by Semafor on Monday, the billionaire activist investor was asked what strategy he would use to pressure the board into reinstating Huang.
Huang resigned from his role on Thursday following the disclosure of extramarital affairs and concerns that he may have been a target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
Ackman said that if Huang's relationships were determined to be a "personal foible as opposed to a corporate defense conspiracy," there could be a "powerful case" for putting Huang back in the CEO seat, though the investor said it would be "unlikely" for him to be involved in such an effort.
"You just present the facts, and you call a special meeting," he said, adding that an activist investor could also partner with Huang, who owns more than 3% of the company.
Said special meeting would be a shareholder vote on reinstating Huang. The now-former CEO's involvement would not only help the company meet the threshold for calling one — which requires at least 15% of the voting power — but also send a public message that the founder wants to return.
"You call a special meeting, the writing will be on the wall very quickly, I would expect, at which point you don't even have to go the meeting," Ackman said. "Just put him back in, make some changes to the board, and push forward."
A spokesperson for Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.
Ackman, who has defended Huang since the Nvidia founder's affairs were publicized, said the situation is an "interesting activist setup," given that Huang is a heralded founder who would have plenty of shareholder support.
"I think the only cloud is there is some legal uncertainty about what actually went down," Ackman said. "It would be helpful to know that answer before you pursue that."

At 2:20 p.m. Eastern time Nov. 17, the Federal Emergency Management Agency and Federal Communications Commission plan to conduct a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, which was announced in September.
According to some posts on social media, however, the test will be followed by a catastrophic 90-day electric and/or Internet blackout, plunging the world into darkness and chaos.
The claim may have felt unusually plausible, given several large failures in digital and physical infrastructure in the days leading up to the test — a Microsoft Outlook outage Nov. 12, a nationwide aircraft ground stop Nov. 13 due to a failure in telecommunication infrastructure, and software outages at several major banks on Nov. 16.
Add to that the curious claim that a 2023 episode of "The Simpsons," the long-running animated TV show somewhat notorious for predicting the future, featured a plot centered around a global blackout that began on Nov. 17. It all seemed to line up.
Snopes readers contacted us ahead of the Nov. 17 emergency alert test, asking for a review of these rumors.
We reached out to FEMA, the FCC and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency for comment on the rumor, asking about the agencies' involvement in the EAS test and the nation's protections against attacks on Internet and electric infrastructure. None of them replied to us by the time of publication.
As with all predictions of cataclysmic events, though, we urge readers to take this one with a grain of salt. There is no evidence indicating that a 90-day blackout will follow the nationwide EAS test, for any of the countless reasons posed online — be it a grand plan from the government, a targeted cybersecurity attack or just because "The Simpsons" said so.
Because Snopes requires substantial evidence to rate a story, however, and we can neither predict nor travel into the future, we're leaving this claim unrated until Nov. 17 has come and gone.
The EAS test
FEMA, in coordination with the FCC, is required by law to conduct a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System at least once every three years, according to its website. The last nationwide test of the EAS, familiar to many Americans as the loud, warbling "beep beep beep" that comes on TV or radio before a severe weather warning or an Amber Alert, occurred Oct. 4, 2023.
In the 2023 test, FEMA and the FCC also sent test emergency alerts to cellphones. However, FEMA's webpage says it will not be testing cellphone alerts this time around. The agency also noted that it may reschedule the test if an actual emergency or severe weather happens Nov. 17. The backup test would be conducted Dec. 3.
No information about the test suggests that any sort of digital blackout will follow, for any reason. If the supposed blackout is supposed to be an act of sabotage by a foreign adversary, why would they have announced the attack beforehand? If the supposed blackout was planned by the United States government, meanwhile, why would it have neglected to warn everyone beforehand through official channels?
The 'Simpsons' episode
As for "The Simpsons" — Snopes has covered many claims implying that the sitcom predicted this or that future event.
The show's oracular reputation grew out of the few times where an absurd plot device ended up being a spot-on prediction, as perhaps most famously happened in a 2000 episode in which Lisa Simpson becomes president and inherits a budget crisis from Donald Trump. (Notably, Trump briefly considered running as the Reform Party's nominee in that year's presidential election.)
We chalk it up to the show's longevity — more than 850 episodes over 38 seasons — above anything else. "The Simpsons" routinely satirizes current real-world events, so given enough opportunities, it's unsurprising the writers occasionally come off as having the gift of prophecy.
In this case, the episode, titled "It's a Blunderful Life," was real, and did feature a plot based around a blackout starting on Nov. 17. Beyond that, the episode's plot bore no resemblance to the claim at hand.
The episode aired Nov. 19, 2023, as the sitcom's Thanksgiving special. It begins decades into the future, as the Simpson family sits down to eat Thanksgiving dinner and Lisa tells everyone to light a candle in remembrance. When asked why by her grandchild, Lisa recounts that a "great blackout" nearly destroyed Springfield. She opens a diary labeled "Apocalyptic Memories" to Nov. 17 (no year is given), and begins explaining as the camera cuts to a shot of the Simpson home "six days before Thanksgiving."
But, there's a problem for the fantasists here — Thanksgiving isn't on the same day each year. In 2023, when the episode aired, Thanksgiving fell on Nov. 23, conveniently, six days after Nov. 17. In 2026, however, Thanksgiving is on Nov. 26, meaning that if the year in the episode truly was 2026, Lisa should have opened the diary to Nov. 20 (i.e., six days before). Sorry to spoil anyone's doomsday prepping.
For more reading, we also previously explained a recent surge in government messaging around emergency preparedness, and a Department of Defense initiative that aims to keep military bases operational for at least 90 days without relying on civilian infrastructure.

The World Health Organisation warned on Friday (November 13, 2026) of surging respiratory illnesses in Gaza, with worse expected after heavy rains flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians.
“The numbers already show the pressure. Acute respiratory infections are 33,000 cases higher than at the same time last year,” Dr. Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told reporters in Geneva from Jerusalem.
Poor living conditions and severe overcrowding are driving up infections as Gaza’s population is squeezed into an ever-smaller area, WHO said. The crunch has worsened as the Israeli military expands its control by advancing the “Yellow Line” — a demarcation established under October’s U.S.-brokered ceasefire.
“That means people are living in more crowded conditions, where of course the spread between humans of a virus is much more prone to spread,” Ms. Van De Weerdt explained.
The Israeli military told Reuters the Yellow Line aims to protect Israeli civilians and army troops from threats and that adjustments to its location follow the ceasefire agreement and international law, and are not intended to harm the civilian population.
“The IDF categorically rejects the claim that it operates to deliberately reduce the area available to the civilian population in the Gaza Strip.”
COGAT, the Israeli military agency that coordinates aid, said that more than 93,000 tents and over 8,600 trucks carrying tarpaulin sheets, blankets and winter clothing have entered Gaza since the Board of Peace, UN agencies and NGOs launched the winterisation plan. Equipment intended for the reconstruction of Gaza will be permitted to enter only after Hamas has been fully disarmed, it added.
Last week COGAT said that it had stepped up efforts to improve sanitary conditions before the heavy rain, in coordination with international organisations.
Respiratory infections currently make up 11% of all consultations, with the WHO expecting cold weather, flooding, overcrowded shelters and poor ventilation to push these numbers higher.
“It is shocking that just a few days of rain really showed us what the coming months will bring. And winter has not even fully set in. The worst really is yet to come,” Ms. Van De Weerdt said.
Nearly a million displaced people in Gaza live in flood-exposed areas, and 400,000 of them are in locations that are considered at extremely high risk, according to the WHO.
The agency said flooding heightened the risk of contaminated water, while standing water gave mosquitoes and pests more places to breed. Dampness encouraged mould and bacteria that are major drivers of respiratory infections, especially in young children, it said.
While the majority of medicines are getting into Gaza, the WHO faces difficulty getting laboratory supplies, which it says are vital for diagnosing patients before they can be treated.
“To prevent outbreaks, we really call to let laboratory equipment enter Gaza today, so that we can avoid a public health disaster on top of a disaster.“
COGAT said Israel has facilitated the entry of all medicines requested by international aid organisations and has not rejected any requests received, adding that X-ray machines, oxygen generators, batteries, generators, and other equipment have entered Gaza.

Bengaluru/Mumbai: In a strong statement about the future of the Tata Trusts, Jimmy N. Tata, the late Ratan Tata's younger brother, has warned that institutions started by Sir Ratan Tata and Sir Dorabji Tata to help the Indian people are being used for family control—a change he says was never what the founders wanted, as they had no children and left their wealth to public trusts that cannot be ended.
Jimmy has accused Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata of taking control of Tata Sons by adding his family members to the Trusts, and wants the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to make the holding company become public ‘without delay’.
The accusations are detailed in a two-page “Record of conversation with Mr. Jimmy Tata on 10th November 2026”, reviewed by Mint and signed by both Jimmy N. Tata and retired defence secretary Vijay Singh.
Jimmy, 85, a permanent Trustee of Sir Ratan Tata Trust, the second-largest shareholder of Tata Sons, has mostly stayed away from the group’s public matters and is Noel’s half-brother. He does not take part in board discussions at the Trusts and does not use his vote either.
Tata Trusts collectively own 65.9% of Tata Sons.
Jimmy and Singh support Tata Sons chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran. Despite his “overwhelming support (including 4–1 in Tata Sons board and a unanimous resolution passed by Tata Trusts), Noel sought to block him arbitrarily by invoking the onerous veto provisions in the amended Articles of Association without providing any justification or accountability,” the document says.
The Economic Times first reported on Monday that Jimmy Tata came out in support of Chandrasekaran and endorsed listing Tata Sons.
The document alleges that a four-year tenure limit, applied to some trustees but not others, is being used to sideline dissenters. It cites “the targeting of Mr. Venu Srinivasan (whose term expires in December) because he opposed the induction of Noel Tata’s son into the Sir Ratan Tata Trust, alongside the earlier removal of Mr. Vijay Singh for authoring a factual article.”
“What has transpired in recent time is that the trusts are being filled with family members of the present Tata Trust Chairman, thereby securing a degree of control over Tata Sons that was never the settlors’ intention,” the document says.
“It is entirely inappropriate for more than one family member to serve on a given trust; doing so effectively confers ownership rights over the trusts’ significant shareholding in Tata Sons at no consideration whatsoever. Such an arrangement is untenable and amounts to a back-door takeover of Tata Sons.”
It connects the problem to changes in Tata Sons’ Articles of Association around 2013-14, which it says gave the Trusts’ chairman “unfair, controlling veto powers”.
Listing, the document argues, would “dismantle the pervasive culture of secrecy, impose statutory accountability” and force a rewrite of the Articles.
It calls on RBI to “enforce strict timelines for listing without delay and ensure that breaking up the group is not permitted”, and on the government and the Charity Commissioner to “step in to protect the original objects of the trusts for the people of India.”
On Monday, RBI told Tata Sons to comply with its rules for upper-layer non-banking financial companies, “including the requirement of listing by your company”.

Romelu Lukaku, Belgium’s all-time leading scorer, announced his retirement from international football on Monday after a 16-year career in which he scored 94 goals in 135 games.
The 33-year-old striker, the fifth-highest scorer in men’s international football history, helped Belgium finish third at the 2018 World Cup during its most successful period.
“These 16 years I gave all I had for the national team. I went through every emotion possible,” Lukaku said on Instagram.
“I played with amazing teammates that I will always be grateful for. I want to thank them all. I want to thank all the coaches as well for pushing and trusting me to help the team. It was a nice ride, and I enjoyed every single moment.
Lukaku played in four World Cups and three European Championships.
“I will never forget those moments,” he said. “I’m at peace with my decision to stop here. It was amazing; it was enjoyable. I’m grateful - thank you.”
Lukaku was an unused substitute in Belgium’s 4-1 home win over Italy in the Nations League on Sunday.
He began his club career at Belgian side Anderlecht before spells with teams including Chelsea, Everton, Manchester United and Inter Milan. He currently plays for Turkish club Fenerbahce.

European Union countries on Monday accused Russia of trying to drag out talks on ending the war in Ukraine while it bombs power plants and other infrastructure to make life even harder for civilians as winter closes in.
At talks in Brussels, EU foreign ministers said the priority should be to secure a ceasefire and then a real peace agreement. They said that Russia started the nearly five-year war and must back down rather than make fresh demands of Ukraine and its Western backers.
“Let’s not blur the picture right now. What we need to see is a ceasefire,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said before chairing the meeting. “We don’t see it at the moment. We see that Russia is really escalating.”
After negotiations in Abu Dhabi last week, the United States encouraged Ukraine and its backers to agree to a Russian demand for a new security framework for Europe, suggesting that it might help bring peace.
But the Europeans see that as a Russian attempt to weaken NATO by obliging the military alliance to pull troops and equipment back westward, similar to the way they were deployed before the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999.
Russia again accused of delaying tactics
That demand is “really absurd,” Kallas said. “If we look at the history, none of these countries has ever attacked Russia.” She said Russia’s tactic is always to demand more even though “they started the war. They are the aggressor. And there’s one victim.”
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee, whose country currently holds the EU’s rotating presidency, said that despite the talks, “Russia has clearly not changed its position. It is continuing its attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure.”
McEntee said the EU will agree on more sanctions later Monday “trying to in particular attack the financial mechanism by which Russia is waging this war.” The ministers will also look at ways to help Ukraine endure the coming winter.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said: “Europe has a security architecture – we don’t need a new one, we just need respect from everyone for the existing security architecture.” He said that is "the foundation for any conceivable agreement, from the European point of view.”
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys also insisted that Europe does not need another security framework, saying that Russia cannot be trusted and has already broken past agreements anyway.
“It’s very clear that we don’t need another one. We already have one. Secure Ukraine, strong Europe, strong trans-Atlantic bond,” he told reporters. “It’s not about the rules. Rules are working. The problem is that Russia is breaking them.”
Little progress in US-led talks
U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have positioned themselves as mediators and have been talking to Russia and Ukraine for just over a year. In that time, no lasting ceasefire has been agreed, and little obvious progress has been made toward peace.
Major differences remain over the control of territory and future security arrangements.
European leaders and officials, including Kallas, have expressed skepticism about the talks. The only tangible progress has been exchanges of prisoners, which are often used by warring parties as a trust-building measure during peace talks.
At a summit in Dublin last week, EU leaders agreed that Europe should be represented in future talks by a team of security advisers from France, Germany, the U.K., Italy and Poland as well as senior officials from the EU’s main institutions.
The Europeans concede that as Ukraine’s biggest backers they cannot also act as mediators. Their role will focus on security arrangements, reconstruction and Ukraine’s future. Only Ukraine itself can decide on matters involving its sovereignty, they said.

Taking Korea's toughest exam from behind bars
- Published
Students intently focus on maths formulas written on a board before lowering their heads and taking notes as the teacher works through a sum.
The teacher's voice and the scratch of pens fill the room.
At first glance, this could be any classroom in South Korea.
But thick metal bars cover the windows and the students are wearing blue prison uniforms and rubber shoes emblazoned with the words "Korea Correctional Service".
This is Mandela Boys' School, an education facility for young prisoners inside the Seoul Southern Correctional Institution in Guro, south-west Seoul. In South Korea, young people who are sentenced to imprisonment by a criminal court must serve their time in prison.
"The boys here have committed serious offences and received criminal sentences," Jeong Yeo-gyeong, a correctional officer in the Korea Correctional Service's social reintegration division, told the BBC.
"As well as theft, there is a high proportion of serious offences, including violence, bodily injury, sexual violence and robbery."
But by opening educational institutes like Mandela, authorities are hoping to give these young offenders a chance to better their lives after they serve out their sentences.
Opened by the justice ministry in March 2023, it allows boys who were aged 17 and under when their sentences became final to prepare for school equivalency exams as well as the Suneung - the country's notoriously difficult university entrance examination - while still serving their sentences.
Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.
Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.
The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.
A total of 551,864 people have applied to take this year's Suneung on 19 November.
Around 30 prisoners are enrolled in the Suneung preparation class at Mandela Boys' School, and 11 of them have applied to take this year's exam.
Park Soo-young (not his real name), a 17-year-old inmate, has been at the Mandela Boys' Suneung preparation class for two months and hopes to study social welfare.
He tells the BBC that he had dreams of becoming a police officer before committing the crime that landed him behind bars.
He says he could not bring himself to look properly at his mother during his trial. When he turned towards her after his sentence was announced, she was crying.
"Seeing her like that, I broke down too. I wondered how I was going to live from then on, and how I could look after my mother, who was on her own. I think I kept crying for about a week while I was in the detention centre."
Looking back on his offence, he says he feels "very ashamed that I couldn't control that impulse". If he could meet his younger self, he would tell him: "Control that impulse. If you do, everything will be different."
"I'd grab myself by the collar and shake myself as I said it."
He hopes the Suneung and university will offer him a chance to start again.
"Once I'm out, I need to cut ties with the friends and people I used to know and start a new life. I think university is the only way to do that. Going to university would let me leave the area where I used to live, move somewhere else and start something new. That's why I began studying again."
But he describes beginning Suneung preparation as "a struggle every day".
"But the teachers don't let anything slip past. They keep helping us until we understand. If I don't understand something, I put my hand up and they come over and explain it.
Sometimes, if I've missed something, I keep working at it on my own. If I still can't get it, I ask the students next to me to explain," he said.
Park's day begins at 06:30 with a morning check by prison officers. He starts memorising English vocabulary and working through Korean reading passages early in the morning.
"I learn English words whenever I can, even before breakfast. From 07:00, I work through a Korean passage, something like literature or speech. We have to come down to the classroom at 08:00, so we have another check and then come down for lessons."
During breaks, students make calls to their families or leave the classroom for scheduled visits. In the evening, they return for supervised study. Once the day's activities are over, they must go back to their cells together.
Park says he studies until 22:00 before finishing for the day. If he wants to study longer hours, he needs permission from a prison officer.
But even if gets a good result this year, Park will not be allowed to leave prison and attend university straight away. He is only due to be released in 2028, but plans to use this exam as experience and continue studying next year.
"This time, I want to experience how the Suneung works and how competitive it is. Then, next year, I'll work hard from the start so I can get in the year after that."
Some former students from Mandela Boys' School have managed to get into university, according to the justice ministry.
Others have continued their studies after leaving prison, including by enrolling in residential exam preparation academies.
The inmates are taught by a team of seven prison officers, all of whom hold teaching certificates. Each is responsible for a subject.
Visiting instructors provide classes in the humanities, arts and sport, while university student volunteers help with learning. Professional psychological counselling is also available.
Park Min-yong, who applied to work here in 2023, teaches science. And alongside Suneung lessons, he works with the students' to change their habits and behaviour.
One thing he often tells them is that they need to "learn how to become adults".
He believes that while studying in itself does not necessarily turn inmates away from a life of crime, the experience of having worked hard at something: staying with a concept that makes little sense, revisiting a wrong answer and continuing even when grades do not improve straight away, is valuable in itself.
"Studying properly means pushing yourself to your limits, and that takes considerable stamina and patience," he says.
"Whether they chose to do it or not, the experience of persevering, enduring and not giving up easily may help them to some extent when they face the difficulties of life after release."
He says the material they encounter while preparing for the Suneung also gives them new things to think about.
Korean reading passages cover literature, society, science and philosophy. Students have to consider a character's perspective, examine the evidence behind an argument and understand unfamiliar concepts. They also encounter explanations that differ from their own and have to reconsider what they think.
"They gradually learn that it's not just about their own personal view - that these concepts and relationships have been developed through a shared understanding among many people," Park said.
There are difficult moments too.
Park says students sometimes cheat in classroom tests even while he is watching.
"They cheat as if it's nothing. They give each other answers, even when I'm watching them. Some repeat it after being told off. There may be an element of doing it deliberately, but often they haven't thought it through. They don't think about the impact their actions or words could have on others."
The boys also have a strong desire for recognition, he says.
"It's all the time. 'Look how much I've done. Look how much my grades have improved. I've done this much - haven't I done well?' They're always like that. They're hungry for it."
Not everyone agrees with this initiative though.
One criticism is that young people who have not committed crimes also face fierce competition for university places: so there is some anger that the state provides offenders with separate education and opportunities to prepare for this exam.
Father Jeong Min-ha, of the Archdiocese of Seoul's correctional ministry committee, worked with Seoul Southern Correctional Institution from September 2023 until last year.
He acknowledges these criticisms.
"Studying gives them a sense of achievement and time to look seriously at their own lives. That's why I think it matters. I think that is the most important part of rehabilitation."
Of course, there is no guarantee.
Park recalls a student who had done well at the school but later returned to prison.
"He was doing well when he left, but in the end he came back. So something went wrong. I'd hoped he would carry on with what he'd been doing here, but he couldn't. That's disappointing."
According to the justice ministry's 2026 corrections statistical yearbook, 35.5% of prisoners aged under 20 who were released in 2021 were imprisoned again within three years. That was about 1.7 times the overall rate of 21.2%, and the highest of any age group.
But Park hopes the students will continue learning after they leave prison. "We don't know what the outcome will be," he says.
"They say the way to clear a glass of dirty water is to keep pouring clean water into it, rather than trying to remove each bit of dirt. I hope they fill their minds with good things, learn to use their energy and intellect in the right way, and put that learning into practice at the right time and place."
Additional reporting by Hosu Lee.

Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as authorities braced for more protests ahead of the US president’s arrival in the city for a leaders’ summit.
Organisers claim as many as 10,000 people will join protests against Trump in the Philippine capital on Tuesday, when he will attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds are expected to try to walk to the summit site.
Authorities have arrested nearly 300 people in widespread protests in held in the days leading up to the summit, with large parts of the capital closed off and tight security in place.
Some burned effigies of Trump and faced off with police officers armed with batons and shields. Slogans on placards called the American leader the world’s “number one terrorist” in protests held on Monday.
Demonstrators angry at the cost-of-living and energy shock caused by the Iran war, and the new US-led Pax Silica initiative on AI and critical minerals, tried to reach the summit at the Philippine International Convention Center on Monday, but were blocked by police.
Pax Silica has sparked tensions in the Philippines over plans to build a tech hub outside Manila that critics say will affect water and energy supplies, and displace members of the Ayta Indigenous community.
Large sections of central Manila were closed to the public as part of the security cordon, and public holidays instituted for the Asean summit.
Trump will meet with the leaders of Australia, Japan and India on Tuesday night before heading to Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. There he will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and hold trilateral talks with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The backlash against Trump follows the ouster of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, and allegations members of the US administration, including the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, knew about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump’s delegation was expected to include businessman Elon Musk.
Protest leader Renato Reyes blamed the arrests in Manila on the heavy handed response of the government on the president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr., calling Monday the largest single day of police arrests since Marcos came to office in 2022.
“It is really crazy that the Philippine government is rolling out the red carpet for someone who has been so flatly rejected by the American people,” Reyes said.
“Trump started a war that devastated the global economy and pushed oil prices in the Philippines to historic highs. It has caused untold suffering on the Filipino people.
“So yes, Trump will have to pay for his crimes and he will have to be answerable, not just to the American people, but to the people of the world.”
The Philippine national police said some officers were injured during confrontations with demonstrators opposed to the summit, including when objects were allegedly thrown at officers.
Pax Silica will include a technology hub planned at New Clark City in Tarlac, about 120km from Manila.
Intended to bolster western stocks of AI technology and reduce “excessive dependencies” on single source supply chains, including from China, Pax Silica will provide chips and critical minerals to 25 participating signatory governments.
Amnesty Philippines said demonstrations should not be forcibly or violently dispersed.
“Reports of arrests during the protests demand immediate scrutiny,” director Ritz Lee Santos III said.
“Authorities must explain the specific grounds for each arrest and any continued detention. Anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights must be released immediately.”

The US Supreme Court dealt President Donald Trump a setback in his drive to cancel billions of dollars in federal grants, leaving intact a ruling that the administration was probably acting illegally by targeting research projects he said were “DEI programs.”
With no noted dissents on Monday, the justices rejected an appeal by the administration in a clash with faculty members and researchers at the University of California.
The rebuff keeps in place a federal appeals court ruling that for now requires the National Science Foundation and National Endowment for the Humanities to continue funding $59 million in grants. The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals said Trump probably violated the Constitution’s free speech clause by discriminating against the grantees because of their viewpoints.
“It means that the 9th Circuit ruling stands and all of the grants that were cut off based on the perceived viewpoint of the research must continue to be restored,” said Erwin Chemerinsky, dean of the University of California’s Berkeley Law and the lead lawyer for the researchers. He said the appeals court ruling would also serve as an “important precedent” for other court’s around around the country.
Even so, the high court’s sidestepping of the case leaves unanswered questions about a controversy that raged during Trump’s first months in office last year. Trump directed agencies to terminate grants that involved diversity, equity and inclusion, as well as “gender ideology” and “environmental justice.”
The Justice Department said it will “continue to advocate for the executive branch’s lawful authority to administer federal funding programs and for the termination of taxpayer-funded DEI initiatives.”
In its appeal, the Trump administration contended that the Constitution lets the government choose to fund only those projects that align with its perspective. US Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that the ruling by the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals would “hamstring every future administration” if not reversed.
“The First Amendment provides the government significant flexibility when it acts as patron to subsidize speech,” argued Sauer, the administration’s top courtroom lawyer. “The government may itself promote favored viewpoints, including by disbursing public funds to private entities.”
In rejecting the government, the 9th Circuit said the Supreme Court has distinguished between a decision not to fund a program at all and a rejection of particular applicants because of their views.
“Because the agencies’ termination of grants is aimed at the suppression of viewpoints with which the government disagrees, it likely violates the First Amendment,” the appeals court said in a 3-0 decision.
The University of California group urged the Supreme Court not to take up the case, saying the 9th Circuit applied “clearly established law.” The researchers said the blitz of terminations upended cutting-edge studies in science, medicine and other areas.
“The stakes for the researchers, and for the public that benefits from their work, could not be higher,” the group told the high court.
Much of the grant cancellation occurred under the direction of the Department of Government Efficiency, the Elon Musk-led effort that tore through the federal government last year, firing workers, dismantling agencies and canceling billions of dollars in spending. DOGE, as the office is known, claimed to have canceled $110 billion in grants and contracts, though the actual savings to the government might have been far less than that.
The administration drew criticism for the wholesale, and in at least some cases erratic, nature of the terminations. The New York Times reported in March that DOGE officials relied on ChatGPT to select which National Endowment for the Humanities grants to target.
In the University of California case, the researchers faulted the administration for relying on keywords, including “diversity,” to determine which grants were problematic. They say the approach scooped in projects with titles mentioning “Leaf Diversity” and “Diversity Within the Legume Rhizobia Mutualism.”
The case is Trump v. Thakur, 26-210.

Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, bank trouble, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder
Maybe the trouble started with the AI billionaire and the Silicon Valley uproar that followed talk of his infidelity, including with an alleged Chinese spy. Or maybe it was the Microsoft outage that, depending on how you looked at it, either cast millions of frustrated workers adrift or spared them from a daily, unrelenting electronic avalanche.
Then, just as it seemed things were calming down after a weekend of airline chaos, United Airlines announced a widespread outage on Monday afternoon (Nov 16) and several top US banks began reporting significant slowdowns, with transactions sometimes not going through.
“We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible," a Chase spokesperson said in a statement.
America has been hearing that for days. From seemingly everywhere.
The prime example began Friday afternoon, when US aviation authorities ordered the grounding of planes across the country. That was when many began to think that something was up.
Just ask Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, trying to fly out of Newark Liberty International Airport when his cancelled flight led to a few beers with his brother in an airport bar and eventually a night in a hotel. Saturday morning, he was back at the airport to try again.
“There’s a lot of weird stuff going on,” Amasio said. “It makes one think.”
His first thought was dark: “We talk about how wars aren’t done with bombs anymore. They shut down airspace or a power grid. They can cripple an economy.”
Throw in a few more examples just from Friday - a cruise ship that overturned in New Orleans when a tanker slammed into it, suspicious drones over a US air base in Britain, a bomb found near an ethanol plant in Illinois - and perhaps things seem even weirder, opening the door for a writer who has been picking at America’s fears for generations to offer his own explanation.
“The aliens have landed,” Stephen King wrote in a Friday afternoon post on the social platform X. “That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic.”
The official explanations for the thousands of grounded jetliners and hours of email and other computer troubles were far more prosaic.
A technology upgrade on the nation’s air traffic control system had overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours, administration officials said.
By Saturday morning, air travel was already smoother and Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said airline schedules should be back to normal by late Sunday.
Microsoft, for its part, said Saturday that its services had been fully restored, saying the problem “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” following a recent network change.
The outage is believed to have affected many millions of people around the world. The banking problems began after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects through the financial system.
On Monday, United said its tech problem was affecting departing flights, not planes in the air.
Chase said its problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and it was working to bring services back online.
'IS THIS A CYBERATTACK?'
Maxine Gustafson, a 34-year-old physician assistant from Minneapolis, was in line to pick up a hastily booked rental car at Chicago’s O’Hare airport on Friday afternoon so she and colleagues could get home from a work training.
Gustafson said the week's mishaps made her feel afraid and helpless.
“It makes you think, like, is this a cyberattack?” she said. “We don’t have control over a lot of this stuff.”
Both the FAA and Microsoft said there were no signs that malicious activity had been behind the troubles.
Tori Perkins, 34, was hoping for a Saturday flight at Terminal 2 at San Diego International Airport, where 11 of the 62 flights already were listed as cancelled that morning and the same number were delayed. Crowds were normal.
“It’s one of those things where I don’t necessarily believe what the government says,” said Perkins, who seemed to take the setback in stride. “I don’t know what’s true because there are so many people saying different things.”
Perkins, who lives in Hawaii, was in San Diego on a layover on her way to see family in Florida. She spent Friday night at the airport.
She was not surprised that Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy had made a plea on Friday for tens of billions in more funding to upgrade the country’s notoriously outdated air traffic system.
“It sounds like more of the same,” she said.
The FAA has already replaced thousands of copper wire connections with fibre optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved US$12.5 billion in funding. The White House has been pushing for US$30 billion more to complete the work.
BRIGHT SPOTS EASE CONCERNS
Sometimes chaos brings out the best in people.
Corbyn Wascher was stuck on the tarmac at Charlotte Douglas International Airport for four hours while heading back to Moline, Illinois, from Miami, where he had been at an education conference.
He said everyone was cordial on the plane, talking to one another and stretching their legs. He was impressed with the American Airlines staff, who handed out water, pretzels and biscotti snacks, though they were clearly under stress.
“The stewardesses were amazing,” said the 37-year-old high school teacher.
Back at the Newark airport, Caroline Ruiz had caught a few hours of sleep by a heating vent. She wasn’t sure what time it was as she waited for someone to bring her a meal she was promised after the cancellation of the first leg of her 24-hour trip to Australia. She hoped to get started later Saturday.
It was two days in a row, she noted, where she had been betrayed by technology.
Though maybe one of those days didn’t count as a betrayal.
“I kind of got a free day yesterday” because the Microsoft systems were down.

At least 17 people were killed in two separate shootings in South Africa over the weekend, police have confirmed.
Nine people, including three women, were found dead with gunshot wounds inside a shack in the informal settlement of Jeffsville, located near the capital of Pretoria.
Eight others were found dead inside a vehicle in Sweetwaters outside the city of Pietermaritzburg, located near the coastal city of Durban.
Police have not yet established a motive for either of the killings.
The shooting in Jeffsville is reported to have taken place on Sunday night but no arrests have been made. In Pietermaritzburg, police said they had not yet identified the victims.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world, averaging about 60 every day.
While there is no standard global definition of mass shooting, in South Africa police define a mass shooting as when three or more people are shot in a single attack.
The country also has high rates of gun crime, including shootings related to local political rivalries.
Authorities say that many of the mass shootings are linked to criminal gangs fighting turf wars or using violence to establish control over communities and areas. The mass killings also tend to happen in the country’s poorest communities
A report from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime found that there had been 43 killings in South Africa this year that were suspected to be politically motivated.
In September, at least 17 people were killed in a mass shooting at a bar in Gauteng. All of the victims, including four women, were declared dead at the scene by the ambulance service.
Last month, at least two people were killed after a gunman opened fire at a memorial service in Katlehong township, located southeast of Johannesburg.
The two victims were members of the youth league of the African National Congress (ANC) party, the largest party in South Africa’s Parliament which describes itself as a “disciplined force of the left”.
The suspected gunman turned himself in while the South African Police Service said that the shooting was being investigated by a political killings task team.

Indian music label and film studio T-Series and digital entertainment company Hungama Digital Media Entertainment have teamed up to launch FastTV, a microdrama platform backed by an INR3 billion ($32 million) commitment from the two partners.
The money will fund original programming, technology, and growing and activating its customer base. T-Series and Hungama own the venture in equal shares.
The launch arrives as the short-episode format surges worldwide. According to the companies, microdrama generated $11 billion in global revenue last year and is on track to top $14 billion by the close of 2026. In India, two in three viewers of the format first came across it within the past year.
FastTV’s originals are being written specifically for mobile screens by writers, directors and actors drawn from Indian film and television. The series span multiple genres and languages, with episodes built to be watched in one go and picked up again the following day. The partners plan to adapt the stories into India’s many languages and take them to audiences in the 190 countries where Indian content already finds viewers.
Hungama spent the past 18 months designing and building the FastTV platform along with the AI production technology that powers it, for which it has applied for a patent, and is contributing both to the joint venture. The companies said the system lets stories be developed, produced and localized across languages fast enough to keep up with the format, and tailors the viewing experience to each user. T-Series will supply original music and soundtracks for FastTV’s series.
“We see immense potential in combining compelling storytelling, world-class music and technology to create a distinctive viewing experience,” said Bhushan Kumar, chair and managing director of T-Series. “With FastTV, our endeavor is to develop a strong Indian content ecosystem that can resonate with audiences not just in India, but across the world.”
T-Series, which runs the most-subscribed music channel on YouTube, has produced more than 180 films, including “Animal,” “Kabir Singh,” “Drishyam 2” and “Border 2.” Hungama has run digital platforms spanning music, video, games and immersive media for two decades and says it reaches more than 300 million users. In the last 12 months it has recast itself as an AI-first business with its own AI studio.
“India does not need another microdrama app. It needs a company built for the way a billion people now watch: stories written for the phone, told in minutes and made to travel,” said Neeraj Roy, founder and CEO of Hungama.
FastTV’s first slate of originals is in development, and programming and genre details will follow in the coming weeks.
