Triumph or flop? The Rugby League World Cup that split opinion
- Published
Has the 2026 Rugby League World Cup been a success or not?
It depends on who you listen to - and perhaps where in the world you are.
The men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments provided plenty of stories - from Kalyn Ponga's return from a broken arm in 23 days, to Jodie Cunningham's mangled ear,, external to the England wheelchair team's golden ladder, to the men's group format that caused widespread bafflement.
But was the World Cup a triumph? The northern and southern hemisphere perspectives provide contrasting answers.
For the fourth tournament running, Australia won the men's and women's titles, with New Zealand unable to deliver a twist in either final.
Tonga and Samoa brought vibrancy and passion - performing to a level that underlined why they are being elevated to Tier One status. The large Polynesian population in the USA - which will co-host the 2030 men's and women's World Cups - is likely to be key in spreading the rugby league word further around the world.
England's Wheelchair World Cup win, in a thunderous final against their old foes France, offset some of the disappointment felt when Brian McDermott's men and Stuart Barrow's women went home early.
And unlike when the game was emerging from post-pandemic constraints in 2022, the tournament has also worked financially by posting a profit.
"This whole tournament's been incredible," said Australia men's captain Isaah Yeo.
"Not just the fans here for New Zealand and Australia, but just everyone. I thought it was all outstanding.
"I think it's to date the most competitive and the best World Cup there's been. I think that's only going to continue to grow."
That sentiment has been endorsed repeatedly by Australian television broadcaster Channel Seven, which paid a reported A$12m (£6.1m) for exclusive domestic free-to-air coverage of the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments.
Not everyone has been able to feel that positivity, though.
The decision to cut the men's tournament from 16 teams to 10 reduced the overall number of matches - and deprived teams such as Jamaica and Greece of a chance to build on the feelgood factor they provided as debutants in 2022.
That decision was made after Australia stepped in to stage the tournament, postponed for a year when scheduled hosts France pulled out for financial reasons.
For those who did get to the party this time, it has not always been an even contest. The disparity between the haves and have-nots has been significant.
While the Jillaroos and Kangaroos players will each receive equal payments of $40,000 (£20,500) for competing, Wales will reportedly spread a total of $15,000 (£7,689) across their women's and wheelchair teams., external
Viewer access to the World Cup has varied too. While Australia had free-to-air live television coverage, fans in the UK only got it for the wheelchair final, shown on BBC iPlayer. For all other games, they needed a Premier Sports subscription, which was also the only way to watch the tournament in North America.
With many matches staged at times when British and American viewers were likely to be in bed, it feels as if a chance to spread the game's gospel has been missed.
Festival feel or competitive balance? Or neither?
Many of the players at this World Cup were Australia-based, as they play club rugby in either the NRL's men's competition or its Women's Premiership.
That helped the International Rugby League - the world governing body - to keep costs down, after it spent a vast sum transporting players from the southern hemisphere to England four years ago.
Paring back the men's competition also helped on the costs front, though another supposed benefit - cutting out the lopsided group-stage scorelines of four years ago - has not been evident.
France and the Cook Islands both conceded more than 180 points in the group stage, while scoring a combined 58.
Former England international Ryan Hall told BBC Radio 5 Live earlier this month that the men's World Cup had suffered for being slimmed down - with Scotland, Ireland, Italy and Wales also missing out.
"I don't think it is a World Cup," Hall said. "The essence of any World Cup in any sport is that it's a festival of the sport.
"Compare it to the football World Cup. Curacao were one of the 48 teams in the World Cup.
"I'm not saying rugby league could get 48 teams in the World Cup because that's not achievable, but [they could] certainly [have] more than 10.
"It's meant to be a festival and showcasing everyone of all levels of different countries who's eligible to play."
A format that contained no quarter-finals came in for widespread criticism from pundits, external before a ball was kicked.
The men's tournament featured one group of four and another of six. But two teams went through from both groups, and not everyone in the six-team pool played each other.
In the words of Castleford Tigers head coach Paul Rowley, the former England hooker: "It's trying to make a square with five sides." England captain George Williams, during the build-up, called the format "weird".
And England turned out to be the major losers. The draw left them with no margin for error as an underprepared and jet-lagged squad faced a dangerous Tonga side first up, and lost 30-12.
And ultimately, McDermott's side paid the price. Of the 26 teams across the three World Cups, only one side won two out of three group games and still failed to make the semi-finals: England's men.
- 'We got disrespected' - Walsh and Australia make World Cup point 
  - Published8 hours ago
- Ruthless Australia win record fourth Women's World Cup 
  - Published11 hours ago
- Sharks, ladders and a four-year plan - how England won World Cup 
  - Published2 days ago
A growing audience?
An October and November tournament brings a different vibe depending on where you are. The last World Cup, in the UK, was staged as the temperatures dropped. This time around, it was held with co-hosts Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea heading towards summer.
Fans have gone to games in T-shirts and shorts instead of thick winter garments - and tellingly, average footfall increased.
That is despite the fact that the capacity 52,000 crowd in Brisbane for finals night was lower than the 67,000 at Old Trafford four years ago.
In 2022, the men's group stage - spanning 24 games - was watched by an average crowd of 9,811, itself down on the 14,345 figure from 2013, when England and Wales played hosts.
This time around, the average crowd rose to 21,360. It probably helped that there were fewer group games. It certainly helped that every Australia match was well attended, and that there was strong backing for New Zealand, Samoa, Tonga and Papua New Guinea, who played twice in their capital Port Moresby.
Lessons have also clearly been learned from 2022's heavily criticised ticket pricing structure.
Instead of adults paying more than £20 to attend matches, it has been a more friendly A$19, which equates to £9.74 per ticket.
But while attendances at this year's tournament are up, there is still work to be done around the women's game.
The sight of more empty seats than supporters in grounds for a number of double-headers is hardly a good look for the organisers or broadcasters.
Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner notably raised the issue after her team defeated Samoa 40-0 in their Pool A opener at the home of Parramatta Eels on 16 October.
That match had followed Samoa's men thrashing France 78-4 - but in a stadium with a capacity of 30,000, many of the recorded 13,174 crowd had dispersed before the women's game got under way, with the stands appearing barely 20% full.
"Let's get around women in sport, right? All women in sport, particularly at this Rugby League World Cup," Skinner said. "We've got a lot of talented women across all the teams and the message would be to stay and support that.
"Something really cool's happening in this generation of sport, with our ladies, and you're going to miss history-making moments at this World Cup, no doubt."
Sadly for Skinner and her peerless team, it was a pattern that was repeated in Sunday's final, with the stands in Brisbane's Suncorp Stadium only filling as kick-off time for the men's game approached.
Northern hemisphere indifference?
Four years ago, the Rugby League World Cup was shown free-to-air in the UK by the BBC, with record-breaking viewing figures.
Almost 30 million people tuned in to watch the five-week extravaganza.
This time, the action has largely been behind a paywall. Premier Sports has shown all the World Cup matches live. The BBC showed the wheelchair final live, plus online highlights of selected games from all three tournaments.
In addition, it provided live radio coverage of all men's matches and some women's games, plus live text commentaries on selected games.
Rights were awarded by the International Rugby League - and not the Rugby Football League. Last month, IRL chair Troy Grant told the iPaper that it made the decision to go with Premier because the BBC did not offer enough money - though no other free-to-air broadcaster made a suitable offer either.
Former England international Jon Wilkin highlighted the issue during a BBC Radio 5 Live discussion at the start of this month, saying: "The World Cup should have been on the BBC.
"There is no doubt in my mind as a public service broadcaster, this had so many reasons to be a slam dunk home run to be free to air on the BBC. It had to be."
In response, a BBC spokesperson said: "We must make difficult choices to deliver the savings required while continuing to serve audiences as effectively as possible."
And therein lies a problem for the sport in the northern hemisphere, where more backing, more financial support and more coverage is needed to reverse the fortunes of the Super League and international teams largely bound to that competition.
The financial gulf to southern hemisphere's elite competitions was laid bare, when the NRL struck a record A$5.3bn (£2.78bn) television deal over seven years in July.
Super League's TV deal with Sky Sports, which expired at the end of 2026, was worth around £21.5m per year.
Even with the pending announcement of a deal to bring NRL investment into Super League, that particular playing field is a long way from being levelled.
And it means that when the next World Cup comes around, Australia can expect to be favourites to win the men's and women's tournaments again.

Two Celebrity Cases Put a Spotlight on British Courts’ Gag Orders
Russell Brand and the TV personality David Walliams both persuaded courts to suppress misconduct allegations against them. Some say the libel laws need to change.
Two recent cases have brought new attention to the ways that British laws can allow the wealthy and powerful to silence their critics.
The first was the rape and sexual assault trial of the comedian Russell Brand. Before his conviction last week, Mr. Brand had obtained an injunction prohibiting another accuser from telling almost anyone — including the police, her family and most doctors — about her claims that he assaulted her. (Mr. Brand has denied her allegations.) That injunction, first revealed by Dan Neidle, a tax lawyer and free-expression activist, apparently remains in force.
In the second instance, two British news organizations were temporarily blocked from reporting allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams, a television personality and author of children’s books, before a judge declined to make the injunction permanent. The Guardian newspaper and ITV News, a British broadcaster, published investigations last week into the allegations, which Mr. Walliams denies.
Though both men now face public scrutiny, the revelations of how they used court injunctions — essentially gag orders — to protect their reputations have provoked no shortage of public and political outrage. Judges in other cases have issued “super injunctions,” which prohibit publishing any information even about the injunction itself.
“What will the government do to prevent these abuses of process, and stop the abusive injunctions and super injunctions which stop scrutiny, accountability and the work of the free press?” Nick Timothy, the shadow justice minister, asked in Parliament on Tuesday.
The British government is now “looking at what we can do,” Alex Davies-Jones, the government minister responsible for victims of crime and violence against women and girls, said in response.

On Wednesday, Mississippi’s Senate race was officially called for Democrat Scott Colom, who will become the first Black person to represent the state in the US Senate since Reconstruction, more than 140 years ago. Colom’s win is a stunning, historic upset — and for many Black Democrats, like Rep. Bennie Thompson, it’s been a long time coming.
“A rich message, but a poor campaign”: How Scott Colom beat the odds in Mississippi
Rep. Bennie Thompson on his 50-year fight to see a Black senator from Mississippi.
Thompson, who also won his race last week, has represented Mississippi’s majority-Black Second Congressional District since 1993. Over the years, the 78-year-old lawmaker has frequently invoked the story of his father, who was never able to cast a vote because of racist Jim Crow laws that enforced segregation until the mid-1960s.
I sat down with Thompson for Today, Explained to talk about Colom’s run for Senate, how he won, what it means for Thompson personally.
Below is an excerpt of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Your dad was never able to cast a vote during his lifetime because of Jim Crow laws. And I wonder, growing up in Mississippi, what did you learn about who was allowed to participate in democracy?
You were a second-class citizen. That means you could go to school, but you couldn’t go to school with the white kids. Or the one swimming pool in town was for white kids, and the Black kids had to swim in the creeks or the ponds around the community. No lifeguard, no anything. My mama and daddy paid taxes, but they weren’t allowed to vote. My uncle fought in World War II; defended democracy all over the world, but when he came back home, he had to ride a segregated train behind the white German prisoners.
Jesus.
So you had the white soldiers, the white German prisoners, and the Black soldiers. And that was the order of the day. It was something that we grew up with.
When you were young, I wonder, did you associate the right to vote with the ability to change things? Like, if we get to cast a ballot, then we get to fix this mess?
The best thing that I can say is I went to Tougaloo College [near Jackson, Mississippi]. And on that college campus, I met Martin Luther King Jr., I met Stokely Carmichael, I met Harry Belafonte, I met Sammy Davis Jr. — all of the major civil rights icons of the day.
That was how we cut our teeth into civil rights and voting rights. The first campaign I worked on was Mrs. Hamer’s campaign for Congress.
Fannie Lou Hamer, the civil rights icon.
And I now represent that district.
But I remember telling my mother that, oh, I had gone to Ruleville, Mississippi, to help register Black people to vote for Congress. And my mama said, “Well, I don’t know why you way up there.” Said, “Black people don’t vote here in Bolton.” And so it hit me. And Lord have mercy. In my own hometown, you know, I was in the same situation. And we did voter registration. We did all kind of things.
“For me, having gone through those life experiences and now to see a Scott come along, you know, it not only brings tears to your eye, but it also says that there’s hope.”
We brought Head Start to the community, and started understanding that real freedom comes with political freedom. And so we started holding meetings about what we wanted to do. We decided to run three people for the board and the three African Americans won.
But it really wasn’t a good four years on that term because the current mayor didn’t want any progress. So we ran an all-Black slate: mayor, clerk, alderman. We won every position.
We’re talking about 50 years ago, and all these challenges that you faced, all these challenges to being able to vote, being able to assume office, being able to function as a mayor in a town that is so segregated. Fifty years later, Scott Colom is winning in Mississippi.
I want to ask you to reflect on when you became aware of his candidacy and what you thought about the potential there.
One of the challenges that I’ve had to deal with is that every time I run for public office, I’ve always been the first. But I wanted to create some kind of vehicle to get other people engaged. So we formed the Mississippi Black Leadership Institute. Well, Scott Colom was in the first class. And he really said, “I want to run for something. I don’t know what it is.” He said, “But there’s a district attorney’s position that’s available. It’s three counties.”
We helped Scott put his campaign together. We hooked him up with various people, and he beat a 28-year incumbent as district attorney.
Why do you think he won?
Well, because he had the fire in the belly. And he never met a stranger. And so we prepared him, and he’s one of our star pupils of that class. And look, uh, when the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee would not support him, they—
They would not support him.
They would not support him. But this was my — Bennie Thompson’s position is that Northeasterners were still looking down on Southerners.
Well, did you call them up and scream at Chuck Schumer or somebody and say, “Guys, I am telling you, we got one here who can win?”
Look, we did everything that the system says you should do. We gave the demographics. That district [Colom] represented was not a majority-African American district. He beat that sitting district attorney in a majority-white district because he had a plan and he had a message. We had a rich message, but a poor campaign. Because we couldn’t get our DSCC to help.
Have you called any of those people in national leadership and said, “I told you so?”
Oh yeah. All of a sudden, the week before the election, they’re going to say, “Well, we’re going to be able to do this, but we’re going to shoot the spot and we’ll send it to you.” So you really didn’t give us the money. You know what I’m saying?
So that’s all right. We’re going to keep doing our low budget, social media-attractive thing. And so it took off.
You are 78 years old? Do I have that right?
Yep.
This has been most of your life. The fight for this has been most of your life.
Yep.
You sit here today, we sit here today. Where is your head at in all of this? Did you lock yourself in the bathroom and cry for 10 minutes?
No question. I’m happy for Scott personally. His trajectory is tremendous. But you know, it’s been a tough journey. We had a poll tax put on us that we had to pay money to be a registered voter. We had to interpret sections of the Constitution. In many instances when my mama registered — my mama had a college degree, she was a teacher — but the person who asked her to interpret the Constitution was an elementary school graduate. You see what I’m saying?
I sure do.
And so for me, having gone through those life experiences and now to see a Scott come along, you know, it not only brings tears to your eye, but it also says that there’s hope. There’s hope for young African Americans that at some point, the choice will be, do I stay or leave? It won’t be, “Well, when I get an education, I have to go somewhere else to seek a career.”
And so that’s the exciting part. I’m just really happy. And for a guy who’s been in it over 50 years and been called everything but a child of God, because I’m trying to elevate people who look like me to where I know if they have it, they’ll do a great job. So for Bennie Thompson, Scott’s victory is a dream come true.

There’s nothing like the feeling of a brand-new planner, and I've found the best planners if you're shopping for something new for 2027. Whether you're looking to get a little more organized or just love having somewhere to write everything down, the beginning of the year is a great time for a fresh start, and most planner companies have their 2027 planner designs already available.
The world of planners might seem simple if you've only browsed your local Target or bookstore to see what planners they might have on hand. But there's a wide world of options out there that can perfectly suit your needs, especially if you're willing to build your own travel notebook or write in the dates on an undated paper planner, or open to trying your first Japanese-style planner.
After years of testing and a constant stack of planners on my desk, I've found these standout favorite planner styles that could benefit everyone. If you're looking for a tech companion to your paper planner, check out my guides to the Best Digital Wall Calendars and Best Digital Notebooks to help keep your calendar and thoughts organized digitally.
Updated November 2026: I've updated the information in this guide to reflect planner availability as 2026 comes to an end and 2027 designs become available. I'm also currently testing 2027 designs from Plum Paper, Laurel Denise, My PA Planner, and Sterling Ink, plus an undated design of Aura Estelle if you're looking for a planner you can start using in December 2026 into the new year.
The Best Planners
If you need a single planner that can do it all and won't burn through your back-to-school budget, this is the one. The Roterunner Purpose Planner is an undated planner that has monthly spreads, weekly spreads, and two full open pages for each week, so there's plenty of room to write longer lists or a project brainstorm. Each monthly and weekly spread has a ton of premade checklist sections for you to use, too. There's even space to track your meals, water intake, and gratitude. It's a planner that actually helps me stay organized and gives me space to track and take notes without running out of room.
The undated nature makes it easy to pick up anytime and use for whichever months you need. Fell off the boat for a few months? No problem. No pages will go to waste when you can fill them in as you go. It only covers six months, but I actually like that; it once again feels like a feasible commitment, especially if you're waffling on how much paper planner you want to promise to use. I love the massive B5 size ($35) since it's finally enough space for me and all my various to-do lists and brainstorms, but there's also a smaller (and cheaper!) A5 ($28) size. It's truly my go-to planner since it has so much space for me to both use the pre-made lists and the open space to actually stay organized and put all my ideas, plans, and notes into one planner. Most others make me feel like I need a companion notebook, but not the Roterunner.
The covers come in a variety of simple colors, and in both hard cover or soft, but the butter-soft faux leather soft cover is my favorite of the bunch. Get it in B5 size if you're always looking for more room in your journals and planners—you won't regret it.
If you're getting into planners, there's no way you won't hear about Hobonichi at some point. There are a few different planners the brand makes, with the Techo being the most popular model. I tested the similar Hobonichi Cousin, which adds weekly spreads to the front of the planner after the monthly overviews. While I don't typically prefer a daily planner style, I was surprised by how much I liked using the Hobonichi. All of Hobonichi's planners use Tomoe River S paper, which is super thin but won't bleed through to the other side. It's also super smooth to the touch and to write on. I liked adding my own structure to the daily pages; I sketched a box to separate my to-do lists and habit trackers from my hourly agenda for the day, and then would usually freeform the rest of the page based on what was on my mind. The Cousin I tested and photographed is an A5 size, while the standard Techo is the smaller A6.
Hobonichi's 2027 editions are here, so you can stock up on your planner for next year right now, plus tons of colors, covers, and other accessories, some of which are unique to 2027. I recommend picking out a protective cover since I did ding up my soft cover quite a bit, and that was just from being used around the house with an occasional trip in a bag. There are little quotes in the corners, but I got a Japanese version instead of an English one, so I can't actually read mine. But honestly, I'm glad I did; I prefer the Japanese lettering to English words on the corners of each page.
I've been obsessed with travel notebooks this year. A travel notebook uses bands to connect three or four notebooks together, and I love using this system to build a customized planner designed for my exact needs. It makes it easy to change the design, too, since you can just switch out a single notebook when it's full.
I really like Cloth & Paper's Travel Notebook Collection. There are 13 different notebooks you can choose from to include in your travel notebook, ranging from classic weekly and monthly spreads to more unique options like a daily wellness notebook and a task planner. It's really a great option if you want a couple of specific things, or even just a regular monthly and weekly notebook plus a blank notebook in the back you can fill with to-do lists and replace anytime without needing an entirely new planner. It's great for students, too, because you can have a notebook dedicated to tracking your assignments and syllabus for the semester. You'll need to create your own, though, as Cloth & Paper doesn't have a dedicated academic notebook for you to select.
I tried both the A5 Slim and the Pocket Plus size, and I really prefer the A5 Slim for a traditional planner experience. The Pocket Plus would be fun to bring on a trip; I wish I'd had it on my latest trip to store little mementos and important things like parking receipts, and could have also written out notes and the plan for the week-long trip. But otherwise, the larger A5 slim was much easier to write on and use for my daily notes and planning.
You'll want the Clear Vinyl Travel Notebook Cover ($23 to $25) no matter which size you choose, which includes elastic bindings to bring all the notebooks you buy together, and you can also pick up more colorful elastic options to add a little more personality to your planner.
I've heard a lot of good things about Erin Condren. Founded in 2005 by Erin Condren, it's known for the LifePlanner that's full of various spreads and productivity tools that you can customize, but there are other variations of planners you can find from the brand. While you'll usually customize your Erin Condren planner if you shop directly on the site, there's a predesigned Target line you can shop that won't give you options, but will give you a well-made planner that's ready to go immediately.
I've been testing the Erin Condren Academic Planner you'll find at Target, but it's sold out as we head into the new year; Erin Condren's website has similar, but more expensive options with more cover and customization options. This base version from Target is a great fit for students and people with deadline-style or client-based work they want to organize. Each month has two pages following the monthly spread to set your most important to-dos and dates, but also a full page to track the month's deadlines and what class (or client, or in my case, story beat) they're for. After that, there are weekly spreads with long columns for each day, and seven blocks of four lines that you can label with things like specific classes, clubs, or organizations, or parenting and household tasks, as I track. It's been a really easy planner to add into my lifestyle, even though it's made for students. There's a class tracker in the front of the planner, too, which I skipped using, plus a detailed holiday calendar, and the back has project and exam pages, plus blank note pages, and even a simple sheet of stickers with things like “Exam,” “Midterm,” and “Paper Due.”
Academic planners usually start in August, so you probably don't want a planner like this if you want something fresh for the new year. But it's still my favorite I've tried if it's your preferred style. Erin Condren does have annual layouts and its popular LifePlanner designs available in 2027 layouts, and other specific designs like budget planners and teacher lesson planners if you're looking for something specific, too.
Honorable Mentions
Like I said, there's a huge world of planners out there. Here are a few that the Reviews team and I at WIRED have tested and enjoyed.
More Planners I’ve Tried
Agendio Basic Planner starting at $48: This is a completely customizable planner. I liked it, and you have the option to design your own pages, and the folder-style cover will protect both the pages and binding. I didn't love the customization tools or abilities as much as I wanted to, and there are a lot of steps to create your planner. I preferred the custom tools of Plum Paper over it. It's a good planner if the pages and binder-style are what you're looking for, and you can find some preset options that usually start around $48 for the smallest page size and black-and-white print.
Ban.do 12-Month Planner for $20: If you're looking for another affordable option but want something with more personality than the Roterunner above, Ban.do's planners are fun and colorful and even come with a page of stickers. Laurel Denise Nancy Academic Planner for $44: These planners are cool because you'll look at the month and your weekly at the same time, as the slim weekly pages lay on top of the monthly spread. Some Planner Accessories
Looking for what to pair with your planner? Here are some of our team's favorite daily tools and planner accessories.
Passion Planner Passion Highlighters for $20: If your planner could use a little color, I really like Passion Planner's highlighter sets. They're nice and thin-tipped to fit into slim planner lines, and I especially like the vintage colors for adding color without it feeling neon-bright. You can use the highlighters to organize your plans by type (I like to do red for work, blue for my kid, yellow for things like doctor's appointments, and green for my social life) or color-code your class subjects like we used to do with ringed notebooks.
Pilot Metropolitan Fountain Pen for $34: I never understood the appeal of a fountain pen until I bought one. A properly smoothed fountain pen nib requires very little pressure to write with and seems to glide across the page with a soft, satisfying scratching sound. I know, I'm one of those people now. Much of my initial skepticism came from the perceived complexity of caring for and using a fountain pen, which is very much overblown. My favorite pen of the dozen I've tested is the Pilot Metropolitan with the fine nib. It's easy to work with, taking either prefilled ink cartridges, which you can pop in and out without ever spilling any ink, or you can fill it yourself using a converter and the ink of your choice. I started off using the cartridges, but eventually my quest for a waterproof ink led me to the converter and this sketching ink. Once a week or so, I dip the Metropolitan nib in the bottle of ink and twist the converter to fill the chamber with ink—that's all there is to it. Whichever fountain pen you find works best for you, you’ll find you'll have a quite simply better writing experience. —Scott Gilbertson
Plum Paper Seasonal Stickers for $10: There are a lot of stickers out there you could use for your planners, but my favorites—especially for the holidays—are from Plum Paper. They're beautiful and fun, and are mostly nice and small to fit into small lines or monthly charts without eating up the entire section. I like that there's a mix of shapes and styles, and you can also shop stickers for themes like home, fitness, wellness, and baby milestones. Planner Alternatives
Not everyone needs or wants a rigid planner. If you just need daily to-do lists or are a fan of bullet journals, consider getting a great notebook instead.
Maybe you just want a plain, lined notebook. One of our former reviewers recommended the Midori MD Notebook, and I found it to be a nice small size if you're looking for something minimal. It comes in lined, unlined, or dot-grid, and uses paper made from cotton pulp (just like money!) Midori’s notebooks are designed to fit inside notebook or journal covers (which you can find all over Etsy). The pages are a subtle off-white and have a weight and texture that draw you in.
One of our reviewers skips a planner entirely and instead writes down his to-do list on a 3-by-5 index card. He puts that index card into his pocket with a pocket-sized memo book like this one from Field Notes ($13 for three), where he jots down notes throughout the day to use for the next day's to-do list. Both the notebook and index cards fit inside a waxed canvas notebook cover to keep them safe from the elements (or just his pocket). It's an affordable and easy-to-manage system.
FAQs
Why Choose a Paper Planner?
Studies show that it's good for your brain to write things down. Sure, you could put your calendar in an online tool, but putting pen to paper activates more brain connectivity. We're more likely to remember and learn things if we write them down by hand, so using a paper planner for your to-do list can make it easier to remember. Plus, it's fun! You're given a creative space to let out everything you need to remember, from appointments to the day's tasks, and customize it in a way that best helps you stay organized.
What Style Paper Planner Is Best for You?
Paper planners mainly come in two styles: weekly and daily. Daily planners have an entire page dedicated to each day, while weekly planners have an entire week spread across just two pages. These aren't the only options (monthly is another popular one, for example, but not as popular as these two styles), but they're the most common you'll see. I like daily planners for folks who have a really busy schedule they want to plan out, and long daily to-do lists. Weekly planners are great if you want to be able to write down a few things per day but don't need an entire page.
What Sizes Do Planners Come In?
Here are a couple common planner sizes. My favorite are the larger sizes since I like lots of room to doodle, but the smaller A5 is a popular choice for a book-sized planner that won't take up too much space. Not all paper planners use the same sizing names—Moleskine, for example, calls its A5 size a large—so you'll want to check measurements before you purchase.
- A5 (5.8 by 8.3 inches)
- Regular/Medium / B5 (7 by 9 inches)
- Large/Letter (8.5 by 11 inches)
- Personal/Pocket (3.5 by 5.5 inches)

Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO.
Tech leaders are convinced that Jensen Huang’s exit was a plot against him
David Sacks, Tim Sweeney, and other big names in tech are raising questions about the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation.
At the center of this theory is the reporting from The New York Times that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, one of multiple women Huang is accused of having an affair with, is a Chinese spy. US agencies haven’t confirmed whether this is the case, and President Donald Trump claims he was unaware of any spy allegations. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang set off the events that led to his resignation; subsequent reporting suggested he had an affair with two employees at Nvidia, including one of his direct reports. The revelation raised new questions around whether Nvidia customers, including Megaspeed, were funneling chips to China in circumvention of export restrictions. Last year, Nvidia intervened in a chip-smuggling probe surrounding the Singapore-based company, according to Bloomberg.
David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about The New York Times’ reporting. In a post on X, Sacks points to an article from CNN, which says US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday, saying: “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.”
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney said, “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.”
SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce released an interim final rule on Monday in an attempt to address this loophole.
More than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter, calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”

Health officials in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin announced two more measles deaths late last week, bringing the national tally of confirmed measles deaths this year to 10. The total includes the deaths of at least four infants: two in Pennsylvania, one in New York, and one in Wisconsin.
Wisconsin health officials said the latest measles death—the second for the state—was in a child. Pennsylvania’s health department did not reveal the age or other details of the latest death—the state’s seventh—besides revealing it was of an unvaccinated resident in Montour County. Overall, the seven deaths in Pennsylvania include two in Jefferson County, three in Lancaster County, and one in Mifflin, in addition to the new death in Montour. An eighth death was reported in Franklin County, but state health officials have not confirmed it.
For all the states with deaths so far, health officials have noted that they’re the first deaths in decades. Multiple outbreaks are underway across the country, pushing the national tally of cases to nearly 5,500 across 47 states and jurisdictions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania’s case count alone is over 1,500, and Wisconsin is reporting nearly 650.
Lost status
With outbreaks that have been smoldering and flaring since last year, the US has reportedly lost its measles elimination status—as medical and public health experts have widely expected it would. A panel of experts for the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization, convened last week to review US measles data and assess its elimination status. The PAHO is set to announce its conclusion and the review’s other findings on Tuesday, November 17. But sources broke the news to The Wall Street Journal on Friday that the panel had found that the US had indeed lost its status.

Meta is testing Direct, a standalone messaging app for Instagram
It’s only available in Turkey and Thailand for now.
Meta is working on a dedicated messaging app for Instagram that could also expand the reach of the app's DMs. The company is starting to test Direct, a new standalone app that brings Instagram's inbox to a separate app, but doesn't require an existing Instagram account to use. Direct will only be available in Thailand and Turkey for now, Meta said in an update.
Direct looks pretty similar to Instagram's inbox at first glance. It has an almost identical layout, with existing chats carrying over from the main app if you log in with your Instagram credentials. It even has some of the same personalization features, like the ability to set custom backgrounds for individual threads and Instagram's status update feature, Notes.
But while Instagram users can log in with their existing accounts, Direct doesn't actually require an Instagram login. People can also sign up for Direct with their email address or phone number, and they'll still be able to message friends in the app. However, it sounds like messaging without a linked Instagram account won't be quite as convenient. Meta notes that users without Instagram credentials will need to manually add contacts to the app via their Instagram username or a QR code in order to start conversations.
Meta says it's also bringing some of Instagram's safety features to Direct. The app won't allow people to start chats with accounts they aren't already connected with via their contacts. And parents will be able to monitor who their teen is chatting with and how much time they spend in the app if they use the company's parental control features. Additionally, Meta says it will "use technology to detect and act on potentially inappropriate interactions with young people," though it's vague about what exactly that will entail.
The test of Direct is an interesting move for Meta. Instagram head Adam Mosseri often notes that messaging is Instagram's most-used feature. But he was also reluctant to give Threads its own inbox because it seemed "redundant" to use multiple apps to reach the same people when Meta briefly considered bringing Instagram's inbox to Threads. He said at the time that mirroring the Instagram inbox could cause "notification routing weirdness" and generally seemed like a less than ideal experience for most people.
The app also raises questions about whether Direct would compete with WhatsApp in the countries where it's rolled out. It's unlikely an Instagram-centric app would replace WhatsApp for many people, but it could eat into that app's engagement if non-Instagram users can use Direct to message friends instead.
That may also be why Direct seems fairly limited for now. Meta describes it as a test that will only be available to people in Turkey and Thailand for the time being. But if the app is a success, it's likely the company will consider expanding it to more places.

The charging mistakes that could ruin your Nintendo Switch's battery
Don't let bad charging habits turn your battery from Super to Super Smashed.
As great as handheld consoles can be, from the familiar-feeling Switch 2 to the Steam Deck OLED that still holds up against other PC handhelds, their batteries really are their Achilles' heel. There's only so much playtime you can squeeze out of any portable device, and the more powerful the console, the shorter that tends to be. Moreover, most recent handhelds aren't designed for quick battery replacement. It's doable — Nintendo even provides instructions — but it's not like slapping a few AAs into a flashlight.
On a long enough timeline, all Switch batteries are bound to degrade until your console is only usable when docked. It's just a fact of lithium-ion technology. But if you're careful about how you charge, you can prolong this fate. If you're lucky, you might push things off until Nintendo's next-gen console arrives, whether that's the Switch 3 or another innovation.
Mostly, this is a matter of how often you charge your Switch, and to what percentage. There are some additional factors to consider, though, and we'll touch on those so you can put the free Mario Kart 8 Deluxe Switch 2 update through its paces.
The charging tricks you need for your Switch
Never let your Switch drain to zero. Lithium-ion batteries have a finite number of charge cycles, and letting the battery die burns through them faster. Granted, the number of cycles is going to be well into the hundreds for any device, even beyond the 800 mark in the case of the Switch 1. But as you progress towards the end of that limit, your battery is going to offer diminished capacity. Nintendo also warns that you should charge once every six months, if you're not actively using it, to avoid permanently losing the ability to charge.
You should also avoid charging to 100% unless you need as many hours as you can get. That's because the optimal charge for lithium-ion batteries is both more than zero and less than full. On most devices, the rule of thumb is between 20% and 80%. On the Switch 2, though, Nintendo has added a Stop Charging Around 90% option, which you can find under System Settings. Just remember to toggle this off and wait a few minutes longer when you're heading out on a trip to maximize your time.
Another important factor is ambient temperature. Realistically, you may be unlikely to store or use a Switch beyond its official operating range, which is 41 to 95 Fahrenheit (5 to 35 Celsius). Charging in extreme heat can, however, accelerate capacity loss, so you might want to avoid leaving your console in sunlight for prolonged stretches, or charging outside in climates with intense summer heat. Notably, while extreme cold can have an impact, it shouldn't be permanent.
Why you might not be able to replace your Switch's battery
A Switch is a complex device with delicate electronics, and the battery is embedded inside, rather than in an easily accessible compartment. Making a mistake could break something critical. In fact, Nintendo strongly urges contacting its Customer Service department instead of doing things yourself, and there's no official DIY guide for any Switch 1 model.
While there is an official guide for the Switch 2, Nintendo notes that only consoles with the BEE-001(-01) marking contain user-replaceable batteries, as far as the company is concerned. On top of that, you need Nintendo's BEE-003(-01) Battery Replacement Kit, a careful touch, and an electrically grounded surface. A large enough static shock could fry circuitry.
The good news here is that if you charge your Switch properly, the odds of it surviving until your next upgrade without a battery swap are pretty good. It's more a question of whether anyone you pass it along to will enjoy the same luxury.

- The claim that Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth awarded a commendation medal to a different person than the soldier who reprimanded his group Nov. 11 at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is unfounded.
- The rumor stems from social media users comparing a blurry image of one side of the soldier's face with a sharper frame from a video showing the other side of the soldier's face. Aside from the apparent asymmetricality, no evidence has been offered that the images — which differ greatly in angle, lighting and distance — show different men.
- A Pentagon spokesperson told Snopes, "As shown in the photos, Secretary Hegseth welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026."
On Nov. 11, video footage captured a U.S. Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Virginia reprimanding Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and his entourage after one of them talked and laughed out loud on the steps of the monument. The next day, Hegseth was photographed ostensibly awarding that same soldier a commendation medal in a Pentagon ceremony. 
Almost immediately, posts (archived) on X and Facebook popped up comparing images of the soldier taken at the tomb with one of Hegseth awarding him the medal in an apparent attempt to sow doubts it was the same person.
People claimed the sentinel's ears looked completely different in the two images and suggested the medal recipient was a body double. Several Snopes readers asked us if it was true Hegseth gave the medal to a doppelganger instead of the actual soldier.
(X user @JamesTate121)
The argument, as summarized in one post, went as follows:
Even though it's not the same side ears, most pairs of ears are pretty symmetrical. The details of the ear of the guy he gave the comm medal to, claiming it was the soldier who reprimanded his group, is totally different shape and physical attributes.
If it were true that most pairs of human ears are symmetrical, the argument might stand, but researchers say perfectly symmetrical facial features are the exception, not the rule. When you add to that the differences contributed by angle, lighting and distance in photographs, arguing that the appearance of asymmetricality, especially in photographs, is definitive proof that a pair of ears don't belong to the same person is bound to fail.
In the above collage, a blurry image of one side of a soldier's face is contrasted with a sharper frame from a video showing the other side of a soldier's face, and it's true they don't seem very symmetrical. Does that mean both ears can't belong to the same person? Not at all. Nor has any other evidence been offered to support the claim it isn't the same man in both photographs. The claim is therefore unfounded.
Snopes contacted the Department of Defense to confirm the identity of the soldier. A spokesperson responded, "As shown in the photos, Secretary Hegseth welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026."
As Snopes has previously reported, soldiers have guarded the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington since March 1926. The Arlington National Cemetery website states that the guards initially "discouraged visitors from climbing or stepping on the Tomb." The 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment has guarded the monument since April 6, 1948. Barbara Starr, CNN's former Pentagon correspondent, told the network (at 11:24) on Nov. 11 that sentinels correct any visitors who do not act with "respect and silence" at the tomb.
For further reading, Snopes has investigated numerous claims about Hegseth. Snopes has also covered many "body double" claims over the years.

The meme appeared to have used outdated census estimates for the population of Texas, which increased by nearly 2.5 million people between 2020 and 2025. Even still, Snopes could not replicate the meme's alleged findings.
After Democrats in Texas flipped control of the state House of Representatives and won the governorship during the 2026 midterm elections, a meme circulated suggesting there may have been election fraud in the historically Republican stronghold.
According to the meme, the number of registered voters exceeded the number of voting-age citizens in counties across the state. Several social media posts relayed the image, which showed a map of Texas' 254 counties, including on Instagram and Facebook. Some posts on X also shared the meme, including one that said "97 counties are over the adult-citizen count" (archived):
The meme claimed the counties in red had more registered voters than adult citizens, and the ones in yellow had at least 10% more registered voters than adult citizens. The image gave numbers for only six counties as evidence of its claim — Collin, Denton, Fort Bend, Montgomery, Parker and Williamson — saying that in each of them, the number of registered voters exceeded the number of adult citizens.
The meme cited as its sources the Texas secretary of state's November voter registration figures and Census 2020-24 adult citizen estimates.
We could find no evidence for the meme's claim. Using the most recent U.S. Census' adult citizen estimates (2024) in these counties and comparing them with the Texas secretary of state's numbers on voter registration per county, we could not replicate the image's alleged findings. For this reason, we rate the claim false.
The meme carried a watermark for the X account @_Patriot1776Q_. We reached out to the account asking for more information about the numbers and we will update this report should we receive a response.
It should be noted that Texas' population was the fastest-growing in the country between 2024 and 2026, and our calculations do not account for this growth due to the fact that the U.S. Census' most recent estimate for adult citizens is for 2024. (This also means that comparing the number of registered voters in 2026 to an older, smaller population estimate, as the meme claims to do, would be a flawed comparison.)
An attempt to replicate the meme's calculations
In January, the Redistricting and Voting Rights Data Office of the U.S. Census published its estimates for citizens of voting age by race and ethnicity for 2024. Snopes uploaded that data into a spreadsheet organized by state and county, with the six counties the meme mentioned highlighted them in yellow.
Next, we pulled data about registered voters and actual voters in each county in Texas. (To reflect population changes, we included July 2025 U.S. Census data and calculated the estimated number of adults, citizens and noncitizens combined, per county.)
We compiled the data for the six counties used in the meme and six more among those marked yellow — that is, counties where there were supposedly at least 10% more registered voters than adult citizens. Our calculations did not demonstrate the map's claim.
In an attempt to replicate the meme's numbers, we used the 2024 estimated number of adult citizens against the 2026 number of registered voters. For these numbers to be accurate and definitive, we would need to have 2026 actual numbers of adult citizens in these counties, as opposed to estimates.
For example, the meme said there were 34,319 more registered voters in 2026 in Montgomery County than there were registered adults based on 2020-2024 estimates. We found there were in fact 20,076 fewer adult citizens (based on the 2024 estimate) than there were registered adults in 2026.
The meme also said Parker County counted 111% registered voters relative to the number of estimated number of adult citizens. Our calculation found 108%. Once again, this number did not reflect the updated number of adult citizens in the county in 2026; Parker County is reportedly one of the fastest-growing counties in the nation.
Texas also places voters "in suspense" before removing them from the voter rolls when election officials believe a registered voter may have moved. This means that the number of registered voters reported for a county includes people who may no longer live in that county. Parker County, for example, had just under 9,000 voters in suspense in November, according to the state.
It also should be noted that voter turnout across Texas was roughly 50% in the 2026 midterms, and no county had more votes than adult citizens.
For further reading, Snopes also debunked the claim that Texas "found" 20 million votes to flip it to a Democratic majority.

Apple's most expensive smartphone—the iPhone Duo—lacks one of the company's hallmark features: Face ID. The folding phone is already jam-packed with a hinge and multiple display layers, leaving no room for the TrueDepth sensor required for biometric face authentication. The Duo relies on Touch ID instead.
That's changing now in a software update. On Monday, Apple announced that it's bringing facial recognition to the iPhone Duo as part of the iOS 27.3 developer beta update. But since it can't rely on the tried-and-true Face ID system without those crucial components, it's borrowing the feature from the company's recently launched smart display, the HomeView.
The HomeView personalizes the display content for up to six people in a household, with its camera recognizing people who step in front of it. (It also uses voice data for recognition when someone asks Siri a command.) This “person recognition” technology is protected by the Secure Exclave—different from the Secure Enclave chip that houses Face ID data—a memory-protected space in Apple's A20 Pro processor. As WIRED's Lily Hay Newman writes, it's still not as comprehensive as Face ID, and could be more susceptible to attacks.
Rumors abound that Apple is racing to add proper Face ID to the second-generation iPhone Duo. Still, tight development cycles might mean the feature may not arrive until the third generation in 2028. That also points to limitations in the Duo's new face recognition tech.
You cannot use it to authenticate payments or unlock sensitive content, like your banking app. You'll still need your thumbprint or passcode to approve Apple Wallet purchases. Instead, it's designed to unlock the foldable without tapping a finger on the Touch ID sensor. There is also a time-based limitation. For face recognition to work, it needs a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication within a 45-minute window. This capability is also restricted to the front screen and camera—it doesn't work if the iPhone Duo is unfolded. Also in iOS 27.3, Apple has a new toggle that lets you lock your iPhone Duo when you close it.
Google's newer Pixel folding phones are the only ones on the US market with secure facial authentication, though it's not as effective in the dark as Apple's Face ID. Samsung's facial biometrics on its Galaxy phones aren't strong enough to protect sensitive content and are largely used to unlock the device.
Apple’s willingness to roll out a watered-down version of Face ID is a rare compromise for the company—and shows just how much of a friction point Touch ID has become for Duo owners.

"Crystal Palace and Thomas Frank feels like a very good fit," added Robinson.
How big a challenge does Frank face?
Thomas Frank has a lot of work to do as Crystal Palace have undoubtedly been the worst team in the Premier League so far this season, ranking bottom not just in points (seven) but also goal difference (-14) and expected goal difference (-8.1).
It's the defence where Frank will have to focus most of his attention. Not only have Palace conceded the most goals (24) but they've also faced the most shots (189) and have the worst expected goals against (xGA) figure in the league (21.9).
Their attack has actually not been too bad. While only Hull have taken fewer shots, the Eagles have created really good chances and have perhaps been unlucky not to score a few more goals given the opportunities they've had.
There is also one significant factor in Frank's favour. Although Palace may be bottom of the Premier League, they are certainly not cut adrift as they sit just two points from safety.
The side propping up the table at this stage have had an average of just three points in the past 10 seasons, but for as bad as they've been, Palace have seven - the most the bottom side have had after 10 games for 24 years.

Vallari Sheel wishes she could carry a camera or a pair of binoculars without being asked what her father does for a living. Once, looking at a tree in her south Delhi neighbourhood, about 50 metres away from her home, a man in a car screamed at her: “You have been clicking photos here for 10 days. What are you going to do with them?”
Sheel, an urban ecologist, spends hours observing trees of all types in all seasons. She often travels by car for her own safety, worries about the impact of her work on her family, and has clear guidance for her female interns when they are, inevitably, approached: don’t engage, don’t respond.
“It’s the men who ask such intrusive questions: Who are you? Where are you from? What does your father do?” she says.
Sheel was recounting these experiences atop Delhi’s oldest fort inside Sanjay Van, a sprawling city forest overlooking a 12th-century minaret. She was one of about 20 women who had gathered on a crisp Sunday morning in October to enjoy nature, safely. Many had never experienced a forest before.
Among the group were a scientist who had stopped birding since she moved to Delhi, a psychiatrist who can’t find a safe place to run, and an environmental planner who cycles everywhere. For many women, simple pleasures such as enjoying nature have become beset by gender crimes.
“The city feels designed to crush any form of freedom, any form of exploration,” says Neha Sinha, who organised the walk. Author of My Wild City: Finding Nature, Meaning, and Hope in India’s Capital, Sinha has been organising these walks for two years.
During her own walks around the city’s forts, forests and wetlands to observe the diminishing number of fireflies, flying foxes, howling jackals, leopards and hyenas, civets and owls, and groves of 350-year-old trees, she has faced the wrath of men. She has changed her route countless times to mislead stalkers, and been asked by men on the street how much she would charge for sex.
“As has everybody else,” she says. “Nearly every woman I know has called a cop saying ‘I have a stalker.’ In a culture that tells you not to go out … how do you make nature your own?”
Two weeks before the women gathered on the walking trails of Sanjay Van, dotted with ruellias, vajradantis and jaal trees, hundreds of people had joined a protest in Delhi over the gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park.
Their demand was to make public spaces safer for women. The government’s response was to ban entry to public parks after sunset.
For Alankrita Narayan, a wildlife conservation student who often needs to work alone at night, that rule was unhelpful. During an internship, she recalls, her organisation trained her for worst-case scenarios in the jungle: What if something happens to your partner? What if you encounter a man carrying a weapon? What if you encounter a forest officer asking for sexual favours?
“And I was like, where did the animal come in here? What if I’m caught alone and a leopard comes in front of me? And they were like, ‘Oh, don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into,” she says. Sinha agrees: “Animals have rules.”
Paroma Mukherjee, a photographer, recalls the advice she once got from a well-known photographer: be inconspicuous, wear clothes that blend in, keep your equipment small. “But then, he was a man. So he could blend in,” she adds.
“Men can pee on the road and we can’t even carry a camera,” another woman says. “You know, we had to take a detour today to avoid a lonely stretch on our way here,” says another. “I carry a pepper spray,” another adds.
On group walks, the women pick up and drop off each other at their homes, wait outside the forest gate until everyone has arrived, and stick together in isolated areas. “I always tell women, ‘Don’t go alone’,” Sinha says.
“We started the walk at 7am today, which is late for birdwatching, but everybody could not leave home while it was still dark,” she says.
However, the group agree that many of these measures might not work for women from less privileged backgrounds, who then miss out.
“No woman in the city is fully free,” Sinha says.
Walking as a woman is an act of resistance, as is observing nature. “Because you’re actually slowing down when you do that,” she says. “It’s so different from the instant gratification culture that we have today. It is more of an immersion, rather than conquering. Both are very political acts.”
In the heart of New Delhi, where India’s senior officials and dignitaries live, there are thousands of fruit bats that swarm out of their roosts every evening to feast on mahua trees.
“And on very clear wintry nights, when everything is silent, I even hear jackals crying and laughing from my home. It’s almost like a parallel city,” Sinha says.
Over three hours, the women collect cuttings, peer and marvel at speckle-like flowers through a pocket microscope, discuss the colonial concepts of wild plants labelled as weeds, chat about the drongo, black kite and tailorbird they spotted, and the next walk.
“Can we do it at night?” someone asks. “What would the forest look like at night?”
Sinha describes a previous night walk experience when frogs had put up an orchestral noise, fireflies lit the bushes and jackals were laughing. “It was the most eerie, magical, bewitching atmosphere I have ever experienced,” she says.
Men, she points out, can simply go ahead and enjoy such experiences, but women have to create an ecosystem around them to be able to.
But, she promises her enthusiastic group, she will try to arrange a night walk.

An Intriguing Approach to Slow Alzheimer’s Shows Mixed Results
The device, a headset delivering light and sound, is based on the theory that audiovisual stimulation can evoke brainwave responses that might help preserve neurological function.
The largest trial to date of a headset device that delivers flickering light and sound in an attempt to slow the progression of Alzheimer’s has delivered mixed results.
The device is based on the theory that audiovisual stimulation can evoke brainwave responses that might help preserve neurological function and clear waste from the brain. The idea is appealing because, if such a treatment works, it could provide an accessible non-drug alternative to Alzheimer’s medications that are expensive and carry significant safety risks.
Results of the study of the device, presented on Monday evening at a major Alzheimer’s conference, showed that the 12-month trial involving participants with mild to moderate Alzheimer’s did not achieve its primary goal. The overall group of patients who used the audiovisual device did not experience slower cognitive decline than those who used an inactive placebo device called a sham.
Patients with moderate Alzheimer’s showed no benefit at all from the system, called Spectris, according to data provided by the company, Cognito Therapeutics, which sponsored the trial. But for patients with mild Alzheimer’s, data generally suggested they could experience slower decline with the device, particularly if they used it nearly every day for close to the recommended 60 minutes.
Based on that, Cognito’s chief executive, Christian Howell, said the company planned to seek Food and Drug Administration approval.
“The signal we found in the mild population is really incredible,” Mr. Howell said in an interview. He attributed the trial’s failure to meet its primary goal to “the lack of treatment effect” in patients with moderate Alzheimer’s, but said that for mildly impaired patients, “there is a very clear path for us to the F.D.A.”

Chris Degnan thought he was done with operating jobs after leaving Snowflake. But golf and startup advisory work left him wanting more.
“I was done,” Degnan, Cognition’s new chief revenue officer, said on an episode of Kleiner Perkins’ podcast released on Monday. “No intent to take an operating job — none.”
But after 18 months away from full time work, he said he was not as happy as he expected to be.
“It’s all well and good that I could go and play golf every single day of the week at 10 in the morning,” he said. “It’s not fulfilling.”
Degnan joined Cognition, the maker of the AI coding agent Devin, in September after initially declining outreach about the job. The company’s president, Russell Kaplan, eventually persuaded him to take a meeting.
After learning more about its growth, Degnan said he woke up the next day with a realization: “Either I’m never going to do another operating job, which was in the cards, or I’m going to do this.”
Degnan’s move to Cognition also sparked a public clash with Factory, a rival AI coding startup where he had been an advisor and board observer. In September, Factory CEO Matan Grinberg said the company had terminated Degnan, accusing him of holding undisclosed discussions with Cognition while advising Factory on confidential matters.
Degnan denied sharing Factory information, saying Cognition had never asked for it and that he would never provide it. He announced his new role as Cognition’s chief revenue officer shortly afterward.
Before he announced his retirement, Degnan was at Snowflake for over a decade, and rose from a sales leader to CRO at the software-as-a-Service company.
'10 times more fulfilling'
The decision to come to Cognition put him back at the center of the AI frenzy.
“You’re in the middle of this insane thing,” he said, referring to the market’s AI momentum. “In a month on the job, it’s 10 times more fulfilling.”
Degnan added that the draw to return to work is less financial than personal.
“I have the luxury of not having to do these things,” he said. “I’m having a ton of fun doing it.”
Degnan is among a growing list of chief executives who have boomeranged back to work after stepping down.
Google cofounder Sergey Brin stepped down from a management role at Alphabet in 2019, but later said he was working at Google “pretty much every day,” drawn back by the pace of AI.
Michael Dell left the CEO job at Dell in 2004, but resumed it at the board’s request in 2007.

Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
- Published
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.
Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.
Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there have been multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.
The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.
"Due to the threat of repeated shelling, emergency workers are constantly forced to periodically suspend work and retreat to a safe place," it added.
The DSNS said the death toll had risen to at least 72 people making it one of the deadliest single incidents since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".
He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.
BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.
Oleksiy said rescue crews operated under a constant threat of attack. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead," he said.
BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.
A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.
While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.
Fears of second strike heard on police radios
Local people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.
Bodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.
Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.
The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.
Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.
Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.
Trevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures.
His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.
Ball and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.
International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.
Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".
Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.
Additional reporting by Margaryta Maliukova, BBC Monitoring

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.

Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.

TRMNL Frame is a $1300 full-color e-paper display that looks like real art

TRMNL, the company known for e-paper frames and kits, just launched its biggest and most colorful product yet. Frame is a 31.5-inch full color e-paper display mounted in a handmade wooden frame, designed to show paintings, photos, maps, graphics and other still images in a more natural way than LCD or OLED screens. Though not cheap, it features high-quality materials and will be released in limited numbers to start with.
If you've never heard of TRMNL, the company has had some buzz of late with its e-paper displays sold in frames or kits. Thus far, products like the DIY (kit) and OG (picture frame) have been strictly black and white or grayscale, because "TRMNL is not a television.
