Do school cellphone bans work? New study says yes – but it's complicated
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
The rise of smartphones in the U.S. coincided with a dramatic slide in K-12 students' reading and math achievement. Now, new research suggests putting students' phones in locked pouches during the school day may help restore some of those historic losses.
"Around 2013, U.S. students started losing 2-3 weeks of learning each year," says Harvard University's Tom Kane, one of the new study's co-authors. "It's been a slow leak that, over time, has put U.S. 8th graders almost a year behind. Strict cellphone bans seem to plug about half of that leak."
Or the equivalent of 1-2 weeks of learning a year, according to the study released Tuesday. That's a small but, according to Kane, statistically significant improvement.
"That could add up over time, just as the initial declines did," adds Dartmouth College's Douglas Staiger, another co-author.
The study's authors say it is the first nationwide analysis of student-level test scores in math and reading both before and after schools enforced locked-pouch cellphone bans. It was a joint effort between Harvard's Center for Education Policy Research, Dartmouth and NWEA, a K-12 testing and research organization.
Kane, Staiger and their teams analyzed a nationwide sample of more than 3 million elementary-, middle- and high-school students over the past five school years, comparing the test scores in schools that adopted phone pouches to the scores at similar schools that did not.
Not only did strict cellphone bans appear to trigger small learning gains, the researchers say, those gains didn't seem to fade out after the first year of implementation. Instead, Kane says, the gains appeared to continue, year after year – at least up to three years after adoption.
Research on phone bans is mix
Tuesday's headline finding, that locking phones during the school day led to small but statistically significant improvements in math and reading scores, comes with an important caveat:
A separate study, from April, found that these pouches had "close to zero" impact on student test scores – and if there was a benefit, it was not statistically significant.
"Overall, we didn't find evidence of meaningful achievement gains," says Brian Jacob, a co-author of that April study and a professor of education policy at the University of Michigan.
What should we make of these seemingly contradictory results?
Both are large-scale studies by well-respected teams of researchers. The April study has been peer-reviewed; the more recent study has not.
Both studies similarly focused on schools' adoption of lockable pouches made by the for-profit company Yondr. According to Tuesday's paper, more than 3,300 schools nationwide began using the pouches between the '19-'20 and '25-'26 school years. Typically, schools that use the pouches require that students put their phones in them at the beginning of the day and don't get them back until the end of the school day, when the pouches are unlocked by a school administrator with a special magnetic device.
But the two studies also differ in key ways. The April study pooled school-level mean test scores at several thousand Yondr-adopting schools, while Tuesday's study used student-level scores at the 844 schools that use both Yondr pouches and tests administered by NWEA.
Simply put, the study released Tuesday had more fine-grain, student-level data, but the study released in April was able to examine a much larger sample of schools.
But the two studies' findings also aren't as different as they may seem. Jacob and his co-authors did find statistically significant gains with Yondr pouches in high school math. It's just that those gains were offset by ban-related learning losses in middle school.
Overall, Jacob says, the new study "is encouraging. And if [the benefit] really persists and accumulates over time, it really could be a meaningful benefit. I think we'll just have to wait and see if that happens."
Another co-author of that April study, Tom Dee, a professor at Stanford University's Graduate School of Education, says of Tuesday's findings, "I hope they are right that these very small test score gains will aggregate and add up over time. However, I'm not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans."
Taken together, Dee says, he considers the results from these early studies into cellphone bans "largely disappointing," and insists "we need continued study on this topic."
Kane sees the results differently. Even if the benefit is small, he argues, relative to the cost – roughly $25 per student – these pouches still make financial sense for schools. "That's still a lot less than having to pay teachers for an extra week or two of instruction."
When it all went wrong
For nearly a quarter-century, from 1990 to 2013, math achievement among fourth- and eighth-graders rose steadily. Reading scores also improved.
Then around 2013, student test scores began a sustained tumble that continued through the COVID-19 pandemic and has only recently begun to slow. For years, politicians and pundits blamed pandemic-era school closures for the losses, but the data tells a different story.
"Particularly in reading, test scores were going down for four to six years before the pandemic," Stanford University researcher Sean Reardon told NPR earlier this year. "In fact, you wouldn't really know there was a pandemic effect if you just looked at the last 10 or 12 years of test scores. There's been just a steady kind of decline regardless of the pandemic."
Which raises the question: What happened around 2013?
Possible explanations abound. The federal government began stepping back from holding schools accountable for low test scores. Many schools also saw funding cuts in the wake of the Great Recession.
This new study is the latest to make the case that the mass adoption of cell phones by children and teens also helped fuel those test score declines.
The researchers note that, in 2011, fewer than a quarter of teen students had access to smartphones. By 2018, 95% did. And similar rates in other industrialized countries coincided with similar student achievement declines.
Now, Kane says, he wants to study students' smartphone and social media use outside of school.

Ronaldo, Maradona, Baggio - what happened to the World XI?
- Published
Soren Colding wasn't expecting the call. "The Laudrup brothers, Peter Schmeichel, there might have been some cancellations," he jokes.
Eventually, the Danish FA turned to a Brondby defender who had played a handful of times for the national team.
The assignment? He would be expected to mark Ronaldo and Gabriel Batistuta as part of a Europe XI against the Rest of the World at Marseille's Velodrome.
It was December 1997, and Colding's team-mates would include defenders Fernando Hierro and Alessandro Costacurta, a midfield duo of Zinedine Zidane and Paul Ince, and Patrick Kluivert and Alen Boksic up top.
This was a star-sprinkled cast - one player from each of the competing nations at the following summer's World Cup joining forces before the draw took place.
"Of course, when you see those names, it was just more or less a dream come true," explains the Dane.
Colding was flown to France and chauffeured to the hotel. His driver offered to hang around in case the full-back fancied an impromptu shopping trip. There was no need. Instead, he discovered a bag of Fifa goodies in his room.
"There was the biggest Adidas bag I have ever seen in my life," he smiles. "I found a training suit and went down to lunch.
"Then I saw all the other guys on round tables - they were sitting with their agents, their wives, their family, their friends in normal [clothes]. Then the Danish guy turned in. Nobody knows who he is, in his Adidas training suit!"
Colding struck up a friendship with South Africa defender David Nyathi and the pair were whisked off to a 45-minute training session that afternoon. Not all the big names took part, but one Argentine offered a taste of what was to come.
"Batistuta was there and just to see him and his moves, you thought, 'Okay, it's gonna be a nice evening tomorrow'," remembers Colding, who also got to link up with European boss Franz Beckenbauer.
"He was pretty cool. He was saying, 'what is your position? Defender? OK, can you play left defender?' No problem - I'll play wherever you place me!"
Come game day, 38,000 fans packed in to see peak Ronaldo. Months earlier, Il Fenomeno completed a world-record move to Inter Milan on the back of 47 goals in 49 games in one sensational season at Barcelona.
The 21-year-old was the most exciting player on the planet.
"It was crazy, actually," recalls Colding, who previously faced the forward when Denmark's under-21s played Brazil in Florianopolis before the 1996 Olympics.
"That was almost the same team as they played with at the World Cup in '98. So we lost 5-1. Just to see his speed and how he played - I played against Roberto Carlos in that game as well - that was just another level. I thought, 'what is going on here?'
"When I saw him there again, it was just to see what is actually reachable for a football player, because that was next level tremendous. His speed and his touch are unbelievable, and also his power.
"And still, just a small, shy guy. You know, he just wants to play football, and all these people are around him protecting him. Just to see when a star like him joins an event like that, how many people around him, agents and followers, how should you navigate all that?"
Ronaldo, captaining Carlos Alberto Parreira's side, was at his blistering best, scoring twice and setting up the other three as Rest of the World won 5-2 - Batistuta also netted twice, before Zidane responded.
"You start thinking what if you injured some of them," explains Colding. "You are a defender, you don't want goals against you, so you have to fight - that's how I am.
"How hard should you go to them? Should you just let them go? No. I would not just let them run and score. I tried to do my best, that was probably not good enough!"
When Maradona came to Wembley
This wasn't the first outing for a World XI, in fact such Fifa exhibition matches had been taking place since England hosted an all-star side in front of a reported 100,000 fans at Wembley in 1963 to celebrate the Football Association's centenary.
They became a semi-regular occurrence as testimonials or charity fixtures, with huge names appearing across eras from Eusebio and Zico to Roberto Baggio.
But the biggest coup was arguably luring Diego Maradona to Wembley a year after winning the World Cup with Argentina and scoring his 'Hand of God' goal against England.
Jon Smith, who represented the Napoli star, explains in his book 'The Deal' how Maradona was offered around £250,000 and flown from Naples on a private jet to take part in an anniversary game against the Football League.
"In fairness, he wanted to shake hands with the team and say 'sorry if I offended you'," Smith tells BBC Sport. "He genuinely believed his talent was God-given.
"He was sort of two people. He was lovely, Diego, when you were with him. When he crossed the white line he was Maradona. So the Hand of God was an expression of 'I am God's footballing representative', if you like.
"It was madness, because you can imagine how the media were all over it. It was a bit special."
Napoli and Argentina welcomed the opportunity for Maradona to generate some good PR in England, helped by Bobby Robson's Football League side winning 3-0 - Bryan Robson netting twice and Norman Whiteside grabbing the other.
"I remember introducing him to Bobby Robson," adds Smith. "He put his hand out, and Bobby said 'I'm not shaking that hand!', which I thought was lovely - he did shake the other hand!"
'It wouldn't happen now'
One of the final games saw a Ronaldinho XI take on a Shevchenko XI at Nou Camp in February 2005 to raise funds for victims of the 2004 tsunami.
Andriy Shevchenko's stacked squad included Zidane, David Beckham, Alessandro Del Piero, Thierry Henry, Raul, Paolo Maldini and Steven Gerrard.
Ronaldinho could call on Ronaldo, Kaka, Cafu, Adriano, Javier Zanetti, Didier Drogba and Samuel Eto'o, though it was Southampton's Henri Camara who scored twice in a 6-3 win for the Brazilian's team.
But things have moved on, and it is hard to imagine clubs releasing their star players for such an exhibition nowadays.
"The whole world of football has changed," says Smith. "You used to have testimonial games and testimonial years because players got paid okay but by the same token weren't earning £100k a week.
"It wouldn't happen now because the business of football is so much bigger, you can't risk the players - if they get injured playing for their country, that annoys everybody.
"But beyond that they are owned by big corporations and in some cases countries, so you just wouldn't allow your player to go out and do that."
Colding went on to play 27 times for Denmark, featuring at the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000, but retains fond memories of representing the Europe XI.
"Now, to come up with the idea to make a game like this, in combination with the draw, I think everyone will say you are crazy," explains Colding.
"But at that time it was perfectly planned and a fantastic event to be a part of. As players, we have a tremendous relationship between each other.
"It shows all the spectators you can be enemies on the field, but you can actually be friends and gather together in this kind of event.
"That for me sends a signal to all that we are a community in football and we can actually make great things together that not only is a question of money."
In fact, he still has his Europe shirt - a reminder of coming up against Ronaldo and Batistuta and being a team-mate of Zidane almost 30 years ago.
"It doesn't smell very good, actually," laughs Colding. "Sometimes, when I go in the garage with my kids and tell them about it and what actually happened, I see in their eyes, they don't really believe that I was a part of that game.
"That was not about money - we didn't get anything to join - it was just because you represent your country, so it was a great experience, it's also about having fun.
"You know, as small kids, you don't start by saying, 'I want to earn 20 million'. No, you start because it's fun to play football."

Following a terrorist attack on November 11 at a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) checkpoint in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kulgam district, a video went viral on social media with the claim that retired Indian Army officer and journalist Pravin Sawhney described Indian military and counter-terrorism drives in the valley as “false flag operations”.
Social media users claimed that Sawhney said that operations against the Kulgam attack, the Balakot airstrikes, and Operation Sindoor were orchestrated for political gains.
X user @RedDeFactoIND (Red Vanguard) shared the viral clip, which shows an interview conducted by The Wire. (Archive)
𝗘𝘅-𝗔𝗿𝗺𝘆 𝗢𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗲𝗿 𝗗𝗿𝗼𝗽𝘀 𝗕𝗼𝗺𝗯𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗹🚨: Pravin Sawhney in Recent Interview for Wire said, “Another false flag, just like Pulwama and Pahalgam,This is a pattern”
Indian journalists and influencers are now openly questioning the government’s narrative.
The voices from within are getting louder.
#CRPFSoldiers #CRPFCampAttack #kulgamattack #Kulgam #KulgamTerrorAttack
— Red Vanguard (@RedDeFactoIND) November 12, 2026
In the viral clip, the interviewer can first be heard saying (translated from Hindi): “Sushant, I want to know from you…the theme of your latest essay is the politicisation of army…During the false flag operations like Balakot and Pahalgam, the way the Bharatiya Janata Party used the military for political gains. My second question is that today while there is a war-like situation in the world…is testing the Pralay missile is an indication of a new false flag operation?”
“On one side China is occupying [Indian land], on the other there are CJP protests…Rahul Gandhi…,” the interviewer goes on to say before his voice is abruptly cut off.
The interviewee then seems to respond with, “Two things are very clear. One, for false flag operations like Balakot and Pahalgam, Operation Sindoor was launched but the Indian army failed. Second, my answers are within your questions.”
Several other users on X and Facebook also circulated the same video with identical claims. Among them were X handles @KaurUdhoke3 and @HinduReformer, along with multiple public Facebook pages focusing on South Asian geopolitics. [Archives: 1, 2]
Fact Check
A closer look at the viral video reveals noticeable lip-sync discrepancies and an unnatural, monotonous cadence in the voices of both men in the interview, which are salient features of AI-generated audio manipulation.
Further, columnist and strategic affairs expert Sushant Singh has been misidentified in the viral video as Pravin Sawhney. In the viral video itself, the interviewer refers to the interviewee as Sushant, and not Pravin. Below is an image of Sawhney, who does not appear in the viral clip.
On November 13, Singh himself took to X to debunk the clip, clarifying that the video was AI-generated, and highlighting that users had also misidentified him.
This is AI generated video of an old interview, which completely fabricates my conversation with @ashubh. This Pakistan-made AI video clip not only gets my identity wrong but creates what was never said.
The original full interview of March 2025 is here: https://t.co/Y6teNLJDfg
— Sushant Singh (@SushantSin) November 13, 2026
In his post, Singh also attached a link to the original YouTube interview from which the visuals were taken. Alt News examined the original video uploaded on The Wire’s official YouTube channel in March 2025.
Comparing the viral clip with the March 2025 interview confirms that the visual frames, including Singh’s attire, the background setting, and lighting, are identical. However, the audio track in the viral clip has been changed using AI.
In the original interview, Singh makes no mention of Kulgam, Pulwama, Balakot, or any ‘false flag operations’. Instead, he is heard discussing civil-military relations and institutional oversight.
To sum up, a manipulated video of journalist and strategic affairs analyst Sushant Singh is circulating on social media with users misidentifying him as journalist and FORCE editor Pravin Sawhney. The claim that the speaker in the video termed India’s counter-terrorism measures in Kulgam and Pulwama ‘false flag operations’ is false as well.

The Food and Drug Administration on Monday approved a new breast cancer drug from Roche, teeing up the launch of a medicine that the Swiss company has said could become its top-selling product ever.
The approval of Wilserdly, also known as giredestrant, was one of the most important regulatory decisions Roche had been awaiting. It also gives the company another foothold in breast cancer treatments, a field in which it has a storied history with the drug Herceptin through its subsidiary Genentech, though in recent years it’s fallen behind rival pharma companies in oncology.
The approval is specifically for patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that has picked up a mutation in the ESR1 gene, a sign that the tumor is developing resistance to standard treatments. The evERA trial showed that the drug, an oral treatment known as a selective estrogen receptor degrader, or SERD, extended the time period before patients’ tumors progressed.

An iOS update did include a "Remote Control" feature that appeared to be enabled automatically.
The feature was introduced as part of the iOS 26 update, not iOS 27, and it does not allow users to remotely access a phone's "activity." Rather, it expands the functionality of the previously existing "Live Listen" accessibility feature. It is only functional on devices signed into the same Apple account, and it requires a user to intentionally initiate a Live Listen session on that device.
A rumor has circulated online since October that Apple released an update automatically enabling an option for outsiders to remotely access a phone's activity.
The claim spread on social media platforms such as Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived). Many of the posts offered warnings about the feature and instructions on how to turn it off, like this one (archived) from a Facebook user:
If you have an iPhone and installed the iOS 27 update, you might not know that Apple turned ON the option for someone to remotely access your activity on your phone.
In short, Apple did put out a "Remote Control" feature in an update, but not iOS 27, as posts claimed. According to their Settings app, the feature released in iOS 26, and the assertion that the feature allowed "someone to remotely access" activity on users' phones was overstated. As such, we have rated this claim as mostly false.
(Screenshot from iPhone/Snopes illustration)
We reached out to Apple for more information about the "Remote Control" feature and to ask whether the iOS 26 update automatically enabled it across all devices. We will update the story if we receive a response.
According to the Apple Support website, Live Listen allows an iPhone to "act like a microphone," allowing users to "hear a conversation in a noisy area or even hear someone speaking across the room." It was originally intended to work with hearing aids, but was expanded in iOS 12 to include AirPods or Beats earphones.
The iOS 26 "Remote Control" setting added new functionality to the feature, allowing Apple devices like iPads and Apple Watches to view and control Live Listen sessions, as long as they are nearby and signed into the same Apple Account.
For example, a student in the back of a noisy lecture hall could put their phone next to their professor at the start of class and remotely control a Live Listen session from their iPad signed into the same Apple account, allowing them to pause, resume and view a transcript of the picked-up audio without getting up from their seat.
Live Listen is situated within the "Accessibility" menu, indicating that Apple intended the feature especially for those with hearing-related difficulties.
(Screenshot from iPhone)
Remote control of a user's Live Listen session can only take place if that user intentionally started the session, and it only provides access to a transcript of audio near the user's iPhone. A bad actor who gained access to a device signed into a user's Apple account wouldn't be able to start a Live Listen session on that user's device using "Remote Control" — that user would have to be the one to start the session. Because of this, there is little risk of someone using the feature nefariously.
Based on user testimony and our own testing, the feature did appear to be automatically enabled as of the iOS 26 update. However, official Apple developer notes (archived) for the update made no mention of the terms "Remote Control" or "Live Listen."
For further reading, Snopes investigated the extent to which incognito mode protects users' data, and found it might be less than most users expected.

Pope Endures Grueling Travel in South America Weeks After Surgery
When doctors operated on Pope Leo XIV’s lung in October, some wondered if he’d postpone a long-planned trip to South America. It’s gone well so far.
Flying with Pope Leo XIV over the Andes, halfway through the pontiff’s 12-day trip to South America, the journalists traveling at the back of the plane suspected something was amiss.
They had expected the pope to come out from behind the business-class curtain and take questions, as he had on previous papal flights. Instead, Vatican officials abruptly told the press corps that the pope would not be speaking with them on the nearly five-hour flight from Argentina to Peru.
Was the pope, who had been diagnosed with lung cancer less than a month earlier, feeling ill? Was he too exhausted to talk? Was he taking a nap?
“It’s evident he’s well,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, who heads the Vatican’s communications department, when asked why the pope wasn’t taking questions. “He’s running circles around us.”
It was perhaps inevitable that Leo’s every action on this journey, so soon after surgery to remove a lobe of his right lung, would be scrutinized for signs of fatigue or illness, particularly as the Vatican is not known for its transparency.
The three-country trip, which began in Uruguay and concludes in Peru on Monday, involves a grueling schedule of 12 flights, two helicopter rides, nine Masses, 36 speeches and numerous meetings with local bishops and community members.

The body of a horse that placed eighth in Australia’s Melbourne Cup two weeks ago and recently fell ill has been found dumped in skip bin in Sydney.
The horse So You Are, a five-year-old gelding, was put down after it suffered from a severe bout from colic and was taken to hospital on Monday for surgery.
The same day, Gregg Jowett posted to his personal social media account a video that showed a dead horse inside a skip bin in Sydney. Guardian Australia has chosen not to publish the video.
“I’m at the tip. It’s a fucking horse. They tipped a horse in the fucking bin at the tip,” he can be heard saying in the video.
“[I’m] quite shocked about that; that’s not normal. Please let me know if I’m wrong, but that’s not normal.”
Jowett later told Guardian Australia he didn’t know when he found the horse that it was So You Are, or a horse that had competed in Australia’s most famous race, the Melbourne Cup.
“I’m just disgusted by it,” he said.
The horse’s trainer, Bjorn Baker, said the handling of So You Are’s remains had compounded an already devastating loss.
“Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the apparent handling of So You Are’s remains,” he said in a statement.
“He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death.
“I understand the hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances, and I expect a full explanation of what occurred.
“My thoughts remain with [So You Are breeders] the Ramsey family, and with all my staff, for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss.”
Dr Jonathan Lumsden, the managing partner of REC Equine Specialists, which treated So You Are after he was brought to the service with colic, apologised “unreservedly for the distress caused by footage shared on social media today”.
“Despite the best efforts of our veterinary team, he could not be saved and was humanely euthanised under anaesthesia,” Lumsden said.
“After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried.
“What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him. We are deeply sorry.
“So You Are was in our care. We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that. We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change.
“We have spoken with So You Are’s owners and trainer to apologise personally,” he said. “We are working with our disposal provider and the facility operators, together with Racing NSW, to establish how this happened and to put in processes to ensure it never happens again.”
Lumsden said the service had, effective immediately, stopped using the contract provider and was undertaking a review of how other providers care for horses after death.
“Out of respect for So You Are and those who loved him, we ask that the footage not be shared further,” Lumsden said.
David Harris, the minister for gaming and racing, said Racing NSW had launched an investigation into the incident.
“This is a concerning incident, the racing legislative framework and Racing NSW as the sport’s controlling body has measures in place to safeguard racing integrity and animal welfare,” he said.
Georgie Purcell, the Animal Justice party MP for northern Victoria,
 
said the incident should “force serious questions the industry’s so-called duty of care”.
“The racing industry breeds these horses and profits for them but fails the most basic obligation to treat them with dignity after death,” she said.

LED lights have become an everyday reality in homes, offices, public places and significantly, our screens. And while their energy efficiency is welcome, for many people, their increased use has led to eye discomfort: this includes sleep issues, a blinding sensation while driving at night, redness and watering. Ophthalmologists say this problem is on the rise and point to multiple factors behind it, including brightness levels, positioning of the light, its temperature, colour-tone, and flickering effects.
Apart from lighting up our homes and workplaces, LED lights are now in every gadget, including mobile phones, laptops as well as television sets. Constant exposure can cause mild to extreme visual discomfort, glare, eye strain, and even headaches for some people. This is a genuine visual concern experienced by many people, says Sugato Paul, consultant, ophthalmology at Manipal Hospital, Broadway, Kolkata. Dr Paul explains that discomfort is primarily associated with high luminance and excessive brightness. “Many cool-white LEDs have a relatively higher proportion of short-wavelength (blue) light, generally in the 400–500 nm range. This can increase the perception of brightness, contribute to visual discomfort and make certain individuals more susceptible to glare under specific circumstances,” he says.

Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister applied for a new passport this week.
Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She crossed the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.
Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.
Her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.
Hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had already returned in anticipation.
On Monday, a British lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina wrote to the Bangladesh high commission in Delhi requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.
“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.
Hasina has rejected the charges against her and claimed the tribunal that convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” said the Awami League leader.
Since Hasina’s conviction, the Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government, which was close to Hasina while she was in power, has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.
This week, the Bangladesh government said that, as a “terrorist”, Hasina would only be allowed to return via an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty.
Aminul Islam, the chief prosecutor of the tribunal that sentenced Hasina, said there was “no legal scope” for her to be issued a new passport as she was a “convicted fugitive”.
Islam emphasised that Hasina would be hanged if she returned, as the deadline for her to appeal against her conviction had passed. “Sheikh Hasina has no option but to face the execution of the verdict,” he said.
Despite the abuses and oppression that mired her 15 years in power and subsequent conviction for crimes against humanity, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many of whom have been driven underground.
Analysts said they believed her decision to return was driven by an attempt to revive her support base and destabilise the newly elected government, led by Tarique Rahman. It came to power in February during Bangladesh’s first democratic election in decades.
The government has since struggled with inflation and protests that shut down garment factories, which the Awami League hopes to use to its advantage.
Another Awami League leader said all those in exile intended to follow Hasina back to Bangladesh, despite many of them facing serious criminal charges and having been given lengthy prison sentences in absentia.
“Some of us have been sentenced in absentia by kangaroo courts, and we know we will be jailed. But we are ready to face the consequences and return to our own people. We will fight this politically,” said the senior leader, who is based in India.
Some senior party figures have returned in recent months, including the former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. He was immediately arrested on his return in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder during the 2024 uprising.
Exiled Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.
Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press: “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people.”

Where are the goddesses? Why Devdutt Pattanaik's remarks have triggered a debate
Are Hindu goddesses worshipped as much as we believe? Mythologist and writer Devdutt Pattanaik has questioned the place of women in Hindu religious imagery, arguing that female deities are increasingly missing from representations of popular gods. His remarks on Rajdeep Sardesai's show have triggered a debate over India's traditions of goddess worship.
Mythologist and author Devdutt Pattanaik has stirred a debate over the place of women in Hinduism after arguing that the worship of goddesses does not necessarily translate into the "worship of women in India". In an interview with India Today Group's consulting editor Rajdeep Sardesai, Pattanaik questioned the widespread belief that Hinduism accords women a prominent position because of its pantheon of female deities.
In the interview released on Saturday, Sardesai asked Pattanaik, "Is mythology reflecting society or is it presenting in a sense an aspiration that society has consistently failed to fulfill?... Why is there such a gap if it's reflecting society between the powerful position of women in Hindu mythology and the subordinate position of them in society?"
"We don't worship women in India. Who said we worship women in India?" Devdutt Pattanaik said, pointing to the apparent disconnect between the prominence of goddesses in Hindu mythology and the subordinate position of women in Indian society. He also argued that despite the worship of goddesses, contemporary Hindu religious imagery increasingly sidelines female deities. Pattanaik said most of the gods are featured without their consorts.
Pattanaik's remarks have drawn criticism, with several people pointing to India's extensive traditions of goddess worship, including prominent Shakti shrines and temples where female deities are the presiding gods. The debate has also raised questions about whether the representation of goddesses alongside male deities can be separated from the broader question of women's position in religious and social life.
WHERE ARE THE WOMEN? ASKS DEVDUTT PATTANAIK
Explaining his argument, Devdutt Pattanaik pointed to what he sees as the growing absence of female deities from popular representations of Hindu gods.
"We built a Ram temple without Sita saying that he's a child but didn't show his mother. We are worshipping Krishna without Radha," he said.
He also cited temples dedicated to Krishna in Pandharpur, Udupi and Tirupati, arguing that female consorts are not always represented in the same shrine as their male counterparts.
"Our gods today, look at the posters across India. Shiva is shown without Shakti. Durga is shown without her family. Krishna is shown with Arjun more than Radha. Strange, no? In a battlefield rather than Madhuban. And Ram seems to be always alone. Why? In every poster he's alone. So where are the women?" he asked.
Pattanaik argued that the representation of goddesses had also undergone a transformation over time. Referring to older Tantric temple imagery, he said goddesses were depicted sitting on the laps of male deities and looking into their eyes.
"The goddess was erotic. So the erotic goddess becomes the romantic goddess. And finally, now gods are all about solitude," he said.
He also attributed some of these changes to the influence of Buddhism and Jainism, arguing that religious traditions and their representations of male and female deities evolved with changing social and economic circumstances.
CRITICS POINT TO INDIA'S GODDESS TRADITIONS
However, his assertion that women are not worshipped in India has faced criticism from those who argue that it overlooks the country's extensive and continuing traditions of goddess worship.
India has several prominent temples where the goddess is the principal deity, including the Meenakshi temple in Madurai, Kamakshi temple in Kanchipuram, Kamakhya temple in Assam and Vaishno Devi shrine in Jammu and Kashmir. These traditions are central to Shakti worship, in which the feminine divine is not merely a consort to a male god but the principal object of devotion.
Critics have also pointed to the prominence of Durga, Kali, Lakshmi and Saraswati in household worship, festivals and religious practices across regions. They argue that the absence of a female consort, in particular representations of male deities, cannot, by itself, establish that goddess worship has diminished, or that women are not worshipped.
MYTHOLOGY, SOCIETY AND THE POLITICS OF REPRESENTATION
During the conversation, Rajdeep Sardesai also challenged Pattanaik on whether the prominence of goddesses in Hindu mythology could reflect an aspiration that society has failed to fulfil, rather than its actual treatment of women.
Pattanaik disagreed with the suggestion that mythology presents an idealised version of society.
"No. It reflects society," he said.
He further argued that images of goddesses should not automatically be read as evidence of matriarchy or women's empowerment.
"If I see a Kali image where she's dancing on top of Shiva, does it mean matriarchy/feminism? And if I show you Lakshmi at the feet of Vishnu, does it mean patriarchy? This is lazy scholarship," he said.
The conversation also touched upon the changing position of women in religious imagery, with Pattanaik questioning why contemporary representations increasingly show male gods in isolation.
His remarks have reopened a larger debate over how Hindu traditions are interpreted, who gets to define their history and whether the evolution of religious imagery reflects changing social attitudes.

On September 27, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy posted a video on X with the words “GAME CHANGER.” “Introducing ‘SMART’—the new air traffic management tool that saves YOU time, cuts back DELAYS, and makes your flying experience BETTER,” he wrote. This was a new AI-infused air traffic control system. Almost three weeks later, that post would get a new life, as a nervous joke, as the FAA issued a national groundstop on Friday the 13th that instantly threw the world’s airline schedules into chaos. The administration quickly announced that there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and no sign that SMART had anything to do with the communications failure at the heart of the government’s decision to suspend flights. But when asked on Friday night whether he could definitively rule out AI failure, Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin could only say, “There’s nothing certain right now.”
New systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway. Take, for instance, the Cessna Caravan that took off from Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California, and flew south to Phoenix on a calm September morning. The plane, a single-engine turboprop, then turned east to Fort Worth, stopped at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, and finally arrived at Dare County Regional Airport off the coast of North Carolina. The zigzag, coast-to-coast trip covered 3,200 miles; along the way, the aircraft navigated busy airspace and maneuvered to avoid storms.
None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls.
According to Joby Aviation, the company that carried out the project, a safety pilot was aboard the Cessna at all times—but never needed to intervene. The pilotless trip marked a major milestone in aviation. The air travel industry has long been technologically conservative, and with good reason: When human lives are at stake, it’s better to be time-tested and a little dated than cutting-edge and unpredictable. But AI is making inroads into aviation with unprecedented speed. The effects now are hard to see, but the changes in the offing are huge, promising to remake the economics of air travel and transform how people and things move around in the sky. A big question remains, though: Can we trust this technology to be reliable and safe?
Depends who you ask. “We're introducing all this new technology to improve the system, and it's going to be a disaster,” says a recently retired FAA employee. “This is literally a Pandora's box that we are going to regret.”
Aviation’s embrace of AI traces back to the early 2000s, when advances in batteries and microelectronics suddenly made drones much more capable and inexpensive. The surge convinced officials that robots and humans would eventually need to share the airways, and that new infrastructure would be necessary to allow that. At the time, virtually all aircraft were human-piloted, and there was no way for drones to avoid human-flown planes or each other.
In 2007, the federal government rolled out a sweeping project called Next Generation Air Transportation System—NextGen, for short—that mandated broad changes to the air travel system over the decades to come. Among its provisions was the requirement that, by 2020, aircraft in the United States be equipped with ADS-B, a system that constantly sends radio signals telling everyone in the vicinity where you are and where you’re headed.
With a road map to robot-friendly skies in place, big players like Amazon and Walmart began working on ambitious plans for drone delivery services. In 2014, Google unveiled Project Wing, a drone delivery offering that by 2018 was ferrying food, coffee, and medication to 164 homes near Canberra, Australia. The next year, the pilot program was expanded to Christiansburg, Virginia. Costs were high and service slow, but those early programs weren’t meant to become viable businesses. Instead, they were providing Google with operational experience for the years to come.
Around the same time, a host of startups began working on a related kind of vehicle: electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs, also known as electric air taxis. These are, essentially, oversized drones (with room for pilots, for now) designed to carry a small number of people a short distance. By 2022 there were 600 different models under development. Soon, their manufacturers promised, cheap, short aerial hops would be commonplace. Joby was among those leading the charge: In 2020, the company unveiled the design of its S4 model, which it said would be able to carry a pilot and four passengers 100 miles or more at speeds of up to 200 mph. The S4’s maiden flight took place last year.
A commercial launch seemed just around the corner. But deadlines kept getting pushed back. As it turned out, engineering a flying autonomous robot was just part of the overall problem. You also needed to design an airspace that they could operate in, train humans to pilot or supervise them, develop an economic framework within which they could earn money, and so on. “It's a very important, safe, careful dance,” says Greg Bowles, Chief Policy Officer at Joby Aviation.
Silicon Valley’s speed has long been in conflict with air travel norms. “Aviation regulation has been conservative and prioritizes reliability, because the consequences of failure are severe,” says Mary Schiavo, an aviation lawyer and former inspector general in the Department of Transportation. “Certification standards and airworthiness require proof and demonstrated safety, and that usually means incremental rather than radical change.” The FAA was in no rush to let unproven robots go careening around the national airspace.
AI faced another kind of resistance in Europe. In 2017, aircraft manufacturers Airbus and Dassault asked the EASA, the European Union’s version of the FAA, to consider allowing airliners to operate with a single pilot in the cockpit. Traditionally, airliners require multiple pilots to divide the considerable workload of flying a plane and to ensure that if one pilot becomes incapacitated, the other can carry on. In Airbus’ vision, automated systems would shoulder the copilot’s workload and even take over entirely if needed.
That idea horrified pilots. The European Cockpit Association, a union of airline pilots, lodged a strong protest. Such a move “would remove an independent safety professional from the flight deck and give operators greater influence over the safety judgments that a pilot would otherwise make,” the union explained to me in an email. Last year, EASA shelved the plan.
Nevertheless, AI pressed onward. In 2023, the FAA began issuing waivers to allow delivery-drone flights beyond the visual range of operators; by the end of this year it could make the rule change permanent. Some of the biggest players are already pushing ahead aggressively. This past August, Amazon announced that it planned to expand its drone delivery service to 500 locations across the country by the end of the year. Walmart is planning drone delivery from 270 store locations by the end of 2027.
The ultimate goal is far larger. Industry insiders say that in a maximal vision of the technology’s build-out, hundreds of thousands of drones will be servicing most or all of the US population. “In five to 10 years, it’s going to be completely ubiquitous,” Anthony Vittone, chief operating officer of the drone technology company DroneUp, told me in a story for Sherwood News last year. “People are going to be, like, ‘I don’t know how I lived without it.’”
Joby and other eVTOL companies haven’t progressed quite as fast, but they, too, are moving ahead. In April, Joby flew the first-ever point-to-point eVTOL flight within New York City, from John F. Kennedy Airport to three heliports in Manhattan. The company has carried out similar flights in California and Texas, all under the auspices of the eVTOL Integration Pilot Program (eIPP), a federal initiative rolled out by the Trump administration this past March to demonstrate the capabilities of modern drones and eVTOLs.
These demo flights, Bowles says, are just the “front edge” of the Joby S4’s operational rollout. Next will come demonstration flights with nonpaying passengers, demonstration flights with paying passengers, and finally flights that will take passengers from A to B. “All of that is permitted under eIPP, with increasing levels of oversight,” he says.
To start, these flights will have human pilots, but it’s very expensive to pay one human to fly around a handful of paying passengers; for the model to make any economic sense, the aircraft will have to fly themselves. And if self-driving is a tough challenge for cars, it’s all the more so for aircraft, where an unexpected control system failure isn’t just dangerous but likely deadly.
Given the scale of the challenge, the entry point of AI into human passenger flight won’t be as flashy as piloting eVTOLs; it’ll occupy a more modest, behind-the-scenes role. Already, data companies like Palantir and aviation industry stalwarts like Jeppesen and Thales are selling AI-enabled software that lets regulators, airlines, and flight dispatchers sift through masses of data to identify risks and plan aircraft and crew scheduling.
In September, the FAA announced that it deployed software built by the Boston-based data company Air Space Intelligence. The new AI-powered tool is called “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories,” or SMART, and it’s aimed at “fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace.” The program isn’t intended to replace controllers, the government says, but to make doing their jobs easier by using predictive AI to head off scheduling snags. “Combining SMART with our ongoing hardware upgrades gives us the tools to cut flight delays, optimize traffic, and keep airspace capacity across the country open—all while maintaining our gold standard of safety,” FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said in a press release.
The system is supposed to help controllers make decisions, not make those decisions for them. But if the program feeds nonsensical information into the system, will human operators be able to catch the mistake? “This is the Trump/DOGE/Musk effect,” says the recently retired FAA employee, who asked to remain anonymous. “They’re pushing through all this new technology without any understanding of the complexity of the national airspace system.”
Some lawmakers are also concerned about SMART. On October 13, almost two dozen Democratic lawmakers reportedly sent a letter to the Government Accountability Office asking it to review the program, citing fears that it might “hallucinate safety-critical information.”
Then there’s the question of whether SMART could worsen the chronic shortage of air traffic controllers. The FAA hopes that the technology lessens the shortage by requiring fewer workers; other industries, though, have yet to see AI-generated efficiencies actually materialize. Even if the software doesn’t directly replace humans, the efficiency could be used to justify a workforce reduction. In May, the FAA reduced its staffing target for active air traffic controllers from the 2024 goal of 14,633 down to 12,563, citing “modern staffing models and scheduling tools.”
Some are more optimistic than others. “I think the SMART program is an important improvement,” Schiavo says. “No one wants the current aviation environment with midairs, runway incursions, myriad near misses, delays, groundings, loss of separation, and long taxi or clearance wait times.”
Michael McCormick, a professor of air traffic management at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, also sees advantages to a predictive tool. “When you have the computing capability to look at the entire trajectory of the aircraft, you can see where the conflicts are going to be,” he says. “And the general axiom in air traffic control is that the sooner you know about a potential conflict, the less effort is required to resolve it.”
That sounds great, but building machines that do a good job most of the time is one thing; machines that can function at the level of reliability required by aviation is another. At present, researchers are focusing on so-called deterministic neural networks—models trained offline whose weights are frozen before being deployed in the real world. These can’t hallucinate, but they may harbor other risky failure modes. In a 2021 paper, Darren Cofer, a researcher at Collins Aerospace, pointed out that when such systems find themselves in situations they haven’t encountered before in training, they can generate “unexpected (and potentially dangerous) outputs.”
The stakes will be even higher when AI software starts making real-time air traffic control decisions, which will start in airspace devoted to autonomous aircraft. According to McCormick, that’ll most likely be select corridors near drone hubs and eVTOL vertiports. With swarms of robot aircraft zipping back and forth, things will be too hairy for human pilots and controllers. “The objective is not to use traditional air traffic control,” he says, “because it would overwhelm the national airspace system if it tried to handle that volume and complexity of airframes moving around.”
With two systems working side by side—one with human decisionmakers, the other with AI—we’ll have a real-time basis to compare the performance of both approaches. Any computer-based system can potentially be hacked; any AI system creative enough to ideate novel solutions could also hallucinate crucial details. Without a human in the loop, seemingly obvious mistakes might go unnoticed until it’s too late.

After Democrats in Texas flipped a U.S. Senate seat, won 14 U.S. House seats and the governor's office in the 2026 midterm elections, a claim (archived) circulated that the wins happened only because the party fraudulently "found" 20 million new voters who all voted blue.
For example, an X user wrote, "There's no chance Texas found 20 million new voters who voted exclusively 100% for Democrats. It's fraud!"
The same text also circulated on Facebook (archived) and other social media platforms.
We found no proof that the Democratic Party in Texas fraudulently "found" and registered 20 million new voters to skew races in their favor in the Nov. 3 elections. The claim appeared to conflate a separate, unproven claim about the number of new voters nationwide with the number of new voters in Texas alone.
Therefore, we rate this claim false.
Texas had just over 19 million registered voters by mid-October, according to its secretary of state. Figures from that office showed the number of registered voters had risen by about 2% since the presidential election in 2024. The number of registered voters rose about 5.4% between the 2022 and 2024 elections. An additional 20 million voters would have created a 107.4% increase in registered voters since 2024 or a 113.2% increase since 2022.
The state's unofficial voter turnout figures showed that 9,850,031 people voted in person or by mail in the state's 2026 midterm elections — a little more than half of Texas' registered voters.
Given the figures from the Texas secretary of state, it wasn't possible for Democrats to have fraudulently "found" 20 million people to tip the state's elections, because fewer than half that number voted in the elections at all. A sudden doubling of the number of registered voters would have raised alarm bells with officials. This did not occur.
The origin of the "20 million" figure was unclear, but it may have come from a bar chart that claimed to show that House Democrats gained 20 million voters across the entire U.S. between 2022 and 2026. The fact-checking organization Lead Stories reported on this graph and found no credible source for its projected 2026 voter numbers.
Rather, Lead Stories pointed to the University of Florida's General Election turnout tables, which showed 123,540,000 ballots counted nationwide in the 2026 midterms by Nov. 6. The same source showed 112,030,874 ballots counted in the 2022 midterms, the most recent equivalent race. The bar chart claimed 126 million people had voted in House races in 2026, around 2.5 million more than the University of Florida's estimate.
The university's figures suggested an increase of 11,509,126 ballots counted between the 2022 and 2026 elections, around half of the 20 million figure the unsourced bar chart suggested.
It wasn't possible to determine how many more individual voters had voted for House Democrats in 2026 vs. in 2022 because state officials had not yet certified their election results at the time of this writing and when the graph circulated.
Regardless of the accuracy of the graph or claim, it was true that Democrats picked up a sizable number of votes in their House and Senate races to secure control of both chambers nationwide. Pollsters credited young voters, male voters and Hispanic voters with securing Democratic wins.
At the time of this writing, there were no credible allegations of widespread fraud.
The false claim played into election fraud theories about bad actors "finding" votes in elections. Snopes has previously reported on variations of this claim in the form of noncitizen voting (which rarely happens), duplicate ballots (which are extremely difficult to produce) and vote spikes (which are a natural part of vote counts).

What is happening in Sudan? The civil war the world forgot
The conflict in Sudan has been described as a war on civilians – and the facts are devastating

Since April 2023, Sudan has been in the grip of one of the deadliest civil wars in a generation. As many as 150,000 people are believed to have been killed and millions displaced.
Right now it is the largest humanitarian crisis, the largest displacement crisis and the largest hunger crisis in the world.
The UN has warned that attacks in Darfur bear the “hallmarks of genocide” and the brutality and widespread use of rape as a weapon of war is unprecedented.
There are no signs of an immediate ceasefire or an end to the conflict, which has been described by humanitarians and Sudanese families as a war on civilians.
How did the war start?
Sudan’s war broke out in April 2023. A vicious power struggle between Sudanese army chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and General Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, or “Hemedti”, head of the powerful paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), exploded into open fighting across the country.
The two generals had once been uneasy allies. They joined forces after the 2019 popular uprising unseated the country’s longterm autocrat Omar al-Bashir, forming a joint government with a civilian prime minister.
At the time there were concerns about a deadly military crackdown on protesters and the involvement of the RSF, that with its precursor the Janjaweed – had already been accused of committing crimes, atrocities, and ethnic cleansing in Darfur, targeting non-Arab communities. (Both sides denied all accusations).
By 2021, the two generals staged a coup. But their power struggle reached breaking point in April 2023, mainly over plans to bring the 100,000-strong RSF under army command.
Fighting first erupted in the capital, Khartoum, and quickly spread across the country, morphing into an international proxy conflict.
Rights groups including Human Rights Watch have said there is mounting evidence that the UAE has bankrolled the RSF in breach of arms embargoes, which the Emirates denies. The RSF in turn accuses the army of being backed by Egypt and Iran.
Where is the fighting now?
The front lines have shifted dramatically. After losing control of Khartoum to the RSF, the army retook the capital in March 2025. But by October 2025, in the west, the RSF had captured El Fasher, the army’s last stronghold in Darfur, after an 18-month siege and slaughter.
This year, a UN independent fact-finding mission for Sudan said the RSF’s ethnically targeted killings, widespread sexual violence and enforced disappearances bore the “hallmarks of genocide”.
The SAF (Sudan Armed Forces) and its affiliated militias have also been accused of atrocities by UN investigators, which the SAF also denies.
Since then, the war’s centre of gravity has moved to the Kordofan region, which links Darfur to central Sudan.
El Obeid: the new front line
El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, is now one of the most important battlegrounds of the war. Its position at a crossroads linking the country’s central and western regions makes it strategic. Until very recently, it was almost completely surrounded by RSF fighters and under partial siege.
The city of around half a million people is also now home to an estimated 100,000 displaced people. But it offers little safety. It has been under intense drone strikes. The UN has warned that the patterns of violence seen in El Fasher are now emerging in El Obeid.
Key facts and figures
- Death toll: There is no official death toll. Conflict monitor Acled says it has verified nearly 60,000 dead, although other estimates say as many as 150,000 have been killed
- Humanitarian crisis: Nearly 34 million people across Sudan need aid, while 21 million lack health services; this has led to Sudan becoming the largest humanitarian crisis in the world, according to the WHO
- Displacement: At least 14 million people have been forced from their homes, a quarter of the population, making it the world’s largest displacement crisis. Neighbouring countries host over 4.4 million Sudanese refugees
- Sexual violence: Conflict-related sexual violence in Sudan is unprecedented in terms of the scale, prevalence and brutality of its widespread use as a weapon of war, according to the UN’s human rights office
- Children: An estimated 825,000 children under five are expected to suffer from severe acute malnutrition in 2026. Unicef has documented the rape of children as young as one year old
- Famine: Around 20 million people or 40 per cent of the population face high levels of acute food insecurity, according to the IPC, the UN-backed global hunger monitor. Famine was confirmed in El Fasher in 2024 and in Kadugli, South Kordofan, in September 2025. Sudan is also the world’s largest hunger crisis right now.
- Drought: The IPC warned in October that Super El Niño-induced drought is compounding conflict and driving a growing risk of famine in Darfur and Kordofan. It also found that the drought now covers more than half of the country
- Healthcare: The WHO has verified 217 attacks on healthcare since April 2023, resulting in thousands of deaths. In 2026, 37 per cent of health facilities were reported to be non-functional
- Aid: As of 8 October, the UN’s $2.9bn appeal for Sudan is 40 per cent unfunded
- Genocide: In February 2026, a UN fact-finding mission said RSF atrocities in El Fasher bore the “hallmarks of genocide” against non-Arab communities

Inbound Manchester United coach Mauricio Pochettino said that he leaves his stint with the US men’s national football team a “much better” coach as he winds up his stint in charge.
Pochettino will lead the side for the second leg of its CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinal second leg against Haiti before departing to join the English heavyweight club.
Long-time assistant Jesus Perez, along with Pochettino’s son and team fitness coach Sebastiano, and goalkeeping coach Toni Jimenez have all already departed to begin working with the players.
“They are in advance, they are preparing all there, because Wednesday when we will arrive, it is going to be non-stop,” Pochettino said on Monday.
“For me, it’s not difficult, I think we are well prepared to switch quick.”

“Like a player from the national team to the clubs. From one game that you don’t play well to another that you need to be ready again. From one action to the next action.”
Pochettino reflected on the difference between club football and international management, saying, “it’s easy, no, from Monday to Saturday to prepare for the game? OK, you control everything. You have control and access to everything, and you come prepared.”
With national teams, “when you arrive and maybe you have a few days to train, but you need to perform -- in the way that you want to play, in the way the opponent plays -- to prepare all these situations demands to be very clinical, and to find different ways to approach the players.
“In the last few years we learnt a lot in how to approach and create an impact in one meeting, in one exercise on the field, in one message.
“Now we are a very complete coaching staff. We don’t say we are going to win all the games. But I think we are much better.”

Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term?
- Published
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages.
The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes.
Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.
Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers.
The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.
Elected in 2023, Tinubu undertook a series of economic reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidies, the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates, and tax reforms.
"That manifesto was trying to get Nigeria back on its feet, given the condition of the country at that time, slipping into austerity," Joshua Osiyemi, who heads Tracka, a platform launched by the BudgIT Foundation, which is a non-profit organisation that aims to make government financial data easier to understand.
The reforms, although considered necessary by some economists, have been painful for many Nigerians.
"Fuel prices went up, and everything that Nigerians consume skyrocketed," Osiyemi told the BBC.
"Most Nigerian families are saying they cannot survive on 10,000 naira [$7.40; £5.50] a day," he said, referring to a survey conducted by his organisation.
Analysis by Nigeria's International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) found that the price of imported rice rose by 184% between May 2023, when Tinubu took office, and October 2025. Other staples, including beans, garri (cassava flour) and bread, also recorded substantial increases.
In a sign that the reforms might be starting to pay off, SBM Intelligence, a security risk consulting firm, found that the cost of preparing a pot of jollof rice fell by 11.5% between June and September 2026, the sharpest decline it had recorded in the 10 years it has been running its Jollof Index.
However, this has not translated into significant relief for most households.
"Nigerians spend more and more of their income on basics," said Ikenna Okonkwo, head of research at SBM Intelligence.
The reforms were praised by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for their effectiveness.
Nigeria's headline inflation stood at 14% in September 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, down from a high of 34% in 2024. The gap between the official and parallel exchange rates has also narrowed.
Tinubu has said the removal of fuel subsidies freed up more than one trillion ($740m; £550m) naira in government resources in just the first two months.
Following widespread complaints about the rising cost of living, he recently said he would work to reduce the cost of fuel but denied that this was a return to the subsidy. For decades, many Nigerians have seen cheap fuel as one of the few perks of living in Africa's largest oil producer.
His administration subsequently announced a 125bn naira intervention package for small businesses, including grants for smaller enterprises and loans for manufacturers.
Atiku has criticised Tinubu's decision to remove the fuel subsidy.
"My position stands! I will restore subsidy to make life easier and affordable for Nigerians," Atiku wrote on X.
However, restoring the fuel subsidy could prove challenging given Nigeria's economic realities.
"The current budget for Nigeria in 2026 is about 68.32tn naira, with 15.8tn going towards debt servicing. So, we are not fiscally strong enough to say that we want to return to the subsidy," Osiyemi said.
While Tinubu's reforms are lauded for restoring some stability at the macroeconomic level, they have also created instability in households.
Two months away from elections, the cost of living and economic hardship are the major issues for many voters.
"These kinds of things can get punished in polls," said Okonkwo of SBM Intelligence.
To address this, Tinubu promised to lower the cost of living, grow the economy by 6% and halve youth unemployment if he wins re-election. Achieving these targets will require increased oil and agricultural production.
But much of Nigeria's agricultural production is concentrated in the north, where insecurity has made farming increasingly difficult.
Osiyemi says many farmers are reluctant to return to their fields.
"They're not sure whether when they go to their farms, they have the chances of also coming back home, to meet with their family."
To address insecurity, Tinubu proposes recruiting an additional 28,000 military personnel and 50,000 police officers.
"The security situation, especially in the north, is more complex than a matter of just recruiting more soldiers," Okonkwo said.

  - Published21 August
The threats include jihadists, kidnap gangs and conflict between herders and farmers in central Nigeria.
Insecurity is also a major priority for Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, who came third in the 2023 presidential election and attracted significant support from young Nigerians.
He unveiled his 2027 Governance Agenda on 10 November, under the campaign slogan "A New Nigeria is Possible", placing national unity at the top of his priorities, followed by security.
"Nobody will kidnap school children and disappear into the bush. If you kidnap children and go into the bush, you will not be alone there. We will come after you," he said.
Further, delivering on those ambitions will also depend on improving electricity supply, particularly for businesses and industries. Tinubu promises to increase available electricity generation towards 10,000MW.
"There is nothing in the manifesto about where that investment is going to come from because it will cost a lot of money," said Okonkwo.
Another huge challenge facing Nigeria is the power sector, which has suffered from years of underinvestment.
The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission says the country had installed generation capacity of 13,625MW at the end of 2024, but generated an average of just 4,223MW during the year.
Nigeria's power sector has failed to produce at capacity due to ageing infrastructure, inadequate maintenance, gas supply constraints and funding challenges.
The government has also privatised electricity distribution, but distribution companies have struggled to invest in infrastructure, including local transformers and metering systems, partly because of low profit margins.
"The government cannot increase tariffs to an extent where people will revolt, and that also keeps investors away because they don't look at the Nigerian power sector as somewhere that they can make money," said Okonkwo.
Unreliable electricity supplies force many households and businesses to rely on generators, pushing up the cost of living and doing business.
The manifesto also promises to build 200,000 affordable homes. This is a fraction of Nigeria's estimated housing deficit, which a technical committee set up by the housing ministry put at 14.9 million units in 2025.
For Nigerians to feel a meaningful improvement in their lives, the reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined in the manifesto, analysts say.
"Some of the items in the manifesto seem bloated, but if they can be committed to it, I want to believe that quite a number of these items that they have here are very much achievable," Osiyemi said.
"The big thing, if the APC wins, which they have to do and is a tall order, is to regain the trust of Nigerians," Okonkwo said.
Nigeria's 2023 presidential election saw Tinubu declared winner with 8.79 million votes, ahead of Atiku and Obi. Tinubu's victory came amid growing economic hardship after eight years of Muhammadu Buhari's APC government.
"APC were able to win because opposition was divided between two very strong candidates with two regional bases. In the end, we still go down to basic questions like the region you are from and tribal sentiments," Okonkwo said.
As Nigeria heads towards the 2027 elections, Tinubu, Atiku and Obi are once again central to the contest, but the opposition faces a familiar challenge - building a united front and support beyond regional strongholds.
"It will play out like it did in 2023," Okonkwo said.
"The APC are in a stronger position being the incumbent party and the momentum that some of the opposition candidates had in 2023 has faded."

Cyclone Akvan, brewing over the Bay of Bengal, is expected to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm before approaching the Andhra Pradesh coast on November 19, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said in its latest forecast on Monday (November 16).
The weather system, currently positioned over the southeast and adjoining southwest Bay of Bengal, is likely to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Monday evening and a severe cyclonic storm by Tuesday evening, November 17.
Thereafter, it is expected to move northwestwards and reach the west-central Bay of Bengal near the Andhra Pradesh coast around the night of November 19 as a very severe cyclonic storm.
The approaching cyclone has prompted authorities in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha to step up preparedness measures, including identifying vulnerable areas and evacuating people ahead of the expected heavy rainfall.
Here's what we know about Cyclone Akvan's expected landfall, wind speed, rainfall forecast and the states likely to be affected.
According to the IMD, the deep depression is likely to move northwestwards and cross the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Nellore and Tuni by noon on November 20 as a very severe cyclonic storm.
The system was moving north-northwestwards at a speed of around 6-8 kmph during the six hours preceding the IMD's Monday morning bulletin.
At 8.30 am on November 16, it was centred over the southeast and adjoining southwest Bay of Bengal, near latitude 11.2°N and Longitude 86.4°E, about 630 km east-northeast of Trincomalee (Sri Lanka), 690 km west of Sri Vijaya Puram (Andaman & Nicobar Islands), 700 km east-southeast of Chennai (Tamil Nadu), 800 km south-southeast of Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh) and 910 km south of Gopalpur (Odisha).
It is very likely to continue to move north-northwestwards, intensify further into a Cyclonic Storm over the central parts of south & adjoining westcentral Bay of Bengal in the evening of today, the 16th November and into a Severe Cyclonic Storm over westcentral Bay of Bengal in the evening of 17th November, 2026. Thereafter, it is likely to intensify further and move west-northwestwards and cross Andhra Pradesh; Yanam coasts between Nellore and Tuni, by noon of 20th November, 2026 as a very severe cyclonic storm with the maximum sustained wind speed of 120-130 kmph gusting to 145 kmph.
