On the heels of the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.
In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.
US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”
Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.”
The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold.
In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department said it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”
Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The New York Times reported.
Trump officials clash on new rule
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy. Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former company, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe.
Megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions.
Whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move. Instead, Lutnick initially favored looser controls that Nvidia claimed would ensure global dominance of US technology. (A Commerce Department spokesperson told NYT that Bessent has never confronted Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed.)
Any companies found violating the rules could face a “range of consequences,” the Commerce Department said after reportedly bending to Bessent’s pressure campaign. Those include possibly facing new import restrictions, stricter license requirements, downgrading their status in the US export control regime, or other changes to their company’s or their base country’s entity-list designations.
New rule may not be aggressively enforced
Although the summary of the rule change said that “Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion” of the anti-diversion policy, it’s unclear how aggressively the Commerce Department might enforce the rule, NYT noted.
Bessent has publicly criticized Lutnick for failing to sanction Megaspeed, and NYT reported that ultimately, enforcement of the stricter rules—which Bessent helped draft—“would be up to the Commerce Department.”
“The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said on a CNBC appearance. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”
There’s even a push to oust Lutnick over his position on chips, but The Guardian reported that Donald Trump confirmed he has no plans to replace the AI industry-friendly commerce secretary. On Monday, Trump told reporters that Lutnick was right to delay blacklisting Megaspeed, because “if you didn’t delay it… you could have a blow-up with China.”
At the press gaggle, Trump aligned with China in saying that there’s no evidence yet that Alice Huang was a spy. He also joined a band of prominent tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, saying that it wasn’t a “bad idea.”
“Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” Trump said. “She may not be a spy.”
However, US investigators have alleged that they found “Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China,” CBS News reported.
Trump thinks China won’t react to rule change
China is unlikely to welcome the new rules, as it has consistently accused the US of fabricating the spying claims to justify imposing additional chip restrictions.
However, a senior Trump official, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive policy matters, told the NYT that Trump “did not expect countermeasures from China in response.”
Trump will be in China for an economic summit this week, including a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new curbs could potentially disrupt those talks, according to Hong Yuan, a researcher and secretary-general of the Center for American Military Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Hong told the People’s Daily that China will likely view the rule change as politically motivated.
“Before any judicial causality was established, Washington handed down a political conviction, substituting suspicion for proof, espionage for personal contact, and an industrial embargo for private conduct,” Hong said. “The issue is not the cause of tighter controls, but a political catalyst.”
The new policy could hurt the US, experts told the Chinese outlets. Analysts told the South China Morning Post that the policy could “accelerate Chinese companies’ shift to domestic AI chips.” Other experts told the People’s Daily—which is the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party—that “the cost of switching back to US platforms will rise” over time. If that happened, it could potentially lock in Chinese technology over America’s in “the world’s largest single consumer market for chips,” experts said.
Sun Chenghao, senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, told the People’s Daily that “what US companies stand to lose could be customers and technological influence for years to come.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

For a woman who has been a witness to some of the most significant political moments in modern Indian history, Sonia Gandhi likes to insist her life has been far from remarkable. “Oh, I don’t know that I would say it’s an extraordinary story,” she says, shifting uncomfortably.
It’s hard to reconcile this modest characterisation with the course her life has taken over the last 79 years. Born to a working-class family in a small town in northern Italy, today she sits at the heart of Indian political power, having weathered assassinations and personal tragedy to become one of the country’s most influential figures. She held Indira Gandhi’s bloodied body after the then-prime minster, her mother-in-law, was gunned down at their home in Delhi in 1984. She then became India’s first lady when her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, took his mother’s place as prime minister. And when Rajiv, too, was killed, she threw aside her distaste for politics to step up and lead his fragmenting party. In 2004, having taken Congress to electoral victory, she famously turned down the prime minister post. She can still boast of being the longest-serving president of Congress, both when India’s oldest political party was in power and later, when it became the flailing opposition. When Gandhi stepped down in 2017, her son Rahul was appointed her successor.
Gandhi’s entrance into Indian politics began in Cambridge in the 1960s when, at 18, while she was studying at a language school, she fell in love with a bright-eyed boy at a Greek restaurant. At the time, she had no idea that Rajiv was heir to India’s most consequential political dynasty. “It was a coup de foudre,” she says. “After that, nothing else really mattered. He was, first of all, a handsome man. But I think his eyes told of the way he was – of his inner self. He was loving, he was comforting, he was caring. Everything I could have possibly dreamed of.”
Only later would she learn that Rajiv’s grandfather was Jawaharlal Nehru, Indian freedom fighter and the country’s first prime minister, and his mother was Indira Gandhi, who in 1966 became India’s first female prime minister.
Does she still recognise herself in that innocent Italian girl who was swept off her feet and transplanted to an alien land and culture? “Not really,” she says quietly. “Too much has happened, too much has changed.”
We meet at the grand white Delhi bungalow she has lived in for 36 years – a relic of British colonial rule, where peacocks roam the grounds. It was in this house in 1991 that Gandhi heard her husband had been assassinated by Sri Lankan Tamil separatist terrorists. Over the years, as she took on the mantle of Congress leader, her home became the centre of party operations.
The ghosts of Congress leaders past loom large in her study. A painting of Nehru, photographs of Rajiv, a carved stone bust and portraits of Indira line the walls, while a painting of Mahatma Gandhi, the freedom fighter who shaped the ideology of Congress, also hangs prominently. Heavy gilded tomes fill the floor-to-ceiling wooden bookshelves, and a long meeting table dominates the space, but the vibrant rugs, patterned blinds and scattered antiques suggest Gandhi’s own light touch.
In a dark blue sari and maroon blouse, her signature neat grey hair pushed back with a black headband, Gandhi looks every inch the composed Indian political matriarch as she sits on the sofa. The only hint of her heritage is softly accented English and recognisably Italian gesticulation.
She has, she confesses, been very nervous and tense about our meeting. Gandhi has not done an interview in a decade, and throughout her life in the public eye, has tried fiercely to maintain her privacy. She has only agreed to this rare meeting to discuss her forthcoming memoir, a strikingly personal account of her life, and has asked her daughter Priyanka, also a senior Congress leader, to sit in for moral support.
India’s media has often cast her as cold and aloof, yet today she seems warm, open and often a little unsure of herself. She’s anxious about how personal the book is, worried it will be eviscerated by the Indian media, but suggests that after years of “horrible and crazy things written about me”, it will be comforting for people to know “the truth”.
Gandhi has good reason to be nervous of the press. In today’s India, the mainstream media landscape has been crushed into submission by the hardline, rightwing Modi government and is largely devoted to promoting the prime minister’s agenda, while mercilessly attacking the Congress party, in particular the Gandhi family. She does not hold back on criticism of Narendra Modi – accusing him of being an “authoritarian force bent upon changing the very nature of our country” – and of his party, BJP, which she says has “systematically dismantled our democratic institutions”.
The Hindu nationalist vision of India that Modi has enacted over his 12 years in power is directly opposed to the pluralistic, secular India that was championed by successive Congress leaders and which remains enshrined in India’s constitution. It has led to well-documented oppression of the country’s minority groups, in particular its 200 million Muslims.
“More than disappointing, it’s very painful, having known a different India,” Gandhi says. “In parliament, we are not allowed to debate. In the past, there were discussions, there were meetings between the opposition and the government, there was consultation. Now the opposition counts for nothing.”
Since Modi came to power, she has had barely any interaction with him; he tends to avoid eye contact when they’re in a room together – a stark contrast to the past, when opposition leaders would often meet the government and “treat each other with cordiality”.
A “Congress-free India” is one of the openly declared goals of Modi’s BJP, resulting in highly personal attacks on Gandhi and her children, who have found themselves with numerous police cases filed against them. As we talk, Gandhi’s phone lights up with a call from her son Rahul – later, we learn a judge has just cleared him of defamation in one of these many cases, this time for criticising Modi’s home minister back in 2018. “They are very vindictive and vicious. There doesn’t seem to be a heart there,” Gandhi says.
So effective is the BJP’s crackdown on any form of dissent or criticism – what Gandhi describes as an “atmosphere of fear” – that her memoir almost didn’t see the light of day in India. Penguin Random House India were originally meant to release the book domestically, but after she sent them the manuscript she was met with a deafening silence. Gandhi says simply that Penguin were “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and that after she refused to make certain suggested edits, the publisher dropped the book, just a week before it was due to be announced. It will now be published by another imprint. In a statement, the publisher denied dropping the book, adding, “Any suggestion that Penguin Random House India decided not to publish Belonging because the author declined editorial changes does not accurately reflect the circumstances.”
Gandhi admits she was disappointed, though not altogether surprised, at what she sees as an attempt to censor her book. It is far from an isolated incident. In the days before we meet, Gandhi’s 26-year-old grandson, who is an artist and curator, is forced to take down dozens of his photographs depicting political protests that had been due to go on show in Delhi.
Gandhi had an early insight into the difficulties and loneliness of being a female leader in India’s deeply patriarchal society. When she arrived in India in 1968, she and Rajiv moved in with his mother, who at that time was two years into her first term as prime minister. Her husband, also a politician, had died years before.
They lived all together in another crumbling colonial Delhi bungalow, in relatively close and modest quarters. To outsiders, Indira was often seen as severe, an “iron lady”, and Gandhi admits that, to begin with, she was deeply intimidated by her formidable mother-in-law. Yet while Indira was imposing in public, she could be vulnerable in private, once confiding to Gandhi how terrified she was when she first bcame prime minister.
“In the newspapers she was portrayed as tough or harsh, but at home she was just like any other mother,” Gandhi says – although Indira’s notoriously explosive temper, frequently directed at political colleagues, would erupt through the house on occasion. Gandhi’s memoir recounts one incident where Indira lost her temper during a family dinner and threw her thali plate across the table.
Gandhi’s book documents the hostility Indira grappled with, both from political opponents and rightwing groups, but also from the old guard of her own party. “I saw her work day and night, constantly under pressure, constantly attacked,” Gandhi says. “It did affect her, like it would anyone. And of course, in that position, there is a loneliness. She had many interests and many friends, but it is a lonely kind of life.”
For several years, Gandhi says, her own life was “carefree”. She and Rajiv were madly in love, often embarrassing their children with public displays of affection that were highly unusual in Indian households at the time. “For this man, I was ready to do everything, to lose even my Italian identity,” she says. Rajiv was working as a commercial airline pilot, and as relations warmed with her mother-in-law, Gandhi set about redecorating the austere Delhi bungalow with some Italian flair, and learning how to cook Kashmiri food. After a traumatic miscarriage, she gave birth to two children, who were doted on by Indira. Even her pangs for fresh Italian ingredients, impossible to find in India in those days, eventually ebbed.
But in 1975 Indira would make the most controversial decision of her political life. Amid mounting political unrest, economic hardship and a concerted effort by the opposition to bring down the Congress government, Indira decided to impose a state of emergency on the country, in a bid to instil order. The repercussions were profound: the constitution was suspended, civil liberties and democratic freedoms abandoned, the media silenced and opponents detained en masse without trial. It lasted for almost two years, and is still seen as the darkest period of India’s democracy; it is regularly used to tarnish the Congress party today.
According to Gandhi, the family was split on the decision. Rajiv was against the move, telling his mother to wait for the next election, but her hotheaded younger son Sanjay pushed for it, arguing at one family dinner that the opposition would destroy his mother and telling her, “They must be stopped.” Sanjay’s forceful influence over his mother was a great source of public controversy at the time. Gandhi recalls that it inflamed tensions within the family, too; Rajiv attempted to confront his mother, but she refused to listen. “Keeping Sanjay in check could have prevented much of the damage that followed,” Gandhi writes in her book.
Today, she says it was a mistake for Indira to call the emergency, and that she believes her mother-in-law came to feel the same. “I always feel that Mrs Gandhi was a democrat at heart,” she says. “I know that many would laugh at this, but I believe she was never comfortable in the course of the emergency. I think it was sitting heavy on her.”
In the following years, Indira would lose one election and be returned to power in another. Rajiv would also be persuaded to enter politics after the premature death of Sanjay. But by 1984, darkness came to their door again.
Months of escalating violence had stricken the north Indian state of Punjab. As separatist militants prepared to declare an independent Sikh state, Indira authorised a military operation at one of the holiest sites in Sikhism, the Golden Temple in Amritsar, where the group were hiding out. The operation caused cataclysmic damage, killing Sikh pilgrims as well as militants, and led to desecration of the temple by tanks and heavy weaponry. Gandhi says that when her mother-in-law was shown images of the devastation, tears rolled down her face.
For Sikhs in India, it was a profound and painful attack on their religion, and Indira was inundated with threats. “She told us what to do in case she died – so she knew,” Gandhi says. “She was making preparations for her death. She told Rahul he must be brave and not to cry.” That summer Indira took her grandchildren on a trip to her ancestral home of Kashmir; Gandhi believes this was to “say goodbye”. Indira also defied advice to remove her Sikh bodyguards – something that turned out to be a fateful decision.
Gandhi was at home on 31 October when she heard what sounded like fireworks going off. Sprinting over to Indira’s office next door, she was confronted by her mother-in-law’s bloodied body, riddled with bullets, lying on the ground. Indira’s own Sikh bodyguards had opened fire on her in retribution for the attack on the Golden Temple.
What came next remains seared on Gandhi’s memory. After Indira was put into a car, she held her bleeding body and tried to revive her mother-in-law as they raced to the hospital. “There was blood everywhere and I realised she wasn’t replying to my questions. It seemed as if she had already gone,” she says.
Even after so many years, the story is clearly painful to recount and she speaks hesitantly, her soft voice growing even quieter. “I remember the drive from the house to the hospital was excruciating. There wasn’t much traffic, but it felt so slow. I also knew that because she wasn’t speaking, it must be over.”
Gandhi admits there are still parts of that experience she can’t bring herself to discuss. “I never talk about it. Only if I’m asked, then I struggle to.” Indira would be declared dead at the hospital. Her body was still lying there, cold, when Rajiv broke the news that he had been asked to step in as prime minister. Gandhi had begged him to stay out of politics and describes that conversation as a “knife going into my heart”.
In the aftermath of Indira’s death, she was traumatised and depressed, living “like a ghost”. Rajiv, too, had no time to grieve. Newly announced as prime minister, he immediately had to deal with deadly anti-Sikh riots that erupted after Indira’s death. He would later be accused of not doing enough to stop the bloodbath. “Rajiv never really showed his pain,” Gandhi says. “I remember seeing him in his mother’s study, on one of the chairs where she sat, with tears. But in public he felt he had to hide it.”
Fear took over their lives. The house became a fortress, with uniformed commandos stationed in the children’s bedrooms. Rahul and Priyanka were pulled out of school and no longer allowed to roam freely. She would worry if Rajiv didn’t come back from an engagement on time. He, meanwhile, would always want her by his side. “Fear was a very real thing,” she says. “My thought was always: he will be killed next.” By 1991, her premonition had come true.
A silence settles over the room as Gandhi struggles to recall how she went on living after Rajiv’s death. A Sri Lankan separatist militant had set off a suicide bomb while he was on the election trail, killing him instantly. Throughout our conversation, she still refers to Rajiv as “Papa”, as he is known to their children.
Priyanka, who sits on the sofa with us, interjects gently. She tells me how her mother would sit in the dark all day, listening to Mozart’s Requiem, engulfed by grief. “You were angry at him,” she says, speaking to her mother. “When you used to cry, you used to shout: how has he left me, why did he leave?”
Gandhi sits quietly for a moment. “After my mother-in-law was killed, we thought that, as we were always together, if something happens to one, it will happen to the other one,” she says. They had even written notes on how they wanted their funerals.
Yet when Gandhi’s sister pleaded for her to return to Italy, the thought was unfathomable. “India was my home, my children’s home,” she says. Gandhi last went back to Italy four years ago, when her mother died.
She found out later that, prior to the attack, Indian intelligence had intercepted death threats against Rajiv by the Sri Lankan separatist Tamil Tigers, angered over India’s intervention in the country’s civil war. However, these had been ignored by the newly elected government, who instead took away his top-level security. She still believes the truth of a wider conspiracy behind his death has yet to come out. The most recent commission to investigate it was shut down by the Modi government. “I don’t think we will get the truth now,” she says with a sigh.
Crucially, just as the foundation of her world was shattered, a wind of change was blowing across north India. A claim that a mosque in the city of Ayodhya was built on the ruins of an ancient Hindu temple had been gaining traction among hardline, rightwing Hindu nationalist organisations and political groups. In December 1992, supporters of the movement – including BJP figures – violently tore down the mosque.
Gandhi recalls crying as she witnessed the demolition on television. She says she knew then that they faced “a long battle for the secular nation that Mahatma Gandhi, Nehru and their colleagues had strived to build”. She accepts that failures of her own party in part contributed to the rise of the BJP and its hardline Hindutva politics. “I think we have been too complacent in many ways. There was a laissez-faire kind of an attitude,” she says. In 2024, Modi delivered on the BJP’s longstanding promise and inaugurated a vast Hindu temple in the place where the mosque had once stood.
Throughout her memoir, Gandhi is open about her distrust of politics, describing it as “menacing”, driven by “ambition, greed and hypocrisy”. But with Congress facing an existential threat and looking likely to fracture, Gandhi succumbed to mounting pressure and agreed to become its president in 1998. It was a decision, she says, driven by a sense of duty to her lost husband. Not only did she have to fight against her own ingrained shyness, she also had to take on political opponents in Hindi, her third language.
She insists she never had political ambition. Despite helping the party to win the most votes in the 2004 election, she shocked everyone by refusing to become prime minister. “It was clear in my mind I would never do it,” she says. “It was just not me.” Nonetheless, until she stepped back from the day-to-day of Congress leadership a few years ago, she had little time for herself. She would carry books to political events, history and autobiographies, to read on the way home. Music, both Indian classical and European operas, also became her solace. Having previously studied art restoration, “once in a while, I would slip away to an art exhibition”.
Today she stays out of the messy day-to-day of politics, though is still kept in the loop by her daughter and attends the occasional meeting. She finds joy in her small vegetable patch, but more than anything in spending time with her children and two grandchildren. Theirs has always been a dog-loving family (Priyanka once had seven golden retrievers) and Gandhi is devoted to her two jack russells, Noorie and Lapo, who were gifts from her son.
Nonetheless, the fortress of security that surrounds her home is a stark reminder of the restrictions still imposed on her freedom. Armed police man the barricades on the road outside, and my car is thoroughly inspected by security before I am allowed to drive through a towering metal gate and into her driveway.
While she was once credited with reviving the fortunes of Congress, over the past decade the Gandhi family have overseen its calamitous decline. Their previous government, in power till 2014, was marred by allegations of rampant corruption. (“In almost every single instance, the ministers resigned,” is Gandhi’s defence.) After taking over from his mother, Rahul lost the last three general elections to Modi, and Congress remains in power in only a few states. Meanwhile, the BJP’s Hindutva has become the country’s dominant political ideology. As the family has maintained its control, Congress has been unable to shake off allegations that it is nepotistic and run by political elites.
Why can’t Congress free itself from the Gandhi family’s leadership, I ask? She is dismissive, perhaps a nerve touched. “You would have to ask the party,” she says. Gandhi also skates over the question of nepotism, simply saying, “We all fight elections: we win them, we lose them. All of us have.” But after so many losses, can a Gandhi-led Congress still be a credible alternative to the BJP? While she is adamant they can, many in the country remain unconvinced.
It is true that we are meeting at an interesting moment, for both Modi and the bruised opposition. As gen Z youth erupted on to the streets in protest against the government over the summer – satirically calling themselves the “Cockroaches” after an online joke transformed into a serious political movement – the long-crushed space for dissent has opened up.
In recent weeks, young Indians have once again been taking to the streets against the government, despite being met with draconian state force. The question of whether they can shake the BJP’s grip on power remains to be seen; so far, the Cockroach movement has kept its distance from the opposition alliance. But “what encourages me is young people are coming out and demonstrating,” Gandhi says. “With determination, they’re calling out the government on things that are not right. I feel like this is a real shift.”
Congress, too, has become more energised than it has been for many years. Images of Rahul and Priyanka being manhandled by police as they tried to protest against the government have gone viral in recent weeks. After once pleading with her children to stay out of politics, Gandhi now says, “It’s good that they’re there. Now more than ever before.” The Gandhi family, it seems, are not done just yet.

Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban
- Published
FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono has been given a 12-match suspension by the Spanish football federation's disciplinary committee after his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel during the closing stages of the second-tier match between their two respective sides on 2 November.
De Miguel died the following day, aged 30.
The disciplinary committee said it had to base its decision "on the facts expressly recorded in the referee's report", which stated the player "was sent off for 'violently striking an opponent in the chest with his leg, using excessive force, while the ball was in play'.
"The tragic outcome of the incident, resulting in the death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda, is public knowledge."
The committee added the "nature of the conduct described and the accompanying circumstances" means that "the maximum sanction, a 12-match suspension, is justified".
Separately, the federation has decided the game between the two sides, which was abandoned seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred, will not be replayed.
"This avoids having to resume play from the precise moment at which the tragic incident occurred," it said.
The teams were drawing 2-2 at the time and that result will now stand, with a federation committee saying that was the "most respectful course of action, given the extraordinary and tragic circumstances of this case".
Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on 4 November, in which he said he was experiencing "the most difficult days" of his life and felt "enormous pain" about De Miguel's death.
On Thursday, FC Andorra manager Carles Manso said Equatorial Guinea international Owono is yet to decide whether he will return to football following the incident.
Manso said Owono is currently spending time with his family and is "completely free to make any decision" with regard to a potential return, adding: "What we have to do is support him in every way and be close to him.
"We will give him space so that he feels completely free to make any decision, whether he wants to return, when, or if he does not want to return.
"When he feels it is appropriate and when he feels genuinely ready to take a decision like that [he will do so]."

In mid-November, following a nationwide halt to U.S. flight departures, social media users shared claims about connections between Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy; his son-in-law, U.S. Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso, a Wisconsin Republican; and Air Space Intelligence — the company behind a new artificial intelligence-powered system used by the Federal Aviation Administration.
On Nov. 13, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after communications problems affected air traffic control facilities. The incident happened three days after the agency announced the nationwide expansion of an AI-supported traffic management system called SMART, developed by ASI.
Some posts claimed Alfonso had financial ties to ASI or received the FAA contract through Duffy, while others linked the company to the shutdown. For instance, one Facebook post (archived) read:
On Friday, the FAA grounded every plane in America.
The AI air traffic system at the center of it belongs to Air Space Intelligence. In June, Sean Duffy's department gave them an $875 million contract.
Before that, the company's PAC donated to Duffy's son-in-law, 26-year-old Michael Alfonso. He just won Duffy's old seat in Congress.
Americans deserve answers.
Another post (archived) on X stated, "Sean Duffy's son in law owns the AI company responsible for this FAA disaster yall."
Versions of the claim circulated on multiple social media platforms, including Reddit, X, Instagram and Facebook. Snopes readers also asked whether Alfonso or Duffy owned ASI, whether Alfonso received a multimillion-dollar FAA contract and whether campaign donations influenced the deal.
In short, Air Space Intelligence's PAC did contribute to Alfonso's campaign in March, and the company later received an FAA contract worth up to $875.95 million. However, we found no evidence that Alfonso owned ASI or that the donation influenced the contract award. The FAA also denied that the company's SMART system caused the Nov. 13 shutdown, and rather pointed to problems with its older communications network.
Alfonso's team said he had no part in awarding the FAA contract and that the campaign donation broke no laws or ethics rules, adding, "Nobody trades an $875 million federal contract for a $2,500 check." The FAA said in a statement that "each FAA contract goes through a rigorous, competitive process guided by nonpartisan career experts and personnel." We have also reached out to Air Space Intelligence and will update this report if we receive a response.
Here's what we know about the rumor:
ASI's PAC donated to Alfonso's campaign
According to a filing with the Federal Election Commission, Air Space Intelligence's political action committee donated $2,500 to Alfonso's congressional campaign on March 31:
(Federal Election Commission)
Alfonso's campaign also reported the same contribution:
(Federal Election Commission)
Some social media posts and articles, however, mentioned a larger sum of $12,500. That likely stemmed from a Raw Story article, which cited that amount, but later issued a correction.
News outlets reported on Alfonso's campaign donations even before the FAA shutdown. For instance, in March, ProPublica reported that his campaign received money from lobbyists and companies with interests before the Department of Transportation.
Did Alfonso or Duffy have financial ties to ASI?
Some social media posts claimed Alfonso owned Air Space Intelligence. Snopes readers also asked whether he invested in the company or benefited financially from its FAA contract.
However, we found no evidence supporting these claims. Neither Alfonso nor Duffy was listed among ASI's founders or executives. Alfonso's financial disclosure from April also didn't list any investment in ASI, although it only covered the period until October 2025. Similarly, Duffy's 2026 financial disclosure didn't list ASI among his investments.
In a statement to Snopes, Alfonso said, "Family ties don't earn anyone special treatment, and my father-in-law knows better than anyone that I think for myself." His team did not directly answer whether he ever owned shares or had any other financial interest in ASI.
Who received the $875M FAA contract?
Some social media posts claimed that Duffy awarded a multimillion-dollar FAA contract directly to his son-in-law, sometimes describing it as a no-bid contract. For example, one Bluesky user wrote, "In a surprise to no one, Sean Duffy gave a No Bid contract to his son-in-law to install the AI program into the FAA's system."
However, the USAspending.gov database showed the contract was awarded to Air Space Intelligence, not Alfonso:
(www.usaspending.gov)
The contract began on June 23 and could run for 12 years. Its maximum potential value is $875.95 million, but this does not mean ASI has already received all of that amount.
"No laws or House Ethics rules were violated," Alfonso's team told us via email, adding that "By law, PACs can give up to $5,000 per election. Nobody trades an $875 million federal contract for a $2,500 check."
According to federal records, the FAA received 12 offers before awarding the contract to ASI. The records classified the award as competitive, although they did not identify the other bidders or explain how ASI was selected. Bloomberg reported "the startup beat out larger competitors Palantir Technologies Inc. and Thales SA."
The FAA said in a statement that: "each FAA contract goes through a rigorous, competitive process guided by nonpartisan career experts and personnel. The FAA awarded the contract to Air Space Intelligence (ASI) following an innovative challenge with three vendors who demonstrated the highest levels of reliability, operational performance, and efficiency." The agency did not say whether Duffy was personally involved in the decision, or whether there was any potential conflict of interest involving him or Alfonso.
The FAA announced its search for a company to develop the system in September 2025, months before ASI's PAC donated to Alfonso's campaign, and announced ASI as the winner in June. We found no public evidence that the donation influenced the contract award.
Alfonso's team said he had no part in awarding the FAA contract, pointing out that he was a congressional candidate at the time, and not a government official. In a statement to Snopes, Alfonso also said, "I can't be bought," adding that he would consider each bill separately, including any future FAA funding requests, and "vote based on what's best for Wisconsin."
What caused the Nov. 13 FAA shutdown?
The FAA said its new AI system, SMART, did not cause the nationwide flight shutdown on Nov. 13. During a news briefing the next day, Duffy explained it "is a system that's not tied into or connected to the systems that went down yesterday. It's a tool that gives a prompt to one of our flight managers that they can accept or deny, but it's just better information flowing to them," summarizing that "SMART had zero impact on the occurrences yesterday."
Similarly, ASI wrote on X on Nov. 13 that the "current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC."
According to a Nov. 15 statement, the issue involved the FAA's older communications network. The agency identified two possible locations connected to the problem: a site in Arkansas, where contractor L3Harris was installing a new router, and another in Texas. L3Harris confirmed in a news release it was cooperating with the FAA's investigation. As of this writing, the exact cause of the shutdown was still under investigation.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ethan Lin, the 40-year-old cofounder and CEO of travel platform Klook, who is based in Hong Kong. The following has been edited for length and clarity.
In 2014, I left a stable banking job to cofound Klook, a platform where people can book travel experiences.
I was 27, had no experience in tech or product, and bootstrapped the business with the savings my cofounders and I had built up. Now, the company is almost 2,000 employees-strong across 25 offices.
As a 40-year-old CEO, I spend most of my time on work and fitness. Here's how I bring my A-game on busy work days.
An 8 a.m. dopamine boost
Fitness is really important to me. It's a dopamine boost in the morning; it works better than coffee.
Each week, I go to the gym five to six times, mostly in the morning before work, around 7 or 8 a.m. That helps me wake up.
I have a light meal, and then I hit the gym for some strength training. I participated in Hyrox in Bangkok a few weeks ago. Klook is Hyrox's travel partner across Asia, and I like to show support.
After my morning workout, I have a light meal that helps me start the day feeling very energetic.
I reach the office around 9 a.m., then AI automations help me kick off
I have several AI projects in the works that help me keep on top of my game.
I have an AI automation set up that sends me a weekly Monday morning summary email, giving me a quick refresh on what's happening each week.
Other AI automations work like think tanks for me, acting like a consultant, industry expert, communication strategist, analyst, and so on, brainstorming with me. One thing I enjoy about AI is that it feels like you're working with many experts every day.
When it comes to drafting emails, I feed AI the skeletons of the content and structure and let it write a draft for me because English isn't my first language, but the critical thinking and judgment have to come from me.
I need to remind myself to be mindful because they all sound right, and I need to be the one deciding what information is really suitable for me.
Before AI, when you worked on a project or task or sent emails, you would get a few hours or days of break before you got a response, or the next piece of information. Right now, that part is pretty much instant, so we end up basically working nonstop. I feel like I'm being mentally challenged more and more every day.
I scroll through customer complaint emails — and enjoy reading them
I'm copied on all Klook customer inquiry or complaint email chains, and I enjoy reading them every day as they come in. In the last 12 years, that's one habit I haven't changed.
The emails often look like: "I booked a day for this activity, but can I change to another day? The system doesn't support it," or "I wrote my name wrong. Can I get entry into this venue without the right name? Can you change it?"
It's something AI can help summarize, but I like to get them randomly every day, even on weekends, because you cannot predict when a customer will submit a complaint. It's like TikTok — swipe, swipe, you never know what's coming next. It's quite addictive.
I don't respond directly to them — that would be a bit awkward — but scrolling through complaints gives me enough frequent data points and real case studies to get a sense of our customers' problems. When we actually conduct analyses or prioritize which problems to solve, I have enough tangible examples.
I'm in the office until at least 7 p.m.
Most days, I'm in the office until 7 to 8 p.m., although other days can get quite late. That's also why I try to protect my morning workouts to kick-start the day, as my evening workouts aren't guaranteed.
As a CEO, my time is very fragmented: I spend half an hour on one task, 15 minutes on another, and an hour on something else. I get sucked into a lot of projects and meetings but often don't have time to sit and think about how they're linked to see if anything's missing.
Every week, I block off two to three hours from my calendar for personal reflection. I'll use that to finish a project or task, or consolidate information.
My second workout, followed by bed at 1 a.m.
After work, about twice a week at night, I hit cardio. I do a light zone-two run. That means a four- to eight-kilometer run at a not-too-crazy pace, depending on how busy my day has been. This helps me build endurance and sleep better, although I'm already a pretty deep sleeper.
The last hour or so of my day is my quiet time. This involves some email clean-up, prepping for the next day, and reading things outside technology and travel to give myself a different perspective.
I'm normally asleep by 1 a.m.

The headlines may be dominated by artificial intelligence and electoral politics, but beneath it all, another debate constantly simmers, forever threatening to erupt.
Men weren’t always “bad at friendship”
History has a solution for the male loneliness crisis.
I write, of course, of the great male friendship debate.
On one side: writers, journalists, and academics who fret over rising male loneliness, the emotional impact of friendless men on their partners, and the threat to society posed by atomized and isolated fellas. On the other: those who defend male friendships built around shared activities rather than heart-to-hearts.
These arguments often talk past each other. But the historian Tiffany Watt Smith offered me a way to think differently about both: that the gender roles undergirding the conversation are not nearly as fixed as they seem.
“I can definitely tell you that men in the past had much more intimate and romantic and involved friendships than we see today, for sure,” said Smith, who has published a number of books on the histories of friendship and emotions. “The idea that women are the kind of great experts in friendship is a really modern idea.”
I talked with Smith about Aristotle’s idea of the “perfect” friendship (it has to be between two dudes), how gendered notions of friendship inverted in the 19th century, and what men seeking deeper emotional connection from their buddies can learn from the past. You can hear that conversation and and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Smith, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
How do male friendships today compare to those of the past?
For thousands of years, it was really men who were considered the great experts in knowing how to form the highest kinds of friendships and the most intimate kind of bonds. And their friendships were considered the most meaningful and enduring and deep kind of friendships.
If you look back at David and Jonathan in the Bible or Achilles and Patroclus in the Iliad, you see these very dynamic, committed male friendships. When we look at the writings of Aristotle in the fourth-century BC, he’s talking about the deepest kind of friendship. He calls it the perfect friendship.
And this is between two men who he sees as soulmates. And he does say that there are other kinds of friendship, which are lesser friendships. He says you might make friends because it’s kind of convenient or because you enjoy doing the same kinds of things, or maybe you’re trying to help each other out. There’s a kind of quid pro quo-type of friendship. So he does see these kinds of friendship all around him. And he says women do those kinds of friendships.
One of the most famous pieces of writing about friendship ever is Michel de Montaigne’s essay “On Friendship.” Montaigne was a 16th-century essayist and lawyer, and he had this very, very close and committed friendship with another writer called La Boétie. And then after La Boétie died very unexpectedly, Montaigne wrote about their friendship and he said they had this kind of ideal friendship, the kind that Aristotle wrote about, this meeting of souls, and that this was rare and extraordinary.
And he was very explicit. He said, “Men can have these kinds of friendships.” But he very explicitly said, “Women are just incapable of having this kind of perfect friendship. They don’t have the kind of emotional stamina. They’re not clever enough. They’re not educated enough. Their souls aren’t strong enough, essentially, to withstand the complexities and difficulties of friendship.” So it’s a complete inversion from what we see today.
You used this word when you started: romantic. What did you mean by that? Was the Aristotelian conception of a perfect male friendship, was there a kind of romantic element in the way that we use the word romance?
Historians call this style of friendship “romantic friendship.” It doesn’t necessarily mean that they were having a physically active relationship or that they were having sex. They did see themselves as a partnership, and some of these male friends talked about themselves as married. This was a marriage of soul.
“Friendship is something that we have to negotiate on an individual basis. Each friendship is completely singular and we have to work out its rules.”
There’s a very important tombstone in Christ’s College in Cambridge, which commemorates these two doctors in the 16th century who basically lived their whole lives together. They traveled together, they did their research together and so on. And when they died, they were buried together. And the tomb does look like a conventional tomb between a husband and wife.
Now, we don’t know anything about their relationship in practice. I mean, the thing that really matters is the fact that this friendship, because it was commemorated as a friendship, the fact that it could be commemorated so vividly and publicly in such an extravagant way shows us that this is a culture that accepts and idealizes this kind of male friendship.
So how do we get from there to here?
Beginning in the 18th century and certainly by the 19th century, there’s a series of things that happen. One is that we get a distinction between the public space of the workplaces, cities are expanding, offices start to exist. The male sphere is fashioned as one of being in public, being a more rational sphere, and the female sphere starts to be connected with the home and intimacy and emotion.
Those ideas have been kind of floating around for a while, but they start to get really consolidated in the 19th century. And at the same time, a new ideal of femininity starts to emerge and it becomes a real sort of middle-class aspirational goal for women that they have very close friendships, almost as evidence that they can do all of these things.
Young girls in this era are taught a very particular style of friendship, which is, again, it’s very romantic. There’s lots of kissing and declarations of love and so on, but also it’s shown to be very committed. It’s very thoughtful, it’s very caring. And this is seen to be a kind of training ground for motherhood and for marriage.
At the end of the 19th century, we start to portray male friendships as kind of blundering and superficial and lacking in intimacy. And then of course, men carry on having close friendships, but by the beginning of the 20th century, another nail in the coffin, as it were, happens, which is that there’s a rise in understanding of homosexuality across Europe and America, and gay culture becomes much more visible.
In that moment, men become really anxious about having intimate and close relationships with other men. They’re worried about what that looks like and how that might be read. And that, in addition, leads to these anxieties about close male friendships.
If some guy is hearing this and is interested in having more fulfilling friendships, but he doesn’t know how to get there, where might he start?
The thing about history is that it shows us how much things have changed, but it also reminds us that things keep changing and can change again.
We’ve had this amazing history of these very romantic, intense, effusive male friendships. I think a lot of men probably would find that kind of overwhelming and unappealing as a model of friendship, but is there something in between? And one of the things I think that is important to remember is that we can make these changes and these shifts in style and these shifts in the patterns and our approaches to friendships.
One thing that I think it’s really worth listeners remembering is that since friendship has changed in the past, it can change again. There’s nothing biologically innate about the inability to make friends.
Which is freeing, the fact that friendship is not a fixed category for men or for women and that things can be what you want them to be. You’re not held back by some innate aspect of our biology.
I think that’s absolutely true. We get this notion that, well, men are sort of naturally worse at making friends or something, or they naturally have less kind of desire to connect with other people. That’s completely not true. The history of male friendships shows us that that is completely not true. So we can be released from that idea.
There isn’t an obvious, perfect, one-size-fits-all version of friendship. Friendship is something that we have to negotiate on an individual basis. Each friendship is completely singular and we have to work out its rules. What is my style of friendship? What is your style of friendship? How can we find something in the between so that we understand how to communicate and how not to hurt each other and how to build trust between each other?

CAA has signed Hybe to rep its artist roster including K-Pop behemoth BTS, along with the South Korean giant’s IP and brands. The companies will collaborate across content, brand partnerships, sports, licensing, merchandising and live experiences.
Hybe’s acts also include such groups as Katseye, Tomorrow X Together, Seventeen and many more.
“This partnership with CAA marks an important step in expanding creative possibilities for Hybe’s artists,” Hybe CEO Jason Jaesang Lee said in a statement. “By bringing together our complementary strengths and global networks, we aim to extend the reach and value of our artists and their IP across content, brands, and live experiences. Together, we will explore new creative opportunities that transcend borders and formats, bringing audiences closer to our artists through more immersive and meaningful experiences.”

Added CAA CEO and co-chair Bryan Lourd: “Hybe has created a cultural movement. Hybe artists do not just entertain; they connect with audiences in extraordinary and innovative ways that define the future of our industry and the intersection of art, influence and fandom. We are honored to help carry that forward, building on CAA’s experience and relationships across the region, to show the world what is possible when two organizations that believe in creative talent come together.”
Hybe, which rebranded from Big Machine Entertainment in 2021, is a global entertainment lifestyle platform company built on music and technology. With operations across Korea, Japan, the U.S., Mexico, China, and India, it runs numerous record labels including Bighit Music, Belift Lab, Source Music, Pledis Entertainment, Koz Entertainment. Hybe America is behind Blue Highway Records, music publisher Big Machine Music and Quality Control Music, along with Hybe’s labels in Latin America and the U.S. Hispanic market.
Beyond music, Hybe continues to expand across concerts, video content, gaming, original stories, retail, and fan platforms.

The Karnataka government has reportedly halted the registration of new taxis operated by Vingroup-backed Green SM days after clearing its operation within the state. Alongside this, the transport department is said to be planning to make fare meters compulsory for all cabs, including those operating through ride-hailing platforms such as Ola and Uber. Transport Minister Byrathi Suresh cited the need to protect the interests of local taxi owners and drivers as an explanation for the ban, as per a report by Moneycontrol. The state government has directed transport department officials to stop registering new Green SM taxis until further orders, even as around 100 vehicles operated by the company have already been registered to ply on Karnataka roads. That said, the state government is yet to take a final call on whether Green SM will be allowed to continue its operations in Karnataka. Questions sent to Green SM remained unanswered at the time of publication. The story will be updated upon receiving a response. The latest action follows protests by Bengaluru-based private transport associations such as Karnataka Rajya Chalakara Parishath and Peace Auto Union. The e-taxi operator, part of Vietnam's Vingroup, which also operates electric car OEM Vinfast, received an aggregator licence from the Karnataka Transport Department in November 2026, valid until September 2031. Protesting associations have questioned the licensing process and alleged that Green SM's vehicles were registered without meeting mandatory requirements, including digital fare meters, taxi display boards, GPS equipment and driver documentation. They have also raised concerns about the impact of another large fleet operator on the earnings of existing taxi drivers, particularly those who have taken loans to purchase their vehicles, seeking an examination of the permissions granted to the company and the potential impact on local operators from the Karnataka Governor. Taxi and auto unions in the state have a long track record of opposing ride-hailing platforms like Uber, Ola and Rapido for their fares, compensation practices and vehicle formats like bike-taxis. Green SM's planned Bengaluru entry is part of a wider India expansion strategy. It is already operational in Delhi NCR and Hyderabad and touched the 15 Lakh rides milestone earlier this month. Green SM started India operations in June this year. It is now preparing to expand across six geographies, and has secured aggregator licences in Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka, with plans to enter Bengaluru and Chennai. Ride-Hailing Platforms Face Regular Roadblocks Karnataka also plans to introduce mandatory fare meters for all taxis, including those operating through app-based aggregators, the state’s transport minister said. The transport department is preparing the necessary draft rules and legal provisions, with the government warning that vehicles found violating the prescribed fare requirements could be seized. The proposed move follows complaints from taxi owners and drivers seeking a uniform fare structure and alleging that aggregators have been exploiting them. The emphasis on physical meters comes as cab aggregators like Uber, Ola and Rapido face increasing scrutiny over fare structures, additional charges and booking practices. In August, the transport department issued notices to Ola, Uber and Rapido over alleged violations of government-notified fares following complaints from driver associations that the aggregators were charging passengers fares different from those prescribed by the state government and were not paying drivers the stipulated amounts. More recently, the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) imposed penalties on Rapido and Ola over prompts asking passengers to increase their payments when drivers were not accepting the original fares. The regulator found that messages and prompts suggesting additional payments constituted dark patterns, including confirmed shaming. The CCPA also said it had initiated proceedings against Uber and Namma Yatri over similar practices, with investigations ongoing. However, the proposal remains under judicial scrutiny after the Supreme Court questioned FSSAI's proposed 365-day voluntary compliance period. FSSAI is yet to notify the final regulations, noting that it could take approximately four months to prepare and finalise the draft amendment regulations.

On the intervening night of November 8 and 9, over 250 PM2.5 data points from Delhi were missing on the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) website, according to an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
Scientist and air quality analyst Manoj Kumar tweeted the statistics in the early hours of November 9. According to him, out of the 59 monitoring stations, as seen on the official website of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), only 14 stations reported complete data, while the remaining 45 had at least one missing hourly observation.
Missing hourly PM2.5 data raises concerns over Delhi’s air quality assessment.
Since midnight on 8 November until 5 am on 9 November, 227 hourly PM2.5 observations were missing across 59 CPCB monitoring stations in Delhi. Only 14 stations reported complete data, while the remaining 45 had at least one missing hourly observation.
A key concern is that many missing readings occurred when concentrations approached the monitoring instruments’ upper measurement limit of 1,000 µg/m³. These observations should not simply be treated as missing when calculating hourly or daily averages or deriving AQI. Doing so could underestimate pollution levels. For a conservative assessment, such readings should be flagged as potentially exceeding the measurement range, with 1,000 µg/m³ considered as a lower-bound value rather than treating them as zero or excluding them without qualification.
Mundka recorded the highest number of missing hourly observations (10), followed by Dwarka Sector 8, IIT Delhi, Nehru Nagar, Pusa IITM and Uttam Nagar, with eight missing hours each.
There is also an unusual pattern at some stations. IGNOU Maidan Garhi, Cantonment Area, Siri Fort and Tikri Kalan recorded PM2.5 concentrations below 30 µg/m³ (Cleanest) during parts of this episode. Given the pollution levels elsewhere, these readings warrant verification for possible instrument or data-quality issues before being used in final averages or AQI calculations.
Reliable air-quality assessment during pollution episodes requires both complete data and transparent treatment of readings that exceed instrument measurement limits.
— Dr. Manoj Kumar (@manoj_kumar_nr) November 9, 2026
Air Quality Index, or AQI, turns air quality data for eight pollutants into one number and one name, providing an easy-to-understand picture of air quality. According to the All India AQI Dashboard, the pollutants are PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, Pb, and NH3. (Lead is not monitored at every station.)
Delhi’s average AQI on the night of Diwali was as follows, according to the CPCB.
However, between 1 am and 3 am on the Diwali night, over 30 monitoring stations were not showing any PM2.5 data. Over the course of the night, more stations failed.
A day after, as the mystery of missing data caused an outrage, the hourly air quality readings missing from the CPCB website became available on the Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) website, which showed that the PM2.5 concentration went up to a staggering 3500 micrograms per cubic metre and beyond, which is around 60 times its standard value.

Why does the Missing Data Matter?
India’s air quality figures come from monitoring stations run by state pollution control boards and committees, such as DPCC in Delhi. Stations send their readings to CPCB every 15 minutes. CPCB calculates each station’s AQI by finding a sub-index for every pollutant and taking the highest one. It then publishes the results on its portal, the SAMEER app and its daily bulletin.
A sub-index is the AQI score for a single pollutant on its own. Each pollutant is measured in different units and has a different “safe” range. For example, PM2.5 is in micrograms per cubic metre, and CO is in milligrams per cubic metre. So CPCB converts each pollutant’s reading to the same 0-500 scale, and that converted number is its sub-index.
If the PM2.5 has a sub-index of 75, SO2 has 63, and NO2 has 38, the station’s overall AQI is the highest of these, so here it is 75, driven by PM2.5. One bad pollutant is enough to push the AQI into a worse category, even if the others are fine.
If one looks carefully at the above screenshot from 12 midnight on November 9 from the Anand Vihar monitoring station, one would see that the 24-hour average of the PM2.5 pollutant is the 24-hour average AQI for that particular monitoring station. One would also note that the highest average sub-index determines the AQI.
Now, if PM2.5, which gives a measure of fine particulate matter in the air and is also highest during Diwali due to the bursting of firecrackers, goes missing, the average AQI reading underestimates the pollution in the air to a great extent. According to a Hindustan Times report, if one considers the released readings, Delhi’s AQI for 24 hours until 9 am on November 9 was 384 on a 500 scale against the 370 figure published by CPCB.
Why did the Data Go Missing?
According to Kumar’s post on X (shared when the missing data had not been released), Mundka recorded the highest number of missing hourly observations (10), followed by Dwarka Sector 8, IIT Delhi, Nehru Nagar, Pusa IITM and Uttam Nagar, with eight missing hours each.
Interestingly, the highest reading also came from Mundka at 3,744 µg/m³ at 2 am on November 9. JNU was at 3,023 at 4 am the same night and NSUT’s West Campus at 3,008 at 5 am. Eleven of DPCC’s stations went past 2,000 micrograms per cubic metre.
The CPCB released an official statement on November 10 addressing the data gaps, saying that particulate analysers like PM2.5 were calibrated for 0-1,000 µg/m³. Under the automated validation, hourly readings beyond that range are treated as “outside range” and left out of the computation. CPCB conceded this “may appear as a data gap” during extreme episodes like Diwali firecracker bursting. Those hours don’t count towards the 24-hour average for that station. It also stated that the methodology for processing data beyond the system’s design range is “under review”, with internal deliberations underway.
On November 11, Kumar posted on X, if the 255 missing PM2.5 data points were replaced with 1,000 µg/m³, the upper measurement limit cited by CPCB, the average showed a 49% increase, from 269 to 400 µg/m³.
Alt News spoke to Kumar, who also told us that while the DPCC continued to record data above 1000 micrograms per cubic metre, it was the CPCB, the body ultimately entrusted with calculating and releasing AQI findings, that did not register it. “DPCC had measured and displayed PM 2.5 concentration above 1000 on that day. But it was not reflected on the CPCB website.”
Explaining the process and the gaps, Kumar said, “Let’s say that the instrument’s operating range is between 0 and 1000. But if it is going above 1000, there will be some uncertainty, but uncertainty can be estimated.”
Even in his November 9 post, Kumar made the point that the readings had gone missing as the concentration readings approached 1000. “These observations should not simply be treated as missing when calculating hourly or daily averages or deriving AQI. Doing so could underestimate pollution levels. For a conservative assessment, such readings should be flagged as potentially exceeding the measurement range, with 1,000 µg/m³ considered as a lower-bound value rather than treating them as zero or excluding them without qualification,” he wrote.
Furthermore, to calculate AQI, one would need to have at least 16 hours in a day, if not all 24 hours of data. So missing out on important data points during peak pollution periods underrepresents the AQI value.
It’s also worth noting that aur quality monitoring is not cheap: A 2018 Hindustan Times report put the cost of a conventional station at up to Rs 5 crore.

As Gaza floods overwhelm displacement sites, municipal teams in Al Maghazi refugee camp face a difficult trade-off: Pumping floodwaters out of shelters means taking away fuel needed to supply residents with drinkable water.
“The diesel we use for these pumps comes from the allocation for the wells that are supposed to pump water,” says municipal engineer Imad Abdel Jawad, and this is at a time when their supply is already insufficient.
Rainstorms swept through Gaza over the weekend of November 7 and 8, overwhelming damaged sewage networks and makeshift shelters. In some tents in Al Maghazi, the water was well over a foot deep, Jawad says.
For Hanan Saied, 46, the storm soaked the bedding and clothing she shares with her seven children. She lives in a shelter in Al Maghazi with mud walls, cracks, and plastic sheeting covering the roof, which WIRED Middle East visited.
“The house flooded, and stones and mud fell on us,” Saied says. “The bedding was soaked, and the children’s clothes were soaked.”
Her children used buckets to move water away while her eldest son tried to repair the shelter. Saied spent the night holding her daughter, Sara, who she says has asthma, trying to keep her warm.
Gaza’s Government Media Office has said at least 70,000 tents sheltering displaced Palestinians had flooded within 12 hours.
On 8 November, the Israel account on X, run by Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, posted, “Contrary to popular belief, Israel does not control the weather.” The post did not explicitly mention Gaza floods.
The flooding comes after widespread destruction of Gaza’s housing. An April assessment by the European Union, United Nations, and World Bank found that more than 371,888 housing units had been damaged or destroyed and around 1.9 million people internally displaced, often repeatedly.
By 8 November, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) estimated that 1.4 million people—65 percent of Gaza’s population—were living in tents or shelters. Humanitarian partners had received appeals from more than 26,000 households whose shelters or belongings had been damaged.
In Al Maghazi, Jawad describes five displacement sites across the camp’s western and northern areas. Parts sit on low ground where rainwater accumulates without an outlet.
His teams used pumps to move water outside the displacement sites. But the problems extend beneath the streets.
Israeli bombardment has damaged sewage manhole covers in Al Maghazi, Jawad says. Other covers have been stolen or deteriorated over time. The resulting openings allow rainwater to pour into sewage networks unable to accommodate the extra volume, causing wastewater to overflow.
“The sewage networks become unable to accommodate the quantities of sewage in addition to the rainwater that leaks into the manholes because the covers are missing,” he says.
Replacement covers are unavailable locally, while materials needed to fabricate alternatives are scarce and expensive. The municipality cannot afford all the work required. Keeping the water supply running takes priority.
“I consider spending money on maintaining wells or maintaining generators to operate water wells a higher priority than allocating some of that money to maintaining sewage manhole covers,” Jawad says.
These shortages extend across Gaza. In its November 5 report, OCHA said Israeli authorities continued to impose particularly tight restrictions on engine oil, lubricants, spare parts, and new generators. Systems for pumping floodwater and sewage were already failing.
Restoring more sustainable power supplies, the agency added, depended on Israeli permission to import solar panels, reconnect the electricity grid, and restart Gaza’s power plant.
The Israel Defense Forces did not respond to WIRED Middle East’s request for comment on restrictions affecting the entry of equipment and supplies needed for flood prevention and infrastructure repairs.
Jawad says trucks and earth-moving machinery are needed to bring material to displacement sites where water collects on muddy ground, improving conditions beneath and around tents.
The consequences also reach clinics. Dr Asma Saleh, a general practitioner at the Al Maghazi clinic of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA), reports an increase in children presenting with respiratory and gastrointestinal illnesses as the rainy season begins.
Saleh says the clinic sees around 120 children daily, including approximately 22 with influenza-like illness diagnosed from symptoms and 13 with gastroenteritis.
“The inhumane living conditions, collapse of infrastructure, the flowing streets contaminated with sewage, and the shortage of medical supplies are all factors that profoundly impact the health care system in Gaza,” she says.
For Saied, the immediate concern is getting Sara through the next storm. Her daughter has more frequent asthma attacks during winter, she says, and the family has neither a nebuliser nor electricity to operate one.
“My older son spent hours repairing our worn shelter using simple tools, but I don’t know what to do during upcoming storms."
This story originally appeared in WIRED Middle East.

In mid-November, an alleged Truth Social post by U.S. President Donald Trump claiming that disruptions to food and banking services were imminent spread on social media.
A screenshot of the alleged post circulated on TikTok, Threads, and Facebook several days before customers at a handful of major U.S. banks experienced service outages on Nov. 16. JPMorgan Chase confirmed that a technical issue was behind the disruptions, according to the Associated Press.
The purported screenshot read:
URGENT: New intelligence and global developments indicate there could be serious disruptions to our food supply, banking system, and critical services in the coming weeks. To protect your family, I strongly recommend that Americans take the following steps immediately:
- Stock up on at least 90 DAYS of food, water, and essential supplies.
- Withdraw your cash from the bank and keep it on hand.
- Be prepared for potential internet and cell service outages.
This is about being prepared, not panicking. The risks are real, and it's better to be ready now than to be caught off guard later.
I want to thank Diane Cavoto, who has been sounding the alarm on this for months. She has been right, and her guidance has helped many Americans get prepared.
Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J TRUMP.
(Accessed via X)
We found no evidence of Trump sharing the above post on any of his social media accounts. As such, we've rated the screenshot fake.
Searches for variations of the quote on Google, DuckDuckGo (archived) and Bing uncovered no reporting from reliable media outlets connecting it to the president, which would have been the case if it were authentic. We searched for various phrases within the purported post, including "New intelligence and global developments," "Stock up on at least 90 DAYS of food" and "This is about being prepared, not panicking," none of which returned any relevant results.
Likewise, searches of Roll Call's archive of Trump's posts on X and Truth Social and Trump's Truth, a website dedicated to archiving his Truth Social posts, did not return any results for posts resembling the screenshot.
As of this writing, we were unable to determine who originally shared the fake post.
For further reading, Snopes has frequently debunked many fake quotes attributed to Trump.

A molecular signal in the blood helps identify microscopic changes that precede the development of ovarian cancer, researchers have found, in a potential diagnostic breakthrough for a disease often discovered after it has already spread.
For decades, efforts to detect ovarian cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumours, the researchers noted in their report published on Tuesday in Nature Medicine.
“We asked a fundamentally different question: What if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” study leader Rajan Gogna of the Hoag Family Cancer Institute in Newport Beach, California, said in a statement. Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes.
The precancerous lesions are known as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC). The new study found that women with this precursor condition have elevated blood levels of an RNA molecule called Tu-Stroma.
When researchers measured Tu-Stroma in blood, they detected STIC in 92.3% of affected women and correctly identified 98.2% of healthy women. In women with genetic risk factors for ovarian cancer, approximately 72% of positive results would be accurate, while negative results would be correct nearly 100% of the time, they reported. “For women at high risk, this could transform how we approach prevention,” co-author Esha Madan, also of Hoag, said in a statement.
Many such women face difficult decisions about preventive surgery to remove their fallopian tubes and ovaries. “Today, decisions about preventive surgery are largely guided by inherited risk, without knowing whether precancerous lesions are actually present,” Madan said. “Our discovery could eventually provide that missing biological information.”

Dust off that Hitachi and put your Slack on “Do not disturb,” because AO3 is back online, baby.
After weeks off the internet due to an unspecified security incident, the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the nonprofit that runs the hugely popular fan fiction forum, announced on November 15 that service had been restored.
“We understand that the wait and uncertainty surrounding AO3’s return have been difficult, and we apologize for the inconvenience,” the statement reads. “We greatly appreciate your support during the downtime, and continued patience as our volunteers work hard to return AO3 to its full functionality.”
The news came as a pleasant surprise to AO3’s devoted fans, as the website had announced in late October that restoring service could take between two to four weeks. To that end, the OTW statement says that some of the site’s features, such as user icons and external work importing, have been temporarily disabled in order to expedite the site’s return. It also warned that users “may experience a delay before AO3 loads,” due to “high traffic.”
Founded in 2007, AO3 is one of the most popular fan fiction forums on the internet, boasting more than 11 million users and over 18 million original works. Following its temporary shutdown, many devastated fans started sharing Google Docs of their favorite fanfics, sparking some concerns among authors worried about AI scraping and their work being posted to other websites without their permission. Others resorted to other platforms to get their Dramione or Hollanov fix, such as Tumblr, which reported a 75 percent jump in new sign-ups among users between the ages of 18 and 25, according to data shared with WIRED.
Throughout the 17-day shutdown, AO3 has remained vague about the causes of the security breach. In its statement announcing its return, OTW said that while it has “no reason to believe that the user database was compromised,” it can’t rule out the possibility; the website recommends users change their passwords “as a precaution.” The site is also pairing with a security firm “to help prevent future incidents.”
Though the suggestion prompted some concern on social media, for the most part fans are jubilant about the end of the “AO3 apocalypse,” as some have referred to the shutdown.
“Ao3 returned on a Sunday,” one fan wrote in a tweet that has 1.2 million views. “Just like Jesus.”
