US has lost measles elimination status, global health authorities say
The U.S. has lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago.
Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country's status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion this week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country.
PAHO had planned a public announcement on Nov. 17.
In public health parlance, measles elimination depends on a country's sporadic outbreaks ending within a year. That's no longer happening in the United States.
"It's a very sad moment," said Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who was not involved in PAHO's decision.
"Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death," Schuchat said.
Measles outbreaks are entirely preventable: Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, so when almost everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus can't spread.
In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized with measles in the U.S. More than 8,000 people have been sickened in outbreaks that have cost roughly $125 million in medical care, public health response, and productivity losses, Johns Hopkins University researchers estimate.
States have reported 13 measles-associated deaths, including a 7-month-old in New York and infants in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin in recent months. Babies typically aren't vaccinated before they're a year old.
PAHO, an international group that oversees health in the Americas and works with the World Health Organization, based its assessment on two analyses: one by the CDC and another by an independent group of measles experts.
Researchers anticipated this conclusion after an outbreak in Utah surpassed the one-year mark in June.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, Emily Hilliard, attributed the resurgence of measles to vaccination gaps that opened years before this administration. Indeed, rates of childhood vaccination have steadily declined since the COVID pandemic started.
But many scientists also blame the Trump administration for spreading vaccine misinformation and stifling a swift, strong response to outbreaks.
For example, the administration cut millions of dollars from children's immunization programs run by state health departments and terminated funds for research on vaccine hesitancy.
After Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sacked CDC director Susan Monarez in August 2025, she told Congress she was fired because she would not preapprove changes to vaccine recommendations "without reviewing the evidence."
Monarez added that "we already have seen the largest measles outbreak in more than 30 years" and that, "if vaccine protections are weakened, preventable diseases will return."
Spokespeople for HHS and the White House defended the administration, and Kennedy, who led a prominent anti-vaccine organization before he took the helm at HHS. "The President and the Secretary have repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, coordinated with states, and facilitated the deployment of vaccine doses across the country," White House spokesperson Allison Schuster wrote in an email.
Past administrations sounded alarms
For more than three decades, the federal government treated measles as a preventable tragedy, with sizable outbreaks triggering national efforts to boost vaccination and stop the virus from spreading.
That's no longer the case, said Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a new initiative that educates the public about vaccines and assists health workers responding to outbreaks.
Stinchfield was a pediatric nurse at a children's hospital in Minnesota during the nation's last surge of measles before elimination, from 1989 to 1991. She recalled an entire ward devoted to children with measles and the enormous effort required to prevent the virus from spreading to kids with cancer and weakened immune systems.
Two children at the hospital died of measles. "That changed my career forever," she said.
Back then, she said, the federal government "saw the urgency." Officials held press conferences, spoke on the news about vaccines, issued clinical guidelines, and published reports in the CDC's flagship journal — the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, or MMWR — that drove policies.
When data suggested that some children weren't mounting a strong response to a single dose of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, a CDC advisory committee recommended two doses of the shot.
When CDC analyses found that many children with measles hadn't been vaccinated due to cost, the government launched the Vaccines for Children program to make immunizations available free of charge to underinsured families.
Cases plummeted. By 2000, the CDC and PAHO determined that measles was no longer a national threat — measles transmission had been eliminated.
"Elimination" allows for occasional outbreaks, because measles is not eradicated worldwide and a small fraction of people, such as young infants, can't be protected by vaccines.
People infected abroad sparked occasional outbreaks after U.S. elimination, but — until now — those fizzled out because of herd immunity, when 95% of people within a community are immunized. In those situations, outbreaks peter out and vulnerable people are protected.
It would be 14 years before another significant outbreak in the U.S. Then in 2015, the virus took off among unvaccinated children at Disney parks in California, giving rise to outbreaks elsewhere. Congress saw some 125 cases as an emergency and summoned the CDC's Schuchat to testify on the situation.
"Vaccination wasn't a partisan issue," she recalled. "This was about problem-solving: What can we do about this?"
National television aired a video of then-U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy talking with Sesame Street's Elmo about vaccination. HHS officials worked with vaccine experts on strategies to boost public confidence in vaccines. California and Vermont tightened vaccine requirements.
In 2019, House and Senate committees met again about measles, as a large outbreak took hold in Orthodox Jewish communities in New York and New Jersey took hold. Congress asked HHS leaders how the administration planned to curb the rise of vaccine misinformation online.
"Internet fraudsters who claim that vaccines are not safe are preying on the unfounded fears and daily struggles of parents, and they are creating a public health hazard that is entirely preventable," Lamar Alexander, then a Republican senator from Tennessee, said at the time.
Alex Azar, health secretary during the first Trump administration, and then-CDC Director Robert Redfield held a press conference stressing the "importance of on-time vaccination."
And during the 2014, 2015, and 2019 outbreaks, the CDC's MMWR published detailed articles within weeks of data collection. Timing matters since the reports guide emergency response. "The MMWR is the voice of the CDC," Schuchat said, "alerting the nation, the media, clinicians, and public health experts to events that require action."
'The dog didn't bark'
Just after President Donald Trump took office in 2025, a measles outbreak exploded in West Texas. Within seven months, it surpassed the size of any in the U.S. since 1992, spread to Mexico and at least three other states, sickened more than 4,500 people in the two countries, and killed at least 16.
Instead of broadcasting clear, repeated messages on the importance of measles vaccines, Kennedy falsely claimed on Fox News that they lead to "deaths every year."
Congress didn't call a hearing, and HHS didn't send funds until after the emergency in West Texas had subsided. Besides an annual measles update, the MMWR didn't publish a single report on the outbreaks that year.
"A lot of this is the dog didn't bark," said Dorit Reiss, a vaccine policy researcher at the University of California Law San Francisco. "Something that normally happens isn't happening."
Political appointees have delayed or blocked several MMWR articles, according to multiple CDC officials whom KFF Health News agreed not to identify because they feared retaliation for speaking with the press. "There's a deliberate effort to downplay vaccine-preventable diseases by the administration," one official said.
"Measles reports from West Texas and New Mexico were intentionally shelved," another scientist at the agency said. In April, The Washington Post reported that Jay Bhattacharya, who temporarily led the CDC this year and remains head of the National Institutes of Health, had blocked the publication of a study in the MMWR finding that COVID vaccines halved the likelihood of emergency department visits.
"The suggestion that HHS is deliberately suppressing information about measles or other vaccine-preventable diseases is false," Hilliard, the HHS spokesperson, said in an email to KFF Health News.
Hilliard said Kennedy and the CDC have provided approximately $100 million in additional funding to respond to outbreaks. The timing of MMWR reports, she added, varies due to factors such as data analysis and scientific review.
More than a year after data was collected from Texas, a few reports came out in the CDC's journal. One study on 60 people hospitalized for measles in West Texas revealed that two required intubation and mechanical ventilation and that a baby born to a mother with measles experienced dangerous brain swelling due to the virus.
The MMWR still hasn't published detailed reports on massive outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah, and Pennsylvania. The CDC's national measles update hasn't appeared in the MMWR this year either. Instead, the journal has featured less urgent articles on scientific techniques that may help characterize future outbreaks.
CDC scientists told KFF Health News that they continue to analyze data but no longer expect to publish their findings in the MMWR because the process has become slow, opaque, and unpredictable. An urgent CDC report on the risks of measles to pregnant women was withheld, The Washington Post reported recently.
"We have two CDCs now," an official at the agency said. "One is staffed by CDC scientists and civil servants who are committed to public health, and the other is political appointees who go in and change the website."
The CDC's measles dashboard counts four fewer measles deaths than state health departments have reported this year. Kennedy has disputed some deaths and made unsubstantiated claims that Pennsylvania health officials misrepresented data.
Kennedy personally instructed the CDC to alter language on a webpage that said vaccines do not cause autism, he told The New York Times last year.
The page now suggests a potential link between the two and no longer lists a slew of peer-reviewed studies that rigorously searched for an association and found none. These have been replaced with speculation about a correlation and unsubstantiated accusations that the scientific establishment has buried a potential link in order "to prevent vaccine hesitancy."
The Trump administration has muddied the message on vaccines in other ways, Reiss said. Trump incorrectly said in August that the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine could be "quite lethal," and he repeated the debunked idea that vaccines may cause autism.
Stephen Miller, now Trump's White House chief of staff, has falsely said doctors "pump your kids full of shots days after birth with no understanding of the long-term consequences." Recommended vaccines and the vaccine schedule have been thoroughly studied.
Kennedy has made such claims for two decades, including as health secretary. "Having top leadership disseminating rumors, disinformation and flat-out falsehoods has been unforgivable," Schuchat said.
When pressed by journalists and Congress, Kennedy and Trump have recommended measles vaccines. But they haven't repeated the message clearly and unprompted on social media or on the podcasts and videos that Kennedy regularly appears in.
Kennedy also replaced vaccine experts on a panel advising the CDC with fringe researchers holding anti-vaccine views. And under his leadership, the CDC has laid off or forced out many vaccine specialists, including all of those in a group that partners with community organizations and pharmacies, the Immunization Services Division partnership branch.
At the same time, Kennedy has devoted resources to searching for potential harms from vaccines, including through an attempted clinical trial considered unnecessary and unethical by medical societies and the WHO.
To regain measles elimination status, the current U.S. outbreaks must end — then, future outbreaks must stop spreading within a year, said Paul Rota, a microbiologist and former CDC official. With outbreaks expanding in several states, he said, that moment isn't on the horizon.
"Bigger fires create more embers, and any one of those embers can seed another fire," he said.

Phage therapy, which uses bacteriophages to selectively eliminate harmful bacteria, holds significant potential in combating antimicrobial resistance (AMR), said Dr. Kalyan Chakravarthy Koganti, sepsis and infectious diseases specialist at SHRI Hospital, Guntur.
He said this while sharing his research experience during a press release, after presenting his team's scientific findings at an international symposium jointly organised by the Chinese University of Hong Kong and reputed biomedical research journals.
Dr. Kalyan said his team's research presentation on phage therapy received appreciation from participants at the symposium. Dr. Sutharsan Govindarajan, associate professor and phage biologist, SRM University-A.P., also presented research conducted by the team.
He described the event as an enriching learning experience, particularly the discussions on the wider applications of bacteriophages in diagnostics and therapy, including cancer research. Chuanbin Mao, chair of the symposium, has been researching bacteriophages for 25 years and has contributed extensively to scientific literature, he said.
Dr. Kalyan noted that bacteriophages selectively target disease-causing bacteria without harming human beings, making them promising alternatives when antibiotics fail.
His team has administered phage therapy to a few patients at its centre with encouraging results. In collaboration with SRM University-A.P. and Szeged University, Hungary, the team has been working to advance its availability in India.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta is suing OpenAI over the cyberattack a group of its rogue models launched against the AI platform Hugging Face in July.
The lawsuit, filed in San Francisco Superior Court on Monday, alleges that OpenAI, one of the world's leading AI developers, endangered the public by testing its advanced models without having adequate safeguards in place. The suit asserts that the incident was foreseeable and preventable, and that OpenAI misled the public about the safety of its experiments.
"OpenAI's actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society," Bonta said in a statement. He added, "In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law — no matter the product or the company."
The hack, Bonta said, "was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability."

Around 86% of the spending on measures against tuberculosis (TB) in 2025 came from domestic sources, the recently released Global Tuberculosis Report 2026 by the World Health Organisation (WHO) said, even as the reduction in international donor funding to combat the infectious disease remains a cause of concern.
TB cases remain one of the leading causes of death from a single infectious agent, with a quarter of all cases concentrated in India in 2025. The report notes that $22 billion is needed annually for TB prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care to achieve the global targets agreed on at the 2023 United Nations high-level TB meeting by 2027.
In absolute terms, Brazil, China, India, the Russian Federation, and South Africa accounted for $3.7 billion (65%) of the total of $5.63 billion provided from domestic sources in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).
The report notes that international donor funding fell by 14%, from $1.1 billion in 2024 to $0.94 billion in 2025, having been relatively stable at about $1.1–1.3 billion per year between 2015 and 2024.
Financing for TB research and innovation, at $1.2 billion in 2023, also continued to fall far short of the global target of $5 billion per year. Progress to date has been constrained by the overall level of investment, said the report.
“TB mostly affects adults in their most productive years. However, all age groups are at risk. Over 80% of cases and deaths are in low- and middle-income countries. In 2025, the largest number of new TB cases occurred in the WHO South-East Asia Region (35%),’’ said the report.
South-East Asia Region
The WHO on Friday (November 13, 2026) called on countries in the South-East Asia Region to accelerate action to end TB. The latest TB estimates show the region accounts for 3.6 million people who developed TB in 2025 — 34% of the global total — and 4,00,000 TB-related deaths, or 35% of the global total. "These numbers are a stark reminder that TB remains one of the Region’s most pressing public health and development challenges,” said Nilesh Buddha, officer-in-charge, WHO South-East Asia Region.
A release issued by the regional office added that in 2025, $1.03 billion was available for TB prevention and care in the region, with 91% from domestic sources. Yet this represented only around 16% of global TB funding, despite the region accounting for 34% of global cases. "Closing this gap in resources is critical to sustaining progress," the WHO said.
“Ending TB is not simply a health sector responsibility. It requires leadership across government, sustained investment, strong health systems and communities at the centre of the response. We have tools to prevent, diagnose and treat TB. What is needed now is the commitment to ensure they reach everyone who needs them, without delay or financial hardship,” said Dr. Buddha, adding that ending TB by 2030 will depend on countries turning political commitments into measurable action, with greater urgency and scale.
Far from target
Meanwhile, the Global TB Report said that across the world, about 50% of people treated for TB and their households face total costs (direct medical expenditures, non-medical expenditures, and indirect costs such as income losses) that are catastrophic (more than 20% of total household income). This is far from the target of the WHO End TB Strategy of zero.
In 2025, globally there were an estimated 0.96 million new TB cases that were attributable to undernutrition, 0.92 million to diabetes, 0.73 million to alcohol use disorders, 0.69 million to smoking, and 0.55 million to HIV infection.

Indian entrepreneur and podcaster Raj Shamani has overtaken global podcasting heavyweights Joe Rogan and Steven Bartlett to become the world’s most-subscribed podcaster on YouTube. His flagship show, Figuring Out With Raj Shamani, has crossed 22 Mn subscribers on the platform, surpassing Bartlett’s The Diary Of A CEO, which has 21.9 Mn subscribers, and Rogan’s The Joe Rogan Experience, which has 21.2 Mn subscribers. Launched in 2021 from Indore, Figuring Out has witnessed rapid growth in 2026, adding 8 Mn subscribers since the beginning of the year. The show now generates approximately 1.4 Bn monthly views across platforms, while international audiences account for 22% of its YouTube subscriber base. The podcast features conversations with prominent personalities across business, politics, science, and entertainment. Its guest list this year included French President Emmanuel Macron, neuroscientist Andrew Huberman, business professor Scott Galloway, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Shamani has also interviewed Indian startup founders including Eternal’s Deepinder Goyal, Zerodha’s Nithin and Nikhil Kamath, CRED’s Kunal Shah, and the founders of Mamaearth, OYO, boAt, Lenskart, and Nykaa. The podcast records 220-230 interviews a year and publishes about 150. Figuring Out Media employs more than 120 people across content, distribution, investments, and education. Shamani said he started the show to give people a way to learn from founders and other leaders regardless of where they grew up or whom they knew. The latest subscriber milestone comes as the entrepreneur looks to expand beyond podcasting and build a broader global media business through Figuring Out Media. As part of its expansion plans, the company is looking to develop commercial partnerships and tap international audiences. It has also roped in global entertainment and sports agency William Morris Endeavor (WME) to support its expansion and partnered with brands such as Levi's and ASUS. The development comes amid growing competition among creators and media companies to build large-scale digital content businesses, with YouTube emerging as an important distribution and monetisation platform for long-form video podcasts. Shamani is among a host of Indian podcasters growing in popularity, including BeerBiceps host Ranveer Allahabadia and Zerodha cofounder Nikhil Kamath, who hosts the ‘WTF is’ show.

Owono did not deserve 12-match ban - Pique
- Published
FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique says goalkeeper Jesus Owono did not deserve the 12-match suspension he received following his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel late on in the second-tier match between Andorra and Tenerife on 2 November.
De Miguel died the following day, aged 30, and a disciplinary committee from the Spanish football federation confirmed Owono's ban last week.
In a video posted on social media, Pique said players past and present, plus coaches and other goalkeepers, felt the incident was "an accident".
The former Spain and Barcelona defender added: "I truly believe that imposing the maximum sanction on Jesus for this action puts him in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened."
- Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision 
  - Published3 November
- Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban 
  - Published3 days ago
The 12-match suspension was the maximum punishment Owono, 25, could have received, as the disciplinary committee could only consider the offence on the pitch and not "the tragic outcome of the incident".
Following the decision, Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera said he accepted the regulations do not specifically account for what happened, but acknowledged the ban "might feel light".
Pique also highlighted a recent on-field incident in Spain, when Albacete winger Jose Corpas accidentally kicked Sabadell midfielder Quadri Liameed in the head during a Spanish second division match.
Nigerian Liameed was knocked unconscious but was later discharged from hospital following medical checks, while Spaniard Corpas was shown a straight red card and handed a three-match ban.
"Fortunately Quadri is fine, the consequences in this case were not fatal, and the committee decided to sanction Corpas with three matches," Pique said.
"With all this, my reflection is: what is being sanctioned, the action or the consequences?"
Owono has withdrawn from Equatorial Guinea's squad for Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Zimbabwe this month, and Pique said it was unlikely he would return to action as soon as his suspension is served.
He added: "Jesus is going to need far more than 12 matches before he is available and able to compete.
"No sanction is going to bring [De Miguel] back to us."

U.N. talks seek to rein in 'killer robots' as fears over AI weapons grow
GENEVA — Negotiations on possible rules for the use of lethal autonomous weapons, also known as 'killer robots' are underway at the United Nations in Geneva.
Supporters of controls on autonomous weapons say this week's U.N. conference on Certain Conventional Weapons (or CCW), which meets just once every five years, is the last best chance to agree rules before it is too late.
Warfare technology has advanced rapidly in the last few years, with some experts warning that the world is just months away from having weapons that can choose targets and make the decision to kill autonomously.
In Ukraine and Gaza, AI-assisted weapons have already been used to take out targets, with Ukrainian civilians reporting being 'hunted' by drones as they shop or go to school. But these are still controlled remotely by humans.
Humanitarian organizations say the decision to kill – and responsibility for that choice – must stay in human hands. Ahead of this week's meeting, the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Pope have all called for legally binding rules. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that allowing fully autonomous weapons to kill would be 'crossing a moral red line'.
What are the risks?
The Red Cross is especially worried that existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – cannot be fully respected by autonomous weapons. War is often chaotic and confusing, and the situation can change rapidly. Under the Conventions, soldiers who are wounded or in the process of surrendering can no longer be targeted.
Georgia Haines, a legal adviser with the Red Cross, worries that autonomous weapons will not be able to distinguish between a soldier who is still fighting, one who is wounded and one who wants to surrender.
'The risk is that, based on the technology we are seeing, they are not able to understand in the same way that a human is the contextual signals. And so the risks are incredibly high that there will be a misidentification of a target.'
Meanwhile, human rights groups warn that the technology behind AI-assisted weapons is becoming increasingly cheap and easy to use. The more it is adopted by the military, the greater the danger of proliferation and its use by terrorist groups or law enforcement agencies in repressive regimes. In theory, a swarm of autonomous drones could be programmed to kill everyone wearing a red sweater, everyone carrying a poster or even everyone speaking a certain language.
Many of the countries now meeting in Geneva take such concerns very seriously. At least 50, including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France and Germany, are calling for a strict timetable to agree on binding rules governing autonomous weapons.
But among states that are already developing and using semi-autonomous weapons, there is pushback. The United States, Russia and Israel have indicated they are set to oppose legally binding rules, with Washington proposing a five-year timetable to draft non-binding guidelines instead.
The U.S. is traditionally a late adopter of international treaties. It did not ratify the Ottawa Convention on landmines, for example, although it did, over time, stop deploying them and reduce its stockpiles.
Under President Trump, doubts about international law have grown. Washington has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court, and just this weekend, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in a keynote speech to the Federalist Society, warned against "quoting laws to men with swords."
The problem for states meeting in Geneva is that U.N. negotiations on limiting specific weapons are supposed to be conducted by consensus. This was achieved in 1995, when countries agreed to a ban on blinding lasers, but other agreements have proved elusive. With landmines, countries frustrated by the delay finally took negotiations outside the U.N. process to create the Ottawa Convention.
This week, there may be a compromise: a longer or even open-ended negotiating period to come up with rules that individual states can adopt as binding or non-binding. For diplomats supporting such a solution, it is a way to ensure at least some progress. For campaigners, it is less than ideal, with one likening it to kicking a very dangerous can down the road.

The Best Apple 3-in-1 Travel Chargers
Featured in this article
A 3-in-1 travel charger that can power up my iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods is one of the first items I pack for any trip. I've tried out plenty of options, but these are my favorite chargers for keeping the holy trinity of Apple gadgets going strong while on vacation or a work trip.
Many of these picks will also happily charge Qi2 Android phones and other devices that support wireless charging. Since space is at a premium when traveling, they all feature clever compact designs.
If you want something for your desk or nightstand when you're back home, check out our Best Apple 3-in-1 Wireless Charging Stations guide, and for power on the go, read our Best Travel Adapters, Best Power Banks, and Best MagSafe Power Banks guides.
Updated June 2026: I've added a new charger from Satechi, added details on Qi2 25W and StandBy and Nightstand modes, reorganized this guide, and updated prices.
Other Good 3-in-1 Travel Chargers
Kuxiu Qi2 25W Travel Charging Station for $78: This charger folds down to an impressively small package, and it feels sturdy with a silicone-covered metal construction. It can hit 25 watts for supported Qi2 W25 phones, comes in a few different finishes, and ships with a 45-watt power adapter and USB-C cable in the box. Unfortunately, I don’t like the way it looks, and I found it awkward to get all three devices charging at once. It’s actually so compact that it feels crowded.
UAG 3-in-1 Travel and Desktop Charger for $165: This charger was close to earning a top spot until I clocked the price. It’s a very smart 3-in-1 charging kit that folds flat and comes in a snazzy zip-up bag with a 4-foot braided USB-C cable and 25-watt power adapter, including plugs for the US, UK, and Europe. You can prop your iPhone at different angles on the MagSafe stand, and it works well with StandBy mode and Nightstand mode for your Apple Watch, but it’s not Qi2-certified, so you won’t get the stated 15-watt charging for an iPhone. Ultimately, it’s just too expensive.
Aukey MagFusion Z Qi2 3-in-1 Foldable Charging Station for $80: This clever 3-in-1 charging station folds flat and feels durable, but it’s kind of heavy for travel. I found my Apple Watch tended to lean on one side on the charger and didn’t work with Nightstand mode unless I folded it above the main charger, which is also the position required for the iPhone to sit in landscape orientation for StandBy mode.
Mophie 3-in-1 Travel Charger With MagSafe for $150: This little travel kit comes with a carrying case, charging brick, and USB-C cable. The square stack unfolds to reveal three wireless chargers in one elongated pad. The iPhone sticks magnetically to the center (15 watts), and the Apple Watch dock supports Nightstand mode. There's also a grooved spot for the AirPods. It feels great, is compact, and is pretty lightweight all around.
Twelve South Butterfly 2-in-1 MagSafe Charger for $80: This is an uber compact 2-in-1 charger that looks like a hockey puck. Open the Butterfly, and you'll find two pads that are attached via a rubbery silicone material. You can fast charge an Apple Watch on one—even popping the charger up to take advantage of Nightstand mode—and the other circle lets you recharge your MagSafe iPhone at 15 watts. It's a super compact solution, and Twelve South includes a 30-watt power source and cable with international plug adapters.
Native Union Voyage 2-in-1 MagSafe Charger for $100: For a slightly lower price, reviews editor Adrienne So likes Native Union's Qi2 butterfly solution, which doesn't include plug adapters but does come in a tidy travel pouch and has a cable.
Avoid These Chargers
Mous Travel Charger: While the compact folding nature of this charger and the low price impressed me, it gets kinda warm when you charge all three of your Apple devices, and the AirPods spot is finicky.
MagSafe and Qi2, Explained
Most of my picks are MagSafe or Qi2-certified wireless chargers. That means they take advantage of the magnets embedded in the back of the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16, and iPhone 17 ranges. The magnets ensure perfect alignment, enabling faster and more efficient wireless charging.
Qi2 is a wireless charging standard that Apple worked with the Wireless Power Consortium to develop. Compared to the original Qi standard, it brings MagSafe-style magnetic charging, enabling faster charging rates and improved efficiency. Apple updated the iPhone 12 and newer to support Qi2, but it’s not just for Apple phones; other phones can get Qi2 certification. While Qi2 Android phones are still thin on the ground, you’ll find Qi2 in Google's Pixel 10 series, and there are Qi2-ready phones that add magnets via a compatible case.
Qi2 charging mostly goes up to 15 watts, but the Qi2.2 update, branded as Qi2 25W, goes up to 25 watts. Support for Qi2 25W is currently very limited, and includes the iPhone 17 range and the Pixel 10 Pro XL.
If you use a case, ensure it is a MagSafe or Qi2 compatible case. A normal case will weaken the pull of the magnets in the device and will not stick to chargers as well. If your case is too thick, your phone may not charge at all.
MagSafe is also available in the AirPods charging case (depending on your model). Apple's AirPods and AirPods Pro with the wireless charging case will work with nearly all of the standard Qi wireless charging pads on these chargers (as will many third-party wireless earbuds), but if you have AirPods with MagSafe, then you can hook them up to the magnetic mounts as well.
What Are StandBy and Nightstand Modes?
I mention StandBy and Nightstand modes throughout this guide, but what are they?
StandBy mode was introduced in iOS 17. When you place your iPhone on a charger in landscape orientation, it turns the screen into a smart display to show the time (with different clock designs to choose from), photos from your library, or widgets. If you have an iPhone that supports an always-on screen, you can choose to have the display automatically turn off after a certain amount of time when the iPhone isn't in use or if the room is dark. Head to Settings > Standby to customize it.
Nightstand mode shows the time on your Apple Watch when the watch is sitting upright and charging, so it can serve as a beside clock. You can customize this on your Apple Watch by heading to Settings > General > Nightstand mode.

Plea in SC seeks contempt action against lawyer over remarks on CJI, hearing tomorrow
A little after 2pm on Monday, advocate Singhal made alleged derogatory remarks against CJI Kant while complaining against non-listing of his case.
The Supreme Court agreed to hear on Wednesday a petition by the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA), seeking contempt action against an advocate who made alleged defamatory comments against Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant on Monday.
The SCBA filed the petition on Tuesday, after Attorney General (AG) for India R Venkataramani granted consent to initiate criminal contempt proceedings against advocate Pravin Singhal, under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.
“I cannot hear this matter. But I will list it tomorrow,” CJI Kant said.
His remarks came after SCBA secretary Pragya Baghel termed Singhal’s remarks “extremely scandalous and unpardonable”, and requested the court to allow listing of the matter along with another contempt petition filed against Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut and senior journalist Nikhil Wagle listed for 2 pm before a bench of justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi.
A little after 2pm on Monday, advocate Singhal made alleged derogatory remarks against CJI Kant while complaining against non-listing of his case. He said he had requested for listing the matter on November 2 but did not receive any response for the past 15 days.
When the CJI told the lawyer that he will examine the case, the latter said the matter was urgent and that he did not wish to wait.
To this, justice V Mohana, who was sharing the bench along with the CJI and justice Joymalya Bagchi, said: “You cannot mention like this. You please wait.”
Singhal then raised his voice and made alleged derogatory remarks at CJI Kant. He was removed by the security guards.
As lawyers assembled in the hall demanded the CJI initiate suo motu contempt action, he said the advocate already faces contempt proceedings and is not a member of SCBA. It could not be immediately ascertained which contempt proceedings the CJI was talking about.
The SCBA, however, took up the matter and wrote to Venkataramani, alleging Singhal’s statements are unacceptable and must be deprecated. The association sought consent to file the contempt petition against the lawyer.
“Having regard to the extremely scandalous and unpardonable conduct and remarks in the open court by Pravin Singhal, I consider it a fit case for granting my consent under section 15(1)(b) of Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 for initiating criminal contempt against Pravin Singhal,” the AG said.
This is the third time the SCBA has taken the lead in initiating criminal contempt action over remarks made against the CJI.
Last year, the association had filed a criminal contempt petition against advocate Rakesh Kishore, who attempted to throw his shoe on a bench headed by then CJI BR Gavai, when the court was in session on October 6, 2025. The SCBA sought guidelines to be framed in order to prevent such incidents.
Recently, the SCBA filed a criminal contempt petition against MP Sanjay Raut and journalist Nikhil Wagle for publishing objectionable posts on social media against the CJI. The alleged posts were made after CJI Kant conveyed his refusal on October 12 to meet Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and Rajya Sabha Leader of Opposition Mallikarjun Kharge over issues regarding alleged irregularities in the Election Commission.

Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.
Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.
A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.
Untangling humans from the weather
Fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without big fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.
Weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.
Human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.
The double-sided role of humans in fire also adds to the difficulty. Humans do start fires, but they also put them out. Firefighters contain fires that could have gone worse if no action had been taken and can keep them from spreading. Humans can also take preventative actions, such as clearing flammable material.
Sometimes the line between starting fires and preventing them becomes blurred. One way to clear out flammable material is to intentionally set fires to make future fires more manageable. However, these fires are hard to distinguish from other fires through satellite monitoring.
A natural experiment in staying home
An experiment is one way to find out how humans affect wildfires. If everyone stayed home under the same weather, their impact on fires would be revealed. This is why Wang’s research team focused on the COVID-19 era. It was what’s called a “natural experiment,” in which experimental conditions arose without any action by researchers.
Wang explained: “Human activity and climate normally vary together, because seasons, farming calendars, and weather all shape both fire and human behavior. The early-2020 lockdowns produced an abrupt, large-scale drop in human mobility, and the timing differed across countries while the weather did not change in the same way. This gave us a natural experiment.”
The researchers defined the period of restricted mobility by checking regional lockdown orders and mobile phone location data. Data from NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Suomi NPP satellite helped the team track fires. Its VIIRS sensor detects heat signatures from fires at a spatial resolution of 375 meters. Each hot spot the satellite detects counts as an active-fire detection, meaning one large fire can appear as multiple spots. However, the satellite records both wildfires and prescribed burns without distinguishing between them. As a result, the intent behind each fire remains unknown.
In the study, detections during the 2020 restriction periods were compared with those from the same weeks in 2013–2019. Weather conditions weren’t exactly the same as in past years, which was accounted for.
The results show that areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the recent-past average. The drop varied by vegetation type. In forests, fires decreased by about 27.7 percent, while grasslands decreased by 8.4 percent. Shrublands, savannas, and croplands didn’t show much difference. The researchers interpret this to mean that humans are a major cause of fires in forests and grasslands.
Controlling for weather factors was important in the study. Without adjustments, the drop was only 5.8 percent, which was not statistically significant. After controlling for weather, however, the estimated decline increased to 12.3 percent. If weather in 2020 were more favorable to fires than in previous years, it might have masked some of the human impact.
The 12.3 percent decrease in fire detections doesn’t mean that humans directly caused this share of fires. Restricting human activity shrank both humans’ impact on starting fires and likely limited their impact on extinguishing them. The 12.3 percent figure is the net effect after these two opposing forces partly cancel out.
Wang said, “The 12.3 percent is a net effect, not the share of fires caused by humans; opposing changes in ignition and suppression mean it does not capture the full magnitude of human influence.”
Not every fire went quiet
In regional data, some areas experienced a considerable increase in fire after human mobility was restricted. Most of South America, southern Africa, and northeast Asia saw an increase in fire during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Notable increases include 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India, and 70.7 percent in Honduras.
There are no direct field data showing why this occurred. The researchers inferred that diminished fire suppression capacity resulted in more fires in these locations, but Wang acknowledged, “It is an inference, not a direct observation.” That inference was based in part on earlier studies that suggested that weaker fire management in Colombia and Madagascar contributed to increased fires.
One line of evidence is how fires reacted to different levels of mobility loss, based on fire counts in 0.5-degree grid cells. In countries with fewer fires, fire declined in almost a straight line as mobility decreased. But countries that experienced more fires showed a slow increase that leveled off at about 27 percent on average as mobility fell. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that different mechanisms were at work. The steady decline fits fewer human-driven ignitions, while the gradual rise points to weakened suppression. But Wang mentioned that there could be other reasons, such as changes in local land use.
Mobility restrictions may also have disrupted fire management activities, which could mean that fewer fires were set for management purposes. The researchers examined 12 countries with records of prescribed burning. The area burned by prescribed fires in 2020 decreased by about half compared to the 2013–2019 average. Of course, the locations and sizes of prescribed burns also shift from year to year with fire return intervals and land-management cycles, which complicates this analysis.
When areas subjected to prescribed burning were excluded in those 12 countries, the decline in fires there shrank from 45.3 percent to 27.8 percent.
This research has limits partly because it relied on mobile phone data to track human movement. This kind of data might not capture human activity in rural areas where coverage may be limited. Also, the analysis focused only on the first half of each year, so the impact on regions where fires happen more frequently in the latter half of the year, such as the western US, may not have been fully captured.
Wang explained that this quasi-experimental design provides strong associational evidence but is not a controlled experiment.
Understanding the human Impact
Wang emphasized that the study is not an evaluation of fire policies. The analysis does, however, suggest that there’s no single ideal policy response. Where fires decreased, human ignition seems to dominate. In those areas, reducing accidental ignitions through public education and maintaining beneficial prescribed burning can be important. On the other hand, areas where fires increased might need to address reduced monitoring and suppression. Maintaining firefighting and patrol capacity during disruptions can be important there.
Wang added, “Overall, a uniform policy is unlikely to work, and strategies should be tailored to local human-fire relationships.” Fire-risk projections might benefit from accounting for human behavior. That way, more accurate fire projections can be made even as weather and society change.

Paraguay’s ousted president moved to military prison after reports of gym and suite in custody
Former Paraguayan President Santiago Peña is being moved to a military prison as he awaits trial over the collapse of Ueno Bank
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay -- A Paraguayan judge on Monday ordered former President Santiago Peña moved to a military prison after reports that he had been held in a suite with a private gym, as he awaits trial over the implosion of a major digital lender, which toppled his government earlier this month.
Judge Osmar Legal ordered Peña transferred from the Presidential Escort Regiment, a military base in the capital, Asunción, where local media reported that his quarters also included a private bathroom and a spacious dining room.
Under the court order, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press, Peña will now be held at the Viñas Cué military prison, apart from other detainees.
President Pedro Alliana opened a news conference Monday by announcing that he had ordered the dismissal of the regiment’s commander, Col. José David Daiub, following allegations that Peña had received special treatment there.
Alliana, who served as Peña’s vice president, pledged to give prosecutors whatever resources they need to investigate the bank’s collapse.
“Paraguayans deserve to know the truth,” he said.
Peña is in pretrial detention on charges including breach of trust, criminal association and administration for personal gain. Prosecutors allege that he used his influence to steer public money to Ueno Bank, a lender used by more than half Paraguay’s adults, as its executives made large insider loans to companies linked to the bank’s owners. He denies wrongdoing.
Paraguay’s central bank seized Ueno on Nov. 3 after declaring it insolvent, freezing the accounts of nearly 3 million customers and more than $850 million in public funds, and disrupting payments for households and small businesses. Three days later, the Senate removed Peña from office, and Alliana took over. A judge ordered Peña jailed the next day.
Ueno’s dizzying growth had become a symbol of Peña’s effort to sell landlocked Paraguay to foreign investors as a low-tax, business-friendly hub. A former International Monetary Fund official and one of the Trump administration’s closest allies in the region, Peña won access in Washington and on Wall Street. That was unusual for a country of Paraguay’s size and economic weight.
The bank launched its digital brand in 2022 and by June had 2.9 million customers in a country of about 6 million. It even sponsored the national soccer team.
But Ueno was also intertwined with Peña’s government. He held a stake in Ueno’s parent company until last year and appointed the bank’s former chairman, Carlos Carvallo, to lead the central bank. Carvallo also faces charges in the case.
Since Peña’s arrest, authorities have searched two of his four homes, one in Asunción and a mansion in the resort town of San Bernardino, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) away.
Prosecutors say the mansion was built partly with about $577,000 in loans that Ueno granted Peña while he was president, and investigators found a vault hidden behind a false wall there. They have also asked the United States, Luxembourg and Argentina for help tracing money that may have been diverted from the bank.
Alliana acknowledged that the crisis had shaken Paraguayans’ faith in their banks. “The closure of Ueno Bank has deeply affected numerous Paraguayan families,” he said.
More than 1.8 million depositors have so far received about $640 million, Alliana said, from a deposit guarantee fund that Paraguay created in 2003 after a series of financial crises wiped out dozens of banks and finance companies.
Most small savers have been repaid in full. The fund has paid out up to about $19,600 per person, out of a guarantee of about $36,700, and authorities haven't said when the rest will be paid. Investors in Ueno’s mutual funds aren’t covered and must wait for the bank to be liquidated.
Still, more than 75% of the roughly $2.8 billion deposited at Ueno, much of it belonging to larger savers and public institutions, has yet to be returned.
For pension funds that had money at Ueno, Alliana said that authorities have preliminarily identified about $600 million in viable assets at the bank, such as loans expected to be repaid, that they plan to use to reimburse the funds. It remains unclear how much of the pension money and other public deposits will be returned.
Teachers walked off the job and blocked roads across the country last week to demand the return of their retirement savings, and retirees’ groups have pressed Alliana and Congress to pass an emergency law to guarantee it. That followed days of unrest in Asunción after Ueno’s collapse, when thousands of people took to the streets demanding their money back and Peña’s ouster, at times clashing with police.

The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
- Published
In 2020, Sanjay Mandava flew down from Chicago to Chennai in southern India to resolve a personal land dispute.
Over the next few months, he was running around between government offices to access a dozen records that would conclusively prove that the property belonged to his family.
Just a sale deed dating back to when his parents bought the land was not enough. Authorities asked him to produce a string of other documents.
Frustrated by the experience, he built Landeed - an AI-led digital platform that enables users to aggregate fragmented, multi-source land-records, verify titles and conduct legal checks at the click of a few buttons, across 24 states in India.
He's solving a problem that is uniquely Indian.
"In the US or UK, when you purchase a property, the government verifies ownership. In India by contrast, we follow presumptive titling - the buyer is responsible for establishing ownership. A sale deed merely records the transaction - multiple other documents may be needed to prove title," Mandava told the BBC.
These include building certificates, property tax receipts and land survey maps among others.
The system is rife for misuse - property disputes account for a bulk of civil litigation cases in the country where some 80% of household wealth is held in real estate.
Landeed has mapped large swathes of India using geo-spatial technology and data from state land revenue departments, registration offices, survey records and municipal databases.
Using this, it has linked registered properties to their official land identification and survey numbers and ownership records.
An additional AI-layer can read these titles, extract information and spot inconsistencies within minutes - a process that takes lawyers and brokers several days.
With the largest repository of title data in the country, consisting of 1.8 billion documents, the app is now used by millions of individual and enterprise customers while doing real estate transactions.
The app is among a burgeoning list of Indian start-ups trying to address some of India's most complex challenges in sectors ranging from legal-tech to healthcare, infrastructure, education and agriculture using AI.
Unlike the US and China which have a global dominance in building frontier language models like ChatGPT, India's AI revolution is happening downstream in data centre infrastructure and consumer applications rather than in research.
Start-ups are solving issues for everything from pothole detection to tribal language translation to assisting overworked public-health professionals with medical tasks - often working with highly fragmented, multilingual datasets in extremely cost sensitive industries.
Bengaluru-based YouTube teacher Gaurav Sen's AI app detects potholes using a dash-cam, satellite-based navigation and an AI vision model to analyse images.
It then identifies civic officials responsible for fixing them and sends them this data. He got viral attention recently given how widespread the menace of potholes is across India's urban sprawls.
On last count, there are at least half a dozen other similar offerings that map and report road damage to authorities across the country.
"A municipal corporation can take the app and use it on public buses and taxis, to access real-time, updated data on road conditions," Sen told the BBC.
In Mumbai on India's western coast, Fractal Analytics - among the few Indian listed AI companies - has deployed its AI tool "Vaidya" in hospitals run by the local civic authority.
The app allows citizens to receive AI-generated, simplified summaries of their lab reports in multiple languages, identify nearby healthcare facilities based on their needs and gives doctors AI-guided pre-consultation support such as medical history and medication details of patients.
It also provides hospital administrators with a public health dashboard based on aggregated, anonymous insights from lab reports accessed through its tie-up with municipal hospitals, giving them crucial visibility into emerging infections or other disease trends.
This boom has led to a surge in funding for AI start-ups - up 265% year-on-year according to Inc42, external, a start-up information platform. They raised over $1bn in the first nine months of this year amid a relatively muted fundraising environment for the broader ecosystem.
Yet, these companies face an uphill task in commercialising their ideas and taking them beyond pilot.
"The cost of building in India is sometimes much higher than what Indian customers are willing to pay," Fractal's co-founder Srikanth Velamakanni told the BBC at his sprawling office overlooking Mumbai's film city.
"The computing power needed to run an AI model is the same whether it is built in India or the US - but American customers have a far bigger paying capacity than those here."
Indian AI founders are also being forced to build around scarcity, with availability of high quality chips at the right scale and price, a major impediment for many.
"I believe I am building one of the most impactful things for this country," says Mandava.
"But I am starved for GPUs [chips that perform millions of calculations and help train AI models]. I have a hellish time trying to acquire them," he says.
The country has promised its start-ups 38,000 GPUs through its government-led AI mission, external, but demand for this compute power is far greater than supply.
Cumbersome regulation and bureaucracy are other major challenges.
Without these fundamental issues being addressed, there's a risk that Indian AI companies will build shallow solutions that a next generation of founders will immediately make redundant, say experts.
"Someone like a Google will probably laugh if I tell them of my pilot. To make it sustainable and hard to replicate, it will have to be much more sophisticated," says Sen, displaying a self-awareness of where his product currently stands.
From a lack of experienced talent to the struggle to turn successful pilots into recurring government contracts to heavy dependence on expensive foreign technology, Indian founders are powering through many odds.
"We can still do it. We don't want protection, but propel us, give us the weapons to compete against the best," Mandava says, when asked what he wants from policymakers.
"To quote Jay-Z - I can't help the poor if I'm one of them," he adds.

Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm in 12 hours. Lisbon saw 183 flights cancelled on Wednesday, around a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.
After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.
Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.
Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.
Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.
A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.

The spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is threatening modern medicine despite progress in combating drug-resistant bacteria, senior World Health Organization officials said Monday, November 16, 2026.
WHO officials said countries had expanded efforts to tackle AMR, but warned that progress in prevention, diagnosis and the appropriate use of antibiotics remained too slow to meet global targets.
Bacteria have long evolved resistance to medicines designed to kill them.
The widespread use of antibiotics in human health, animal husbandry and food production has accelerated the problem, making AMR one of the leading causes of infectious-disease deaths worldwide.
"Antimicrobial resistance is widespread and threatening the future of modern medicine," said Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, interim head of antimicrobial resistance at the WHO. "Unlike COVID-19, which was very visible, drug-resistant infections have been taking people's lives for years without us noticing it and raising the alarm as we should," said Nyemazi.
In 2021 alone, AMR was directly responsible for more than one million deaths and linked to some 4.7 million others, said the agency.
A WHO investigation in 183 countries into the progress of the fight against antimicrobial resistance this year revealed that nearly nine countries in 10 had a national action plan against the phenomenon. In 2017, the figure was only around four in 10.
But only 42 countries -- less than one in five -- said they had a plan that was financed, implemented and monitored, said Pravasha Prakash, an AMR technical officer with the global health agency.
"Countries are moving forward in every step but progress still needs to be speeded up to reach the 2030 targets," she added.
Poor access to diagnostics
One of the main weaknesses remains access to diagnostics. Only 36% of countries had a national reference laboratory capable of testing for resistance in all bacteria and fungi monitored by the WHO -- well short of the 80% target set for 2030.
"Without testing, clinicians must treat without knowing the cause of infection or which antibiotic will work," said Sylvia Bertagnolo, head of surveillance for AMR at the WHO.
The latest global surveillance data show that in 2023, one in every six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections flagged to the WHO was resistant to antibiotics used to treat it.
As a result, the WHO has announced the release of two new tools designed to help countries strengthen their diagnostic capacities.
The first defines the tests that should be available at every level of the healthcare system, from primary care centres to referral hospitals. The second compiles 73 laboratory procedures, from sample collection to the identification of pathogens and antibiotic susceptibility testing.
The WHO has estimated that AMR could cause some 39 million deaths between now and 2050.
There needed to be improved use of existing antibiotics, at a time when the development of new treatments is failing to keep pace with the rise of resistance, it said.
Infection prevention, vaccination, improved access to water and sanitation, and the appropriate use of antimicrobials are the main levers to combat the issue, it added.

Karnataka mulls tobacco ad ban in public places, eyes smoking zones at tech firms
The Karnataka government is weighing a public tobacco advertising ban and designated smoking zones at technology companies. The proposals extend its campaign against tobacco promotion amid concerns about celebrity endorsements influencing children.
The Karnataka government is considering a ban on tobacco advertisements in public places, including those displayed on the rear of Bengaluru Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC) buses, as part of efforts to curb the promotion of tobacco products.
The state government is also mulling the introduction of designated smoking zones in technology companies, with a proposal to ensure employees smoke only in these designated areas and not elsewhere on office premises.
The developments come as Karnataka Health Minister and Congress leader UT Khader on Tuesday criticised actors and celebrities for endorsing pan masala and tobacco-related products, warning that such advertisements could influence children and encourage addiction.
Speaking to reporters, Khader questioned the responsibility of celebrities who promote products that can harm public health, particularly when their endorsements reach young audiences.
“If people develop an addiction to these products and eventually end up in hospital, who will be there to take care of them? Apart from their parents, who else will stand by them?” he asked.
KARNATAKA STEPS UP TOBACCO CONTROL
The proposed measures come against the backdrop of Karnataka's decision to impose a one-year ban on the manufacture, storage, transportation, distribution and sale of gutkha and pan masala products containing tobacco or nicotine.
The prohibition was issued through a notification dated August 10, 2026, under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. It covers products containing tobacco or nicotine, including those marketed separately but intended to be mixed by consumers.
Karnataka had earlier taken steps to curb tobacco promotions on public transport. In January, then Transport Minister Ramalinga Reddy issued a directive to the managing directors of the state's four transport corporations — Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (KSRTC), Bengaluru Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC), North West Karnataka Road Transport Corporation (NWKRTC) and Kalyana Karnataka Road Transport Corporation (KKRTC) — prohibiting all direct and indirect advertisements promoting tobacco consumption on buses and at bus stands.

Two days after Diwali was celebrated across India, on November 10, Tuesday, the nation woke up to grim newspaper headlines and reports highlighting the sharp deterioration of air quality across major cities. According to reports, 93 Indian cities appeared among the world’s 100 most polluted locations, several parts of Delhi reportedly witnessed a staggering Air Quality Index (AQI) of 3,000+, and six cities recorded an AQI above 1,000 at 9 pm on Diwali night.
Newspaper reports suggested that despite bans and restrictions, the bursting of firecrackers remained untethered across states, resulting in not only a severe surge in air pollution, but major fire accidents, noise pollution, and several people, stray animals and birds suffering burn injuries.
The front page of the Delhi edition of The Times of India on Tuesday led with a report headlined ‘Delhi pollution on Diwali rockets to worst in 5 yrs’.
“Delhi saw its most polluted Diwali day in five years, with AQI touching 376 at 4pm Nov 8, the worst since 2021. The city, however, narrowly escaped its worst post-Diwali pollution day in five years, with Monday’s AQI touching 370 at 11am before improving to 344 by 4pm, better than 2025’s post-Diwali air quality,” the report read, while highlighting that “several monitoring stations failed to report crucial AQI data”.
The front page also carried reports on the death of 10-year-old Rishi Garg in Delhi’s Narela after suffering a deep injury on his chest while bursting a firecracker; the hourly PM2.5 concentration at Jahangirpuri surging to 4,985 µg/m³ on Diwali night, which is 83 times the daily national ambient air quality standard; and X “locking” the account of TOI photojournalist Anindya Chattopadhyay after he posted visuals of smog in Delhi, citing violation of its rules.
The Mumbai edition of the paper on Tuesday reported “a record number of firecracker accidents” across the city on Diwali, with the headline ‘390 fires caused by crackers across Mum region on Diwali’. The report highlighted that the local train services on the Western line were disrupted due to a fire damaging signalling cables between Virar and Nalasopara. It noted that over 60 people suffered burns across Mumbai Metropolitan Region and over 30 stray animals and birds sustained burn injuries due to crackers, among various other major accidents and mishaps across MMR.
Similarly, the Kolkata edition led with a story on firecracker-related noise complaints. With the headline, ‘This Diwali, city seeks max number of noise complaints’, the report highlighted the widespread bursting of banned high-decibel firecrackers across the city, well beyond the permissible hours, making Sunday night one of the noisiest in recent years. Kolkata’s air quality deteriorated sharply over the same period, with readings lying between the “very poor” and “severe” categories from Sunday night to the intervening morning, and PM2.5 rising from 74 to 409 in Ballygunge and 115 to 444 in Salt Lake within a span of 2 hours, the report highlighted.
The front page Delhi edition of The Indian Express on Tuesday carried the lead story on pollution with the headline ‘Delhi wakes up to toxic post-Diwali air, 8 stations in ‘severe’ zone’. It reported that the capital had recorded its “worst” Diwali-day air quality in the last five years. Pollution levels rose sharply after sunset and remained elevated into the following morning, with PM2.5 concentrations touching nearly 5,000 µg/m³ at some monitoring stations. India’s 24-hour national ambient air quality standards prescribe a safe limit of 60 µg/m³ for PM2.5 and 100 µg/m³ for PM10.
The lead story of the Hindustan Times carried the headline, ‘Delhi pollution monitors went dark as AQI surged on Diwali’. According to the report, 43 of Delhi’s 59 air quality monitoring stations went “blank” on Diwali night just as PM2.5 readings surged towards 1,000 µg/m³. The data gaps reportedly affected the calculation of the capital’s daily AQI, raising questions about the reliability of pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours.
The front page also featured reports on Punjab recording nearly 200 stubble burning incidents on November 9, Monday; the sale of firecrackers continuing in Delhi despite a Supreme Court ban; and the rampant bursting of firecrackers leading to an increase in ambient noise levels across most monitoring stations in Delhi.
The Telegraph featured a collage showing the contrast of visibility of Delhi’s India Gate before and after Diwali, with photographs taken on October 30 and November 9 respectively. With the lead headline reading ‘Diwali cocktail of cacophony’, the front page reports covered the aftermath in both Delhi and Kolkata, highlighting data gaps in Delhi’s pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours and administrative inaction in Kolkata.
“Slackness in the seizure of banned fireworks. Stalls selling crackers at almost every neighbourhood. Lackadaisical police response to noise complaints. Political endorsement at the highest level in the name of religion. Several factors made this Diwali the most deafening in years, according to environmentalists, former pollution control board members, Opposition politicians and ordinary Calcuttans,” the report read.
The Telegraph reported that this Diwali celebration was Delhi’s most polluted Diwali in five years. It noted that, over 18 hours, from 10 pm on Sunday to 4 am on Monday, 59 air quality stations in the national capital should have recorded 1062 hourly readings; however, around 24% are missing from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data.
On Kolkata’s exceeding noise pollution levels, the report stated that “even a minister and an MLA from the BJP complained of the “unbearable” noise…However, asked about the rampant violation of noise pollution norms, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari politicised the issue, saying it was the “communists” and those unnerved by the “stupendous rise of Sanatan” that were complaining.”

The Hindu on Tuesday carried a standalone image of thick smog enveloping Rashtrapati Bhavan on Monday morning with the caption ‘Pollution unlimited’. On Page 6, it further reported that air pollution levels in Delhi had spiked to 200 times the World Health Organization’s recommended limits during Diwali.
Hospitals Report Burn Patients; Doctors Raise Concerns
“I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival,” Dr Vijay Hadda, professor, department of pulmonary medicine and sleep disorders at AIIMS, told ANI on Monday.
He said that the green crackers reduced emissions by only 30 per cent, but as far as the particulate matter was concerned, 70 per cent of the emissions remained the same as conventional firecrackers. He raised concerns over people breathing this ‘poisonous’ smoke and said, “You should understand that you are simply inhaling poison and exhaling it.”

Many of my colleagues who are otherwise completely healthy have been calling me and saying, “I am unable to get rid of this irritation. It feels as though something is stuck in my throat.” We saw patients during our last OPD session, and they have returned again today. This happens every year, but somehow, we all forget. The general public forgets, and even policies remain somewhat in a grey area, making it difficult to understand how they should be interpreted. Overall, the situation is not good at all. In the aftermath of Diwali, doctors in Delhi began reporting an alarming number of juvenile patients, including newborns, arriving with breathing difficulties, even as hospitals are witnessing a significant rise in respiratory illnesses. According to reports, 397 patients with Diwali-related injuries were treated at four major hospitals in Delhi. The cases included burns, firecracker injuries and eye trauma.
AIIMS reported 42 burn injury cases by 11 am on November 9. Of these, 37 were caused by firecrackers. Eleven patients sustained major injuries, while 31 had minor injuries. Eight were admitted, including one in critical condition. Moreover, 18 of the 42 patients were under 18, including six below the age of 10. An eight-year-old child at AIIMS was in critical condition after sustaining burns over 45 per cent of their body surface area. Safdarjung Hospital recorded 135 burn injury cases. Of these, 129 were attributed to firecrackers and six to traditional diyas. Seven patients sustained major burns requiring hospital admission. The hospital also treated 35 children with firecracker-related injuries in its outpatient department.
Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital treated 41 patients with burn injuries from 9 am on Saturday. 18 of these injuries were reportedly caused by firecrackers, with two patients requiring admission. Eight patients were hospitalised overall, while approximately 10–12 of those treated were children. Guru Tegh Bahadur Hospital reported 172 patients with firecracker burns and other Diwali-related injuries within 24 hours. Among them were 25 children and 56 women. Thirty-four patients also suffered eye injuries.
The toll was not limited to burn injuries. The Dr Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences at AIIMS received nearly 110 patients with eye injuries on Sunday and during the early hours of Monday, most of them with firecracker-related ocular injuries. 18 patients suffered corneal perforations or lacerations and underwent surgical intervention.
In Pali, Rajasthan, sparks from firecrackers being burst on a road reportedly reached a firecracker shop near Swarn Mandir in Falna town, gutting three shops and killing two people. One person sustained burn injuries and three others were initially reported missing.

Wider access to diabetes technology needs policy support, experts say
Continuous glucose monitors and automated insulin delivery systems drastically improve glycaemic control and cut hospitalisations, yet steep out-of-pocket costs and socioeconomic disparities leave a massive adoption gap
Technology can improve monitoring and support treatment decisions |Image used for representational purpose only
| Photo Credit: Wikimedia commons
Diabetes management is moving beyond periodic finger-prick tests and clinic visits, with technologies such as continuous glucose monitors (CGMs), insulin pumps and mobile applications providing more detailed information on glucose levels and helping patients make day-to-day decisions about their care.
CGMs use a sensor placed on the arm or abdomen to measure glucose levels at regular intervals, offering a picture of fluctuations through the day and night. Insulin pumps deliver insulin continuously, while automated insulin delivery systems combine CGM readings with algorithms to adjust insulin delivery. Mobile applications can bring together information on glucose levels, food intake, physical activity and medication.
